title: Seeing What the Vehicle Sees: Video-Augmented Virtual Reality for Physical Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles are expected to improve road safety and efficiency, but passengers often remain uncertain about what the vehicle perceives and why it acts as it does. Virtual reality (VR) offers a safe and repeatable medium for presenting this information, yet most passenger-facing VR studies rely on fully simulated vehicles or pre-scripted scenarios, so the motion and perception shown to the user do not originate from a physically operating autonomous system. This paper presents a video-augmented VR framework that couples a physical ROS 2 autonomous robot vehicle to a Unity 6 application deployed on a Meta Quest 3S headset. The vehicle state and live onboard camera stream are transmitted over two independent communication channels, allowing the virtual vehicle to mirror the physical robot's motion while the passenger simultaneously views the vehicle's first-person camera feed and its navigation decisions through an in-vehicle dashboard interface. We evaluate the framework over 20 repeated closed-loop navigation trials. The system achieves a mean state-update latency of 29.63 ms, a mean relative route-progress error of 2.28% between the physical and virtual vehicles, and video delivery at 10.006 frames per second with 0.25% frame loss. All monitored navigation decisions were correctly reflected in the VR interface with no missed or incorrect notifications. The results indicate that the framework can support temporally synchronized, semantically consistent, and accurate route-progress representation for immersive observation of physical autonomous-vehicle behavior.

AI.tldr: A video-augmented VR framework links a real ROS2 autonomous vehicle to a Unity-based VR interface on Meta Quest 3S, enabling synchronized motion and real-time first-person camera and navigation decisions in VR with low latency and accurate route progress.
AI.motivation: Improve passenger understanding, trust, and comfort in autonomous vehicles by providing a physically grounded, temporally synchronized VR representation of the vehicle's perception and decisions. Address limitations of prior VR studies that rely on fully simulated or scripted scenarios.
AI.method: Couple a physical ROS 2 autonomous robot vehicle with a Unity 6 application on Meta Quest 3S. Transmit vehicle state and onboard camera via two independent channels so the virtual vehicle mirrors the physical robot's motion while the passenger views the real camera feed and an in-vehicle dashboard showing navigation decisions.
AI.result: Evaluated over 20 closed-loop trials. Mean state-update latency: 29.63 ms. Mean relative route-progress error: 2.28%. Video delivery at 10.006 fps with 0.25% frame loss. All navigation decisions were correctly reflected in VR with no missed or incorrect notifications.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates temporally synchronized, semantically consistent, and accurate representation of physical autonomous-vehicle behavior in VR, enabling immersive observation and potential improvements in user understanding and trust.

title: ShieldVLA: Feasibility-Aware Safety Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models demonstrate strong generalization in robotic manipulation and navigation, but existing fine-tuning methods provide limited safety guarantees. Current approaches primarily rely on Lagrangian optimization that enforces safety through soft penalties on expected cumulative cost, often resulting in residual constraint violations or overly conservative behavior. Moreover, learning safety in visual domains is challenging due to the absence of dense per-step safety annotations. We propose ShieldVLA, a safety-aligned fine-tuning framework for VLA models based on Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability. ShieldVLA learns a model-free approximation of the HJ reachability value function directly from visual observations to estimate the safe operating region. The learned safety critic gates policy optimization by separating reward maximization within feasible regions from recovery near unsafe states, avoiding persistent reward-cost trade-offs. To enable scalable supervision in visual environments, we introduce rubric-based VLM safety scores that convert semantic safety feedback into structured critic targets without requiring manual cost labels. Across five navigation and manipulation benchmarks spanning multiple VLA backbones, ShieldVLA reduces cumulative safety cost by 57% on average and improves task success rate by +0.13 over SafeVLA.

AI.tldr: A safety-focused fine-tuning framework for Vision-Language-Action models, ShieldVLA, uses Hamilton-Jacobi reachability to learn a model-free safety value function from visual input, gating policy optimization to separate safe exploitation from recovery, and rubric-based VLM safety scores for scalable supervision; it achieves lower safety cost and higher success across benchmarks compared to SafeVLA.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA fine-tuning often relies on soft Lagrangian penalties for safety, which can leave violations or be overly conservative, and visual safety lacks dense per-step annotations. There is a need for scalable, reliable safety guarantees in vision-based control.
AI.method: ShieldVLA learns a model-free approximation of the HJ reachability value function directly from visual observations to estimate safe regions. A safety critic gates policy optimization to optimize rewards within safe regions and drive recovery as needed near unsafe states. To scale supervision, rubric-based VLM safety scores convert semantic safety feedback into structured critic targets without manual cost labels.
AI.result: On five navigation/manipulation benchmarks across multiple VLA backbones, ShieldVLA reduces cumulative safety cost by 57% on average and improves task success rate by +0.13 over SafeVLA.
AI.conclusion: ShieldVLA provides a scalable, safety-aligned fine-tuning framework for VLA models, offering improved safety guarantees and task success without dense per-step safety annotations, by leveraging HJ reachability and rubric-based, model-free safety learning.

title: Harnessing human expertise for high-precision robotic assembly in industrialized construction: A sample-efficient installer-in-the-loop interactive reinforcement learning framework
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables. Published in Advanced Engineering Informatics
summary: Industrialized construction imposes stringent precision requirements on robotic assembly of modular components such as prefabricated window units. In tolerance-critical operations, the central bottleneck is not only mechanical clearance but also converting tacit installer expertise into data-efficient autonomy under sparse acceptance feedback, contact variability, and millimeter-scale constraints. We present an installer-in-the-loop interactive reinforcement learning framework that acquires expertise through offline teleoperated demonstrations, sparse event-driven binary takeovers at contact-failure boundaries, and acceptance-aligned terminal rewards, logged under a unified schema for traceable offline-to-online adaptation. A temporally abstract action-sequence policy built on Q-chunking with Flow Q-Learning captures multimodal recovery maneuvers under sparse terminal rewards, while a non-updating warm-start phase stabilizes the offline-to-online transition. The framework is evaluated in MuJoCo across the workflow from suction acquisition through clearance-limited seating, under structured staging and end-to-end randomized placement. Within a defined stress-test regime with 2 mm per-side clearance, bounded pose perturbations, and friction randomization, the pipeline attains 100\% autonomous seating with 12--15 min of cumulative installer supervision over 3.0 h of online training, and reaches the 95\% success milestone in approximately 0.5 h and 1.5 h in the two experiments. We also report wall-clock adaptation time, cumulative takeover minutes, intervention-rate decay, and stage-wise failure attribution to inform supervision budgeting. Ablations isolate the complementary contributions of temporal abstraction, installer intervention, and warm-start value calibration.

AI.tldr: Installer-in-the-loop reinforcement learning enables data-efficient autonomous seating of prefabricated window units under tight tolerances, achieving near-fully autonomous operation with limited supervisor time in MuJoCo simulations and stressing regimes.
AI.motivation: Industrialized construction imposes millimeter-scale precision and sparse feedback; tacit installer expertise must be converted into data-efficient autonomy that handles contact variability and failure boundaries.
AI.method: Offline teleoperated demonstrations plus sparse event-driven takeovers at contact-failure boundaries, acceptance-aligned terminal rewards; a temporally abstract action policy (Q-chunking with Flow Q-Learning) handles multimodal recoveries; a non-updating warm-start phase stabilizes online adaptation; logs unify offline-online data for traceability; evaluated in MuJoCo from suction capture to seating under staged and end-to-end randomized placement with friction variety.
AI.result: Achieves 100% autonomous seating with 12–15 minutes of installer supervision over 3 hours of online training under 2 mm per-side clearance; reaches 95% success in ~0.5 h and ~1.5 h in the two tests; reports wall-clock adaptation time, cumulative takeover minutes, intervention-rate decay, and stage-wise failure attribution; ablations confirm the value of temporal abstraction, installer intervention, and warm-start calibration.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides traceable offline-to-online adaptation for precision assembly, enabling data-efficient autonomy in tolerance-critical tasks, with clear metrics for supervision budgeting and insights into what components drive performance.

title: Learning Manipulation-Sufficient Representations via Outcome Bottlenecks
summary: Networked manipulation endpoints couple perception to actuation across compute- and bandwidth-limited links, yet commonly exchange dense geometric states optimized for fidelity rather than action outcomes. A stochastic representation is learned with a policy-free, action-conditioned outcome bottleneck: marginal outcome log-loss supplies distortion and a KL term regularizes rate. The construction is motivated by the minimal statistic that preserves the outcome distribution of every admissible action, while the implemented finite model is evaluated as a rate-regularized mixture predictor. The same encoder and outcome head support grasp selection, singleton conformal filtering, active viewpoint selection, and latent test-time adaptation. A finite-probe theorem identifies the local level-set tangent space with the null space of an outcome Jacobian. The synthetic oracle verifies this result; on scanned objects, an analytic surrogate agrees with measured simulator invariances within \(0.56^\circ\). Across 11,979 simulated grasps on 13 objects, a reconstructed-geometry wrench score attains 0.542 AUC against lift success and falls below chance on curved objects, while our representation attains 0.876. At 25\% commitment, executed-grasp success is 0.503 versus 0.984. The 512-byte interface is \(288\times\) smaller than one RGB-D frame and runs at 16\,ms per CPU decision. Independent synthetic points track the tested conformal levels; scanned-object all-pair coverage is reported as a clustered empirical diagnostic. On unseen objects, within-scene AUC falls to 0.569, and a full-feedback update raises empirical mean pairwise coverage from 0.728 to 0.883.

AI.tldr: A rate-regularized, outcome-conditioned representation compresses networked manipulation states into a compact, policy-free bottleneck that preserves action outcomes, enabling multiple tasks with high efficiency and favorable in-distribution performance; notable results include a 512-byte interface, 16 ms decision, and strong grasp-outcome AUC, with some generalization gaps on unseen objects.
AI.motivation: Networked manipulation links are bandwidth- and compute-constrained. Dense geometric states optimized for fidelity waste bandwidth and may not optimize action outcomes. The minimal statistic that preserves the outcome distribution for all admissible actions motivates a finite, rate-regularized representation that can support multiple manipulation tasks and end-to-end efficiency.
AI.method: Learned stochastic representation via a policy-free, outcome-conditioned outcome bottleneck using marginal outcome log-loss plus a KL-divergence term to regularize the communication rate. A finite-probe theorem identifies the local tangent space with the null space of the outcome Jacobian. A shared encoder and outcome head support tasks including grasp selection, singleton conformal filtering, active viewpoint selection, and latent test-time adaptation. Experimental evaluation uses a rate-regularized mixture predictor as the finite model, synthetic oracle, analytic surrogate, and 11,979 simulated grasps on 13 objects.
AI.result: The representation attains 0.876 AUC for the grasp outcome task, outperforming a reconstructed-geometry wrench score of 0.542 AUC (which fails on curved objects). At 25% commitment, grasp success is 0.503 versus 0.984 for a baseline. The interface is 512 bytes and runs at ~16 ms per CPU decision. Unseen objects yield AUC of 0.569; full-feedback update raises mean pairwise coverage from 0.728 to 0.883. Independent conformal diagnostics and within-scene coverage metrics are reported, with 0.56° invariance in a synthetic surrogate vs analytic surrogate on scanned objects.
AI.conclusion: A compact, rate-regularized, outcome-preserving representation can support multiple manipulation tasks with efficient runtime and favorable in-distribution performance. It exhibits some generalization gaps on unseen objects and curved geometries, but the finite-probe theory provides geometric insight into when outcome changes lie in the tangent space. Overall, the approach demonstrates practical compression of networked manipulation information toward action-oriented fidelity.

title: Personalized and Explainable Blood Pressure Estimation from PPG via Hybrid CNN--Morphological Features
summary: Continuous cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring using photoplethysmography (PPG) offers a promising solution for personalized healthcare. However, existing methods have two major limitations. Handcrafted feature-based approaches rely on precise fiducial point detection and are limited to short-term analysis, while deep learning models, despite their accuracy, often operate as black boxes with limited physiological interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose a physiology-guided hybrid framework for personalized BP estimation that couples a convolutional neural network (CNN) branch capturing global and local waveform dynamics with a morphology-prior branch that explicitly encodes person-specific vascular characteristics. By embedding a morphology-based feature set that explicitly encodes individual vascular characteristics, the proposed framework enhances personalization and reduces dependence on large-scale training datasets. Evaluated on a subset of the MIMIC-III database under a subject-specific (personalized) testing protocol, the proposed personalized physiology-guided hybrid approach achieved mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 3.77 mmHg for systolic BP and 2.36 mmHg for diastolic BP, corresponding to relative improvements of 43.7% and 32.4% over a subject-specific (personalized) CNN-only baseline. SHAP-based analysis confirmed that the introduced morphology-prior features align with individual vascular characteristics, reinforcing per-subject interpretability. These findings highlight the potential of personalized, physiology-guided hybrid learning with novel morphological descriptors for accurate and explainable BP monitoring in real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A physiology-guided hybrid model improves cuffless BP estimation from PPG by integrating morphology priors with CNN, achieving accurate per-subject MAEs and interpretability with SHAP, reducing data needs.
AI.motivation: Address two major limitations: reliance on precise fiducial point detection and short-term analysis in handcrafted features, and lack of interpretability in deep learning models, by introducing personalized physiology-guided components.
AI.method: A CNN branch captures global/local waveform dynamics while a morphology-prior branch encodes person-specific vascular characteristics via a morphology-based feature set. The framework is trained for subject-specific personalization and uses SHAP to interpret feature importance.
AI.result: On a subset of MIMIC-III with subject-specific testing, MAEs are 3.77 mmHg (systolic) and 2.36 mmHg (diastolic), with relative improvements of 43.7% and 32.4% over a CNN-only personalized baseline. SHAP analysis confirms the morphology-prior features align with vascular characteristics, enhancing interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Physiology-guided hybrid learning with morphology descriptors yields accurate, explainable cuffless BP monitoring and reduces dependence on large-scale datasets, supporting real-world personalized hypertension management.

title: BudgetBench: A Budget-Tiered Protocol and Pilot Harness for Memory Strategy Evaluation in Local Large Language Model Agents
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/aviskaar/budgetbench
summary:
For local large language model agents, active context is a scarce resource: memory capacity, prefill latency, cache growth, and service objectives all constrain how many input tokens each call can afford. We present BudgetBench, an active-budget protocol and reference harness that treats the per-call input-token budget as the independent variable when comparing memory strategies. Holding the model, task, sampler, and decoding fixed, it sweeps budgets over 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, and 32K tokens and records quality, budget utilization, latency, and, as a first-class outcome, budget-violation rates. The core contribution is this reusable measurement surface: a swappable MemoryStrategy contract, explicit budget enforcement, deterministic or versioned graders, prompt-audit metadata, and reproducibility artifacts, released at https://github.com/aviskaar/budgetbench.
  We substantiate the protocol with pilot studies rather than final rankings. Across a local qwen2.5:1.5b pilot (89 items each on SWE-bench Verified and LongBench v2), a hosted 50-item Qwen3 30B-A3B LongBench replication with exact tokenization, and a 500-item LongMemEval oracle study scored by the official GPT-4o evaluator, the harness exposes budget-compliance failures, non-monotonic quality curves, and operating points that single-budget evaluation hides. The budgeted-versus-full-context direction remains unresolved: the local slice is near-null and the hosted replication favors full context in point estimate. We report results transparently, including that the early pilot's tokenizer approximation undercounts some served-model prompts, so its violation rows are tokenizer-approximation diagnostics, not claim-bearing results; all timings are operational diagnostics. The reusable contribution is the protocol, harness, and failure-reporting discipline needed to scale fixed-budget memory-strategy evaluation.

AI.tldr: BudgetBench provides a fixed-budget evaluation framework for local LLM agent memory strategies, enabling systematic comparison across token budgets with explicit budget enforcement, graders, and reproducibility artifacts; pilot studies reveal budget-compliance failures and non-monotonic quality curves, with protocol and harness released on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Local LLM agents face scarce input-token budgets due to memory, latency, cache, and service-objective constraints. A reusable, transparent benchmarking surface is needed to compare memory strategies under fixed budgets, not just single-budget evaluations.
AI.method: BudgetBench defines a protocol that sweeps per-call input-token budgets (2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K) while keeping model, task, sampler, and decoding fixed. It introduces a swappable MemoryStrategy contract, explicit budget enforcement, deterministic/versioned graders, prompt-audit metadata, and reproducibility artifacts, all exposed via a reference harness. Results are meant to be reproducible and comparable across implementations.
AI.result: Pilot studies across multiple setups (local qwen2.5:1.5b, hosted Qwen3 30B-A3B LongBench replication, and 500-item LongMemEval study) identify budget-compliance failures, non-monotonic quality curves, and distinct operating points that single-budget evaluations miss. Tokenizer approximations in early pilots can undercount prompts, making some violation rows diagnostics rather than claims. The harness exposes budgeted-versus-full-context dynamics and emphasizes transparent reporting over final rankings.
AI.conclusion: The core contribution is a reusable protocol, harness, and failure-reporting discipline for scalable fixed-budget memory-strategy evaluation; the paper acknowledges unresolved direction between budgeted and full-context performance and releases artifacts at GitHub for reproducibility.

title: ZGCM-1: A Fully Open and Extremely Efficient Foundation Model for Math and Agentic Search
summary: In this work, we present ZGCM-1, a fully open 7B dense foundation model trained from scratch with extreme data, system, and algorithmic efficiency. ZGCM-1 is founded on a core premise: compact models cannot passively memorize the open web, but can overcome parametric capacity limits by coupling deliberate internal thinking with active external tool use. To support this paradigm across a 256K context, we develop an end-to-end, high-efficiency open training recipe: Architecture & System Co-design: interleaved gated sliding-window and full attention, and a stable FP8 Muon optimizer; Progressive Curriculum & MDP Mid-Training: context scaling across 16K, 64K, and 256K, and the reformulation of interaction traces into Markov Decision Processes. Furthermore, we establish an AI-native R&D workflow where agent swarms autonomously manage cluster operations, data curation, and rapid diagnostic evaluation. Extensive evaluations show that ZGCM-1-7B is competitive across 7B model family on general benchmarks. On several challenging mathematical reasoning and agentic search suites, it remains competitive with frontier models orders of magnitude larger, such as Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.1. We also show that our pre-training design offers a ~4.2x efficiency improvement in 16K pre-training time-to-loss. Across the full development lifecycle, we distill eight actionable empirical findings-spanning architectural scaling, SFT quality pruning, long-context generalization, and agentic co-training dynamics. To facilitate community research, we open-source model weights from the pre-training, mid-training, and post-training stages, intermediate checkpoints, training code, per-stage data and data recipes, and W&B logs.

AI.tldr: ZGCM-1: a 7B dense foundation model trained from scratch with extreme efficiency and 256K context, leveraging architecture/system co-design, progressive context scaling, and agentic tool use; claims competitive performance vs much larger models and significant training-time efficiency, with open-source release.
AI.motivation: Overcome the parametric capacity limits of compact models by coupling deliberate internal reasoning with active external tool use, enabled by huge context and AI-native R&D workflows.
AI.method: Architectural design with interleaved gated sliding-window and full attention; stable FP8 Muon optimizer; Progressive Curriculum with context scaling to 16K/64K/256K; reformulation of interaction traces into Markov Decision Processes; AI-native agent swarms for cluster ops, data curation, and rapid diagnostics; open training recipe and data pipelines.
AI.result: ZGCM-1-7B is competitive on general benchmarks within 7B family; on challenging math reasoning and agentic search tasks it matches frontier models much larger (e.g., 235B- and 5.1B-class gaps); ~4.2x efficiency in 16K pre-training time-to-loss; eight empirical findings across scaling, pruning, long-context generalization, and co-training dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that compact models can close the gap with larger models through architectural and data-efficiency innovations and agentic training processes; provides open releases to accelerate community research.

title: The optimal-transport cartogram: world population as a Brenier map
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Code, experiment records and figure provenance: https://github.com/philippbogdan/historical-cartogram
summary: A contiguous cartogram is a map whose area is proportional to a quantity such as population. The defining condition, that the Jacobian determinant of the deformation equals the density, is one equation for two unknown functions, so every cartogram method adds a tie-breaker, usually implicitly. Optimal transport makes the tie-breaker explicit: among all density-equalising maps of the frame onto itself, take the one that moves the population least in the mean-square sense. By Brenier's theorem that map is the gradient of a convex potential, so it has no local rotation anywhere and cannot fold. We compute this map for the world population of 2025 on a 4096 by 4096 Mercator grid (10 km cells) from the GHS-POP raster, using the fixed-point Monge-Ampère iteration of Benamou, Froese and Oberman with spectral Poisson solves, continuation in the population share and an ocean-only buffer, on a laptop GPU. Against a Gastner-Newman diffusion cartogram of the same density we find the same transport cost to within 0.4 per cent and density errors of a few per cent for both, but a median local rotation of 8.8 degrees for diffusion against 0.01 for transport, and a median anisotropy of 6.30 against 3.93. The construction extends to local refinement, by transporting a city's 100 m population onto the area measure the global map assigns to it, and to a semi-discrete counterpart: 8,192 Laguerre cells of 1.00 million people each. Code, data provenance and every figure's inputs are public.

AI.tldr: Optimal-transport cartograms minimize population movement while preserving density, yielding maps with negligible local rotation and moderate anisotropy compared to diffusion-based methods. The approach matches diffusion-cost but reduces local distortion, and extends to local refinement and semi-discrete variants; code and data are public.
AI.motivation: Provide an explicit, principled tie-breaker for density-equalising cartograms (minimize movement) and ensure maps are free of local rotations and folds, enabling accurate, scalable cartography.
AI.method: Compute the Monge–Ampère equation via a fixed-point Monge–Ampère iteration (Benamou, Froese & Oberman) with spectral Poisson solvers, continuation in population share, and an ocean buffer on a 4096×4096 Mercator grid for 2025 world population (GHS-POP). Implement on a laptop GPU; compare against Gastner–Newman diffusion cartograms; extend to city-scale refinement (100 m) and a semi-discrete Laguerre-cell representation (8192 cells of ~1 million people). Code, data provenance and inputs are public.
AI.result: Transport cost matches diffusion within about 0.4%; density errors are a few percent for both methods. Median local rotation: 0.01° (transport) vs 8.8° (diffusion). Median anisotropy: 3.93 (transport) vs 6.30 (diffusion). Extensions include refining to city scale and a semi-discrete 8192-Laguerre-cell model; all outputs and inputs publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Explicit optimal-transport cartograms deliver density-equalising maps with far lower local distortion than diffusion-based approaches while preserving comparable transport cost and accuracy; the method is scalable, reproducible, and adaptable to multi-resolution and semi-discrete representations.

title: Self-Evolving AI for Humanoids: Mechanisms, Safety, and Evaluation of Post-Deployment Self-Improvement
comment: The paper includes 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, and is considered for publication
summary: Humanoid robots are becoming an important part of embodied artificial intelligence, driven by advances in reinforcement learning for locomotion, world models for prediction, and vision-language-action models for general control. However, most of these systems remain static after deployment. A policy is trained offline for a fixed objective and then frozen, even though the tasks, environments, and robot bodies keep drifting over time. An emerging paradigm of self-evolving agents aims to address this problem by allowing systems to improve from their own post-deployment experience. Since most existing studies focus on disembodied software agents, this survey examines how self-evolution changes when an agent has a physical body. We first define self-evolution for humanoids and represent a deployed robot using a state tuple that includes its policy, perception, memory, workflow, and body. This state is updated by an evolution operator in a slow outer loop with a lifelong objective. We then organize the literature into four complementary mechanisms of self-evolution, presented in increasing order of autonomy: self-learning, self-adaptation, self-optimization, and self-generation. Since changes to a humanoid can introduce physical hazards, we treat safety and uncertainty as key design dimensions of the evolution operator, and further formulate admissible evolution as a constraint enforced by a world-model verification gate within a human-oversight envelope. Finally, we present that evaluation should track the robot's evolving trajectory rather than a fixed checkpoint, and we identify the lack of a benchmark designed specifically for self-evolving humanoids. Moreover, we outline open challenges spanning AI algorithms, on-board systems, and governance.

AI.tldr: A survey framing self-evolving humanoid agents, introducing a formal state-and-evolution operator, and a four-stage autonomy taxonomy (self-learning, self-adaptation, self-optimization, self-generation) with safety as a design constraint. It highlights evaluation on evolving trajectories, notes the lack of benchmarks, and outlines cross-cutting AI, hardware, and governance challenges.
AI.motivation: Offline-trained policies degrade in changing tasks, environments, and bodies; need for autonomous, safe self-improvement in embodied agents to maintain performance and adaptivity.
AI.method: Proposes a formal state tuple for deployed robots (policy, perception, memory, workflow, body) updated by a slow outer-loop evolution operator with a lifelong objective. Organizes literature into four mechanisms—self-learning, self-adaptation, self-optimization, self-generation—and analyzes safety/uncertainty as design dimensions via a world-model verification gate within a human-oversight envelope.
AI.result: Provides a cohesive taxonomy and design framework for self-evolving humanoids, including safety constraints and evaluation design, and identifies gaps such as benchmarks and governance for future work.
AI.conclusion: Calls for open challenges across AI algorithms, on-board systems, and governance to advance self-evolving humanoids, plus the need for benchmarks tailored to evolving embodiments.

title: Part Grounding, Not Action Knowledge: Locating the Bottleneck in VLM Affordance Prediction
summary: Benchmarks agree that vision-language models reason poorly about low-level manipulation, but an aggregate accuracy score does not say which step fails. We separate two steps that affordance questions conflate: identifying which part of an object to act on, and knowing what action that part requires. Across 19 articulated objects we asked eight models, spanning three developers, what motion a robot should apply. Under an open prompt, push was produced once in 64 evaluations where it was correct, despite being correct for 8 of 19 objects and appearing in the offered label set every time. Inspecting the outputs showed why: models described a different part than the one being scored, e.g. explaining how to pick up a camera rather than press its button. Naming the target part raises action accuracy by 0.32 to 0.63 for every model, from 0.158-0.474 to 0.684-0.947, and push recall from 0-1/8 to 7-8/8. No model beats a constant answer that ignores the image under the open prompt; once the part is named, all eight do. Asked to describe the same part in free prose with no label set, models produce pressing language for 6 to 8 of 8. These results are hard to reconcile with missing action knowledge, and instead point to part grounding as the dominant bottleneck, a pattern that holds across all three model families and does not diminish with capability. Naming the part supplies the grounding variable, so this bounds what a perfect part detector would offer rather than demonstrating a general model of mechanics. Two supporting results agree: on real photographs only three of eight models localize grasp points better than a constant baseline, and on rendered objects none do. We also document two measurement errors of our own, a threshold that let a constant baseline score 0.929 and a labelling rule wrong on 4 of 19 objects, both caught only by testing our numbers against trivial alternatives.

AI.tldr: Part grounding is the main bottleneck for affordance reasoning in vision-language models; naming the target part dramatically boosts action accuracy and push recall across 19 articulated objects and eight models, while open prompts fail. Evidence spans three model families and reveals two measurement errors.
AI.motivation: Disentangle whether failures in low-level manipulation stem from action knowledge or misidentification of the object part to act on; quantify the impact of grounding on action commands.
AI.method: Evaluate eight models (three developers) over 19 articulated objects. Compare open-prompt prompts (target: push) versus explicit naming of the target part. Measure action accuracy and push recall. Analyze free-prose descriptions without labels. Extend tests to real photographs and rendered objects. Report measurement anomalies discovered.
AI.result: When the target part is named, action accuracy rises from 0.158–0.474 to 0.684–0.947; push recall rises from 0–1/8 to 7–8/8. Under open prompts, push is produced only once in 64 evaluations, though correct for 8 of 19. Models often describe a different part than the one scored. In free prose without labels, models produce pressing language for 6–8 of 8. Real photos yield grasp-point localization better than baseline for only 3/8; rendered objects show none. Two measurement errors are identified: a threshold that yields a constant baseline 0.929 and a labeling rule wrong on 4/19, uncovered by benchmarking against trivial alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Part grounding is the dominant bottleneck across model families and capabilities. Providing the grounding variable by naming the part bounds what a perfect part detector could offer, rather than proving a general model of mechanics. Improving part identification should be the priority to advance manipulation-through-language systems.

title: A derivative-fidelity failure mode in physics-informed neural networks: strengthened benchmark evidence from function-value training
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) use automatic differentiation to impose differential-equation residuals, but good agreement in function values does not necessarily imply accurate derivatives. This paper formulates derivative fidelity as a failure mode of PINNs and tests it with one-dimensional benchmarks. Multilayer perceptrons are trained only on function values for sin(x) and exp(x), while second derivatives obtained by automatic differentiation are evaluated separately. The hypothesis is strengthened by additional tests over training-point density, activation functions, endpoint-dense evaluation, and both L2 and maximum-error diagnostics. The results show that visually accurate function approximation can coexist with substantially larger second-derivative errors, especially near high-curvature boundary regions. The experiment provides a diagnostic protocol for distinguishing value accuracy from physics-residual reliability.

AI.tldr: PINNs can yield accurate function values but may have large errors in higher-order derivatives; derivative fidelity is a separate failure mode that warrants diagnostic testing.
AI.motivation: To diagnose and quantify the gap between function-value accuracy and derivative (second-derivative) accuracy in PINNs, which affects physics-residual reliability.
AI.method: Train multilayer perceptrons on 1D functions sin(x) and exp(x) using only function values; compute second derivatives via automatic differentiation; compare to true second derivatives; explore the impact of training-point density, activation functions, endpoint-dense evaluation, and both L2 and maximum-norm diagnostics.
AI.result: Second-derivative errors can be substantially larger than function-value errors, especially near high-curvature boundary regions; visually convincing function approximations do not guarantee accurate derivatives; the study proposes a diagnostic workflow to separate value accuracy from physics-residual reliability.
AI.conclusion: Derivative fidelity in PINNs is a distinct failure mode; evaluating derivatives is essential for assessing physics-residual reliability; the paper provides a practical diagnostic protocol based on 1D benchmarks to distinguish derivative fidelity from function-value accuracy.

title: Converge Then Diversify: Decoupling Convergence and Diversity in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimisation
summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (MOBO) is a sample-efficient approach for optimising expensive black-box functions with multiple objectives. In MOBO, the goal is to adequately approximate the Pareto front; that is, to obtain a high-quality solution set with 1) good convergence (closeness to the Pareto front) and 2) good diversity (spread across the Pareto front). Existing MOBO methods typically aim to accomplish these two tasks simultaneously, i.e., driving the search towards the Pareto front while maintaining a diverse set of nondominated solutions, such that the solutions, ideally, can gradually approach the entire front. When sufficient search budgets are available, this approach is effective. However, considering both convergence and diversity throughout the search is not easy and requires careful design. Under very tight budgets, there may not be enough solutions generated to be able to simultaneously approach the entire Pareto front. To address this issue, this paper proposes a \textit{converge-then-diversify} (CTD) approach that decouples convergence and diversity into two stages. In the first stage, CTD focuses on convergence, aiming to quickly drive the search toward a single point on the Pareto front. In the second stage, CTD focuses on diversity, aiming to spread solutions across the front. We present two simple instantiations of CTD by using widely adopted acquisition functions in the area. Experimental results show that, across all 446 pairwise comparisons, CTD statistically outperforms state-of-the-art methods in 72.9\% of the cases, performs equivalently in 21.1\%, and is statistically worse in only 6.1\%, with the advantage being particularly evident in settings with very tight evaluation budgets or in high-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: Proposes converge-then-diversify (CTD) for multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) to decouple convergence and diversity into two stages, improving performance under tight budgets.
AI.motivation: Balancing convergence (closeness to the Pareto front) and diversity (spread across the front) in MOBO is difficult, especially under very limited evaluation budgets; existing methods struggle to achieve both simultaneously.
AI.method: Two-stage CTD: (1) converge stage targets rapid convergence to a single Pareto-front point using standard acquisition functions; (2) diversify stage spreads solutions across the Pareto front; two simple instantiations of CTD are demonstrated using widely adopted acquisition functions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation over 446 pairwise comparisons shows CTD outperforms state-of-the-art methods in 72.9% of cases, is equivalent in 21.1%, and worse in 6.1%; gains are pronounced with tight budgets and in high-dimensional problems.
AI.conclusion: CTD offers a simple, effective mechanism to decouple convergence and diversity in MOBO, yielding robust gains under budget constraints; suggests potential for broader instantiations and theoretical analysis.

title: Computing the minimal perimeter polygon for digital objects in the triangular tiling
summary: This work presents an algorithm, together with its correctness proof, to determine the minimum perimeter polygon (MPP) for digital objects given as regular complexes in the triangular plane tiling. Such objects are edge-adjacency-connected sets of triangle tiles that have no end tiles, and the point set union of all their tiles forms a simple polygon. Nevertheless, the boundary paths of the objects are not assumed to be simple. Then the MPP is a weakly simple polygon that coincides with the relative convex hull (i.e., geodesic hull) of a set $A$ with respect to a simple polygon $B$, where $A\subset B$, but $A$ is not necessarily a polygon, in fact it is generally not connected. Our MPP algorithm relies on constructing and iteratively constraining cones of visibility through forthcoming boundary tiles, it uses the structure of the canonical boundary path, the MPP frontier is the shortest polygonal curve following this path. We also propose a boundary tracing algorithm to obtain such paths from the objects.

AI.tldr: Algorithm for minimum-perimeter polygon (MPP) of digital objects on triangular tiling; computes weakly simple MPP as relative convex (geodesic) hull of a potentially disconnected subset A within a simple polygon B; uses visibility cones, canonical boundary path, and shortest frontier; includes a boundary tracing algorithm.
AI.motivation: Provide a guaranteed tight boundary (minimum perimeter) representation for digital objects formed by triangular-tiling tiles, even when boundary is not simple and A may be disconnected, by relating MPP to a relative convex hull.
AI.method: Iteratively construct constraining cones of visibility through boundary tiles; exploit canonical boundary path; define MPP frontier as the shortest polygonal curve along this path; develop a boundary tracing algorithm to extract the canonical paths from the object.
AI.result: Proof of correctness; characterization of MPP as a weakly simple polygon equal to the geodesic hull of A with respect to B; algorithm outputs the MPP and a tracing method.
AI.conclusion: Shows that MPP coincides with the relative convex hull in the triangular grid setting; provides a practical method to obtain the boundary of digital objects with minimal perimeter.

title: GzDRL: Reproducible and Scalable Deep Reinforcement Learning with Gazebo
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: We present GzDRL, a novel single-process reinforcement learning (RL) framework for Gazebo that overcomes longstanding bottlenecks in scalable, reproducible robotics experimentation. Unlike conventional middleware-based RL-Gazebo integrations that suffer from nondeterminism and irreproducibility, GzDRL introduces a systematic, middleware-free environment-stepping mechanism that directly synchronizes agent actions and physics updates. This design enables deterministic, high-throughput data collection, efficient vectorization, and reproducible RL training and evaluation. Comprehensive benchmarks demonstrate that GzDRL achieves the highest workstation throughput among the evaluated frameworks while remaining competitive with GPU-accelerated simulators on laptop hardware, and maintains precise agent-environment synchronization, multi-agent scalability, and experiment-level reproducibility. We further validate sim-to-real transfer by deploying learned policies directly onto a physical quadrotor, without fine-tuning. Our results establish GzDRL as an accessible and reproducible platform for advancing RL in robotics and automation.

AI.tldr: GzDRL is a middleware-free, single-process RL framework for Gazebo delivering deterministic, scalable, reproducible robotics RL with strong sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: To overcome nondeterminism, irreproducibility, and bottlenecks of middleware-based RL-Gazebo integrations, enabling deterministic, high-throughput, reproducible experimentation in robotics.
AI.method: A middleware-free environment-stepping loop that directly synchronizes agent actions with physics updates in a single process, enabling deterministic execution, vectorization, and multi-agent scalability; comprehensive benchmarks; sim-to-real validation on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning.
AI.result: GzDRL achieves the highest workstation throughput among evaluated frameworks, is competitive with GPU-accelerated simulators on laptop hardware, preserves precise agent-environment synchronization and reproducibility, and demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: GzDRL provides an accessible, reproducible platform for RL in robotics, enabling deterministic data collection, scalable experimentation, and direct sim-to-real transfer without middleware overhead.

title: Synthetic Leprosy Image Generation Using Mask-Conditioned Latent Diffusion and Transfer Learning from Large Chronic Wound Datasets
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Code and data pipeline: https://github.com/Yusufa09/SyntheticImageGeneration
summary: Machine learning for neglected tropical diseases is limited by data, not algorithms: public annotated image sets for leprosy (Hansen's disease) number in the hundreds, orders of magnitude below what generative models require. We ask whether a model trained on abundant chronic wound photography transfers to this low-data regime. We build a three-stage pipeline. First, a DeepLabV3-ResNet50 segmentation network (validation Dice 0.876, IoU 0.799) supplies lesion masks for two wound datasets that ship without them. Second, we assemble a mask-conditioned latent diffusion model from Stable Diffusion 1.5 components and train it on 3,280 region-of-interest wound crops, widening the UNet input convolution from 4 to 11 channels to admit three mask feature maps and a blurred low-frequency context latent. Third, we fine-tune this model on 708 leprosy image-mask pairs drawn from 764 images of approximately 150 patients. We evaluate with LPIPS perceptual distance, anchored by a real-versus-real baseline computed on the same 242 anchor images as the cross-set comparisons; without that reference the cross-set distances cannot be interpreted. The generated set shows no mode collapse: its internal perceptual diversity (0.662) is statistically indistinguishable from that of the real leprosy set (0.672, 95% CI [0.664, 0.680]). Generated images sit 0.044 LPIPS outside the real distribution - measurably apart, but under half of one standard deviation. Fine-tuning shifted the output distribution only marginally, which we trace to lesion geometry reaching the network through input concatenation alone. Chronic wound photography is therefore a viable donor domain for leprosy lesion synthesis: low-level appearance transfers well, and the remaining barrier is semantic control rather than image quality.

AI.tldr: Cross-domain lesion synthesis for leprosy using a three-stage pipeline; chronic wound images serve as a donor domain to train a mask-conditioned latent diffusion model; perceptual diversity preserved; minor distribution shift; semantic control remains the main barrier.
AI.motivation: Assess whether models trained on abundant chronic wound data can transfer to the data-scarce leprosy domain and enable realistic lesion synthesis.
AI.method: Stage 1: Train DeepLabV3-ResNet50 to produce lesion masks on two wound datasets lacking masks (validation Dice 0.876, IoU 0.799). Stage 2: Build a mask-conditioned latent diffusion model from Stable Diffusion 1.5; modify UNet input to 11 channels to accept three mask feature maps plus a blurred low-frequency context latent; train on 3,280 ROI wound crops. Stage 3: Finetune on 708 leprosy image–mask pairs from 764 images of ~150 patients.
AI.result: No mode collapse; perceptual diversity of generated images (0.662) is statistically indistinguishable from real leprosy (0.672, 95% CI [0.664, 0.680]). Generated set sits 0.044 LPIPS outside the real distribution (within half a standard deviation). Cross-set distances require an anchor, but with the anchor, interpretation is possible. Fine-tuning shifted the distribution only marginally, attributed to lesion geometry entering the model via input concatenation. Chronic wound photography appears to be a viable donor domain for leprosy lesion synthesis, with low-level appearance transferring well; main barrier is semantic control rather than image quality.
AI.conclusion: Chronic wound imagery is a viable donor domain for leprosy lesion synthesis. Low-level appearance transfers well, but achieving semantic-level control remains the key challenge for practical use.

title: Land Art as a Big-Data Climate Sensor
summary: Robert Smithson's 1970 land artwork Spiral Jetty, located in the north arm of Utah's Great Salt Lake, has alternated between submergence and exposure during severe lake decline. We analyze 1,744 co-registered Landsat 4-9 and Sentinel-2 image chips spanning every year and calendar month from 1984 to 2025. A 14-feature complexity signature combines Shannon entropy, multiscale permutation entropy, fractal dimension, lacunarity, gray-level co-occurrence texture, intensity statistics, and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 features. These measurements are compared with a 42-year monthly climate and hydrology panel from NASA GISTEMP, USGS NWIS, Open-Meteo, and the Global Carbon Budget. Bootstrap analysis shows that Shannon entropy is a weak proxy and does not support an earlier small-sample claim of positive correlation with global temperature. By contrast, coarse-scale permutation entropy and mean intensity track lake elevation strongly, with Spearman correlations of 0.85 to 0.88 and 95 percent confidence intervals excluding zero. The third principal component of the ResNet50 embeddings emerges without supervision as an AI climate axis, correlating 0.86 with cumulative CO2 and -0.83 with lake elevation. Image complexity leads lake stage by about three years, with Pearson r = 0.58 at lag +3 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.40 to 0.73. STL decomposition reveals a non-monotonic trend that rises from 1984 to 2015 and declines sharply thereafter as the lake approaches record-low elevations. Partial correlations controlling for month and sensor confirm robustness to seasonal and sensor effects. These results refine the art-as-thermometer metaphor into an art-as-leading-indicator-of-hydrological-state interpretation. The dataset, feature pipeline, and analysis code are released as a public benchmark.

AI.tldr: A 1984–2025 analysis of Spiral Jetty using Landsat/Sentinel imagery shows image-derived complexity metrics, especially coarse-scale permutation entropy and mean intensity, reliably track lake elevation and predict lake state up to ~3 years in advance. An unsupervised AI-climate axis from ResNet50 embeddings correlates with CO2 and lake level. The study provides a public benchmark (data, features, code) and highlights art as a leading indicator of hydrological state, with robust statistics (bootstrapping, partial correlations, STL).
AI.motivation: To quantify hydrological state and its climate associations via art-based remote sensing features, testing whether image complexity metrics can lead or reflect lake state and climate drivers, and to promote reproducible benchmarks.
AI.method: Compile 1,744 co-registered Landsat 4-9 and Sentinel-2 image chips (1984–2025). Build a 14-feature complexity signature including Shannon entropy, multiscale permutation entropy, fractal dimension, lacunarity, gray-level co-occurrence texture, intensity statistics, and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 embeddings. Compare with a 42-year monthly climate/hydrology panel (NASA GISTEMP, USGS NWIS, Open-Meteo, Global Carbon Budget). Use bootstrap to assess entropy proxies, compute Spearman correlations (rho 0.85–0.88 for coarse entropy and mean intensity with lake elevation), perform PCA on ResNet50 embeddings to find an unsupervised AI climate axis (correlating 0.86 with CO2 and -0.83 with lake elevation), analyze lead-lag with Pearson r=0.58 at +3 months/years lag, and apply STL decomposition and partial correlations controlling for month and sensor. Release dataset, feature pipeline, and code as a public benchmark.
AI.result: Findings show Shannon entropy is a weak proxy for climate linkage. Coarse-scale permutation entropy and mean image intensity strongly track lake elevation (Spearman 0.85–0.88; CIs exclude zero). The third ResNet50 PC yields an AI-derived climate axis correlating 0.86 with cumulative CO2 and -0.83 with lake elevation. Image complexity leads lake stage by about three years (r=0.58 at lag +3; 95% CI 0.40–0.73). STL reveals a rise from 1984–2015 followed by a sharp decline as lake reaches record lows. Partial correlations confirm robustness to month and sensor effects. The work reframes art as a leading hydrological indicator and provides a public benchmark for future studies.
AI.conclusion: Image-derived complexity metrics, especially coarse permutation entropy and mean intensity, can serve as leading indicators of hydrological state in lake systems, with an AI-climate axis capturing major climate drivers. The public benchmark enhances reproducibility and cross-study comparability of image-based hydrological proxies.

title: Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: When we speak of recursive self-improvement (RSI), are we speaking of a phenomenon, a mechanism, or a prospect? Towards autonomous and evolving intelligence, RSI is being claimed at many scales, while no single framework that formally describes these emerging instances exists. Its counterpart in the classical realm, iterative policy improvement, is characterized by generalized policy iteration (GPI), a framework of broad applicability with well-understood theoretical properties, but only where the update principle and the evaluation base lie outside the agent. In this paper, we propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that describes iterative policy improvement and RSI as two cases of a single learning paradigm. GAI defines the agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a system and models the learning process as a cycle of agent evaluation and agent improvement. Two pivotal dials then distinguish the instances: whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent and whether the standard it is measured against is grounded outside it. The former dial delineates the boundary between GPI and RSI, and the latter determines a system's polarity as anchored, goal drift, or fully self-referential. Moreover, we use these coordinates to place existing systems on the same two axes and make the defects of recursive self-improvement statable one condition at a time. We see this paper as a first step toward exploring a formal characterization of RSI that rests on the classical account, makes existing systems comparable, and provides a principled basis for analyzing and designing new ones.

AI.tldr: Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI) unifies iterative policy improvement (GPI) and recursive self-improvement (RSI) within a single, agent-centric learning framework. It treats an agent as a configurable configuration of modifiable components and frames learning as a cycle of evaluation and improvement. Two binary dials—whether the improving mechanism is inside the agent, and whether the evaluation standard is grounded outside—map RSI and GPI onto a two-dimensional space, clarifying polarity (anchored, goal drift, fully self-referential) and enabling cross-system comparison, analysis of RSI defects, and principled design.
AI.motivation: There is no single formal framework that captures RSI across scales. While Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI) has broad applicability in classical RL, it assumes the update principle and evaluation base lie outside the agent. The authors seek a formal, unified account that subsumes both GPI and RSI, enabling systematic analysis, comparison, and design of evolving autonomous systems.
AI.method: Propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI). Define the agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a system and model learning as a cycle of agent evaluation and agent improvement. Introduce two pivotal dials: (1) whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent (inside) vs outside (external), and (2) whether the standard for evaluation is grounded outside the agent vs internal. Use these axes to distinguish GPI from RSI and to classify systems into polarity categories (anchored, goal drift, fully self-referential). Map existing systems onto the axes to analyze RSI defects condition-by-condition.
AI.result: GAI yields a two-axis taxonomy that unifies GPI and RSI and provides a framework to place existing systems on a common plane. It makes RSI defects analyzable one condition at a time and offers a principled basis for analysis and design of new RSI-capable systems.
AI.conclusion: GAI is framed as a first formal step toward a formal RSI characterization that rests on the classical account, enabling direct comparison with GPI, and supplying a principled scaffold for analyzing and designing future autonomous, evolving agents.

title: Flip Graphs for Eight Points in Three Dimensions Are Connected
summary: We prove that every configuration of four through eight points in three-dimensional space, with no four points coplanar, has a connected full geometric flip graph under $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ flips. Every point remains fixed and present throughout the sequence. The proof brings each tetrahedralization into placing form at a convex hull vertex: the tetrahedra not incident to that vertex fill the convex hull of the remaining points. This reduction allows us to establish connectivity by induction, using the connectivity of regular tetrahedralizations. The main geometric tool is radial projection, which turns the tetrahedra incident to a hull vertex into a planar triangulation. When this planar triangulation is regular, varying its lifting heights produces legal spatial flips that progressively shrink the region occupied by the incident tetrahedra and reach placing form. Planar lifting criteria and compatibility constraints between the projections at different hull vertices resolve the remaining small cases. For eight points, at most 35 flips are needed to reach placing form.

AI.tldr: Connected full geometric flip graph for 4–8 point configurations in R^3 (no four coplanar) under 2↔3 flips; fixed points; eight-point bound of 35 flips to reach placing form.
AI.motivation: Understand connectivity of geometric flip graphs for 3D tetrahedralizations with a fixed vertex set; extend planar flip results to 3D by using a canonical placing form as the end state.
AI.method: 1) Reduce to placing form by selecting a hull vertex; 2) Radial projection maps incident tetrahedra to a planar triangulation; 3) If the planar triangulation is regular, vary lifting heights to realize legal 3D flips that shrink the incident region; 4) Use planar lifting criteria and cross-vertex compatibility to handle remaining small cases; 5) Prove connectivity by induction on point count using regular tetrahedralizations; 6) derive an explicit bound (≤35 flips) for eight points.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the full geometric flip graph is connected for configurations of 4–8 points with no four coplanar; every configuration can be transformed to placing form via 2↔3 flips with all points fixed; eight-point case requires at most 35 flips to reach placing form.
AI.conclusion: Radial projection and planar lifting are effective tools to transfer 3D flip connectivity problems to planar triangulation problems, enabling a clear inductive proof and explicit flip bounds for small point sets.

title: Physical Kernel: Structured Visual Latents for Dark Manipulation
summary: We study dark manipulation: after a brief lit Write encodes z0 = Enc(rgb), a policy pi(z) and open-loop dynamics f(z,a) complete contact-rich skills without further pixels (dark_f). On ManiSkill StackCube (n=160; seed packs 0/1000), dark_f attains 68.1% stacked on the five-rung chain (near_A -> grasped -> lifted -> on_B -> stacked), compared with 35.6% for per-step lit_reenc and 0% for freeze/encode_black. On a shared Write->HOLD protocol (n=40), occlusion and camera-aligned GT contact-neighbor masks drive lit lift from 43% to 0%, while dark_f holds 82.5%; shuffling actions inflates dynamics MSE by ~9.4x; write-time appearance shifts break encoding (night: 0% stacked), yet the same shifts during HOLD leave dark_f lift unchanged; Write length Tw is flat once the stop phase is reached, while earlier stops and write-time blur/JPEG sharply cut stacked. A dedicated pi_write reaches 35% vision-budget stacked (n=80); matched Dreamer-style/pixel nulls without privileged geom stay at 0%. Privileged state-RSSM MPC reaches ~35% stacked with 9D dark observations -- a stronger-observation null, not a matched visual baseline.

AI.tldr: Latent-state policies (dark_f) can robustly perform contact-rich manipulation with open-loop dynamics using only latent encodings, surpassing several pixel-based baselines in several tasks and under occlusion/temporal perturbations, though pixel-based or privileged-observation baselines can match stronger cases.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether manipulation tasks requiring contact can be solved in a latent space without continuous pixel input, and assess robustness to occlusion, timing shifts, and encoding perturbations across different evaluation protocols.
AI.method: Encode an RGB image to a latent z0 via Enc(rgb); a policy pi(z) operates with open-loop dynamics f(z,a) to complete skills; evaluate on ManiSkill StackCube (n=160; seeds 0/1000) and a Write->HOLD protocol (n=40). Compare against lit_reenc and freeze/encode_black baselines. Use metrics such as percentage of successful stacking across task stages (five-rung chain). Analyze effects of occlusion, GT masks, action shuffling, temporal shifts, and write-time blur/JPEG. Additional trials include a dedicated pi_write (n=80) and Privileged state-RSSM MPC (9D observations).
AI.result: dark_f achieves 68.1% stacked on the five-rung chain (near_A -> grasped -> lifted -> on_B -> stacked) vs 35.6% for per-step lit_reenc and 0% for freeze/encode_black. Under Write->HOLD, lit lift drops from 43% to 0% while dark_f maintains 82.5%; action shuffling inflates dynamics MSE ~9.4x. Write-time appearance shifts break encoding (night: 0% stacked) but HOLD shifts do not affect dark_f lifting. Write length Tw is flat after the stop phase; earlier stops and write-time blur/JPEG sharply reduce stacking. A dedicated pi_write reaches 35% vision-budget stacked (n=80); Dreamer-style/pixel nulls without privileged geometry stay at 0%. Privileged state-RSSM MPC reaches ~35% stacked with 9D dark observations, indicating a stronger-observation null relative to matched visual baselines.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space manipulation (dark_f) demonstrates robust, competitive performance on several contact-rich tasks without pixel input, outperforming several pixel-based baselines under occlusion and temporal perturbations. However, performance still lags pixel-enabled or privileged-observation baselines in certain settings; incorporating richer observations (e.g., 9D dark observations) or targeted latent representations can close the gap. Overall, latent encodings enable persistent stacking success under challenging conditions that degrade pixel-based approaches.

title: Don't Just Look, Intervene: Perturbation Based Region Labeling for VQA Images
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) should rely on visual evidence that directly determines the correct answer, but supervision for grounding visual reasoning is often expensive to obtain manually or tied to dataset-specific annotation primitives. We instead introduce model-causal visual evidence as an annotation target, defined as the set of image regions whose counterfactual intervention changes a model's answer distribution for a given image-question pair. Based on this principle, we introduce Counterfactual Search for Grounding Regions (CSGR). CSGR is a scalable pipeline that proposes candidate regions, perturbs them, measures their effect on answer sensitivity, and aggregates this evidence across multiple judges to approximate answer-critical regions in VQA data. To assess whether CSGR annotations contain a useful supervision signal, we plug them into three existing grounding-aware training routines: attention steering, Visual CoTfinetuning, and latent visual reasoning. These experiments test whether the proposed annotation scheme can provide a useful supervision signal across multiple ways of consuming region labels, rather than introducing a new way of using them. Across competing automatic region-labeling mechanisms, CSGR annotations provide the most consistent gains over Cross Entropy-only finetuning in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations, indicating that the proposed labeling scheme captures useful region-level information.

AI.tldr: Proposes model-causal visual evidence as grounding annotation via Counterfactual Search for Grounding Regions (CSGR); shows CSGR annotations improve grounding-aware VQA training across multiple schemes, with in-domain and out-of-domain gains.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of scalable grounding supervision for visual reasoning; use counterfactual perturbations to identify answer-critical regions.
AI.method: CSGR pipeline: propose candidate regions, perturb them, measure effect on answer distribution (sensitivity), aggregate across multiple judges to approximate answer-critical regions in VQA data.
AI.result: CSGR annotations yield the most consistent gains over Cross Entropy-only finetuning across in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations compared to other region-labeling methods.
AI.conclusion: Model-causal visual evidence is a useful supervision signal for grounding in VQA and can generalize across different grounding strategies; scalable region-level supervision can enhance VLM performance.

title: LLMs or Naive Bayes? Old Gems or New Ways
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to the Proceedings of Practice and Experience in Advanced Research Computing (PEARC '26), Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
summary: Large language models (LLMs) prompt a recurring question in research computing: should classical methods like Naive Bayes (NB) be retired? We benchmark Complement Naive Bayes against zero-shot and few-shot LLMs spanning four model families and a 37x range in scale (27B to a 1T-parameter mixture-of-experts) across text classification tasks. LLMs dominate only in zero-data regimes (98.0% vs 88.2% on Amazon Polarity sentiment), and even that win is contamination-prone: on a low-contamination sentiment task NB beats the zero-shot LLM (81.7% vs 73.0%). However, once labeled data is available (e.g., AG News), NB reaches 89.1% accuracy, statistically indistinguishable from the zero-shot 27B LLM (89.0%) and better than the 397B frontier model (84.8%), at thousands of samples/sec on a commodity CPU. Fine-tuned DistilBERT reaches 90.6% but at far lower throughput than NB at batch size 1 (Table 2). Our measured GPU throughput analysis shows small-LLM batched inference is 40-486x slower than NB CPU inference (the multiplier depends strongly on the host CPU), exposing a structural gap bounded by memory bandwidth, with roughly two orders of magnitude lower energy per sample. For resource-constrained HPC practitioners performing text classification with labeled data, NB remains the optimal choice. We show the decision line is task-dependent (NB reaches LLM parity around $N \sim 10^4$ labels for topic classification, while zero-data sentiment favors the LLM at all N tested) and provide a Kubernetes Helm operator that automates model selection using configurable thresholds and verifiable Prometheus metrics.

AI.tldr: Complement Naive Bayes (CNB) remains competitive with large language models (LLMs) for text classification when labeled data is available, and even matches or surpasses some LLMs in zero-shot scenarios for certain tasks, while offering far higher throughput and energy efficiency on CPU. The decision boundary is task-dependent and shifts with data size; the authors provide a Kubernetes Helm operator to automate model selection.
AI.motivation: Assess whether classical methods like NB can retire in light of powerful LLMs by benchmarking CNB against zero-shot and few-shot LLMs across a wide scale range and multiple tasks, and to quantify trade-offs in accuracy, throughput, and energy on CPU/GPU. Explore the data regimes where CNB remains advantageous in HPC contexts.
AI.method: Benchmark Complement Naive Bayes against zero-shot and few-shot LLMs spanning four model families and scales from 27B to 1T parameters (mixture-of-experts) across four text classification tasks. Evaluate on labeled data (e.g., AG News) and zero-shot/data-scarce settings (e.g., Amazon Polarity). Measure accuracy, throughput (samples/sec) on commodity CPU for CNB and on GPUs for LLMs, including energy per sample. Compare against fine-tuned DistilBERT and report a task-dependent decision boundary (e.g., NB parity at N ~ 10^4 for topic classification). Provide a Kubernetes Helm operator to automate model selection with thresholds and Prometheus metrics.
AI.result: LLMs dominate zero-shot performance in several tasks (e.g., Amazon Polarity: 98.0% vs 88.2% for CNB–though contaminated results show NB beating a zero-shot LLM on a low-contamination sentiment task: 81.7% vs 73.0%). With labeled data (AG News), CNB reaches 89.1%, statistically indistinguishable from zero-shot 27B LLM (89.0%), and outperforms the 397B model (84.8%). DistilBERT achieves 90.6% but at far lower throughput than CNB on CPU. GPU throughput for small LLMs is 40–486x slower than CNB CPU inference, leading to ~100x higher energy per sample. NB delivers thousands of samples/sec on commodity CPU. The decision boundary is task-dependent: NB parity around N ~ 10^4 labels for topic classification; zero-shot sentiment favors LLM across tested N. A Helm operator automates model selection with configurable thresholds and Prometheus metrics.
AI.conclusion: For resource-constrained HPC practitioners with labeled data, CNB remains optimal. The study emphasizes a task-dependent choice between CNB and LLMs, with practical implications for throughput and energy efficiency. It also provides a deployable tooling artifact (Helm operator) to automate model selection based on thresholds.

title: Vibe Patenting: Evaluating LLM Judges for Professional Patent-Drafting Agents
summary: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate and improve AI-generated outputs, yet their reliability for complex professional work remains unclear. We study this problem through Vibe Patenting, an end-to-end patent-drafting testbed for AI-agent evaluation. A separately-invoked LLM judge evaluates generated patent drafts and provides structured feedback for iterative revision. Across multiple inventions and drafting-agent configurations, judge-guided revision consistently improves judge-assessed quality, while unguided revision tends to saturate. Notably, iterative judge feedback enables a low-reasoning agent to approach the performance of a substantially more expensive high-reasoning agent. Stronger models and increased reasoning generally improve judge-assessed drafting quality, while domain-specific agentic workflows provide further gains. We validate the judge against independent evaluation by a professional patent attorney and find meaningful but strongly metric-dependent agreement and systematic calibration differences. These results highlight both the utility and limitations of LLM judges as evaluators and optimization signals for complex professional workflows.

AI.tldr: LLM judges can guide iterative patent drafting and improve output quality, with judge-guided revisions outperforming unguided edits; iterative feedback lets simpler agents rival more expensive ones; stronger models and domain-specific workflows help; evaluation agreement with professionals exists but is metric-dependent and calibration-sensitive, highlighting utility and limitations of LLM judges as evaluators and optimization signals.
AI.motivation: Assess reliability and utility of LLM-based judges as evaluators for complex professional tasks, here patent drafting, and understand how judge feedback shapes iterative improvements and agent performance.
AI.method: End-to-end patent-drafting testbed (Vibe Patenting) where a separately invoked LLM judge evaluates drafts and provides structured feedback for iterative revision. Compare judge-guided vs unguided revisions across multiple inventions and drafting-agent configurations; vary model strength, reasoning depth, and domain workflows; validate against a professional patent attorney.
AI.result: Judge-guided revisions consistently improve judge-assessed drafting quality; unguided revisions saturate. Iterative judge feedback enables a low-reasoning agent to approach the performance of a substantially more expensive high-reasoning agent. Stronger models and increased reasoning generally improve quality; domain-specific workflows provide additional gains. Judge-agreement with the attorney is meaningful but metric-dependent and calibration differs.
AI.conclusion: LLM judges are useful evaluators and optimization signals for complex professional workflows but have limitations, including metric-dependence and calibration differences. The results support deploying judge feedback to drive iterative improvements while acknowledging evaluation variability and the need for human benchmarking.

title: Low-Dimensional Embeddings for Gaussian Kernels on Manifolds
summary: The Gaussian kernel is a widely used similarity measure underlying kernel methods such as kernel PCA and spectral clustering, but computing Gaussian kernel distances for many pairs of points can be expensive. Using Random Fourier Features (RFF), Chen and Phillips [ALT 2017] showed that for points in a $d$-dimensional Euclidean ball in ${\mathbb R}^N$, $t=Ω((d/\varepsilon^2)\log(dR/\varepsilon))$ features suffice to preserve all pairwise Gaussian kernel distances within a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ factor with high probability. We establish a uniform relative-error embedding theorem for the more general setting of an arbitrary positive-reach submanifold $\mathcal M\subset{\mathbb R}^N$ of intrinsic dimension $d$. We show that $t=O((d/\varepsilon^2)\log(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal M)^2N^{2d}/(\operatorname{vol}(B_1^d(0))^2\operatorname{rch}(\mathcal M)^{2d}\varepsilon^{2d+1}δ)))$, or approximately $O((d^2/\varepsilon^2)(\log N+\log(1/(\varepsilonδ))))$, RFFs suffice, with probability $1-δ$, to preserve the Gaussian kernel distance between every pair of manifold points up to relative error $\varepsilon$. Thus the bound depends only logarithmically on the ambient dimension and on manifold parameters such as volume and reach, while retaining the $1/\varepsilon^2$ Euclidean rate. We also prove a topological consequence: under the same RFF embedding, persistent homology is preserved in the sense that weighted Cech and Rips filtrations built from Gaussian kernel power distance are $(1\pm\varepsilon_\star)$-interleaved, where $\varepsilon_\star$ accounts for both distance distortion and kernel-weight approximation.

AI.tldr: Random Fourier Features (RFF) are extended from Euclidean balls to arbitrary positive-reach submanifolds. The authors show a uniform relative-error embedding for Gaussian kernel distances requiring t = roughly O((d/ε^2) log(...)) features, with probability 1−δ, where d is intrinsic dimension and the log-term depends on manifold volume, reach, and ambient dimension. They also prove that Gaussian-kernel-based filtrations (weighted Čech/Rips) are (1±ε_*)-interleaved, preserving persistent homology.
AI.motivation: To reduce the cost of computing Gaussian kernel distances in kernel methods when data lie on low-dimensional manifolds, by generalizing prior RFF bounds from Euclidean balls to manifolds and establishing topological stability.
AI.method: Derive uniform relative-error embedding bounds for Random Fourier Features in the setting of a positive-reach submanifold M ⊂ R^N of intrinsic dimension d. Obtain the feature count t = O((d/ε^2) log(vol(M)^2 N^{2d} /(vol(B_1^d)^2 rch(M)^{2d} ε^{2d+1} δ))). Show that with probability at least 1−δ, all pairwise Gaussian distances on M are preserved within (1±ε). Prove a topological consequence: weighted Cech and Rips filtrations based on Gaussian kernel power distance are (1±ε_*)-interleaved, preserving persistent homology.
AI.result: A uniform relative-error embedding result for Gaussian kernel distances on manifolds using RFF, with feature count t ≈ O((d^2/ε^2)(log N+log(1/(εδ)))) and high-probability guarantees. Topological persistence is preserved up to an ε_*-level interleaving.
AI.conclusion: RFF-based Gaussian kernel embeddings extend to manifolds with positive reach, yielding scalable guarantees where ambient dimension affects only logarithmically, governed by intrinsic dimension and manifold geometry (volume, reach). The topological invariants inferred from Gaussian-kernel filtrations remain stable under the embedding, enabling reliable kernel-based learning and topological data analysis on manifold-valued data.

title: Conflict-Predictive Variable Horizons in Multi-Drone Distributed Model Predictive Control
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, is already submitted to IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics as journal-paper (current status "under review"). I think this is again more eess.SY, but also if my last paper is published there, i am still not allowed to use that category, please decide for yourself
summary: In distributed model predictive control for multi-drone collision avoidance, a fixed prediction horizon forces a compromise: a short horizon is inexpensive but reacts late to approaching neighbors, whereas a long one anticipates conflicts at a per-step cost that grows superlinearly with its length. We propose a conflict-predictive variable horizon that each drone sets locally, leaving the distributed model predictive control itself unchanged. From a short history of observed positions, a drone extrapolates the flight lines of its neighbors, tests each against its own using confidence funnels that narrow with prediction range, and obtains each time to conflict in closed form. The horizon is then the smallest admissible value whose planning window covers the farthest predicted conflict. It collapses to its minimum in clear airspace and grows only when a conflict lies ahead.
