AI.method: Introduce OrchSLM as a routing framework that unifies existing non-interactive orchestration methods and treats their design choices as controllable parameters. Use OrchSLM as a systematic probe to examine how orchestration behavior emerges from task structure, model-pool composition, and multi-agent consensus.
AI.result: Shows that orchestration behavior emerges from diverse knobs; reveals how task structure, pool composition, and consensus shape routing decisions and the effectiveness of cached-sample orchestration.
AI.conclusion: OrchSLM provides a principled, modular framework to analyze and design non-interactive orchestration of heterogeneous SLMs, offering actionable insights into managing trade-offs among performance, cost, and privacy in agentic pipelines.

title: Bridging Thought and Action: Taming Long-Horizon Instability in Open-Source LLM Agents with a MetaTool-Enhanced ROS Framework
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems (TCDS)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled more natural human-robot interaction, but open-source models often exhibit unstable long-horizon reasoning and inefficient action execution when deployed in agentic robotic frameworks. This paper presents an enhanced ROS-Agent based architecture that improves task reliability and execution efficiency for agentic robotic systems using open-source LLMs. The proposed system introduces a novel intermediate mechanism, termed the MetaTool, which enforces structured planning prior to action execution. Given a natural-language command, the MetaTool induces the LLM to generate a pseudo-code plan of intended tool invocations, which is stored in the ROS-Agent's scratchpad and persists throughout execution. By explicitly separating planning from execution, the proposed approach reduces execution loops and improves deterministic behavior. The architecture is validated on a custom mobile robotic platform with multimodal perception and motion control capabilities. Experimental results on real-world interactive tasks demonstrate improved task completion and contextual consistency, with up to ~24% gains on complex tasks compared to the baseline framework.

AI.tldr: ROS-Agent architecture with MetaTool enforcing planning-before-execution via a pseudo-code tool plan stored in a scratchpad; improves reliability and efficiency; demo shows up to ~24% gains on complex tasks vs baseline.
AI.motivation: Open-source LLMs in robotics often suffer unstable long-horizon reasoning and inefficient action loops; separating planning from execution can improve determinism and task success.
AI.method: Introduce MetaTool within an enhanced ROS-Agent. Given a natural-language command, MetaTool prompts the LLM to generate a pseudo-code plan of intended tool invocations, stored in the scratchpad and persisted during execution; execution follows the plan, reducing execution loops; validated on a custom mobile robot with multimodal perception and motion control.
AI.result: Improved task completion and contextual consistency; up to ~24% gains on complex tasks relative to the baseline framework.
AI.conclusion: Explicit planning via MetaTool enhances reliability, efficiency, and determinism in agentic robotics using open-source LLMs by separating planning from execution.

title: Pixel-wise Planarity for High-Precision Monocular Plane Segmentation
comment: To appear at ECCV 2026. Code available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/PixelwisePlanarity
summary: Plane segmentation from a single RGB image remains challenging due to imprecise region grouping and geometrically inconsistent supervision, often leading to over-segmentation and false planar detections. We propose instead a pixel-wise planarity prediction framework for robust monocular plane segmentation. Building on a pretrained monocular geometric backbone predicting depth and surface normals, we introduce a dedicated planarity head that estimates per-pixel planarity confidence. During inference, predicted depth, normals, and planarity are combined in a lightweight region-growing procedure that enforces geometric consistency when forming plane segments. We further analyze existing plane ground-truth annotations and demonstrate substantial geometric inconsistencies under strict distance thresholds. Across multiple datasets, our method achieves improved geometric precision and segmentation quality compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches, while improving computational efficiency. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/PixelwisePlanarity.

AI.tldr: Pixelwise planarity prediction for monocular plane segmentation using a dedicated planarity head on top of a depth+normal backbone; combines depth, normals, and per-pixel planarity confidence in a lightweight region-growing step to enforce geometric consistency, achieving improved geometric precision and efficiency; includes ground-truth geometric inconsistency analysis.
AI.motivation: Monocular plane segmentation is prone to imprecise region grouping and geometrically inconsistent supervision, causing over-segmentation and false planes. A per-pixel planarity estimate with a geometry-aware inference could improve segmentation quality and robustness.
AI.method: Utilize a pretrained monocular backbone that predicts depth and surface normals. Add a planarity head that outputs per-pixel planarity confidence. During inference, fuse depth, normals, and planarity to perform a lightweight region-growing procedure that enforces geometric consistency to form plane segments.
AI.result: Outperforms prior state-of-the-art in geometric precision and segmentation quality across multiple datasets while being more computationally efficient. The authors also analyze ground-truth annotations and reveal substantial geometric inconsistencies under strict distance thresholds.
AI.conclusion: A pixel-wise planarity prediction framework with a planarity confidence head and geometry-aware region-growing yields robust monocular plane segmentation, improving accuracy and efficiency. Code and models are publicly available.

title: Discovering and Preserving Category Correlation Knowledge via Adaptive Reciprocal Knowledge Distillation
comment: Accepted by 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Knowledge distillation aims to improve the performance of lightweight student models by transferring knowledge from larger and more powerful teacher models. However, a substantial size gap between teacher and student models often impedes effective knowledge transfer. Most existing approaches adopt a static, one-way teacher-to-student distillation paradigm, which overlooks the dynamic nature of student learning and fails to provide targeted guidance on hard samples. In this paper, we propose adaptive reciprocal knowledge distillation (AR-KD), a novel method that improves knowledge transfer by simplifying the teacher's output distribution. Specifically, AR-KD performs reciprocal adaptation on the teacher by matching its class correlation matrix to the student's relational representation, which reshapes the teacher's prediction structure to better suit the student's capacity. This relational alignment mitigates the collapse of inter-class dark knowledge caused by overconfident teachers, enabling the student to learn from richer and more compatible supervisory signals. We evaluate AR-KD on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k classification datasets, where it outperforms state-of-the-art knowledge distillation baselines. Specifically, AR-KD improves student performance across homogeneous and heterogeneous setups: up to 7.13% accuracy gain for students, 1.42% to 4.15% higher than vanilla KD on average, and further improvements when integrated with other advanced methods. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ARKD/.

AI.tldr: Adaptive reciprocal knowledge distillation (AR-KD) aligns the teacher's class correlations with the student's relational representation to simplify teacher outputs, enabling better knowledge transfer across large teacher–student gaps and yielding strong gains on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k.
AI.motivation: To address inefficiencies in static one-way KD when teacher–student capacity gaps are large and the teacher’s overconfident outputs collapse inter-class dark knowledge, hindering transfer of useful information to the student.
AI.method: Reciprocal adaptation by matching the teacher's class correlation matrix to the student's relational representation, effectively reshaping the teacher's output distribution to be more compatible with the student’s capacity; evaluated on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k, with improvements in both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings.
AI.result: AR-KD outperforms state-of-the-art KD baselines, achieving up to 7.13% accuracy gain for students, and 1.42%–4.15% higher than vanilla KD on average; further gains when integrated with other advanced methods; code released.
AI.conclusion: Relational alignment between teacher and student via AR-KD mitigates collapse of inter-class dark knowledge from overconfident teachers, enabling richer, more compatible supervisory signals and effective knowledge transfer across varying model capacities.

title: Grounded Adjudication of Variations across Extracted TimeLines (GAVEL): Comparing Clinical Timelines Against Their Case Reports
summary: Existing pipelines for clinical timeline extraction from case reports are evaluated using an expert reference and are limited by imperfect reference annotations and imprecise event alignment. We developed GAVEL, an LLM judge protocol that compares two timelines with the case report and returns a discrepancy type, verdict, and report passage for each difference. We evaluated the event matcher, reviewed 2,738 findings from GPT5.6sol and DeepSeek V3.2, ranked six LLM extractors and two human annotators, and tested GAVEL guided merging. True match rates were 60% immediately below and 48% immediately above the 0.10 cutoff. Manual review confirmed 89.4% and 88.6% of findings. Across 126 reports, merged timelines were preferred in 77.0% of comparisons (95% CI, 69.8 to 84.1%) and reduced discrepancies attributed to the evaluated timeline from 7.63 to 0.85 per report. GAVEL supports report-based comparison and revision without treating either timeline as ground truth.

AI.tldr: GAVEL is an LLM judge protocol for comparing two clinical timelines against case reports, reporting discrepancy type, verdict, and relevant passage per difference; it merges timelines to reduce discrepancies without assuming a ground truth.
AI.motivation: To address imperfect reference annotations and imprecise event alignment in clinical timeline extraction from case reports, enabling robust timeline revision and comparison.
AI.method: Evaluate an event matcher; audit 2,738 findings from multiple LLM extractors; compare two pipelines with GAVEL-guided merging across 126 reports; measure discrepancy reduction and user preference.
AI.result: GAVEL yields 60% true matches just below and 48% just above a 0.10 cutoff; manual review supports 89.4% and 88.6% finding accuracy; merged timelines preferred in 77.0% of comparisons, reducing discrepancies per report from 7.63 to 0.85.
AI.conclusion: GAVEL enables report-based comparison and revision of timelines without ground truth, improving consistency and preferability of merged timelines.

title: Chance-Constrained Belief-Space Maneuver Planning for Autonomous Collision Avoidance Under Uncertainty
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables, Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies (AMOS) Conference 2026
summary: Increasing conjunction frequency in low Earth orbit places growing pressure on spacecraft operators to determine not only whether an encounter requires mitigation, but whether sufficient information is available to commit to a maneuver. This work formulates this information-action tradeoff as a belief-space planning problem for conjunctions between a maneuverable spacecraft and an unmaneuverable secondary object. The planner represents the uncertain orbital states as Gaussian beliefs and uses a chance-constrained belief-space Monte Carlo tree search framework to reason over possible future tracking updates before time of closest approach (TCA). A terminal chance constraint limits the probability of reaching TCA above a prescribed collision-risk threshold, allowing the planner to wait for informative tracking while intervening when deferral becomes too risky. We evaluate the approach on eight historical conjunctions from NASA's Conjunction Assessment Risk Analysis dataset. By varying the secondary-object measurement quality and tracking cadence, we generate a total of 96 distinct evaluation scenarios. Across the evaluated conditions, the planner reaches TCA without maneuvering in approximately 40% of episodes while maintaining no terminal collision-risk violations. In contrast, fixed-time rule-based maneuver policies resolve more encounters without maneuvering when intervention is deferred closer to TCA, but at the expense of increasing terminal risk violations. The fraction of episodes reaching TCA without maneuvering depends strongly on tracking quality and measurement cadence, ranging from 76% under accurate, frequent measurements to approximately 18%-20% under the poorest tracking conditions. These results show that tracking quality and frequency are not only inputs to collision-risk estimation: they can determine when intervention becomes necessary.

AI.tldr: Belief-space planning with chance-constrained MCTS for conjunctions in LEO; evaluates information-update vs maneuvering trade-off; tracking quality critically affects safe deferral.
AI.motivation: Address the information-action tradeoff in conjunction mitigation under uncertainty by deciding when to wait for informative tracking versus intervene, within a principled risk framework.
AI.method: Gaussian-belief state representation; chance-constrained belief-space Monte Carlo Tree Search; terminal collision risk constraint; evaluation on NASA CA Risk Analysis data across 96 scenarios with varying tracking quality and cadence.
AI.result: Planner reaches TCA without maneuvering in ~40% of episodes with zero terminal collision risk violations; fixed-time policies defer interventions near TCA but incur higher terminal risk; deferral efficacy scales with tracking quality (76% to ~18-20%).
AI.conclusion: Tracking quality and frequency are central to collision-risk estimation and intervention timing; the approach offers a rigorous mechanism to delay maneuvering when informative updates are expected and to intervene when risk becomes unacceptable.

title: Evaluation of MLLM-Agnostic Plug-and-Play Keyframe Selection Methods for Long Video Understanding
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot process every frame of a long video because of limitations in visual-token and computational budgets. Three primary approaches have been proposed to enhance their long-video understanding capabilities: (i) Retraining an MLLM on a large video corpus and/or extending its input length; (ii) Training an adapter for a specific MLLM that takes the entire video and the query as input and selects the most relevant video frames; and (iii) Developing a training-free, plug-and-play (PaP) adapter that is MLLM-agnostic. We refer to the third approach as PaP keyframe selection. A PaP method may use only candidate video frames without considering the query, or it may use both candidate video frames and the query. The first approach is prohibitively expensive. The second approach requires substantial training time and computational resources, but it is accessible to many because an adapter contains significantly fewer trainable parameters than an entire MLLM. The third approach has the lowest computational cost and is therefore broadly accessible. To the best of our knowledge, only five PaP methods have been reported within the past year. All of these methods have been evaluated on one or more video question-answering benchmarks and have demonstrated improvements in long-video understanding. However, the methods were evaluated on different benchmarks using different MLLMs. We present a comprehensive evaluation of these five methods using three MLLMs across three long-video understanding benchmarks. Our results show that QAaF achieves the best performance in 13 of the 15 aggregate evaluation settings, while FOCUS ranks second overall. These results provide a common experimental reference for comparing training-free keyframe-selection methods for MLLMs.

AI.tldr: Training-free keyframe selection methods for long-video MLLMs are comprehensively evaluated across three MLLMs and three benchmarks; QAaF dominates (13/15 wins), with FOCUS second, establishing a common reference for comparison.
AI.motivation: MLLMs struggle with long videos due to visual-token and compute constraints; training-free keyframe selection offers a scalable, model-agnostic solution that avoids costly retraining or heavy adapters.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of five PaP keyframe-selection methods (including QAaF and FOCUS) across three MLLMs and three long-video QA benchmarks, standardizing experimental settings to compare performance.
AI.result: QAaF achieves the best performance in 13 of 15 aggregate settings; FOCUS ranks second overall, indicating strong and consistent gains across models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified benchmark and reference for training-free keyframe-selection methods; QAaF emerges as a leading method, highlighting the viability of PaP adapters for long-video understanding and the need for standardized evaluation protocols.

title: Criticality in Dissimilar Decomposition and Undersampling of Random Datasets with Anomalies
summary: Training datasets for upcoming LLMs would include a significant amount of AI text/image data generated from current LLMs. In such a scenario, it is important to understand how this affects batch decompositions and thereby, the performance of the resultant new LLM. In this paper, we consider AI generated data as anomalies ``linked" to main data points and study decomposition and undersampling properties of the overall random dataset. We use redundancy graphs and iteration techniques to obtain bounds for the minimum size of a strongly dissimilar (SD) decomposition and demonstrate a phase transition phenomena, wherein the minimum size is essentially determined by the \emph{main} data points when the number of anomalies is small and is ``taken" over by the anomalies above a certain threshold. We also establish a size criticality result for the strong similarity of a randomly undersampled dataset and illustrate our results with examples involving categorical datasets, whose overall space size is much larger than the size of the dataset.

AI.tldr: AI-generated data in training sets acts as anomalies affecting SD decomposition and undersampling; a phase transition occurs where deviation hinges on main data vs anomalies; bounds via redundancy graphs; illustrated on high-cardinality categorical data.
AI.motivation: To understand how AI-generated data within training corpora influences data decomposition, undersampling properties, and ultimately LLM performance.
AI.method: Model data with redundancy graphs; apply iterative decomposition to bound the minimum strongly dissimilar (SD) decomposition size; analyze phase transition in dominance between main data points and anomalies; derive size criticality for strong similarity under random undersampling; provide categorical dataset examples with large space sizes.
AI.result: Derived bounds on the minimum SD decomposition size; demonstrated a phase transition in which anomalies dominate the decomposition size beyond a threshold; established a size criticality result for strong similarity under undersampling; illustrated concepts with high-cardinality categorical data examples.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated data can disproportionately affect decomposition and undersampling behavior in training datasets; the identified phase transition and size criticality have implications for data curation and model robustness during iterative training of future LLMs.

title: Token Efficient Task Execution via Application Behavior Modeling for Web Agents
summary: The strong performance of AI Agents across an impressive variety of tasks is driving an unprecedented investment in agentic infrastructures, however the cost of processing tokens is fast increasing. Web agents automate the execution of web-application tasks described in natural language, by analyzing the web-application's user interface (UI) and interacting with it. This work introduces OdoBot, a novel web-agent architecture that completes tasks at a fraction of the cost when compared to conventional web agents. This is achieved by leveraging a behavioral model of the underlying application constructed by analyzing successful task-execution demonstrations. Our experiments with 45 tasks on the Canvas Learning Management System (LMS) demonstrate that OdoBot uses 44% and 80% fewer tokens than two state-of-the-art competitor agents (Agent-E and WebVoyager), while also surpassing WebVoyager in terms of task success rate.

AI.tldr: OdoBot, a web-agent architecture, reduces token cost by leveraging a behavioral model learned from successful task demonstrations, achieving substantially lower token usage than Agent-E and WebVoyager and higher task success on 45 Canvas LMS tasks.
AI.motivation: To address the rising token-processing costs of AI agents in web automation and improve efficiency without sacrificing success rates.
AI.method: Build a behavioral model of the target application from successful task-execution demonstrations and integrate it into a web-agent (OdoBot) that analyzes the UI and interacts to complete tasks at lower token cost.
AI.result: On 45 Canvas LMS tasks, OdoBot uses 44% fewer tokens than Agent-E and 80% fewer tokens than WebVoyager, while surpassing WebVoyager in task success rate.
AI.conclusion: A demonstration-based behavioral-model web agent can substantially reduce token costs while maintaining or improving task success, indicating a promising direction for cost-efficient web automation.

title: STAGE: Diagnosing Semantic Transfer at Grounded Execution in Embodied Agents
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. 24 pages, 7 figures
summary: Embodied language grounding requires more than identifying the referent of an instruction: recovered semantics must also control the action an agent exposes. We study this missing link as a semantic-action gap, where instruction semantics are recoverable but weakly expressed in native continuous actions. We introduce SAT-Bench, a fixed-observation counterfactual benchmark that holds the visual scene and agent state fixed while changing only instruction semantics. On LIBERO target-name and pixel-grounded relation swaps, target recovery reaches 100.0% and 95.8%, whereas OpenVLA action sensitivity remains only 6.8% and 7.7%. The gap persists across 1,000 additional compositional and temporal/procedural counterfactuals, with overall action sensitivity of 6.1%. Hidden-state, threshold-free, cross-policy, and rollout diagnostics further support this semantic-action transfer failure. We introduce VISA, a lightweight execution-time interface that converts recovered semantics into ALLOW, DEFER, target-consistency, and verified-selection decisions. VISA reduces invalid-instruction blind execution from 92.7% to 2.8% while preserving 94.0% of normal commands, and verified selection further improves target-consistent action exposure without updating the underlying policy. Overall, embodied language evaluation should measure semantic-action transfer, not semantic parsing alone.

AI.tldr: Identifies a semantic-action gap in embodied language grounding and introduces SAT-Bench and VISA to evaluate/bridge semantics to action; results show high semantic recovery but low action sensitivity, and substantial improvement in preventing invalid executions with minimal policy updates.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate semantic parsing or target identification but not how recovered semantics translate into concrete actions. The authors argue that true embodied grounding requires semantic-to-action transfer, and that measuring this transfer is essential for reliable agent behavior.
AI.method: Introduce SAT-Bench, a fixed-observation counterfactual benchmark that keeps scene and state constant while varying instruction semantics across LIBERO target-name and pixel-grounded relation swaps. Report target-recovery and action-sensitivity metrics, plus diagnostics (hidden-state, cross-policy, rollout). Develop VISA, a lightweight execution-time interface converting recovered semantics into decisions (ALLOW, DEFER, target-consistency, verified-selection) to reduce invalid blind executions without changing the underlying policy.
AI.result: On LIBERO tasks, target recovery reaches 100.0% and 95.8%, while OpenVLA action sensitivity remains only 6.8% and 7.7%. Across 1,000 additional counterfactuals, overall action sensitivity is 6.1%. Diagnostics support semantic-action transfer failure. VISA reduces invalid-instruction blind execution from 92.7% to 2.8% and preserves 94.0% of normal commands; verified selection further improves target-consistent action exposure without policy updates.
AI.conclusion: Embodied language evaluation should quantify semantic-action transfer, not just semantic parsing; SAT-Bench and VISA offer a practical framework to diagnose and mitigate the semantic-action gap and improve safe, reliable instruction execution.

title: Preserving Subject-Clarity in Image Outpainting with Multiscale Wavelet Supervision
summary: Commercial and advertising images are frequently affected by poor framing, partially cropped subjects, truncated text or logos, and insufficient context, all of which can reduce subject clarity, i.e., the ability of an image to clearly communicate its primary subject. Image outpainting offers a scalable solution by extending image boundaries and recovering missing content and context. However, existing diffusion-based outpainting methods often produce visually plausible completions while degrading subject fidelity through structural inconsistencies, semantic drift, or loss of fine-grained detail. To address this limitation, we propose a subject clarity outpainting framework that combines vision-language model (VLM)-guided semantic conditioning with multiscale wavelet supervision for subject-localized detail preservation. To support training, we develop a subject-centric data curation pipeline that constructs subject-intersecting outpainting pairs from advertising and natural images. The resulting objective introduces no additional inference cost and is designed to be compatible with diffusion-based backbones. Across four advertising and natural-image benchmarks, our method improves subject clarity, reducing subject-centered DreamSim error and FID on average by 3.0% and 2.4% over matched supervised fine-tuning, and by 10.8% and 7.7% over the strongest state-of-the-art approach per dataset, respectively.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based outpainting method enhances subject clarity by using VLM-guided semantic conditioning and multiscale wavelet supervision, with a subject-centric data pipeline; it improves subject clarity metrics over fine-tuning and SOTA without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Commercial and advertising imagery suffer from framing, cropped subjects, and incomplete context, which reduces subject clarity. Existing diffusion-based outpainting can preserve plausibility but harms subject fidelity; there is a need for a method that maintains fine-grained subject details and alignment.
AI.method: Proposes a subject clarity outpainting framework that combines vision-language model-guided semantic conditioning with multiscale wavelet supervision to preserve subject-localized detail. Introduces a subject-centric data curation pipeline to construct subject-intersecting outpainting pairs from advertising and natural images. The objective adds no inference cost and is compatible with diffusion backbones.
AI.result: Across four advertising and natural-image benchmarks, the method reduces subject-centered DreamSim error by 3.0% and FID by 2.4% over matched supervised fine-tuning, and by 10.8% and 7.7% over the strongest state-of-the-art per dataset, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The framework improves subject clarity in diffusion-based outpainting without increasing inference cost, and demonstrates robust gains across both advertising and natural-image domains.

title: Do Tabular Foundation Models Still Need Feature Engineering?
summary: Feature engineering has long been a cornerstone of tabular machine learning. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are pretrained on a wide range of tabular datasets and applied via in-context learning. Their rise raises a natural question: does manual feature construction still matter as these models become more capable? To answer this, we perform a controlled study across several versions of two major TFM families, testing a wide range of existing feature engineering techniques on benchmark datasets from TabArena. We find a consistent pattern: feature engineering gains are concentrated in earlier model generations and become negligible for the strongest models. These results suggest that stronger TFMs depend less on explicitly engineered input representations. In a complementary experiment, however, adding in-context information from related datasets still improves performance. Our findings indicate a shift in the source of performance gains for stronger TFMs: re-representing existing inputs becomes less effective, while providing additional task-relevant context remains beneficial.

AI.tldr: As tabular foundation models improve, manual feature engineering becomes less impactful, while context from related datasets remains beneficial.
AI.motivation: Assess whether explicit feature engineering retains value across generations of TFMs on tabular tasks.
AI.method: Controlled study across several versions of two major TFM families; evaluate many feature engineering techniques on TabArena benchmarks; also test adding in-context information from related datasets.
AI.result: Feature engineering gains are concentrated in earlier model generations and vanish for the strongest models; in-context information from related datasets provides performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Stronger TFMs rely less on engineered input representations; gains shift from re-representation to contextual information; practical implication: focus on providing task-relevant context to TFMs rather than extensive feature engineering for top models.

title: Fraglingo: Molecular Design via Attachment-Aware Autoregressive Fragment Generation
summary: Molecular design is most effective when generation mirrors the edits chemists actually make: extending a scaffold, replacing a substituent, or decorating a scaffold at a specified attachment site while optimizing molecular properties. Fragment-based molecular design naturally supports this workflow, yet existing approaches often separate fragment selection from attachment prediction, first choosing a fragment from a fixed vocabulary and then predicting how it should be connected. This decoupling restricts generation to a closed fragment vocabulary and treats attachment as a separate prediction problem. We introduce Fraglingo, an autoregressive fragment-based molecular generator that jointly models fragment identity and attachment in a continuous latent space. Fraglingo predicts an attachment-aware fragment embedding and retrieves the next fragment through latent-space nearest-neighbor search. To encode attachment context, we introduce a wildcard-anchored readout that represents the growing molecule from the perspective of its active attachment site, enabling the predicted embedding to capture both the molecular context and the required attachment. Because generation operates in a continuous embedding space rather than over fixed fragment identifiers, new fragments can be added to the inference-time vocabulary without retraining, provided their embeddings can be computed by the trained fragment encoder. This retrieval-based formulation provides a unified generation primitive for molecule generation, scaffold generation, scaffold decoration, and molecular optimization. On controlled property-conditional benchmarks, Fraglingo achieves stronger joint property control than comparably trained baselines while maintaining competitive validity, uniqueness, and novelty. Furthermore, Fraglingo generalizes to fragment libraries up to 4x larger than those used during training without retraining.

AI.tldr: Fraglingo is an autoregressive fragment-based molecular generator that jointly models fragment identity and attachment in a continuous latent space, enabling attachment-aware embeddings and latent-space retrieval to generate molecules, scaffolds, or decorations with scalable vocabulary and improved joint property control.
AI.motivation: To overcome decoupled fragment selection and attachment in fragment-based design, which limits vocabulary and joint optimization; aims for a unified, scalable generation primitive.
AI.method: An autoregressive model operating in a continuous embedding space; predicts an attachment-aware fragment embedding and retrieves the next fragment via latent-space nearest-neighbor search; uses a wildcard-anchored readout to encode context from the active attachment site; allows adding new fragments at inference time if their embeddings can be computed by the trained encoder; a retrieval-based generation primitive for scaffold generation, decoration, and molecular optimization.
AI.result: On controlled property-conditional benchmarks, Fraglingo achieves stronger joint property control than comparably trained baselines while maintaining competitive validity, uniqueness, and novelty; generalizes to fragment libraries up to 4x larger than those used during training without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Fraglingo presents a unified, scalable fragment-based generation framework that uses continuous embeddings and retrieval to integrate fragment identity and attachment, enabling dynamic vocabulary growth and robust property optimization across scaffold generation tasks.

title: Constraint-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Variable Impedance Control in Contact-Rich Robotic Insertion
summary: In robotic insertion under uncertain contact, the axial force limit and the appropriate controller gain vary across tasks. As a result, a single fixed gain is unlikely to remain suitable across different task conditions, making conventional impedance controllers reliant on manual retuning. To eliminate manual retuning, we propose Constraint-Grounded Reinforcement Learning (CG-RL), a variable impedance framework for online gain adaptation. Conditioned on the force limit and contact feedback, the policy outputs a residual motion, an insertion rate, and a requested gain. The controller projects this gain into the admissible range without exposing the range itself to the policy. This separation allows a single policy to operate under different force limits without retraining or manual retuning. We evaluate CG-RL on simulated oblique insertion across five training seeds. CG-RL achieves an $85.8\pm7.7\%$ (mean $\pm$ SD) success rate of insertions without violating the force limit, while keeping the applied gain within the admissible range. As a comparison, a fixed-gain baseline using the midpoint gain achieves a success rate of $50.1\%$. The policy adapts its insertion rate continuously to the specified force limit and further generalizes to more permissive force limits above the training range. In contrast, the same actor without force-limit input does not exhibit this adaptation. The applied gain is guaranteed to remain within the admissible range, while force-limit satisfaction is validated empirically rather than guaranteed formally.

AI.tldr: Constraint-Grounded Reinforcement Learning (CG-RL) for online gain adaptation in robotic insertion under uncertain contact. A policy conditioned on force limits and contact feedback outputs residual motion, insertion rate, and a requested gain, which is projected into the admissible range to avoid exposing the range to the policy. Demonstrates improved insertion success (85.8% ±7.7%) over a fixed-gain baseline (50.1%), with the policy adapting insertion rate to force limits and generalizing to higher force limits. Gains stay within bounds; force-limit satisfaction is empirically validated rather than formally guaranteed.
AI.motivation: Axial force limits and optimal controller gains vary across tasks in robotic insertion under uncertain contact. A fixed gain necessitates manual retuning. The aim is to automatically adapt impedance gains online to diverse task conditions without manual retuning.
AI.method: CG-RL framework conditioned on force limit and contact feedback. The policy outputs a residual motion, an insertion rate, and a requested gain. The gain is projected into the admissible range (not exposed to the policy). A single policy operates across different force limits without retraining. Evaluated on simulated oblique insertions across five training seeds.
AI.result: CG-RL achieves 85.8% ± 7.7% success rate without violating force limit, outperforming a fixed-gain baseline at 50.1%. The policy continuously adapts insertion rate to force limits and generalizes to more permissive force limits beyond training. The actor without force-limit input fails to adapt. The applied gain remains within the admissible range; force-limit satisfaction is evidenced empirically.
AI.conclusion: A single policy with gain projection can handle varying force limits without retraining, ensuring the gain stays within admissible bounds. The approach improves insertion success under uncertain contact and eliminates manual retuning, though force-limit satisfaction is supported empirically rather than formally guaranteed.

title: (How) Do MLLMs Report Bistable Images Like Humans?
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 31 pages, 46 figures, 2 tables
summary: Bistable images such as the duck-rabbit are classic stimuli in which one image supports multiple mutually incompatible interpretations, typically reported one at a time in humans. We ask whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show similar report behavior and what internal computations support it. Using the LLaVA family, we study two tractable dimensions: modulability, whether reports can be biased by bottom-up visual cues and top-down linguistic priors, and exclusivity, whether responses commit to a single interpretation. We test both on the canonical duck-rabbit and on synthetic Visual Anagrams to mitigate memorization confounds. Behaviorally, both visual and linguistic manipulations systematically shift reports in human-consistent ways, while responses remain predominantly exclusive. Mechanistically, these effects arise from competing image-token representations, distinct pathways for bottom-up and top-down modulation, and a link between exclusive reporting and object-count encoding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rtakatsky/mllm-bistable-images.

AI.tldr: MLLMs exhibit bistable-reporting behavior with modulability and exclusivity, driven by competing image-token representations and distinct bottom-up/top-down pathways; human-consistent shifts occur under visual and linguistic cues, yet responses remain mostly exclusive; object-count encoding links to exclusivity; code available.
AI.motivation: To determine if multimodal LLMs can mirror human bistable perception (as with the duck–rabbit) and to uncover the internal computations that support modulable and exclusive reports.
AI.method: Evaluate LLaVA-family models on bistable stimuli (duck-rabbit, Visual Anagrams). Systematically manipulate bottom-up visual cues and top-down linguistic priors to assess modulability and exclusivity. Use synthetic Visual Anagrams to reduce memorization confounds. Analyze behavioral reports and mechanistic underpinnings, including image-token representations, pathways for bottom-up/top-down modulation, and the connection to object-count encoding.
AI.result: Behaviorally, reports shift systematically with both visual and linguistic manipulations, aligning with human patterns; reports remain predominantly exclusive (one interpretation at a time). Mechanistically, effects arise from competing image-token representations, distinct bottom-up vs. top-down modulation pathways, and a link between exclusive reporting and object-count encoding.
AI.conclusion: MLLMs can produce controllable bistable reports that resemble human bistable-illusion responses. The underlying computation involves competing representations and modality-specific modulation pathways, with object-count encoding underpinning exclusivity. The work provides data/code to enable replication and further study.

title: Scalable partial information decomposition for symptom networks via supervised embeddings
summary:
Pairwise relationships among mental-health symptoms are routinely summarised asscalar edge weights, which cannot express whether two symptoms carry overlapping information about a third or information that appears only in combination. Partial information decomposition (PID) addresses this gap but is computationally intractable beyond a few sources.
  We introduce embedding-based PID (ePID), a scalable pipeline that compresses all nonfocal symptoms into a low-cardinality discrete embedding and computes a tractable two-source PID, yielding source-unique, remainder-unique, redundant, and synergistic components for each ordered source-target pair. We benchmarked 13 candidate embeddings on synthetic Bayesian networks calibrated to PHQ-9 and on 83 real-world datasets across five PID measures.
  A supervised Agglomerative Conditional Information Bottleneck (ACIB) embedding recovered the reference decomposition most accurately of the 13 embeddings tested, and did so for every PID measure yielding non-negative atoms once four or more symptoms were compressed (synergy recovery r = 0.92). The two instruments then diverged sharply. In PHQ-9 networks (UK Biobank,N = 154,291; Xinxiang student sample, N = 24,292) the surrounding symptom context carried most pairwise dependence through redundant and remainder-unique channels; synergy contributed 6 to 9%, and no directed edge was synergy-dominated in either cohort. In the 28-item Interpersonal Reactivity Index, 45% of source pairs were. The identical pipeline, applied without parameter changes, therefore returned opposite profiles for the two instruments, each consistent with how that instrument was constructed.
  By separating overlapping from interaction-dependent information, ePID provides a scalable, model-agnostic complement to standard symptom-network methodology to distinguish redundant and synergistic contributions to observed correlations.

AI.tldr: Embeddings-based partial information decomposition (ePID) enables scalable two-source PID by compressing nonfocal symptoms into a low-cardinality discrete embedding, yielding source-unique, remainder-unique, redundant, and synergistic components for each ordered source-target pair. An Agglomerative Conditional Information Bottleneck (ACIB) embedding best recovers reference decompositions across many datasets; drugs results show instrument-specific information profiles in PHQ-9 and IRI networks, with redundancy and remainder-unique channels dominating in PHQ-9 and synergy limited, while the IRI yields opposite profiles.
AI.motivation: Partial information decomposition (PID) captures overlapping and interaction-dependent information among multiple sources but is computationally intractable beyond a few sources; there is a need for scalable methods to analyze information decomposition in symptom networks.
AI.method: Compress nonfocal symptoms into a low-cardinality discrete embedding using 13 candidate embeddings; compute a tractable two-source PID for each ordered source-target pair; recover atoms: source-unique, remainder-unique, redundant, and synergistic. Benchmark on synthetic Bayesian networks calibrated to PHQ-9 and 83 real-world datasets across five PID measures; identify best embedding (ACIB) via supervised training to maximize accuracy and non-negativity of atoms (synergy recovery r = 0.92).
AI.result: ACIB embedding most accurately recovers the reference decomposition and yields non-negative atoms when four or more symptoms are compressed (synergy recovery r = 0.92). In PHQ-9 networks (UK Biobank N=154,291; Xinxiang N=24,292), surrounding context carries most pairwise dependence through redundant and remainder-unique channels; synergy contributes 6–9%; no synergy-dominated directed edges observed. In the 28-item Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), 45% of source pairs were [text cut off]; however, the pipeline produced opposite profiles for the two instruments, consistent with how each instrument was constructed.
AI.conclusion: ePID offers a scalable, model-agnostic complement to traditional symptom-network analyses by separating overlapping and interaction-dependent information, enabling clearer attribution of redundant versus synergistic contributions to observed correlations.

title: From Legal Text to AI-specific Risk Sources: A Systematic Analysis of the EU AI Act's High-Risk Requirements
summary: The EU AI Act introduces mandatory requirements for high-risk AI systems with the explicit goal of ensuring the development and operation of trustworthy AI. At the same time, AI risk management practices rely on structured risk taxonomies to systematically identify and treat AI-specific risk sources. As both the AI Act and established risk taxonomies aim to address AI-induced risks, a natural question is whether they align in the risk sources they cover. However, no clear mapping exists between the risks implicitly addressed by the Act's high-risk requirements and established taxonomies, leaving practitioners without a structured basis for aligning regulatory obligations with AI risk management practice. This paper presents a systematic classification of the requirements extracted from the EU AI Act Section 2 (Requirements for high-risk AI systems), revealing that only a minority directly address AI-specific risk sources, while the majority impose organizational process and documentation obligations. From the AI risk-related requirements, a consolidated list of distinct AI-specific risk sources is derived. The resulting EU AI Act Risk Source List takes an important step towards bridging the gap between legal obligation and AI risk management practice, providing a structured reference for explicit comparison between existing AI risk taxonomies and the risk sources implicitly addressed by the EU AI Act. Important Note: This is the authors' preprint. The paper was presented at the 4th International Conference on Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Multidisciplinary Applications. A link to the conference's official proceedings will be provided upon publication.

AI.tldr: Systematic classification of EU AI Act high-risk requirements reveals AI-specific risk sources are a minority; introduces EU AI Act Risk Source List to bridge regulation and AI risk management.
AI.motivation: Regulatory requirements and AI risk taxonomies currently lack a clear mapping, leaving practitioners without a structured basis to align compliance with AI risk management.
AI.method: Extract requirements from EU AI Act Section 2, perform a systematic classification to identify AI-specific risk sources, consolidate into an AI Act Risk Source List, and discuss its use for comparing risk taxonomies with Act-addressed risk sources.
AI.result: Most high-risk requirements are organizational/process/documentation; only a minority address AI-specific risk sources. A consolidated list of AI-specific risk sources (EU AI Act Risk Source List) is derived to facilitate explicit comparison with existing AI risk taxonomies.
AI.conclusion: The Risk Source List bridges legal obligations and AI risk management practice by providing a structured reference; enables explicit alignment of risk taxonomies with Act-specified risk sources; preprint presented at a conference.

title: Runtime-Incremental Transformer for Reinforcement-Learning-Based Adaptive Control
summary: Learning-based adaptive control of robotic manipulators with non-observable friction memory has been addressed by attention- based meta-controllers whose number of attention heads is fixed before training and is tuned by costly offline search. At long memory horizons, such fixed-capacity controllers are prone to catastrophic failures on a sizeable fraction of training seeds. The present paper introduces a runtime mechanism that grows and prunes the heads of the attention block during reinforcement learning, governed by two signals: the effective rank of the on-policy context distribution, which triggers growth when representational capacity becomes insufficient, and the per-head output magnitude, which flags redundant heads for removal. Policy continuity at growth events and a quantitative bound at prune events are established analytically. On a two- link manipulator with Stribeck friction, the proposed mechanism attains full success across all memory regimes, eliminating the long-horizon failure mode and removing the need for offline tuning of the head count.

AI.tldr: Dynamic growth and pruning of attention heads during RL-based manipulator control to handle non-observable friction memory, removing offline head-tuning and reducing long-horizon failures.
AI.motivation: Fixed-capacity attention heads in attention-based meta-controllers fail catastrophically on long memory horizons; need a runtime mechanism to adapt representational capacity and prune redundancy.
AI.method: During RL training, grow heads when the effective rank of the on-policy context distribution indicates insufficient capacity; prune redundant heads when per-head output magnitude indicates redundancy; ensure policy continuity at growth and provide a quantitative bound at prune; analytic guarantees; no offline head-count search.
AI.result: In experiments on a two-link manipulator with Stribeck friction, the method achieves full success across memory regimes, eliminates long-horizon failures, and removes the need for offline head-count tuning.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, data-driven adaptation of attention-head count yields robust RL-based control under non-observable friction memory and mitigates dependence on offline architectural tuning, demonstrated on a simple manipulator model.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Multimodal Facial State Analysis: Tasks, Methods, and Resources
summary: Facial state analysis plays a crucial role in understanding human expressions, psychological modeling, and human computer interaction. Traditional unimodal vision-based methods are often limited by environmental sensitivity and weak interpretability. Multimodal facial state analysis addresses these issues by integrating complementary cues from visual, audio, textual, physiological, and other related modalities. This survey emphasizes two key aspects: on one hand, multimodal learning enables contextual semantic understanding for improved facial state reasoning and leverages interpretable language generation to enhance model explainability; on the other hand, multi-task learning allows simultaneous analysis of expressions, action units (AUs), and face-based soft biometrics (e.g., age, gender), effectively capturing fine-grained expressions and improving cross-scene generalization. This survey reviews core tasks, representative methods, and datasets in multimodal facial state analysis, focusing on facial expression recognition, AU detection, and face-based soft biometric estimation, and emphasizing the unique value of language in providing contextual semantics, enhancing reasoning, and generating explanations. The survey aims to provide an up-to-date overview of the literature and to highlight future research directions for multimodal, interpretable, and multi-task adaptive facial state analysis.

AI.tldr: This survey synthesizes multimodal facial state analysis, highlighting language-guided context and multi-task learning to improve recognition of expressions, AUs, and soft biometrics, and outlining datasets and future directions.
AI.motivation: To overcome unimodal limitations (environment sensitivity, limited interpretability) by leveraging complementary modalities and interpretable language-enabled reasoning.
AI.method: Comprehensive review of core tasks (facial expression recognition, AU detection, soft biometric estimation), modalities (visual, audio, text, physiological), fusion strategies, language-augmented reasoning, and multi-task learning; analysis of representative methods and datasets; discussion of evaluation practices and gaps.
AI.result: Multimodal learning enhances contextual understanding and model explainability via language; multi-task learning improves fine-grained analysis and cross-scene generalization; language-enabled explanations emerge; current datasets and benchmarks vary in modality coverage and bias; open research directions identified.
AI.conclusion: Provides up-to-date overview and directs future work toward more interpretable, multimodal, and multi-task facial state analysis with standardized benchmarks and exploration of language-driven explanations.

title: GradRepair-ODE: Certified Gradient Repair for Neural ODE Training
summary: Neural ordinary differential equations use numerical solvers inside the training loop. The solver determines the forward trajectory and also affects the gradient passed to the optimizer. That coupling creates a reliability problem for scientific machine learning and continuous-time generative modeling, including diffusion probability-flow ordinary differential equations and flow-matching models. Under loose step sizes, stiff dynamics, chaotic sensitivity, or event discontinuities, a differentiable ODE pipeline can return a finite gradient whose direction is numerically suspect. We introduce GradRepair-ODE, a reliability framework for checking, repairing, and rejecting ODE gradients at the optimizer step. The method computes several gradient candidates, compares them with directional finite-difference checks and solver diagnostics, diagnoses likely numerical failure modes, repairs selected gradients through path switching or stricter recomputation, and rejects steps whose descent direction cannot be certified. In six synthetic ODE systems, GradRepair-ODE leaves low-risk systems unchanged, repairs Robertson and Lorenz gradients to cosine similarity 1.000 against a strict reference, reduces unsafe accepted steps from 37 to 0, and rejects an event-discontinuous case instead of applying an uncertified update. The paper argues for a simple change in the training contract: an ODE gradient should reach the optimizer with numerical evidence attached.

AI.tldr: GradRepair-ODE provides a reliability framework to check, repair, and possibly reject ODE gradients during neural ODE training to ensure trustworthy optimization, by combining multiple gradient candidates, directional finite-difference checks, and solver diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Neural ODEs couple solver behavior to gradients, causing unreliable updates under stiff, chaotic, or discontinuous dynamics; a trustworthy gradient is crucial for scientific ML and continuous-time generative models.
AI.method: Compute multiple gradient candidates; compare with directional finite-difference checks and solver diagnostics; diagnose numerical failure modes; repair gradients by path switching or stricter recomputation; reject steps when descent direction cannot be certified.
AI.result: Across six synthetic ODE systems, the method leaves low-risk systems unchanged, repairs Robertson and Lorenz gradients to perfect cosine similarity with a strict reference; reduces unsafe accepted steps from 37 to 0; rejects an event-discontinuous case instead of applying uncertified update.
AI.conclusion: Advocates a shift in training contracts: ODE gradients should be delivered to the optimizer with attached numerical evidence of their reliability.

title: Asclepius: An Adaptive Harness for Long-Horizon Clinical Agents
summary: LLM agents are predominantly benchmarked on short, single-task trajectories, yet real deployments run for hours under contention, surfacing a different class of failures. We use the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES), in which an agent manages an entire emergency-department shift under continuous time and resource pressure, as a testbed: long-horizon execution failures manifest measurably in a single rollout under structured, multi-dimensional grading. On CES, current agents reach the correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap. We attribute this gap to three long-horizon failure modes, each operationalized as a per-trace counter: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. We then introduce Asclepius, an adaptive agent scaffolding with a self-evolving harness that rewrites the operating manual between shifts from trace-level feedback, an externalized clinical skills library for high-stakes regimen knowledge, and three isolated subagents that partition per-turn decisions across the patient queue. On held-out batches never observed during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) over a strong baseline agent framework while preserving diagnostic accuracy, with consistent gains across five LLM judges from three model families; on the full ten-batch set, improvements reach 25% on critical actions and 13% on timeliness. The three failure modes form a coupled bottleneck: decisive reductions appear only when all three components act together.

AI.tldr: Long-horizon failures in LLM agents under continuous, multi-task stress are prevalent, revealing gaps beyond short, single-task benchmarks. An adaptive scaffolding (Asclepius) with a self-evolving harness, a clinical-skills library, and three specialized subagents significantly improves critical actions and timeliness without sacrificing diagnosis accuracy.
AI.motivation: Address the disparity between benchmarked short-horizon performance and real-world, long-horizon deployment where agents must manage ongoing, resource-constrained environments such as emergency departments; identify and mitigate failure modes that hinder timely, complete actions while preserving diagnostic ability.
AI.method: Evaluate LLM agents in the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES) simulating an entire ED shift under continuous time/resource pressure. Define per-trace counters for three long-horizon failure modes: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. Develop Asclepius, an adaptive harness that rewrites the operating manual between shifts from trace feedback, integrates an externalized clinical-skills library, and deploys three isolated subagents to partition per-turn decisions across the patient queue. Assess performance on held-out batches and the full dataset across five LLM judges from three model families.
AI.result: On held-out batches never seen during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) over a strong baseline while preserving diagnostic accuracy, with consistent gains across judges. On the full ten-batch set, critical actions improve by 25% and timeliness by 13%. The gains emerge only when all three components act together, indicating the three failure modes are a coupled bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon failure modes are a bottleneck for deployed LLM agents; an adaptive scaffolding strategy (Asclepius) that combines a self-evolving harness, externalized expertise, and modular subagents yields robust improvements in critical actions and timeliness while maintaining diagnostic accuracy across model families.

title: An MRI-Guided Robotic System to Improve Hippocampal Access for Epilepsy Interventions
summary: This paper presents an MRI-guided robotic system that improves hippocampal access by delivering a curved needle-like laser ablator through the foramen ovale, a natural opening in the base of the skull. Both the delivery path and the curved nature of the needle improve upon current clinical straight-line laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) as measured by hippocampal cannulation percentage. We describe the design of the robotic system which includes positioning, aiming, and curved needle deployment stages, followed by experimental results assessing cannulation percentages using MRI images in phantoms. In three curvilinear, single-insertion experiments, we achieved cannulation percentages of 93.5%, 96.5%, and 60.4%, exceeding reported clinical averages of 50-60%. Seizure control is believed by physicians to be a function of hippocampal volume treated, and our system provides a means of treating a greater volume of the hippocampus with LITT-based interventions.

AI.tldr: An MRI-guided robotic system delivers a curved needle-like laser ablator through the foramen ovale to enhance hippocampal access for LITT, achieving high cannulation percentages in phantom tests that exceed clinical averages.
AI.motivation: Improve access and ablation coverage of the hippocampus for laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT), addressing limitations of straight-line cannulation by leveraging a curved needle path and a natural skull aperture to increase treated hippocampal volume and potentially improve seizure control.
AI.method: Design and evaluation of an MRI-guided robotic system with three stages: positioning, aiming, and curved-needle deployment. Experimental assessment used MRI in phantoms; three curvilinear, single-insertion experiments to measure cannulation percentages.
AI.result: Cannulation percentages achieved: 93.5%, 96.5%, and 60.4%, surpassing reported clinical averages of 50–60%.
AI.conclusion: The curved-needle LITT approach via the foramen ovale enables a larger hippocampal volume to be treated, which physicians believe correlates with seizure control; the system provides a method to increase targeted ablation of the hippocampus beyond conventional straight-line approaches.

title: Sampling headroom is not selection gain: a compute-value audit of test-time scaling for video world models
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) can improve generation only when additional compute produces better candidates and the system can reliably identify them. This distinction is especially important for video world models, where a wider sample pool may contain stronger rollouts without improving the output that is ultimately selected. We introduce the Compute-Value Audit (CVA), a sequential framework that asks whether extra sampling creates opportunity, observable signals provide a reliable state, that state supports a beneficial action, and the resulting gain exceeds the full entry fee of generation and verification. On 192 Physics-IQ scenes, expanding the pool from 4 to 16 candidates increases oracle quality by +9.23 IQ (95% CI [+7.44, +11.14]), but Flow, Cycle, and VideoReward fail to recover this headroom reliably. Across three generators, none of twelve adaptive-depth policies outperforms uniform compute; they recover only 42-69% of the measured entry fee. A matched-60-NFE Predict-and-Perturb intervention on VideoPhy2 is likewise negative across three fresh-seed replicas. These negative results are not universal: anchor-explorer passes all four stages in a sparse PRM800K setting, MMLU-Pro exposes the gap between predictive state and useful action, and a privileged paired future establishes a positive video upper bound. Together, these results show that sampling headroom has deployment value only when it can be converted into a reliable decision whose benefit survives the complete compute charge. Code is available at https://github.com/YuhuaJiang2002/sampling-headroom-is-not-selection-gain.

AI.tldr: A sequential Compute-Value Audit (CVA) tests whether extra sampling is worth compute; findings show headroom often does not translate into actual selection gains; results vary across models and tasks.
AI.motivation: To distinguish when test-time scaling (TTS) improves generation quality versus wasted compute, especially in video world models where more samples may not improve the final chosen output.
AI.method: CVA's four-stage audit: detect opportunity, reliable state signal, state-action compatibility, and payoff exceeding full compute cost; empirical evaluation on Physics-IQ scenes across multiple generators and policies; comparisons include adaptive-depth policies, Predict-and-Perturb, anchor-explorer, MMLU-Pro, privileged paired future; code and data referenced.
AI.result: Expanding pool from 4 to 16 increases oracle quality by +9.23 IQ (CI [+7.44, +11.14]); Flow, Cycle, and VideoReward do not reliably recover this headroom; across three generators, adaptive-depth policies recover 42-69% of the entry fee; Predict-and-Perturb intervention negative across three fresh-seed replicas; some setups show positive bounds (anchor-explorer in sparse PRM800K; privileged paired future); MMLU-Pro exposes gaps between predictive state and useful action; overall, sampling headroom has deployment value only if it translates into a reliable decision whose benefit survives full compute cost; code: https://github.com/YuhuaJiang2002/sampling-headroom-is-not-selection-gain.
AI.conclusion: Headroom from sampling is only valuable in deployment when it can be converted into a reliable decision whose payoff remains after accounting for the full compute and verification costs; results are task- and model-dependent, with mixed success across evaluated settings.

title: Task-Aware Federated Fine-Tuning for MoE-based Large Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become a widely adopted architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs), as it improves model capacity while limiting computational overhead through sparse expert activation. This property makes MoE-based LLMs particularly attractive for resource-constrained distributed environments. However, federated fine-tuning of MoE-based LLMs remains challenging under heterogeneous client data. Since clients often correspond to different task preferences, directly aggregating their local updates may weaken expert specialization and introduce conflicting update directions on shared experts. To address these challenges, we propose FedTAR, a task-aware federated fine-tuning method for MoE-based LLMs. FedTAR establishes the association between local updates and task preference via routing outputs. Specifically, we apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to both routing features and local updates to extract low-dimensional task coordinates and update directions. Based on the task coordinates, FedTAR performs intra-cluster aggregation among clients with similar task preferences and inter-cluster aggregation across different task groups. The aggregated update is then reconstructed through the learned task-to-update mapping, ensuring that the final update remains aligned with task-specific optimization directions. In this way, FedTAR preserves expert specialization and mitigates destructive interference among heterogeneous clients. We evaluate FedTAR on four benchmark tasks under different non-IID settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedTAR consistently outperforms strong federated fine-tuning baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: FedTAR is a task-aware federated fine-tuning approach for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs that uses SVD on routing outputs and local updates to derive task coordinates, enabling intra- and inter-cluster aggregation to preserve expert specialization and improve performance under non-IID data.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning of MoE-based LLMs suffers from heterogeneous client tasks that cause conflicting updates to shared experts, harming specialization and performance; a task-aware aggregation strategy is needed to align updates with task preferences.
AI.method: Compute the association between local updates and task preferences via routing outputs. Apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to routing features and local updates to extract low-dimensional task coordinates and update directions. Cluster clients by task coordinates and perform intra-cluster aggregation among similar-task clients, plus inter-cluster aggregation across different task groups. Reconstruct the aggregated update through a learned task-to-update mapping to align with task-specific optimization directions, preserving expert specialization and reducing destructive interference.
AI.result: Evaluated on four benchmark tasks under different non-IID settings; FedTAR consistently outperforms strong federated fine-tuning baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware, SVD-guided routing and aggregation effectively maintain expert specialization and mitigate interference in MoE-based LLM federated fine-tuning, yielding strong performance under heterogeneous data.

title: AutoTailor: Automatic, User-Aligned Capability Selection and Adaptation for Web Agents
summary: Web agents can utilize reusable tools to reduce the cost and latency of low-level browser interaction, but automatically discovered tool collections can be large, redundant, and poorly aligned with user demand. We present AutoTailor, a meta-agentic framework for constructing and maintaining a compact set of trajectory-derived Model Context Protocol (MCP) APIs. Offline, AutoTailor converts web trajectories into parameterized browser-automation programs, applies a Quality Filter to remove APIs with unsuitable granularity and redundant functionality, and applies a Usage Likelihood Filter to prioritize broadly useful capabilities while preserving semantic coverage. Online, Dynamic Reselection monitors task outcomes and API usage, identifies recurring coverage gaps, adds relevant candidates, and prunes persistently unused capabilities. We evaluate AutoTailor on 106 WebArena Postmill tasks. Offline filtering reduces the initial 1,283 unrefined APIs to 87, and Dynamic Reselection produces a 33-API set. With reasoning and acting (ReAct) fallback, this set achieves 90.6% correctness, compared with 87.5% for ReAct alone, while reducing average total request-token cost by 57.8% and latency by 29.4%. Without ReAct, it achieves 60.1% correctness, marginally matching the performance of unrefined set, while reducing request-token usage by 94.9%. Together, these results show that static filtering produces a compact inventory of APIs expected to support core, high-likelihood tasks, while dynamic reselection further tailors that inventory to observed user needs. This combination improves accuracy and latency while sharply reducing token usage and end-to-end cost, demonstrating the value of user-aligned capability management for efficient web agents.

AI.tldr: AutoTailor creates a compact, task-aligned set of browser-automation APIs (MCP) by offline quality and usage filtering and online dynamic reselection, reducing redundancy and cost while preserving semantic coverage and improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Web agents rely on reusable tools, but discovered tool collections are large, redundant, and misaligned with user demand. There is a need for a compact, adaptive inventory of APIs that covers core tasks with high likelihood, while staying aligned to observed use.
AI.method: Offline: convert web trajectories into parameterized browser-automation programs; apply Quality Filter to remove overly granular or redundant APIs; apply Usage Likelihood Filter to prioritize broadly useful capabilities while preserving semantic coverage. Online: Dynamic Reselection monitors outcomes and usage, identifies recurring coverage gaps, adds relevant candidates, and prunes persistently unused capabilities.
AI.result: Evaluated on 106 WebArena Postmill tasks. Offline filtering reduced 1,283 unrefined APIs to 87. Dynamic Reselection produced a 33-API set. With ReAct fallback, correctness is 90.6% (vs 87.5% for ReAct alone); average total request-token cost down 57.8%; latency down 29.4%. Without ReAct, 60.1% correctness, token savings 94.9% vs unrefined set.
AI.conclusion: Static filtering yields a compact inventory of core, high-likelihood APIs; dynamic reselection tailors the inventory to observed needs, together improving accuracy and latency while sharply reducing token usage and end-to-end cost, illustrating the value of user-aligned capability management for efficient web agents.

title: Differential Realizability of Static Control Allocation in Multirotors: An Impossibility under Nonredundant Full Actuation and a Pseudoinverse Obstruction under Redundant Actuation
summary: Control allocation for multirotors with bidirectional propellers is commonly formulated in signed-thrust variables, where the wrench map is linear. The signed-quadratic map from physical rotor speed to thrust, however, is not a local diffeomorphism at zero speed. This work derives two distinct consequences. Under nonredundant full actuation, a single-propeller reversal removes one instantaneous task direction; hence, no global continuously differentiable exact static allocator exists over the complete task space. Under redundant actuation, the physical task map may remain regular, yet a transverse pseudoinverse zero crossing requires an unbounded rotor-speed derivative. We define differential realizability as regularity of the physical lift of an actuator-output section, derive exact and first-order validity conditions, and distinguish structural rank loss from an allocator- induced rate singularity. A local nullspace deformation repairs isolated pseudoinverse reversals, while a global fixed-orthant construction establishes existence of regular sections at the cost of persistent task-preserving internal actuation.

AI.tldr: The signed-quadratic rotor model creates fundamental singularities for control allocation: no global differentiable exact allocator in nonredundant full actuation, and potential rate singularities in redundancy; introduces differential realizability and two remedies (local nullspace deformation and global fixed-orthant construction) with trade-offs.
AI.motivation: To understand fundamental limitations of control allocation for multirotors with bidirectional propellers due to nonlinear thrust-speed mappings and to establish criteria for when a differentiable allocator exists and how to repair singularities.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of the signed-quadratic thrust map, derivation of exact and first-order viability (validity) conditions for differential realizability, and characterization of singularities. Proposes a local nullspace deformation to repair isolated pseudoinverse reversals and a global fixed-orthant construction to guarantee regular sections at the cost of persistent internal actuation.
AI.result: Shows that in nonredundant full actuation a single prop reversal eliminates an instantaneous task direction, ruling out a global C1 exact static allocator over the full task space. With redundancy, the map can stay regular yet a transverse pseudoinverse zero crossing causes an unbounded rotor-speed derivative. Defines differential realizability, distinguishes structural rank loss from allocator-induced rate singularity, and demonstrates two remedies: a local nullspace deformation to fix isolated pseudoinverse reversals and a global fixed-orthant strategy to ensure regular sections, trading complete task preservation for actuation persistence.
AI.conclusion: Differential realizability provides a rigorous framework to diagnose and repair actuation-induced singularities. The proposed local and global remedies offer pathways to maintain regular task lift in bidirectional multirotors, albeit with trade-offs between flexibility, rate behavior, and internal actuation requirements.

title: Interpretable Temporal Video Reasoning with EventGraph and EventField
comment: Submitted to WACV 2027. Preprint; 9 pages, 7 figures. Copyright may be transferred without notice
summary: We present a structured temporal video reasoning pipeline built around a discrete EventGraph, a continuous EventField, and a human-readable EventGlyph view. On a calibrated EPIC-KITCHENS subset of 10 videos and 50 temporal reasoning questions, EventField+Glyph achieves 0.98 overall accuracy, which is higher than the caption baseline by +0.40 (paired p = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}) and direct VLM-only QA by +0.20 (p = 0.0063) on this subset. We further evaluate annotation-source variations, including manual, heuristic, and heuristic+Gemini pipelines, and find that the best structured method stays above the caption baseline across settings. We also include cross-video pair benchmarking and an appendix gallery of glyph outputs for all studied videos. Overall, the results indicate that structured temporal representations can support both performance and inspectability by preserving symbolic structure, capturing temporal continuity, and providing human-readable diagnostics for video reasoning.

AI.tldr: A structured temporal video reasoning pipeline using discrete EventGraph, continuous EventField, and EventGlyph achieves state-of-the-art-like accuracy on a subset of EPIC-KITCHENS, outperforming caption baselines and VLM-only QA, with robust performance across annotation sources and providing interpretable glyph diagnostics.
AI.motivation: To enable interpretable, high-level symbolic reasoning about video dynamics by preserving temporal structure and providing human-readable diagnostics, addressing limitations of unstructured captioning or black-box QA.
AI.method: Proposes a pipeline with discrete EventGraph, continuous EventField, and EventGlyph; evaluate on EPIC-KITCHENS subset (10 videos, 50 questions); compare against caption baseline and VLM-only QA; assess manual/heuristic/heuristic+Gemini annotation pipelines; cross-video benchmarking; appendix gallery of glyph outputs.
AI.result: Achieves 0.98 overall accuracy on the subset; outperforms caption baseline by 0.40 (paired p=1.1e−5) and VLM-only QA by 0.20 (p=0.0063); best structured method remains above caption baseline across annotation settings; provides cross-video pair benchmarking and glyph outputs; demonstrates improved performance and inspectability via structured representations.
AI.conclusion: Structured temporal representations enhance video reasoning by preserving symbolic structure and temporal continuity, enabling interpretable diagnostics while maintaining high accuracy.

title: Specification Oracles
summary: Specifications face a basic tradeoff: leave details out, and important questions go unanswered; record every detail separately, and the specification becomes large and prolix. We investigate whether a language model can serve as a compact, living specification oracle by learning facts about a target and answering questions about it directly. We compare two ways of storing the learned facts: external text notes and changes to the model's weights.
