Across four families of 596-fact worlds and two Qwen2.5 model sizes, weight-only oracles benefited substantially more from structure: with the 7B model, their accuracy integrated across storage capacities was 18.5 percentage points higher on structured than unstructured worlds, compared with 1.1 points for note-sheet oracles. This advantage came at a substantial storage cost, with the smallest adapter requiring approximately 175 KiB compared with a maximum note budget of 16 KiB. Adapted weights therefore exploited latent structure more successfully, while external notes required substantially less object-specific storage.

AI.tldr: Weight-based learned knowledge in LMs yields higher accuracy when exploiting structure, at higher storage cost; notes are cheaper but less effective.
AI.motivation: Assess whether LMs can serve as compact living specification oracles by storing facts either as editable weights or external notes, and quantify how structure affects performance.
AI.method: Compare weight-only and note-based storage across four families of 596-fact worlds and two Qwen2.5 sizes; measure accuracy across structured vs unstructured worlds; report storage costs.
AI.result: Weight-only encodings gained 18.5 percentage points more accuracy on structured vs unstructured worlds for 7B model; note-based encodings gained only 1.1 points. Smallest adapter ~175 KiB; note budgets up to 16 KiB. Weight adapters exploit latent structure; notes require less object-specific storage.
AI.conclusion: Adapted weights better leverage latent structure to serve as compact living specifications, but with higher storage cost; external notes offer cheaper storage but lower accuracy gains. Implications for designing living specification systems.

title: Toward a Decision-Assurance Layer for AI-Assisted Flight Planning in Air Traffic Management
summary: Generative AI is increasingly being used informally in Air Traffic Management (ATM) for tasks such as flight plan generation, trajectory interpretation, and constraint checking. Although these tools can reduce workload and accelerate planning, their non-deterministic outputs create safety and operational risks in human-in-the-loop settings. This paper proposes the AI Trust and Assurance Layer (ATAL), a model-agnostic decision assurance architecture that evaluates whether AI-generated flight-planning outputs are sufficiently reliable for operational use. ATAL combines semantic stability under prompt variation, operational consistency of structured outputs, and normative constraint validation against domain rules, and maps these signals to a Decision Readiness Level (DRL) for human operators. An ATM-inspired experimental study shows how unsafe, inconsistent, or misleading outputs can be identified before influencing flight-plan validation or execution. Although demonstrated in aviation, the framework is also transferable to other safety-critical decision-support domains that require human oversight under regulatory constraints.

AI.tldr: Proposes ATAL, a model-agnostic decision assurance layer for AI-assisted ATM that maps AI-generated flight-planning outputs to a Decision Readiness Level using semantic stability, operational consistency, and normative constraint validation.
AI.motivation: Non-deterministic AI outputs in safety-critical, human-in-the-loop ATM tasks pose safety and operational risks; a verification layer is needed to determine when AI outputs are trustworthy for use.
AI.method: Introduce ATAL architecture; combine semantic stability under prompt variation, operational consistency of structured outputs, and normative constraint validation against domain rules; map these signals to a Decision Readiness Level (DRL) for operators; validate via an ATM-inspired experimental study.
AI.result: Able to identify unsafe, inconsistent, or misleading outputs before flight-plan validation or execution; demonstrates framework’s potential in aviation and transferability to other safety-critical domains.
AI.conclusion: ATAL provides a transferable, model-agnostic decision assurance framework for safety-critical AI-assisted decision-support, enabling human oversight under regulatory constraints.

title: From Vision to Harvest: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multi-Arm Robotic Fruit Harvesting
summary: Multi-arm robotic harvesting offers a promising path to improve harvesting efficiency and reduce reliance on manual labor. However, practical deployment remains challenging because the system must generalize across diverse environments while efficiently coordinating multiple arms in a shared workspace. Existing methods often require substantial data collection in target environments or rely on simplifying assumptions that limit planning quality. In this work, we introduce the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on zero-shot multi-arm fruit harvesting planning. Our benchmark uses real-world apple and citrus orchard images and compares a VLM-based planning pipeline with a traditional perception-and-planning pipeline. The VLM pipeline directly generates harvesting sequences and waypoints for each arm, while a lightweight trajectory verifier checks for collisions. Our results show that frontier VLMs can generate effective multi-arm harvesting plans zero-shot, but a practical deployment remains limited by accurate 3D waypoint generation and collision-aware coordination. These results highlight both the promise and current limitations of pretrained VLMs for multi-arm robotic harvesting.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking zero-shot multi-arm fruit harvesting with pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using real orchard images; compares VLM-based planning to traditional pipelines; frontier VLMs show promise but 3D waypoint generation and collision-aware coordination limit deployment.
AI.motivation: Address generalization across diverse environments and efficient coordination of multiple arms, reducing data collection in target environments and avoiding simplifying planning assumptions.
AI.method: Introduce the first comprehensive benchmark for pretrained VLMs on zero-shot multi-arm harvesting planning. Use real-world apple and citrus orchard images. A VLM-based planning pipeline directly generates harvesting sequences and per-arm waypoints; a lightweight trajectory verifier checks collisions. Compare against a traditional perception-and-planning pipeline.
AI.result: Frontier VLMs can generate effective zero-shot multi-arm harvesting plans; but deployment is limited by inaccurate 3D waypoint generation and collision-aware coordination.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained VLMs show promise for zero-shot planning in multi-arm harvesting, but practical deployment requires improvements in 3D waypoint accuracy and integrated collision-aware coordination; benchmark highlights both potential and current limitations.

title: TryOnReward: Learning Foveated Consistency for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Virtual Try-On
summary: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to dress a person with the reference garment, producing visually reasonable results aligned with human preferences. Turning this preference-oriented goal into an actionable objective relies on a scoring function aligned with human taste. However, classic fidelity metrics exhibit weak correlation with human judgments, and generic VLMs fail to provide the discriminative granularity demanded by try-on quality evaluation, which hinges on faithfully preserving garment and person details. This shortcoming is further exacerbated in the reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) optimization and leads to severe reward hacking. To this end, we present TryOnReward, a fine-grained reward model tailored for VTON. Built on a vision-language backbone, it adopts a foveation calibration objective that grounds each quality dimension in the relevant region to avoid global shortcut learning. Meanwhile, TryOnReward jointly optimizes pairwise preferences and per-dimension quality scores via margin-aware supervision, leveraging both relative and absolute quality signals. For model training and evaluation, we build TryOnReward-100K, a human-annotated per-dimension rating dataset, alongside TryOn-Bench and TryOnRewardBench, two benchmarks covering diverse real scenarios. Extensive experiments confirm that TryOnReward significantly outperforms generic judges in human preference alignment, and when serving as the RFT reward function, it consistently yields human-preferred try-on results across multiple baselines.

AI.tldr: Presents TryOnReward, a fine-grained, region-aware reward model for virtual try-on (VTON) that improves alignment with human judgments and reduces reward hacking, aided by three new datasets for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between traditional fidelity metrics (which poorly correlate with human judgments) and the nuanced, region-specific quality aspects of try-on results; mitigate reward hacking in reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) by grounding quality signals in relevant image regions.
AI.method: Introduce TryOnReward: a vision-language backbone with a foveation calibration objective that grounds each quality dimension to the appropriate region; jointly optimize pairwise preferences and per-dimension scores via margin-aware supervision; create TryOnReward-100K (human-annotated per-dimension ratings) and two benchmarks (TryOn-Bench, TryOnRewardBench). Evaluate against generic judges and multiple baselines in RFT settings.
AI.result: TryOnReward significantly outperforms generic judges in aligning with human preferences; when used as the RFT reward, it yields human-preferred try-on results across multiple baselines.
AI.conclusion: A region-grounded, fine-grained reward model with margin-aware supervision and dedicated datasets enhances human-aligned evaluation and reduces reward hacking in VTON RL, advancing the practical effectiveness of reinforcement-fine-tuned try-on systems.

title: ReCAST: Reward Credit Assignment across Timesteps for Online Diffusion Reinforcement
summary: Training diffusion models with multiple rewards requires distinguishing user preference from reward informativeness. User preference determines how much each reward should contribute to the overall objective; reward informativeness determines when its feedback is useful during denoising. Some rewards can meaningfully evaluate a sample as soon as global structure emerges, but others become informative only when the sample is nearly clean. To address both questions jointly, we propose ReCAST (Reward Credit ASsignment across T}imesteps), the first method, to our knowledge, for per-reward, timestep-dependent credit assignment in diffusion reward fine-tuning. ReCAST separates user preferences from temporal allocation through a reward-by-timestep weight matrix $W$, whose row sums match the user-specified reward budgets $λ$, while its column sums are equal, assigning the same total weight to each denoising step. Under these marginal constraints, ReCAST allocates weight according to each reward's informativeness, quantified by its Rényi discriminability gain at each step. These gains telescope to the total discriminability between the reward-induced positive policy and the current policy, providing a basis for temporal credit assignment. We evaluate ReCAST by training SD3.5-Medium under two distinct four-reward settings, each across five reward budgets $λ$. ReCAST improves the training rewards in one setting and matches them in the other, improves every held-out judge in both, and is preferred by an independent LLM-as-a-Judge. Together, these results show that ReCAST yields improvements that generalize beyond the training rewards and support its core principle: assigning each reward greater weight at the denoising timesteps where its feedback is most informative.

AI.tldr: ReCAST introduces per-reward, timestep-dependent credit assignment for diffusion reward fine-tuning using a reward-by-timestep weight matrix with row sums equal to user budgets and equal column sums across timesteps; weight allocation is based on Rényi discriminability gain, enabling temporal credit assignment and improved generalization.
AI.motivation: To separate user preference from reward informativeness and allocate feedback across diffusion timesteps where it is most informative.
AI.method: Define W, a reward-by-timestep matrix with row sums λ (budgets) and column sums equal; compute informativeness via Rényi discriminability gain per step and telescope gains to discriminability between reward-induced positive policy and current policy; apply to diffusion reward fine-tuning (SD3.5-Medium) under two four-reward settings and five budgets.
AI.result: ReCAST improves training rewards in one setting and matches them in the other; enhances all held-out judgments in both settings; preferred by an independent LLM-as-a-Judge.
AI.conclusion: Per-reward, timestep-dependent credit assignment under marginal constraints based on reward informativeness improves diffusion reward fine-tuning and generalizes beyond training rewards.

title: Carbon-Aware Routing for Function Calling in Edge-Cloud LLM Systems
comment: 2026 IEEE 33rd International Conference on Electronics, Circuits and Systems (ICECS)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) with function-calling capabilities are becoming critical for modern agentic AI systems. Nevertheless, current deployments typically route inferences to powerful cloud-based models, incurring significant energy use and carbon emissions. We address this sustainability challenge with a carbon-aware routing framework that distributes function-calling queries across a three-tier edge-cloud architecture, combining edge and cloud LLMs on heterogeneous hardware. At its core, a lightweight k-NN predictor operating in a unified semantic-lexical embedding space estimates query-specific accuracy, delay, and power consumption on each edge tier. These predictions are then combined with real-time grid carbon intensity to route every query to the lowest-emission tier capable of executing it successfully. Evaluated on state-of-the-art function-calling benchmarks and LLM families, our framework matches cloud-level accuracy while reducing operational carbon emissions by $4\times$ on average.

AI.tldr: A three-tier edge-cloud LLM routing framework uses a k-NN predictor in a semantic-lexical space and real-time carbon intensity to route function-calling queries to the lowest-emission tier that can meet accuracy and latency requirements, achieving cloud-equivalent accuracy with ~4x lower carbon emissions.
AI.motivation: Mitigate energy consumption and carbon footprint of cloud-heavy LLM deployments by distributing inference across heterogeneous hardware and leveraging real-time grid carbon intensity.
AI.method: Three-tier edge-cloud architecture; lightweight k-NN predictor operating in a unified embedding space to estimate per-tier accuracy, delay, and power; routing policy uses these predictions plus real-time grid carbon intensity to select tier; evaluation on function-calling benchmarks and multiple LLM families.
AI.result: Matches cloud-level accuracy; reduces operational carbon emissions by 4x on average.
AI.conclusion: Carbon-aware routing with edge-cloud LLMs is viable for sustainable, high-accuracy function-calling; scalable across heterogeneous hardware; future work could explore broader deployment, latency guarantees, and dynamic workloads.

title: How Well Do Pseudo-Rigid Body Models Capture Real Plants? In-Field Validation of Simulated Blueberry Canes
summary: Many labor-intensive tasks in fruit production such as pruning require physically interacting with the plant (e.g., pushing, pulling, bending limbs, etc.). Due to increasing labor shortages, there is widespread interest in the adoption of robotics in this area. When the robot must physically interact with the system, a deformable model of the plant is beneficial. Coupled, spring-loaded beams have been used in prior work to build deformable plant models in simulation for learning, planning, and control, but this approach has rarely been validated against the mechanical properties of real-world plants. In this paper, we use this rigid-body model, grounded in real material properties and beam bending theory, to simulate the deformation of blueberry canes under loading. To validate the model, we simulate the canes in MuJoCo and compare their behavior with real-world data collected from probing canes at a commercial farm with a custom testbed. We perform sensitivity analysis on several key modeling variables and show that this approach is highly sensitive to the plant diameter calculations and a priori flexural modulus estimation, which is dependent on season and blueberry variety. We also share our dataset of live blueberry cane deformation, including RGB-D images and measured forces and displacements.

AI.tldr: Rigid-beam, spring-loaded model for deformable plant behavior validated against real blueberry canes; high sensitivity to diameter and a priori flexural modulus; dataset of deformation data released.
AI.motivation: Labor-intensive pruning tasks require physical plant interaction; robotics need accurate deformable plant models for learning, planning, and control. Existing models lack real-world validation against material properties.
AI.method: Create a deformable plant model using coupled rigid bodies linked by springs, based on beam bending theory. Simulate deformation in MuJoCo and validate against field data from probing blueberry canes with a custom testbed. Conduct sensitivity analysis on modeling variables and share a dataset including RGB-D data and measured forces/displacements.
AI.result: MuJoCo simulations reproduce observed cane deformation and reveal that model accuracy is highly sensitive to plant diameter calculations and the a priori flexural modulus (which varies with season and blueberry variety). The authors also release a live blueberry cane deformation dataset.
AI.conclusion: Rigid-body beam-based deformable plant models are viable for learning, planning, and control in robot-plant interaction, but accurate parameterization of geometry and material properties is crucial. Dataset release facilitates broader validation and parameter study.

title: Filling the Unseen: Scene Extrapolation via 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted to ACM Multimedia (ACM MM) 2026. 9 pages
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting achieves photorealistic reconstruction within training view distribution, yet it degrades on out-of-distribution novel views, exhibiting holes in unobserved regions and artifacts in observable areas. Recent works formulate this task as extrapolation and interpolation and try to address it with generative models, but remain limited in extrapolation scale and quality. They repeat a generate-reconstruct-shift cycle to progressively build a scene, which introduces accumulated errors with every step conditioning on previous outcomes. In this work, we propose a holistic framework for extrapolation and interpolation. We devise an independent camera view detection mechanism to enable parallel conflict-free extrapolation, circumventing the reliance on the aforementioned error-prone cycle. Building upon this, we design a hierarchical pipeline that extrapolates independent and dependent camera views separately. Additionally, previous methods overlook inconsistency between generated and original images, resulting in compromising well-reconstructed areas. We propose a plug-and-play Quality-Aware Mask (QA-Mask) module, enabling selective utilization of generated data. By calibrating learning weights with pixel-wise rendering quality, it prevents generation-induced degradations on well-constructed areas. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our framework, with QA-Mask generalizing to multiple generative reconstruction models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a holistic extrapolation/interpolation framework for 3D scene reconstruction that avoids error-prone cycles by using independent camera view detection for parallel extrapolation, a hierarchical pipeline for independent/dependent views, and a QA-Mask to selectively fuse generated data based on pixel-wise quality, achieving superior results and generalization.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting excels within training view distributions but fails on out-of-distribution views, creating holes and artifacts. Prior generative-then-reconstruct cycles introduce accumulating errors. There is a need for scalable, parallel extrapolation and consistency-aware data fusion.
AI.method: (1) Independent camera view detection enabling parallel, conflict-free extrapolation to avoid cycle-based error accumulation. (2) A hierarchical pipeline that extrapolates independent and dependent camera views separately. (3) QA-Mask, a plug-and-play module that weighs generated pixels by rendering quality, selectively incorporating data to prevent degradation of well-reconstructed areas.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the framework's superiority. The QA-Mask improves robustness and generalizes to multiple generative reconstruction models, yielding better extrapolation/interpolation performance than prior methods.
AI.conclusion: A holistic, parallelizable extrapolation/interpolation framework with quality-aware data integration outperforms existing cycle-based approaches and generalizes across models.

title: Certifiably Interpretable Training of ReLU-MLPs for Boolean Tasks with Guaranteed Truth-Table Generalization
summary:
As compute scales, models evolve, and training algorithms advance, our ability to explain the increasingly powerful AI systems they enable is eroding. To help safeguard interpretability, we introduce a specialized training algorithm (MACCHIATO) that jointly constructs (i) an explicitly structured $\operatorname{ReLU}$-MLP from partial truth-table observations and (ii) an explicit Boolean circuit over signed literals with $\{\operatorname{AND},\operatorname{OR},\operatorname{XOR}\}$ gates certifying what its subnetworks compute and how they compose. Intuitively, we iteratively project the residuals of a Boolean function onto low-dimensional $\{\operatorname{AND},\operatorname{OR},\operatorname{XOR}\}$-circuit classes and exactly compile the resulting circuit into a $\operatorname{ReLU}$-MLP; we combine $\operatorname{ReLU}$-MLP circuit compilation, ESPRESSO logic minimization, and influence-based variable selection.
  Roughly speaking, our interpretability certificate is complemented by a statistical guarantee: under the theorem's influence-recovery conditions, if each of the $m$ stage-wise residuals depends on at most $\log_2(B)$ bits, a sample-splitting variant of our algorithm trained on $T$ observations returns a six-layer $\operatorname{ReLU}$-MLP (counting the input layer) of width $\mathcal{O}(mB)$ with truth-table error $\mathcal{O}\bigl(\sqrt{m(B+\log(m/δ))/T}\bigr)$.
  On synthetic random-junta tasks, our networks outperform depth- and hidden-width-matched Adam-trained MLPs in several data-sparse or projection-aligned regimes, while the trained ReLU-MLPs are stronger in others. Moreover, in our explicit PyEDA truth-table implementation, the iterative procedure completes in regimes where flat ambient-dimensional ESPRESSO exceeds the three-hour computational budget.

AI.tldr: MACCHIATO jointly learns a structured ReLU-MLP and an explicit Boolean circuit; uses iterative projection of residuals onto {AND, OR, XOR} circuits and exact compilation into a ReLU-MLP; provides an interpretability certificate with influence-recovery guarantees; demonstrates data-sparse regimes where interpretable models outperform standard MLPs, with practical computation via PyEDA/ESPRESSO.
AI.motivation: To address eroding interpretability of increasingly powerful AI systems by constructing verifiable, jointly interpretable architectures that couple neural networks with symbolic circuits and provide formal guarantees.
AI.method: Iteratively project residuals of a Boolean function onto low-dimensional circuit classes ({AND, OR, XOR}), compile the resulting circuit into a six-layer ReLU-MLP; integrate ESPRESSO logic minimization, PyEDA truth tables, and influence-based variable selection; analyze under influence-recovery conditions and sample-splitting to bound sample complexity.
AI.result: On synthetic random-junta tasks, the MACCHIATO networks outperform depth- and width-matched Adam-trained MLPs in data-sparse or projection-aligned regimes; ReLU-MLP performance is stronger in other regimes; the implemented truth-table version completes within feasible budgets; provides a six-layer ReLU-MLP with width O(mB) and truth-table error O(sqrt{m(B+log(m/δ))/T}).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a viable path to interpretable AI via jointly learned, verifiable architectures that fuse neural and symbolic components, with formal guarantees under specified conditions; performance gains are regime-dependent and computationally bounded by logic-minimization steps.

title: A Hybrid Agentic AI Framework for Intelligent Supply Chain Analytics
summary: Efficient utilization of supply chain analytics for decision making remains a significant challenge for planners, as critical tasks such as database querying, key performance indicator (KPI) analysis, demand forecasting, and performance diagnosis require heterogeneous expertise spanning data engineering, operations research, and domain knowledge. In this work, we propose an agentic system for supply chain analytics that bridges the gap between business decision-making and technical expertise, where a coordinator agent interprets user intent and delegates sub-tasks to specialized agents. The system supports both exploratory analysis and deterministic workflows, enabling planners to transition between ad hoc questions and structured processes. Domain logic is encapsulated within specialist agents and prompts, yielding a scalable, modular, and auditable design and lowering the cost of functional extension through prompt-centric development. We evaluate the proposed architecture on a test environment that replicates multi-echelon inventory management operations. Results show that our multi-agent design achieves a 90\% accuracy, which is competitive with a single agent baseline while reducing input token usage by roughly fourfold, substantially improving scalability and cost-efficiency. Furthermore, we provide case studies to demonstrate interpretable suboptimality detection and automated forecast optimization, illustrating how agentic architectures can effectively combine open-ended exploratory analysis and deterministic supply chain analytics workflows, and provide a practical pathway toward more accessible and extensible decision-support systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes an agentic, multi-agent architecture for supply chain analytics enabling exploration and deterministic workflows; achieves 90% accuracy on a test environment with 4x token efficiency; includes interpretable suboptimality detection and forecast optimization case studies.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between business decision-making and technical expertise in supply chain analytics; reduce reliance on specialized data engineering; deliver a scalable, auditable, and prompt-centric decision-support system.
AI.method: A coordinator agent interprets user intent and delegates tasks to specialist agents; domain logic is encapsulated in prompts and agents; supports both exploratory analysis and deterministic workflows; evaluated in a multi-echelon inventory management simulation; performance metrics include accuracy and token usage; case studies on suboptimality detection and forecast optimization.
AI.result: Achieves 90% accuracy, competitive with a single-agent baseline; ~4x reduction in input token usage; improved scalability and cost-efficiency; demonstrates interpretable suboptimality detection and automated forecast optimization.
AI.conclusion: Agentic architectures enable combining open-ended exploratory analytics with deterministic supply chain workflows; modular, auditable, and cost-effective; validated through simulations and case studies, offering a practical path toward accessible decision-support systems.

title: Compositional Shift Algebra: Extrapolating Mixed Robot Shifts Without Mixed Finetuning
summary: Robot deployments rarely change one mechanism at a time: cameras, action interfaces, and physical dynamics often shift together. Prior adaptation recipes either finetune a new model for every mix or attempt to select which module to update. We instead learn shift operators on a modular stack z{=}E(o), a{=}g(z,u), z'{=}f(z,a) and compose them. Compositional Shift Algebra (CSA) fits single-factor observation, policy, and dynamics operators from exact-reset probes, then extrapolates held-out mixed shifts by operator composition---without mixed-shift finetuning. On ManiSkill StackCube, residual CSA matches an oracle mixed inverse on held-out mixes (success 1.0 over 10 seeds) while beating best-single / zero-shot / parameter-average baselines by { approx}67 pp. RGB-D vision-in-the-loop composition remains near oracle and far above non-compositional arms; a delay commutator stress shows ordered necessity for policy timesdelay. On a second task (PickCube), residual CSA again reaches compose 1.0 vs. 0.33 non-compositional (n{=}10), and an L1 vision controller without privileged cube/goal poses or grasp flags in the control loop retains compose 0.95 vs. 0.00. Main-track upgrades freeze PushCube (+33 pp), PegInsertion joint8 / pose7 EE (+67 pp each), and thin BC under frozen CSA (+67 pp); deeper BC and fair adapt baselines still need compose (+67 pp each), vision-localized BC needs compose (+56 pp), and delay favors ordered/few-shot deploy. We report Intervention-Gated Adaptation as a negative control.

AI.tldr: Proposes Compositional Shift Algebra (CSA) to learn and compose modular shift operators across perception, action, and dynamics, enabling zero-shot extrapolation to mixed shifts without finetuning; achieves near-oracle performance on ManiSkill StackCube and PickCube, outperforming single-model baselines by large margins.
AI.motivation: Robotic deployments experience simultaneous shifts in cameras, interfaces, and dynamics. Existing adaptation either fine-tunes per mix or selects modules to update; a compositional, extrapolative approach is needed to handle unseen mixed shifts from single-factor probes.
AI.method: Model the robot stack with modular operators z=E(o), a=g(z,u), z'=f(z,a). Learn single-factor shift operators from exact-reset probes and compose them to handle mixed shifts without finetuning (Residual CSA). Evaluate on ManiSkill StackCube (RGB-D, vision-in-the-loop) and PickCube, testing against oracle mixed inverse and various baselines; include delay/ordering stress and a negative-control Intervention-Gated Adaptation.
AI.result: Residual CSA matches oracle mixed inverse on held-out StackCube mixes (success 1.0 over 10 seeds); outperforms best-single / zero-shot / parameter-average baselines by ~67 percentage points. RGB-D vision-in-the-loop composition near oracle and robust to delays; on PickCube, residual CSA achieves compose 1.0 vs non-compositional 0.33 (n=10); L1 vision controller without privileged data retains compose 0.95 vs 0.00. Reported gains across tasks include main-track upgrades and sensitivity to order/delay; negative control noted as Intervention-Gated Adaptation.
AI.conclusion: CSA enables robust compositional generalization to mixed shifts without finetuning, via operator composition on a modular robot stack; yields strong cross-task performance, with evidence that proper ordering and few-shot deployment influence success; defines a clear boundary via negative control.

title: Multi-View Structure-from-Motion Enables Oriented Projective Shape Analysis in Three Dimensions
summary: Projective shape analysis provides a geometric framework for studying landmark configurations in digital images acquired by pinhole cameras. In the classical projective shape (PS) model, three-dimensional configurations ($k$-ads) are represented as points in $(\mathrm{RP}^3)^q$, $q = k - 5$. A nonparametric test is developed in Patrangenaru et al. [12], for this framework, to determine whether an object matches a design blueprint, with each configuration reconstructed from a single uncalibrated stereo pair. Such two-view reconstructions are identified only up to a 3D projective transformation, which may reverse orientation, so that the sign-blind PS summary was the only available, before oriented projective shape (OPS) was recently considered. Multi-view Structure-from-Motion (SfM) technology removes this obstruction: its bundle adjustment is identified up to an orientation-preserving projective transformation. In this paper we revisit a well-cited three-cube object, from Patrangenaru et al. [12], with $n = 8$ SfM reconstructions built in Agisoft Metashape Professional 2.3.0, and validate our implementation by reproducing the published stereo construction from the original data. This allows us to perform what is to the best of our knowledge the first three-dimensional OPS analysis, compute its extrinsic total-variance index and perform statistical inference in this novel setting. Due to the high concentration of SfM data, the OPS index is asymptotically one-half the PS index, a structural consequence of concentration rather than a property of the object. Here our blueprint hypothesis is not rejected for any of the $q = 14$ non-frame landmarks, while the SfM reconstructions are about 26 times more concentrated than the stereo ones, a substantial gain in reconstruction precision. Sample-size, photograph-count, and frame-ordering analyses support the robustness of these conclusions.

AI.tldr: Extends projective shape analysis to oriented projective shape (OPS) within multi-view SfM, validating OPS on a well-known three-cube object using 8 SfM reconstructions. Finds OPS concentration is stronger than PS, enabling robust statistical inference without sign ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Address sign/orientation ambiguity in two-view projective shape by adopting orientation-preserving transformations via OPS, leveraging SfM reconstructions to improve precision and enable 3D OPS inference.
AI.method: Uses 8 SfM reconstructions (Agisoft Metashape) of a well-studied 3D object; reconstructs q=14 landmarks (k=9) and computes extrinsic total-variance index under OPS; compares with stereo-derived PS analysis; assesses blueprint hypothesis and robustness across sample size, photo count, and frame order.
AI.result: OPS index is asymptotically half the PS index due to concentration, a property of concentration rather than object; blueprint hypothesis not rejected for all 14 non-frame landmarks; SfM reconstructions show ~26× higher concentration than stereo reconstructions, indicating substantial precision gains.
AI.conclusion: Oriented projective shape analysis is practically viable for 3D objects with SfM data, delivering tighter inference and resolving orientation ambiguity; high data concentration in SfM enhances statistical power.

title: Efficient Online Inverse Optimization with $O(d)$ Regret
summary: We give a deterministic algorithm for online inverse linear optimization with regret $O(d)$, uniform in the horizon and $O(d^{2})$ time per round. A bound of this order was obtained recently by Dewasurendra, settling a question of Gollapudi et al.\ and of Oki and Sakaue, but by an improper rule that enumerates covers at every scale and costs $T^{Θ(d)}$ a round; ours is the first efficient such bound and the first proper one. We build on the variable-metric framework of Sakaue et al., adding a self-normalized rank-one update, and we replace the $\log\det$ potential by the trace power $\tr(H^{-1/2})$, which is bounded outright and removes the $\ln T$. The bound also holds against an expert that does not optimize, and we give corruption-robust and rank-adaptive variants, and an application to convex minimization.

AI.tldr: Deterministic online inverse linear optimization with regret O(d) and per-round time O(d^2); first efficient and proper bound matching recent but inefficient results.
AI.motivation: Resolve open questions on achieving low-regret bounds for online inverse optimization with a scalable, proper algorithm, robust to non-optimizing adversaries and adaptable to rank changes.
AI.method: Extend the variable-metric framework of Sakaue et al. with a self-normalized rank-one update; replace log-determinant potential with trace power potential tr(H^{-1/2}) to obtain a bound without log T; ensure efficiency (O(d^2) per round).
AI.result: Achieves regret O(d) uniformly in horizon; per-round complexity O(d^2); the bound also holds against an expert who does not optimize; provides corruption-robust and rank-adaptive variants; applicability to convex minimization.
AI.conclusion: First efficient and proper bound of this type, improving over a recent but inefficient/ improper construction; broadening robustness and applicability for online inverse optimization and related convex problems.

title: Planning or Learning: Reliability and Cost in Multi-Asset Maintenance
summary: Industrial maintenance systems involve multiple interacting assets and shared resources, making it challenging to balance reliability and operational cost using a single decision framework. While recent work has focused on reinforcement learning (RL) for maintenance scheduling, direct comparisons with planning approaches under identical settings remain limited. In this work, we empirically compare planning and RL for multi-asset bearing maintenance using run-to-failure data. We examine how these methods behave when balancing preventive maintenance against tolerable failures across a range of failure penalty scenarios. We observed a consistent behavioral difference driven by objective formulation. Planning enforces reliability as a hard constraint and produces zero-failure policies whose total cost is largely insensitive to the magnitude of failure penalties. RL agents optimize expected cost and often trade off preventive maintenance against occasional failures as penalties vary, resulting in lower costs under low-penalty regimes but persistent non-zero failures even when penalties are high. We also investigate lightweight constraint mechanisms, including reward shaping and action masking, to encourage RL's reliability. From a practical perspective, planning may be more suitable when strict reliability is required and deployment horizons are short, whereas RL may provide cost-efficient policies when limited failures are acceptable and long-run operational efficiency is prioritized. Overall, this study clarifies the trade-offs between reliability and cost in multi-asset maintenance and suggests that planning and RL are complementary approaches. Beyond these findings, the controlled benchmark protocol itself that unifies environment, cost model, and evaluation across paradigms, offers a reusable template for comparing decision-making approaches in other maintenance settings.

AI.tldr: Empirically compare planning and reinforcement learning (RL) for multi-asset bearing maintenance under run-to-failure data; planning yields zero-failure policies with stability across penalty levels, while RL minimizes expected cost and trades preventive maintenance with occasional failures; lightweight constraint mechanisms can steer RL; planning favored for strict reliability and short horizons, RL for cost efficiency and long horizons; both are complementary and a benchmark protocol is proposed for cross-paradigm evaluation.
AI.motivation: Clarify trade-offs between planning and RL in maintenance decision-making by evaluating them in the same setting, using identical data and cost models, to guide practitioners on method selection and to establish a reusable benchmarking protocol.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing planning and RL under run-to-failure data for multi-asset bearing maintenance. The analysis spans a range of failure-penalty scenarios. The study investigates hard constraint enforcement (planning) versus learned cost optimization (RL) and explores lightweight RL constraint mechanisms (reward shaping, action masking). Outcomes are analyzed in terms of reliability (failures) and total cost, with a discussion of horizon length and practical deployment.
AI.result: Planning enforces reliability as a hard constraint, producing zero-failure policies and cost largely insensitive to penalty magnitude. RL optimizes expected cost, trading preventive maintenance against failures, yielding lower costs under low penalties but non-zero failures under high penalties. Lightweight constraints can nudge RL toward reliability. Practically, planning suits strict reliability and short horizons; RL suits cost efficiency and long horizons. The study also offers a reusable benchmark protocol for cross-paradigm comparison in maintenance.
AI.conclusion: Planning and RL are complementary approaches; the choice depends on reliability requirements and horizon length. The research advances an integrated benchmarking framework that unifies environment, cost model, and evaluation across paradigms, enabling robust comparisons and extension to other maintenance settings.

title: Does Online Gravity Estimation Matter? Revisiting a Silent Design Split in LiDAR-Inertial Odometry
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Code, evidence, and video: https://github.com/jiejie567/rethink-lio-gravity
summary: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) systems differ in whether they continue estimating gravity after initialization. We compare four gravity-bias state configurations in each of FAST-LIO2 and LIO-SAM, then separately test a gravity-direction factor. Across 12 dataset sequences evaluated with FAST-LIO2, fixing gravity under continuous LiDAR correction produces mean paired changes in vertical and 3D position errors with 90% confidence intervals within $\pm 2\%$. Tests on 4 sequences with LIO-SAM likewise show no consistent benefit from online gravity. Multi-second LiDAR outages, unlike reduced range or field of view, reveal trajectory-dependent costs of fixing gravity. A history-matched 23D-to-21D switch places the repeatable 3D error increase after LiDAR updates resume. Under 5-s outages, a direction factor from the same IMU used for preintegration improves accuracy on Hall05 but worsens both errors with online gravity on TUHH. Dynamic-start tests also show fixed-bias failures at particular starting phases. We recommend keeping gravity and accelerometer bias online for robustness; use a direction factor only after verifying vertical and 3D accuracy gains under the intended operating conditions.

AI.tldr: Online gravity bias yields no universal gains over fixed gravity in LIO; effects vary with outages and datasets; maintaining online gravity and bias is robust; gravity-direction factors may help in select cases after verification.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of gravity-bias handling in two LIO systems under varied outages and configurations; quantify accuracy changes and reliability.
AI.method: Evaluate four gravity-bias configurations in FAST-LIO2 and four in LIO-SAM across multiple datasets; test a gravity-direction factor; simulate multi-second LiDAR outages and mode switches; report vertical/3D errors and 90% CIs; dynamic-start tests.
AI.result: Fixed gravity under continuous LiDAR correction yields changes within ±2% in FAST-LIO2; no consistent benefit from online gravity in LIO-SAM; outages reveal trajectory-dependent costs of fixing gravity; 23D-to-21D switches place error increase after LiDAR resumes; a direction factor helps in Hall05 but hurts TUHH under online gravity; dynamic-starts show fixed-bias failures.
AI.conclusion: Keep gravity and accelerometer bias online for robustness; apply gravity-direction factor only after verifying vertical and 3D gains under intended conditions.

title: BEACON: Behavior and Appearance Control for Subject-Specific Video Generation
summary: Generating human-centric videos that preserve both visual identity and person-specific expressive behavior remains a fundamental challenge. In addition to reproducing appearance, a model must replicate the facial behaviors that characterize how a subject expresses emotion over time. However, most state-of-the-art methods condition generation on a single reference image, which contains no information about these temporal dynamics. As a result, they tend to preserve the subject's visual identity but often produce expressions with limited variation and weak subject specificity. To mitigate this issue, we introduce BEACON, a lightweight framework for person-specific video generation that produces more expressive videos by disentangling visual identity from expressive behavior. BEACON conditions generation on two complementary signals: a reference image encoding the identity and a reference video capturing subject-specific facial dynamics. By conditioning on these complementary signals, BEACON generates videos that better preserve both the subject's appearance and characteristic facial dynamics, while also supporting identity-expression transfer. Our experiments on the MEAD and RAVDESS datasets show that by fine-tuning on approximately 2,000 pairs and updating about 1% of the pretrained Wan video diffusion model, BEACON improves facial expressivity over state-of-the-art video generation methods while maintaining competitive identity preservation.

AI.tldr: BEACON disentangles identity from expressive dynamics using a dual-reference conditioning (identity from an image, dynamics from a reference video) to produce more expressive, identity-consistent talking-head videos with minimal fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art video generation often relies on a single reference image, which captures appearance but ignores temporal facial dynamics, leading to limited expressivity and weak subject specificity.
AI.method: BEACON is a lightweight framework that conditions a diffusion-based video generator on two signals: a reference image for identity and a reference video for subject-specific facial dynamics. It is trained with ~2,000 paired data and updates about 1% of the Wan video diffusion model to enable identity–expression transfer.
AI.result: On MEAD and RAVDESS, BEACON achieves improved facial expressivity over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive identity preservation.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling visual identity from expressive behavior via dual conditioning yields more expressive, subject-specific video synthesis, achievable with modest fine-tuning and small datasets.

title: Learning to Solve Hard Problems in RL for LLMs by Never Giving Up
comment: Blog post mnoukhov.github.io/posts/ngu and code available at github.com/mnoukhov/never-give-up
summary: We demonstrate that training LLMs with RL does not improve performance equally across a dataset. RL shows large improvements on easy problems that an LLM is already good at solving, but small improvements on hard problems. We call this the Matthew Effect in RL for LLMs, after the phenomenon of cumulative advantage from economics and network science summarized as "the rich get richer". The naive explanation is that hard problems require more compute to find a solution. We argue that modern RL methods are exacerbating the issue by wasting too much compute on easy problems and instead should dynamically reallocate how they use compute. We introduce Never Give Up (NGU), a simple adaptive sampling method that keeps generating samples for a problem until one is correct. By leveraging asynchronous RL, this naturally uses fewer samples to filter out easy problems and allocates more compute to solving harder problems. We investigate the design choices that affect NGU, such as off-policy robustness, and develop a set of best practices. On the math benchmark Deepscaler, NGU improves performance per compute, especially on harder problems. On a recent coding task, Manufactoria, standard GRPO with a per-test reward fails to fully solve problems that have a range of easy and difficult tests. NGU iteratively improves, solving harder and harder tests, until it learns to fully solve coding problems.

AI.tldr: NGU adaptive sampling reallocates compute to harder problems in RL for LLMs, reducing the Matthew Effect and improving compute efficiency on math and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Mitigate unequal performance gains across a dataset when training LLMs with RL by allocating more compute to hard problems.
AI.method: Propose Never Give Up (NGU), an adaptive sampling method using asynchronous RL; evaluate design choices (off-policy robustness) and provide best practices; compare to GRPO on Deepscaler and Manufactoria.
AI.result: NGU improves performance per compute on Deepscaler, especially on hard problems; in Manufactoria, NGU iteratively solves harder tests, eventually fully solving coding problems where per-test reward GRPO stalls.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, adaptive compute allocation via NGU reduces the Matthew Effect and offers a practical path to more efficient RL for LLMs; applicable to diverse tasks with mixed difficulty.

title: Causal multi-modal AI for personalized chemosensitivity prediction
summary: Chemotherapy improves survival for some patients with breast cancer, but doctors cannot reliably predict who. Current guidelines rely on recurrence scores as a proxy for treatment benefit, which may contribute to the overprescription of chemotherapy. Here we present a causal multi-modal AI model that predicts personalized chemosensitivity using routinely collected pathology and clinical information. We developed our model on a multi-national dataset of 9,141 patients (twelve cohorts, nine countries) and evaluated it on another 1,994 patients (five cohorts, three countries). The model generated treatment-specific recurrence probabilities for each patient, with near-perfect calibration and strong prognostic discrimination across both 5- and 10-year follow-up horizons. Moreover, its chemotherapy benefit predictions demonstrated robust predictive performance, and out-performed existing recurrence-score-based tests. Compared to the standard of care, using the model to support personally tailored therapeutic decisions could reduce the number of patients receiving chemotherapy by 30% while achieving the same recurrence-free rate. Tumors predicted to be highly chemosensitive displayed concordant molecular and morphological programs of proliferation, cell cycle progression, and replication stress. The model's predictive capabilities transferred zero-shot to non-breast cancers, indicating our causal multi-modal AI approach may provide a universal strategy to predict treatment outcomes across cancer types.

AI.tldr: A causal multi-modal AI model predicts personalized chemosensitivity in breast cancer using pathology and clinical data, outperforming recurrence-score tests and potentially reducing chemotherapy by ~30% while preserving recurrence-free survival; shows underlying biology of chemosensitive tumors and transfers zero-shot to non-breast cancers.
AI.motivation: Reduce overtreatment by chemotherapy in breast cancer by moving beyond recurrence-score proxies to directly predict individual chemosensitivity and treatment benefit.
AI.method: Train and validate a causal multi-modal AI model on 12 cohorts (n=9,141) across 9 countries, with external validation on 1,994 patients from 5 cohorts in 3 countries. The model integrates routine pathology and clinical data to output treatment-specific recurrence probabilities and estimated chemotherapy benefit. Calibration and discrimination assessed for 5- and 10-year outcomes; comparative performance vs. recurrence-score-based tests; biological characterization of predicted chemosensitive tumors; zero-shot transfer to other cancer types.
AI.result: The model achieved near-perfect calibration and strong prognostic discrimination for 5- and 10-year recurrence. It predicted chemotherapy benefit with robust predictive performance and outperformed existing recurrence-score-based tests. Implementing the model could reduce chemotherapy use by ~30% while maintaining same recurrence-free rate compared to standard care. Highly chemosensitive tumors showed concordant molecular/morphological programs (proliferation, cell cycle, replication stress). The predictive capability transferred to non-breast cancers in zero-shot fashion.
AI.conclusion: A unified causal multi-modal AI framework can personalize chemotherapy decisions in breast cancer with superior predictive accuracy over traditional recurrence scores and with potential for broad applicability across cancer types.

title: How to Better Train VLAs: Lessons Learned From the REAL-I Challenge at ICRA 2026
summary: How can robot policies learn more effectively from a fixed demonstration budget? The first Real-world Embodied AI Learning (REAL-I) Challenge at ICRA 2026 examined this question through simulation, real-robot evaluation, and an on-site final on a shared dual-arm humanoid platform. We describe the challenge tasks, data and deployment interfaces, and competition results, then compare the approaches contributed by NUS-CLEAR, RCL-Lab, and Deeptouch.ai. Their systems combined pretrained vision-language-action models and task-specific imitation policies with different strategies for data curation, staged adaptation, checkpoint selection, and action-space design. The team reports highlight the importance of adapting to the deployment environment while retaining prior capabilities, treating demonstration quality at an appropriate temporal scale, and suppressing errors in inactive robot components. They also expose the limitations of offline action-prediction metrics for forecasting closed-loop success. These observations motivate a view of fixed-data robot learning that integrates data, adaptation, evaluation, and deployment.

AI.tldr: REAL-I Challenge assesses learning from fixed demonstration budgets for real-world embodied AI, using simulation and on-site evaluations; combines pretrained vision-language-action models with imitation policies; findings stress deployment-adaptation balance and limits of offline metrics.
AI.motivation: Understand how to maximize data efficiency and reliable deployment for real-world robot manipulation under a fixed data budget.
AI.method: Multi-faceted evaluation: simulation, real-robot testing, and on-site deployment on a shared dual-arm humanoid; compares approaches from NUS-CLEAR, RCL-Lab, and Deeptouch.ai; integrates pretrained vision-language-action models with task-specific imitation policies; employs data curation, staged adaptation, checkpoint selection, and action-space design.
AI.result: Shows that adapting to deployment environments while preserving prior capabilities is crucial; highlights the role of demonstration quality at the appropriate temporal scale; emphasizes suppressing errors in inactive components; reveals limitations of offline action-prediction metrics for predicting closed-loop success; advocates a holistic fixed-data learning framework spanning data, adaptation, evaluation, and deployment.
AI.conclusion: A call for integrating data collection, model adaptation, evaluation, and deployment into a unified fixed-data robot-learning paradigm; stresses environment-specific adaptation and data-quality considerations, beyond offline metrics.

title: Forward-Facing Near-Infrared Adds Little to Colour for Farm-Machinery Traversability: A Site-Disjoint Evaluation of Sensor-Dependent Spatial Leakage
summary:
Near-infrared (NIR) imaging does not consistently outperform standard color cameras for daytime agricultural traversability once spatial data leakage is eliminated. Prior benchmarks suggesting an NIR advantage used sequence-level splits that permitted spatially autocorrelated imagery into test sets, artificially inflating NIR performance, especially on difficult paddy-boundary segmentation.
  When evaluated across strictly held-out recording sites using the AI Hub autonomous driving corpus, none of the four tested configurations (color, NIR, a luminance control, or their fusion) reliably surpasses standard color across any of the five traversability classes. Furthermore, apparent performance gains observed at a single held-out site completely fail to replicate when the held-out site is rotated, demonstrating that the observed benefits were site-specific artifacts rather than generalizable improvements.
  Correcting for spatial leakage erases the apparent lead of NIR entirely rather than uniformly degrading performance across all sensor types. Consequently, adding a forward-facing NIR camera to a daylight agricultural vehicle sensor suite remains unproven, and evaluations compromised by location leakage risk distorting sensor rankings and misleading procurement decisions.

AI.tldr: NIR imaging does not outperform standard color for daytime agricultural traversability when spatial leakage is eliminated; prior NIR gains were artifacts of sequence-level leakage and site-specific biases.
AI.motivation: Assess whether NIR offers real, generalizable advantages for daytime traversability in agriculture and correct biases from spatial leakage in prior benchmarks.
AI.method: Evaluate four sensor configurations (color, NIR, luminance control, and their fusion) on strictly held-out recording sites using the AI Hub autonomous driving corpus, across five traversability classes; analyze the impact of spatial leakage by rotating held-out sites and testing site generalizability.
AI.result: No configuration reliably beats color across any traversability class on strictly held-out sites. Apparent gains at one site do not replicate when the site is rotated. Correcting for spatial leakage neutralizes any NIR lead.
AI.conclusion: Spatial leakage largely drives perceived NIR advantages; adding a forward-facing NIR camera to daylight agricultural sensor suites remains unproven. Evaluations prone to location leakage can misrank sensors and misguide procurement.

title: A Machine Learning API for Earth Observation Data Cubes Based on openEO
summary:
Earth Observation (EO) data are increasingly organized as spatio-temporal data cubes, while machine learning (ML) methods operate on tabular feature matrices or structured tensor inputs. This mismatch forces platform-specific transformations that are difficult to reproduce or transfer across cloud infrastructures. The openEO specification provides a unified interface for EO data access and processing across heterogeneous backends, but lacks a standardized approach for ML integration.
  We propose a process-level ML specification for openEO structured into three stages: model initialization, model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and model management. It supports classical algorithms such as Random Forest and SVM, as well as deep learning architectures for time-series and spatial patch-based modeling, including TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, and foundation model inference. Three prototype implementations in R and Python demonstrate feasibility across diverse technology stacks. A crop type mapping use case demonstrates cross-backend interoperability by submitting an identical process graph to independent R and Python backends and comparing predictions and evaluation metrics.
  Two further use cases demonstrate deep learning on time series and foundation model inference, each executed on a dedicated backend. The prototypes reveal, however, that full cross-backend portability requires deeper harmonization of serialization formats and execution semantics than the process level alone can enforce; backend library versions and preprocessing conventions outside the specification's boundary also affect reproducibility. Addressing both through explicit backend conformance profiles represents the most important near-term direction. The specification advances the reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms.

AI.tldr: A three-stage process-level ML spec for openEO enabling ML on EO data cubes, with prototypes in R/Python; demonstrates cross-backend feasibility but highlights need for backend conformance for full portability.
AI.motivation: EO data cubes are growing as spatio-temporal data, while ML workflows require tabular/structured inputs; openEO lacks a standardized ML integration path, hindering reproducibility and portability across clouds.
AI.method: Propose a process-level ML specification with three stages: model initialization, model actions (training, tuning, inference, validation), and model management. Supports classical algorithms (Random Forest, SVM) and deep learning for time-series/spatial patches (TempCNN, Temporal Attention Encoders, foundation model inference). Three prototype implementations in R and Python across backends; use cases include crop type mapping to test cross-backend interoperability and additional DL/time-series and foundation model workloads.
AI.result: Prototype implementations demonstrate cross-backend interoperability to some extent (identical process graphs yield comparable predictions/evaluations). Full cross-backend portability is hindered by differences in serialization formats, execution semantics, backend library versions, and preprocessing conventions outside the specification boundary.
AI.conclusion: The spec enhances reproducibility, portability, and accessibility of ML workflows on EO data cubes across cloud platforms, but achieving full portability requires explicit backend conformance profiles to harmonize serialization, execution semantics, and preprocessing conventions.

title: How User-AI Mistreatment Occurs and Matters in Conversational Systems?
comment: Accepted by the 10th Workshop on Online Abuse and Harms (WOAH 2026) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Safety research often focuses on model-generated harms, but users may also direct hostility, coercion, and adversarial pressure at models. Understanding how and when that occurs is essential for accurately interpreting model behaviour, alignment drift, and real-world deployment risks. In this paper, we audit 777K English LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations with two independent detectors: an eight-category lexicon for hostility directed at the model, and the dataset's moderation signal; and show that they capture different, weakly overlapping phenomena. The lexicon identifies insults, threats, and jailbreak coercion aimed at the assistant, while moderation flags are dominated by toxic-content solicitation rather than hostility at the model. Together, they mark about 5% of user turns; adjusting the narrower lexicon-harassment union for measured precision puts mistreatment aimed at the assistant at 0.90%. These absolute rates describe arena-style evaluation traffic and should not be read as deployment-wide base rates. We find that user hostility varies 13-fold across models, driven largely by who each model attracts rather than by model behaviour: first-turn hostility spreads far wider than post-response hostility, and more than fifteenfold separates the extremes even after deduplicating opening prompts. Within conversations, assistant apologies are consistently associated with higher odds of next-turn hostility under both detectors; the effect survives restricting to non-refused prior turns and to jailbreak-free conversations, and is positive in 20 of 23 models. Yet across models, more apologetic models receive less hostility overall. Finally, hostility also shows temporal structure, with coercive openings front-loading the first turn while affective hostility accumulates over a session. We release the lexicon, the detector cross-validation pipeline, and all derived tables.

AI.tldr: Audits 777K LMSYS-Chat-1M dialogues for user-directed hostility toward assistants using two detectors, revealing they capture different phenomena; around 5% of turns flagged; after precision tuning, about 0.9% mistreatment; hostility varies widely across models; first-turn hostility spreads more widely; apologies correlate with higher odds of next-turn hostility; shows temporal patterns; releases lexicon and detection pipeline.
AI.motivation: Address the gap that hostility directed at models (not only model-generated harms) can affect interpretation, alignment drift, and deployment risk; quantify and characterize such hostility and its detectors.
AI.method: Two independent detectors are used: (i) an eight-category lexicon for hostility directed at the model, and (ii) the moderation signal from the dataset. The study analyzes 777K English LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations, compares detector coverage, reports rates and distribution across models, examines turn-level and session-level dynamics (e.g., first-turn vs. subsequent hostility, apologies effects), deduplicates opening prompts, and releases the lexicon, cross-validation pipeline, and derived tables.
AI.result: Lexicon and moderation detect overlapping but distinct hostility signals; combined they mark ~5% of user turns; a precision-tuned narrower lexicon-estimate yields ~0.9% mistreatment. Hostility varies ~13-fold across models, driven by model-attractiveness rather than behavior. First-turn hostility spreads wider than post-response hostility; more than 15x separation across extremes after deduplication. Inside conversations, assistant apologies correlate with higher odds of next-turn hostility under both detectors, surviving controls; but across models, more apologetic models have less hostility overall. Hostility displays temporal structure: coercive openings front-load initial turns, while affective hostility grows over a session. The authors release the lexicon, detector cross-validation pipeline, and derived tables.
AI.conclusion: The work provides public detectors and datasets for studying user-directed hostility toward models, emphasizes that absolute rates depend on evaluation context (arena-style traffic) and model attractivity, and offers resources to better understand and audit deployment risks related to user-directed hostility.

title: GROOVE: Geometry-Guided Reduction of Operational-Space Jerk in VLA Execution
summary: Chunked vision language action (VLA) policies execute several commands per query, but jerk within chunks and across replanning boundaries can induce oscillatory motion and sharp actuator transients. We present GROOVE, an online regulator that searches directional correction regions around the raw three dimensional end effector (EEF) path, without retraining or additional VLA inference. It optimizes the new chunk using delivered commands as boundary conditions, reducing boundary and within chunk jerk while bounding cumulative translation and local axis angle deviation from the raw plan after every command. Using quadratic programs (QPs), GROOVE generates a cube reference and thirteen directional candidates, then selects the one with the lowest command space jerk under a reference relative deviation cap. On a held out LIBERO benchmark, GROOVE achieves the largest reductions among the evaluated methods, reducing translational and rotational EEF jerk by 33.02% and 43.42%, respectively, with task success of 95.75% versus 93.75% for raw execution. Across 50 matched UR5e pairs with measured execution timing, it reduces translational and rotational tool center point (TCP) jerk by 16.39% and 19.49% and joint current slew by 29.09%.

AI.tldr: GROOVE is an online regulator for chunked vision-language action policies that reduces end-effector and TCP jerk by online-quadratic-program optimization over directional corrective regions, without retraining, leading to improved smoothness and high task success on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Chunked VLA policies can cause jerk and oscillations at chunk boundaries and during replanning, producing sharp actuator transients. An online method that smooths the path without retraining or re-inference can improve motion quality and safety while preserving task success.
AI.method: GROOVE searches directional correction regions around the raw 3D end-effector path and optimizes the new chunk using delivered commands as boundary conditions. It uses quadratic programs to generate a cube reference and thirteen directional candidates, then picks the candidate with the lowest command-space jerk under a relative deviation cap.
AI.result: On LIBERO: translational EEF jerk reduced by 33.02% and rotational EEF jerk by 43.42%; task success 95.75% vs 93.75% for raw execution. On 50 matched UR5e pairs: translational TCP jerk reduced by 16.39%, rotational TCP jerk by 19.49%, and joint current slew by 29.09%.
AI.conclusion: GROOVE provides a practical, training-free online regulation of chunked VLA policies, achieving substantial jerk reductions and maintaining or improving task success across hardware (LIBERO benchmark and UR5e pairs).

title: Structure-Token Evidence-Anchored Reasoning for Scientific Chart Understanding
summary: Scientific charts encode quantities in axes, legends, and geometric marks, yet large vision-language models still treat them as natural photographs. Visual in-context examples do not expose the coordinate frame; unconstrained chain-of-thought can name a plausible number that was never read from a bar. We present STEER (Structure-Token Evidence-anchored Reasoning), which freezes a Llama-3.2-Vision encoder and inserts three modules: a chart structure graph encoder (CSGE) that binds ticks, legend items, and marks; evidence-anchored step reasoning (EASR) that forces every arithmetic step to cite a graph node; and weak-parser strong-reasoner alignment (WPSR) that uses a specialized table extractor only as a teacher of node attributes. On ChartQA, STEER reaches 82.70 average relaxed accuracy versus 80.16 for ChartGemma and 76.40 for a LLaVA-CoT backbone trained on the same mix. Gains widen on CharXiv reasoning (33.60 vs. 29.20 InternVL Chat V1.5) and ChartQAPro CoT (40.70 vs. 37.17 Qwen2-VL-7B), where OCR shortcuts disappear. Ablations show that dropping node serialization or numeric candidate constraints undoes most of the reasoning lift.

AI.tldr: STEER improves chart QA by enforcing structure-aware reasoning: binding chart elements into a graph, citing graph nodes for each calculation, and using a dedicated table extractor as a teacher. It freezes a vision encoder and adds three modules, achieving state-of-the-art results on ChartQA and gains on other benchmarks with ablations confirming the importance of node serialization and numeric constraints.
AI.motivation: Modern vision-language models treat charts as generic images, failing to expose coordinate frames and leading to plausible-but-read-from-chart hallucinations. There is a need for structure-aware reasoning that grounds arithmetic steps in chart components (ticks, legends, marks) to improve accuracy and reliability.
AI.method: Freeze a Llama-3.2-Vision encoder. Introduce three modules: (1) chart structure graph encoder (CSGE) that binds ticks, legend items, and marks into a graph; (2) evidence-anchored step reasoning (EASR) that requires every arithmetic step to cite a graph node; (3) weak-parser strong-reasoner alignment (WPSR) that uses a specialized table extractor as a teacher to supervise node attributes. Evaluations are conducted on ChartQA, CharXiv reasoning, and ChartQAPro CoT benchmarks.
AI.result: STEER achieves 82.70 average relaxed accuracy on ChartQA, surpassing ChartGemma (80.16) and LLaVA-CoT (76.40). Larger gains are observed on CharXiv reasoning (33.60 vs. 29.20) and ChartQAPro CoT (40.70 vs. 37.17). OCR shortcuts disappear under STEER. Ablations show that removing node serialization or numeric candidate constraints largely cancels the performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly encoding chart structure and enforcing evidence-based reasoning significantly improves chart QA performance and reduces reliance on OCR shortcuts. The three-module design is validated by ablations, highlighting the critical roles of node-level serialization and constrained numeric reasoning.

title: On the Potential of Multi-Task Learning in Predictive Process Monitoring
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60)
summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts how ongoing organizational processes unfold, enabling information systems to move beyond execution support toward proactive analysis and monitoring. Although deep learning has improved prediction accuracy in PPM, most approaches follow a single-task learning (STL) setup, training a separate model per task. This increases maintenance effort and overlooks potential synergies. Multi-task learning (MTL), which jointly learns multiple prediction targets in one model, offers a promising alternative, yet its effectiveness in PPM remains underexplored. It remains unclear whether and under which settings MTL improves upon STL, which prediction tasks benefit most from joint learning, which task combinations are particularly synergistic, and if and how tasks should be balanced. To fill this gap, we present the first comprehensive empirical study of MTL for PPM, evaluating a variety of task combinations, neural architectures, and optimization methods. Overall, our results position MTL as a strong paradigm for PPM: we see substantial improvements in next-activity prediction and inherent mitigation of class imbalance using MTL, while task balancing is especially critical under low-capacity models.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive empirical study of multi-task learning in Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM). Demonstrates substantial gains in next-activity prediction and inherent mitigation of class imbalance with MTL; emphasizes the importance of task balancing, especially for low-capacity models.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in understanding MTL's effectiveness for PPM: which task combinations are synergistic, which architectures and optimization methods work best, and how to balance tasks to maximize gains.
AI.method: Systematic empirical evaluation across diverse task combinations, neural architectures, and optimization strategies in PPM, comparing multi-task learning against single-task baselines and analyzing synergy and balancing effects.
AI.result: MTL yields substantial improvements in next-activity prediction and mitigates class imbalance; task balancing is particularly critical for low-capacity models.
AI.conclusion: MTL is a strong paradigm for PPM. Practitioners should consider MTL for multi-target PPM tasks, with careful attention to balancing; further work needed on identifying synergistic task combinations and effective balancing strategies.

title: FLoKD: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Federated Low-Rank LLM over Wireless Networks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of natural language processing tasks. However, conventional fine-tuning typically relies on centralized data collection, bringing in privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative LLM fine-tuning without sharing raw client data, but its deployment over bandwidth-constrained wireless networks is hindered by the communication overhead of model-parameter transmission. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces the number of trainable parameters, its communication cost still increases with model scale. Knowledge distillation avoids parameter sharing via output logits, but token-level logits in LLMs incur high communication cost due to sequence length and vocabulary size. Reducing logits lowers the cost but weakens supervision and degrades accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose FLoKD, an adaptive knowledge-distillation framework for federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs over wireless networks, which communicates intermediate LoRA activations as the distillation signal rather than logits or full parameters. Since transmitting all blocks over the entire public dataset remains costly, we further propose a transformer block importance scoring framework that selectively transmits the most informative blocks, and two dataset selection strategies that discard public samples deviating from the local data distribution and prioritise those most informative for distillation. Extensive experiments across multiple generative language datasets, including WikiText-103, PTB, and Dialog, demonstrate that our proposed framework reduces communication overhead by 50-65% while achieving rapid convergence to competitive perplexity compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: Adaptive federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs using distillation signals from intermediate LoRA activations, with selective transformer-block transmission and dataset selection to cut communication while preserving perplexity.
AI.motivation: Address privacy concerns and high communication costs in federated LLM fine-tuning over bandwidth-limited wireless networks; overcome LoRA's communication scaling and logits-based distillation inefficiency.
AI.method: FLoKD framework: adaptive knowledge-distillation that uses intermediate LoRA activations as the distillation signal; transformer-block importance scoring to selectively transmit the most informative blocks; two dataset-selection strategies to discard samples not aligned with local data or most informative for distillation.
AI.result: Achieves 50–65% reduction in communication overhead and rapid convergence to competitive perplexity across WikiText-103, PTB, and Dialog datasets compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Transmitting intermediate activations with selective block transmission enables efficient federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs over wireless networks while maintaining accuracy; demonstrates a viable path to privacy-preserving, communication-efficient FL for large models.

title: Decentralized Multi-Robot Task Allocation Under Degraded Communication: A Benchmark of Performance, Reliability, and Computation
summary: Selecting a decentralized Multi-Robot Task Allocation (MRTA) method for embedded deployment on autonomous platforms requires considering more than route performance alone. We benchmark six decentralized MRTA allocators (CBAA, ACBBA, PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, and DGA) in the Collaborative Visit (CV) scenario to characterize tradeoffs among MinMax and MinSum travel, communication robustness and demand, allocation reliability, computational burden, and scale sensitivity. The core study uses 500 paired ten-target instances across 25 ideal and degraded communication conditions spanning Bernoulli loss, Gilbert--Elliott loss, and Rayleigh fading, with additional campaigns examining pre-allocation, execution-integrated computation, and sensitivity to grid size, robot density, and target load. Across the 24 impaired core conditions, DGA and DMCHBA achieved the lowest mean MinMax travel at 24.49 and 24.78 steps, respectively. HIPC narrowly led mean MinSum travel at 66.95 steps, followed by DGA at 67.22, with both methods occupying the top two in every impaired condition. DMCHBA had the lowest publication intensity at 2.08 publications per team step. In ten-target pre-allocation, HIPC and DMCHBA remained viable and stable in every tested condition, while ACBBA, PI, and DGA lost stability or viability as communication degraded. Under ideal delivery, median full-protocol computation $\Cterm$ in the primary ten-target comparison ranged from 4.88 ms for DMCHBA to 1.346 s for DGA. Static route quality preserved DGA and DMCHBA as the leading MinMax methods, while DGA led MinSum at three of four target loads and HIPC led at 50 targets. Static and execution-integrated computation rankings diverged as task load increased.
