The results identify distinct allocator operating regions across route objective, communication behavior, reliability, and computational constraints.

AI.tldr: DGA and DMCHBA excel on MinMax; HIPC excels on MinSum; stability under degraded comms is allocator-dependent with distinct operating regions.
AI.motivation: Evaluate tradeoffs of decentralized MRTA allocators under realistic communication impairments to guide embedded deployments.
AI.method: Benchmarked six decentr MRTA allocators (CBAA, ACBBA, PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA) in the Collaborative Visit scenario using 500 paired ten-target instances across 25 ideal/degraded communication conditions (Bernoulli loss, Gilbert-Elliott loss, Rayleigh fading); additional campaigns on pre-allocation, execution-integrated computation, grid size, robot density, and target load; measured MinMax/MinSum travel, communication robustness, allocation reliability, computational burden, scale sensitivity; computed full-protocol computation times; observed performance across impaired conditions.
AI.result: DGA and DMCHBA achieved the lowest mean MinMax travel in impaired conditions (24.49 and 24.78 steps). HIPC narrowly led MinSum travel (66.95 steps), with DGA close (67.22); both top in every impaired condition. DMCHBA had the lowest publication intensity (2.08 pubs per team step). In ten-target pre-allocation, HIPC and DMCHBA remained viable; ACBBA, PI, and DGA degraded. Under ideal delivery, full-protocol computation ranged 4.88 ms (DMCHBA) to 1.346 s (DGA). Static routing preserved DGA/DMCHBA as leading MinMax; DGA led MinSum in 3 of 4 target loads, HIPC led at 50 targets. Rankings diverged between static and execution-integrated computation as task load increased.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized MRTA allocators exhibit distinct operating regions with tradeoffs among route quality, communication resilience, reliability, and compute, implying that allocator choice should align with deployment priorities (MinMax vs MinSum, tolerance to loss, and available computation).

title: Capability-Routed Visual Retrieval and Evidence Threading for Long-Context Document Question Answering
summary: Annual reports, diligence packs, and infographic dashboards bury numbers in page images: axes, cell grids, and footnotes that OCR pipelines flatten and that page-level visual retrievers still treat as interchangeable in-context examples. We keep a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct generator and a ColPali / VisRAG-Ret page index, and insert three modules. A capability-aware visual router (CAVR) tags each retrieved page as text, table, chart, layout, or mixed and mixes specialist experts before generation. Weak-to-strong page selection (WSPS) distils a frozen 7B answerability teacher into a 3B selection head so ranking is no longer a single InfoNCE score. Visual evidence threading (VET) builds layout-anchored paths of length at most three and lets the generator read the thread rather than a flat top-$k$ list. On gold-page DocVQA / ChartQA / InfographicVQA the 7B system reaches 96.3 / 90.1 / 85.4. Under the VisRAG top-3 protocol the mean generation accuracy is 62.74 versus 59.39 for the same backbone with concatenation. On MMLongBench-Doc retrieve-then-read, F1 moves from 19.2 to 22.6 and multi-page accuracy from 16.4 to 21.2. ViDoRe nDCG@5 after WSPS reranking is 83.6, with TAT-DQA financial reports at 70.4.

AI.tldr: Modular capability-aware retrieval+reading pipeline improves document QA on infographics, charts, and long documents by tagging pages with CAVR, distilling WSPS selection, and threading visual evidence via VET; shows gains over baselines on DocVQA-style tasks and long-form datasets.
AI.motivation: OCR-driven page flattening obscures structure in annual reports, diligence packs, and infographics. The goal is to preserve content typology (text/table/chart/layout) and build evidence-aware reading paths to improve answerability and accuracy.
AI.method: Three modules added to a frozen 7B generator with VisRAG-Ret index: (1) CAVR capability-aware visual router tagging pages as text, table, chart, layout, or mixed and fusing specialist experts before generation; (2) WSPS weak-to-strong page selection distills a 7B teacher into a 3B selection head for ranking beyond a single InfoNCE score; (3) VET visual evidence threading constructs layout-anchored paths (length ≤3) so the generator reads a thread instead of a flat top-k; evaluated on gold-page DocVQA/ChartQA/InfographicVQA, MMLongBench-Doc, with VisRAG top-3 and ViDoRe nDCG@5.
AI.result: Gold-page DocVQA/ChartQA/InfographicVQA: 96.3, 90.1, 85.4 accuracy. VisRAG top-3: mean generation accuracy 62.74 vs 59.39 with concatenation. MMLongBench-Doc: F1 22.6 vs 19.2; multi-page accuracy 21.2 vs 16.4. ViDoRe nDCG@5: 83.6; TAT-DQA financial reports: 70.4.
AI.conclusion: A modular, capability-aware architecture with CAVR, WSPS, and VET yields notable improvements in document-level question answering and long-form retrieval-to-read tasks, demonstrating better utilization of page structure and evidence threading over flat retrieval schemes.

title: One Spectrum, Two Resources: Data-Memory Scaling in Autoregressive Prediction
summary: How much learned memory is needed to benefit from more data? We show that the two resources are governed by one predictive-energy spectrum in a positive-entropy autoregressive retrieval source. Each coordinate contributes its query probability times the squared radius of its unknown logit. Writing $μ$ for the resulting energy spectrum, we prove the minimax law $\mathfrak R^*_{\rm value}(n,B)\asymp_R Φ_μ(n^{-1})+Φ_μ(τ_B), Φ_μ(t)=\int\min\{x,t\}\,μ(\mathrm dx),$ for $n$ prediction blocks and a learned state with at most $2^B$ values. Data set the resolution $1/n$; memory sets the level $τ_B$ reached by optimal bit allocation. The complete curve also recovers the positive spectrum. Energy-dimension pairing is essential: two causal sources with identical block-energy and block-dimension marginals have different data and memory exponents. A masked query-key attention head learns the route and values, realizing the law with explicit routing, format, and arithmetic errors. Further results give exponent-adaptive allocation, finite-precision realization, and compute-precision laws under two-sided arithmetic assumptions. Experiments recover the data-memory collapse and coupling exponents, explain the routing and allocation mechanisms, and examine weight-only quantization across six pretrained-model scales.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a minimax data-memory trade-off for learned memory in autoregressive models via a predictive-energy spectrum, showing data and memory are governed by a single spectrum and that energy-dimension pairing dictates distinct exponents even for sources with identical margins.
AI.motivation: Quantify how data and learned memory scale together in autoregressive systems and derive principled laws governing data-memory trade-offs, routing, and precision.
AI.method: Introduce an energy spectrum μ based on query probabilities and squared logit radii. Derive the minimax risk R^*_{value}(n,B) ~ Φ_μ(n^{-1}) + Φ_μ(τ_B) with Φ_μ(t)=∫ min{x,t} μ(dx). Analyze a masked query-key attention head implementing optimal routing; study exponent-adaptive allocation, finite- and compute-precision laws; provide explicit routing and arithmetic error characterizations.
AI.result: Establishes a data-memory collapse governed by the energy spectrum; demonstrates that two causal sources with identical block-energy and block-dimension marginals yield different data/memory exponents; validates routing and allocation mechanisms; shows results across six pretrained-model scales and provides exponent-adaptive and finite-precision laws.
AI.conclusion: Energy-dimension pairing is central to understanding data-memory interplay; the framework yields explicit routing, allocation rules, and precision laws, enabling principled design of memory and computation budgets in learned autoregressive systems.

title: $τ$-Elicitation: Benchmarking multi-turn entity extraction in voice agents
summary: Voice agents often need to collect names, addresses, identifiers, dates, and times exactly, yet end-to-end benchmarks obscure where capture fails. We introduce $τ$-Elicitation, a 200-task voice benchmark spanning 10 entity types, controlled difficulty, caller realisms, and three environments. A matched text agent passes all tasks, but four voice configurations achieve robust exact success from 0.14 to 0.41. Agents increase verification for hard and unfamiliar entities and sometimes for incorrect captures, but not for their weakest caller voice; only 24 to 37 percent of verified errors are repaired. A scaffold that prescribes spelling, read-back, correction, and confirmation raises robust Pass$^3$ by 14 to 31 points, at a cost of 21 to 28 seconds per call. Realisms such as spelling variations and restarts do not detectably affect exact success; mispronunciation increases repair effort. These results identify strategy selection and successful recovery as the central bottlenecks in exact spoken entity collection.

AI.tldr: 200-task τ-Elicitation benchmark shows bottlenecks in exact data capture by voice agents; scaffolds improve robustness at cost; broad realism effects are limited.
AI.motivation: End-to-end benchmarks miss where capture fails; need granular evaluation of exact data collection across entities, dialects, and caller realism.
AI.method: Evaluate 200 tasks across 10 entity types and three environments; include matched text agent as upper bound; test three or four voice configurations; introduce Pass^3 scaffold with spelling/read-back/correction/confirmation.
AI.result: Robust exact success ranges 0.14–0.41 across voice configurations; verification increases for hard/unfamiliar entities and some incorrect captures; 24–37% of verified errors are repaired; Pass^3 raises robust success by 14–31 points at 21–28 s per call; spelling variations/restarts do not affect exact success; mispronunciation increases repair effort.
AI.conclusion: Strategy selection and recovery are central bottlenecks; scaffolds can raise robustness but with latency cost; future work should optimize error detection, repair strategies, and adaptivity to caller voice.

title: Learning In-Hand Object Reaching to General 6D Poses
summary: In-hand manipulation allows multi-fingered dexterous hands to reconfigure grasped objects without releasing and regrasping them. This improves manipulation efficiency by reducing repeated grasp acquisition and large arm motions. However, most learning-based methods focus on reorientation, continuous rotation, or translation, whereas many tasks require joint control of object position and orientation. We formulate this capability as in-hand 6D object pose reaching: starting from an existing grasp, coordinated finger motions move the object to a palm-relative target pose. We present POISE (Palm-relative Object reaching In SE(3)), a sim-to-real reinforcement learning framework for this task. POISE combines diverse stable-grasp initialization, goal- and geometry-conditioned control, an adaptive 6D goal curriculum, and a compact reward scheme for pose reaching and grasp preservation. In simulation, diverse initialization raises held-out-grasp success from 40.1% to 51.5% and post-drop recovery from 33.8% to 72.9%; the curriculum raises full-range success from 6.2% to 59.5%. On hardware, the grasp-maintenance reward improves three-target sequence success from 20% to 80%. In real-world experiments, POISE reaches successive 6D targets without manual reset across multiple object geometries and wrist orientations, and recovers from external disturbances. To support further research in dexterous manipulation, we will release our code at https://junxiaolin.github.io/poise-website/.

AI.tldr: A sim-to-real reinforcement learning framework (POISE) enabling in-hand 6D object pose reaching from an existing grasp, with a palm-relative SE(3) goal, large gains in stability and recovery via diverse grasp initializations and curriculum, achieving robust hardware transfer and no-reset operation.
AI.motivation: Current dexterous manipulation methods focus on reorientation/translation; many tasks require simultaneous control of object position and orientation in-hand. There is a need for joint in-hand 6D pose control that is robust to grasp variations and disturbances and transferable from simulation to real robots.
AI.method: POISE: Palm-relative Object reaching In SE(3). A sim-to-real RL framework that learns coordinated finger motions to move a grasped object to a palm-relative 6D target. Key components include diverse stable-grasp initialization, goal- and geometry-conditioned policies, an adaptive 6D goal curriculum, and a compact reward design emphasizing pose reaching and grasp preservation. Training in simulation with diverse initializations; transfer to real hardware with grasp-maintenance rewards and disturbance handling.
AI.result: In simulation, held-out-grasp success improves from 40.1% to 51.5%; post-drop recovery from 33.8% to 72.9%; full-range success with curriculum rises from 6.2% to 59.5%. On hardware, three-target sequence success with grasp-maintenance reward grows from 20% to 80%. Real-world experiments demonstrate sequential 6D target reaching without manual resets across multiple objects and wrist orientations and resilience to disturbances.
AI.conclusion: POISE enables robust, autonomous 6D in-hand pose reaching with sim-to-real transfer, broadening dexterous manipulation capabilities and enabling longer-horizon tasks without manual resets; code will be released to advance research.

title: Frame-Synchronous Hand Gesture Detection by Projected Winding Order
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Implementation, evaluation and figure-generating code: https://github.com/Amey-Thakur/GESTURE-FX. Live deployment: https://amey-thakur.github.io/GESTURE-FX/. The evaluation runs in a browser against the shipped modules, so every figure can be reproduced by opening a page
summary:
Gesture recognition on video is normally posed as classification: label each frame, then act on the label. That is adequate for control, where a command may be obeyed several frames late without a user noticing, and inadequate for synchronisation, where an output must be aligned to the frame on which the gesture physically occurred. We take the synchronisation problem for one common movement, the rotation of an open hand about its long axis, and show that it admits an exact solution needing no classifier, no training data and no calibration.
  Let s be the normalised two-dimensional cross product of the two palm edges at the wrist and the outer knuckles, under the projection the camera already performs. We prove that s factorises as k(theta)cos(theta) with |k| > 0 everywhere, so s vanishes exactly when the palm is edge-on and its sign tracks the face presented to the camera. Detection is therefore a zero crossing of one scalar, which yields an instant rather than an interval, and we prove the criterion invariant to image mirroring, hand scale and handedness, all from its algebraic form rather than from the landmark estimator.
  A two-handed interaction uses four fingertips as a window onto a restyled version of the same scene. We give a coverage predicate that stays correct when the hands cross, where the usual triangulation does not, and derive each free parameter of the three stylisation operators from a noise statistic rather than by inspection.
  Against a corpus with exact ground truth the criterion detects 95% of flips with no false positive in 240 near-miss sequences, and places each within 6.7 ms on average of the instant it occurred, a sixth of the interval at which the hand is observed, against 23.0 ms for reporting the bracketing sample. Reporting an event more finely than one samples follows from treating a gesture as the zero of a continuous quantity rather than a label.

AI.tldr: Proposes a classifier-free, exact synchronization method for a common hand gesture rotation, using a scalar s that zero-crosses exactly when the gesture occurs; robust to mirroring, scale, and handedness, with high timing precision and extension to two-handed interactions.
AI.motivation: Classifying gestures is often adequate for control but insufficient for precise temporal alignment. The work addresses exact synchronization (instantaneous event detection) for a common hand motion.
AI.method: Define s as the normalized 2D cross product of palm edges at the wrist and outer knuckles under camera projection. Prove s factorizes as k(theta) cos(theta) with |k|>0, so s vanishes when the palm is edge-on and flips sign with facing direction. Detect zero-crossings of s as instantaneous events, invariant to image mirroring, scale, and handedness. Extend to two-handed interactions using four fingertips and introduce a coverage predicate that remains valid when hands cross; derive stylisation parameters from a noise statistic rather than inspection.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a ground-truth corpus shows 95% detection of flips with no false positives in 240 near-miss sequences. Timing accuracy is 6.7 ms on average after the true event, far earlier than the bracketing sample at 23.0 ms. The approach enables precise event reporting by treating a gesture as the zero of a continuous quantity rather than a label.
AI.conclusion: The criterion provides an exact, training-free, calibration-free mechanism for instantaneous gesture event detection, with robust invariances and a principled extension to two-handed scenarios; it shifts synchronization from classification to precise zero-crossing detection.

title: Pretraining for Sample-Efficient Neural Interfaces
comment: 15 pages, including references and appendix; 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/bentang18/MAPA
summary: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) decode neural activity to restore lost function. Typically, training a high-performance neural decoder requires a large labeled dataset to be collected from every new subject. One way to reduce the labeled data cost is self-supervised pretraining, which learns general neural representations from unlabeled recordings that accumulate across subjects. However, for intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) recordings, self-supervised learning has been challenging due to differences in contact placement and neuroanatomy between subjects. We propose MAPA, an otherwise vanilla masked autoencoder with two spatial encodings, an anatomical region embedding and a relative positional encoding, which together enable it to learn neural representations that transfer to unseen subjects and across various tasks. MAPA sets a new state of the art across all three regimes of the Neuroprobe benchmark without fine-tuning: within-session, cross-session, and cross-subject. In the cross-subject regime, a linear probe on MAPA's features needs only ${\sim}164$ labeled trials to reach the accuracy that takes 3,500 without pretraining. Our results show that self-supervised pretraining can scale across heterogeneous iEEG recordings and reduce the labeled data needed for accurate decoding in new subjects.

AI.tldr: A masked autoencoder with anatomical region and relative position encodings learns transferable iEEG representations, achieving state-of-the-art transfer across within-session, cross-session, and cross-subject tasks with minimal labeled data for cross-subject decoding.
AI.motivation: Reduce labeled data requirements for neural decoders in BCIs by leveraging self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled iEEG data, addressing subject-specific heterogeneity in contact placement and neuroanatomy.
AI.method: MAPA is a vanilla masked autoencoder augmented with two spatial encodings—an anatomical region embedding and a relative positional encoding—to learn neural representations from unlabeled iEEG recordings. It is evaluated on the Neuroprobe benchmark in three regimes (within-session, cross-session, cross-subject) without fine-tuning; decoding performance is assessed with linear probes on the learned features.
AI.result: MAPA achieves new state-of-the-art across all three regimes without fine-tuning. In the cross-subject regime, a linear probe on MAPA features requires ~164 labeled trials to reach the accuracy that would require 3,500 trials without pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining with MAPA scales across heterogeneous iEEG recordings and substantially reduces the labeled data needed for accurate decoding in new subjects, supporting transferability across tasks and subjects.

title: Identity Is More Than Recall: A Benchmark for Persistent Identity in Deployed AI Agents
comment: 27 pages, 2 figures, including 18 pages of supplementary material
summary: Persistent agents need evaluations that distinguish identity facts they can recall from those they express and enact. We introduce PAI-Bench, a provider-neutral benchmark for fidelity to a versioned, update-governed identity contract. It separates recall, composition, behavioral enactment, resistance, persistence, lineage, and role-conditioned updates while keeping scoring oracles outside the target process. Two frozen campaigns cover sixteen synthetic profiles, thirty-two probes, and three independently initialized target configurations, yielding 1,536 retained responses. A judge-independent literal audit finds direct-parent identifiers in 48/48 atomic responses but only 1/48 implicit self-portraits. On eight profiles, explicit field cues increase joint presence of three identity identifiers from 0/8 to 7/8 under the same four-sentence instruction. A separate startup body-label substitution increases full-designation presence from 1/8 to 7/8 while parents remain absent. These contrasts reveal prompt-dependent component selection and component-specific sensitivity to startup cues in the tested deployments. Replaying identical factorial responses also yields a Claude headline mean 12.5 percentage points below Astra's, demonstrating evaluator sensitivity separately from target behavior. The studies use single target samples per condition, with post-hoc audits and follow-ups. PAI-Bench provides a reproducible evaluation protocol for measuring factual availability, identity expression, and behavioral enactment as distinct aspects of identity-contract fidelity.

AI.tldr: PAI-Bench is a reproducible, provider-neutral benchmark to measure fidelity of persistent agents to a versioned identity contract across recall, expression, and enactment, highlighting prompt-driven component selection and evaluator sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To disentangle factual recall from identity expression and behavioral enactment, enabling objective evaluation of persistent agents' adherence to an identity contract over updates, while keeping scoring external to the target model.
AI.method: Two frozen campaigns with 16 synthetic profiles, 32 probes, and 3 independently initialized target configurations, yielding 1,536 responses; judge-independent audits; explicit field cues; startup body-label substitutions; factorial responses; cross-model comparisons (Claude vs Astra); single-target-per-condition design; post-hoc audits and follow-ups.
AI.result: Direct-parent identifiers observed in all atomic responses; implicit self-portraits are rare (1/48); explicit cues increase presence of identity identifiers (0/8 to 7/8); startup cue increases full-designation presence (1/8 to 7/8); prompt-dependent component selection and sensitivity to startup cues; evaluator sensitivity evidenced by Claude vs Astra differences; limitations include single target samples per condition and post-hoc auditing.
AI.conclusion: PAI-Bench provides a reproducible protocol to measure factual availability, identity expression, and behavioral enactment as distinct aspects of identity-contract fidelity.

title: When Do Learned Priors Help Visual Inertial Estimation? A Controlled Study of Prior Integration, Calibration, Initialization, and Backend Consistency
summary: Learned components are increasingly integrated into geometric visual--inertial estimators to provide motion, depth, bias, uncertainty, or confidence cues. Yet it remains unclear whether gains arise from useful learned priors or from changes in the backend, calibration, initialization, temporal association, or evaluation gauge. We present a controlled framework for learning-augmented visual--inertial estimation that separates fusion gain from the incremental value of a learned prior and evaluates four evidence layers: local motion consistency, global trajectory accuracy, physical-state correctness, and numerical consistency. We instantiate the framework with a MonoViT-based monocular motion prior added as a local relative-motion factor to an unchanged VINS backend. We compare Original VINS and learned-prior VINS under matched sensor streams, timestamps, initialization, frontend/backend settings, and camera--IMU extrinsics, while probing calibration, initialization, state coupling, scale, bundle adjustment, and loop closure. On KITTI, with fixed reference extrinsics, translation APE RMSE is 31.4 m for Original VINS and 31.8 m with the learned prior. Across four recordings, the prior changes mean APE by only -0.2%, while a five-times-higher weight worsens it by 8.2%. Online extrinsic updates increase mean APE by 45.7% and 52.1%, respectively, while mean RPE changes by less than 2%. These results show that fusion performance alone cannot establish the value of learned priors. Reliable evaluation requires same-backend controls and joint analysis of prior compatibility, calibration, initialization, global drift, physical-state error, and backend consistency.

AI.tldr: Presents a controlled framework to evaluate learned priors in visual–inertial estimation and shows that fusion gains do not guarantee improved performance; robust evaluation requires same-backend controls and joint analysis across multiple evidence layers.
AI.motivation: Clarify whether improvements from learned priors come from the priors themselves or from changes in backend calibration, initialization, and evaluation methods; establish a rigorous evaluation protocol for learning-augmented VINS.
AI.method: Introduce a controlled framework with four evidence layers (local motion consistency, global trajectory accuracy, physical-state correctness, numerical consistency). Instantiate with a MonoViT-based monocular motion prior added as a local relative-motion factor to an unchanged VINS backend. Conduct matched comparisons between Original VINS and learned-prior VINS under identical sensor streams, timestamps, initializations, frontend/backend settings, and camera–IMU extrinsics, while varying calibration, initialization, state coupling, scale, bundle adjustment, and loop closure. Evaluate on KITTI dataset using translation APE RMSE and RPE." ,
AI.result: On KITTI, with fixed extrinsics, translation APE RMSE is 31.4 m for Original VINS and 31.8 m with the learned prior. Across four recordings, the prior changes mean APE by -0.2%, while increasing a five-fold weight worsens it by 8.2%. Online extrinsic updates raise mean APE by 45.7% and 52.1%, respectively; mean RPE changes are <2%. These findings indicate that fusion performance alone does not establish the value of learned priors, and reliable evaluation must control backends and jointly assess prior compatibility, calibration, initialization, global drift, physical-state error, and backend consistency.
AI.conclusion: Fusion gains from learned priors do not guarantee improved VINS performance when backend/configuration changes are controlled; rigorous, multi-layer evaluation is essential to determine the true value of learned priors and avoid misattribution.

title: CANAL: Channel-Aware Noise Allocation for Differentially Private Feature Distillation in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Medical image segmentation needs diverse training data, but hospitals hold complementary scans they cannot share for privacy and regulatory reasons. Knowledge distillation can bridge this gap by exporting learned feature representations instead of images, but those representations still encode patient-specific anatomy and remain vulnerable to membership-inference and feature-inversion attacks. Adding calibrated Gaussian noise restores a differential-privacy guarantee, yet three issues have been overlooked. First, prior DP feature-distillation pipelines re-sample noise at every student iteration, so each patient image is released many times and the privacy cost composes over those releases, growing by orders of magnitude. We present a sample-once-per-image release, realized by a single precomputation pass, under which each patient contributes one release. Second, uniform noise is wasteful because channels differ in task importance. Using task-gradient energy as the importance measure, we derive CANAL, a closed-form water-filling allocation that gives important channels proportionally less noise, and prove it strictly minimizes importance-weighted distortion at a fixed budget. Third, the clipping caps and importance scores that drive the allocation are themselves data-dependent, so releasing them in the clear silently breaks the guarantee. We give a DP-honest budget split that charges each to the privacy budget, so the reported epsilon is the true epsilon. Across three medical segmentation benchmarks spanning dermoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound, CANAL retains more task-relevant signal than uniform noise at the same privacy budget.

AI.tldr: CANAL: sample-once-per-image DP feature distillation for medical segmentation with channel-wise noise via water-filling based on task-gradient energy; DP-honest budget split; empirical gains on dermoscopy/colonoscopy/ultrasound.
AI.motivation: Address privacy risks in collaborative medical imaging via knowledge distillation. Prior DP feature-distillation re-sampled noise per iteration, used uniform noise across channels, and used data-dependent clipping that leaks budget. Need single-release, channel-aware noise, and honest accounting.
AI.method: Single precomputation pass releases one DP-perturbed feature per image. CANAL uses closed-form water-filling to allocate Gaussian noise across feature channels based on task-gradient energy, giving important channels less noise. Use DP-honest budget split to report true epsilon; provide proofs of optimality (minimizes importance-weighted distortion under fixed budget).
AI.result: Outperforms uniform-noise baselines in retaining task-relevant signal at the same privacy budget across three medical segmentation benchmarks (dermoscopy, colonoscopy, ultrasound).
AI.conclusion: CANAL enables a tighter privacy-utility trade-off for DP feature-distillation in medical segmentation, with a practical, principled, and auditable privacy accounting framework; promising for multi-institution collaborations.

title: A Three-Axis Stress Test of LLM vs Classical ML for Network Intrusion Detection under Distribution Shift and Adversarial Evasion
summary: Large language models are increasingly benchmarked against classical machine learning for network intrusion detection (NIDS), almost always using same-dataset evaluation, and that protocol turns out to be incomplete. Evaluating XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA on two independently collected NetFlow v2 networks across three axes (same-dataset performance, cross-dataset transfer, and adversarial evasion) reveals no universal winner. The two models are statistically tied same-dataset. XGBoost wins decisively under cross-dataset distribution shift, by 15 points of F1 and 25 points of balanced accuracy; on the target network RoBERTa-LoRA's false positive rate reaches 0.78, leaving it barely above chance despite a superficially moderate F1. RoBERTa-LoRA wins decisively under adversarial evasion, by roughly 17 points of F1 at a representative mid-range perturbation strength, while both models hold false positive rates below 0.01 throughout. The model an evaluator would recommend therefore depends entirely on which axis is tested, not on same-dataset accuracy alone. A staged feature-leakage ablation improves cross-dataset transfer non-monotonically, indicating the leakage signal is distributed across the feature representation rather than confined to a few columns, and cross-dataset transfer between our two networks is strongly directional. These results argue for evaluating NIDS models along multiple independent robustness axes, and with more than one metric per axis.

AI.tldr: No universal winner between XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA for NIDS; performance depends on evaluation axis. Cross-dataset transfer favors XGBoost; adversarial evasion favors RoBERTa-LoRA; same-dataset performance is tied. Multi-axis, multi-metric evaluation is necessary for robust NIDS assessment.
AI.motivation: Challenge the dominance of same-dataset evaluation in NIDS and demonstrate that robustness and generalization require multi-axis assessment across different dataset shifts and adversarial conditions.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA on two independently collected NetFlow v2 networks across three axes: same-dataset performance, cross-dataset transfer (distribution shift), and adversarial evasion. Includes a staged feature-leakage ablation to study leakage effects. Metrics reported include F1, balanced accuracy, and false positive rate. Cross-dataset transfer is characterized as strongly directional.
AI.result: On the same dataset, XGBoost and RoBERTa-LoRA are statistically tied. Under cross-dataset distribution shift, XGBoost wins decisively (≈+15 F1, +25 points balanced accuracy); RoBERTa-LoRA suffers high FPR on the target network (≈0.78). Under adversarial evasion, RoBERTa-LoRA wins decisively (~+17 points F1 at mid-range perturbation), with both models maintaining FPR < 0.01. No universal winner; the preferred model depends on tested axis. A staged feature-leakage ablation shows non-monotonic transfer improvements and indicates leakage is distributed across features; cross-dataset transfer between networks is directional.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of NIDS models should be performed along multiple independent robustness axes, with more than one metric per axis. Cross-dataset transfer and feature leakage analyses reveal nuanced, axis-dependent performance, challenging the reliance on same-dataset accuracy as a sole performance surrogate.

title: Solar Intelligence
summary: Solar energy decision support is fragmented across dashboards that provide data without explanation, research papers are slow to parse, and general-purpose language models are not solar domain specific and answer without evidence. This paper introduces Solar Intelligence, a hybrid retrieval-augmented framework that unifies structured solar analytics, evidence-grounded scientific question answering, and machine learning forecasting in one system. The platform integrates daily NASA POWER solar and meteorological data, Biosphere 2 ground-sensor readings, and a curated corpus of research papers and institutional reports. Structured queries use DuckDB SQL; scientific questions are answered by a hybrid retriever that fuses BM25 and ChromaDB dense embeddings via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with responses grounded through a language model (llama3.2:3b). An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model produces daily forecasts of irradiance, temperature, and wind speed. The system is exposed via FastAPI, Streamlit, and an MCP server, so it can be used as an application, an API service, or an agent tool - by students, researchers, and energy analysts.

AI.tldr: Hybrid retrieval-augmented Solar Intelligence platform unifies structured solar analytics, evidence-grounded QA, and ML forecasting using DuckDB, BM25+ChromaDB with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, Llama3.2-3b grounding, and XGBoost forecasts; deployable via API and UI for researchers and analysts.
AI.motivation: Solar decision support is fragmented across dashboards and literature; there is a need for an integrated, evidence-grounded, domain-specific system that combines structured analytics, literature-backed QA, and forecasting.
AI.method: Integrates NASA POWER solar and meteorological data, Biosphere 2 sensor readings, and curated research corpus. Structured queries executed via DuckDB SQL. Scientific questions are answered by a Hybrid Retriever that fuses BM25 and ChromaDB dense embeddings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with responses grounded by a language model (Llama3.2-3b). Daily forecasts produced with XGBoost for irradiance, temperature, and wind speed. Exposed through FastAPI, Streamlit, and an MCP server for use as app, API, or agent tool.
AI.result: Conceptual architecture and workflow demonstrated; evidence-grounded QA and daily meteorological forecasts are achievable within the integrated platform.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid retrieval-augmented solar intelligence framework can streamline decision support by unifying data analytics, literature-backed insights, and forecast capabilities in a single, accessible system.

title: Force-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hybrid Sensorless Force Estimation for Wheeled-Legged Loco-Manipulation
summary: Force-controlled loco-manipulation requires a whole-body policy to coordinate locomotion and arm motion while regulating end-effector interaction forces. This is challenging under floating-base dynamics and changing support contacts, particularly when end-effector force/torque sensing is unavailable for control. This paper presents a force-aware reinforcement learning approach with hybrid sensorless force estimation for wheeled-legged loco-manipulation. The proposed method provides a structured estimate of the end-effector force as an explicit policy observation, enabling force-guided contact behavior without using an end-effector force/torque sensor for control. The force estimate is obtained by combining generalized momentum observation, contact-constrained wrench projection, and temporal residual learning: the model-based components extract the physically structured part of the whole-body disturbance, while the residual network compensates the remaining motion-dependent bias. The estimated force is integrated into a mode-conditioned whole-body policy with an axis-wise force/position selector, allowing free-space motion, pure force regulation, and hybrid force/position control within one controller. Simulation results demonstrate improved sensorless force estimation and force-control performance. Hardware experiments further validate the proposed controller through quantitative valve-rotation and hybrid wiping evaluations, together with force-guided door opening and zero-force human-guided motion on a real wheeled-legged platform.

AI.tldr: Sensorless, force-aware whole-body policy for wheeled-legged loco-manipulation using a hybrid physics-ML force estimator and mode-conditioned control.
AI.motivation: Enable robust force-controlled loco-manipulation under floating base and changing contacts without relying on end-effector force sensing.
AI.method: Hybrid force estimation: generalized momentum observation + contact-constrained wrench projection + temporal residual learning; integrate into a mode-conditioned whole-body policy with axis-wise force/position selector enabling free-space motion, force regulation, and hybrid force/position control.
AI.result: Improved sensorless force estimation and force-control in simulation and hardware; demonstrated on a wheeled-legged platform with tasks like valve rotation, wiping, door opening, and zero-force human-guided motion.
AI.conclusion: Shows practical viability of sensorless force-aware loco-manipulation, combining physics-based components and learning residuals to enable versatile end-effector force control without force/torque sensors.

title: SomBench: Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Machine Learning in Lunar Science
summary: Lunar orbital missions, such as Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Kaguya/SELENE, Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory, and Lunar Prospector, among others, provide rich multi-instrument observations, but their heterogeneity in sampling, projection, and conventions limits reproducible machine learning (ML). We introduce SomBench, a unified, spatially-aligned, ML-ready lunar dataset aggregating 30+ co-registered layers from ten instruments across four missions, spanning 1 meter to 20 kilometer/pixel and covering 82 degree latitude in 90 Lunar Transverse Mercator zones with two polar stereographic caps. An image-anchored tiling pipeline yields pretraining-ready multimodal tile views with leakage-safe splits, distributed as netCDF with Parquet catalogs. An application benchmark suite spans impact processes, volcanic history, and polar volatiles. Baseline experiments with ResNet-50 and SwinV2-B models confirm that each benchmark task is learnable from the released inputs, establishing reference points for future model development.

AI.tldr: SomBench is a unified, ML-ready lunar dataset that aggregates 30+ co-registered layers from 10 instruments across four missions, spanning scales from 1 m to 20 km per pixel, and covering 82° latitude with LTM zones and polar caps. It provides an image-anchored tiling pipeline, leakage-safe splits, netCDF/Parquet packaging, and a benchmark suite; baseline models show learnability across tasks.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneity in sampling, projection, and conventions across lunar missions hinders reproducible machine learning. A unified, spatially aligned, ML-ready dataset is needed to enable robust cross-mission analyses and model development.
AI.method: Aggregate 30+ co-registered layers from 10 instruments across four missions into a single, spatially aligned dataset; span scales 1 m to 20 km/pixel; map to 82° latitude in 90 Lunar Transverse Mercator zones with two polar caps; implement an image-anchored tiling pipeline to produce pretraining-ready multimodal tile views; enforce leakage-safe splits; package as netCDF with Parquet catalogs; develop an application benchmark suite on impact processes, volcanic history, and polar volatiles; validate with baseline experiments using ResNet-50 and SwinV2-B.
AI.result: A unified, ML-ready lunar dataset (SomBench) with 30+ co-registered layers from 10 instruments across 4 missions, multi-scale alignment, tiling pipeline, leakage-safe splits, and benchmark tasks. Baseline experiments demonstrate that each benchmark task is learnable from the provided inputs.
AI.conclusion: SomBench provides a reproducible, cross-mission ML resource for lunar science, establishing reference points for future model development and enabling robust multimodal analyses across missions.

title: Adaptive Phase-Switching for Communication-Efficient Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, 7 appendices. Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society. Code and analysis data: https://github.com/jerryadamsfranklin/fedlora-protocols
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models with low-rank adaptation reduces per-client trainable parameters, but client-to-server communication remains the dominant cost. Existing accounting for federated LoRA protocols omits the asymmetric transition round when a protocol changes aggregation mode, and reports savings that ignore grouped-query attention shapes. This paper measures per-round upload and download bytes for a bidirectional B-only federated LoRA protocol and places five methods, three from prior work, on a single communication-quality frontier. The frontier has a knee, which an adaptive phase-switching aggregator, ReverseAdaptive, locates by monitoring the relative improvement in global training loss against a dimensionless threshold rather than by fixing a phase boundary in advance. On TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat with Alpaca, ReverseAdaptive attains 40.5 percent measured round-trip savings over FLoRA at a held-out instruction-following loss cost of 0.0063. It outperforms FFA-LoRA, which freezes the first of the two LoRA factors at initialization, by 0.0182 in held-out loss, more than twenty times the largest per-method seed standard deviation on that metric, so learning that factor before freezing it produces better adapters. The same threshold transfers across model scales without retuning, and the quality cost of the transition is stable across the two datasets tested.

AI.tldr: Adaptive phase-switching in federated LoRA (ReverseAdaptive) reduces round-trip communication by ~40% while maintaining or improving held-out performance across models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning of large language models with LoRA lowers trainable parameters but is dominated by client-server communication. Existing accounting omits asymmetric transitions and grouped-query attention shapes, complicating fair comparison across methods. A unified, quality-aware frontier is needed to assess compression vs. performance.
AI.method: Introduce ReverseAdaptive, an adaptive aggregator that locates the frontier knee by monitoring relative global loss improvement against a dimensionless threshold, enabling automatic phase switching between aggregation modes. The study measures per-round upload/download bytes for a bidirectional B-only federated LoRA protocol and compares five methods (three from prior work) on a single communication-quality frontier. Evaluation uses TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat with Alpaca, with threshold transfer across model scales.
AI.result: On TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat with Alpaca, ReverseAdaptive achieves 40.5% measured round-trip savings over FLoRA. It attains a held-out instruction-following loss cost of 0.0063 and outperforms FFA-LoRA by 0.0182 in held-out loss. The improvement is more than twenty times the largest per-method seed standard deviation, indicating strong stability. The same threshold transfers across model scales without retuning, and the quality cost of the transition is consistent across two tested datasets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive phase-switching (ReverseAdaptive) effectively identifies the knee on the communication-quality frontier, delivering substantial communication savings with stable, improved model quality. A dimensionless loss-improvement threshold enables robust cross-scale transfer and reduces reliance on fixed phase boundaries; learning or freezing LoRA factors in a data-driven manner yields gains.

title: Safety as a Constraint: Fine-Tuning a LLM Recommender to Explain Itself
summary: Traditional recommender systems are typically trained to predict what item users will interact with next, but not why. However, offering personalized evidence for why a user might like the predicted item is an important way to enhance the service and to raise the likelihood that the user will be genuinely interested in the recommendation. This service can be delivered by integrating a frontier-model call into the member-facing pipeline, but it will add extra cost and latency. In this paper, we train a recommender LLM to generate personalized explanations for its reccomendation, based on the user's watching history at a large video streaming service. We impose two requirements on the generated explanation: it must be faithful to the elements of the shows it links, and it must be strictly non-harmful to the user. To this end, we first train two LLM-judge reward models covering three specific criteria, and propose constrained GRPO to incorporate these different criteria. On a held-out real-world testing set, our fine-tuned model improves the all-three-criteria PASS rate rises from 0.649 to 0.956 under our own judges and from 0.677 to 0.931 under an independent judge, where as the frontier generator performs similar to the untuned recommender baseline. We conduct further experiments to show that the model's language and recommendation abilities remain unchanged. Based on these results, we conclude that an LLM-based recommender can be fine-tuned on other complex tasks without compromising its original recommendation performance, thus provide insights for further agentic user interface powered by a single model.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning a recommender LLM with constrained GRPO and LLM-judge rewards yields explanations that are faithful and non-harmful, improving evaluation PASS rates without degrading recommendation ability.
AI.motivation: Provide personalized explanations to boost trust and engagement while avoiding the extra cost/latency of frontier models.
AI.method: Train LLM-judge reward models for faithfulness and non-harmfulness; apply constrained GRPO to optimize across criteria; fine-tune an LLM-based recommender on real user watching history; evaluate on held-out real-world data with both internal and external judges; compare to frontier generator and an untuned baseline.
AI.result: PASS rates improved from 0.649 to 0.956 (own judge) and 0.677 to 0.931 (independent judge); frontier generator performs similarly to untuned baseline; language and recommendation ability preserved.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-based recommender can be fine-tuned on complex tasks like explanation generation without sacrificing core recommendation performance, enabling agentic user interfaces powered by a single model.

title: GeomVLA: Unifying Scene, Motion, and Action in 3D
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project page: https://ziyin-xiong.github.io/geomvla.io/
summary: We present GeomVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that unifies perception, latent scene motion prediction, and action generation within a shared robot-centric 3D coordinate frame. Our approach lifts pretrained VLM features into spatially grounded 3D scene tokens using depth and camera calibration, while retaining the semantic representations learned during VLM pretraining. We further introduce a 3D Scene Trajectory Denoiser, a task-conditioned module that learns a latent representation of how scene points are expected to move in 3D. Rather than executing the predicted trajectory as an open-loop plan, GeomVLA extracts intermediate motion tokens from the trajectory denoiser and uses them to condition a 3D flow-based action denoiser through geometry-aware attention. GeomVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN, competitive performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0, and outperforms strong baselines in real-world manipulation settings without robot-action pretraining. Extensive ablations show that future-motion reasoning alone is insufficient: the primary gains are associated with maintaining geometric consistency among scene representation, motion prediction, and robot actions throughout the perception-to-action pipeline.

AI.tldr: GeomVLA unifies vision-language perception, 3D scene motion prediction, and action generation in a robot-centric 3D frame by grounding VLM features into 3D tokens, using a 3D Scene Trajectory Denoiser and a 3D flow-based action denoiser; achieves state-of-the-art on CALVIN and competitive results on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0, with primary gains from geometric consistency across the perception-action pipeline.
AI.motivation: To bridge perception, motion understanding, and action in a single architecture by leveraging pretrained VLMs while explicitly grounding in 3D geometry, enabling robust manipulation without robot-action pretraining.
AI.method: Lift pretrained VLM features to spatial 3D scene tokens using depth and camera calibration; introduce a 3D Scene Trajectory Denoiser to learn a latent representation of how scene points move in 3D; extract intermediate motion tokens to condition a 3D flow-based action denoiser via geometry-aware attention; operate in a unified robot-centric 3D frame.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on CALVIN; competitive on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0; outperforms baselines in real-world manipulation without robot-action pretraining; ablations show that gains come from maintaining geometric consistency across perception, motion prediction, and actions rather than future-motion reasoning alone.
AI.conclusion: Geometric-consistent integration of perception, motion prediction, and action is crucial for effective vision-language-action robotics; the approach demonstrates strong real-world performance and underscores the importance of geometry throughout the pipeline.

title: The MODA General Attribute Suite: A Four-Track Evaluation Benchmark for Fashion Attribute Extraction
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Benchmark suite, scorers, split builders, prediction files with hashes, and model weights at https://github.com/hopit-ai/Moda_ner
summary: Fashion attribute extraction is evaluated inconsistently: results are reported as single aggregate numbers across image types that pose different problems, fields that are not visible in an image are scored as ordinary negatives, and the effect of vocabulary mismatch between datasets is acknowledged but not measured. We release the MODA General Attribute Suite, a four-track benchmark that keeps these problems separate by construction. Each track (localized garment crops, catalogue product images, applicability-aware full-body photographs, and product text) carries its own frozen test set, input contract, metric, and leakage unit, and the tracks are never averaged. The protocol requires label-blind prediction, SHA-256 commitment of prediction files before any label is opened, a fail-closed scorer, and a 10,000-sample paired cluster bootstrap at each track's natural leakage unit; promotion requires a positive interval on every track rather than a favourable mean. We release the scorers, the split builders, our own prediction files with their hashes including the runs we lose, and the MODA_NER(V) model checkpoints for three of the four tracks. The text model is not distributed; its benchmark is. We report baseline results, six interventions that did not improve them, and the limitations of the evidence.

AI.tldr: MODA General Attribute Suite: a four-track, non-aggregated benchmark for fashion attribute extraction with strict evaluation protocol, leakage control, and released artifacts; baseline results reported, six interventions failed to improve, and three model checkpoints released.
AI.motivation: Address inconsistent fashion attribute evaluation across image types, problems, and vocabulary mismatches by separating evaluation into four dedicated tracks with track-specific test sets and metrics.
AI.method: Four tracks with frozen test sets, input contracts, metrics, and leakage units; label-blind prediction; SHA-256 commitment of predictions; fail-closed scorer; 10,000-sample paired cluster bootstrap at each leakage unit; promotion requires a positive interval on every track; track-specific artifacts released (scorers, split builders, predictions with hashes, and MODA_NER(V) checkpoints for three tracks); text model benchmark is the only one distributed; six interventions tested; results include baseline results and limitations.
AI.result: Baseline results reported; six interventions that did not improve them; limitations of evidence acknowledged; resources released include scorers, split builders, predictions, and three MODA_NER(V) model checkpoints; text model benchmark provided as benchmark.
AI.conclusion: MODA establishes a rigorous, track-specific benchmarking framework to address inconsistent evaluation in fashion attribute extraction, enabling robust cross-track comparisons while mitigating leakage and vocabulary mismatch effects.

title: Operational Range Bounding in Spectroscopy: A Safety Cage Framework for Machine Learning Models
summary: Ensuring the reliability of black-box machine learning models in safety-critical space missions remains a significant challenge, particularly when ground-truth is unavailable for validation. Although machine learning models offer a powerful means to augment standard pipelines by extracting transmission spectra from complex exoplanetary light curves, their susceptibility to unmodelled instrument anomalies, stellar activity, and domain shifts introduces unquantified risks. This study evaluates a modular safety cage architecture that operates as a parallel monitoring layer to assess the validity of a prediction without modifying the underlying estimator. By monitoring different runtime indicators, including uncertainty quantification, out-of-domain detection, and influence functions, the framework constrains the model's operational domain to a verified region. A controlled evaluation is conducted under both in-domain and cross-domain conditions, using datasets from the 2019 and 2021 editions of the Ariel Data Challenges. The results reveal that model failure is multifaceted and that no single indicator captures all failure modes, demonstrating the need for indicator fusion. The application of safety-driven rejection strategies shows that a modest 20% reduction in data coverage results in error reductions between 45% and 65% across different domains and evaluation metrics. Using a formalised coverage-risk framework, a systematic analysis of indicator combinations is performed to identify configurations that maximise risk-ranking accuracy and optimise the trade-off between data coverage and scientific performance. Safety cages provide a transparent mechanism for detecting unreliable predictions and represent a critical step towards the safe deployment of data-driven models in scientific applications, such as astrophysics, where ground truth is seldom available.

AI.tldr: A modular safety cage monitors black-box ML for exoplanet spectroscopy by fusing multiple runtime indicators (uncertainty, OOD, influence functions) to gate predictions; single indicators fail to capture all failure modes; a 20% reduction in data coverage yields 45–65% error reductions; a coverage-risk framework optimizes indicator configurations; safety cages enable transparent detection of unreliable predictions for safe deployment in astrophysics.
AI.motivation: Ensure the reliability of data-driven predictions in safety-critical space missions where ground-truth validation is often unavailable.
AI.method: A parallel safety cage layer monitors predictions using multiple indicators (uncertainty quantification, out-of-domain detection, influence functions). It performs indicator fusion within a formal coverage-risk framework, evaluating in-domain and cross-domain performance on ARIEL 2019/2021 data challenges, with safety-driven rejection to constrain the operational domain.
AI.result: No single indicator captures all failure modes; fusion of indicators improves risk ranking and reduces risk more effectively. A modest data-coverage reduction (≈20%) yields substantial improvements in error metrics (≈45–65%) across domains. The formal framework identifies configurations that balance coverage and scientific performance.
AI.conclusion: Safety cages provide a transparent mechanism to detect unreliable predictions and are a critical step toward safe deployment of data-driven models in scientific contexts like astrophysics, where ground truth is scarce.

title: FedV-KGQA in Practice: Design Lessons and an Interactive Prototype
comment: Accepted at the ISWC 2026 Posters and Demos Track; to appear in the ISWC 2026 Companion Volume (CEUR-WS)
summary: Knowledge graph question answering usually assumes that one system can reach the whole graph. In practice, facts are often held by organizations that share entity identifiers but own disjoint relation types, so no single party sees a complete reasoning chain. This poster presents the empirical findings of FedV-KGQA on multi-hop question answering over such vertically partitioned graphs. Each silo enriches its local graph and trains a knowledge graph embedding on its own triples. A server then concatenates the silo-specific entity views, anchors the projected question at the topic entity, and ranks candidates by similarity. Raw triples and relation embeddings never leave a silo. Comparing the FedV-KGQA experiments with one another yields three results. First, federated fusion recovers most of the centralized accuracy, while a single silo recovers little. Second, anchoring and enrichment matter more than the choice of embedding model. Third, the cheapest encoder depends on the target accuracy rather than on parameter count. This poster paper contributes that cross-experiment comparison, four design lessons drawn from it, and an interactive prototype that runs real inference and traces the full pipeline, per question, on released checkpoints.

AI.tldr: Federated vertical-partition KGQA can approach centralized accuracy when silos enrich local graphs and are anchored at the topic entity; anchoring and enrichment outweigh embedding model choice, and cost-optimal encoders depend on target accuracy.
AI.motivation: In many real-world scenarios, factual data is distributed across organizations that share identifiers but own disjoint relation types, making a single global graph inaccessible. A privacy-preserving federated approach is needed for reliable multi-hop QA over such disjoint graphs.
AI.method: Each silo enriches its local KG and trains a KG embedding on its triples. A central server concatenates silo-specific entity views, anchors the projected question to the topic entity, and ranks candidate answers by similarity. Raw triples and relation embeddings never leave their silos. Experiments compare configurations to derive insights, and an interactive prototype traces the full pipeline per question on released checkpoints.
AI.result: Federated fusion recovers most of the centralized accuracy, while a single silo performs poorly. Anchoring and enrichment matter more than the particular embedding model. The cheapest encoder depends on the target accuracy rather than parameter count. The work also provides four design lessons from cross-experiment comparisons and an interactive prototype with end-to-end inference and per-question trace.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the viability of FedV-KGQA for privacy-preserving multi-hop question answering over vertically partitioned graphs, offers concrete design guidance (four lessons), and delivers a prototype that enables real inference with full pipeline tracing.

title: LePlanner: An Iterative Amortized Controller For World Models
summary: World models trained with joint-embedding predictive architectures learn compact, structured latent representations from physical interaction, yet planning in these latent spaces typically relies on one of two costly approaches. Search-based planners such as CEM, MPPI, and iCEM optimize action sequences through many predictor rollouts, achieving strong performance at the cost of high per-decision compute and latency. Policy-based methods amortize inference into a single forward pass but can degrade on contact-rich tasks where the demonstration distribution is multimodal. We propose LePlanner, an amortized iterative controller that learns to construct and refine latent action sequences through a frozen world-model predictor. LePlanner is trained with an arrival-and-hold objective that encourages the controller to reach the goal at the earliest feasible horizon and remain there. This addresses horizon-reset procrastination, a failure mode in which repeated receding-horizon replanning continually postpones goal arrival. An additional action-Gaussian loss keeps generated actions near the support of the offline dataset. Across navigation, contact-rich manipulation, and continuous-control environments, LePlanner matches or exceeds search-based planners while requiring an order of magnitude fewer predictor evaluations and 3-49x lower wall-clock time per decision. It achieves success rates of 98% on PushT, 100% on Reacher, 100% on TwoRooms, and 92% on the OGBench Cube task. These results show that much of the structure discovered through online search can be amortized into a lightweight iterative policy, enabling fast, horizon-aware, nonlinear physical control without online optimization.

AI.tldr: LePlanner is an amortized iterative controller that builds latent action sequences via a frozen world model. Trained with an arrival-and-hold objective to minimize horizon procrastination and an action-Gaussian loss to stay near offline data, it matches or surpasses search-based planners with far fewer predictor evaluations and faster decision time.
AI.motivation: Planning in latent world-model spaces faces a trade-off: (i) search-based planners (CEM/MPPI/iCEM) are accurate but computationally expensive; (ii) policy-based methods are fast but can fail on multimodal, contact-rich tasks. There is a need for fast, horizon-aware planning that leverages learned structure without online optimization.
AI.method: LePlanner is an amortized iterative controller that, at inference, constructs and refines latent action sequences using a frozen world-model predictor. Training uses an arrival-and-hold objective to encourage early goal arrival and maintenance, plus an action-Gaussian loss to keep actions within the dataset support. This yields a lightweight, horizon-aware policy that imitates the planning behavior of search-based methods without their compute burden.
AI.result: Across navigation, contact-rich manipulation, and continuous-control tasks, LePlanner matches or exceeds search-based planners while requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer predictor evaluations and 3-49x lower wall-clock time per decision. Reported success rates include 98% (PushT), 100% (Reacher), 100% (TwoRooms), and 92% (OGBench Cube).
AI.conclusion: Much of the structure discovered via online search can be amortized into a lightweight iterative policy, enabling fast, horizon-aware nonlinear physical control without online optimization.

title: RxScribe Bench: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Indian Outpatient Prescriptions
summary: Prescription transcription errors are not interchangeable. A model that fabricates a drug and a model that misreads a legible dose pose very different clinical risks, yet prescription-transcription accuracy is typically reported as a single blended figure that treats the two as equivalent. We introduce RxScribe Bench, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on handwritten prescription digitization that decomposes performance into four axes tied to clinical severity, rather than folding everything into a single aggregated score. Given only a prescription image and an output schema, a model produces a structured record, which is then compared field by field against a human-authored ground truth of identical shape, with each field also labeled for visibility and legibility. The four axes isolate distinct failure modes, namely Correctness, Hallucination, Engagement, and Robustness. The Robustness axis withholds its hard-field results rather than reporting one when the supporting sample falls below a minimum-evidence threshold. We evaluate frontier vision-language models on real prescriptions across independent cold runs per image, and find that no single model wins across all four axes.

AI.tldr: A benchmark, RxScribe Bench, assesses handwritten prescription digitization by breaking performance into four clinically meaningful axes instead of a single score, revealing diverse model strengths and weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Prescription transcription accuracy is often aggregated into a single metric, masking distinct clinical risks (e.g., correct values vs. misread or invented content). A nuanced, axis-based evaluation aligns evaluation with clinical severity.
AI.method: Provide a prescription image and an output schema; models generate a structured record; compare field-by-field to a ground truth with per-field visibility/legibility labels; evaluate four axes—Correctness, Hallucination, Engagement, Robustness; Robustness results withheld below a minimum evidence threshold; real prescriptions evaluated with independent cold runs per image.
AI.result: Evaluated frontier vision-language models across real prescriptions; no single model dominates all four axes, highlighting heterogeneous strengths and weaknesses across the axes.
AI.conclusion: An axis-based evaluation reveals nuanced model performance, enabling targeted improvements for clinical safety and robustness, rather than relying on a single aggregated accuracy metric.

title: GeoTTER: Leveraging Local Geometry of Optimal Transport for Zero-Shot Classification
summary: We present GeoTTER, a novel framework that redefines optimal transport in the realm of zero-shot classification. Conventional methods often suffer from miscalibration and a lack of adaptability, as they rely on fixed cost matrices derived solely from pre-trained model embeddings. In contrast, GeoTTER addresses these limitations by incorporating two key techniques. First, to alleviate high-frequency label jaggedness (sample-level manifold jitter that assigns neighboring embeddings to different classes), GeoTTER integrates local geometric structure into the optimal transport formulation via graph-Laplacian smoothing, a technique grounded in spectral graph theory that enforces neighborhood consistency. Second, to correct coherent angular drift (a low-frequency orientation bias in which large groups of samples share the same angular offset from their true label prototypes), we fuse clustering-guided cost components with a globally adjusted transport cost, achieving a multi-objective optimization that respects both global distribution constraints and latent data structure. With a median improvement of +6.82% compared to zero-shot and +2.13% compared to OTTER, GeoTTER shows robust improvements across a diverse set of benchmarks.

AI.tldr: GeoTTER reframes zero-shot OT by integrating graph-Laplacian smoothing and clustering-guided cost fusion to mitigate local and global miscalibrations, achieving notable gains over zero-shot and OTTER.
AI.motivation: Fix miscalibration and rigidity of fixed-cost OT in zero-shot classification by leveraging local geometry and clustering structure to better reflect data manifold and label prototypes.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (i) graph-Laplacian smoothing to enforce neighborhood consistency and reduce high-frequency label jaggedness; (ii) incorporate clustering-guided cost with a globally adjusted transport cost to address coherent angular drift, yielding a multi-objective OT optimization.
AI.result: Reported median improvements of +6.82% vs zero-shot and +2.13% vs OTTER across diverse benchmarks, indicating robust performance gains.
AI.conclusion: GeoTTER demonstrates that combining local geometric regularization with clustering-informed cost components yields robust, adaptable zero-shot OT performance and improved calibration.

title: Cost Characterization of Vertically Partitioned Federated Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted at DMKG'26: 2nd International Workshop on Data Management for Knowledge Graphs, co-located with ISWC 2026; to appear in CEUR-WS proceedings
summary: Knowledge graphs are increasingly distributed across autonomous organizations that share an entity space but own disjoint subsets of relations, forming a vertical partition. Answering a multi-hop query may require combining facts from several silos, making the partitioning strategy a key data management decision that affects communication, indexing, load balance, and query latency. However, the costs associated with different partitioning strategies remain insufficiently studied. We formalize vertical partitioning as a design space and compare four strategies: semantic domain grouping, frequency-balanced partitioning, co-occurrence graph-cut partitioning, and random partitioning. We evaluate them using five metrics: communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, and end-to-end query latency. Three of the five prove to be determined by the graph and the silo count rather than by the partition, which reduces the design problem to two conflicting axes, cross-silo path length and load balance. Experiments on MetaQA and PathQuestion use a fixed federated knowledge graph question-answering architecture based on TransE embeddings and a frozen BERT encoder across three silo configurations. By keeping the learning model unchanged, we isolate the effect of partitioning and show that the trade-off between locality and balance holds only where each silo can hold several relations, weakening as the number of silos increases. The study provides practical guidance for deployments constrained by cross-silo reasoning or by silo load.

AI.tldr: Vertical partitioning of distributed knowledge graphs is framed as a design space over four strategies; three metrics are largely determined by graph structure, leaving cross-silo path length vs. load balance as the main trade-off, with implications that weaken as silo count grows.
AI.motivation: To understand how partitioning strategies in vertically partitioned knowledge graphs affect query performance, communication, indexing, and load, especially for multi-hop cross-silo queries.
AI.method: Formally define vertical partitioning; compare semantic domain grouping, frequency-balanced, co-occurrence graph-cut, and random partitioning. Evaluate across five metrics (communication cost, candidate index size, cross-silo path length, load balance, end-to-end query latency) using fixed federated QA architecture (TransE embeddings, frozen BERT) over three silo configurations, using datasets MetaQA and PathQuestion.
AI.result: Three of the five metrics are largely determined by the graph structure and the number of silos rather than the partition strategy. The remaining trade-off lies between cross-silo path length and load balance. Increasing the number of silos weakens the locality-versus-balance trade-off. The study isolates partitioning effects by keeping the learning model fixed and provides guidance for deployments constrained by cross-silo reasoning or silo load.
AI.conclusion: The design space of vertical partitioning reduces to two conflicting objectives—minimizing cross-silo path length and maximizing load balance. The results offer practical guidance for real-world deployments where cross-silo reasoning or silo load are critical constraints.

title: ReWeight: Leveraging Human Data for VLA Post-Training via Demonstration Retrieval and Sample Weighting
summary: Post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models for specific robots and tasks requires in-domain demonstrations, yet collecting diverse robot data is costly. Egocentric human demonstrations provide a scalable alternative, but directly mixing human and robot data can introduce cross-embodiment discrepancies and degrade policy performance. To address this challenge, we introduce ReWeight, a framework that incorporates human data into VLA post-training through demonstration-level retrieval and sample-level weighting. ReWeight learns a cross-embodiment visuomotor representation that combines visual observations with future actions to measure behavioral similarity between human and robot demonstrations. Based on optimal transport, it retrieves human demonstrations relevant to the target robot data and assigns larger weights to samples with smaller cross-embodiment discrepancies. We evaluate ReWeight using $π_{0.5}$ across eight simulation tasks and four real-world tasks under both clean and randomized settings. In simulation, ReWeight improves the average success rate of post-trained $π_{0.5}$ from 39% with only robot data and 44% with randomly mixed human-robot data to 57%. In the physical experimental setting, it achieves an average success rate of 68.8%, outperforming the baselines by 28.8% and 13.8%, respectively. Overall, ReWeight provides an effective paradigm for transforming abundant egocentric human experience into transferable supervision for robot learning. (Project webpage: https://reweight-vla.github.io/)

AI.tldr: ReWeight introduces a cross-embodiment retrieval and sample-weighting framework to leverage egocentric human demonstrations for post-training vision-language-action policies on robots, using an optimal transport-based retrieval and a learned cross-embodiment visuomotor representation to reweight samples by behavioral similarity.
AI.motivation: Collecting diverse robot data is costly; egocentric human demonstrations offer abundant data but suffer from cross-embodiment discrepancies that can degrade robot policy performance. A retrieval-and-weighting approach aims to fuse human and robot data effectively for post-training.
AI.method: Learn a cross-embodiment visuomotor representation that encodes visual observations and future actions; use optimal transport to retrieve human demonstrations relevant to target robot data; assign higher weights to samples with smaller cross-embodiment discrepancies during post-training.
AI.result: In simulation, post-training π0.5 success rate improves from 39% (robot-only) and 44% (mixed) to 57%. In real-world tasks, average success reaches 68.8%, outperforming baselines by 28.8% and 13.8%. Evaluations span eight simulated tasks and four real tasks under clean and randomized settings.
AI.conclusion: ReWeight provides an effective paradigm to transform abundant egocentric human experience into transferable supervision for robot learning in post-training VLA settings, with demonstrated gains in diverse tasks.

title: GaugeDefect: Detecting Surface Anomalies by Curvature of Feature Transport
comment: Accepted at the 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision (PRCV 2026)
summary: Industrial anomaly localization has advanced rapidly with feature-based, reconstruction-based, and distillation-based methods. Most of these methods score a region by asking how unusual its local appearance or feature representation is with respect to normal training images. This is a strong and practical formulation. In this work, we study a complementary geometric cue for cases where an abnormal region may still contain locally plausible visual features. Thin scratches, small dents, and disrupted repeated patterns often do not make every local patch individually abnormal; instead, they disturb how nearby features vary and connect across the surface. We propose GaugeDefect, a geometric method for surface anomaly localization based on the curvature of feature transport. Given a feature lattice, we estimate a local feature frame at each node and compute orthogonal transports between neighboring frames. The accumulated transport around a small closed loop gives a holonomy matrix, whose deviation from identity measures feature-transport curvature. After calibration on normal training images, unusually large curvature indicates a local inconsistency in the feature field. The curvature here is not the physical curvature of the inspected object, but a representation-space measure of neighborhood inconsistency. This makes the method applicable to curved surfaces, textured materials, and non-planar industrial objects. Its main role is to improve localization of subtle surface disruptions, while often producing sharper responses near defect boundaries as a natural consequence of the curvature signal.

AI.tldr: GaugeDefect introduces a geometry-based anomaly localization method that measures feature-transport curvature (holonomy) over a feature lattice to detect local neighborhood inconsistencies, effective for subtle surface defects on curved or textured objects.
AI.motivation: Standard region-wise anomaly scoring can miss defects that preserve local patch plausibility but disrupt how nearby features vary across a surface. A representation-space geometric cue is needed to capture such neighborhood inconsistencies, especially on non-flat geometries.
