AI.method: Construct a feature lattice on the surface, estimate a local feature frame at each node, compute orthogonal transports between neighboring frames, and accumulate transports around small closed loops to form holonomy matrices. The deviation of these holonomies from the identity quantifies curvature. After calibrating on normal data, large curvature indicates local inconsistency. Curvature serves as a representation-space anomaly score that is applicable to curved surfaces and textured materials.
AI.result: The curvature-based measure improves localization of subtle surface disruptions and tends to produce sharper responses near defect boundaries. It broadens applicability to curved/non-planar industrial objects and acts as a complementary cue to existing anomaly localization methods.
AI.conclusion: Feature-transport curvature provides a geometric cue for surface anomaly localization in representation space, enabling effective detection on non-planar geometries and enhancing boundary-focused responses.

title: Rolling Day-Wise Mortality Prediction in Critically Ill Patients With AKI on CRRT Utilizing Machine Pressure Waveforms
summary: Critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) face high mortality, yet current risk assessment relies primarily on clinical parameters from electronic health records (EHR) and ignores minute-level circuit pressure waveforms generated by CRRT machines that track the extracorporeal circuit's interaction with the patient. Clinicians therefore cannot see deterioration as it develops. Risk is reassessed only when labs are drawn, while this continuous record is discarded because it is contaminated by shared-device records, non-physiological minutes, and sensor artifacts. To make the stream usable, we aligned machine records to charted therapy intervals to prevent cross-patient leakage, removed priming and downtime minutes, tuned denoising on a synthetic spike-injection benchmark, and masked unobserved intervals rather than imputing them. On this cleaned stream, we define a rolling day-wise task and a transformer-based stacked ensemble that late-fuses a window-reduced sequence transformer with classical models using circuit-instability features and clinical EHR variables. In a leak-safe benchmark on the multi-center CRRTnet cohort (976 patients, 4,585 treatment days), the machine-only model had the lowest standalone prognostic value (AUROC 0.625), followed by the EHR-only model (0.717). Integrating EHR and machine streams reached a one-day mortality AUROC of 0.766. SHAP attribution showed that circuit-instability descriptors raised the machine share of the top 15 combined-model features from 3 to 7 (20.0% to 46.7%), highlighting filter pressure, transmembrane pressure (TMP), and access-to-return difference (ARD). To our knowledge, this is the first patient-level mortality prediction incorporating CRRT machine data, turning a discarded bedside stream into a continuous risk signal.

AI.tldr: A multi-center study demonstrates that incorporating continuous CRRT machine data with EHR improves mortality risk prediction for critically ill AKI patients, using cleaned, leak-safe streams and a transformer-based ensemble.
AI.motivation: CRRT machine data are an untapped, high-resolution source reflecting real-time circuit dynamics and patient condition; integrating it with EHR could enable earlier and more accurate mortality risk assessments.
AI.method: Clean and align CRRT machine records to therapy intervals, remove priming/downtime, denoise with a synthetic spike-in benchmark, and mask unobserved intervals. Develop a rolling day-wise task and a transformer-based stacked ensemble that fuses a window-reduced sequence transformer (machine data) with classical models (EHR) using circuit-instability features and EHR features.
AI.result: In a leak-safe benchmark on 976 patients and 4,585 treatment days (CRRTnet), machine-only AUROC = 0.625; EHR-only AUROC = 0.717; combined model AUROC = 0.766 for one-day mortality. SHAP showed circuit-instability descriptors increased the machine stream’s top feature share from 3 to 7 (20.0% to 46.7%), with key contributions from filter pressure, TMP, and ARD.
AI.conclusion: This study pioneers patient-level mortality prediction by leveraging CRRT machine streams, demonstrating that integrating bedside machine data with EHR yields the strongest predictive performance and offering interpretable insights via SHAP.

title: GeoSkill:Experience-Driven Hierarchical Skill Learning with Collaborative Revision forGeospatialAgents
summary: Geospatial agents are increasingly expected to support recurring and evolving analytical tasks rather than execute isolated workflows. In such settings, effective agents must distill prior execution experience into reusable geospatial procedural knowledge to guide future planning and tool use. However, existing memory-augmented paradigms struggle to summarize both long-horizon tool-chain orchestration experience and tool-level invocation constraints in geospatial analysis, while directly relying on LLM self-reflection to update experience often leads to misattribution and unreliable revisions. To address these challenges, we propose GeoSkill, an experience-driven hierarchical skill learning framework for geospatial agents. GeoSkill comprises two core components: (i) a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB), consisting of a Planning Skill Bank and a Tool Skill Bank, which respectively distill high-level task-planning experience and tool usage constraints, enabling structured representation and cross-task reuse of historical execution experience; and (ii) a Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism, where Judge, Critic, and Refiner collaboratively perform error identification, skill-level defect localization, and targeted modification, preventing misattributed and unreliable revisions from polluting the skill bank. GeoSkill learns and validates skills from historical executions during development, and freezes the skill bank for retrieval-only guidance on unseen tasks during deployment. Extensive experiments on EarthBench and ThinkGeo demonstrate that GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving both end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.

AI.tldr: GeoSkill is an experience-driven hierarchical skill learning framework for geospatial agents that uses a two-part Skill Bank (Planning and Tool) and a collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) mechanism (Judge-Critic-Refiner) to convert historical execution data into reusable skills, guard revisions, and freeze the skill bank for deployment. It improves end-to-end task accuracy and tool reliability on EarthBench and ThinkGeo.
AI.motivation: Geospatial agents must generalize from past executions by distilling long-horizon planning and low-level tool constraints into reusable knowledge. Existing memory-augmented approaches struggle with long tool chains and tool-usage constraints, and self-reflection-based updates cause misattribution.
AI.method: 1) Develop a Hierarchical Skill Bank (HSB) with a Planning Skill Bank and a Tool Skill Bank to capture high-level task planning experiences and tool usage constraints for cross-task reuse. 2) Implement Collaborative Trace-driven Skill Revision (CTSR) where Judge, Critic, and Refiner identify errors, localize skill defects, and apply targeted modifications to keep the skill bank reliable. 3) Learn and validate skills from historical executions during development and deploy with a frozen, retrieval-only skill bank for unseen tasks.
AI.result: Empirical results on EarthBench and ThinkGeo show that GeoSkill effectively transforms historical execution experience into reusable hierarchical skills, improving end-to-end task accuracy and tool-execution reliability in geospatial tasks.
AI.conclusion: GeoSkill enables reliable, reusable geospatial planning and tool-use knowledge by structuring past experience into hierarchical skills and enforcing disciplined revisions, with a deployment-time retrieval-only skill bank for unseen tasks.

title: Co-Speech with You: Training-Free Personalization of Robot Co-Speech Gestures
summary: Personal robots should adapt their co-speech gesture style to a new user without requiring model retraining. We present a training-free personalization pipeline that combines a frozen audio-conditioned diffusion prior with a gesture style encoder and lightweight conditioning adapters. The encoder is first trained to discriminate speaker identities and then jointly refined with the adapters using the diffusion objective, enabling a reusable style embedding to be extracted from approximately 10 seconds of enrollment motion through a single forward pass. To support this setting, we also release a Quest~3 capture application and a dataset of spontaneous co-speech motion from ten participants. We evaluate the system on held-out speakers using Style Recognition Accuracy (SRA) and Fr'echet Gesture Distance (FGD) to measure personalization and motion quality. Our approach improves SRA from 27.6\% for the frozen prior to 69.5\% while preserving motion quality (FGD 34.2 versus 34.8), and replacing the enrollment embedding with another person's reduces SRA to 11.4\%. The generated gestures are retargeted to a physical NAO robot, and this improvement also transfers to the robot deployment setting, where speech is synthesized using five TTS voices, retaining 67.3\% SRA.

AI.tldr: A training-free personalization pipeline for co-speech gesture synthesis that adapts to new users without retraining, achieving high style recognition while preserving motion quality and transferring to robot deployment with multiple TTS voices.
AI.motivation: To enable personal robots to adopt a new user’s co-speech gesture style without costly retraining or per-user data collection, facilitating natural human-robot interaction across devices and voices.
AI.method: Use a frozen audio-conditioned diffusion prior combined with a gesture style encoder and lightweight conditioning adapters. The encoder is first trained to discriminate speaker identities, then jointly refined with adapters using the diffusion objective. A reusable style embedding is extracted from ~10 seconds of enrollment motion via a single forward pass. They release a Quest 3 capture app and a 10-participant spontaneous co-speech motion dataset.
AI.result: On held-out speakers, Style Recognition Accuracy (SRA) improved from 27.6% with the frozen prior to 69.5%; Fr'echet Gesture Distance (FGD) remained comparable (34.2 vs 34.8). Replacing the enrollment embedding with another person drops SRA to 11.4%. When retargeted to a NAO robot, and with speech synthesized by five TTS voices, SRA remains at 67.3%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free personalization pipeline significantly boosts personalization success without sacrificing motion quality and generalizes to real robot deployment and varied synthesis voices, enabling scalable co-speech gesture customization.

title: Multimodal-Multiresolution Foundation Model for Lunar Remote Sensing
summary: We present a multimodal foundation model for lunar remote sensing, pretrained from scratch on SomBench, a geographically partitioned corpus of nearly two million co-registered tile bundles spanning 11 modalities at two spatial scales (1 m/pixel and 100 m/pixel). The model adapts the TerraMind masked-token architecture with two lunar-specific extensions: acquisition geometry is provided as explicit context, and meter- and hundred-meter-scale tiles are trained jointly so that a single set of weights covers both resolutions. FlexiViT patch embeddings allow adaptation to different patch sizes without retraining, while modality-wise inputs enable flexible multimodal fine-tuning. Qualitative generation experiments suggest the model learns meaningful cross-modal correspondences, including terrain derivatives from elevation and illumination-consistent reflectance from geometry. We evaluate on four benchmarks: crater detection at WAC and NAC scales, irregular mare patch (IMP) segmentation, and polar ice prospectivity regression. Across tasks, the pretrained model matches or outperforms ImageNet-pretrained baselines and an architecturally identical random-init control. On multimodal ice prospectivity regression, pretrained variants achieve the best results, while the random-init model outperforms most baselines, suggesting gains arise from both the architecture and pretraining. Label efficiency is notable for WAC crater detection, where the pretrained model trained on 50% of the data exceeds the strongest ImageNet baseline trained on the full dataset. Among adaptation strategies, LoRA matches or surpasses full fine-tuning on crater detection and IMP segmentation while using far fewer trainable parameters, whereas full fine-tuning performs best for ice prospectivity regression. We release the pretrained checkpoint, benchmark datasets, and fine-tuning code to support reproducible lunar AI research.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal lunar foundation model trained from scratch on SomBench across 11 modalities and two spatial scales; extends TerraMind with explicit acquisition-geometry context and joint 1m/100m tile training; uses FlexiViT embeddings and modality-wise inputs; shows competitive or superior performance to ImageNet baselines and random init on crater detection, IMP segmentation, and polar ice prospectivity; demonstrates data efficiency and effective fine-tuning (LoRA); release of pretrained model, datasets, and code.
AI.motivation: Leverage diverse lunar remote-sensing modalities and resolutions to enable robust, data-efficient, and scalable analysis across key tasks by learning cross-modal correspondences and geometric-consistent representations.
AI.method: Adapt TerraMind masked-token architecture with lunar-specific extensions: 1) acquisition geometry provided as explicit context; 2) joint training of 1 m/pixel and 100 m/pixel tiles with shared weights; 3) FlexiViT patch embeddings to accommodate varying patch sizes without retraining; 4) modality-wise inputs to enable flexible multimodal fine-tuning; 5) pretraining on SomBench (≈2M co-registered tile bundles spanning 11 modalities and two scales). Qualitative generation indicates meaningful cross-modal correspondences (e.g., terrain derivatives from elevation, illumination-consistent reflectance from geometry).
AI.result: Across four benchmarks—crater detection at WAC and NAC scales, irregular mare patch (IMP) segmentation, and polar ice prospectivity regression—the pretrained model matches or surpasses ImageNet-pretrained baselines and a architecturally identical random-init model. Pretrained variants achieve best results on ice prospectivity regression; the random-init model often outperforms most baselines, suggesting gains arise from both architecture and pretraining. Label efficiency is notable: for WAC crater detection, the pretrained model trained on 50% of data exceeds the strongest ImageNet baseline trained on full data. Among adaptation strategies, LoRA matches or exceeds full fine-tuning for crater detection and IMP segmentation while using far fewer trainable parameters; full fine-tuning performs best for ice prospectivity regression. The work releases pretrained checkpoints, benchmark datasets, and fine-tuning code to support reproducible lunar AI research.
AI.conclusion: Jointly training a multi-scale, multi-modal lunar foundation model with acquisition-geometry context and flexible patch embeddings yields competitive, data-efficient performance across multiple lunar remote-sensing tasks, highlighting the value of architecture and large-scale multimodal pretraining for planetary AI. The release of resources supports reproducibility and further research.

title: Generative Interpretability via Scalable Neuro-Symbolic Models
summary: As the use of Large Language Models moves from chatbots into agentic systems, where outputs become actions with irreversible consequences on reality, the existing paradigm on AI Interpretability research, post-hoc interpretability, is structurally inadequate for safe and trustworthy model deployment: it explains behavior after the fact but cannot audit or intervene in an inference computation before it commits to an output. We therefore argue for a shift toward \emph{generative interpretability}, an architectural property under which a model's inference pass natively exposes semantically meaningful checkpoints that are human-understandable and amenable to causal intervention. We show the merits of generative interpretability as comparison to other interpretability research paradigms, and propose Neuro-Symbolic Models as a concrete instantiation.

AI.tldr: Generative interpretability is proposed as a shift from post-hoc explainability toward exposing semantically meaningful, auditable checkpoints during an inference pass; Neuro-Symbolic Models are proposed as a concrete instantiation.
AI.motivation: The rise of agentic LLMs with irreversible real-world effects makes post-hoc interpretability inadequate for safe deployment; there is a need for architectures that allow real-time auditing and causal intervention during inference.
AI.method: Conceptual argument for generative interpretability, comparing it to existing interpretability paradigms, and proposing Neuro-Symbolic Models as a concrete instantiation of the approach.
AI.result: The authors argue for generative interpretability, demonstrate its merits relative to other paradigms, and present Neuro-Symbolic Models as a concrete path to realization.
AI.conclusion: Generative interpretability is needed for safe and trustworthy AI in agentic systems; exposing actionable checkpoints during inference and leveraging Neuro-Symbolic architectures can enable causal intervention and auditing.

title: Enhancing Event Candidate Acquisition for Event Linking
summary: Event linking associates event mentions in text with entries in a knowledge base (KB), or identifies them as out-of-KB events. Although existing methods use different architectures, candidate event acquisition can still be weakened by short ambiguous mentions, noisy arguments, and evidence that is unevenly useful for retrieval. We present MACE, a Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition method that refines event structure before linking. MACE uses evidence-specialized LLM agents to acquire time, location, participant, and event-type evidence, exposes intermediate queries to candidate-event lookup tools, and lets a coordinator revise the evidence set before final candidate construction. Experiments on two event linking benchmarks show that adding MACE to different event linking models consistently improves accuracy. These results show that MACE improves event linking through better candidate event acquisition without modifying the event linking model.

AI.tldr: MACE improves event linking by multi-agent evidence gathering to refine candidates, yielding consistent accuracy gains across models without modifying the linking architecture.
AI.motivation: Candidate-event acquisition in event linking is weakened by short ambiguous mentions, noisy arguments, and unevenly useful evidence, leading to suboptimal retrieval performance.
AI.method: MACE introduces multiple evidence-specialized LLM agents that extract time, location, participant, and event-type evidence; intermediate queries are exposed to candidate-event lookup tools; a coordinator can revise the evidence set before final candidate construction, integrating with existing event-linking models without changing them.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on two event-linking benchmarks shows consistent accuracy improvements when MACE is appended to various event-linking models.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, evidence-focused pre-processing via MACE enhances event linking by improving candidate acquisition without altering the core linking model; this approach may generalize to similar retrieval-heavy NLP tasks, albeit with potential concerns about complexity and dependence on LLMs.

title: Rethinking the Implications of Human Feedback for Preference Learning in Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: In Human-Robot Interaction, the standard approach to learn a reward model that represents human preferences for robot behavior consists of three steps. First, the robot collects limited direct evidence from human feedback (e.g., positive or negative binary feedback). Then, the robot utilizes the direct evidence to derive accepted or rejected labels to feasible but unchosen actions using fixed implication rules. Finally, the robot updates the reward model with both the direct and derived evidence. Unfortunately, the fixed rule can hinder preference learning: in a user study with two collaborative simulation environments, human-provided implication labels often differed from the standard fixed rule, and using the human labels substantially improved reward learning with the Preference Learning from Implicit and Explicit Feedback (PIE) algorithm. Consequently, we propose IMPLIED, an implication modeling method that treats fixed-rule implications as an initial guide while learning to infer and revise accepted and rejected action labels over time. Across evaluations on recorded human-robot interaction trajectories and a physical robot pizza-making study, IMPLIED predicts human implications more accurately than the fixed rule approach and LLM baselines, approaching the performance of a human-label oracle. In turn, IMPLIED reduces preference-estimation error and leads to robot actions that are more often rational with respect to a combined reward (which includes the true preference reward and a task-specific reward) compared to baselines. By learning to reason about the implications of human feedback, this work enables more faithful and efficient robot behavior adaptation during human-robot collaboration.

AI.tldr: IMPLIED is an implication modeling method in human-robot interaction that learns to infer and revise accepted/rejected action labels derived from human feedback, outperforming fixed-rule implications and LLM baselines, and approaching a human-label oracle in accuracy, leading to better reward estimation and more rational robot behavior.
AI.motivation: Fixed-rule implications can misalign with human intent and impede preference learning; human-derived implications often diverge from standard rules, motivating a method that learns and revises implications over time.
AI.method: Treat fixed-rule implications as an initial guide and iteratively infer and revise accepted/rejected action labels based on human feedback; evaluate on recorded HRI trajectories and a physical pizza-making study; compare against fixed-rule implications and LLM baselines, and relate to PIE.
AI.result: ImPLIED achieves higher accuracy in predicting human implications than fixed-rule and LLM baselines, approaches the performance of a human-label oracle, reduces preference-estimation error, and yields robot actions that are more rational with respect to a combined reward.
AI.conclusion: Learning to reason about human feedback implications enhances faithful and efficient robot adaptation in HRI, enabling more effective collaboration.

title: LLaDA-UI: Bringing Block-wise Diffusion to Vision-Language GUI Agents
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) achieve high decoding efficiency through block-parallel, arbitrary-order generation, making them attractive for latency-sensitive applications. GUI agents represent a natural testbed for this paradigm, as they must repeatedly perceive screen states and emit structured, spatially grounded actions in real time. However, whether dLLMs can be extended into capable multimodal GUI agents while preserving their parallel decoding advantage remains an open question. We present LLaDA-UI, a 16.7B-parameter MoE-based, block-wise diffusion vision-language GUI agent. LLaDA-UI follows a two-stage training pipeline: general multimodal pre-training aligns a native-resolution vision encoder with the LLaDA2.0-mini-base diffusion language backbone, followed by GUI-agent supervised fine-tuning on diverse mobile, desktop, web, and grounding data. Across widely adopted grounding benchmarks and navigation benchmarks spanning multiple platforms, LLaDA-UI substantially outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-7B and surpasses Qwen3-VL-8B on four of six reported GUI benchmarks. These results establish block-wise diffusion as a practical generative paradigm for multimodal GUI agents.

AI.tldr: LLaDA-UI is a 16.7B MoE diffusion LLM that acts as a multimodal GUI agent using block-wise generation; two-stage training (multimodal pretraining + GUI fine-tuning); it improves GUI benchmarks over strong VL baselines, underscoring block-wise diffusion as viable for real-time, spatially grounded GUI tasks.
AI.motivation: Assess whether diffusion-LMs with parallel, block-wise decoding can be extended into capable, multimodal GUI agents without sacrificing latency advantages, addressing real-time perception-action loops across mobile/desktop/web platforms.
AI.method: A two-stage training pipeline: (1) general multimodal pre-training that aligns a native-resolution vision encoder with the LLaDA2.0-mini-base diffusion backbone; (2) GUI-agent supervised fine-tuning on diverse data covering mobile, desktop, web, and grounding tasks. Model: 16.7B parameter MoE-based, block-wise diffusion architecture.
AI.result: On standard grounding and navigation benchmarks across multiple platforms, LLaDA-UI substantially outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-7B and surpasses Qwen3-VL-8B on four of six GUI benchmarks, demonstrating the practicality of block-wise diffusion for multimodal GUI agents.
AI.conclusion: Block-wise diffusion is a practical and effective generative paradigm for multimodal GUI agents, enabling real-time, spatially grounded action generation while maintaining competitive performance against strong VL baselines.

title: Attention Is All You Need (to Avoid Spurious Oscillations)
summary: Can attention move a shock across several cells in one update without breaking it? We develop a conservative, fixed grid finite-volume scheme in which a CFL-conditioned attention flux selects upstream information according to the transport required by the current time step. One-dimensional inviscid Burgers transport is used as the central mechanism test: the same learned flux remains reliable in the conventional small-step regime and, with a time step four times larger, preserves sharp shocks while using one stage per update. A standard fifth-order WENO scheme with third-order strong-stability-preserving Runge-Kutta time integration (WENO-5+SSP-RK3) is included alongside controlled Forward Euler comparisons to separate flux selection from time integration. The learned attention shifts upstream with the local transport reach and becomes more selective near shocks; inference-time interventions and retrained ablations show that transport-scale information and state-dependent selection contribute directly to performance. Directional two-dimensional scalar Burgers transport and the one-dimensional shallow-water system then test whether the conservation-scale-selection principle transfers beyond the original scalar setting. The results support attention as a learnable information stencil for conservative large-step shock transport, while identifying finite candidate reach and problem-dependent robustness as the present limits.

AI.tldr: Learned attention-guided flux in a conservative finite-volume scheme enables large-step shock transport while preserving sharp discontinuities; demonstrates transferability beyond 1D Burgers to 2D scalar Burgers and shallow-water, with limitations on reach and robustness.
AI.motivation: Reduce numerical dissipation and improve shock transport quality under large time steps by learning a flux stencil that selects upstream information based on local transport requirements.
AI.method: Develop a CFL-conditioned attention flux within a fixed-grid finite-volume scheme; evaluate on 1D inviscid Burgers; compare to WENO-5+SSP-RK3 and Forward Euler; extend to directional 2D Burgers and 1D shallow-water; perform ablations and inference-time interventions to assess what flux uses.
AI.result: The learned flux remains reliable in standard small-step regimes and, with a time step four times larger, preserves sharp shocks using a single stage per update. Attention shifts upstream proportional to transport reach and becomes selective near shocks. Transport-scale information and state-dependent selection contribute to performance. Generalization to 2D and shallow-water shows promise; limits include finite candidate reach and problem-dependent robustness.
AI.conclusion: Attention can serve as a learnable information stencil for conservative large-step shock transport, enabling shock-preserving updates beyond traditional small-step regimes, though robustness and reach are current constraints requiring further development.

title: Recoverability as a System Primitive for Long-Horizon AI Agents
summary: AI agents can be interrupted while editing files, calling tools, or carrying out multi-step tasks. Restarting repeats completed work, but continuing from unverified or outdated progress can carry earlier errors forward. A saved state is not necessarily a suitable place to resume. We introduce recoverability as a system primitive that makes reuse an explicit decision: select a supported starting point and a permitted recovery action, or withhold automatic continuation. Its behavioral contract binds that choice to supporting evidence, execution, and independent checks. A reference architecture connects persistence, validation, and control, with complementary runtime instances testing distinct responsibilities. Four deterministic and 20 paired file challenges demonstrate that accurate restoration and successful completion can conceal disallowed starting points. Progress controls attribute retained work to shared restoration. Event-time tests show that permission must also constrain the action, and that independently held policy evidence can expose violations even after an effect occurs. These findings establish why recovery decisions need their own evaluation, beyond restored bytes and final task success. Within supplied policies and a declared trust model, the contribution is a common, testable interface for retaining justified progress and making the conditions for its reuse explicit and enforceable.

AI.tldr: Introduces recoverability as a system primitive for AI task resumption, requiring explicit, justified recovery decisions with supporting evidence and validation.
AI.motivation: Interruption-safe task editing risks rework and propagation of errors; saved states may be unsuitable for resumption; recovery must be a deliberate, policy-driven choice.
AI.method: Proposes a reference architecture linking persistence, validation, and control; deploys multiple runtime instances; evaluates with four deterministic and 20 paired file challenges; conducts event-time tests; analyzes retained progress and policy evidence.
AI.result: Demonstrates that accurate restoration can obscure disallowed starting points; progress controls help attribute retained work; independent policy evidence can reveal violations even after effects; emphasizes evaluation of recovery decisions beyond bytes or final outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Offers a common, testable interface for justified progress retention within supplied policies and trust models, enabling enforceable recovery decisions and exposing violations; supports systematic testing and accountability for reuse of work.

title: What Makes an Efficient VLA? Navigating Action-Head Design, Scaling, and Latency
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine a pretrained vision encoder, a language backbone, and an action head, but their relative contribution has not been established under controlled, latency-paired conditions. We fix the backbone families (SigLIP2 and Qwen2.5) and the training pipeline, sweep action-head design and module scale, and pair each configuration with measured on-device latency. The study yields three findings. First, action-head performance is governed primarily by initialization rather than decoder architecture, loss, or inference budget: copying the last transformer layers of the language backbone into the head is the single largest lever, at no latency cost, and the only axis that helps at every module scale. Alignment also explains the other axes: flow matching and a heavier decoder pay off only while the head is misaligned and reverse once it is aligned, and extra inference passes give no measurable benefit; expressiveness appears to substitute for missing alignment. We read this as representation transfer: the aligned head keeps attending to the instruction's object nouns and stays close to the backbone in weight space rather than relearning to act from scratch. Because we reach alignment only through initialization, we offer this as the account that best organizes the measurements, not a demonstrated cause, and name the control that would settle it. Second, capacity pays only after alignment: the aligned action head is the highest-return module to scale. Third, those returns diminish sharply near the size today's $π$-series VLAs already use, so further growth buys little in-domain accuracy for its latency. These specify EffVLA, a compact model matching the strongest open-source VLAs on standard LIBERO, leading on most LIBERO-Plus perturbation axes at lower latency, and transferring to a real SO-ARM101 arm with the recipe unchanged.

AI.tldr: Aligned, initialization-driven action heads dominate VLA performance under fixed backbones; alignment governs the benefits of flow matching and heavier decoders, while extra inference passes offer no gains. Capacity helps only after alignment, and gains saturate near current model scales. Proposes EffVLA, a compact, low-latency model that matches or surpasses strong open-source VLAs on LIBERO benchmarks and transfers to real hardware with unchanged recipe.
AI.motivation: To dissect the relative contributions of vision encoder, language backbone, and action head in Vision-Language-Action models under latency-constrained, controlled conditions, and to determine how architecture, initialization, and training interact with on-device latency.
AI.method: Fix backbone families (SigLIP2, Qwen2.5) and training pipeline; systematically sweep action-head designs and module scales; measure on-device latency for each configuration; analyze alignment, representation transfer, and the effects of capacity and decoder depth; evaluate on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus perturbations; transfer results to a real SO-ARM101 hardware platform.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) Action-head performance is driven by initialization (copying last transformer layers from the language backbone into the head is the strongest lever, with no latency cost; alignment explains other axes; extra passes yield no benefit; expressiveness substitutes for alignment); (2) Capacity benefits appear only after alignment, with aligned heads yielding the highest returns as modules scale; (3) Gains saturate near current π-series VLA sizes, giving diminishing in-domain accuracy improvements for additional growth. This leads to EffVLA, a compact model matching top LIBERO VLAs on standard perturbations with lower latency and successfully transferring to SO-ARM101 with the unchanged recipe.
AI.conclusion: The study proposes EffVLA, a compact VLA that achieves strong performance at low latency, by emphasizing initialization-driven alignment of the action head and recognizing that capacity benefits materialize post-alignment; growth beyond current scales yields diminishing returns. The results suggest a practical design principle: prioritize alignment-infused initialization for the head, and treat capacity expansion as valuable mainly after alignment is established.

title: Target-Checked Reliability Score Refinement for Video Question Answering
summary: Video-language models can answer multiple-choice questions with high confidence yet be wrong. We study whether answer-level reliability scores can be improved under target shift without retraining the models or changing their answers. We collect option-probability lists from three fixed video-language models under four deterministic video samplings and represent cross-view changes and cross-model agreement as a response graph. Using a labeled target pilot, we compare the original score, defined as the probability assigned to the chosen answer, with a histogram-based gradient-boosting (HGB) score trained on the development datasets and a regularized logistic-regression score trained on the target pilot. A candidate replaces the original score only when repeated video-level checks indicate a positive, stable improvement. We develop this rule on public VideoQA benchmarks and Video Hallucination Diagnosis (VHD), a controlled diagnostic dataset for shared high-confidence errors. Ranking quality is measured by the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), where lower is better. On a held-out 963-question HERBench split, the method reduces mean AURC across the three models by 16.64% (95% confidence interval (CI), 12.12 to 22.61%); the smallest model-level gain is 11.39%. On a separate held-out 911-question Perception Test split, the mean reduction is 18.87% (95% CI, 15.43 to 22.14%). For InternVL3.5, the target check retains the original scores. Using the same outputs, the method outperforms seven training-free baselines in mean AURC on both datasets. It also improves AUROC, reduces calibration error, and lowers the error rate at 50% coverage by 6.50 and 6.58 percentage points.

AI.tldr: A training-free, post-hoc reliability booster for video-language models under target shift, using cross-view response graphs and learned score estimators (HGB and logistic regression) to improve answer-level confidence without changing predictions; yields substantial AURC and calibration gains on HERBench and Perception Test across multiple models.
AI.motivation: Answer-level reliability degrades under distributional shift; retraining large video-language models is expensive; a training-free mechanism to improve reliability is desirable.
AI.method: From three fixed models and four video samplings, collect option-probability lists; compute original score (probability of chosen option). Build a response graph capturing cross-view changes and cross-model agreement. Train histogram-based gradient boosting (HGB) on development data and a regularized logistic regression on a target pilot to predict more reliable scores. Apply a replacement rule: replace the original score with the learned score only if repeated video-level checks indicate stable improvement. Evaluate on HERBench and VHD-derived splits; measure AURC, AUROC, calibration error, and error rate at 50% coverage.
AI.result: On held-out HERBench (963 questions) across three models, mean AURC reduced by 16.64% (CI 12.12–22.61%), with at least 11.39% for the smallest model. On Perception Test (911 questions), mean reduction 18.87% (CI 15.43–22.14%). For InternVL3.5, target check retains original scores, but overall method outperforms seven training-free baselines on both datasets. Also improves AUROC, reduces calibration error, and lowers error rate at 50% coverage by about 6.5 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: A practical, training-free post-hoc reliability mechanism improves answer-level confidence under target shift without modifying model outputs, achieving meaningful gains in ranking quality and calibration across datasets and multiple models; effectiveness varies by model (e.g., InternVL3.5 less affected).

title: Toward Optimal Switching Regret for Multi-Armed Bandits with Oblivious Adversary
summary: We study switching regret in adversarial multi-armed bandits, where the learner competes with an arm sequence that changes at most $S$ times. When $S$ is known, an optimal expected regret of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ is obtainable [Auer et al., 2002]. However, when $S$ is unknown, Marinov and Zimmert [2021] show that this guarantee is impossible under an adaptive adversary. In this paper, we show that a single algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{(S+1)KT})$ expected regret for every $S$ against an oblivious adversary, resolving an open problem of Auer et al. [2019b]. Our algorithm combines a fixed-share learner initialized with a small learning rate and dyadic-interval subroutines that search for local improvements using randomized learning rates and implicit exploration. Importantly, a non-uniform prior favors following the main learner, keeping the cost of maintaining many subroutines small. When the subroutines accumulate sufficient improvement over the main learner, its learning rate doubles, allowing adaptation to the unknown number of comparator switches $S$.

AI.tldr: A single algorithm achieves near-optimal switching regret for unknown S against oblivious adversaries in adversarial bandits, resolving an open problem by combining a fixed-share learner with dyadic-interval subroutines and adaptive learning rates.
AI.motivation: Address the unknown-switches setting in adversarial bandits. Previous work showed optimal regret with known S, but unknown S is hard under adaptive adversaries; the paper proves that optimal regret is possible against oblivious adversaries.
AI.method: A composite algorithm: a fixed-share learner with a small learning rate, plus dyadic-interval subroutines that search for local improvements using randomized learning rates and implicit exploration. A non-uniform prior favors the main learner. When subroutines collectively improve, the main learner’s learning rate is doubled to adapt to S.
AI.result: For every S, against an oblivious adversary, the algorithm achieves Õ(√((S+1)KT)) expected regret, matching the known-S bound and resolving the open problem.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that unknown-switching non-stationarity can be handled optimally against oblivious adversaries using a hierarchical, adaptive algorithm that balances maintenance cost via non-uniform priors and triggers learning-rate doubling based on subroutine gain.

title: Windowed A-K-MDP
summary: Markov decision processes (MDPs) are used to support decision-making in conservation of biodiversity, but policies, even over small state spaces, can be difficult to interpret for conservation managers. K-MDP methods address this problem by building simpler MDPs with at most K abstract states. We show that the previously proposed A-K-MDP algorithm that relies on selecting a discretisation divisor using binary search can skip better abstract states. To fix this issue, we propose Windowed A-K-MDP, an algorithm that generates every distinct feasible partition induced within a declared divisor window and evaluates candidates until reaching the ideal value loss (J = 0) or exhausting the family of candidates. Across 33 K-MDP instances, Windowed improved 25 and tied 8.

AI.tldr: Windowed A-K-MDP exhaustively explores partitions within a divisor window to avoid missing better abstract states, improving performance over A-K-MDP (33 instances: 25 improved, 8 tied).
AI.motivation: Improve interpretability of decision policies derived from MDPs in biodiversity conservation by producing simpler abstractions with at most K states that managers can understand and apply.
AI.method: Introduce Windowed A-K-MDP: for a declared divisor window, generate every distinct feasible partition induced within that window, evaluate candidates, and continue until ideal value loss J=0 or all candidates are exhausted.
AI.result: In 33 K-MDP instances, Windowed A-K-MDP improved the solution in 25 instances and tied in 8, evidencing superior or equivalent performance to the prior A-K-MDP approach.
AI.conclusion: Windowed A-K-MDP provides a more thorough search of feasible partitions within a divisor window, mitigating the risk of skipping better abstractions caused by binary-search discretisation, and yields better or comparable value losses across tested instances.

title: Mobile Multi-Robot Navigation under Runtime Uncertainty via Koopman Operator Learning and Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
summary: In this work, we developed a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) framework that employs learned dynamics via the Koopman Operator theory for mobile multi-robot navigation. We formulated and solved NMPC problems using a lifted bilinear Koopman-based model that accurately predicts affine input systems affected by perturbations and uncertainties. Two exemplary multi-robot navigation problems are considered: target reaching and formation control. The output of our method enables closed-loop multi-robot navigation and formation control in environments populated with obstacles, whereby the Koopman operator-based model used in the NMPC formulation addresses runtime uncertainties, namely, various degrees of random wheel slipping. We validated the effectiveness of our method for both problems via extensive numerical simulations in different environments with wheeled robots affected by different amounts of slip and without knowledge of their true dynamic models.

AI.tldr: Koopman-based NMPC with a lifted bilinear model for multi-robot navigation under slip disturbances, validated by simulations for target reaching and formation control.
AI.motivation: Need robust NMPC for multi-robot navigation under model uncertainties and disturbances (e.g., wheel slip) in obstacle-rich environments.
AI.method: Learned Koopman operator-based lifted bilinear model to predict affine input systems with perturbations; formulate and solve NMPC; apply to target reaching and formation control; simulate wheeled robots with varying slip and unknown true dynamics.
AI.result: Enables closed-loop multi-robot navigation and formation control in obstacle-rich environments; robust to runtime uncertainties (wheel slip); validated through extensive numerical simulations across different slip levels without knowledge of true dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Koopman-based NMPC with lifted bilinear dynamics is effective for robust multi-robot navigation under runtime uncertainties; promising for real-world deployment pending further experiments and analysis.

title: Reliable Egocentric Action Anticipation via Temporal Reliability Suppression and Compositional Graph Decoding
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Towards Real-time Multimodal Contextual Assistants (Wearable AI Workshop)
summary: Wearable action anticipation systems must remain reliable despite missing frames, masking, and sensor noise, yet existing egocentric anticipation methods largely assume clean observations. We identify two complementary failure modes under temporal corruption: unreliable temporal evidence during encoding and implausible, low-support verb-noun compositions during decoding. We address them with a lightweight framework combining Temporal Reliability Suppression (TRS) and Robust Verb-Noun Graph (RVG) decoding. TRS predicts a per-frame suppression score from the projected input embedding and uses it as a learned key-side attention penalty at every encoder block and to derive reliability-weighted temporal pooling. RVG re-ranks verb-noun pairs using a PMI-based compatibility graph constructed from training labels. Under corruption-augmented training, TRS+CA+RVG reaches 29.1% average corrupted accuracy and 88.2% relative robustness across six corruptions, including three mechanisms absent during training, while reducing rare verb-noun predictions from 15.4% to 1.1%. Multi-seed and diagnostic experiments show that TRS responds to synthetic masking; shuffled-graph and frequency-only controls further indicate that RVG gains depend on genuine pairwise compatibility rather than marginal-frequency effects alone.

AI.tldr: A lightweight framework TRS+RVG improves robustness of egocentric action anticipation under temporal corruption by suppressing unreliable temporal evidence and re-ranking verb-noun pairs with a PMI graph; corruption-augmented training yields substantial gains in corrupted accuracy and reduces rare predictions.
AI.motivation: Real-world wearable/action anticipation systems encounter missing frames, masking, and sensor noise, causing unreliable temporal evidence during encoding and implausible verb-noun outputs during decoding. The work targets these failure modes to enhance reliability.
AI.method: Introduce Temporal Reliability Suppression (TRS): per-frame suppression scores are predicted from projected input embeddings and used as a learned key-side attention penalty in every encoder block; also used to derive reliability-weighted temporal pooling. Introduce Robust Verb-Noun Graph (RVG): PMI-based compatibility graph built from training labels to re-rank verb-noun pairs. Train with corruption-augmented data to improve robustness; evaluate under six corruptions.
AI.result: With corruption-augmented training, TRS+RVG achieves 29.1% average corrupted accuracy and 88.2% relative robustness across six corruptions, including three mechanisms unseen during training. It also reduces rare verb-noun predictions from 15.4% to 1.1%. In ablations, TRS responds to synthetic masking; RVG gains require genuine pairwise compatibility rather than marginal-frequency effects.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TRS+RVG framework effectively addresses both encoding-time unreliability and decoding-time incompatibilities under temporal corruption, yielding substantial improvements in robustness for egocentric action anticipation and reducing spurious verb-noun predictions. The results indicate the benefits depend on real temporal cues and genuine verb-noun compatibility rather than frequency alone.

title: When Greedy Sampling Explores: KL-Regularized Contextual Bandits without Eluder-Dimension Dependence
summary: We study KL-regularized contextual bandits under both reward and preference feedback. We show that greedy sampling can achieve logarithmic regret without explicit dependence on the eluder dimension. For reward feedback, we establish an eluder-dimension-independent regret bound for a simple greedy algorithm that directly samples from the Gibbs policy induced by the estimated reward. We further extend this result to preference feedback under both the general preference and Bradley--Terry models, while also sharpening existing dimension-dependent guarantees. Our analysis reveals a trade-off between greedy sampling and upper confidence bound-style exploration: greedy sampling enjoys stronger guarantees when KL regularization is sufficiently strong, whereas additional exploration becomes preferable as the regularization weakens.

AI.tldr: Greedy sampling in KL-regularized contextual bandits achieves logarithmic regret independent of eluder dimension for reward feedback, extendable to preference feedback; shows a trade-off between greedy sampling and UCB-type exploration depending on KL strength.
AI.motivation: To obtain regret guarantees for KL-regularized contextual bandits under both reward and preference feedback, without relying on eluder dimension, and to understand exploration strategies under different regularization levels.
AI.method: Proves a regret bound for a simple greedy algorithm that samples directly from the Gibbs policy induced by the estimated reward; extends analysis to general preference and Bradley–Terry models; sharpens existing dimension-dependent guarantees.
AI.result: Eluder-dimension-independent logarithmic regret bound for reward feedback; extension to preference feedback with both models; characterization of the KL strength threshold that favors greedy vs exploration; improved bounds for dimension-dependent settings.
AI.conclusion: Greedy sampling with sufficient KL regularization yields strong regret guarantees; as regularization weakens, additional exploration becomes advantageous; provides practical guidance on exploration strategy in KL-regularized contextual bandits with reward and preference feedback.

title: Drift-Constrained Optimization: Only Direction Matters in Fine-Tuning Instruct Models
summary: Fine-tuning instruct models often improves target performance while inducing behavioral drift from the reference model, which can degrade existing capabilities. Rather than treating this drift as an uncontrolled consequence of optimization, we specify a behavioral drift budget before optimization and ask how to boost the target-task performance within it. Locally, behavioral drift induces a shared geometry anchored at the reference model, with the drift budget defining a boundary within this space. In this space, drift determines distance from the reference, leaving update direction as the remaining degree of freedom. Fine-tuning updates can therefore be compared through their directional efficiency, naturally reformulating fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem. This reformulation makes a concrete prediction: changing the accessible directions can qualitatively alter the outcome of fine-tuning. We test this prediction in a stringent QA-only setting, where strong instruct models are fine-tuned only on final answers but must still generate multi-step reasoning at inference. Despite this mismatch, a coarse layer-selective probe reverses the failure of QA-only fine-tuning and reveals the existence of effective directions, with multiple neighboring configurations improving target performance while preserving reasoning and general capabilities. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation. Over more than 100 languages, the resulting models match or outperform dedicated translation systems and provide a stronger initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. Our results suggest that fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent. https://github.com/CONE-MT/DCO and https://huggingface.co/collections/LLaMAX/dco

AI.tldr: A drift-budgeted, direction-focused fine-tuning framework that searches for effective update directions within a bounded parameter-change region, improving target tasks (reasoning, translation) while preserving core capabilities.
AI.motivation: To control and understand behavioral drift during fine-tuning by constraining the allowed model changes and analyzing how the direction of updates, rather than their magnitude, affects outcomes.
AI.method: Define a drift budget anchored to a reference model to create a geometry of permissible updates; reformulate fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem within this drift space; use a coarse layer-selective probe in a QA-only fine-tuning setup to identify effective directions; evaluate on Qwen-3-8B and Qwen-3-14B across reasoning and translation tasks.
AI.result: Identified multiple neighboring update directions that substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation without sacrificing reasoning or general capabilities; translations across 100 languages match or exceed dedicated systems; improved initialization for subsequent RL; demonstrated that the outcome of fine-tuning depends on the chosen directions, not just the amount of change.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning should be viewed as selecting productive update directions within a bounded drift space rather than solely increasing magnitude; targeting directionality can yield robust gains in reasoning and translation while maintaining core capabilities.

title: Gradient-Free Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Scalable Safety-Critical Control
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides a principled framework for synthesizing safety certificates and robust controllers for safety-critical robotic systems. However, applying reachability analysis to high-dimensional nonlinear systems remains challenging: classical grid-based solvers suffer from the curse of dimensionality, continuous-time neural solvers require accurate spatial value gradients, and reinforcement-learning-based approaches often suffer from weak boundary anchoring and non-stationary adversarial policy optimization. We propose a discrete-time neural reachability framework for control-disturbance-affine systems that learns backward reachable tubes (BRTs) and backward reach-avoid tubes (BRATs) through Bellman-Isaacs value propagation. Our key idea is to combine equation-driven self-supervision with structured policy learning: rather than computing explicit PDE-gradients, we exploit the bang-bang structure of optimal safety interventions to construct approximate teacher actions from gradient-free value probes, converting adversarial actor learning into supervised policy learning. To stabilize long-horizon value propagation, we leverage the learned actor to train the value function backward from the terminal boundary using a windowed temporal curriculum, where each window is used as the boundary condition for the next window. Across benchmark problems up to 80 dimensions, our method learns accurate reachability value functions while improving stability over existing learning-based solvers. We further demonstrate observation-space scalability on F1-tenth racing with over 16,000-dimensional egocentric inputs. The learned safety filter generalizes zero-shot to unseen tracks and transfers to a physical RC car, achieving real-time robust collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: A discrete-time neural reachability framework for control-disturbance-affine systems that learns backward reachable tubes via Bellman-Isaacs propagation, combining equation-driven self-supervision with supervised policy learning to scale reachability to very high dimensions and enable real-time safety on hardware.
AI.motivation: To overcome the curse of dimensionality in Hamilton-Jacobi reachability and instability of learning-based solvers, by leveraging bang-bang optimal interventions and a curriculum-based backward propagation.
AI.method: Discrete-time neural reachability for control-disturbance-affine dynamics; learn BRTs and BRATs via Bellman-Isaacs value propagation; construct approximate teacher actions from gradient-free value probes exploiting bang-bang structure; convert adversarial actor learning into supervised policy learning; stabilize long-horizon value propagation with windowed temporal curriculum and boundary-conditioned training; test up to 80 dimensions; apply to 16k-dimensional observations; zero-shot generalization to unseen tracks and real RC car.
AI.result: Accurate reachability value functions up to 80 dimensions; improved stability vs prior learning-based solvers; scalable to very high-dimensional observation spaces; zero-shot generalization to unseen tracks; successful transfer to real hardware with real-time robust collision avoidance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates scalable, stable neural reachability for high-dimensional safety-critical systems and effective hardware transfer; the hybrid equation-driven and learning-based approach yields practical, real-time safety guarantees.

title: VectorHarness: Recovering Editable, Relation-Preserving Structure from Scientific Graphics
summary: Converting scientific graphics into editable representations remains a challenging problem for image-to-code generation because of their heterogeneous elements and complex layouts. Recent multi-agent reconstruction systems have advanced this line of work, but often follow a copy-paste paradigm: the reconstructed image closely resembles the original, while complex regions remain effectively uneditable. We instead formulate a different objective, raster-to-authoring reconstruction, which aims to recover an authoring representation that supports native, customized editing rather than mere visual replication. To this end, we present VectorHarness, a multi-agent framework for raster-to-authoring reconstruction that recovers heterogeneous components using type-appropriate native representations. Text, formulas, shapes, connectors, icons, charts, and tables are reconstructed as natively editable objects, while intrinsically image-based regions remain raster content. To systematically evaluate reconstruction quality, we introduce VectorHarness-Bench, which jointly assesses rendering fidelity, raster fallback coverage, executable object edits, and relation-preserving edits. Experiments show that VectorHarness improves executable edit success and relation preservation, reduces avoidable raster fallback, and maintains high visual fidelity across heterogeneous graphics.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent raster-to-authoring system (VectorHarness) reconstructs scientific graphics into editable native elements, using heterogeneous type-appropriate objects for text, formulas, shapes, connectors, icons, charts, and tables, while leaving image-only regions raster; augmented by VectorHarness-Bench for evaluation.
AI.motivation: To overcome copy-paste–oriented reconstructions that visually replicate graphics but yield uneditable regions, enabling native editability and relationship preservation across heterogeneous elements.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework that recovers heterogeneous components as type-appropriate native representations (text, formulas, shapes, connectors, icons, charts, tables) and retains intrinsically image-based regions as raster. It introduces VectorHarness-Bench, a benchmark evaluating rendering fidelity, raster fallback coverage, executable object edits, and relation-preserving edits.
AI.result: Experiments show improved executable edit success and relation preservation, reduced avoidable raster fallback, and maintained high visual fidelity across heterogeneous graphics.
AI.conclusion: VectorHarness enables editable reconstruction of diverse graphics and provides a benchmark suite to quantify rendering quality, editability, and relation preservation.

title: AttnFuse: A Composable DSL for Compiling Attentions to Fused GPU Kernels
summary:
Modern AI systems are built on the Transformer architecture, whose core operation, attention, accounts for the majority of computation and memory cost. Researchers continually propose new attention variants to improve quality, efficiency, or context length, but each variant currently requires expert-written GPU code to run at usable speeds. PyTorch's recent flex\_attention lets researchers describe custom attention patterns in Python and compile them to fused kernels, but its design is limited to modifications applied after the central matrix multiplication, excluding Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), the positional encoding used by every major LLM.
  We introduce AttnFuse, a small DSL for attention that makes pre-multiplication transformations like RoPE first-class operations. Researchers compose ten high-level building blocks to describe a variant, and AttnFuse's compiler emits a single fused GPU kernel for the entire computation. On an RTX 3090, AttnFuse achieves a 2.10$\times$ speedup over flex\_attention on the RoPE+causal pattern. On an H100, it runs a full Llama-3-8B training step within 5\% of PyTorch's hand-tuned backend. Our investigation reveals the Rotation Calculus: whether to fuse RoPE or apply it separately depends on the GPU's compute-to-bandwidth ratio, with a derived crossover that matches measurement. AttnFuse demonstrates that a small, attention-specific compiler can close the gap between flexible research code and production kernels.

AI.tldr: AttnFuse is a DSL and compiler for attention that treats RoPE and pre-multiplication transforms as first-class, enabling a single fused kernel that significantly improves performance over existing Python-level approaches and approaches PyTorch-level backends.
AI.motivation: Current attention variants require hand-tuned GPU kernels; Python-based composition (e.g., flex_attention) lacks RoPE integration and cannot fuse early transforms, hindering research-to-production efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce AttnFuse, a small domain-specific language with ten high-level building blocks to describe attention variants; compiler emits a single fused GPU kernel for the entire computation, including pre-multiplication transforms like RoPE.
AI.result: On RTX 3090, AttnFuse achieves 2.10x speedup over flex_attention for RoPE+causal; on NVIDIA H100, a full Llama-3-8B training step runs within 5% of PyTorch's hand-tuned backend; analysis reveals a Rotation Calculus crossover dependent on compute-to-bandwidth ratio.
AI.conclusion: A compact, attention-specific compiler can bridge research-code and production kernels, enabling faster experimentation and near-production performance for complex attention variants.

title: Degraded but Not Entirely Ineffective: PE-Based Deformable Graph Neural Networks
summary: Many real-world scenarios can be represented using graph-structured data. However, traditional GNNs that transmit messages based on first-order neighbors have long faced several fundamental contradictions: increasing depth leads to over-smoothing, long-range dependencies cause over-compression, fixed neighborhoods restrict the receptive field, and on heterophilous graphs, topological neighbors become a source of noise. Although many works have addressed these issues individually, few mechanisms can simultaneously alleviate all of these challenges. To address the aforementioned problems, we propose a Position Encoding-Based Deformable Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBDSAM) that solves them all in one step. Specifically, we utilize a deformable mechanism in the position space to identify relevant nodes to supplement the original first-order neighbor information of GNNs, allowing traditional GNNs to adapt to heterophilous scenarios. Through diagnostic experiments, we obtained several major findings: current offsets fail to have any effect; subsequently, we analyzed the causes of offset failure and why model performance still improves even after offset failure, pointing out future research directions. Based on these diagnostic experiments, we streamlined the original PEBDSAM, resulting in a simplified version, which we call the Position Encoding-Based Spatial Aggregation Module (PEBSAM). In addition, we propose a PEBSAM-Speed to adapt to large datasets. Finally, we designed the module to be plug-and-play and applied it to GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, achieving desirable results on three homophilous datasets and six heterophilous graph datasets.

AI.tldr: A deformable, position-encoding based spatial aggregation module (PEBDSAM) is proposed to augment GNNs by selecting relevant nodes beyond fixed neighborhoods, addressing depth-related issues and heterophily in a single step; simplified versions (PEBSAM and PEBSAM-Speed) enable plug-and-play use with GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE, with experiments on both homophilous and heterophilous datasets and diagnostic ablations.
AI.motivation: Traditional GNNs suffer from conflicting issues: over-smoothing with increasing depth, over-compression of long-range dependencies, fixed neighborhoods restricting receptive fields, and noise on heterophilous graphs. A unified mechanism is needed to alleviate all these simultaneously while maintaining efficiency and compatibility with existing architectures.
AI.method: Introduce PEBDSAM: a deformable mechanism in the position space that, guided by position-encoding, identifies and aggregates information from relevant nodes beyond first-order neighbors to supplement GNNs. This enables better adaptation to heterophily and expands the effective receptive field. A streamlined version PEBSAM is proposed, plus PEBSAM-Speed for large datasets. The module is designed to be plug-and-play with GCN, GAT, GIN, and GraphSAGE.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows desirable performance on three homophilous and six heterophilous datasets. Diagnostic experiments suggest current offsets have no effect; analysis explains offset-failure causes and why performance still improves, suggesting directions for future work. The simplified PEBSAM confirms viability, and the speed variant enables scalability to larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: PEBDSAM/PEBSAM family provides a unified, plug-and-play solution to mitigate depth-related degradation, fixed receptive fields, and heterophily-induced noise in GNNs, with diagnostic insights guiding future refinement and scalability improvements.

title: Vision-Force Admittance Learning for Peg Insertion into a Movable Hole
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project page: https://ai4ce.github.io/VFAL/
summary: Precise manipulation in dynamic environments, whether induced by a mobile robot base or a target with unknown motion, remains a major challenge in robotics. Manipulation in dynamic environments introduces substantial uncertainty, which fundamentally conflicts with the tight precision requirement of precise tasks such as peg-in-the-hole. We propose a Vision-Force Admittance Learning (VFAL) framework that fuses asynchronous visual feedback with a high-frequency force-based model, using visual pose estimations as a regularization term. VFAL adapts insertion strategies online to dynamic motion while maintaining millimeter-level precision. To obtain robust, low-frequency pose information, we employ state-of-the-art vision foundation models for visual pose estimation. Additionally, we incorporate failure recovery mechanisms to enhance overall robustness. We validate our approach in real-world experiments, demonstrating high success rates and strong adaptability to various pegs and dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: VFAL fuses asynchronous visual feedback with a high-frequency force-based admittance model to enable precise peg-in-hole manipulation in dynamic environments, achieving millimeter accuracy with online adaptation and robust failure recovery.
AI.motivation: Dynamic manipulation under motion induces uncertainty that degrades precision; existing methods struggle with unknown target motion; there is a need for robust, multi-rate fusion of vision and force control to maintain precision.
AI.method: Propose Vision-Force Admittance Learning (VFAL) that uses visual pose estimations as a regularization term in a high-frequency force-based admittance controller; employs vision foundation models for robust low-frequency pose; adapts insertion strategies online; includes failure recovery mechanisms.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show high success rates and strong adaptability across pegs and dynamic environments while maintaining millimeter-level precision.
AI.conclusion: VFAL demonstrates effective multi-rate fusion of vision and force control to achieve robust, adaptive precision manipulation in dynamic settings, with practical applicability and potential for broader manipulation tasks.

title: Harnessing Image Question Dependence for Better VLM Test-time Reinforcement Learning
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning can adapt vision-language models (VLMs) to unlabeled target data, but its effectiveness is fundamentally limited by the reliability of self-generated learning signals. To assess the reliability of consensus-based learning signals, we analyze VLM test-time reinforcement learning across diverse VQA datasets and model sizes, revealing two limitations. First, gains from consensus-based test-time training largely come from answer normalization rather than content correction. Second, many initial VLM responses are incorrect due to the model's limited ability to jointly use the image and the question; consensus rewards derived from these outputs may preserve the resulting grounding errors rather than correct them. Motivated by these, we propose TTIQ, a test-time reinforcement learning framework that harnesses image-question dependence for better vlm adaptation. TTIQ teacher-forces each sampled response under the original image-question pair and its image- and question-ablated variants, using the resulting token-level likelihood changes to estimate dependence on each input. It combines image and question dependence with calibrated confidence to construct a response-level reward that favors jointly grounded responses, and uses the token-level signals to assign greater positive policy credit to tokens supported by both inputs. This design favors responses that are jointly grounded in the image and the question and sufficiently confident, rather than merely popular. Experiments across eight VQA datasets and multiple VLM sizes show that TTIQ achieves the best average performance at every model scale. It further generalizes across VLM families, while models trained on one dataset improve performance on unseen datasets without further training.

AI.tldr: TTIQ is a test-time RL framework for VLMs in VQA that leverages image-question dependence and calibrated confidence to produce rewards favoring jointly grounded, confident responses, addressing failures of consensus-based learning; it shows strong cross-dataset and cross-model-sizes improvements without extra training.
AI.motivation: Two observed issues in consensus-based test-time learning: (1) gains come from answer normalization not content correction, (2) many initial outputs are incorrect due to limited image-question joint reasoning; consensus rewards may preserve grounding errors.
AI.method: TTIQ: teacher-forces each sampled answer under the original image-question pair and under image-ablated and question-ablated variants, measuring token-level likelihood changes to estimate input dependence; constructs a response-level reward from image and question dependence with calibrated confidence, and assigns positive credit to tokens supported by both inputs.
AI.result: Across eight VQA datasets and multiple VLM sizes, TTIQ achieves best average performance at every model scale; generalizes across VLM families; models trained on one dataset improve performance on unseen datasets without further training.
AI.conclusion: TTIQ provides a robust, input-dependent, grounded, and confidence-aware test-time RL framework that improves joint grounding and cross-domain generalization for VLM-based VQA, outperforming consensus-based methods.

title: An Efficient and Modular Framework for Targeted Harm Mitigation in LLMS
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful zero-shot learners but remain prone to misalignment with human preferences, often producing biased, toxic, or otherwise harmful outputs. Existing alignment methods, while effective, are costly and tightly coupled to the model, limiting flexibility and scalability. We propose a modular correction framework that augments pretrained LLMs with Activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters and a context-aware routing mechanism to eliminate harms from misaligned model responses. Our approach enables expert adapters to activate mid-sequence without invalidating the KV cache, allowing low-latency, targeted correction during generation. Each expert is trained to detect and mitigate specific harms, such as bias or toxicity. A learned router dynamically selects appropriate experts based on the models intermediate outputs. We demonstrate that our system improves alignment on standard safety benchmarks while preserving task performance, offering a lightweight and efficient path toward safer and more controllable LLM deployments.

AI.tldr: A modular, low-latency correction framework that augments pretrained LLMs with Activated LoRA adapters and a context-aware router to dynamically activate expert corrections during generation, improving alignment while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Misalignment of LLMs with human preferences leads to biased, toxic, or harmful outputs. Existing alignment methods are costly and tightly coupled to models, hindering scalability and deployment flexibility.
AI.method: Augment LLMs with Activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters and a context-aware router. Experts specialize in mitigating specific harms (e.g., bias, toxicity). Experts can activate mid-sequence without invalidating the KV cache to enable low-latency correction. A learned router selects experts based on intermediate model outputs during generation.
AI.result: Improves alignment on standard safety benchmarks while preserving task performance, demonstrating a lightweight and efficient path toward safer, more controllable LLM deployments.
AI.conclusion: A modular, plug-and-play framework enabling scalable, low-latency harm mitigation in LLMs via per-harm expert adapters and dynamic routing, decoupled from the base model.

title: JaxAHT: A JAX-Based Library for Ad Hoc Teamwork
summary: Ad Hoc Teamwork (AHT) addresses the challenge of designing agents capable of coordinating with novel partners without prior coordination. However, progress in the field is hindered by the prohibitive computational cost of the AHT research lifecycle, the lack of standardized benchmark implementations, and the absence of a diverse, validated evaluation teammate suite. In this work, we introduce JaxAHT, the first open-source, JAX-based library designed to accelerate and standardize the AHT research lifecycle. Leveraging JAX's hardware acceleration and massive parallelization capabilities, JaxAHT provides a unified framework for teammate generation, ego agent training, and evaluation against unseen teammates, achieving approximately 95x wall-clock speedup over PyTorch counterparts. Alongside the library, we contribute a diverse suite of evaluation teammates across the domains of Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked, and Hanabi. To illustrate the value of the framework, we use it to conduct a large-scale, compute-controlled benchmark study comparing teammate generation and AHT agent learning methods, finding that no algorithm consistently performs best, and that agent modeling primarily offers benefits in role-based scenarios with diverse teammates.

AI.tldr: Open-source JAX-based AHT toolkit (JaxAHT) that standardizes and speeds up the AHT lifecycle and provides diverse evaluation teammates; shows no single method dominates; substantial speedups over PyTorch.
AI.motivation: Prohibitive compute cost, lack of standardized benchmarks, and lack of diverse validated evaluation teammates impede progress in Ad Hoc Teamwork.
AI.method: Develop JaxAHT: unified framework for teammate generation, ego-agent training, and evaluation against unseen teammates; leverage JAX for hardware acceleration and parallelization; assemble evaluation teammates across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked, Hanabi; conduct large-scale compute-controlled benchmark comparing teammate generation and AHT learning methods.
AI.result: ≈95x wall-clock speedup over PyTorch; diversified evaluation suite; large-scale benchmark shows no algorithm consistently best; agent modeling provides benefits mainly in role-based scenarios with diverse teammates.
AI.conclusion: JaxAHT enables reproducible, scalable AHT research and reveals nuanced performance depending on teammate diversity and roles; highlights the need for diverse evaluation and careful method choice in AHT.

title: When Faster VLA Deployment Changes Closed-Loop Behavior: Task Success-Latency Analysis of SmolVLA Across PyTorch and ONNX Variants
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) deployment can reduce inference latency while changing closed-loop task behavior. We evaluate HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero on an RTX 2060 (6 GB) in LIBERO Spatial and Object (MuJoCo 3.3.2, LeRobot 0.6.1, seed 42), comparing PyTorch+AMP with ONNX Runtime CUDA Execution Provider (CUDA EP). The main evaluation uses 100 episodes/suite; a paired rollout uses 300 episodes/suite. PyTorch+AMP reaches 70.0%/88.0% Spatial/Object success at 1181 ms p99.
