Requested-FP16 and requested-INT8 ONNX reduce tether-inspect p99 to 601 ms and 532 ms, while Spatial success falls to 41.0% and 40.0% and Object remains at 89.0%. A graph audit shows those artifacts are byte-identical FP32 graphs, so the requested-INT8 row is not operator-level INT8 quantization. A static language-width ablation (16/24/32 tokens) yields Spatial success of 41.0%, 75.0%, and 71.0%; widths 24 and 32 recover much of the Spatial drop while Object success and uniform-bench latency stay approximately stable. Width-24 ONNX Spatial success is comparable to the PyTorch+AMP baseline at roughly half the latency (Wilson intervals overlap; two-proportion chi-squared p=0.53). Context width is an important contributor in this stack; it does not account for every PyTorch-vs-ONNX difference. Deployment evaluation should jointly report latency, artifact inspection, interface constraints, and closed-loop success. Code: https://github.com/rafiqul713/smolvla-libero-onnx.

AI.tldr: Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action deployment across PyTorch+AMP and ONNX Runtime CUDA EP on RTX 2060; ONNX can lower p99 latency with non-quantizing changes but degrades Spatial accuracy; artifact inspection reveals FP32 graphs, not true operator-level INT8; context/width crucial; recommends multi-faceted deployment reporting.
AI.motivation: Understand real-world VLA deployment tradeoffs and validate ONNX Runtime optimizations in LIBERO stack on MuJoCo/LeRobot tasks; identify factors driving latency and closed-loop success.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation on RTX 2060 (6 GB) in LIBERO Spatial and Object tasks; 100 episodes per suite, 300 in paired rollout; compare PyTorch+AMP vs ONNX Runtime CUDA EP; measure p99 latency; perform artifact inspection; static language-width ablation with 16/24/32 tokens; width-24 ONNX analysis; statistical tests (Wilson intervals, two-proportion chi-squared with p=0.53).
AI.result: PyTorch+AMP p99 latency 1181 ms; Requested-FP16 and Requested-INT8 ONNX reduce p99 to 601 ms and 532 ms, but Spatial success drops to 41.0% and 40.0% while Object remains at 89.0%; artifact audit: identical FP32 graphs, so not operator-level INT8 quantization; width ablation: Spatial success 41.0%, 75.0%, 71.0% for 16/24/32 tokens; 24/32 recover spatial performance, while Object success and uniform-bench latency stay roughly stable; width-24 ONNX Spatial success comparable to PyTorch+AMP baseline at about half latency (Wilson intervals overlap; p=0.53); context width is important but does not explain all PyTorch-vs-ONNX differences.
AI.conclusion: Deployment evaluations should jointly report latency, artifact inspection, interface constraints, and closed-loop success; do not assume ONNX-induced speedups reflect true quantization or uniform behavior across tasks; context width materially affects performance and should be reported alongside latency and success metrics.

title: Variational Template Matching with Statistical Fusion for Anomaly Detection in Patterned Structures
summary:
Anomaly detection in structured images is challenging in small-data settings where deep learning approaches are costly or impractical. Classical template matching is simple and interpretable but lacks robustness to geometric variations such as scale, rotation, and perspective.
  We propose a variational template matching framework that represents anomaly templates as a family of transformed instances and performs detection via normalized cross-correlation over this transformation space. To further improve robustness, we introduce a density-based statistical anomaly score derived from local intensity distributions using kernel density estimation (KDE). This produces a smooth representation that captures distributional concentration and tail behavior more robustly than histogram-based methods.
  The structural and statistical signals are integrated through a unified fusion formulation, enabling complementary modeling of geometric similarity and distributional deviation. Experiments on biological cell images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms classical baselines and achieves competitive performance with ResNet-50 under a fully training-free setting, while providing explicit localization. The approach offers an efficient, interpretable, and practical solution for anomaly detection in structured image domains.

AI.tldr: A training-free anomaly detection method that combines variational template matching with KDE-based density scoring, robust to geometric variations and providing explicit localization.
AI.motivation: In small-data regimes, deep learning is costly or impractical. Classical template matching is interpretable but brittle to scale/rotation/perspective changes. A robust, efficient, and interpretable method is needed for anomaly detection in structured images.
AI.method: Represent anomaly templates as a family of transformed instances and detect via normalized cross-correlation over the transformation space. Compute a density-based anomaly score from local intensity distributions using kernel density estimation (KDE). Fuse the geometric similarity and distributional deviation in a unified framework.
AI.result: On biological cell images, the method outperforms classical baselines and is competitive with ResNet-50 under a fully training-free setting, while providing explicit localization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational template matching plus KDE-based scoring offers an efficient, interpretable, and practical solution for anomaly detection in structured image domains, particularly in small-data contexts.

title: FlowTSFM: Turning Encoder Depth into Quantile Transport
summary: Encoder-based time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically rely on deep stacks of independently parameterized Transformer layers, where only the final forecast is supervised and intermediate representations have no explicit predictive role. We introduce FlowTSFM, an encoder architecture that interprets depth as a recurrent transport process: a single Transformer block is iteratively applied with shared parameters, while a quantile-flow objective supervises intermediate states along a prescribed trajectory from a prior distribution toward the final forecast. The objective combines pinball forecasting loss with path-level position matching. With only 38.8M parameters, FlowTSFM achieves competitive performance on GIFT-Eval and TIME, remaining within 1.8-4.6% MASE of stronger baselines while using approximately $3\times$ fewer parameters than a 12-layer Chronos-2 model (119.5M). Beyond accuracy, we introduce CosMean, a scale-free diagnostic measuring whether recurrent updates consistently align toward the final prediction. Under a matched intermediate-state probing protocol, FlowTSFM achieves a CosMean score of 0.919 compared with 0.350 for Chronos-2, suggesting that recurrent parameter sharing combined with path supervision is associated with substantially more structured predictive trajectories at a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: FlowTSFM reframes encoder-based time series foundation models as a recurrent transport process by sharing Transformer parameters across iterative steps and supervising intermediate states with a quantile-flow objective. This yields competitive accuracy with far fewer parameters and a strong diagnostic showing structured predictive trajectories.
AI.motivation: To address inefficiencies in conventional TSFMs where deep stacks with independently parameterized layers produce unutilized intermediate representations; to promote data-efficient, interpretable dynamics and reduce parameter counts.
AI.method: Apply a single Transformer block iteratively with shared parameters to model depth as a recurrent transport; train with a quantile-flow objective that combines pinball forecasting loss and path-level position matching to supervise intermediate states along a trajectory from a prior to the final forecast; evaluate using standard TS benchmarks and introduce a CosMean diagnostic.
AI.result: FlowTSFM uses 38.8M parameters and achieves competitive performance on GIFT-Eval and TIME, within 1.8-4.6% MASE of stronger baselines, while using ~3x fewer parameters than Chronos-2 (119.5M). It outperforms in structural predictability as indicated by CosMean score of 0.919 versus 0.350 for Chronos-2 under matched probing.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent parameter sharing with path-supervised intermediate states yields accurate and parameter-efficient time series forecasting, producing more structured predictive trajectories as evidenced by the CosMean diagnostic, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared with deeper, non-recurrent baselines.

title: MANAS-2: Constrained Reconstruction for EEG Foundation Models
summary: Masked reconstruction is widely used for EEG foundation models, but optimizing reconstruction on low-SNR waveforms does not necessarily produce the most useful latent representation. We introduce MANAS-2, a new EEG foundation model that combines a Raw-Band Hybrid (RBH) masked autoencoder with Constrained Reconstruction (ConRec), a physics-motivated regularizer. RBH jointly reconstructs temporal waveform patches and compact spectral-band targets, while ConRec acts only on the temporal decoder output, penalizing differences in RMS energy between adjacent short windows of the reconstructed waveform. ConRec is intended to shape the encoder by biasing it toward the organization of oscillatory-envelope information. Across seven held-out EEG datasets, adding ConRec to an otherwise identical RBH model increases frozen ridge recovery of six-band spectral power from mean R^2=0.860 to 0.906 and recovery of inter-patch band-energy dynamics from R^2=0.283 to 0.354, while temporal waveform information remains highly recoverable from the frozen latents. Applied to a temporal-only masked autoencoder, ConRec also improves frozen downstream transfer and frequency-dependent latent geometry despite receiving no spectral targets: i.e., the effects of ConRec are architecture-independent. MANAS-2 also outperforms leading EEG Foundation Models on most downstream knowledge-transfer tasks. From the effects of ConRec, we see that a physically motivated constraint imposed through the decoder can make for a more spectrally organized and transferable latent space. MANAS-2 therefore provides a new EEG foundation model built around constrained reconstruction as a mechanism for shaping representation--rather than reconstruction--quality.

AI.tldr: MANAS-2 introduces a Raw-Band Hybrid masked autoencoder with a physics-informed ConRec regularizer for EEG foundation models. ConRec biases the latent space toward oscillatory-envelope information, improving spectral power recovery and band-energy dynamics without sacrificing temporal information, and leading to better downstream transfer and state-of-the-art performance on several datasets.
AI.motivation: Low-SNR EEG reconstruction training does not guarantee useful latent representations. A physics-mituated constraint can shape the latent space to be more spectrally organized, improving transferability.
AI.method: A RBH masked autoencoder reconstructs temporal waveform patches and compact spectral-band targets. ConRec applies a RMS-energy-based penalty on adjacent short windows of the temporal decoder output, guiding the encoder to organize oscillatory-envelope information. The approach is tested on seven held-out EEG datasets, with both RBH and a temporal-only variant, showing architecture-independent improvements.
AI.result: Adding ConRec increases frozen ridge recovery of six-band spectral power from mean R^2 0.860 to 0.906 and recovery of inter-patch band-energy dynamics from 0.283 to 0.354. Temporal waveform information remains highly recoverable in frozen latents. ConRec also improves downstream transfer and frequency-dependent latent geometry in a temporal-only MAE, despite no spectral targets. MANAS-2 outperforms leading EEG Foundation Models on most downstream knowledge-transfer tasks.
AI.conclusion: A physically motivated decoder constraint can produce a more spectrally organized and transferable latent space, making constrained reconstruction a mechanism for shaping representations, not merely improving reconstruction quality; MANAS-2 offers a new EEG foundation model built around this idea.

title: Visible Touch: Rendering Contact for Visuomotor Policies
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). Project website: https://visibletouch.github.io/
summary: Integrating contact information into visuomotor policies remains an open problem. Touch is essential to robust manipulation, yet most modern policies, including pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models, operate from vision and proprioception alone. Existing approaches to closing this gap require specialized tactile hardware, add separate tactile encoders, or commit to non-image policy backbones, all incompatible with the modern paradigm of image-conditioned policies built on pretrained 2D visual representations. Our key insight is that the bottleneck is not the contact information itself, but how it is delivered: when contact signals are exposed in the same spatial frame as the scene the policy already attends to, they become directly usable by any image-conditioned policy without architectural changes. We operationalize this insight in Visible Touch, paired with a custom low-cost magnetic contact sensor that is open-sourced and fabricated from off-the-shelf parts via a parametric CAD-to-mold pipeline. Across the LIBERO benchmark, Visible Touch improves BC-Transformer success by 15.7 percentage points on average in the 2-view setting, with similar gains in the 1-view setting; controlled comparisons show that the contact-integration strategy strongly affects how effectively tactile information is used. The pattern holds when fine-tuning pretrained VLAs: miniVLA on LIBERO gains 25 percentage points on average, and $π_{0.5}$ on four real-world contact-rich tasks gains 30 percentage points with our custom sensor.

AI.tldr: Exposing tactile contact signals in the scene's spatial frame enables image-conditioned visuomotor policies to use tactile information without architectural changes, demonstrated by a low-cost, open-source sensor in Visible Touch that yields large performance gains on LIBERO and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies trained on vision and proprioception lack tactile feedback, and current tactile approaches require hardware or backbones incompatible with image-conditioned 2D visual representations. The bottleneck is how contact information is delivered, not the information itself.
AI.method: Introduce Visible Touch with a low-cost magnetic contact sensor; deliver contact signals in the same spatial frame as the scene; open-source hardware built via parametric CAD-to-mold pipeline; evaluate with pretrained and fine-tuned 2D visual representations (BC-Transformer, miniVLA) on LIBERO and real-world tasks; compare 2-view and 1-view settings.
AI.result: Significant gains: BC-Transformer improves by 15.7 percentage points on average in 2-view (similar gains in 1-view); fine-tuning pretrained VLAs (miniVLA) yields ~25-point gains on LIBERO; on four real-world contact-rich tasks, π0.5 gains ~30 points with the custom sensor.
AI.conclusion: Delivering contact information in the scene frame is an effective, architecture-agnostic way to leverage tactile data in image-conditioned policies; the approach is hardware-efficient, open-source, and yields consistent performance improvements across policies and settings.

title: Adaptive Conformal Redistribution for Inter-class Transitional Uncertainty in Medical Image Classification
summary: Medical image classification is frequently complicated by transitional categories whose feature distributions overlap those of adjacent classes, producing ambiguous decision boundaries. Conformal prediction returns uncertainty-aware prediction sets, but these are not directly actionable in clinical screening, where a single decision is required. This work proposes adaptive conformal redistribution (AdaConRed), a label-free post-conformal decision rule that converts ambiguous prediction sets into refined class assignments. A five-stage pipeline is developed. Vision-language generative augmentation addresses minority-class scarcity; a frozen DermFoundation encoder provides embeddings; a lightweight multi-layer perceptron performs classification; an entropy-modulated, margin-aware nonconformity score constructs adaptive prediction sets; samples predicted as transitional with multi-label sets are reassigned to the most probable alternative class within the set, using only model outputs at inference. Evaluation uses the OSCC oral lesion and ISIC skin lesion benchmarks at a miscoverage level of 0.2. On the 3-class OSCC benchmark, overall accuracy improves from 73.54% to 77.38%, with oral cancer accuracy rising from 64.29% to 82.14% and benign accuracy from 56.57% to 70.20%. Reassignment of transitional samples reduces OPMD accuracy from 84.78% to 80.16%, consistent with the asymmetric cost of missed malignancy. On ISIC, overall accuracy improves from 85.83% to 87.19%, melanoma accuracy rising from 66.04% to 68.34%. AdaConRed outperforms LAC, APS and RAPS under an identical backbone and redistribution rule. Conformal prediction can be extended beyond uncertainty quantification toward actionable decision support where transitional disease categories are present, with gains concentrated in the clinically critical malignant categories. Code repository: https://github.com/saibal436ghosh/AdaConRed.

AI.tldr: AdaConRed turns conformal prediction uncertainty sets into actionable class assignments via a label-free post-conformal rule, boosting accuracy on OSCC and ISIC with preserved miscoverage, and outperforming baselines LAC/APS/RAPS.
AI.motivation: Transitional, overlapping feature distributions create ambiguous decision boundaries in medical image classification. Conformal prediction yields uncertain sets that are not directly actionable in clinical screening; there is a need for a single, actionable decision rule that leverages model outputs.
AI.method: Five-stage pipeline: (1) vision-language generative augmentation to mitigate minority-class scarcity; (2) frozen DermFoundation encoder for embeddings; (3) lightweight multi-layer perceptron classifier; (4) entropy-modulated, margin-aware nonconformity score to form adaptive prediction sets; (5) at inference, reassign transitional samples with multi-label sets to the most probable alternative class within the set, using only model outputs.
AI.result: On OSCC (3-class): accuracy 73.54%→77.38%; oral cancer 64.29%→82.14%; benign 56.57%→70.20%. OPMD accuracy reduced 84.78%→80.16%. On ISIC: overall 85.83%→87.19%; melanoma 66.04%→68.34%. AdaConRed outperforms LAC, APS, and RAPS with the same backbone and redistribution rule.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction can be transformed into actionable clinical decision support in the presence of transitional disease categories, with most gains in malignant classes. Code is available for reproduction.

title: When Compliance Data Masquerades as Evaluation: Measurement Validity for Deployed AI Systems
summary: We argue that a recurring failure in the evaluation of deployed AI systems occurs when data collected for operational monitoring or regulatory compliance are interpreted as if they were designed for comparative evaluation. Automated driving provides a concrete example of this problem. U.S. disengagement and crash-reporting regimes produce valuable operational evidence, but differences in reporting scope, exposure, deployment domain, event capture, and comparator construction limit the safety claims that can be supported from these measurements alone. We frame this issue as a measurement-validity problem in AI evaluation rather than as a transportation-specific data limitation. We argue that comparative claims about deployed AI systems require alignment between the intended capability, measured outcome, exposure opportunity, deployment domain, data-generation process, and evaluation comparator. Using automated-driving safety evaluation as a case study, we propose an evaluation contract that makes these assumptions explicit before operational data are interpreted as evidence of comparative performance. The broader implication is that data useful for monitoring deployed AI systems are not automatically valid benchmarks for evaluating them.

AI.tldr: Monitoring data from operational/regulatory contexts are not automatically valid benchmarks for comparing deployed AI systems; a measurement-validity framework and explicit evaluation contract are proposed, illustrated via automated driving safety.
AI.motivation: There is a recurrent evaluation failure: data collected for monitoring or compliance are misinterpreted as designed for comparative evaluation. Automated driving exemplifies this, where disengagement and crash reports yield evidence but differing scopes, exposures, domains, event capture, and comparator construction weaken safety claims. The problem is framed as a measurement-validity issue rather than a data limitation.
AI.method: Frame the issue through automated-driving safety evaluation as a case study and develop an evaluation contract that makes explicit the assumptions before interpreting operational data as evidence of comparative performance. Define and require alignment among intended capability, measured outcome, exposure opportunity, deployment domain, data-generation process, and evaluation comparator.
AI.result: Propose a measurement-validity framework and an evaluation contract. Demonstrate that operational/monitoring data do not automatically serve as valid benchmarks for comparative evaluation and outline how explicit alignment enables credible comparisons across deployed AI systems.
AI.conclusion: Comparative safety claims require explicit alignment of capability, outcome, exposure, domain, data generation, and comparator. Evaluation contracts should govern the use of monitoring data to prevent invalid benchmarks; data for monitoring should be treated as contextual evidence rather than automatic benchmarks for evaluation.

title: IBBench-Light: A Paired Evaluation of Task-Conditioned Responses to External Directives
summary: An external record may contain a procedure to apply or text to read, depending on the user's request. IBBench-Light tests both uses against the same record. Twelve semantic bases yield 144 matched pairs per model; four quantized instruction models produced 1,152 archived greedy responses. Paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA) requires both members to satisfy their output contracts. Qwen succeeds on 132 execute and 109 process prompts, but only 97 complete pairs, showing what marginal averages omit. We audit literal-target exposure and case normalization, then add 1,722 logged CPU generations to test directive-absent controls, twelve additional semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping. In the pinned Phi rerun, changing the end-of-sequence (EOS) set changes exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. A bounded IHEval comparison uses the same SmolLM2 checkpoint and output budget while preserving its published instruction roles and scorer. The benchmark measures conditional task and output-contract success. Its task margins and paired count need to be read together with the stopping policy.

AI.tldr: The abstract presents a benchmark (IBBench-Light) to assess exact-output-contract adherence (PECA) across LMs using varying records, prompts, and controls; results show sensitivity to EOS and directive controls, with marginal averages obscuring performance, and the value of broader semantic bases and explicit stopping policies.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively evaluate how well instruction-tuned language models comply with explicit output contracts and directives (beyond surface-level accuracy), and to reveal how evaluation choices (EOS, stopping, data auditing) shape measured performance.
AI.method: IBBench-Light protocol: 12 semantic bases yield 144 matched pairs per model; four quantized instruction models yield 1,152 archived greedy responses. PECA requires both outputs to satisfy their contracts. Qwen’s performance is reported on 132 execute and 109 process prompts, with 97 complete pairs. Audits include literal-target exposure and case normalization; 1,722 logged CPU generations are added to probe directive-absent controls; twelve more semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping are tested. The pinned Phi rerun shows EOS-set changes move exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. A bounded IHEval comparison uses the SmolLM2 checkpoint and same budget, preserving instruction roles and scorer. The benchmark measures conditional task and output-contract success; results depend on stopping policy and task margins that should be read together with paired counts.
AI.result: Key results include: (i) Qwen achieves 132 execute and 109 process prompts but only 97 complete PECA pairs, illustrating divergence between marginal averages and actual pairwise compliance; (ii) changing the EOS set in the pinned Phi rerun dramatically alters exact paired success (0/144 → 62/144); (iii) expansion of semantic bases and added controls (1,722 CPU generations, wording changes, stopping) affect the measured success and reveal directionally different outcomes across prompts and bases; (iv) a bounded IHEval test using SmolLM2 confirms the approach preserves instruction roles and scorer while enabling cross-system comparisons; (v) the benchmark foregrounds conditional task and output-contract success as core signals, with margins and paired counts contingent on stopping policy.
AI.conclusion: Exact-paired success is highly sensitive to EOS and directive-controls; marginal averages can misrepresent performance; robust evaluation requires explicit contract definitions, careful pairing, and policy-aware stopping; broader semantic bases and directive-absent testing expose hidden behaviors, underscoring the need for contract-focused benchmarks in instruction-following models.

title: GIFT: Glove-Inferred Force Transfer: Force-Aware Human-to-Robot Skill Transfer from a Wearable Sensing Glove to a Robot Hand Without Tactile Sensors
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Project page: https://tzahsarusi.github.io
summary: Human-to-robot skill transfer from sensing gloves has so far relied on shared hardware: the same tactile glove worn by the demonstrator and the robot, or a learned alignment between two tactile sensors. We present GIFT (Glove-Inferred Force Transfer), a pipeline in which the interface between human and robot is a physical unit rather than a shared sensor: fingertip force is measured in newtons on the human side and estimated in newtons on the robot side. A wearable glove records finger flexion, calibrated fingertip force, and wrist orientation, while a head-mounted camera records the demonstration; no robot is present. At deployment, the robot estimates force from actuator-current residuals relative to a free-space baseline, through a calibrated mapping to newtons, so any position-controlled hand that reports motor current can serve as the deployment platform. The policy uses a glove-space state and predicts finger-position targets; the robot enters only through two calibrated adapters, a retargeting decoder and a force estimator. We evaluate GIFT on a cup grasp-and-hold task with two action-chunking policies trained on the same demonstrations, with fingertip-force inputs retained in one and zeroed in the other. In a 50-rollout evaluation with sample size and metrics fixed before scoring, both policies succeeded in all 25 rollouts. The median of the per-rollout hold-phase grip-force estimates was 53% lower with force inputs: 1.20 N versus 2.55 N (one-sided Mann-Whitney U, p<0.0001). In an observation ablation, a vision-only policy achieved 0/15 grasps, policies given hand-command state acquired the grasp, and the force inputs determined how hard the policy held. A force channel measured on the human hand thus transfers to a robot hand with no tactile hardware, through a retargeting map from five glove channels to seven robot actuators, with no sensor shared between the two.

AI.tldr: GIFT transfers fingertip force from a sensing glove to a robot hand without shared tactile sensors by estimating robot force from actuator-current residuals and a calibrated map, enabling force-aware manipulation with a universal deployment path.
AI.motivation: To enable human-to-robot skill transfer without shared hardware or identical tactile sensors, by decoupling sensing from actuation and using a calibrated force-estimation pipeline.
AI.method: Wearable glove records finger flexion, calibrated fingertip force, and wrist orientation; head-mounted camera records demonstration; at deployment, robot estimates force from actuator current residuals via a calibrated mapping to newtons. A glove-space policy predicts finger-position targets; deployment uses two adapters: a retargeting decoder and a force estimator to map glove channels (5) to robot actuators (7). Evaluation on a cup grasp with two action-chunking policies trained on the same demonstrations, comparing force-informed vs force-zeroed inputs; a vision-only ablation.
AI.result: In a 50-rollout evaluation (metrics fixed beforehand), both policies succeeded in all 25 rollouts; the median grip-force during hold phase was 1.20 N with force inputs vs 2.55 N without (p<0.0001, one-sided Mann–Whitney U). Vision-only policy achieved 0/15 grasps; hand-command-state policies required the force-input to acquire the grasp, and the force-input determined how hard the policy held. A force channel on the human hand transfers to a robot hand with no tactile hardware via a five-to-seven channel retargeting map.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a complete cross-domain force transfer from human glove to robot hand without shared sensors, enabling force-aware manipulation on arbitrary position-controlled grippers by simple adapters and calibrated force estimation.

title: HGSQ: Heatmap-Guided Sparse Query Detector for Real-Time Aerial Small Object Detection
summary: Real-time aerial small object detection is an important visual signal and image processing problem, requiring a detector to preserve fine-grained localization while avoiding redundant computation on large background regions. This paper focuses on this deployment-oriented aerial/UAV setting rather than claiming a universal detector for all object detection scenarios. Existing Transformer-based detectors provide strong global modeling, but their dense query initialization and multi-layer decoder still spend substantial computation on background tokens, which is inefficient when small objects occupy only sparse image regions. To address this problem, this paper proposes HGSQ, a Heatmap-Guided Sparse Query Detector for real-time aerial small object detection. HGSQ uses a lightweight Heatmap Budget Predictor (HBP) to predict a foreground budget map in a single forward pass. The predicted heatmap is then used by three fixed components: Heatmap-Guided Sparse Query Selection (HSQS), which initializes decoder queries from high-confidence foreground positions; Heatmap-Gated Lite Snake Convolution (HGLSConv), which performs local shape refinement only on heatmap-activated small-object regions; and Adaptive Query-Decoder Budgeting (AQDB), which adjusts the query budget and decoder depth according to the estimated object density. Unlike post-hoc heatmap generation, HGSQ treats the heatmap as a real-time computation budget rather than a visualization map during deployment. Experiments on NWPU VHR-10 and VisDrone2019 show that HGSQ achieves 95.10 mAP50 on NWPU VHR-10 and 54.8 mAP50 on VisDrone2019, while reducing GFLOPs to 48.6 and running at 96.0 FPS on an RTX 4070 under our TensorRT FP16 deployment protocol.

AI.tldr: HGSQ introduces a heatmap-guided sparse query detector for real-time aerial small-object detection, predicting a foreground budget to sparsify Transformer queries and refinements, achieving high accuracy with low computation.
AI.motivation: In UAV contexts, small objects occupy sparse image regions; dense-query Transformers waste computation on background regions. A deployment-oriented detector should preserve localization while reducing computation.
AI.method: A Heatmap Budget Predictor (HBP) forecasts a foreground heatmap in one pass. This heatmap informs three fixed components: (1) Heatmap-Guided Sparse Query Selection (HSQS) initializes decoder queries from high-confidence foreground positions; (2) Heatmap-Gated Lite Snake Convolution (HGLSConv) refines local shapes only in heatmap-activated areas; (3) Adaptive Query-Decoder Budgeting (AQDB) adjusts the number of queries and decoder depth according to estimated object density. The heatmap serves as a real-time computation budget during deployment, not just a visualization.
AI.result: On NWPU VHR-10: 95.10 mAP50; on VisDrone2019: 54.8 mAP50. GFLOPs reduced to 48.6; runtime 96.0 FPS on RTX 4070 with TensorRT FP16 deployment.
AI.conclusion: HGSQ demonstrates deployment-oriented efficiency by leveraging heatmap-guided sparsity to maintain high localization accuracy for aerial small objects while substantially reducing computation and enabling real-time performance.

title: Curvature-Independent Regret Bounds for Distributed Online Optimization on Hadamard Manifolds
summary: This work addresses decentralized online Riemannian optimization on Hadamard manifolds. Prior work under geodesic convexity (g-convexity) may require curvature information in the optimization analysis, typically through a finite lower bound on the sectional curvature. Curvature may also enter the step size or contraction factor of tangent-space Riemannian consensus schemes. In this work, we relax the curvature dependence for a narrower class of horospherical convex (h-convex) functions. We study Distributed Riemannian Online Gradient Descent (D-ROGD), which combines local Riemannian h-subgradient updates with an implicit Fréchet-mean consensus. For h-convex and strongly h-convex local objectives, we establish $O(\sqrt{T})$ and $O(\log T)$ static regret, respectively, matching the corresponding Euclidean rates with respect to $T$, with network dependence governed solely by the spectral gap. To our knowledge, these are the first curvature-independent regret guarantees for decentralized online optimization on Hadamard manifolds. Experiments on hyperbolic embeddings corroborate the predicted rates, with no observable degradation due to curvature.

AI.tldr: Curvature-independent regret guarantees for decentralized online Riemannian optimization on Hadamard manifolds using D-ROGD; achieves O(sqrt(T)) static regret for h-convex and O(log T) for strongly h-convex; network dependency via spectral gap; validated on hyperbolic embeddings.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses under geodesic convexity require curvature bounds that influence analysis and parameters; aim to relax curvature assumptions to horospherical convexity to enable curvature-independent guarantees in decentralized online optimization on nonpositively curved manifolds.
AI.method: Proposes Distributed Riemannian Online Gradient Descent (D-ROGD) combining local Riemannian h-subgradient updates with an implicit Fréchet-mean consensus on Hadamard manifolds; analyzes regret for h-convex and strongly h-convex objectives; curvature dependence is removed in the analysis.
AI.result: Proved static regret bounds O(sqrt(T)) for h-convex and O(log T) for strongly h-convex objectives; network dependence arises solely from the spectral gap; claims first curvature-independent regret guarantees in decentralized online optimization on Hadamard manifolds; experiments on hyperbolic embeddings support the rates with no observed curvature degradation.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that curvature dependence can be avoided under horospherical convexity in decentralized online Riemannian optimization, enabling robust performance on Hadamard manifolds and motivating use in hyperbolic embedding tasks.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Cybersecurity and Systems Survey on Threat Landscapes, Defense Architectures, and Open Challenges
summary: The transition from passive foundation models to autonomous, goal-directed agentic AI systems has introduced unprecedented capabilities by coupling recursive cognitive reasoning loops, persistent memory architectures, live tool execution planes, and multi-agent collaboration topologies. However, granting probabilistic neural cores execution authority across filesystems, networks, and cloud infrastructure dissolves classical security perimeters: natural language simultaneously serves as input data, internal control code, and communication protocols, exposing a Turing-complete blast radius where untrusted data represents executable instructions. This survey delivers a comprehensive systems-security reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI, synthesizing 206 foundational studies and regulatory standards. We formalize the general agent architecture as a stateful 5-tuple and establish a 6-dimensional trustworthiness taxonomy covering security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability. We systematically analyze threat surfaces across intra-execution loops and interaction planes, formulate a multi-layered zero-trust defense-in-depth architecture integrating Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, and sandboxed runtimes, review standardized evaluation benchmarks, and map technical controls to international AI governance frameworks.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey and formal framework for trustworthy agentic AI, introducing a 5-tuple agent architecture and a 6-dimension trustworthiness taxonomy, plus a defense-in-depth zero-trust architecture.
AI.motivation: To address systemic security, safety, privacy, explainability, fairness, and accountability challenges posed by autonomous, tool-using AI agents with open execution across software layers.
AI.method: Systematic synthesis of 206 studies and standards; formalization of the agent as a 5-tuple stateful model; development of a 6D trustworthiness taxonomy; threat surface analysis; design of a multi-layer zero-trust architecture (Dual-LLM isolation, Capability-Based Access Control, kernel eBPF probes, sandboxed runtimes); review of benchmarks and governance mappings.
AI.result: A reference framework for trustworthy agentic AI; formalized architecture and taxonomy; identified threat surfaces; proposed practical controls; alignment with international AI governance frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a formalized, comprehensive framework to guide trustworthy agentic AI research and practice, emphasizing layered defense, explainability, and governance alignment.

title: DreamSat-Bench: Development and Initial Testing of a Testbed for AI-Based Pose Estimation from 3D Reconstruction
summary: This paper presents the development and initial testing of DreamSat-Bench, a modular rendezvous and proximity operation testbed designed to benchmark AI-based relative navigation techniques. By integrating a software- and hardware-in-the-loop robotic pipeline, the platform enables a seamless transition from digital simulation to physical reality. DreamSat-Bench unifies state-of-the-art robotic learning tools such as MuJoCo, Isaac Lab, and LeRobot into a single benchmarking platform, utilizing robotic arms to trace 3D trajectories. The platform allows for extensive customization of orbital environments and lighting to evaluate the simulation-to-reality gap. We demonstrate the testbed's utility by evaluating an end-to-end vision-based navigation pipeline that pairs DreamSat, a generative AI framework for single-view 3D reconstruction, with FoundationPose for zero-shot 6-DoF tracking of unseen spacecraft. Initial testing explores mission-representative orbital segments, including fixed-point station-keeping and fly-around characterization. Through a series of parametric studies, we quantify the impacts of reconstruction latency, mesh resolution, orbital range, and illumination geometry on pose estimation accuracy. Finally, a preliminary hardware-in-the-loop campaign qualitatively validates the physical deployment of the pipeline, identifying target symmetry and accumulated tracking drift as critical factors for robust navigation. DreamSat-Bench provides a rigorous framework for maturing autonomous navigation with unprepared space assets in the absence of prior geometric models.

AI.tldr: A modular AI-enabled rendezvous/navigation testbed DreamSat-Bench integrates software/hardware-in-the-loop, combining MuJoCo, Isaac Lab, LeRobot, DreamSat and FoundationPose to benchmark appearance-based navigation for unmodeled space assets, with parametric studies and a preliminary hardware-in-the-loop validation.
AI.motivation: There is a need for robust autonomous relative navigation for unprepared space assets without prior geometric models, and a desire to close the sim-to-real gap by providing a controllable, realistic benchmarking platform for AI-based perception and pose estimation.
AI.method: DreamSat-Bench is a modular testbed that unifies software and hardware through a software- and hardware-in-the-loop robotic pipeline. It uses robotic arms to trace 3D trajectories and supports comprehensive customization of orbital environments and illumination. The end-to-end vision-based navigation pipeline evaluated pairs DreamSat (single-view 3D reconstruction) with FoundationPose (zero-shot 6-DoF tracking). The study conducts mission-representative segments (fixed-point station-keeping, fly-around) and parametric studies varying reconstruction latency, mesh resolution, orbital range, and illumination geometry. A preliminary hardware-in-the-loop campaign qualitatively validates physical deployment and highlights target symmetry and accumulated tracking drift as key factors.
AI.result: The testbed demonstrated utility by evaluating an end-to-end pipeline and quantifying how reconstruction latency, mesh resolution, orbital range, and illumination affect pose estimation accuracy. The hardware-in-the-loop campaign qualitatively validated deployment and identified symmetry and drift as critical factors for robust navigation.
AI.conclusion: DreamSat-Bench provides a rigorous framework for maturing autonomous navigation with unprepared space assets in the absence of prior geometric models and offers a practical path toward sim-to-real maturity of AI-based relative navigation systems.

title: GroundBench: A Factorized, Counterfactual Benchmark for Locating VLM Affordance Failures
summary: A companion evaluation found that naming the target part in a manipulation prompt increased action accuracy by 0.32-0.63 across eight vision-language models, with no model outperforming a constant baseline until the part was named. However, naming the part supplies information that a real system must infer, confounding visual grounding, mechanical reasoning, and category-to-action association. We introduce GroundBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates these explanations through six branch-and-merge conditions, each adding a controlled information bundle, and a counterfactual re-ask targeting a real alternate part visible in the same image. Across three OpenAI models and 1,068 predictions, supplying the target region without its identity leaves action accuracy at or below the 0.53 majority baseline (0.26, 0.26, and 0.53), although the models largely reproduce the supplied region. Supplying identity without location instead yields 0.74, 0.68, and 0.68. Every above-baseline gain in this curated set occurs where the supplied part category itself determines the action. A no-vision control leaves GPT-5's scores unchanged or improved, providing evidence consistent with substantial category-to-action association. GPT-4o mini declines on one condition, so this interpretation is not universal. Adding joint type and motion axis does not improve accuracy across six model-stratum comparisons. On 74 counterfactual pairs from 32 objects, GPT-5 achieves 0.86 pair-weighted compliance with a 0.07 shortcut rate but fails all observed push-to-lift-vertical cases. GroundBench identifies which supplied information changes affordance behavior and tests whether apparently grounded performance can be reproduced through textual shortcuts.

AI.tldr: Naming the target part improves action accuracy across vision-language models, but the gain often reflects category-to-action cues rather than true visual grounding. GroundBench diagnoses the information driving affordances with six branch-and-merge conditions and counterfactuals. Experiments reveal that supplying region without identity performs near or below baseline, while supplying identity without location yields higher accuracy; gains are concentrated where the part category determines the action. A no-vision control and counterfactual tests show textual shortcuts can mimic grounding in some cases, underscoring the need for diagnostic benchmarks to separate grounding, mechanical reasoning, and category-to-action associations.
AI.motivation: To disentangle which information signals underlie model-prompted manipulation actions and to provide a diagnostic benchmark (GroundBench) that isolates visual grounding, mechanical reasoning, and category-to-action mapping.
AI.method: GroundBench employs six branch-and-merge conditions to add controlled information bundles and a counterfactual re-ask targeting an alternate visible part. Evaluations across three OpenAI models (1,068 predictions total) examine effects of supplying target region with/without identity, with/without location, and joint type/motion axis. A separate set of 74 counterfactual pairs from 32 objects tests model behavior and shortcut susceptibility, including a no-vision control.
AI.result: Key findings: supplying the target region without its identity leaves accuracy at or below the 0.53 majority baseline (model scores: 0.26, 0.26, 0.53). Supplying identity without location yields 0.74, 0.68, 0.68. Gains above baseline occur only when the supplied part category determines the action. A no-vision control shows GPT-5 scores unchanged or improve, suggesting non-visual cues or textual shortcuts contribute. GPT-5 achieves 0.86 pair-weighted compliance on 74 counterfactuals with a 0.07 shortcut rate but fails push-to-lift-vertical cases. Adding joint type and motion axis does not improve accuracy across six model-strata comparisons.
AI.conclusion: GroundBench can diagnose which supplied information alters affordance behavior and evaluate whether apparently grounded performance can be reproduced by textual shortcuts. The results imply substantial category-to-action associations and that observed grounding effects may reflect information other than true visual grounding.

title: Online Bayesian Node Classification on Inductive Graphs under Distribution Shift
summary: On evolving graphs, node classifiers must satisfy two key requirements: inductive generalization to newly arriving nodes under distribution shift and calibrated uncertainty for safety-sensitive applications. Standard graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically trained once and address neither requirement. We adapt the Bayesian last-layer (BLL) model by placing random last-layer parameters on top of a deterministic GNN encoder for uncertainty quantification. The categorical softmax likelihood required for classification breaks Gaussian conjugacy, so neither the training posterior nor the test-time streaming update has a closed-form solution. To address both challenges, we introduce a variational Bayesian last-layer (VBLL) objective that jointly trains the encoder and an approximate last-layer posterior by maximizing an evidence lower bound with a Monte Carlo expected log-likelihood. At test time, we freeze the encoder and apply an online Laplace update to the last-layer posterior. This update corresponds to a power-prior Bayesian model with exponential forgetting and a Kullback-Leibler anchor to the training posterior. Across five node-classification benchmarks under distribution shift, online GVBLL is the only method to achieve the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on every dataset. It improves accuracy by up to 17 percentage points on Cora and 14 percentage points on ogbn-arxiv over the strongest non-GVBLL baseline, while remaining competitive in calibration with MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles, Temperature Scaling, and Gaussian-process classifiers.

AI.tldr: Bayesian last-layer on top of a deterministic GNN with a variational objective (VBLL) and online Laplace updates improves uncertainty and accuracy for node classification under distribution shift on evolving graphs.
AI.motivation: Standard GNNs trained once struggle with inductive generalization to new nodes under distribution shift and lack calibrated uncertainty for safety-critical applications.
AI.method: Place random last-layer parameters on a deterministic GNN encoder. Use a variational Bayesian last-layer (VBLL) objective to jointly train the encoder and an approximate last-layer posterior via an evidence lower bound with Monte Carlo expected log-likelihood. At test time, freeze the encoder and perform an online Laplace update to the last-layer posterior (power-prior with exponential forgetting and a KL anchor to the training posterior).
AI.result: On five node-classification benchmarks under distribution shift, online GVBLL achieves best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on every dataset. Improvements reach up to 17 percentage points in accuracy on Cora and 14 on ogbn-arxiv over the strongest non-GVBLL baseline, with competitive calibration alongside MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles, Temperature Scaling, and Gaussian-process classifiers.
AI.conclusion: VBLL with online updating effectively handles inductive generalization and calibrated uncertainty in evolving graphs, outperforming strong baselines under distribution shift and offering robust uncertainty quantification.

title: How Many Thoughts Can a Vector Hold? The Capacity of Reasoning by Superposition
summary: Large language models solve hard problems through intermediate computations across multi-step reasoning. Traditional chain-of-thought encodes these computations as tokens. Recent continuous and recurrent methods instead move partial computations into fixed-dimensional latent states, where a single thought can superpose multiple alternatives. This raises a fundamental design question:what should continuous thoughts preserve as reasoning proceeds? An intuitive approach discards past computations and keeps only the current reasoning frontier. Storing more items seems to dilute states and waste limited representational capacity. We show this intuition can be incorrect. Under identical downstream computations, cumulative superposition retaining full reasoning history can require lower representational dimensions than frontier-only superposition holding only current alternatives. At fixed hidden width, this advantage allows latent reasoners to retain more valid evidence, distinguish more plausible downstream outcomes, and delay the point where compressed states turn unreliable. This counter-intuitive effect emerges because informative historical components coherently reinforce each other, while unrelated alternatives bring random interference. This perspective also answers a practical design question: how should models weight memories accumulated inside latent states when their future use is unknown? Across reusable weighted superpositions, prioritizing a small set of recent or salient items produces weakly-represented memories that bottleneck subsequent attention. Uniform cumulative weighting avoids this flaw, and we prove it is minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning. Our results turn superposition from an observed latent-space effect into a design principle: balanced cumulative memory lets a fixed representational budget support more reliable, reusable computations.

AI.tldr: Balancing memory in latent state is beneficial: retaining full reasoning history under a fixed budget can outperform frontier-only approaches, and uniform (minimax-optimal) weighting of memories yields robust, reusable reasoning.
AI.motivation: Dynamically deciding what to preserve in continuous latent thoughts is crucial for reliable multi-step reasoning. The paper questions the intuition that only the frontier matters and investigates how cumulative memory affects representational capacity and future performance.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of reusable weighted superpositions under fixed hidden width. Compares cumulative full-history vs frontier-only representations. Proves uniform cumulative weighting is minimax-optimal for robust future reasoning and characterizes interference vs reinforcement in memory items.
AI.result: Under identical downstream computations, cumulative superposition retaining full history can require lower representational dimensions than frontier-only, enabling more evidence retention, better outcome discrimination, and delayed unreliability. Uniform cumulative weighting avoids bottlenecks and is minimax-optimal for robustness.
AI.conclusion: A design principle: use balanced cumulative memory in latent states. Allocate memory budget across a broad, uniformly weighted history to support more reliable, reusable computations rather than prioritizing only recent or salient items.

title: Novel Ex-vivo Calf Brain Model with Integrated Sub-Skull Force Sensors to Access Simulated Neurosurgical Procedures
summary: Surgical tissue manipulation demands precision; however, tool-tissue manipulation force magnitudes under realistic conditions are rarely quantified. To address this gap, we proposed and validated a portable ex-vivo force-sensing platform that measures tool-tissue interaction forces across the skull-brain interface during simulated neurosurgery. The system involves fresh calf brain tissue, used as a biological surrogate for brain parenchyma, placed in a 3D-printed human skull model equipped with a 6 degree-of-freedom force/torque sensor and a real-time data acquisition system. Five validation protocols assessed the accuracy and dynamic fidelity of the platform against ground-truth measurement, static accuracy and linearity using calibrated weights (0.5-50 g), minimum detectable force, spatial consistency across different anatomical regions, effect of surgical draping, and long-duration stability. Across protocols, measured forces showed excellent agreement with reference loads (correlation R = 0.9997), with RMSE < 0.005 N and mean relative error under 2%. The platform reliably detected low-magnitude forces down to 1 g (9.8 mN), while surgical drapes introduced no meaningful signal distortion and prolonged recordings exhibited minimal drift. Overall, the proposed framework provides objective, high-fidelity force quantification for skill training and performance assessment using fresh calf brain tissue and may serve as a foundation for force-based evaluation across other surgical procedures. Future work will integrate clinically used surgical instruments to increase procedural realism and will progress toward clinical trials to evaluate usability, educational impact, and translational relevance in practice-adjacent settings.

AI.tldr: Portable ex-vivo force-sensing platform quantifies tool-tissue interaction forces at the skull-brain interface using calf brain in a 3D-printed skull with a 6-DOF sensor; validated with high accuracy and dynamic fidelity across five protocols; supports training and evaluation; groundwork for force-based assessment in surgery.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of quantitative measurements of tool-tissue forces under realistic neurosurgical conditions to enable objective skill assessment and performance benchmarking.
AI.method: Fresh calf brain tissue placed in a 3D-printed human skull model equipped with a 6-DOF force/torque sensor and real-time data-collection. Five validation protocols: static accuracy/linearity with calibrated weights (0.5–50 g), minimum detectable force, spatial consistency across regions, effect of surgical draping, and long-duration stability. Comparison to ground-truth loads; metrics include correlation R, RMSE, and mean relative error.
AI.result: For all protocols, force readings showed excellent agreement with reference, R = 0.9997; RMSE < 0.005 N; mean relative error < 2%. Capable of detecting forces as low as 9.8 mN (1 g). Draping did not distort signals; minimal drift over long recordings.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers objective, high-fidelity force quantification for neurosurgical skill training and performance assessment and may extend to other procedures; future work: integrate clinically used instruments and pursue clinical trials to evaluate usability and educational impact.

title: Task-Based CT Protocol Optimization Using Reinforcement Learning and Virtual Imaging Trials
summary: Protocol optimization in computed tomography (CT) aims to improve diagnostic image quality while reducing radiation dose, but the interdependence of acquisition and reconstruction parameters makes exhaustive testing impractical. We propose a virtual imaging trial framework with reinforcement learning for efficient CT protocol optimization. Sixty-three computational human models with liver lesions were imaged using a validated CT simulator across 468 combinations of acquisition and reconstruction parameters, including tube voltage, tube current, reconstruction kernel, slice thickness, and pixel size. The optimization objective balanced liver lesion detectability, quantified by detectability index d-prime, against radiation dose. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent was trained and conditioned on patient-specific CT localizer embeddings derived from a pretrained vision transformer. On held-out patients, evaluating only 8 protocols per patient, about 2% of exhaustive testing, recovered 98.2% of the exhaustive-search oracle objective. With no patient-specific simulation, surrogate scoring alone achieved 89.7% recovery. Conditioning on the localizer improved zero-simulation recovery by 10.7 percentage points over the localizer-blind policy (paired 95% CI 2.9-19.5; p=0.02). These results show that the proposed framework can substantially reduce exhaustive protocol testing while enabling task-based, dose-aware protocol selection before the diagnostic scan.

AI.tldr: RL-driven virtual imaging trial enables dose-aware CT protocol optimization with limited exhaustive testing while approaching the full exhaustive search objective; patient-specific embeddings improve zero-shot performance.
AI.motivation: CT protocol design involves a combinatorial search over acquisition and reconstruction parameters; exhaustive testing is impractical due to radiation dose and time constraints. A data-driven, task-based, dose-aware optimization framework can reduce testing while preserving diagnostic utility.
AI.method: 63 computational liver models with lesions were simulated in a validated CT pipeline across 468 parameter combinations (tube voltage, current, reconstruction kernel, slice thickness, pixel size). The objective balances lesion detectability (d-prime) with dose. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent was trained, conditioned on patient-specific CT localizer embeddings from a pretrained vision transformer. Evaluation on held-out patients tested only 8 protocols per patient (~2% of exhaustive space) and compared against a surrogate-scoring baseline.
AI.result: 8 protocols per patient recovered 98.2% of the exhaustive-search objective; surrogate scoring alone achieved 89.7% recovery. Conditioning on the localizer improved zero-simulation recovery by 10.7 percentage points (paired 95% CI 2.9-19.5; p=0.02).
AI.conclusion: The proposed virtual imaging trial framework with RL can substantially reduce exhaustive protocol testing while enabling task-based, dose-aware CT protocol selection prior to scanning. Patient-specific embeddings enhance zero-shot performance.

title: Leakage-Safe and Scheduler-Aware Machine Learning for Grid Job Runtime Prediction
comment: Accepted in the 26th International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA 2026)
summary: Accurate job runtime prediction can improve scheduling-aware resource management in grid and distributed computing environments, but prediction models must be evaluated under realistic deployment constraints. This paper revisits CPU burst time prediction on the GWA-T-4 AuverGrid workload trace and reformulates it as leakage-safe pre-execution job runtime prediction. We define the target as job-level runtime, use only submission-time attributes, exclude post-execution variables, and evaluate models under temporal and cold-start settings rather than relying only on random cross-validation. We compare standard regressors, chronological historical baselines, categorical encoding strategies, and CatBoost with native categorical handling. We further add temporal hyperparameter tuning, runtime predictability analysis, feature ablation, error analysis by job length, and a minimal scheduling simulation. After temporal-validation tuning, CatBoost achieves the strongest deployment-oriented result with R^2=0.239, MAE=27,019, RMSE=46,587, and LogMAE=2.646 on the held-out temporal test set. A single-server simulation over all 69,523 held-out temporal test jobs shows that prediction-informed SJF reduces average waiting time by 50.92% relative to FCFS. The results show that random-split evaluation overestimates performance, categorical-native boosting improves temporal generalization, and long-job underestimation remains a scheduler-relevant challenge.

AI.tldr: Temporal-validated leakage-safe pre-execution CPU burst-time prediction using CatBoost; deployment shows SJF reduces wait times by ~51% vs FCFS; random-split evaluations overestimate performance; long jobs remain challenging.
AI.motivation: Accurate, deployment-relevant job runtime prediction under realistic constraints is essential for scheduling in grid/distributed systems; need to rely on submission-time features and test under temporal and cold-start conditions rather than random CV.
AI.method: Reformulate as leakage-safe, pre-execution prediction using only submission-time attributes. Compare standard regressors, chronological baselines, various categorical encoding strategies, and CatBoost with native categorical handling. Include temporal hyperparameter tuning, runtime predictability analysis, feature ablation, error analysis by job length, and a minimal single-server scheduling simulation. Evaluate on held-out temporal test set derived from the GWA-T-4 AuverGrid workload trace across 69,523 jobs.
AI.result: CatBoost with temporal tuning achieves strongest deployment-oriented metrics on the held-out temporal test: R^2=0.239, MAE=27,019, RMSE=46,587, LogMAE=2.646. In a single-server simulation over all 69,523 held-out temporal test jobs, SJF reduces average waiting time by 50.92% relative to FCFS.
AI.conclusion: Random-split evaluation overestimates performance; categorical-native boosting improves temporal generalization; long jobs underestimation remains a scheduler-relevant challenge.

title: Positioning manuscripts in the scientific landscape with agentic AI
summary: Publishing a research manuscript is a routine yet demanding part of scientific life: time-consuming, stressful, and often uncertain in outcome. Recent advances in large language model (LLM)-based agentic AI have shown promise across a range of scientific tasks, and here we ask whether agentic AI can help researchers navigate the publication process itself by reliably inferring a manuscript's eventual publication venue from its content and literature context. We introduce PASS (Publication-oriented Agentic Scientific System), an agentic system that understands manuscripts within their domain-specific literature context and predicts top-matched publication venues. PASS positions each manuscript within its surrounding literature landscape by reconstructing its local scientific neighborhood, tracing its topic trajectory, and reasoning over field-specific journal spaces. Evaluated on a leakage-audited benchmark of over 2,000 preprints across 16 biomedical fields, PASS achieved Top-1 accuracy of 50.3% and Top-5 accuracy of 86.1%, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM baselines and established journal-selection tools. PASS-produced quality scores, such as impact potential and novelty, aligned with independent measures of publication outcome. We also found that the designed literature retrieval module is the strongest performance contributor, particularly for positioning manuscripts relative to nearby work, and that PASS maintained near-full performance from the abstract alone, whereas LLM baselines required the full manuscript text. An independent human evaluation found strong researcher agreement with PASS's manuscript understanding and recommendation rationale. PASS has been released as a public platform (https://ratemypaper.ai/) for broad researcher access.

AI.tldr: PASS is an agentic AI system that predicts suitable publication venues for manuscripts by situating them in their literature context; it outperforms baselines and shows strong agreement with human evaluators, with public release.
AI.motivation: Researchers face time pressure, stress, and uncertainty in publishing. Existing tools often rely on surface features or manual judgment. An agentic AI that understands a manuscript within its domain literature could reliably suggest venues and assess related metrics, potentially streamlining the publication process.
AI.method: PASS reconstructs each manuscript’s local scientific neighborhood, traces its topic trajectory, and reasons over field-specific journal spaces to place the manuscript within its surrounding literature landscape. It uses a literature retrieval module as a key performance driver. Evaluation on a leakage-audited benchmark of >2,000 preprints across 16 biomedical fields. Performance metrics include Top-1 and Top-5 venue accuracy; additional assessments include quality scores (impact potential, novelty) and alignment with independent publication outcomes. Human evaluation corroborates PASS’s understanding and rationale. PASS is released publicly as ratemypaper.ai.
AI.result: Top-1 accuracy 50.3%; Top-5 accuracy 86.1% on the benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM baselines and established journal-selection tools. The literature retrieval module is the strongest contributor to performance, especially for positioning manuscripts relative to nearby work. PASS maintains near-full performance when given only the abstract, whereas baseline models require the full manuscript text. PASS’s quality scores correlate with independent measures of publication outcomes. An independent human evaluation shows strong agreement with PASS’s understanding and recommendations.
AI.conclusion: PASS demonstrates that an agentic AI can meaningfully assist researchers in selecting publication venues by contextually interpreting manuscripts within their literature landscape. The public release enables broad adoption. Future work could broaden domain coverage, further validate generalizability across disciplines, and explore robustness to literature shifts and biases.

title: ITA-LaCAM: A Complete and Scalable TAPF Solver via Assignment-Aware Configuration-Space Search
summary: Combined Target Assignment and Path Finding (TAPF) requires assigning targets for agents while simultaneously planning collision-free paths. We present ITA-LaCAM, a complete and scalable TAPF solver inspired by LaCAM and ITA-CBS. In ITA-LaCAM, each joint-configuration node carries an agent-to-target matching. When a successor is generated, ITA-LaCAM incrementally repairs the matching for the agents that moved and uses the targets to guide PIBT successor generation. This design enables adaptive reassignment without explicitly enumerating the combinatorial assignment space, while preserving LaCAM's completeness and scalability. Across 9,760 benchmark instances on eight maps with 5--200 agents, ITA-LaCAM solved 100% of the instances, compared with 95.6% for IR-TAPF configured with DBS-Hungarian. ITA-LaCAM found an initial solution faster in 84.0% of the comparisons and achieved a lower sum of costs in 65.0% of the instances solved by both methods.

AI.tldr: Complete and scalable TAPF solver ITA-LaCAM combines adaptive agent-to-target matching with LaCAM/ITA concepts, achieving 100% solvability on large benchmarks and outperforming IR-TAPF with DBS-Hungarian in speed and cost.
AI.motivation: TAPF requires both target assignment and collision-free path planning. Existing methods often trade completeness for scalability or require explicit combinatorial assignment enumeration. A complete, scalable approach that adapts assignments during search is desirable.
AI.method: ITA-LaCAM stores an agent-to-target matching at each joint-configuration node. Upon successor generation, it incrementally repairs the matching for moved agents and uses targets to guide PIBT successor generation, enabling adaptive reassignment without enumerating the full assignment space while preserving LaCAM’s completeness and scalability.
AI.result: On 9,760 benchmark instances across eight maps with 5–200 agents, ITA-LaCAM solved 100% of instances (vs 95.6% for IR-TAPF with DBS-Hungarian). It found an initial solution faster in 84.0% of comparisons and achieved a lower sum of costs in 65.0% of instances solved by both methods.
AI.conclusion: ITA-LaCAM provides a complete, scalable TAPF solution with adaptive target reassignment during search, outperforming the DBS-Hungarian-based IR-TAPF baseline on large benchmarks.

title: Pedestrian Crossing Intent Classification From Event-Based Vision Using Convolutional Spiking Neural Networks With Temporal Augmentation
summary: Anticipating whether a pedestrian will cross the road is safety-critical for autonomous vehicles, requiring real-time inference under challenging conditions including motion blur, high dynamic range, and class imbalance. Conventional frame-based deep networks process redundant RGB data at fixed frame rates, limiting their temporal resolution and energy efficiency. In this work we present an end-to-end pipeline that (i) converts real-world driving footage from the Joint Attention in Autonomous Driving (JAAD) dataset into synthetic dynamic vision sensor (DVS) event streams using the v2e simulator, (ii) augments training with the CARLA-simulated DVS sequences of the DVS-PedX dataset under both normal and adverse weather conditions, and (iii) trains a novel convolutional spiking neural network (Conv-SNN) with clip-consistent DVS augmentation to classify pedestrian crossing intent as binary: crossing or non-crossing. We detail all architectural decisions, the exact leaky-integrate-and-fire neuron dynamics with surrogate-gradient learning, the class-balanced loss formulation, JAAD oversampling at 6x, and a 70/15/15 stratified splitting protocol. The trained model achieves 95.83% accuracy and F1 = 0.9695 on the JAAD DVS test set, 97.79% accuracy and F1 = 0.9478 on normal CARLA DVS, and 94.78% accuracy and F1 = 0.8369 on adverse-weather CARLA DVS, all from a 1.07M-parameter architecture trained on CPU. Compared to prior frame-based approaches on JAAD, our method closes or surpasses the reported accuracy while operating natively on sparse temporal representations. We include a thorough analysis of the convergence behaviour across all 15 training epochs, domain transfer characteristics, and a quantitative comparison with representative related work.

AI.tldr: End-to-end convolutional spiking neural network (Conv-SNN) for predicting pedestrian crossing intent using synthetic DVS data, bridging JAAD and CARLA datasets via v2e and DVS-PedX, achieving high accuracy with a 1.07M parameter CPU-trained model and extensive cross-domain evaluation.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical pedestrian intent prediction for autonomous vehicles under challenging conditions (motion blur, HDR, class imbalance). Limitations of frame-based RGB networks in temporal resolution and energy efficiency motivate sparse temporal representations (DVS) and neuromorphic approaches.
AI.method: Convert JAAD to DVS with v2e; augment with CARLA-DVS sequences (normal and adverse weather); train a Conv-SNN with leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons using surrogate-gradient learning; apply clip-consistent DVS augmentation; use class-balanced loss, JAAD 6x oversampling, and a 70/15/15 stratified split.
AI.result: On JAAD DVS: 95.83% accuracy, F1 0.9695; on normal CARLA DVS: 97.79% accuracy, F1 0.9478; on adverse-weather CARLA DVS: 94.78% accuracy, F1 0.8369. Model has 1.07M parameters and is CPU-trained. Outperforms or matches prior frame-based methods on JAAD while operating on sparse DVS data; includes convergence analysis across 15 epochs, domain transfer study, and comparison with related work.
AI.conclusion: Conv-SNNs trained on synthetic DVS data are viable for real-time pedestrian intent prediction in autonomous driving, offering competitive accuracy with sparse temporal representations and robustness across domain shifts and adverse conditions. The work provides detailed architectural and training methodology enabling replication.

title: Certifying Model Upgrades with Slice-Wise Non-Regression and Incumbent Fallback
summary: An updated model can improve an aggregate metric while degrading a slice that matters to a downstream user. We study checkpoint selection subject to non-regression tolerances relative to a retained incumbent. The central distinction is between failing to detect harm and certifying non-inferiority: the former can release harmful updates with high probability when evaluation is noisy. We give a reproducible release procedure that separates candidate search from independent, paired evaluation and returns the exact incumbent when certification fails. Applying established intersection-union and Learn-then-Test principles, we state finite-sample guarantees for one frozen candidate, a finite candidate library, and a prespecified testing order. A joint release decision does not require a slice-count Bonferroni penalty, although certification power can still decrease with the number of slices. In bounded-score simulations, a no-detected-harm gate releases a harmful candidate in 99.7% of trials in one 32-slice setting, compared with 2.6% for an exact non-inferiority gate at a 5% target. A constructed two-block family yields larger certified utility than a scalar path under matched candidate counts. Public digits experiments, including a subsequent continuation that improves average aggregate accuracy, return the incumbent in every run because certification is underpowered. These results establish an auditable protocol and its limitations; they do not establish benefits on foundation-model or multilingual translation upgrades.

AI.tldr: Proposes a reproducible release protocol that selects model checkpoints under non-regression tolerances, separating search from independent evaluation and using finite-sample guarantees across candidate sets and evaluation slices.
AI.motivation: To manage the trade-off between improving aggregate metrics and risking harm on specific user slices when releasing updates, especially under noisy evaluation.
AI.method: Independent paired evaluation with a candidate search stage; use of intersection-union and Learn-then-Test to provide finite-sample guarantees for a single candidate, a finite candidate library, or a preset testing order. No slice-count Bonferroni penalty for joint release decisions; examines effects of testing order and slice count on power.
AI.result: A no-detected-harm gate can release a harmful candidate in 99.7% of trials in a 32-slice setting; an exact non-inferiority gate yields 2.6% under the same target. A two-block construction yields larger certified utility than a scalar path. Public digits experiments always return the incumbent due to underpowered certification.
AI.conclusion: Provides an auditable release protocol with clear limitations: it does not demonstrate benefits for foundation-model or multilingual translation upgrades; certification power can be insufficient, risking harm under noise, and the method trades off auditability against potential risk depending on slice configuration.

title: Homeostatic Continual Learning
summary: In this paper, I formulate a Continual Learning problem and propose a method named "Homeostatic Continual Learning" that enables an AI agent to learn continuously in a changing environment without catastrophic forgetting. The core of the method is to find outliers in the environment data when the agent experiences an outlier in its output. Through this method, the agent gradually completes its model and policy and performs well in more and more contexts. I also suggest that we may use the method to build a world model where the agent factorizes the objects in the world into features, abstract objects into comparable instances of concepts and map concepts to intents through features. I discuss the works needed to render the method practical, the connections to many fields in Artificial Intelligence and the broader implications of the method.

AI.tldr: Proposes Homeostatic Continual Learning (HCL) to mitigate catastrophic forgetting by detecting environment outliers via the agent's outlier outputs, enabling progressive model/policy completion and potential world-model formation through feature-object-concept-intent factorization; outlines practical steps and interdisciplinary relevance.
AI.motivation: Address continual-learning non-stationarity and catastrophic forgetting; leverage outlier signals to guide adaptation and structure world-models by factoring objects into features and concepts, enabling robust long-horizon learning.
AI.method: Core idea: when the agent outputs an outlier, detect corresponding outliers in environment data and treat them as learning signals; implement a homeostatic mechanism to balance knowledge, gradually refine the model and policy; propose world-model construction by factorizing objects into features, abstracting objects into concept-equivalence classes, mapping concepts to intents via features.
AI.result: The abstract presents a theoretical framework with no empirical results; claims potential for reducing forgetting and enabling broader generalization; suggests steps to render method practical and connects to broader AI domains.
AI.conclusion: HCL offers a promising direction for continual learning and world-modeling; practical realization requires cross-disciplinary work and evaluation across tasks and environments; highlights broader implications.

title: Task-Specified Active Metrological Inspection with Measurement-Steered VLA Manipulation and Deterministic Evidence Gating
summary: High-mix low-volume (HMLV) manufacturing requires inspection systems to adapt to changing parts, specifications, and work orders without repeated task-specific programming. Existing inspection automation typically assumes predefined sensing sequences, while general purpose robot agents optimize task completion rather than the completeness and validity of metrological evidence.
