We formulate task-specified active metrological inspection and propose From Requirements to Admissible Metrological Evidence (FRAME), a hierarchical dual-arm framework that converts an inspection instruction and structured specification into traceable conformance evidence. FRAME coordinates learned manipulation with calibrated laser profilometry: a task manager grounds and schedules requirements, active surface correspondence verifies physical-to-specification localization, and evidence memory tracks measurement provenance, admissibility, and coverage. Learned components may propose inspection targets and physical access actions, but deterministic datum-grounded measurement, admissibility checks, coverage auditing, and conformance evaluation prevent incomplete or unverified evidence from authorizing PASS. A series of physical experiments shows that FRAME achieves higher end-to-end inspection reliability, fewer false accepts, and shorter task completion time.

AI.tldr: FRAME is a hierarchical dual-arm framework that translates inspection instructions into traceable metrological evidence, blending learned manipulation and deterministic admissibility checks to improve reliability and efficiency in high-mix low-volume manufacturing.
AI.motivation: To enable flexible, automated inspection across changing parts/specifications without extensive per-task programming, while ensuring evidence completeness and validity of measurements.
AI.method: A three-layer architecture: a task manager grounds requirements and schedules actions; active surface correspondence aligns physical parts with specs; evidence memory tracks provenance, admissibility, and coverage. Uses calibrated laser profilometry for deterministic measurements with learned components suggesting targets/actions but constrained by datum-grounded measurement and conformance checks.
AI.result: Physical experiments show improved end-to-end inspection reliability, reduced false accepts, and shorter task completion times compared with baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic admissibility checks and coverage auditing ensure only complete, verifiable evidence is accepted, supporting traceable conformance from requirements to measurements in high-mix low-volume inspection.

title: Global-Local Contextual Progressive Expansion Network for Martian Landslide Segmentation in Multimodal Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Automated landslide segmentation on Mars is one of the important tasks for understanding its surface processes, and all will aid in future space exploration. However, it remains a relatively underexplored open challenge because landslide morphology is highly variable, foreground regions are often sparse or irregular, and orbital observations combine heterogeneous spectral and topographic cues. In this context, this work investigates the capability of deep learning to address Martian landslide segmentation through an extensive assessment of modern neural segmentation models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to provide such a comprehensive exploration in this domain. We further propose TransCPLES, a U-shaped network that couples Contextual Progressive Layer Expansion feature extraction with Transformer-based contextual reasoning, enabling the model to capture local geomorphic patterns and broader spatial dependencies for more reliable landslide delineation. Experiments on MMLSv2, a seven-band multimodal Martian landslide dataset, show that TransCPLES achieves the best overall performance when evaluated on geographically distinct samples, with consistent delineation across different landslide extents, stable foreground discrimination, and a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost compared with several state-of-the-art convolutional, attention-based, and Transformer-based segmentation models. With this work, we hope to provide a useful reference and encourage further research and development in deep learning for planetary remote sensing. Code will be available after publication.

AI.tldr: TransCPLES, a Transformer-augmented U-Net for Martian landslide segmentation, outperforms CNN/attention/Transformer baselines on the seven-band MMLSv2 dataset, with strong generalization across geographic splits and efficient computation.
AI.motivation: Mars landslide segmentation is challenging due to highly variable morphology, sparse/irregular foregrounds, and multimodal spectral-topographic cues; a comprehensive evaluation of modern segmentation models in this domain is lacking and essential for advancing planetary remote sensing.
AI.method: Proposes TransCPLES, a U-shaped network that combines Contextual Progressive Layer Expansion feature extraction with Transformer-based contextual reasoning; evaluated on MMLSv2 (seven-band multimodal Martian landslide data) against state-of-the-art CNN, attention-based, and Transformer segmentation models.
AI.result: TransCPLES achieves the best overall performance on geographically distinct samples, with consistent landslide delineation across extents, stable foreground discrimination, and a favorable accuracy-to-computation trade-off compared with competing models.
AI.conclusion: Provides a useful reference for deep learning in planetary remote sensing and aims to spur further research; code will be released after publication.

title: A Variational Optimal Transport Operator on Incompressible Flow
summary: We present the Variational Incompressible Optimal Transport (VIOT) operator, a generative neural operator for amortized incompressible density transport. Given a new source-target density pair, VIOT predicts a divergence-free velocity field and generates the full transport trajectory by feed-forward inference, replacing the hour-scale per-pair optimization used by adjoint fluid solvers and differentiable simulation baselines. The system consists of three components: a stream-function or vector-potential representation that enforces incompressibility by construction, a regularized incompressible transport objective that balances endpoint accuracy and flow smoothness, and a Fourier Neural Operator backbone that amortizes the solve across new pairs and grid resolutions. Together, these components make incompressible transport a reusable neural operator that facilitates various transport processes. Further, the generative capability extends beyond the training distribution, with VIOT producing incompressible transports for user-drawn source-target pairs in a real-time interactive system. We demonstrate VIOT on 2D and 3D density-transport benchmarks. Both 2D and 3D rollouts complete in seconds per pair, while per-instance baselines in our 2D comparisons optimize each new pair from scratch and require on the order of an hour, a roughly $10^4\times$ online speedup.

AI.tldr: A neural operator, VIOT, for amortized incompressible density transport that predicts a divergence-free velocity field and generates transport trajectories in seconds, delivering large speedups over per-pair optimizers while generalizing to new source–target pairs in 2D/3D.
AI.motivation: To enable fast, accurate incompressible transport without per-instance optimization, enforcing incompressibility by construction and supporting multiple grid resolutions in real time.
AI.method: Three components: (1) a stream-function or vector-potential representation to enforce incompressibility by construction, (2) a regularized incompressible transport objective balancing endpoint accuracy and flow smoothness, (3) a Fourier Neural Operator backbone that amortizes the solve across new source–target pairs and grid resolutions; inference is feed-forward to generate full transport trajectories.
AI.result: 2D and 3D benchmarks with per-pair rollouts completed in seconds; ~10^4× speedup over baselines that optimize each pair from scratch in 2D; demonstrated real-time interactive generation for user-drawn pairs.
AI.conclusion: VIOT demonstrates that incompressible transport can be treated as a reusable neural operator, enabling fast, generalizable transport across tasks and resolutions with real-time applicability.

title: Surprising Effectiveness of Self-Demonstrations in Enhancing Schema-Ontology Mapping with LLMs
summary: Integrating heterogeneous relational databases into a centralized ontology remains a persistent challenge in enterprise knowledge representation, primarily due to semantic heterogeneity, cryptic schema naming, missing metadata, and the abstraction gap between relational schemas and ontological models. Although large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic reasoning capabilities, we show that directly applying them through one-shot prompting or naive multi-stage pipelines leads to poor performance for schema-ontology mapping. This paper presents a self-demonstration-driven approach that combines a neuro-symbolic task decomposition with a novel mechanism for automatically generating pattern-guided, dependency-aware demonstrations to address this integration challenge. Our approach incorporates two key strategies to achieve substantial accuracy gains over existing LLM-based schema integration methods: (i) a neuro-symbolic decomposition of the task into cascaded sub-tasks, where symbolic constraints structure the search space and LLMs perform semantic reasoning within each focused sub-task, and (ii) self-generated demonstrations guided by domain-agnostic patterns to supervise each sub-task. Experiments on three of the most challenging scenarios from the RODI benchmark show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming (25 percentage points F1 improvements) both traditional schema-to-ontology mapping techniques and recent LLM-based schema-to-ontology and schema matching approaches. Ablation studies further reveal the significant benefits of pattern-guided self-demonstrations and the complementary benefits of neuro-symbolic task decomposition.

AI.tldr: Proposes a self-demonstration-driven, neuro-symbolic approach for schema-to-ontology integration that uses pattern-guided, dependency-aware demonstrations to guide LLM reasoning across cascaded sub-tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the RODI benchmark.
AI.motivation: Enterprise knowledge integration faces semantic heterogeneity, cryptic schema naming, missing metadata, and a large abstraction gap between relational schemas and ontologies. Naive one-shot or multi-stage LLM prompting underperforms for schema-ontology mapping, necessitating a stronger, principled approach.
AI.method: Decompose the task into cascaded sub-tasks using symbolic constraints to structure the search space, with LLMs handling semantic reasoning within each sub-task. Introduce self-generated demonstrations guided by domain-agnostic patterns to supervise each sub-task. Evaluate on challenging RODI benchmarks, comparing against traditional schema-to-ontology methods and modern LLM-based approaches.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance with substantial gains (≈25 F1 points) over both traditional and LLM-based methods. Ablation studies show pattern-guided demonstrations and neuro-symbolic decomposition separately contribute to performance, with their combination yielding the best results.
AI.conclusion: A neuro-symbolic task decomposition with pattern-guided self-demonstrations effectively addresses semantic heterogeneity in schema-to-ontology mapping, enabling more accurate and scalable integration of heterogeneous relational databases into centralized ontologies.

title: VGFM: Expressive Robot Policies via Dense Value Guidance in Flow Matching
summary: Recent robot learning paradigms increasingly rely on large offline datasets of robotic interactions to train control policies. Expressive generative models enable rich and multimodal action representations, expanding the capability of this paradigm for complex robotic control. However, policy improvement with multi-step generative actors remains challenging. In offline reinforcement learning (RL), incorporating value-based objectives along generative trajectories often introduces substantial training complexity, including backpropagation through time (BPTT), auxiliary architectures, or distillation losses. We propose Value-Guided Flow Matching (VGFM), a scalable offline RL framework that enables dense value-guided shaping within a flow-based policy while avoiding BPTT and additional algorithmic overhead. VGFM parameterizes the policy as a conditional flow-matching model in action (x-prediction) space, ensuring that each intermediate flow step produces a valid robot action that can be directly evaluated by a standard offline RL critic. This design allows value guidance to be applied at randomly sampled flow times without differentiating through the entire generative trajectory, while preserving inference-time flexibility by varying the discretization of the underlying flow ODE without retraining. Evaluated on robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks in OGBench, VGFM achieves strong performance across a wide range of tasks under rigorous evaluation protocols. With minimal hyperparameter tuning, these results demonstrate that VGFM provides a simple, scalable, and effective approach for expressive policy learning in long-horizon, goal-oriented robotic control.

AI.tldr: VGFM introduces a scalable offline RL method using a conditional flow-matching policy in action space with value-guided shaping, avoiding backpropagation through time and extra overhead, achieving strong results on robotics tasks.
AI.motivation: Tackle the complexity of incorporating value-based objectives into multi-step generative policies in offline RL, and provide a scalable, non-BPTT solution suitable for long-horizon robotic control.
AI.method: Model the policy as a conditional flow-matching model in action space (x-prediction). Include value guidance by evaluating intermediate flow steps with a standard offline RL critic at randomly sampled flow times, without differentiating through entire trajectories. Allow inference-time flexibility by discretizing the flow ODE differently without retraining. Ensure each intermediate flow step yields a valid action.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance across robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks on OGBench under rigorous evaluation protocols with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: VGFM offers a simple, scalable, and effective approach for expressive policy learning in long-horizon, goal-oriented robotic control, compatible with offline RL and flexible at inference time.

title: ProtoCAM: Interpretable Few-Shot Mask-Guided Prototypical Learning for Breast Lesion Classification in Ultrasound Imaging
summary: Breast ultrasound imaging plays an important role in the early detection and diagnosis of breast cancer, particularly for patients with dense breast tissue. However, developing reliable deep learning models for ultrasound analysis is challenging due to limited annotated medical data and the need for interpretable predictions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes ProtoCAM, an explainable few-shot learning framework for breast lesion classification that integrates mask-guided feature encoding, prototypical metric learning, and gradient-based visual explanations. The proposed approach leverages lesion masks to guide feature extraction and constructs class prototypes within an embedding space to enable robust classification under limited training samples. The framework was evaluated on the BUSI dataset using a stratified group k-fold cross-validation protocol to prevent patient-level data leakage. Experimental results demonstrate ProtoCAM's high performance in low-data scenarios. In a 3-way 5-shot setting, the proposed method achieves a macro F1-score of 0.910, representing a substantial improvement over standard supervised CNN models. Among the evaluated backbone networks, ResNet18 achieved the best performance, reaching a macro F1-score of 91.65% under a 15-shot configuration, providing interpretable insights into the classification decisions. These results highlight the potential of explainable few-shot learning frameworks for reliable computer-aided breast cancer diagnosis in data-scarce medical imaging environments.

AI.tldr: ProtoCAM is an explainable few-shot learning framework for breast lesion classification that uses mask-guided feature encoding, prototypical metric learning, and gradient-based explanations; it achieves strong performance in low-data regimes on BUSI, with ResNet18 achieving 91.65% macro F1 in a 15-shot setting.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of annotated medical imaging data and the need for interpretable predictions in breast ultrasound for reliable diagnosis.
AI.method: Mask-guided feature encoding guided by lesion masks; prototypical metric learning to form class prototypes in embedding space; gradient-based visual explanations for interpretability; stratified group k-fold cross-validation to prevent patient leakage; evaluation in 3-way 5-shot and 15-shot settings with different backbones, notably ResNet18.
AI.result: In 3-way 5-shot, Macro F1 = 0.910. ResNet18 achieves Macro F1 = 91.65% under 15-shot. The approach shows superior performance to standard supervised CNNs under data-scarce conditions and provides interpretable decision insights.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of explainable few-shot learning with mask-guided feature encoding and prototypical reasoning for reliable breast cancer diagnosis in data-scarce ultrasound scenarios; supports clinical potential due to improved accuracy and interpretability.

title: JumpStart Your Policy Learning with Lessons from 160,000 Training Runs
summary: Reliable progress in offline policy learning depends on careful reporting, well-tuned baselines, and evaluation across diverse conditions. Prior work has shown that results can be sensitive to reporting choices, hyperparameter tuning, and dataset properties, but these sources of variability have not been systematically investigated together at the scale needed to understand how they shape conclusions. To address this gap, we present a large-scale empirical study of offline reinforcement and imitation learning, training over 160,000 policies across 114 datasets. At this scale, no algorithm dominates: aggregate performance among the strongest methods is often close, but the leaders differ substantially across environments. We find that proper hyperparameter tuning frequently reshuffles perceived algorithm rankings and that benchmark composition can produce conflicting conclusions. We also study hyperparameter sensitivity and transfer across environments, identifying a simple strategy for deriving strong default configurations. We use our findings to develop a dataset-conditioned recommender that provides task-specific algorithm recommendations for practitioners. Finally, we release JumpStart: a resource suite containing every trained policy, per-model scores and hyperparameters, strong baselines across all environments, training and evaluation code, and an extensible website for retrieving, analyzing, and contributing results. Together, these resources aim to make offline policy-learning research more reliable and enable future work beyond the scope of this study.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of offline reinforcement and imitation learning (over 160k policies across 114 datasets) showing no single algorithm dominates; hyperparameter tuning and dataset composition significantly affect rankings; proposes simple default configurations, a dataset-conditioned recommender, and JumpStart resource to improve reliability and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: To understand how reporting choices, hyperparameter tuning, and dataset properties shape conclusions in offline policy learning, and to move beyond single-dataset or small-scale studies by assessing performance and stability across a broad, diverse set of tasks.
AI.method: Train and evaluate over 160,000 policies on 114 datasets for offline RL/IL; analyze hyperparameter sensitivity and cross-environment transfer; compare leading methods, assess ranking stability, and examine effect of benchmark composition; derive default configuration strategies; develop a dataset-conditioned recommender; release JumpStart with all trained policies, scores, hyperparameters, baselines, code, and an analysis platform.
AI.result: No algorithm is uniformly superior across all environments; strongest methods’ aggregate performance is often close but leadership varies by environment; hyperparameter tuning frequently reshuffles rankings; benchmark composition can lead to conflicting conclusions; a simple strategy for strong default configurations is identified; a dataset-conditioned recommender is built; JumpStart resource suite released to support reproducibility and further research.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the fragility of cross-study conclusions in offline policy learning and provides practical tools (default configurations, recommender, JumpStart) to improve reliability, generalization across tasks, and future research.

title: Partition Scores Are Not System Scores: Deployment-Fidelity Gaps in Decomposed Algorithm Selection
summary:
Oracle-style quantities, including virtual best solvers, selected-portfolio VBS, virtual-best encodings, and best-in-family summaries, are widely reported as upper bounds on what a deployable selector could achieve. In decomposed algorithm selection, an analogous partition-level score grants an oracle choice of the best algorithm within the selected family; once the family selector is fixed, the deployable system must replace that within-family oracle with a learned within-family selector.
  We define the deployment-fidelity gap G(R) as the difference between partition-level and deployable end-to-end utility and derive two accounting consequences: a per-instance margin-regret stability condition that tells us when a partition-time family choice is deployment-optimal, and a sharp partition-only identification interval that, when it strictly crosses zero, prevents the partition-level report from certifying the deployable winner.
  Across five public algorithm-selection benchmarks spanning tabular AutoML and combinatorial CSP/SAT, every decomposed pipeline has positive G(R), ranging from 0.012 on TabZilla to 0.13 on PROTEUS-2014. Four of ten decomposed-versus-flat decisions have sign-changing point estimates; on PROTEUS-2014, a 33-point partition advantage shrinks to a 20-point end-to-end advantage. A training-side validation gap-correction diagnostic recovers the point-estimate deployable sign on all four sign-changing cells; it is a reporting aid, not a substitute for direct end-to-end evaluation. Partition and end-to-end scores should be reported side by side.

AI.tldr: Introduces deployment-fidelity gap G(R) to quantify the gap between partition-level oracle performance and deployable end-to-end performance in decomposed algorithm selection; derives stability and identifiability conditions; empirically shows positive gaps and recommends reporting both partition and end-to-end scores.
AI.motivation: Oracle-style upper bounds (e.g., virtual best solvers, best-in-family) overstate what deployable selectors can achieve. The paper quantifies this gap in decomposed algorithm selection and provides diagnostics to ensure truthful reporting.
AI.method: Define G(R) as the difference between partition-level utility and deployable end-to-end utility. Derive a per-instance margin-regret stability condition and a sharp partition-only identification interval. Empirically evaluate across five benchmarks (AutoML/tabular+combinatorial CSP/SAT), examine decomposed versus flat pipelines, and apply a training-side gap-correction diagnostic.
AI.result: G(R) is positive in all decomposed pipelines (0.012 to 0.13). Four of ten decomposed decisions have sign-changing point estimates; in PROTEUS-2014 a 33-point partition advantage shrinks to a 20-point end-to-end advantage. The diagnostic recovers deployable sign in all four sign-changing cases. Conclusion: report partition and end-to-end scores side by side; gating off partition-level reports without end-to-end validation risks misstatement.
AI.conclusion: Partition-level upper-bound reports are insufficient alone; include end-to-end evaluation and a deployment-fidelity diagnostic to ensure truthful reporting and better guidance for deployment.

title: Learning Communication-Conditioned Generative Policies for Decentralized Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance
summary: In this work, we propose a decentralized communication-conditioned generative framework for multi-agent collision avoidance. Agents generate short-horizon action sequences using a flow-matching policy trained from privileged offline demonstrations with access to global state. The demonstrations do not include explicit communication signals; instead, agents learn to exchange and aggregate latent messages that encode interaction-relevant intent under partial observability. This formulation supports flexible inference at test time, where unconditioned generation corresponds to independent behavior and communication-conditioned generation enables coordinated interaction without centralized planning. The resulting policies operate in a fully decentralized manner at execution time, relying only on local observations and learned messages. Combined with a receding-horizon inference scheme, the proposed approach enables efficient single-step inference of short-horizon action sequences and degrades gracefully under communication dropouts. Extensive simulation results demonstrate near-expert collision avoidance performance and strong generalization to denser, unseen multi-agent scenarios, along with zero-shot transfer to real-robot experiments.

AI.tldr: Decentralized, communication-conditioned policy learning for multi-agent collision avoidance using flow-matching trained from privileged offline data; learns latent messages for interaction intent; test-time supports independent or coordinated behavior without centralized planning; robust to communication dropouts; strong simulation and zero-shot real-robot transfer.
AI.motivation: Enable scalable, decentralized multi-agent collision avoidance under partial observability without relying on a centralized planner or explicit inter-agent signals.
AI.method: Train a flow-matching policy from offline demonstrations with access to global state. Agents learn latent messages encoding interaction intent and aggregate them to communicate under partial observability. At test time, unconditioned generation yields independent behavior, while communication-conditioned generation enables coordination. Execution is fully decentralized; a receding-horizon inference scheme enables efficient single-step inference of short-horizon action sequences and robustness to communication dropouts.
AI.result: Near-expert collision avoidance performance in extensive simulations; strong generalization to denser, unseen multi-agent scenarios; zero-shot transfer to real-robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: A scalable decentralized framework that leverages learned latent communications to enable coordinated multi-agent avoidance without central planning, with robust performance and graceful degradation under communication failures.

title: ConeGaussian: Anti-Aliased Gaussian Ray-Tracing for Generic Central Cameras
summary: In rendering, a camera is a sampling operator that maps each finite pixel to a bundle of rays. Different camera models change the geometry of this bundle, thus making a unified and faithful rendering formulation challenging. Consequently, Gaussian ray tracing supports generic cameras (with optical center) through their inverse ray mappings, yet typically reduces every pixel to a single center ray. This ignores the camera-dependent pixel footprint, causing aliasing under minification, while unconstrained Gaussians expose unsupported frequencies under magnification. We present ConeGaussian, a camera-model-agnostic anti-aliasing framework for Gaussian ray-based rendering. Instead of defining the pixel filter on a camera-specific image plane, ConeGaussian constructs an anisotropic footprint directly from neighboring rays produced by the camera's native inverse mapping. We derive a closed-form response under a locally linear, depth-local, moment-matched approximation of the finite pixel footprint, while the same geometry defines a per-Gaussian training-frequency floor. Notably, by construction, our filtering principle can be used unmodified across calibrated central camera models and multiple Gaussian ray-rendering backbones. Additionally, unlike in mip-splatting, our scene-space frequency floor and filtering enable trivial composition at render time, allowing us to remove excess blurring. On pinhole and strongly distorted fisheye captures, ConeGaussian consistently improves two distinct ray-based backbones, by up to 4.3 dB at 1/8 resolution, and reduces fisheye LPIPS by 30% where perspective screen-plane footprint formulations are not directly applicable.

AI.tldr: ConeGaussian offers camera-model-agnostic anti-aliasing for Gaussian ray rendering by deriving an anisotropic footprint from neighboring rays via the camera's inverse mapping, with a closed-form filter under depth-local assumptions; it improves image quality across camera models/backbones (up to 4.3 dB at 1/8 resolution; 30% LPIPS reduction on fisheye).
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian ray tracing collapses pixels to a single center ray, ignoring camera-dependent pixel footprints, causing aliasing under minification and exposing high frequencies under magnification; a unified, model-agnostic AA framework is needed.
AI.method: Construct an anisotropic pixel footprint from neighboring rays using the camera's native inverse mapping; derive a closed-form filter under a locally linear, depth-local, moment-matched footprint; establish a per-Gaussian training-frequency floor; ensure compatibility across calibrated central camera models and Gaussian backbones; enable scene-space frequency control and avoid excessive blurring, unlike mip-splatting.
AI.result: Empirically improves both pinhole and strongly distorted fisheye rendering, achieving up to 4.3 dB gain at 1/8 resolution and a 30% reduction in fisheye LPIPS where perspective-screen footprints fail.
AI.conclusion: ConeGaussian provides a practical, unified anti-aliasing framework for Gaussian ray-based rendering that preserves detail, reduces aliasing, and integrates with existing backbones across camera models.

title: HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability-Transferability Scheduling for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning
comment: 13 pages. Equal contribution: Hongliang Wei and Xiaobing Tu. Corresponding authors: Xiaobing Tu and Xiaopeng Fan
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed through diverse harnesses that differ in system prompts, tool schemas, control loops, and trajectory formats. The same model can perform unevenly across these interfaces, making robustness to harness variation an important objective. A natural approach is to train a shared policy through multiple harnesses, but doing so introduces a scheduling problem: each training step should favor a harness that currently provides a useful learning signal while also producing an update that benefits the other harnesses. We develop HarnessBandit, an online scheduler that selects one harness per optimizer step. After a group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) update, it observes learnability -- the mean absolute advantage on the batch -- and transferability -- the cosine between a low-dimensional gradient sketch of the current harness and exponential moving averages of the remaining harnesses. The two signals are fused after pooled sliding-window min-max normalization and sampled with a visit-dependent bonus and an explicit exploration floor. We train Qwen3.5-2B across six harnesses on ClawGym and evaluate on PinchBench (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness). HarnessBandit improves over mixed-batch multi-harness training on both benchmarks, while training diagnostics indicate that learnability and transferability provide distinct, evolving signals.

AI.tldr: HarnessBandit is an online scheduler for multi-harness training of language-model agents that selects one harness per optimizer step, balancing learnability and transferability signals to improve robustness across harness variations.
AI.motivation: Robustness to interface/harness variation: different system prompts, tool schemas, and control loops lead to uneven model performance; training a shared policy across harnesses requires a principled scheduling mechanism.
AI.method: Introduce HarnessBandit, which uses a group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) update. After each update it measures learnability (mean absolute advantage on the batch) and transferability (cosine between a low-dimensional gradient sketch of the current harness and EMA of other harnesses). These signals are fused via pooled sliding-window min-max normalization, with visit-dependent bonuses and an explicit exploration floor to select the next harness per optimizer step.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Qwen3.5-2B trained across six harnesses on ClawGym shows improved performance over mixed-batch multi-harness training on PinchBench (in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness). Diagnostics indicate learnability and transferability provide distinct, evolving signals.
AI.conclusion: HarnessBandit enables robust, multi-harness training by effectively balancing current learning signal with cross-harness transferability, leading to better generalization across held-out tasks and harness configurations.

title: Do Not Restart: Residual Completion for Stateful Agent Handoffs
summary: Routing and cascades reduce tool-agent cost by transferring control across models, but stateful handoffs must preserve accepted choices, realized effects, and unfinished obligations. We formulate this as commitment-constrained residual completion and introduce Commitment-Frontier Residual Completion (CFRC). CFRC enforces target-before-proposal, whole-proposal-before-authority, and live-evidence-before-success: it freezes a residual contract from accepted progress, closes the successor continuation into an evidence-linked graph, and admits execution only when the remainder is covered, with live receipts discharging obligations. We establish contract-relative partial correctness, which extends to the original residual request under complete contract construction. Across five environments and two same-provider model pairs, CFRC achieves comparable macro accuracy to strong full-task agents at only 22.0%-34.6% of their inference cost, with additional cross-provider results demonstrating broader transfer.

AI.tldr: CFRC offers commitment-constrained residual completion to enable fast, accurate cross-model handoffs by freezing progress and linking evidence, achieving near full-task accuracy at only 22–35% of the baseline inference cost.
AI.motivation: Reduce tool-agent cost in cascaded model scenarios while preserving accepted choices, effects, and obligations across stateful handoffs.
AI.method: Introduce CFRC with policies: target-before-proposal, whole-proposal-before-authority, live-evidence-before-success; freeze a residual contract from accepted progress; encode successor as an evidence-linked graph; permit execution only when remainder is covered; use live receipts to discharge obligations; prove contract-relative partial correctness and extend to original residual request under complete contract construction; empirical validation across five environments and two provider pairs, with cross-provider transfer.
AI.result: CFRC achieves macro accuracy comparable to strong full-task agents at 22.0%–34.6% of their inference cost; cross-provider results show broader transfer and robustness.
AI.conclusion: CFRC provides a practical, correctness-guaranteed framework for cost-efficient, transferable tool-agent handoffs in cascaded model deployments.

title: Multi-Task Visual Perception Network with LLM Conditioning for Autonomous Navigation
comment: Accepted and presented at the IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence (IEEE WCCI / IJCNN 2026), Maastricht, Netherlands. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted
summary: Long-term navigation for service robots faces crit- ical challenges like the accumulation of odometry drift and sensor error, which progressively degrade 2D maps and renders traditional path planning algorithms (e.g., A*, RRT*, DiPPer, ViT-A*) ineffective over time. To address this, we propose a user-friendly, interactive framework that eliminates the reliance on globally consistent maps. Our approach integrates visual perception with Large Language Models (LLM) to interpret user commands via text or voice. Instead of relying on a drift- prone global map, the system generates a sequential action plan based on local visual cues and egocentric geometric instructions. These action plans are executed sequentially, allowing the robot to navigate known and unknown environments safely. By reset- ting localization relative to immediate targets, our framework effectively works with a minimum accumulation drift strategy, ensuring accurate, efficient, and collision-free navigation without the maintenance overhead of traditional mapping. Experiments on real-world and simulated data have shown significant improve- ments over other methods. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/PraveenSingh24/VL-Navigation.

AI.tldr: Drift-resistant robot navigation using visual perception and LLMs to interpret user commands and generate sequential local plans without relying on global maps, enabling safe, efficient long-term autonomy with resettable localization.
AI.motivation: Long-term navigation suffers from odometry drift and sensor error, which accumulate and degrade 2D maps, rendering traditional planners ineffective over time. A user-friendly framework that avoids reliance on globally consistent maps is needed.
AI.method: Integrate visual perception with Large Language Models (LLMs) to interpret user commands (text/voice). Instead of a drift-prone global map, generate sequential action plans based on local visual cues and egocentric geometric instructions. Execute plans sequentially with localization reset relative to immediate targets, enabling a minimum-drift navigation strategy without heavy mapping overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world and simulated data show significant improvements over baseline methods. The approach maintains accuracy and safety without global maps. The authors provide publicly accessible source code at the given GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Drift-tolerant, map-free navigation achieved through LLM-guided interpretation of user commands and local plan execution reduces mapping overhead while delivering safe, efficient navigation in known and unknown environments.

title: RIGOR: Rig-Informed Geometry for Omnidirectional Reconstruction
summary: Recent developments in feed-forward 3D reconstruction resulted in models which can recover dense scene representations and camera motion solely from an image stream. However, such predictions are prone to becoming inconsistent over long trajectories, specifically in demanding environments with repetitive structures, weak textures and dynamic objects or people. One way to mitigate those challenges is to use an omnidirectional camera, which provides wide spatial coverage and captures richer visual information. Yet, the majority of models do not offer support for 360-degree imagery or require additional fine-tuning. To bridge these two aspects, we present RIGOR: a large-scale reconstruction pipeline for gravity-aligned omnidirectional videos that retains a frozen feed-forward perspective backbone and exploits each panorama as a four-view virtual rig. The rig structure is used to detect and repair locally inconsistent predictions, to retrieve loop closures through cyclic four-view consensus, and to geometrically verify candidate revisits before global optimization. Verified constraints drive a Sim(3) pose graph that corrects accumulated rotation, translation, and scale drift along the sequence. We demonstrate that the proposed consistency mechanisms improve both trajectory accuracy and reconstructed geometry over a feed-forward baseline on challenging construction-site sequences. The code is made available under this link: https://github.com/TangentH/RIGOR.

AI.tldr: RIGOR uses gravity-aligned omnidirectional video with each panorama treated as a four-view rig to locally fix inconsistencies, detect loop closures via four-view consensus, and optimize with a Sim(3 pose graph, improving trajectory and geometry while keeping a frozen feed-forward backbone; code released.
AI.motivation: Addresses long-trajectory drift and geometry degradation in dense 3D reconstruction from image streams, especially under challenging conditions (repetitive structures, weak textures, dynamic objects). Expands beyond standard 360 handling by exploiting panoramic rigs for stronger geometric constraints and loop closure.
AI.method: Each omnidirectional panorama is converted into a four-view virtual rig. Local consistency checks repair predictions; cyclic four-view consensus enables loop closures. Candidate revisits are geometrically verified before global optimization. A Sim(3) pose graph accumulates constraints to correct rotation, translation, and scale drift. The backbone remains frozen to a feed-forward model; global optimization enforces consistency using the rig constraints.
AI.result: Improved trajectory accuracy and reconstructed geometry compared with a feed-forward baseline on challenging construction-site sequences. The authors release code at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Rig-based consistency constraints effectively integrate omnidirectional data to mitigate drift and geometric errors in long trajectories, enabling more robust 360-degree reconstruction without retraining the base model.

title: Training Specialist Models without Reasoning Trajectories for Domain Expert Distillation
summary: Specialist distillation effectively transfers domain expertise to student models via teacher-generated reasoning trajectories. However, when these specialists are trained solely on question--answer pairs without explicit reasoning supervision, what governs the trajectories they generate? In this work, we show that specialist optimization implicitly selects from this latent trajectory space. To isolate and observe this latent distribution, we leverage student distillation not as a downstream goal, but as an agnostic probe---since students inherit no parameterization or optimization constraints from the specialist, inheriting only the sampled trajectories themselves. Through this probe, our empirical analysis unveils a tight governing relationship: across 27 specialist--student pairings, their specialization--generalization profiles correlate exceptionally strongly. Crucially, explicitly controlling the specialist's distributional drift systematically shifts both the teacher and its distilled student along a controllable trade-off between domain precision and general-capability retention. Across chemistry, physics, and multilingual settings, distilled students systematically reflect these specialist-induced profiles, even across divergent model families. Our findings establish a new view of specialist training: when gold reasoning is absent, tuning choices directly control the latent supervision passed to downstream models.

AI.tldr: Specialist distillation without explicit reasoning supervision reveals a latent trajectory distribution; drifting the specialist changes both the teacher and the distilled student, with a strong specialization-generalization correlation across domains and model families.
AI.motivation: When expert reasoning is not explicitly supervised, the trajectories these specialists generate are unconstrained. Understanding and controlling this latent distribution is essential for predicting and shaping downstream student performance.
AI.method: Treat student distillation as an agnostic probe to sample the latent trajectory space from specialist optimization. Analyze 27 specialist–student pairs across chemistry, physics, and multilingual settings, and across divergent model families. Systematically vary specialist distributional drift and observe its effects on both teacher trajectories and distilled students.
AI.result: There is an extremely strong correlation between specialization and generalization profiles across pairs. Distilled students reflect the specialist-induced distributional drift, with a controllable trade-off between domain precision and general-capability retention. The findings hold across domains and model families.
AI.conclusion: When gold reasoning is absent, tuning the specialist’s training choices directly controls the latent supervision passed to downstream models.

title: LLM-Enhanced Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Unified Electric Vehicles-Charging Station-Grid Optimization in Public Charging Systems
summary: In the era of the Internet of Things (IoT), coordinating connected electric vehicle (EV) charging scheduling to balance EV charging satisfaction, station profitability, and smart grid stability presents a complex multi-objective challenge. Existing Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) approaches often struggle with high-dimensional state spaces generated by massive IoT sensing data and conflicting stakeholder interests. This paper proposes a novel LLM-enhanced MARL framework that, for the first time, simultaneously optimizes the Grid, EVs, and Stations within a unified loop. By integrating Large Language Model (LLM), we address two critical bottlenecks: interpretable feature selection and adaptive multi-objective balancing. The LLM analyzes real-time IoT-collected environmental states to extract physically significant features and dynamically assigns weights to conflicting objectives-including profit, user satisfaction, and grid load-using semantic reasoning instead of complex manual tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior market efficiency while reducing training time by over 70%. This approach offers a scalable, transparent solution for efficient and sustainable IoT-enabled urban charging infrastructure management.

AI.tldr: An LLM-enhanced MARL framework optimizes Grid, EVs, and Stations in a unified loop for IoT-enabled EV charging, enabling interpretable feature selection and adaptive multi-objective balancing, outperforming baselines with faster training.
AI.motivation: Address high-dimensional IoT sensing data and conflicting objectives (profit, user satisfaction, grid stability) in EV charging coordination.
AI.method: Integrate LLM into MARL to perform feature extraction and dynamic objective weighting; operate across Grid/EVs/Stations in a single loop; semantic reasoning replaces manual tuning.
AI.result: Significant performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines; improved market efficiency; training time reduced by >70% in experiments.
AI.conclusion: LLM-enhanced MARL offers scalable, transparent management for IoT-enabled urban charging, balancing efficiency, profitability, and grid stability.

title: VLBiMan++: Expanding the Generalization Boundary of Vision-Language Anchored One-Shot Bimanual Manipulation
comment: Under review. Extended journal version of https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21723. The project link is https://hnuzhy.github.io/projects/VLBiManPlus
summary: Generalizable bimanual robotic manipulation requires a reusable task prior that can persist across increasingly diverse tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and execution conditions, thus avoiding the prohibitive cost of large-scale teleoperated demonstrations and policy retraining. In this work, we present VLBiMan++, an extended framework that expands the generalization boundary of vision-language anchored one-shot bimanual manipulation. Starting from a single human demonstration, VLBiMan++ performs task-aware decomposition to identify reusable and adaptable skill components, and employs vision-language grounded geometric adaptation to transfer these skills to novel configurations without retraining. Building on this foundation, we systematically extend generalization along five dimensions: task generalization through diverse and long-horizon skill compositions; object generalization across unseen categories, varying geometries, and more complex articulated or deformable objects; scene generalization under clutter, occlusion, and dynamic interference; embodiment generalization across heterogeneous dual-arm robotic platforms; and deployment generalization through prolonged closed-loop execution under repeated external perturbations. To support this broader scope, we further introduce object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization mechanisms that accommodate changes beyond simple rigid 6-DoF pose variations while preserving reliable bimanual coordination. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that VLBiMan++ maintains strong task success and adaptation capability across these increasingly challenging settings. Overall, VLBiMan++ advances one-shot bimanual manipulation from demonstrating isolated transferability toward a more systematic and scalable framework for generalization across tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and long-term deployment conditions.

AI.tldr: VLBiMan++ generalizes one-shot bimanual manipulation across tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and deployment using task-aware decomposition and vision-language grounded geometric adaptation, plus object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization; validated by extensive real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: To reduce reliance on large-scale teleoperation and retraining while achieving broad generalization, enabling reusable priors across diverse task settings.
AI.method: From a single human demonstration, perform task-aware decomposition to reusable skills; use vision-language grounded geometric adaptation to transfer to new configurations without retraining; extend generalization along five dimensions (tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, deployment); add object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization for non-rigid/object-state changes; conduct extensive real-world experiments.
AI.result: VLBiMan++ maintains strong task success and adaptation across challenging settings; demonstrates generalization across the five axes; real-world experiments show robustness and persistence under perturbations.
AI.conclusion: VLBiMan++ advances one-shot bimanual manipulation toward a systematic, scalable generalization framework across tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and long-term deployment.

title: Towards Practical Precision Agriculture: Real-Time Fruit Detection and Video Analytics on Embedded Edge Hardware
summary: Static-image benchmarks do not capture the computational and temporal requirements of practical orchard video analytics. This study presents an end-to-end framework for real-time fruit detection, tracking, and counting on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super. A lightweight YOLO26s detector is trained independently on four public datasets representing apples, mangoes, blueberries, and strawberries under a common protocol. The models are deployed on embedded platform using PyTorch and TensorRT at FP32, FP16, and INT8 precision. APPLE MOTS is then used for temporal video analytics because it provides orchard sequences with persistent fruit identities, enabling evaluation of multi-object tracking and unique-fruit counting. The selected FP16 TensorRT detector is integrated into an NVIDIA DeepStream pipeline combining hardware-accelerated decoding, ByteTrack tracking, and motion-aware line-crossing analytics. Across the four detection tasks, mean test mAP@50:95 ranges from 0.4957 to 0.8656. On the Jetson, TensorRT FP16 achieves 66.76-74.56 images/s at 13.41-14.98 ms prediction latency, while reducing mAP@50:95 by only 0.0020-0.0054 and gross energy consumption by approximately 64-66% relative to PyTorch FP32. The complete detector-tracker-analytics pipeline reaches 44.96-54.11 FPS and sustains the configured 30-FPS input rate without output-frame loss. On held-out orchard video sequences, HOTA ranges from 0.345 to 0.538, event-level counting F1 from 0.611 to 0.803, and relative count error from 6.2% to 51.6%. Performance varies across acquisition geometries: near-lateral row viewing yields the most stable tracking and counting, whereas forward traversal remains association- and recall-limited despite spatially adaptive counting geometry. These results show that practical edge-based fruit monitoring requires efficient detection and acquisition geometries that support reliable temporal association.

AI.tldr: End-to-end real-time orchard fruit detection/tracking/counting on NVIDIA Jetson using lightweight YOLO26s, FP16 TensorRT, and APPLE MOTS; achieves 30 FPS stable pipeline at edge with mAP 0.50–0.87 and significant energy savings; geometry of acquisition affects temporal association.
AI.motivation: Static-image benchmarks do not capture the temporal and computational requirements of real-world orchard video analytics; need real-time edge processing with persistent fruit identities for reliable tracking and counting.
AI.method: Train lightweight YOLO26s detectors on four public fruit datasets (apples, mangoes, blueberries, strawberries) under a common protocol. Deploy on Jetson Orin Nano Super with PyTorch and TensorRT in FP32/FP16/INT8; select FP16 TensorRT model. Use APPLE MOTS for temporal evaluation; integrate into NVIDIA DeepStream pipeline with hardware-accelerated decoding, ByteTrack tracking, and motion-aware line-crossing analytics.
AI.result: Mean test mAP@50:95 ranges 0.4957–0.8656 across detection tasks. Jetson FP16 TensorRT yields 66.76–74.56 images/s (13.41–14.98 ms per inference) with only 0.0020–0.0054 drop in mAP@50:95 and ~64–66% energy reduction vs PyTorch FP32. End-to-end detector–tracker–analytics pipeline runs at 44.96–54.11 FPS and maintains 30 FPS input without frame loss. On held-out orchard video, HOTA 0.345–0.538, event-level counting F1 0.611–0.803, relative count error 6.2%–51.6%. Performance varies with acquisition geometry; near-lateral views are most stable for tracking/counting; forward traversal is more challenging for association/recall.
AI.conclusion: Practical edge-based fruit monitoring requires efficient detection and acquisition geometries that support reliable temporal association; geometry-aware data collection and robust temporal tracking are essential for real-time orchard analytics.

title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models? It Depends on Who's Judging
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators are increasingly used to score open-ended generation, yet a judge's correlation with human ratings on its development set may not guarantee valid measurement when outputs are closely matched and human preferences are subjective. We study this failure mode through psychological depth in short stories. Seven human readers and an LLM-judge ensemble selected on the original scalar Psychological Depth Scale dataset ($ρ= 0.646$) evaluated 60 blinded, prompt-matched story pairs from GPT-5 vs.\ GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 vs.\ DeepSeek-V3. Human preferences showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was modestly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0--62.9\%), whereas DeepSeek-R1 trailed V3 (42.9\%), and inter-reader agreement was near chance (Krippendorff's $α= 0.070$), with within-reader consistency and recurring weighting patterns suggesting structured heterogeneity rather than random responding. The judge, by contrast, favored reasoning outputs in 89.0\% of dimension-level comparisons and 59 of 60 pairs on aggregate PDS, uniformly across all five evaluator configurations, and its scores were associated with surface features such as sentence length and lexical diversity. These results suggest that development-set performance is insufficient evidence for deployment validity on a shifted distribution, and that point-estimate judges can obscure the heterogeneity in subjective human evaluation.

AI.tldr: LLM-based judges can show high correlation with human ratings on a development set yet fail to provide valid measurement under distribution shift when judgments are subjective and outputs are nearly indistinguishable; human raters exhibit substantial heterogeneity and very low inter-rater agreement, while the judge relies on surface features and favors reasoning outputs, signaling deployment risks from using development-set performance alone.
AI.motivation: To test whether high development-set performance of LLM-based evaluators generalizes to shifted distributions in a setting with subjective judgments (psychological depth in short stories) and closely matched outputs.
AI.method: Evaluate 60 blinded, prompt-matched story pairs from GPT-5 vs GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 vs DeepSeek-V3 using seven human readers and an LLM-judge ensemble selected on the original Psychological Depth Scale dataset (ρ=0.646). Assess correlations with the PDS, dimension-level vs. aggregate judgments, Krippendorff's α for inter-reader agreement, within-reader consistency, and associations with surface features (sentence length, lexical diversity).
AI.result: Humans showed no universal reasoning advantage; GPT-5 modestly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0–62.9%), DeepSeek-R1 trailed V3 (42.9%), and inter-reader agreement was near chance (Krippendorff’s α ≈ 0.070). The LLM judge favored reasoning outputs in 89% of dimension-level comparisons and in 59 of 60 pairs on aggregate PDS, with scores tied to surface features like sentence length and lexical diversity.
AI.conclusion: Development-set performance is insufficient evidence for deployment validity on shifted distributions, and point-estimate judges can mask heterogeneity in subjective human evaluation; robust assessment should account for distribution shift and evaluator heterogeneity.

title: Bypass Observation: A Conceptual Design of a Non-Intrusive Layer-Wise Semantic Extraction Architecture
summary: Large language models reason in high-dimensional hidden-state spaces, while users observe only final outputs. We introduce Bypass Observation, a non-intrusive layer-wise readout architecture that attaches read-only observation heads to selected Transformer layers without feeding their outputs back into the backbone. We consider three variants: a shared LM head across layers, layer-specific heads, and a layer- or step-adaptive head. For full-vocabulary readout, we derive a closed-form overhead approximation governed primarily by V/(12d), with representative estimates ranging from about 30% to 240%, and discuss cost reductions via sparse observation, low-rank factorization, reduced vocabularies, top-k readout, and selective positions. We argue that Bypass Observation can make model computation more observable while remaining only a partial, potentially misleading projection of hidden states. We further distinguish bypass chain-of-thought from conventional chain-of-thought: conventional reasoning tokens enter the autoregressive computation, whereas bypass readouts remain causally external at inference time, although they can still provide training signals in reinforcement learning. Finally, we discuss applications to looped and recurrent-depth Transformers, where iteration-wise readout may expose convergence, oscillation, and potential halting signals. The proposal is conceptual and analytical; systematic empirical validation remains future work.

AI.tldr: Introduces Bypass Observation: attach read-only, layer-wise observation heads to Transformer layers to observe hidden-state computations non-intrusively without feeding back into the backbone. Explores three variants (shared head, layer-specific heads, adaptive head); derives an overhead approximation for full-vocabulary readout (~V/(12d)) and discusses costs and reductions via sparsity, low-rank factorization, reduced vocabularies, top-k readout, and selective positions. Argues that bypass observations improve observability while giving a partial, potentially misleading projection of hidden states; distinguishes bypass chain-of-thought from conventional chain-of-thought; discusses applications to looped/recurrent-depth Transformers; status is conceptual/analytical with empirical validation left for future work.
AI.motivation: Enhance transparency and interpretability of large language models by making hidden-state computations observable through non-intrusive readouts, without altering model behavior during inference or training unless used for signals in RL.
AI.method: Proposes attaching read-only observation heads to selected Transformer layers (three variants: shared LM head, layer-specific heads, and layer/step-adaptive heads); derives a closed-form overhead approximation for full-vocabulary readout; discusses strategies to reduce cost (sparse observation, low-rank factorization, vocab reduction, top-k readout, selective positions); differentiates bypass readouts from conventional chain-of-thought; discusses implications for looped/recurrent-depth Transformers.
AI.result: Framework is analytical and conceptual; provides overhead estimates (V/(12d)) and representative cost ranges (roughly 30%–240%); outlines cost-reduction strategies; offers insights on observability and potential pitfalls; no systematic empirical validation yet; highlights design choices and potential applications including convergence/halting signals.
AI.conclusion: Bypass Observation offers a non-intrusive means to make model execution more observable and potentially informative, at the cost of partial/misleading projections of hidden states; suitable for looped and recurrent-depth architectures; empirical validation remains a future step; serves as a conceptual foundation for further study.

title: BIG-CBF: Behavior-Imagination-Guided Control Barrier Function with Shared Uncertainty for Mobile Robot Navigation
summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a mathematically grounded framework for enforcing local collision-avoidance constraints in autonomous mobile robots, commonly through optimization-based safety filters. However, a minimum-intervention CBF filter lacks task-level maneuver awareness and may fail to select a productive avoidance direction when multiple distinct maneuvers are locally viable, leading to safe but stalled behavior in geometrically ambiguous environments. This paper presents BIG-CBF, Behavior-Imagination-Guided Control Barrier Function with shared uncertainty, a two-rate navigation architecture that separates low-rate maneuver selection from high-rate safety filtering. Over a short horizon, six closed-loop feedback behaviors are imagined and evaluated using analytic CBF compatibility together with a lightweight objective accounting for task progress, freezing, smoothness, and switching. To reduce planning-execution mismatch, the imagination and execution layers share consistent uncertainty sources for relative-motion delay, obstacle prediction, zero-order-hold motion, and command-execution residuals, while a hard CBF remains the final safety authority. In a 3,600-episode comparative benchmark across nine scenarios, BIG-CBF achieves the highest overall task success rate of 99.78% while substantially reducing downstream CBF intervention. On a physical omnidirectional robot with onboard Jetson Orin Nano computation, BIG-CBF completes all 15 evaluation runs without a recorded contact event. Matched hardware comparisons against the non-shared variant further show lower CBF intervention energy and activation frequency, supporting improved consistency between maneuver selection and safety-critical execution.

AI.tldr: BIG-CBF introduces a two-rate navigation framework that combines imagination-guided maneuver selection with a high-rate, safety-first CBF filter to reduce intervention while maintaining safety in ambiguous environments.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of minimum-intervention CBF filters, which can be task-agnostic and stall in geometrically ambiguous situations, by incorporating maneuver-aware planning and shared uncertainty between planning and execution.
AI.method: A two-rate architecture: low-rate planning imagines six closed-loop behaviors over a short horizon and evaluates them for CBF compatibility and task-oriented objectives (progress, freezing, smoothness, switching). The high-rate safety filter enforces hard safety via a CBF. Shared uncertainty sources (relative-motion delay, obstacle prediction, zero-order-hold motion, command-execution residuals) align imagination and execution to reduce planning-execution mismatch. It includes a hard CBF as final safety authority.
AI.result: In 3,600-episode benchmark across nine scenarios, BIG-CBF achieved a 99.78% task success rate and reduced downstream CBF intervention. On a physical omnidirectional robot with Jetson Orin Nano, all 15 runs completed without a contact event. Matched hardware comparisons show reduced CBF intervention energy and activation frequency, indicating improved consistency between maneuver selection and safety execution.
AI.conclusion: BIG-CBF effectively combines imagination-guided planning with a robust safety layer to outperform conventional minimum-intervention CBF filters in both simulated and physical experiments, reducing unsafe interventions while maintaining high task success.

title: From Advertised Improvements to Measured Capabilities: Evaluating ChatGPT Images 2.5 on Forgery Tasks
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures. Ancillary files include the scored manifest for the in-the-wild sample and an arena snapshot
summary: We evaluate whether the improvements advertised for ChatGPT Images 2.5 translate into better performance on forgery tasks with predetermined answers. We compare its Flare and Sunburst API models with GPT-Image-2 re-run in the same week, using receipt-field edits, repeated editing, product placement and fine-print rendering. After image registration, Flare and Sunburst show fewer OCR-detected changes to surrounding receipt text (31.7% and 31.2% versus 44.2% for both GPT-Image-2 baselines), mainly on CORD receipts, without a detectable improvement in target-field correctness. Flare retains fewer earlier edits on CORD receipts, while photo-edit sequences provide little separation between models. Product codes are more often legible with Images 2.5, alongside larger product placement; the analyses do not establish a fidelity gain independent of size. Fine-print improvements remain unresolved below the OCR reliability limit. Refusals are rare and localisation is weak in both generations. At a fixed detection threshold, Community Forensics flags 68.6% of controlled Images 2.5 images averaged across cells, versus 35.9% of self-reported images posted online. These results motivate task-specific evaluation of advertised capabilities and defences, with explicit limits on what automatic checks can establish.

AI.tldr: Evaluates whether ChatGPT Images 2.5 improvements improve forgery task performance; 2.5 reduces OCR-detected changes and improves legibility/placement but does not improve target-field correctness; automatic checks have limits; task-specific evaluation needed.
AI.motivation: To validate advertised capabilities of new image-generation updates against objective forgery-detection tasks and to quantify fidelity and detection metrics across models.
AI.method: Comparative evaluation using Flare and Sunburst API models versus GPT-Image-2 baseline. Experiments include receipt-field edits, repeated edits, product placement, and fine-print rendering; image registration used; metrics include OCR-detected changes to surrounding text, target-field correctness, legibility of product codes, size-related fidelity, and automatic defences (Community Forensics flags) across controlled versus self-reported images.
AI.result: Flare and Sunburst show fewer OCR-detected changes (31.7% and 31.2% vs 44.2% for baselines, mainly on CORD receipts) but no detectable improvement in target-field correctness. Flare retains fewer earlier edits; photo-edit sequences provide little separation between models. Product codes more legible and larger product placement with Images 2.5, yet fidelity gain not independent of size. Fine-print improvements unresolved due to OCR limits. Refusals are rare and localization is weak in both generations. Community Forensics flags 68.6% of controlled Images 2.5 vs 35.9% of self-reported images.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific evaluation is necessary to assess advertised capabilities and defenses; automatic checks have explicit limits on what they can establish.

title: PPDL: A Real-world Industrial User Retention Ratio Forecasting Framework Integrating Physical Priors with Deep Learning
summary: In multi-channel paid user acquisition, early and accurate prediction of user retention at the channel level is crucial for optimizing budget allocation. User retention curves display a pronounced temporal pattern: an initial period of high churn transitions into long-term stability. This pattern is further characterized by regular fluctuations attributable to seasonality and exhibits high serial autocorrelation. These intrinsic properties make such curves highly suitable for analysis within a time-series forecasting framework. However, forecasting user retention ratio for large-scale short-video platform faces three major challenges: significant heterogeneity across channels, pronounced global trend of decay followed by saturation, and short look-back windows. To address these challenges, we propose PPDL, a novel forecasting framework that integrates physical priors with deep learning. We first introduce a trend-residual decomposition component. The trend is modeled using the Weibull distribution, whose parameters are learned via a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Secondly, for the residual component, we design an auxiliary embedding module on top of a deep learning backbone to maintain the channel identity awareness. Finally, to enhance the model's sensitivity to trends, we design a Multiscale Trend-penalized loss function. The proposed approach PPDL is validated through comprehensive experiments on industrial-scale datasets, covering three applications with an average of 30+ channels each. Experimental results show that PPDL achieves improvements across different backbones and significantly outperforms existing online solutions.

AI.tldr: PPDL is a time-series forecasting framework combining a Weibull trend with an MLP, a channel-aware residual embedding, and a multiscale trend-penalized loss to forecast multi-channel user retention under heterogeneity, decay-saturation, and short look-back.
AI.motivation: Accurate channel-level retention forecasting is essential for budget allocation in large-scale short-video platforms, where curves show decay-to-saturation, seasonality, and high inter-channel heterogeneity with limited history.
AI.method: Decompose retention into trend (Weibull-distributed, learned via MLP) and residual. Introduce an auxiliary embedding to preserve channel identity in the residual, on top of a deep learning backbone. Apply a multiscale trend-penalized loss to emphasize trend fidelity across horizons.
AI.result: Empirical validation on industrial-scale datasets (avg 30+ channels per scenario) shows PPDL improves across backbones and significantly outperforms existing online solutions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating physical priors (Weibull trend) with deep learning enhances multi-channel retention forecasting under challenging data conditions, achieving robust performance on real-world industrial data.

title: ViperQ: Order Flow Pattern Recognition via Auction Market Theory for Reinforcement Learning Trading
summary: Reinforcement learning trading systems published in the academic literature overwhelmingly rely on price-aggregate state representations (OHLCV bars) or limit-order-book depth features, leaving microstructure pattern theories from the practitioner literature, namely Auction Market Theory and Market Profile, without a peer-reviewed computational instantiation. We present ViperQ, a reinforcement learning system whose state representation is built explicitly from Auction Market Theory primitives: Volume Point of Control, Value Area position, Low Volume Node flags, Cumulative Volume Delta divergence, and tape-velocity signatures, assembled into a 20-dimensional Z-normalised vector. Two Proximal Policy Optimisation agents are trained with a prospect theory-grounded asymmetric reward function that penalises losing holds at a magnitude consistent with Kahneman and Tversky's loss-aversion coefficient. Evaluated on a held-out twelve-month partition of institutional tick data the agents have never seen, ViperQ achieves +163.6% ROI on TSLA (-27.5% max drawdown, 27,019 trades) and +116.5% ROI on NVDA (-47.8% max drawdown, 12,892 trades) under zero leverage. The results establish Auction Market Theory features as a tractable structured input modality for sequential decision-making on financial time series and motivate further work on microstructure-aware policy learning.

AI.tldr: Introduces ViperQ, a PPO-based RL system that uses Auction Market Theory primitives as a 20D Z-normalised state; demonstrates strong out-of-sample ROI on TSLA and NVDA with zero leverage.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap where reinforcement learning trading research largely uses price-aggregate or depth features, lacking a computational instantiation of Auction Market Theory and Market Profile; tests whether microstructure primitives can structure RL inputs.
AI.method: Construct a 20-dimensional state from Auction Market Theory primitives (Volume Point of Control, Value Area position, Low Volume Node flags, Cumulative Volume Delta divergence, tape-velocity) and normalise to Z-scores. Train two PPO agents with a prospect-theory-inspired asymmetric reward that penalises losing holds. Train on institutional tick data with a 12-month held-out partition, zero leverage.
AI.result: Out-of-sample: +163.6% ROI on TSLA (-27.5% max drawdown, 27,019 trades) and +116.5% ROI on NVDA (-47.8% max drawdown, 12,892 trades).
AI.conclusion: Auction Market Theory features constitute a tractable, structured input modality for sequential decision-making on financial time series; supports further microstructure-aware policy learning research.

title: Orientation Control of Soft Robots via Adiabatic Spectral Submanifolds
comment: This paper has been accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
summary: Soft robots are commonly sought for safety-critical interactions in delicate environments, where accurate position and orientation control is imperative. Model predictive control (MPC) offers a solution, but it requires a model of the robot's infinite-dimensional nonlinear dynamics that is at once accurate and computationally cheap. Recent theory on adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) and their applications to soft robots provide data-driven model-reduction methods to construct such models. Here, we extend these methods to identify aSSMs from enlarged observable datasets and upgrade the currently available aSSM-MPC schemes. Evaluated on a high-fidelity finite-element simulation of a pressure-actuated soft arm, our controller reduces position and orientation tracking error by more than 60% compared to existing data-driven baselines.

AI.tldr: Extends adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) to larger observable datasets for data-driven reduced-order modeling in soft robot MPC; demonstrates substantial accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Soft robots have infinite-dimensional nonlinear dynamics; need accurate yet cheap models for MPC. aSSMs offer data-driven reductions, and this work enlarges the observable data used for identification to improve model fidelity.
AI.method: Identify aSSMs from augmented observable datasets and integrate these reduced-order models into MPC. Evaluate on a high-fidelity finite-element model of a pressure-actuated soft arm and compare tracking performance to existing data-driven baselines.
AI.result: Position and orientation tracking error reduced by over 60% compared with current data-driven baselines.
AI.conclusion: Extending aSSM-based reductions to larger datasets improves MPC performance for soft robots; supports safer and more accurate control in delicate environments; future work could address hardware validation and computational efficiency.

title: YOLO12-MambaScan: An Efficient Object Detector with High-Frequency Enhancement and State-Space Modeling
summary: The rapid development of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology has made aerial-image object detection increasingly important for natural-resource monitoring, traffic management, and disaster response. Detecting small objects in aerial images remains difficult because objects occupy very few pixels, high-frequency cues are easily lost, and global context is hard to model in cluttered scenes. Existing detectors often retain insufficient edge, corner, and texture information. We propose \ours, an aerial-image detector built on the YOLO12 architecture. The model combines a triple-path high-frequency enhancement convolution module (TriPathHFConv), receptive-field coordinate-attention convolution (RFCAConv), and a Mamba-based global-context module. On VisDrone, at an input resolution of 960*960, ours achieves 60.0% mAP@50 and 38.6%mAP@50:95, demonstrating a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off for small-object detection. The benchmark and dataset protocol follow the VisDrone challenge setup.

AI.tldr: An aerial-image detector built on YOLO12 (ours) combines high-frequency enhancement and global-context modules to improve small-object detection in UAV imagery, achieving strong accuracy with efficiency on VisDrone.
AI.motivation: Small objects in aerial images are hard to detect due to few pixels, loss of high-frequency cues, and difficulty modeling global context in cluttered scenes. Edge, corner, and texture information is often underrepresented by existing detectors.
AI.method: Proposed TriPathHFConv (triple-path high-frequency enhancement conv), RFCAConv (receptive-field coordinate-attention conv), and a Mamba-based global-context module, integrated into YOLO12 architecture for 960x960 input.
AI.result: On VisDrone (960x960): 60.0% mAP@50 and 38.6% mAP@50:95, indicating favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off for small-object detection; protocol follows VisDrone challenge.
AI.conclusion: The method enhances high-frequency details and global context to improve small-object detection in aerial imagery, achieving competitive performance with a focus on efficiency; future work could include broader ablations and cross-dataset validation.

title: Benchmarking Optimizers to Solve Inverse Problems with Differentiable Physics Simulators
summary: Solving inverse problems with differentiable physics simulators holds the potential to revolutionize scientific discovery and engineering design, as it enjoys both the strict physical correctness from rigorous numerical physics simulators, and the high efficiency and effectiveness from automatic differentiation and gradient-based optimization.
