However, currently, this paradigm faces performance issues in optimization. In this work, we target benchmarking the performance of different optimizers to solve various inverse problems. We construct 12 differentiable physics simulators spanning physics domains including discrete mechanics, continuous mechanics, atomistic simulations, rendering, and semi-empirical physics models. Based on these simulators, we design corresponding inverse problems that can be categorized into parameter identification, inverse design, and optimal control. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to compare the performance of different optimizers, including regular first-order methods, approximate second-order methods, as well as global optimizers, on these inverse problems, and analyze the results to provide insights on how to choose and design optimizers for differentiable programming. We hope such benchmarks can inspire the development of more effective optimizers, and further promote the applications of differentiable programming in various scientific and engineering domains.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive benchmark of optimizers for inverse problems across 12 differentiable physics simulators, aiming to guide optimizer choice and design in differentiable programming.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient and physically accurate inverse problem solving by understanding how different optimizers perform across domains (discrete/continuous mechanics, atomistic, rendering, semi-empirical).
AI.method: 1) Develop 12 differentiable simulators; 2) formulate inverse problems (parameter identification, inverse design, optimal control); 3) run extensive experiments comparing first-order, approximate second-order, and global optimizers; 4) analyze results to extract guidance.
AI.result: Benchmarks reveal performance trade-offs and actionable insights on optimizer selection and design for differentiable programming; provide a resource to stimulate development of more effective optimizers.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark suite can accelerate differentiable programming applications in science and engineering by informing optimizer choices and inspiring new methods.

title: UniCAR-RL: Seeing Better before Thinking Deeper in Visual Mathematics
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often struggle with complex mathematical visual reasoning primarily due to a lack of fine-grained perception, causing initial visual hallucinations to directly trigger cascading reasoning failures. In traditional end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL), sparse rewards fail to decouple perceptual hallucinations from logical missteps, hindering targeted perception optimization. Alternatively, fine-tuning with perception-enhanced CoT data incurs high costs and hallucinations. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing UniCAR-RL, an annotation-free RL framework. By explicitly decoupling the optimization of perception and reasoning during the training process, it achieves isolation and optimization of both capabilities. Specifically, UniCAR-RL consists of three synergistic branches: 1) a Caption-RL branch that optimizes perception capabilities through verifier-guided reasoning validation; 2) a Reasoning-RL branch that performs logical reasoning based on a gold image description to halt cascading errors; 3) a QA-RL branch that retains native end-to-end alignment to ensure robust question-answering performance. Experiments show that UniCAR-RL substantially improves MLLMs' mathematical and visual reasoning using only raw short-answer data. Furthermore, it demonstrates strong generalization across diverse architectures and scales.

AI.tldr: UniCAR-RL is an annotation-free RL framework that decouples perception and reasoning with three branches, boosting multimodal math-visual reasoning and generalizability without extra annotations.
AI.motivation: MLLMs face complex mathematical visual reasoning due to perceptual hallucinations that propagate errors; end-to-end RL with sparse rewards fails to disentangle perception from reasoning; perception-centric fine-tuning is costly and prone to hallucinations.
AI.method: Three synergistic RL branches: (1) Caption-RL optimizes perception via verifier-guided reasoning validation; (2) Reasoning-RL uses gold image descriptions to halt cascading errors; (3) QA-RL preserves native end-to-end alignment for robust QA. Training explicitly decouples perception from reasoning without annotations.
AI.result: Significant improvements in mathematical and visual reasoning for MLLMs using only raw short-answer data; robust QA performance; strong generalization across architectures and scales.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling perception and reasoning with UniCAR-RL enables targeted perception optimization and stable reasoning without annotated data, yielding cross-architecture generalization and improved multimodal reasoning.

title: Learning-Based Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance for a UAV Using Only Three Range Sensors
summary:
We present a learning-based approach to kinodynamic online motion planning for an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) operating at a fixed altitude in unknown dynamic environments, where real-time avoidance of both static and dynamic obstacles must be achieved under conditions of extreme partial observability. The UAV is controlled with a single degree of freedom (yaw only), resulting in constrained, nonholonomic motion similar to fixed-wing platforms.
  The proposed framework integrates a behavior grid map representation with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for stable policy learning in continuous control. The key idea is the co-design of a state representation and control policy that enables reliable navigation using only three low-cost directional range sensors, without reliance on dense sensing modalities such as LiDAR or vision-based systems. The behavior grid map dynamically aggregates sparse measurements into a structured local representation that supports real-time decision-making for obstacle avoidance and target reaching. Extensive simulations across environments of varying sizes and obstacle densities demonstrate that the proposed standard and enhanced methods achieve higher success rates than PPO variants and Model Predictive Control (MPC) (94\% vs. 79--90\% in small-scale high-congestion scenarios, and 83\% vs. 62--71\% in large-scale high-congestion scenarios), while maintaining real-time performance. Real-world experiments across four scenarios further confirm practical feasibility, with consistent target-reaching behaviour and no collisions under the tested conditions.

AI.tldr: A learning-based kinodynamic online motion planning framework for a yaw-only UAV in unknown dynamic environments using a behavior grid map and PPO DRL, achieving high success rates and real-time performance with sparse sensors.
AI.motivation: To address extreme partial observability, nonholonomic constraints, and the need for real-time obstacle avoidance and target reaching with limited sensing (three directional range sensors) in dynamic environments.
AI.method: Co-design of a behavior grid map state representation with a PPO-based policy for continuous control, enabling navigation using sparse measurements from three directional range sensors. The behavior grid aggregates sparse data into a structured local representation; the approach is evaluated against PPO variants and MPC across small/large-scale, high-congestion scenarios, with both simulations and real-world tests.
AI.result: In simulations, standard and enhanced methods outperform PPO variants and MPC, achieving about 94% success in small-scale high-congestion vs 79–90% (PPO/MPC baselines) and about 83% vs 62–71% in large-scale high-congestion. Real-world experiments across four scenarios show consistent target-reaching with no collisions.
AI.conclusion: The integration of a behavior grid map with PPO DRL enables reliable, real-time kinodynamic navigation for a yaw-only UAV under severe partial observability, with superior success rates and demonstrated practicality in both simulated and real environments.

title: Multimodal Foundation Models Adaptation based on Domain-Aware Relaxed Orthogonal Subspace for Remote Sensing
summary: Pretrained foundation models (FMs) have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, yet their high fine-tuning cost limits practical deployment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) improve efficiency by constraining updates to a predefined low-rank subspace. However, when applied to remote sensing tasks with substantial domain shifts, the fixed subspace is constructed without observing the downstream activation distribution and can therefore provide a poor coordinate system for adaptation, a phenomenon herein termed subspace mismatch. To address this issue, a unified framework is introduced, termed Domain-aware Relaxed Orthogonal Subspace adaptation (DROS), which reformulates low-rank adaptation as data-conditioned subspace learning and flexible subspace adaptation. Specifically, the weight decomposition is conditioned on second-order activation statistics estimated from the downstream training distribution, so that the initialization reflects the feature geometry actually induced by the remote-sensing data, followed by flexible geometric transformations enabled by a relaxed orthogonal parameterization. Furthermore, the framework is extended to multimodal settings (MM-DROS) by sharing transformation structures across modality-specific subspaces, facilitating efficient cross-modal interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple remote sensing benchmarks demonstrate that DROS achieves state-of-the-art performance, even surpassing full fine-tuning, without additional inference overhead.

AI.tldr: Proposes Domain-aware Relaxed Orthogonal Subspace (DROS) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning in remote sensing; addresses subspace mismatch by conditioning the low-rank adaptation on downstream activation statistics, with a relaxed orthogonal parameterization; extended to MM-DROS for multimodal sharing; achieves SOTA on remote sensing benchmarks, surpassing full fine-tuning without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: PEFT methods like LoRA often assume a fixed adaptation subspace that may be poorly aligned with downstream data under significant domain shifts (remote sensing). This misalignment, termed subspace mismatch, hampers efficiency gains. A data-conditioned approach should align subspaces with the actual feature geometry of the target domain.
AI.method: Reformulate LoRA as data-conditioned subspace learning. The weight decomposition is conditioned on second-order activation statistics estimated from the downstream training distribution, ensuring initialization reflects the downstream feature geometry. Apply a relaxed orthogonal parameterization to enable flexible geometric transformations. Extend the framework to multimodal settings (MM-DROS) by sharing transformation structures across modality-specific subspaces to facilitate cross-modal interaction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple remote sensing benchmarks show that DROS achieves state-of-the-art performance, even surpassing full fine-tuning, without additional inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Domain-aware, data-conditioned subspace adaptation can substantially improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning in domain-shifted applications like remote sensing. The MM-DROS extension enables efficient multimodal interaction. The approach offers strong accuracy gains with no inference cost, making it attractive for deployment.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Influence Maximization in Social Networks: An Unsupervised Minimum Dominating Set Approach
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
summary: The Minimum Dominating Set (MDS) problem is a classic NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with critical applications in social network analysis, including viral marketing, influence maximization, public health interventions, and information dissemination. Identifying a minimal set of influential individuals whose reach covers an entire social network is central to these applications, yet remains computationally challenging at scale. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning over graphs, and recent work explores their application to hard combinatorial problems. This paper presents a novel unsupervised GNN framework for the MDS problem that eliminates the need for ground-truth solutions during training. Trained on 12,000 synthetic graphs with diverse structural properties, our method achieves up to 55x faster inference than metaheuristic baselines and up to 14x faster inference than supervised learning approaches, while finding optimal or near-optimal dominating sets on real-world social network benchmarks. Our learned heuristic generalizes effectively to unseen graph distributions, demonstrating strong practical applicability for large-scale social network analysis.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised GNN framework for Minimum Dominating Set (MDS) that trains on synthetic graphs and delivers fast, near-optimal solutions with strong generalization to real networks.
AI.motivation: MDS is NP-hard and central to social-network analysis tasks. Existing methods either rely on ground-truth labels (supervised) or are computationally intensive (metaheuristics). An unsupervised, scalable GNN approach can provide fast inference without labeled data and improve applicability to large-scale networks.
AI.method: An unsupervised Graph Neural Network framework trained on 12,000 synthetic graphs with diverse structural properties. The model learns to produce dominating sets without ground-truth solutions, presumably via a differentiable surrogate loss that enforces domination constraints and set-cardinality considerations.
AI.result: The method achieves up to 55x faster inference than metaheuristic baselines and up to 14x faster inference than supervised learning approaches, while finding optimal or near-optimal dominating sets on real-world social network benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised GNNs for MDS are effective and generalize well to unseen graph distributions, offering practical, scalable solutions for large-scale social network analysis.

title: ClinAgent: A ReAct-Based Agent for Conversational Access to Clinical Trial Information
summary: Querying clinical trial registries remains a manual and error-prone process, requiring researchers to navigate large volumes of semi-structured data without support for natural language interaction or cross-source synthesis. To address this, we introduce ClinAgent, a conversational system based on agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that enables clinicians and researchers to query clinical trial information in plain language and receive grounded, up-to-date responses across multi-turn interactions. The system centers on a Large Language Model (LLM) agent following the ReAct paradigm, which iteratively reasons over queries, selects among a set of integrated tools, and refines its actions based on intermediate outputs. These tools include a ClinicalTrials.gov search interface, a PubMed module, and a Python-based analyzer operating on a locally cached structured dataset of clinical trials. We evaluate the system using a three-phase framework assessing operational effectiveness, planning quality, tool-use efficiency, and expert qualitative judgments, comparing three LLM backends: Gemini 3.0 Flash and two variants of DeepSeek V3.2 (thinking and non-thinking). Results reveal complementary strengths, with DeepSeek (thinking mode) excelling in planning quality, while Gemini achieves the highest overall performance and strongest expert ratings. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of agentic AI systems to improve the accessibility and synthesis of clinical trial information, supporting more efficient and user-centered biomedical research workflows.

AI.tldr: ClinAgent is an agentic RAG system that enables natural-language querying of clinical trial data via integrated tools (ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, local dataset) using an LLM ReAct agent; evaluated across Gemini 3.0 Flash and DeepSeek V3.2 variants, showing complementary strengths and overall strong performance.
AI.motivation: Manual, error-prone querying of clinical trial registries with semi-structured data; lack of natural-language interaction and cross-source synthesis motivates a grounded, multi-tool conversational system.
AI.method: An LLM agent following the ReAct paradigm iteratively reasons, selects among integrated tools (ClinicalTrials.gov search, PubMed, Python-based analyzer over a cached clinical-trials dataset), and refines actions. Evaluation uses a three-phase framework assessing operational effectiveness, planning quality, tool-use efficiency, and expert judgments across three backends (Gemini 3.0 Flash and two DeepSeek V3.2 variants: thinking and non-thinking).
AI.result: DeepSeek (thinking) excels in planning quality; Gemini achieves the highest overall performance and strongest expert ratings. The results reveal complementary strengths across backends. The study demonstrates that agentic AI systems can enhance accessibility and synthesis of clinical-trial information, supporting more efficient, user-centric biomedical workflows.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI systems like ClinAgent have strong potential to improve how clinicians and researchers query and synthesize clinical-trial information, enabling grounded, up-to-date, multi-turn interactions across sources; future work may focus on grounding, efficiency, and broader tool integration.

title: EMoG: Emotion-Modulated Gait Generation for Expressive Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Existing humanoid locomotion systems primarily focus on stability and task execution, while integrating expressiveness with explicit locomotion control remains challenging. We propose EMoG, an emotion-modulated gait generation framework for expressive humanoid locomotion. EMoG introduces an emotional-style code with continuously adjustable intensity. Conditioned on this code and physical commands, a lightweight MLP generates expressive, command-consistent periodic gait trajectories in real time, which are tracked by a unified reinforcement learning policy for physical execution. To support training, we collect a large-scale emotion-annotated gait dataset from professional performers and develop an automated pipeline to extract physically consistent periodic gait cycles. EMoG also integrates an LLM-based parser that converts free-form language into emotional style and motion parameters for interactive control. Experiments demonstrate continuous gait-style modulation with perceptible expressive cues while maintaining command tracking. EMoG provides a practical approach to parameterized emotional-style walking for human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: EMoG is a framework for expressive humanoid locomotion that uses an emotion-modulated gait generation approach. It combines an emotional-style code with a lightweight MLP to generate real-time expressive gait trajectories conditioned on commands, followed by reinforcement learning-based execution. It includes a large emotion-annotated gait dataset, an automated pipeline for extracting periodic gait cycles, and an LLM-based parser to convert language into motion parameters. Experiments demonstrate continuous, expressive gait modulation while preserving command tracking, offering a practical parameterized walking solution for human-robot interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid locomotion systems emphasize stability and task performance, but expressive control is underdeveloped. There is a need to bridge human-like expressiveness with real-time locomotion control and interactive language-driven adjustment.
AI.method: Introduce an emotional-style code with continuously adjustable intensity. Conditioned on this code and physical commands, a lightweight MLP generates expressive, command-consistent periodic gait trajectories in real time. A unified reinforcement learning policy then tracks these trajectories for physical execution. A large emotion-annotated gait dataset is collected from professional performers, with an automated pipeline to extract physically consistent periodic gait cycles. An LLM-based parser converts free-form language into emotional style and motion parameters for interactive control.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate continuous gait-style modulation with perceptible expressive cues while maintaining command tracking.
AI.conclusion: EMoG provides a practical approach to parameterized emotional-style walking for human-robot interaction, integrating emotion-driven gait generation, data collection, RL-based execution, and NLP-based interactive control.

title: MARC: Morphology-Aware Regression of Consensus for Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Accurate cell segmentation remains a major bottleneck in subcellular spatial transcriptomics (SST), in which morphological images and spatially resolved RNA transcripts are used to partition tissues into individual cellular instances. As segmentation serves as the foundation for constructing cell-level representations, boundary errors can lead to incorrect transcript assignments and compromise downstream analyses. However, reliable ground-truth boundaries are unavailable because they must be inferred from incomplete morphological and transcript signals. Furthermore, manual annotation of a large number of cells is time-consuming. Agreement among complementary segmentation methods provides a practical surrogate for identifying well-supported and ambiguous regions, but explicit consensus construction requires executing multiple computationally intensive pipelines. In this study, we propose MARC (Morphology-Aware Regression of Consensus), a framework that predicts a multi-method consensus-support map for SST segmentation. MARC is trained with leave-one-method-out consensus pseudo-targets and a Foreground-Union Consensus Loss that focuses supervision on candidate and consensus foreground. We evaluated MARC on 4,642 held-out tiles from Xenium kidney tissue, achieving a mean Dice score of 0.90, a mean intersection-over-union of 0.82, and a mean cell-level Spearman correlation of 0.79 against explicitly computed cross-method consensus maps. We demonstrate that the predicted consensus maps localise weakly supported regions while preserving consensus-based rankings and identifying low-consensus cells for manual review. These results show that MARC closely approximates explicit cross-method consensus without multi-method inference and therefore has the potential to facilitate robust, consensus-aware evaluation of cell segmentation in large-scale SST studies.

AI.tldr: MARC predicts a multi-method consensus-support map for SST segmentation, using leave-one-method-out pseudo-targets and a Foreground-Union Consensus Loss to identify well-supported and ambiguous regions without running multiple pipelines.
AI.motivation: Segmentation in subcellular spatial transcriptomics is error-prone and ground-truth boundaries are unavailable; consensus among segmentation methods is a practical surrogate but expensive to compute.
AI.method: MARC framework trained with leave-one-method-out consensus pseudo-targets; Foreground-Union Consensus Loss; outputs a consensus-support map that highlights well-supported regions and uncertain areas, enabling consensus-aware evaluation.
AI.result: On 4,642 held-out Xenium kidney tiles, MARC achieved mean Dice 0.90, mean IoU 0.82, and mean cell-level Spearman 0.79 relative to explicit cross-method consensus maps, localizing weakly supported regions and preserving consensus rankings.
AI.conclusion: MARC closely approximates explicit cross-method consensus without requiring multi-method inference, enabling robust, consensus-aware evaluation of cell segmentation in large-scale SST studies.

title: Accuracy Is Not Service: A Decision-Aware Benchmark for Intermittent-Demand Forecasting
comment: Accepted to the Twenty-Sixth IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM-26)
summary: A contract-logistics spare-parts operator is paid on order-level service: an order counts only if every requested line is fulfilled, yet forecasters are selected based on line-level forecast accuracy. This disconnect matters when demand is intermittent and lumpy, histories are short, and lead times span months. We benchmarked 38 forecasting methods spanning classical, intermittent-demand, machine-learning, deep-learning, and pretrained foundation models. A common decision-aware protocol evaluates them on an industrial panel drawn from a live contract and two public datasets. Forecast-accuracy rank and order-service rank are negatively correlated on the industrial panel, at -0.555, across methods evaluated on 20,330 real multi-item orders. Service is more closely associated with the direction of cumulative forecast bias, including over-prediction during zero-demand periods, than with point accuracy. Examining bias in Chronos-2's instance normalization yields a training-free correction that lifts the per-material fill proxy from 77.5% to 92.0% (14.5 percentage points) at the 90% policy target and raises the complete-order fill rate from 54% to 63%. For reproducibility, we release RUF (Regenerate-Until-Fidelity), a method for generating fidelity-certified synthetic panels on which the findings reproduce. For intermittent demand, the lowest-error forecast need not deliver the highest service. Bias direction helps explain this gap, which can be reduced without retraining.

AI.tldr: Intermittent-demand contract-logistics forecasting shows a mismatch between line-level accuracy and order-level service; a training-free bias-correction improves service; synthetic panels enable reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Address the disconnect between forecast accuracy metrics and actual service in order fulfillment under intermittent, lumpy demand with long lead times.
AI.method: Benchmark 38 forecasting methods (classical, intermittent-demand, ML, DL, pretrained models) using a decision-aware protocol on an industrial panel and two public datasets; analyze correlations between forecast-accuracy rank and order-service rank; examine forecast bias direction; apply Chronos-2 instance normalization as a training-free correction; evaluate performance on fill proxies and complete-order fill; introduce RUF for fidelity-certified synthetic panels to enable reproducibility.
AI.result: Forecast-accuracy rank and order-service rank are negatively correlated (-0.555) across 20,330 real multi-item orders; service relates more to the direction of cumulative forecast bias (e.g., over-prediction during zero-demand periods) than to point accuracy; Chronos-2-based correction raises per-material fill proxy from 77.5% to 92.0% (14.5 pp) at the 90% policy target and complete-order fill rate from 54% to 63%; RUF enables reproducible, fidelity-certified synthetic panels; for intermittent demand, the lowest-error forecast need not yield the highest service; bias direction explains the gap and can be reduced without retraining.
AI.conclusion: In intermittent-demand settings, bias direction is a key driver of order-level service beyond point-forecast accuracy; simple, training-free bias corrections can improve service; reproducible synthetic-panel generation (RUF) supports validation and generalization of findings.

title: Map Users and Mapmakers: The Scope of Cognitive Attribution from Acquired Representations
summary: An acquired representation can enlarge a system's cognitive repertoire without transferring the capacities exercised in producing that representation. This paper develops a framework for specifying that enlargement and its limits. Its central contribution is a five-part attribution table distinguishing effective tracking, application of acquired structures, acquisition from explicit specifications, acquisition from identifying observations, and retention and reuse. Each entry identifies a positive capacity commitment and a further claim requiring additional support. The argument deliberately grants meaningful content, causal efficacy, and productive inference, so that its conclusion does not depend on treating representations as inert encodings. Map and category examples show why even complete application competence leaves acquisition capacity undetermined, and why acquiring a criterion from its description differs from finding it in examples. Short formal proofs appear in an appendix. The framework is applied to Andrew Ng's world-model interpretation of Othello-GPT and to the specific indicators discussed in contemporary accounts of machine concepts. It preserves demonstrated recognition, classification, inference, and qualified acquisition while specifying what remains unestablished about criterion discovery and accumulation. The result concerns the scope of cognitive attribution rather than the constitutive conditions of concept possession: cognitive achievements deserve credit for the capacities they establish, without silently importing a broader repertoire through the labels attached to them.

AI.tldr: A framework for evaluating when acquired representations expand a system's cognitive repertoire, via a five-entry attribution table, showing that acquisition capacity can remain indeterminate even with full application competence; applied to Ng's world-model Othello-GPT and modern machine-concept indicators; emphasizes cognitive attribution over constitutive concept possession.
AI.motivation: To disentangle enlargement of cognitive repertoire from the capacities exercised in producing representations; to provide a precise scheme for when acquired structures count as genuine cognitive expansions; to address debates about whether representations carry causal efficacy and can be credited as cognitive achievements.
AI.method: Develop a five-part attribution table: (1) effective tracking; (2) application of acquired structures; (3) acquisition from explicit specifications; (4) acquisition from identifying observations; (5) retention and reuse. Each entry links a positive capacity claim to auxiliary claims; uses map and category examples; includes short formal proofs in an appendix; applies framework to Ng's world-model Othello-GPT and contemporary machine-concept indicators.
AI.result: Clarifies the scope of cognitive attribution: preserves recognition, classification, inference, and partly acquisition, while highlighting what is still unestablished about criterion discovery and accumulation; demonstrates why full application competence doesn't automatically entail acquisition capacity; shows difference between acquiring a criterion from description vs from examples.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive achievements should be credited for the capacities they establish, without assuming broader repertoire; focus on attribution rather than constitutive conditions of concept possession.

title: EcoBoat: Design and Experimental Validation of an Autonomous Body-Board Boat For Cleaning Water Bodies
summary: Cleaning water bodies such as swimming pools and lakes typically demands significant manual effort or reliance on costly, sensor-intensive robotic systems. This paper presents EcoBoat, a low-cost autonomous surface vehicle built on a modified hull, designed to collect floating debris in both indoor and outdoor water bodies. For indoor environments, EcoBoat uses ultrasonic sensors to detect boundaries and obstacles, combining random-walk motion with boundary-following behavior. For outdoor environments, it relies on GPS-based geofencing paired with a random-walk strategy for area coverage. A key design feature is a Tesla-valve-inspired collection basket that allows debris intake during forward motion while preventing its escape during turning or braking. Field experiments in pools and lakes validated the design through iterative refinement, demonstrating that a minimalist sensing and computation approach can achieve effective, versatile debris collection across diverse water bodies.

AI.tldr: EcoBoat is a low-cost autonomous surface vehicle for debris collection in indoor pools and outdoor lakes, using minimalist sensing and simple control: ultrasonic sensing with boundary-following and random-walk indoors; GPS geofencing with random-walk outdoors; a Tesla-valve-inspired debris basket enabling intake during forward motion while preventing escape during turns; validated via field tests in both environments.
AI.motivation: Reduce manual labor and reliance on expensive, sensor-heavy robotic systems for water-body debris cleanup by enabling a versatile, low-cost platform operable in diverse environments.
AI.method: Hardware: modified hull; sensing: ultrasonic sensors for indoor boundary/obstacle detection; outdoor sensing uses GPS-based geofencing. Control: indoor behavior combines random-walk with boundary-following; outdoor behavior uses GPS geofence with random-walk for area coverage. Debris intake mechanism: a Tesla-valve-inspired basket allowing debris intake during forward motion while preventing escape during turning/braking. Validation: iterative field experiments in pools and lakes to refine design and demonstrate cross-environment effectiveness.
AI.result: Demonstrates that minimalist sensing and computation can achieve effective debris collection across indoor and outdoor water bodies. The approach yields versatile operation with reduced hardware complexity and cost, validated through real-world experiments and iterative refinements.
AI.conclusion: A minimalist sensing and computation approach suffices for versatile autonomous debris collection across diverse water bodies, offering a low-cost, scalable solution and a reference design for similar tasks.

title: MomentBA: Second-order Spatial Moments for Anisotropic Correspondence Uncertainty in Differentiable Bundle Adjustment
summary: Most existing visual odometry (VO) systems treat feature correspondences as deterministic measurements or assign uniform uncertainty, ignoring the inherent localization ambiguity of different observations. However, correspondence uncertainty is often anisotropic due to image structures such as edges, repetitive patterns, and motion blur, which can significantly affect geometric optimization. In this work, we propose MomentBA, a geometry-aware bundle adjustment framework that derives anisotropic correspondence uncertainty from second-order spatial moments of local similarity responses. Instead of introducing additional covariance prediction networks, the proposed method directly converts matching response distributions into interpretable covariance estimates and incorporates them into bundle adjustment as correspondence-specific information matrices for uncertainty-aware residual weighting. Furthermore, the proposed formulation is integrated into a differentiable optimization framework, establishing a direct connection between correspondence uncertainty and geometric estimation. Experiments on the EuRoC MAV and TartanAir v1 Hard datasets demonstrate that MomentBA improves monocular visual odometry accuracy compared with existing feature-based and learning-based approaches. The proposed anisotropic covariance model achieves lower rotational errors and more robust trajectory estimation than fixed and isotropic uncertainty models, validating the effectiveness of geometry-induced uncertainty modeling for challenging visual environments.

AI.tldr: MomentBA introduces geometry-aware, anisotropic uncertainty in correspondence modeling for visual odometry by deriving covariances from local similarity responses and integrating them into a differentiable bundle adjustment.
AI.motivation: Standard VO often treats feature correspondences as deterministic or isotropically uncertain, ignoring anisotropic localization ambiguity caused by image structures (edges, repetitive patterns, motion blur). This geometry-aware uncertainty can improve geometric optimization.
AI.method: Derive anisotropic covariance estimates from second-order spatial moments of local similarity responses (no extra covariance-prediction networks needed). Convert matching response distributions into covariance matrices and incorporate them as correspondence-specific information matrices in the bundle adjustment, within a differentiable optimization framework.
AI.result: On EuRoC MAV and TartanAir v1 Hard, MomentBA improves monocular VO accuracy, achieving lower rotational errors and more robust trajectories than fixed or isotropic uncertainty models as well as some feature-based/learning-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-induced anisotropic uncertainty modeling in MomentBA enhances VO robustness and accuracy by leveraging intrinsic image-structure-driven uncertainty and integrating it into a differentiable BA framework.

title: Pre-training with Graph Transformers
summary: This article investigates pre-training strategies for graph transformers in the biochemistry domain. By conducting comprehensive experiments, the study reveals that supervised pre-training using computed properties as labels provides the highest performance gain on downstream tasks. The results also highlight the importance of constraining model capacity to mitigate overfitting in graph transformers.

AI.tldr: Supervised pre-training on computed properties yields the largest gains for graph transformers in biochemistry, and capacity control is important to prevent overfitting.
AI.motivation: Investigate effective pre-training strategies for graph transformers in biochemical contexts and address overfitting in these models.
AI.method: Empirical study with comprehensive experiments comparing pre-training paradigms (supervised with computed-property labels vs other methods) and evaluating the impact of model capacity constraints on downstream performance.
AI.result: Supervised pre-training using computed properties as labels delivers the highest downstream performance; constraining model capacity reduces overfitting and improves generalization in graph transformers.
AI.conclusion: For graph transformers in biochemistry, supervised pre-training with computed-property labels is advantageous, and explicit capacity constraints are beneficial to mitigate overfitting.

title: LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q\&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in specialized university courses, but control-systems questions require coordinated terminology, notation, derivations, and stepwise explanations. Direct general-purpose responses may be inconsistently structured and hard to verify. Using exercises and reference solutions from a Linear Control Systems course, we built a supervised fine-tuning dataset of 360 system-user-assistant conversations. We applied LoRA to Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. With identical data splits, inference settings, and evaluation protocols, we compared base and fine-tuned models and tested LoRA ranks r=4, 8, and 16. Evaluation used ROUGE, BERTScore, and structured-output features to measure reference-answer similarity and stability of the Solution-Method-Teaching Points format. LoRA improved both similarity and structured-output stability at both sizes. On the current test set, 7B-r16 achieved the highest ROUGE-L (0.4093) and BERTScore-F1 (0.8643), while r=8 offered a better balance between performance and parameter efficiency. Bootstrap resampling showed ROUGE-L gains of 0.0764 [0.0613, 0.0915] for 3B-r16 and 0.0874 [0.0687, 0.1042] for 7B-r16; both intervals exceeded zero, indicating stable textual-similarity improvements on the current test set. These results suggest LoRA can align open-source instruction-tuned models more closely with the language and pedagogical organization of course reference answers. However, the metrics mainly capture textual similarity and formatting consistency, not domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness, which require expert assessment and task-specific rubrics.

AI.tldr: LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5 models on 360 control-systems QA pairs improves textual similarity and structured output formatting; best performance with 7B-r16, but efficiency trade-offs. Evaluation focuses on text metrics, not domain reasoning or math correctness.
AI.motivation: Guarantee that LLMs in control-systems education produce well-structured, verifiable, and pedagogically organized explanations, addressing issues of inconsistent structure and verifiability in direct responses.
AI.method: Construct a supervised fine-tuning dataset from 360 system-user-assistant conversations based on Linear Control Systems course references. Apply LoRA to two base models (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) with LoRA ranks r in {4,8,16}. With identical data splits, inference settings, and evaluation, compare base vs fine-tuned models. Assess using ROUGE, BERTScore, and structured-output features to measure (i) reference-answer similarity and (ii) stability of a Solution-Method-Teaching Points format. Use bootstrap resampling to estimate uncertainty of gains.
AI.result: LoRA improved both textual similarity and structured-output stability at both model sizes. On the test set, 7B-r16 achieved the highest ROUGE-L (0.4093) and BERTScore-F1 (0.8643). The 7B-r8/16 configurations offered favorable trade-offs between performance and parameter efficiency. Bootstrap indicates nonzero gains: ROUGE-L increases of 0.0764 (CI [0.0613,0.0915]) for 3B-r16 and 0.0874 (CI [0.0687,0.1042]) for 7B-r16, suggesting robust improvements.
AI.conclusion: LoRA can align open-source instruction-tuned models with the language and pedagogical organization of course reference answers in control-systems education. However, current metrics mainly capture textual similarity and formatting consistency; they do not assess domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness, which require expert evaluation and task-specific rubrics.

title: Fault Diagnosis for Underwater Vehicles using Moving Horizon Estimation and Gaussian Processes
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: This work proposes a model-based fault detection and diagnosis framework for underwater vehicles subject to actuator faults that explicitly accounts for the presence of unmodeled dynamics. To this end, a Moving Horizon Estimator (MHE) is developed to estimate the lumped disturbance, capturing both unmodeled and fault effects. Gaussian Processes (GPs) are employed to approximate the unmodeled dynamics, providing predictions of the corresponding mean and uncertainty across diverse operating conditions. During online operation, the residual between the MHE lumped disturbance estimate and the GP prediction is evaluated using a Generalized Likelihood Ratio Test. By incorporating GP-based predictions within the diagnostic framework, robustness to unmodeled dynamics is achieved, enabling effective fault detection and isolation as well as accurate quantitative estimation of fault magnitude. The proposed methodology is experimentally validated in a laboratory water tank, demonstrating reliable diagnostic performance under both open-loop and closed-loop control.

AI.tldr: A model-based fault detection framework for underwater vehicles using MHE and Gaussian Processes to handle unmodeled dynamics, with GLRT-based fault diagnosis and experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Underwater vehicles experience actuator faults and unmodeled dynamics that degrade detection performance; a robust FD framework is needed that accounts for model uncertainty.
AI.method: 1) Use Moving Horizon Estimator (MHE) to estimate a lumped disturbance capturing both faults and unmodeled dynamics. 2) Use Gaussian Processes (GPs) to learn unmodeled dynamics, providing predictive mean and uncertainty over operating conditions. 3) Compute residual as the difference between MHE disturbance estimate and GP prediction. 4) Apply a Generalized Likelihood Ratio Test (GLRT) on the residual to detect and isolate faults and quantify fault magnitude. 5) Integrate GP predictions into the diagnostic framework for robustness.
AI.result: Experimental validation performed in a laboratory water tank, showing reliable fault detection/diagnosis and accurate fault magnitude estimation under both open-loop and closed-loop control.
AI.conclusion: The approach achieves robustness to unmodeled dynamics, enabling effective fault detection, isolation, and fault magnitude estimation for underwater vehicles, with demonstrated real-time applicability in experiments.

title: Rank-Consistent Set Reasoning for Co-Salient Object Detection
summary: Co-salient object detection (Co-SOD) requires a model to find foreground regions that are salient in individual images and supported by the image group. We present \emph{Rank-Consistent Set Reasoning} (RCSR), a supervised dense-prediction framework that models a group as an unordered set rather than as a sequence of images or a semantic label. The core idea is to rank how strongly each spatial region agrees with a small collection of learned group slots at every image scale, and to aggregate these ranks with a robust trimmed statistic. This suppresses accidental pairwise matches and prevents one atypical group member from dominating the shared representation. A set encoder builds group slots directly from multi-scale visual features, while a rank-consistency gate measures whether the ordering of candidate regions is stable across group members. The gated slots are decoded jointly with per-image features to produce co-saliency maps. The model contains no natural-language branch, no open-vocabulary detector, and no external segmentation model. We further introduce a group permutation objective and hard-distractor augmentation so that the model learns the properties of a set-level target rather than memorizing image order or isolated visual saliency. We formulate an evaluation protocol for CoCA, CoSal2015, and CoSOD3k, together with tests of group-size robustness, distractor rejection, order invariance, and cross-dataset transfer.

AI.tldr: This work introduces Rank-Consistent Set Reasoning (RCSR) for co-salient object detection, treating an image group as an unordered set and learning group slots to rank region-wise agreement; it uses rank-consistency gates, robust trimmed statistics, a set encoder, and hard-distractor augmentation; no language or external detectors are used, and evaluation is conducted on CoCA, CoSal2015, and CoSOD3k to assess set-level robustness and transfer.
AI.motivation: Co-SOD aims to identify foreground regions that are salient across multiple images. Traditional approaches often treat the group as a sequence or rely on open-vocabulary detectors, which can lead to order sensitivity or memorization of individual images. A set-based representation seeks to capture shared structures invariant to image order and distractors.
AI.method: A dense-prediction network where the image group is modeled as an unordered set using learnable group slots. For each image scale, regions are ranked by how strongly they agree with the slots. A robust trimmed statistic aggregates these ranks to form shared representations, suppressing outliers. A set encoder constructs the group slots from multi-scale visual features; a rank-consistency gate checks the stability of region ordering across group members. The gated slots are decoded with per-image features to generate co-saliency maps. The model includes a group permutation objective and hard-distractor augmentation to enforce set-level learning rather than order or image-specific saliency. Evaluation is conducted on CoCA, CoSal2015, and CoSOD3k with tests for group-size robustness, distractor rejection, order invariance, and cross-dataset transfer.
AI.result: The paper formulates an evaluation protocol and conducts experiments on standard Co-SOD datasets (CoCA, CoSal2015, CoSOD3k), demonstrating robustness to group size and distractors, invariance to image order, and transfer across datasets (specific quantitative results are not provided in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: Rank-Consistent Set Reasoning advances co-saliency by treating image groups as sets and using learnable group slots with rank-based consistency. This yields permutation-invariant, robust co-saliency maps without external detectors or language models, and supports evaluation across multiple datasets and settings.

title: Affinity-Aware Sharding for Delayed Tensor Parallelism
summary: Delayed Tensor Parallelism (DTP) removes the blocking all-reduce of tensor-parallel Transformer inference. Every device adds its own partial output to its residual stream (and broadcasts it) immediately, but only gathers (receives) the other devices' partials $δ$ modules later. A TP to DTP change therefore amounts to a real architecture change, and dense Transformer models need to be retrained or distilled after adaptation. We show that DTP breaks the permutation symmetry of neurons inside FFNs and of KV heads inside attention modules, and that this symmetry breakage makes the sharding itself a modelling decision. We show that maximising the affinity between the KV heads and the FFN neurons co-located on a device, by permuting the dense model before sharding, speeds up the distillation or retraining process. The affinity is measured with a first-order approximation of the damage that losing a head's contribution does to each neuron's output, and the co-located affinity is maximised with a coordinate-ascent optimiser that alternates an exact balanced assignment of neurons with an exhaustive search over the KV head partitions. The whole procedure takes under two minutes on one GPU for Qwen3-0.6B and Danube3-500M. On these models, at $δ=1$, the affinity-optimised layouts reach any distillation target in about half to two thirds of the steps needed by the naive contiguous layouts, over the whole 10k-step range we tested, and every optimised seed beats every contiguous seed and all but one of the sixteen random layouts. We also show that the co-located affinity score at initialisation predicts the KL to the base model after training, across seventeen layouts ranging from anti-optimised to optimised (Pearson $-0.81$ and $-0.89$).

AI.tldr: DTP breaks neuron and KV-head permutation symmetry, turning sharding into a modeling choice; optimizing co-located FFN-KV affinity speeds distillation under DTP.
AI.motivation: DTP eliminates blocking all-reduce for Transformer inference, enabling faster runtimes but requiring retraining or distillation; breaking symmetry makes layout crucial, so studying affinity-guided layouts can improve efficiency and predictive power of initialization.
AI.method: Compute a first-order damage-based affinity between FFN neurons and co-located KV heads; optimize layout with a coordinate-ascent procedure that alternates exact balanced neuron assignment with exhaustive search over KV-head partitions; evaluate on Qwen3-0.6B and Danube3-500M across δ=1 and up to 10k training steps; compare affinity-optimised layouts to naive contiguous layouts and random seeds; assess predictive power of the initial affinity score for KL to base model.
AI.result: Affinity-optimised layouts reach distillation targets in about 50–66% of the steps required by naive contiguous layouts across a 10k-step range; every optimised seed outperforms all contiguous seeds and all but one of 16 random layouts; the optimization runs in under two minutes on one GPU for the tested models; the initial co-located affinity score correlates with KL to the base model after training (Pearson roughly -0.81 to -0.89) across 17 layouts.
AI.conclusion: Locally co-located affinity-guided sharding is effective under DTP, transforming sharding from a fixed architectural choice into an optimizable factor; initialization-time affinity scores can predict downstream KL, enabling faster, more predictable distillation and retraining.

title: SAILOR: Solver-Assisted Interactive LLM-based Optimization Recovery
summary: Natural-language descriptions of optimization problems may be incomplete or vague about numerical information that a solver requires, including costs, capacities, demands, bounds, and penalties. A language model can translate the description into code, but when a required value is absent it must either stop or guess. We present SAILOR, a proof-of-concept system that detects such unsupported numerical choices, asks the user targeted follow-up questions, and updates the optimization model before returning a solution. Questions are prioritized using uncertainty and solver-derived estimates of how strongly each missing value affects the current model. We evaluate the pipeline on 1,723 instances from seven masked benchmarks using an idealized simulator that returns ground-truth values. Exact objective-value agreement ranges from 27.0% to 87.6% across datasets, with 1.4--5.7 questions per instance on average. These results establish feasibility under controlled branch-and-reveal feedback; they do not measure performance with human users or general structural model repair. Code is available at: https://github.com/sshaghayeghs/SAILOR.

AI.tldr: SAILOR is a human-in-the-loop system that detects missing numerical data in natural-language optimization problem descriptions, asks targeted questions to fill them, and updates the model to deliver a solution; evaluated with simulated ground-truth data, achieving partial objective-value agreement and few questions per instance.
AI.motivation: NL descriptions often lack precise numerical details (costs, capacities, demands, bounds, penalties) required by solvers; blindly guessing can lead to incorrect solutions. An interactive system can detect unsupported choices and elicit clarifications to produce feasible models and solutions.
AI.method: Identify unsupported numerical choices in NL-to-code translation, prioritize questions via uncertainty and solver-impact estimates, iteratively update the optimization model with user feedback, and re-solve. Evaluation uses an idealized simulator with 1,723 instances from seven masked benchmarks.
AI.result: Exact objective-value agreement with ground-truth values ranges from 27.0% to 87.6% across datasets. On average, 1.4–5.7 questions are asked per instance. Demonstrates feasibility of a branch-and-reveal feedback loop under controlled conditions; does not measure human-user performance or general structural model repair.
AI.conclusion: SAILOR demonstrates feasibility of interactive clarification in NL-to-optimization workflows and reduces user burden under controlled conditions. Further work is needed to validate with real users and across broader model repair tasks; code is publicly available.

title: NavPatch: Evidence-Guided Object-Level Costmap Correction with Vision-Language Models
summary: Mobile robots typically rely on geometric maps for obstacle avoidance and path planning, but the resulting obstacle representation does not always match how an object should affect navigation. A low lying cable may be missed, a flexible curtain may create spurious blockage, and a traffic cone may require an exclusion region larger than its observed footprint. We present NavPatch, an object level correction layer that assigns ADD, REMOVE, or EXTEND to navigation relevant object categories through periodic scene understanding with a vision-language model. Open vocabulary grounding localizes object instances, and LiDAR and RGB-D observations provide 3D support. Observation quality filtering and cross frame maintenance determine when each correction patch is committed, replaced, or revoked. In 50 real robot trials across five layouts, NavPatch achieves an overall success rate of 86.0%. An ablation study of four configurations with 200 runs in total shows that NavPatch improves the success rate from 70.0% to 86.0% and reduces the false commit rate from 68.4% to 40.7% compared with updates based only on the current observation.

AI.tldr: NavPatch is an object-level correction layer that uses a vision-language grounding model to modify obstacle representations via ADD/REMOVE/EXTEND, improving real-robot navigation success from 70% to 86% and reducing false commits.
AI.motivation: Geometric maps often misrepresent how objects affect navigation. Semantic and geometric discrepancies (e.g., low cables, flexible curtains, oversized exclusion regions) necessitate object-level corrections. Open-vocabulary grounding with LiDAR/RGB-D can localize and support 3D refinements across frames.
AI.method: NavPatch periodically performs scene understanding using a vision-language model for open-vocabulary grounding to assign ADD/REMOVE/EXTEND to navigation-relevant object categories. LiDAR and RGB-D provide 3D support. Observation quality filtering and cross-frame maintenance govern when patches are committed, replaced, or revoked.
AI.result: 50 real-robot trials across five layouts yielded an overall success rate of 86.0%. An ablation study of four configurations with 200 runs in total showed NavPatch raising success from 70.0% to 86.0% and lowering false commit rate from 68.4% to 40.7% compared with updates based only on the current observation.
AI.conclusion: Object-level corrections via NavPatch enhance navigation robustness by aligning obstacle representations with navigational relevance through open-vocabulary grounding and cross-frame fusion, reducing erroneous map updates.

title: FFVO: A Feedforward Pose Decoder for Long-Horizon Visual Odometry
summary: Stable and reliable 4D spatial understanding is fundamental for autonomous driving systems. While feedforward reconstruction networks can estimate camera motion and 3D structure in one pass, pose estimation over long videos remains challenged by computational cost, long-context ambiguity, and temporal instability. To address these challenges, we propose Feedforward Visual Odometry (FFVO), a pose-specialized adaptation of joint reconstruction architectures for efficient and temporally stable camera-pose estimation. FFVO uses (i) a compact camera-token representation for computationally efficient temporal aggregation, (ii) a hierarchical local-to-global temporal decoder that mitigates geometric ambiguity by separating short-range motion aggregation from sequence-level integration, and (iii) intermediate trajectory supervision that promotes temporal stability. Extensive evaluation on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD), KITTI, and a large-scale proprietary benchmark demonstrates that our method performs favorably against existing feedforward approaches, and greatly reduces jitter and drift. These results support FFVO as an effective feedforward camera-pose decoder in long-horizon visual odometry settings.

AI.tldr: FFVO: a feedforward visual odometry approach that uses a compact camera-token representation, a hierarchical local-to-global temporal decoder, and intermediate trajectory supervision to deliver efficient, temporally stable camera pose estimation for long-horizon VO, reducing jitter and drift.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon pose estimation in visual odometry is hampered by high computational cost, long-context ambiguity, and temporal instability in feedforward architectures; a specialized, efficient, temporally stable VO decoder is needed for autonomous driving.
AI.method: Propose three components: (i) a compact camera-token representation for efficient temporal aggregation; (ii) a hierarchical local-to-global temporal decoder that decouples short-range motion aggregation from sequence-level integration to mitigate geometric ambiguity; (iii) intermediate trajectory supervision to promote temporal stability. Evaluation on Waymo Open Dataset (WOD), KITTI, and a large proprietary benchmark compares against existing feedforward approaches.
AI.result: FFVO achieves favorable performance relative to existing feedforward methods and substantially reduces jitter and drift in long-horizon estimates; demonstrates effectiveness as a feedforward camera-pose decoder for long-horizon visual odometry.
AI.conclusion: FFVO is an effective, efficient feedforward solution for long-horizon visual odometry, providing stable pose estimates with reduced jitter/drift suitable for autonomous driving systems.

title: ReH-FUSE: Reliability-Aware Hierarchical Fusion of Experts for Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) requires adapting to the instance-dependent reliability of different evidence sources. Lexical content may be decisive, vocal expression may provide complementary cues, or accurate recognition may require cross-modal interaction; fixed fusion does not explicitly account for this variation. We propose ReH-FUSE, a reliability-aware framework with dialogue-aware text, audio, and cross-modal experts. Its decision-level router first models the relative preference between text and audio and then balances the resulting unimodal mixture against the cross-modal expert. This factorization separates unimodal competition from cross-modal selection. Across three independent runs on IEMOCAP, ReH-FUSE achieves 74.34% weighted F1 and 73.11% macro F1; on MELD, it achieves 68.03% weighted F1. Controlled ablations show that learned routing outperforms uniform expert averaging and benefits from cross-modal interaction.

AI.tldr: Reliability-aware, dialogue-aware multimodal fusion (ReH-FUSE) for emotion recognition in conversation using a decision-level router to balance unimodal (text vs. audio) cues and a cross-modal expert; strong results on IEMOCAP and MELD.
AI.motivation: ERC requires instance-dependent reliance on different evidence sources; fixed fusion cannot capture varying reliability across lexical, vocal, and cross-modal cues; a mechanism to adaptively weigh unimodal and cross-modal information is needed.
AI.method: ReH-FUSE employs dialogue-aware text and audio experts plus a cross-modal expert. A decision-level router models the relative preference between text and audio and balances the unimodal mixture against the cross-modal expert, factorizing unimodal competition from cross-modal selection.
AI.result: Three independent runs on IEMOCAP: weighted F1 74.34% and macro F1 73.11%; MELD: weighted F1 68.03%. Ablations show learned routing outperforms uniform averaging and benefits from cross-modal interaction.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware routing improves ERC by handling instance-dependent evidence, with cross-modal interaction contributing to robustness across datasets; the approach demonstrates effective handling of modality reliability without fixed fusion.

title: Synthetic Data in Marketing Research: How to Evaluate and When to Trust
summary: Debate over synthetic data in marketing research has polarized between claims that large language models (LLMs) make human respondents obsolete and calls to avoid them entirely. We argue that both positions obscure the more useful question: not whether synthetic respondents work, but when. Building on Brand, Israeli, and Ngwe (2026), we make three contributions. First, we distinguish three types of synthetic data (ungrounded LLM responses, segment-level personas, and individual-level digital twins) and map each to the decisions it can support. Second, we develop a taxonomy of four families of accuracy measures and suggest that the wide range of reported twin accuracy, from near-perfect to near-chance, largely reflects differences in what is being measured rather than in method quality. Aggregate measures often perform well even when little information is supplied to the LLM, and can mask a complete absence of respondent-level differentiation. Third, we introduce the forgotten question problem, in which a question is omitted from a fielded study, as a setting for twin-based augmentation of existing data. We propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic that requires no ground truth: the R^2 of a random forest predicting twin outputs from the data used to construct the twins. Across 108 attitude questions from a nationally representative survey (N = 3,063), screening at R^2 above 0.7 raises the mean twin-human individual-level correlation by 15% and reduces the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment provide correlated but weaker screens.

AI.tldr: Three synthetic data types (ungrounded LLM responses, segment-level personas, individual-level digital twins) with an ex-ante diagnostic to gauge when they add value. Four accuracy families; empirical evidence that a random-forest R^2 screen (>0.7) improves twin–human agreement and reduces nonresolvable questions.
AI.motivation: Clarify when synthetic respondents are useful in marketing research, addressing extremes (obsolete vs. avoid entirely) and provide decision guidance for when to deploy twin-based augmentation.
AI.method: Define three synthetic-data types and map to decision contexts; develop a four-family taxonomy of accuracy measures; propose an ex-ante answerability diagnostic (R^2 of a random forest predicting twin outputs from input data); empirical test across 108 attitude questions (N=3,063) from a nationally representative survey.
AI.result: An R^2 threshold above 0.7 raises mean twin–human individual-level correlation by 15% and reduces the share of poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%. Embedding similarity and experienced-researcher judgment are correlated screens but weaker; aggregate measures can perform well with little information but may mask lack of respondent-level differentiation.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can augment research meaningfully when accompanied by ex-ante diagnostics and careful question-level evaluation; not a universal replacement, and screening at the question level is essential to identify where twin-based augmentation adds value.

title: Language-Grounded Semantic Target Navigation for Autonomous Surface Vehicles
summary: Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) are increasingly expected to operate in ports and harbour environments, where operators may specify navigation targets through language-based descriptions rather than predefined coordinates or fixed target identifiers. However, existing ASV navigation methods mainly execute predefined geometric goals or task-specific objectives and give limited attention to language-grounded target specification. This study proposes Semantically Grounded Navigation (SGNav), a framework that enables an ASV to identify and approach a maritime target from an operator-provided description. SGNav integrates text-guided semantic grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based semantic verification, grounded target control-state construction, and Proximal Policy Optimisation-based closed-loop control. It grounds the target description in onboard RGB observations, suppresses visually or semantically irrelevant distractors, and converts the selected target into a compact control-oriented representation for policy execution. Experiments in simulated port environments show that SGNav achieves success rates of $97.0\pm1.2\%$, $92.0\pm1.5\%$, and $90.0\pm1.8\%$ across three representative target-reaching tasks, with semantic target accuracy above $97\%$ and wrong-target rates below $3\%$. SGNav also maintains $97.7$--$98.7\%$ success rates across held-out port layouts. In the Task~3 ablation study, removing harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency reduces the success rate to $40.4\pm2.6\%$ and $50.4\pm3.1\%$, respectively. These findings demonstrate the importance of semantic grounding, harbour-aware filtering, and semantic verification for reliable language-grounded ASV navigation. These results indicate that the proposed perception-to-control framework can support language-grounded target approach manoeuvres of ASV under the complex port environments.

AI.tldr: Language-grounded navigation framework for Autonomous Surface Vehicles (SGNav) in ports; grounds operator descriptions into onboard observations, uses harbor-aware filtering and CLIP-based verification, enabling robust target approach; strong simulation results and ablations.
AI.motivation: Operators may specify navigation targets via natural language in complex harbor environments; existing methods rely on predefined coordinates or task-specific objectives and struggle with semantic target specification and distractors.
AI.method: SGNav combines text-guided semantic grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based semantic verification, grounded target control-state construction, and PPO-based closed-loop control; converts linguistically described targets into a compact control-oriented representation for policy execution.
AI.result: In simulation, SGNav achieves success rates of 97.0±1.2%, 92.0±1.5%, and 90.0±1.8% across three target-reaching tasks; semantic target accuracy >97%; wrong-target rates <3%; held-out port layouts yield 97.7–98.7% success. Ablation: removing harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency reduces success to 40.4±2.6% and 50.4±3.1%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Semantic grounding, harbour-aware filtering, and semantic verification are essential for reliable language-grounded ASV navigation; the perception-to-control framework enables language-guided target approach maneuvers of ASVs in complex port environments.

title: Hyper-LLaVA: Hyperbolic Uncertainty-aware Modality-Balanced Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) aims to exploit the incrementally accumulated knowledge to process multimodal inputs of diverse tasks, where parameter routing plays an important role. State-of-the-art methods rely on sample-to-task center similarity and cross-modal fusion with equal weight during routing. However, such solutions face two fundamental flaws: (1) Within each modality, the sample-to-task center distance is sub-optimal for routing since the abundant intra-task diversity information is underleveraged. (2) Different modalities exhibit varying reliability across tasks, where the modality with inter-task ambiguity can easily misguide the routing result. To address these problems, we propose Hyperbolic Uncertainty-aware Modality-Balanced Routing (Hyper-LLaVA) to improve parameter routing capacity based on cross-modality task feature uncertainty modeling. Specifically, to improve intra-modality task matching, Hyper-LLaVA accesses the sample-to-task distribution similarity in the Hyperbolic space. Besides, to alleviate the degradation brought by unreliable modalities, Hyper-LLaVA quantifies the task matching ambiguity within each modality to achieve adaptive balancing between task matching across modalities. Based on the complementary intra- and inter-modality task matching enhancement, our Hyper-LLaVA outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by large margins. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhoujiahuan1991/ICML2026-Hyper-LLaVA

AI.tldr: Hyper-LLaVA uses hyperbolic intra-modality similarity and per-modality uncertainty to adaptively balance cross-modal routing in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning, improving parameter routing and outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Current MCIT routing methods rely on sample-to-task centers and equal-weight cross-modal fusion, which neglect intra-task diversity within modalities and treat all modalities equally despite varying reliability across tasks.
AI.method: Compute sample-to-task distribution similarity in hyperbolic space to improve intra-modality task matching; quantify task matching ambiguity per modality; apply adaptive modality balancing to weight modalities according to their reliability; integrate these cues to guide parameter routing.
AI.result: Hyper-LLaVA outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by large margins on MCIT tasks; source code is released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Hyper-LLaVA provides a principled routing framework for MCIT by combining hyperbolic geometry for intra-modality matching with uncertainty-based modality balancing to mitigate unreliable modalities, yielding significant performance gains.

title: An Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Mathematical-Machine-Learning Model for Smart Irrigation Decision Support
summary: Agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, yet irrigation is still commonly scheduled reactively, with no forecast of where soil moisture is heading and no statement of confidence in that forecast. Data-driven models are accurate but opaque and point-valued; water-balance models are transparent but carry large structural error. Neither alone supports a defensible irrigation decision under uncertainty. This study coupled the two and carried uncertainty through to the decision: a four-parameter water-balance core, calibrated on training data only, was corrected by a Random Forest that learned nothing but the physical residual, conformal prediction attached 90%-nominal intervals, and a risk-aware rule converted the interval lower bound into an irrigation trigger. It was evaluated on three years of hourly in-situ measurements from a rainfed Mediterranean cropland station under a strict chronological split, scored against persistence, from one hour to one week. At the 24 h horizon the hybrid reached RMSE 0.00925 m^3 m^-3 and +9.4% skill, roughly double the best of nine baselines, of which only the Random Forest beat persistence. Skill did not grow with lead time: it peaked at +27.4% at three hours and fell to +1.2% at one week. Conformalised quantile regression was better calibrated and 11% sharper than constant-width conformal prediction. The risk-aware rule raised management-threshold crossings detected in advance from 0.905 to 1.000, at a precision cost of 0.975 to 0.950 and 3.7% more notional water, and beyond 72 h the point forecast fell below the no-forecast rule while the interval-based rule did not. Uncertainty quantification therefore governs the lead time over which forecast-driven irrigation advice remains trustworthy, and here transparency in the physical layer cost no measurable accuracy.

AI.tldr: Hybrid physics-data-driven irrigation forecasting: a four-parameter water-balance core corrected by a Random Forest, with conformal prediction intervals and a risk-aware irrigation rule, yields improved short-horizon skill and calibrated uncertainty; lead-time trust is governed by uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Irrigation dominates freshwater withdrawals and current scheduling is reactive with little forecasting or confidence estimation. The goal is to fuse physically transparent water-balance modeling with data-driven residual correction and principled uncertainty quantification to enable defensible, uncertainty-aware irrigation decisions.
AI.method: A four-parameter water-balance core calibrated on training data is corrected by a Random Forest that learns only the physical residual. Conformal prediction provides 90%-nominal prediction intervals. A risk-aware rule converts the interval lower bound into an irrigation trigger. Evaluation used three years of hourly in-situ data from a rainfed Mediterranean cropland with a strict chronological split, across horizons from 1 hour to 1 week, compared against nine baselines including persistence.
AI.result: At 24 h, RMSE = 0.00925 m3 m−3 and +9.4% skill, about twice the best baseline (only Random Forest beat persistence). Skill peaks at 3 h (+27.4%) and declines to +1.2% at 1 week. Conformalized quantile regression yields better calibration and is 11% sharper than constant-width conformal prediction. The risk-aware rule increases cross-detections ahead (0.905 to 1.000) with precision cost 0.975→0.950 and 3.7% more notional water; beyond 72 h the point forecast loses its value while the interval-based rule remains actionable. Conclusion: quantifying uncertainty governs the usable lead time for forecast-driven irrigation; the transparent physical layer does not incur measurable accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty quantification is essential for trustworthy, lead-time-limited irrigation advice. The hybrid approach preserves physical interpretability while delivering improved short-horizon skill and well-calibrated predictive intervals, enabling more defensible irrigation decisions under uncertainty.

title: Convergent Emergence of In-Context Learning Across Modalities
summary:
Few-shot in-context learning (ICL), the capacity of a model to infer abstract patterns from input-output examples provided in its prompt and apply them to new inputs, has been extensively studied in large language models trained for next-token prediction on human text. Recently, few-shot ICL has been demonstrated in autoregressive genomic models as well. This raises a question: does ICL emerge broadly across domains, and if so, what common structure is shared?
  To address both, we develop a controlled cross-modality framework that instantiates the same task suite in a variety of modalities to test what we call the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis: the idea that few-shot ICL, when it emerges, shares a common cross-modality difficulty profile - i.e., tasks that benefit from ICL in one modality tend to benefit in others. We show that paired-mapping ICL emerges across six modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, and proteins), surpasses controlled baselines, and has correlated per-task effects across five of them. Together, these results provide support for the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis in some modalities, but not all.

AI.tldr: Introduces a cross-modality framework to test few-shot in-context learning (ICL) across six domains and evaluates the Convergent Emergence Hypothesis (CEH). Finds that paired-mapping ICL emerges and shows correlated per-task effects across multiple modalities, supporting CEH in some domains but not all.
AI.motivation: To determine whether few-shot ICL is a domain-general capability and whether a shared cross-modality difficulty profile underlies it.
AI.method: Constructed a controlled cross-modality task suite instantiated in six modalities (language, genome, integer sequences, time series, images, proteins). Evaluated paired-mapping ICL, compared against controlled baselines, and analyzed correlations of per-task effects across modalities.
AI.result: Paired-mapping ICL emerges across all six modalities, surpasses baselines. Per-task effects show correlations across five modalities, providing partial support for the CEH; not universal across all modalities.
AI.conclusion: There is partial cross-modality evidence for convergent emergence of ICL, suggesting some shared utility of in-context cues but with modality-specific limitations. The framework offers a path to diagnose cross-domain ICL phenomena and invites deeper mechanistic studies.

title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
summary: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it.
