Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.

AI.tldr: GLAM is a goal-conditioned latent world model for navigation using a global spatiotemporal memory; GLAM NAV is a complete navigation system built around it that jointly predicts future map representations and waypoint latents to plan navigation. Trained on Habitat HM3D v0.2 ObjectNav data, it shows improved performance over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset.
AI.motivation: Agents need to build memory from partial observations, predict how that memory evolves to support future motion, and convert predictions into actionable plans. This work couples a global map-level latent memory with goal-conditioned planning to enable robust navigation.
AI.method: JEPA-like latent prediction operating on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstructions. GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and current pose. It uses a pretrained waypoint encoder–decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are generated by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scenes and sliced into multi-timescale prediction samples.
AI.result: On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV outperforms a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates the effectiveness of a latent-world-model framework with global spatiotemporal memory for goal-conditioned navigation, enabling joint latent prediction and plan decoding, and yielding improved navigation performance over a baseline in controlled experiments.

title: Development of Low-Cost Real-Time Driver Drowsiness Detection System using Eye Centre Tracking and Dynamic Thresholding
summary: One in every five vehicle accidents on the road today is caused simply due to driver fatigue. Fatigue or otherwise drowsiness, significantly reduces the concentration and vigilance of the driver thereby increasing the risk of inherent human error leading to injuries and fatalities. Hence, our primary motive being - to reduce road accidents using a non-intrusive image processing based alert system. In this regard, we have built a system that detects driver drowsiness by real time tracking and monitoring the pattern of the driver's eyes. The stand alone system consists of 3 interconnected components - a processor, a camera and an alarm. After initial facial detection, the eyes are located, extracted and continuously monitored to check whether they are open or closed on the basis of a pixel-by-pixel method. When the eyes are seen to be closed for a certain amount of time, drowsiness is said to be detected and an alarm is issued accordingly to alert the driver and hence, prevent a casualty.

AI.tldr: Non-intrusive, real-time drowsiness detection via eye-state monitoring using a 3-component standalone system.
AI.motivation: Reduce road accidents due to driver fatigue by providing a non-intrusive alert mechanism.
AI.method: Face detection followed by eye localization and continuous pixel-level eye-open/closed monitoring. If eyes stay closed for a threshold duration, an alarm is triggered. System comprises a processor, camera, and alarm.
AI.result: No quantitative results are reported; the abstract describes system design and prototype without evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The approach is feasible for alerting drowsy drivers but hinges on robust eye-detection under varied conditions; effectiveness requires empirical validation and tuning of thresholds.

title: The Filter Metric is Safety-Critical: Phantom Advantages in Group-Relative RL under Shaped Rewards
summary: Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO and descendants) can discard no-contrast rollout groups through dynamic sampling, while practical implementations expose a configurable filter metric. We identify and quantify a metric-predicate mismatch under composite shaped rewards. When filtering follows the shaped training score rather than the task outcome, all-fail groups retain nonzero within-group spread and pass the predicate; standard-deviation normalization then promotes shaping differences among failures to full-size phantom advantages. In a controlled GSM8K comparison (Qwen2.5-1.5B, LoRA), no filtering and shaped-score filtering end at EM 0.080 +/- 0.112 and 0.040 +/- 0.008, whereas binary-outcome filtering holds 0.754 +/- 0.005 across four runs per arm (three default-seed reruns and one seed-123 run; mean +/- sample SD). On verl's native recipe/dapo trainer, holding model, data, reward and trainer fixed and changing only the metric, the score arm requires no batch refill in any of 40 observed steps and ends at EM 0.160; the accuracy arm refills in 29/40 steps and ends at 0.763. Both use the same custom shaped-reward hook and unmodified trainer/filter code. Prior work established shaping-induced amplification and all-fail filtering; our contribution isolates the metric-predicate semantic mismatch and directly instruments native deletion/refill telemetry. Across tested positive coefficients lambda in {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, unsafe arms collapse; exploratory one-run cells reproduce the failure at 1.5B/7B on MATH and under GSPO, while disabling standard-deviation normalization avoids the observed collapse. Filtering under a composite reward should use a task-outcome signal whose semantics are independent of shaping.

AI.tldr: Filtering GRPO with composite-shaped rewards is misaligned with task outcomes, causing shaping-induced amplification and unsafe all-fail groups when using shaped-score normalization. Binary-outcome/task-outcome filtering avoids this mismatch and yields substantially higher EM on GSM8K; metric choice critically affects performance even with fixed model/training setup.
AI.motivation: To diagnose why filtering metrics in group-relative policy optimization degrade or amplify performance under composite shaped rewards, and to determine whether the predicate semantics should be independent of reward shaping.
AI.method: Empirical study across GRPO-like setups: (1) GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B LoRA; compare no-filter, shaped-score filter, and binary-outcome filter; four runs per arm. (2) verl's native recipe/dapo trainer with fixed model/data/reward/trainer; vary only the metric to switch between score-based vs accuracy-based filtering; measure EM and refill behavior. Explore lambda in {0.1,0.3,0.5}, test SD normalization, and reproduce failures on MATH/GSPO.
AI.result: No-filter EM 0.080±0.112; shaped-score filter EM 0.040±0.008. Binary-outcome filter EM 0.754±0.005 across four runs. On verl trainer, score-arm EM 0.160 with no batch refill in 40 steps; accuracy-arm refills in 29/40 steps ending at 0.763. Positive coefficients (lambda) cause unsafe collapse; disabling SD normalization prevents collapse. Across tests, filtering should rely on a task-outcome signal independent of shaping to avoid metric-predicate mismatch and shaping-induced amplification.
AI.conclusion: Metric-predicate semantics in GRPO under composite rewards must be decoupled from shaping to avoid amplification of shape-induced differences. Task-outcome (binary) filtering provides robust performance, while shaping-dependent filters distort evaluation and can trigger unsafe collapses, especially with SD normalization and positive lambda. Future work should formalize the mismatch and evaluate broader tasks to generalize the recommendation to use shaping-independent task outcomes for filtering.

title: Schizophrenia Detection from EEG Signals: A Transformer Framework with Spectrogram Representation
summary: Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric disorder that affects millions of people worldwide, and its diagnosis remains primarily dependent on clinical assessment. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive approach to investigate brain activity and has shown potential to support automated Schizophrenia detection. However, existing EEG-based classification studies often suffer from limitations including small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing strategies, and evaluation protocols that may not adequately prevent subject-related data leakage. In this study, we propose an EEG-based Schizophrenia classification framework that transforms preprocessed EEG recordings into time-frequency representations using the Short-Time Fourier Transform. The generated spectrogram images are classified using both conventional Machine Learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and XGBoost, and Deep Learning models, including convolutional architectures and CNN-Transformer hybrids. To ensure reliable evaluation, all data partitions are performed at the subject level. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive classification performance, with the CNN-Transformer (CT-SZ) model achieving an AUC-ROC of 88.41% and the CNN + Squeeze and Excitation + Transformer (CST-SZ) achieving an AUC-ROC of 92.88% on the independent test set.

AI.tldr: An EEG-based schizophrenia classification framework using STFT spectrograms, evaluated with subject-level partitions, achieving strong AUC-ROC—up to 92.88% with a CNN-Transformer hybrid.
AI.motivation: Address limitations in EEG schizophrenia studies (small datasets, inconsistent preprocessing, and subject leakage) and establish a robust, reproducible evaluation framework for automated diagnosis.
AI.method: Preprocess EEG data, convert to time-frequency spectrograms via Short-Time Fourier Transform, then classify using conventional ML (SVM, RF, XGBoost) and DL models (CNNs, CNN-Transformer hybrids). Ensure subject-level data partition to prevent leakage; evaluate on an independent test set.
AI.result: CNN-Transformer model (CT-SZ) achieves AUC-ROC of 88.41%; CNN + Squeeze and Excitation + Transformer (CST-SZ) achieves 92.88% AUC-ROC on independent test set; results indicate competitive performance and benefit from time-frequency representations and hybrid architectures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework yields strong, robust performance for EEG-based schizophrenia detection, with the CST-SZ model providing the best results; subject-level partitioning mitigates data leakage, supporting reliable evaluation and potential clinical decision support.

title: Learning Multi-Agent Task Assignment and Navigation in the Factory: from Simulation to Real Robots
comment: This work has been submitted for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown considerable promise for robotic decision-making, yet deploying multi-agent RL (MARL) on physical multi-robot systems in industrial environments remains challenging. This paper investigates the real-world applicability of decentralized MARL for multi-robot multi-machine tending. We propose Feature-fusion Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (FMAPPO), which fuses 2D LiDAR measurements with task-specific state information to enable safe decentralized multi-robot task assignment and navigation. A complete simulation-to-reality pipeline was developed using high-fidelity robotic simulation and ROS2 and deployed on physical mobile-manipulator platforms operating under realistic real-world conditions, with the robotic arms disabled during the experiments. We further investigate the sensitivity of the learned policy to command update frequency, an important consideration for real-world deployment. Comparative evaluation in simulation demonstrated that FMAPPO significantly outperformed state-of-the-art baselines with a large effect size, achieving improvements of 106\% and 21\% in parts delivery and 48\% and 11\% in parts collection over MAPPO and SMAPPO, respectively. FMAPPO also increased machine utilization by 31 and 10 percentage points, respectively, while reducing collisions by 18\% and 15\% and increasing the safety score by 14 and 6 percentage points compared with MAPPO and SMAPPO, respectively. Furthermore, real-world experiments demonstrated that the learned decentralized policies can coordinate multiple robots to service multiple machines while maintaining safe operation under real-world sensing and control constraints. Videos of the real-world experiment are available online https://anonymouspapers123.github.io/FMAPPO/.

AI.tldr: FMAPPO is a decentralized MARL approach that fuses LiDAR and task-state features for multi-robot tending, achieving large simulation gains and validating a real-world ROS2 pipeline; demonstrates safety and coordination under real sensing/control constraints.
AI.motivation: Deploying decentralized MARL in real-world industrial robotics is challenging due to perception fusion, safety, and sim-to-real transfer; the goal is robust, decentralized coordination for multi-robot multi-machine tending.
AI.method: FMAPPO fuses 2D LiDAR measurements with task-specific state features to form augmented observations. It uses a PPO-based MARL framework in a decentralized setting (FMAPPO) and a complete sim-to-real pipeline with high-fidelity simulation and ROS2, with experiments where robot arms are disabled. The study also analyzes policy sensitivity to command update frequency.
AI.result: In simulation, FMAPPO outperforms MAPPO and SMAPPO: parts delivery improved by 106% (MAPPO) and 21% (SMAPPO); parts collection improved by 48% (MAPPO) and 11% (SMAPPO). Machine utilization increased by 31 and 10 percentage points, collisions reduced by 18% and 15%, safety score increased by 14 and 6 percentage points, respectively. Real-world experiments show coordinated decentralized policies enabling safe operation under real sensing and control constraints; videos are available online.
AI.conclusion: FMAPPO demonstrates practical decentralized MARL for real-world multi-robot machine tending, with a robust sim-to-real pipeline and validated safety and coordination improvements; the approach is sensitive to command update frequency, indicating a consideration for real-time control in deployment.

title: GEAR: From Dynamic Encoding to Dynamic Activation in Social Trajectory Prediction
summary: Human trajectory prediction requires modeling both individual motion patterns and social interactions among agents. Existing methods have made substantial progress by using attention mechanisms, graph structures, and temporal encoders to capture dynamic social context. However, most of them primarily focus on how social information is encoded, while paying less explicit attention to how the encoded social context should take effect during future trajectory generation. In this paper, we argue that dynamic social encoding does not necessarily imply dynamic social activation. The same interaction context may require different activation strengths across future horizons and scene densities: social cues should be strengthened when interaction evidence is strong, but suppressed when they are weak or noisy. To address this issue, we propose GEAR, a generation-aware bias activation model for human trajectory prediction. Built upon a bias-decomposed trajectory generation formulation, GEAR dynamically activates the individual-motion and social-resonance bias terms at each future step before final trajectory composition. This allows the model to explicitly control when and how strongly individual and social bias components participate in generation. Experiments on ETH-UCY, SDD, and NBA show that GEAR consistently improves the resonance-based baseline and achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance. Further analyses of activation patterns and density-grouped errors validate the importance of calibrating encoded social context during trajectory generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/GEAR.git.

AI.tldr: GEAR introduces a generation-aware bias activation mechanism that gates individual-motion and social-resonance bias terms at each future step, conditioned on horizon and scene density, to better leverage encoded social context during trajectory generation.
AI.motivation: Many prior works focus on encoding social context but overlook when and how much that context should influence future trajectory generation. Dynamic activation is proposed to adaptively weigh social cues according to horizon, density, and evidence strength.
AI.method: Bias-decomposed trajectory generation with per-step activation gates for two bias components: individual motion bias and social resonance bias. These gates modulate contributions before assembling the final predicted trajectory. The approach is evaluated on ETH-UCY, SDD, and NBA with analyses of activation patterns and density-grouped errors. Code is released.
AI.result: GEAR consistently improves a resonance-based baseline and achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance across the three benchmarks. Activation pattern analyses validate the importance of calibrating encoded social context during generation.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, generation-aware bias activation improves trajectory prediction by explicitly controlling when social context participates in generation, adapting to horizon and scene density.

title: A Multi-Resolution Multi-Domain Pre-Training Framework for Universal Traffic Forecasting
summary: Spatio-temporal traffic data are central to intelligent transportation systems, yet their heterogeneity poses significant challenges for large-scale modeling. Existing pre-trained models often rely on a homogeneous modeling paradigm to handle highly heterogeneous traffic data. This fundamental mismatch not only limits model generalization but also leads to computationally expensive and parameter-inefficient designs. To this end, we propose FlexST, a novel pre-training framework that introduces modularity and adaptivity for traffic modeling. Specifically, we first propose a multi-resolution spatio-temporal diffusion module that captures both short-term fluctuations and long-range trends, effectively reconciling inputs with divergent temporal and spatial resolutions. After that, we construct a domain-adaptive mixture-of-experts that dynamically routes data to specialized sub-networks, enabling selective knowledge transfer while preventing negative interference across diverse domains. Moreover, we devise a unified periodic encoding strategy that injects resolution- and domain-aware inductive biases to harmonize periodic inconsistencies across datasets. Extensive experiments on 23 real-world traffic datasets demonstrate that FlexST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in zero- and few-shot settings, showcasing superior generalization, adaptability and efficiency. This work offers a new direction for building general-purpose pre-trained models capable of handling the complexity and variability of urban traffic systems.

AI.tldr: FlexST enables modular, adaptive pre-training for heterogeneous spatio-temporal traffic data by combining a multi-resolution diffusion module, a domain-adaptive mixture of experts, and a unified periodic encoding, achieving strong zero- and few-shot generalization across 23 real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Traffic data from diverse sensors and regions are highly heterogeneous in spatial and temporal resolutions. Homogeneous pre-training struggles to generalize and is computationally inefficient. There is a need for modular, adaptive architectures that can reconcile multi-resolution inputs and transfer knowledge across domains.
AI.method: 1) A multi-resolution spatio-temporal diffusion module capturing short-term fluctuations and long-range trends across divergent resolutions. 2) A domain-adaptive mixture-of-experts routing data to specialized sub-networks to enable selective knowledge transfer while avoiding negative interference across domains. 3) A unified periodic encoding strategy injecting resolution- and domain-aware inductive biases to harmonize periodic inconsistencies across datasets.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 23 real-world datasets show FlexST significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in zero- and few-shot settings, demonstrating superior generalization, adaptability, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: FlexST offers a new direction for building general-purpose pre-trained models for complex, variable urban traffic systems by leveraging modularity, adaptivity, and principled inductive biases.

title: VeriDx: Earning the Right to Diagnose with Disease-Centric Verification
comment: accepted by EMNLP 2026, 17 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: A correct diagnosis can still be reached for the wrong reasons. In clinical reasoning, every disease hypothesis creates obligations: key evidence must be checked, alternatives must be ruled out, contradictions must be resolved, useful tests must be considered, and closure must be justified. Current evaluations of medical LLMs mostly focus on final answers, local steps, or isolated facts, and therefore miss these hypothesis-induced commitments. We introduce \textbf{VeriDx}, a disease-centric verification framework that links free-form diagnostic reasoning to structured disease profiles. VeriDx tracks whether each hypothesis is satisfied, unresolved, or violated its clinical obligations, exposing failures such as missing critical tests, unresolved differentials, ignored contradictions, unsupported claims, and premature closure. We instantiate VeriDx for complex respiratory diagnosis using guideline-derived disease profiles and expert-annotated longitudinal cases. Our results show that many diagnostic errors are not isolated mistakes, but broken commitments made earlier in the reasoning process.

AI.tldr: VeriDx links diagnostic reasoning to disease profiles to verify each hypothesis, identifying commitments broken during clinical reasoning rather than isolated errors.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLM evaluations miss hypothesis-driven obligations; a framework is needed to audit reasoning commitments across hypotheses, including required tests, differential formation, contradictions, and justified closure.
AI.method: Define VeriDx as a disease-centric verification framework that maps free-form diagnostic reasoning to structured disease profiles, tracking each hypothesis as satisfied, unresolved, or violated; identify missing tests, ignored contradictions, unsupported claims, and premature closure; instantiate with guideline-derived respiratory disease profiles and expert-annotated longitudinal cases.
AI.result: Applied to complex respiratory diagnosis, revealing that many diagnostic errors stem from broken commitments early in reasoning rather than isolated mistakes; VeriDx surfaces these failures.
AI.conclusion: VeriDx provides a principled approach to evaluate and improve clinical reasoning in medical LLMs by auditing hypothesis-level commitments and their satisfaction.

title: Robotic Servo Tracking of Moving Targets with Dynamic Imitation Constraints
summary: Imposing explicit trajectory constraints in robot visual servoing remains challenging. Existing tracking methods achieve fast responses by mapping visual residuals to control velocities, but they have weak constraints on the intermediate motion process, which lead to trajectory discontinuity, oscillation, or conservative behaviors. To enable constrained tracking for moving targets, this paper proposes a servo tracking method based on imitation trajectory constraints. A dynamic model describing the robot approaching a moving target is formulated and analyzed for convergence. A time-scalable deformation mechanism and a trajectory modulation incorporating shape and amplitude components are introduced to generate a series of trajectories in real time, from which tracking points are adaptively determined to form dynamic constraints. The robot velocity is then computed from target pose differentials or tracked key features to follow the constrained trajectory. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve dynamic obstacle avoidance and high-precision convergence compared with several state-of-the-art methods in complex environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces a vision-based servo tracking method that enforces imitation trajectory constraints for moving targets, using a time-scalable deformation and shape/amplitude modulation to generate real-time constrained trajectories, improving dynamic obstacle avoidance and convergence.
AI.motivation: Address trajectory discontinuity, oscillation, and conservatism in existing visual servoing methods by imposing explicit intermediate trajectory constraints for moving targets.
AI.method: Develops a dynamic model of approaching a moving target; introduces a time-scalable deformation mechanism and trajectory modulation (shape and amplitude) to produce real-time trajectory sequences; adaptively selects tracking points to form dynamic constraints; computes robot velocity from target pose differentials or tracked features to follow constrained trajectories.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments show dynamic obstacle avoidance and higher-precision convergence compared with state-of-the-art methods in complex environments.
AI.conclusion: Imposing imitation trajectory constraints via dynamic deformation and modulation yields realizable, constrained tracking for moving targets with improved robustness and accuracy.

title: Restore What Matters: Lessons from Joint Restoration and Recognition
summary: Recognition pipelines typically adopt a restore-then-recognize workflow, yet decades of experience show that generating visually pleasing images seldom translates to improved recognition. We propose a Joint Restoration-for-Recognition (JR$^2$) paradigm: restore only what downstream tasks truly require, with task signals dictating where, how much, and whether restoration is necessary. JR$^2$ rests on three pillars: (i) Physics, employing optics-accurate turbulence simulation, extensible to blur and noise, to ground restoration in real image formation; (ii) Neuroscience, drawing on selective attention and neuroplasticity to direct model capacity toward identity-critical regions and frames while bypassing already-clean inputs; and (iii) Vision & Learning, coupling recognition loss end-to-end through restoration and alignment so that low-level edits maximize high-level identity stability. Evaluations on IARPA-BRIAR show consistent improvements (e.g., TAR@0.01% FAR +0.6; FNIR@1% FPIR -2.5), while a quality gate skips ~70% of clean frames, reducing cost. Ablations confirm physics priors enhance realism, joint training prevents catastrophic forgetting, and selective restoration suffices in many cases. We conclude that better-looking images are neither necessary nor sufficient; restoration modules must be task-driven, selective, and physically aware. Code, pretrained models, and recipes are provided for integration.

AI.tldr: Joint Restoration-for-Recognition (JR^2) reframes restoration as task-driven: restore only what recognition tasks demand, guided by physics, neuroscience, and vision-learning to improve downstream recognition without maximizing image beauty.
AI.motivation: Decades of experience show high visual aesthetics do not guarantee better recognition; need restoration that directly supports identity-focused recognition under realistic image formation.
AI.method: Three-pillars: (i) Physics-based turbulence/blur/noise models to ground restoration in real image formation; (ii) Neuroscience-inspired selective attention/neuroplasticity to allocate capacity to identity-critical regions while ignoring clean inputs; (iii) Vision & Learning: end-to-end optimization coupling recognition loss with restoration and alignment to maximize identity stability while editing low-level pixels.
AI.result: On IARPA-BRIAR, JR^2 yields consistent recognition gains (e.g., TAR@0.01% FAR +0.6; FNIR@1% FPIR -2.5) and a quality gate reduces processing by ~70% of clean frames, lowering cost. Ablations show physics priors improve realism, joint training prevents catastrophic forgetting, and selective restoration suffices in many cases.
AI.conclusion: Images that look better are not necessary or sufficient for recognition; restoration modules should be task-driven, selective, and physically grounded. The work provides code, pretrained models, and practical recipes for integration.

title: Lie to me: Detecting Managerial Evasiveness in Earnings Calls via Conversational Audio Encoders
summary: Earnings conference calls are a primary channel through which managers disclose information under analyst scrutiny. Prior work has linked vocal and lexical cues to future adverse outcomes, but often pools features over an entire call and underuses the interactive structure of Q&A. We propose a two-branch late-fusion framework for detecting managerial evasiveness as a predictor of extrinsic SEC events (primarily late filings): (i) an LLM-as-a-judge that maps Q&A text to an interpretable call-level vector X_text via a structured binary rubric, and (ii) a frozen conversational encoder whose temporal hidden states are read by a DeepVoice-style sequential reader to produce an audio representation h. Late fusion of (X_text, h) yields a call-level risk score p. On n=1,039 calls (212 late filings) with firm-grouped 5-fold CV, fusion reaches AUROC approx. 0.89, versus 0.55 for the text judge and 0.71 for duration alone. These results show that conversational audio dynamics encode managerial evasiveness beyond lexical content and call length, yielding a stronger early-warning signal of adverse SEC outcomes.

AI.tldr: A two-branch late-fusion model combines text-based Q&A analysis via an LLM rubric with audio dynamics from a frozen conversational encoder to predict managerial evasiveness in earnings calls, yielding strong early warning for SEC-adverse events (AUROC ~0.89) beyond lexical cues and duration.
AI.motivation: Earnings calls are a key disclosure channel; existing approaches rely on lexical cues or call length and ignore interactive Q&A dynamics. Detecting evasiveness early could predict extrinsic SEC events like late filings, enabling proactive risk management.
AI.method: Two-branch late fusion: (i) LLM-as-judge maps Q&A text to interpretable vector X_text using a structured binary rubric; (ii) frozen conversational encoder processes audio into temporal representations, read by a DeepVoice-style sequential reader to obtain h. Late fusion of X_text and h yields call-level risk p. Dataset: n=1,039 calls, 212 late filings; firm-grouped 5-fold CV.
AI.result: Fusion achieves AUROC ~0.89; text-only judge ~0.55; duration-alone model ~0.71. Demonstrates that conversational audio dynamics carry predictive information about managerial evasiveness not captured by lexical content or call length.
AI.conclusion: Conversational audio dynamics provide orthogonal, actionable signals for predicting adverse SEC outcomes, offering a stronger early-warning signal beyond text and duration alone.

title: Semantic Knowledge Technologies: what the Semantic Web lost sight of, and what it never had
summary: The Semantic Web set out to give information a machine-interpretable form so that software could integrate and reason over it. Its standards became scientific knowledge infrastructure, but the machine competence it promised did not follow, and the systems now answering questions over scientific knowledge are language models holding no inspectable account of what they know. This paper argues the original goal was right and the technical programme incomplete, states what is missing, and names the extended programme Semantic Knowledge Technologies: the same technical core carried out of its web-publishing origin and applied to knowledge wherever held. The diagnosis is that the standards formalised truth while omitting three things: the conditions under which a claim holds, the operations its terms permit, and any account of what a base covers. Without conditions, contradiction and applicability cannot be judged; without operational grounding, holding a statement confers no ability; without declared coverage, a system cannot recognise the boundary of its own content, which under the open-world assumption cannot be inferred. The paper fixes the word understanding to five measurable tests (check, connect, derive, act, delimit) and sets out a seven-layer architecture in which the first three layers are enabling and the rest the cognitive capabilities they make possible. It then defines three terms the programme implies: Large Knowledge Model, a model whose unit of output is a reference to an addressable claim, not a token; SLKM, the knowledge base an agent builds for itself from declared sources; and Semantic Artificial General Intelligence, stated as a falsifiable position about necessary conditions, not a system. A graded ladder replaces the untestable word general. It is offered as a research agenda, with its weakest points and refutation condition named.

AI.tldr: Reframes the Semantic Web as Semantic Knowledge Technologies: diagnoses missing elements (conditions, operations, coverage), introduces five tests of understanding, a seven-layer architecture, and new concepts (Large Knowledge Model, SLKM, Semantic AGI); posits a graded ladder to replace 'general' and outlines a falsifiable research agenda.
AI.motivation: Explain why the Semantic Web's promise remains unfulfilled and propose an extended program that grounds knowledge in verifiable conditions, operations, and coverage.
AI.method: Critical analysis of the Semantic Web's formalizations, diagnostic framework identifying missing elements, formalization of 'understanding' into measurable tests, architectural proposal, and definitional groundwork for a research program.
AI.result: Diagnoses omissions in existing standards (truth without conditions, operations, or coverage); introduces five tests (check, connect, derive, act, delimit); presents a seven-layer architecture; defines Large Knowledge Model, SLKM, and Semantic Artificial General Intelligence; proposes a graded ladder and a falsifiable research agenda.
AI.conclusion: Advocates Semantic Knowledge Technologies as a coherent extension of the Web's standards, enabling verifiable reasoning and boundary recognition within an open-world setting.

title: REVOLVE: An Automated Closed-Loop Framework for Evolving Robot Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention
summary: Recent advances in data-driven robot manipulation policies have substantially improved task execution and generalization. However, real-world deployment still relies heavily on humans for failure assessment, correction, and environment reset, while models often fail to continually learn from failures and corrective experience. We present REVOLVE (Robot Evolving via Orchestrated Loops, Verification, and Experience), an automated closed-loop framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention. Built on a unified software platform, REVOLVE integrates data collection, policy training and deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning into a single closed-loop workflow. Its Automated Reset and Collection (ARC) architecture automatically resets the environment and intervenes to correct policy failures. Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) continually improves the manipulation policy and agent by feeding real-world interaction and failure--correction data back into policy learning and using an external mismatch memory to refine agent judgments. Experiments across four real-world manipulation tasks show that, after five iterations, REVOLVE improves average policy success rate by 18.5% and agent judgment accuracy by 8.5%, while reducing human effort in data collection and deployment testing by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively. These results demonstrate that REVOLVE transforms real-world deployment into a closed-loop learning process that continually accumulates and uses execution experience, enabling continual evolution of both the policy and supervisory model with substantially less human intervention.

AI.tldr: REVOLVE is a fully automated closed-loop framework for evolving robot manipulation policies with minimal human intervention, combining automated environment reset/correction (ARC) and continual learning via feedback (DLE).
AI.motivation: Real-world robot manipulation relies on humans for failure handling and environment resets, hindering continual learning and deployment at scale.
AI.method: REVOLVE integrates data collection, policy training/deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning into a single loop. ARC automatically resets the environment and intervenes to correct policy failures. DLE uses real-world interaction and failure-correction data, along with an external mismatch memory, to iteratively improve both the policy and the supervisory model.
AI.result: Across four real-world manipulation tasks, after five iterations REVOLVE increases average policy success rate by 18.5% and agent judgment accuracy by 8.5%, while reducing human effort in data collection and deployment testing by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: REVOLVE demonstrates that a closed-loop learning process can continually accumulate execution experience to evolve both policy and supervisory components with substantially less human intervention, enabling scalable real-world robotics learning.

title: StepPrune: Adaptive Sequential Visual Token Selection across Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Visual prefixes account for a major portion of the per-layer computation in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), making visual-token pruning a direct approach to accelerating inference. Existing top-K methods typically evaluate tokens independently and apply a uniform budget to all inputs, overlooking both selection-dependent interactions and variations in visual complexity across samples. In contrast, we propose StepPrune, which formulates visual-token pruning as an adaptive sequential decision process. Conditioned on previously selected tokens and textual context, StepPrune progressively constructs the retained subset and automatically determines its size through a learned STOP action. During training, a variance-preserving noise gate provides a differentiable surrogate for the discrete selection process, whereas during inference, unselected tokens are physically removed before language-model prefill. A grouped selection mechanism further extends StepPrune to high-resolution inputs. Experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3 show that StepPrune achieves the best average normalized performance retention across all evaluated pruning rates on LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3, while remaining competitive on the substantially longer AnyRes prefixes of LLaVA-NeXT. On LLaVA-1.5, StepPrune retains 94.6% of the full-prefix normalized performance while pruning 88.9% of the visual tokens. At a mean retained count of 64, StepPrune reduces prefill latency from 59.95 ms to 40.05 ms, corresponding to a 1.50x prefill speed-up.

AI.tldr: Adaptive sequential visual-token pruning (StepPrune) for MLLMs, achieving high retention with substantial token pruning and latency reduction.
AI.motivation: Visual prefixes dominate per-layer computation; existing top-K methods prune tokens independently with a uniform budget, ignoring inter-token interactions and sample-dependent visual complexity. This motivates an adaptive, context-aware pruning strategy.
AI.method: StepPrune formulates pruning as a sequential decision process conditioned on previously selected tokens and textual context. It incrementally constructs a retained subset and learns a STOP action to determine its size. Training uses a variance-preserving noise gate to provide a differentiable surrogate for discrete selection; at inference, unselected tokens are physically removed before language-model prefill. A grouped selection mechanism extends StepPrune to high-resolution inputs.
AI.result: Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3, StepPrune achieves the best average normalized performance retention across pruning rates on LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3, and is competitive on LLaVA-NeXT’s longer AnyRes prefixes. On LLaVA-1.5, it preserves 94.6% of full-prefix normalized performance while pruning 88.9% of visual tokens, and reduces mean retained prefill tokens to 64, delivering a prefill latency drop from 59.95 ms to 40.05 ms (1.50x speed-up).
AI.conclusion: StepPrune demonstrates that adaptive, sequential pruning with an explicit STOP action and differentiable training surrogate yields strong performance retention at high pruning levels while delivering practical latency improvements, and remains competitive across diverse MLLM benchmarks, including high-resolution inputs.

title: Machine Learning under Imperfect Data: Challenges and Methods
summary: Machine-learning models are commonly developed under an assumption that training and test data are sufficiently complete, balanced, labelled, and drawn from compatible distributions. In practice, one or more of these conditions is often violated. Measurements may be missing or corrupted, rare classes may be poorly represented, supervision may be weak, and the deployment environment may differ from the training environment. These imperfections are usually treated as separate technical problems, although they alter learning through a small number of shared mechanisms: loss of information, biased empirical risk, ambiguous supervision, and unstable representations. This short survey organises representative methods around these mechanisms. It reviews reconstruction and generation, rebalancing and representation calibration, learning with limited supervision, adaptation across domains and modalities, and reliability under distribution change. The discussion highlights the limits of plausible reconstruction, benchmark-specific correction, and adaptation without trustworthy feedback. It concludes with directions for evidence-aware learning, uncertainty-preserving prediction, and evaluation that separates visual plausibility from decision utility.

AI.tldr: A concise survey that organizes ML robustness issues (missing/corrupted data, class imbalance, weak supervision, domain shift) by shared mechanisms and method categories, offering a unified view and directions for future evidence-aware learning.
AI.motivation: Real-world data violate i.i.d. assumptions; a unifying framework is needed to understand how information loss, biased risk, ambiguous supervision, and unstable representations affect learning; the survey aggregates representative methods across related problems.
AI.method: Systematic review organizing representative methods around core mechanisms: (1) reconstruction/generation, (2) rebalancing and representation calibration, (3) learning with limited supervision, (4) cross-domain and cross-modality adaptation, (5) reliability under distribution change; discusses limits and directions.
AI.result: Synthesis of method families, mapping between problems and underlying mechanisms; insights into common limitations such as limits of plausible reconstruction and benchmark-specific corrections; guidance on evaluation and directions for evidence-aware learning and uncertainty-preserving prediction.
AI.conclusion: Future research should emphasize evidence-aware learning, predictions that preserve and quantify uncertainty, and evaluations that separate perceptual plausibility from actual decision utility.

title: MOSCOPT: Mixture-of-Skills Collective Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Natural language prompts and skills serve as the strategic backbone of LLM-based agents. Recent advances in prompt and skill optimization have achieved notable gains, yet all existing methods optimize a \emph{single} text template---missing the synergy among multiple complementary strategies. We propose MOSCOPT, a text-native, parameter-free algorithm that jointly optimizes a pool of $N$ skills and a gating skill $G$ that dynamically selects $K$ skills per step. To effectively optimize the skills, we build the EditAdam with internally maintained dual states. Through the three-phase interleaved updates with EditAdam, the system monotonically improves without gradient or parameter tuning. Extensive experiments and detailed ablations across 5 benchmarks and 3 target LLMs demonstrate that MOSCOPT consistently outperforms all baselines, and confirm that both the mixture-of-skills architecture with selective activation and the collective evolution with three-phase interleaving are essential to its superior performance. Code is released https://github.com/zhangzhenyu13/SummerClaw/tree/master/summerclaw/agent_trainer/algorithms/moscopt.

AI.tldr: MOSCOPT jointly optimizes a pool of N skills and a gating skill to select K per step using a parameter-free, text-native framework with three-phase EditAdam updates, achieving consistent gains over single-template baselines across 5 benchmarks and 3 LLMs.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitation of optimizing only a single prompt template by leveraging synergy among multiple complementary prompting skills in LLM-based agents.
AI.method: Maintain a pool of candidate skills and a gating mechanism G that selects K skills per step. Train without gradients or tunable parameters via three-phase interleaved updates using a novel EditAdam with dual internal states. The approach is text-native and parameter-free, enabling monotonic improvement.
AI.result: MOSCOPT consistently outperforms all baselines across 5 benchmarks and 3 target LLMs. Ablations show that both the mixture-of-skills architecture with selective activation and the three-phase interleaving are essential. Code is released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Mixture-of-skills with selective activation and the three-phase interleaving in MOSCOPT yield superior performance for prompt/skill optimization in LLM agents, demonstrating the value of dynamic, multi-skill collaboration without gradient-based tuning.

title: Skill Composition for Legged Robot Reinforcement Learning
summary: Robots, and humanoid robots in particular, are increasingly competent at individual behaviors, each obtained by training a specialized controller. A specialized skill is quick to train, converges reliably because the problem it faces is narrow, and can be validated on its own, none of which is true of a single end-to-end policy asked to cover everything. What remains fragile is the transition between them. We argue that the composition of independent sub-policies deserves to be treated as a research problem in its own right, rather than as an implementation detail left to whatever mechanism happens to be at hand. Reliable composition is what turns a collection of separate skills into a repertoire that can be used, extended and shared. More fundamentally, if control can be passed between specialized policies safely, and at any moment, the choice of what the robot should do next can be delegated to a component of an entirely different nature, such as a planner, an automaton or a symbolic controller, whose behavior can be inspected in advance. The policies would then only ever have to act, and what the robot can be trusted to do would become verifiable.

AI.tldr: Modular composition of specialized sub-policies is essential for robust robotic behavior; end-to-end policies are brittle. A research framework for safe, verifiable handoffs between policies is proposed to build reusable, extensible repertoires.
AI.motivation: End-to-end policies trained for broad tasks are fragile and hard to verify. Specialized skills train quickly and are reliable in isolation, but their transitions are a weak point. A compositional approach promises a reusable, verifiable robotics repertoire.
AI.method: Proposes a conceptual framework treating policy composition as a core research problem. Highlights the need for well-defined interfaces and reliable handoffs between sub-policies, potentially delegating next-action decisions to planners, automata, or symbolic controllers to enable inspectability and verifiability.
AI.result: No empirical results reported; the paper offers a theoretical framework and design principles for modular, verifiable policy composition and safe transitions between skills.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on the composition of sub-policies can turn disparate skills into a usable, extensible repertoire with verifiable behavior, enabling higher-level controllers to manage and inspect robot actions.

title: Realtime-Venus: A full-duplex interaction system with asynchronous delegation
summary:
Natural interaction in digital and physical environments requires continuous perception and timely responses. Spoken dialogue relies on acoustic and linguistic cues, while video interaction also requires grounding the conversation in evolving visual context. We present Realtime-Venus, a proactive full-duplex interaction system with two separately trained 9B models: Realtime-Venus-Omni for audio-visual interaction and Realtime-Venus-Audio for spoken interaction. Each model serves as a complete conversational frontend, integrating continuous perception, conversational control, and native speech generation through a shared causal timeline for user inputs, model outputs, and delegation events.
  A dual-loop runtime coordinates live interaction with background reasoning and tool execution. Foreground interaction continues while Realtime-Venus-Harness executes tasks asynchronously and returns results for integration into the ongoing dialogue.
  Both models follow a common post-training recipe combining offline understanding, proactive full-duplex trajectories, and delegation workflows.
  Among the evaluated online models, Realtime-Venus-Omni achieves the highest scores on six of eight video benchmarks, including StreamingBench (70.2%), OVO-Bench (64.7%), and Daily-Omni (81.3%). Across eight audio understanding and spoken question answering benchmarks, Realtime-Venus-Audio leads the compared models on MMAU (78.0%), MMAU-Pro (63.2%), Llama Questions (83.8%), and Speech CMMLU (67.8%), while matching the best VoiceBench AlpacaEval score of 4.81. On Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5, Realtime-Venus-Audio responds to 75% of user interruptions and achieves continuation rates of 97%, 88%, and 86% under backchannels, other-directed speech, and background speech, respectively, exceeding Gemini 3.1 Live and GPT-4o on all three continuation metrics.

AI.tldr: Realtime-Venus is a dual-9B, full-duplex multimodal dialogue system with separate Omni (audio-visual) and Audio (spoken) models, sharing a causal timeline and a dual-loop runtime for live interaction and asynchronous delegation, achieving strong benchmarks across video and audio tasks.
AI.motivation: Enable proactive, continuous perception and timely, grounded responses in both audiovisual and spoken interactions by unifying perception, conversational control, and native speech generation within a shared timeline and delegation workflow.
AI.method: Two independently trained 9B models: Realtime-Venus-Omni for audio-visual interaction and Realtime-Venus-Audio for spoken interaction. Each serves as a complete conversational frontend with continuous perception, control, and speech generation. A dual-loop runtime coordinates foreground interaction with a background reasoning and tool-execution Harness; tasks are delegated asynchronously and integrated into ongoing dialogue. A common post-training recipe combines offline understanding, proactive full-duplex trajectories, and delegation workflows.
AI.result: Omni achieves highest scores on six of eight video benchmarks (e.g., StreamingBench 70.2%, OVO-Bench 64.7%, Daily-Omni 81.3%). Audio leads across eight audio benchmarks: MMAU 78.0%, MMAU-Pro 63.2%, Llama Questions 83.8%, Speech CMMLU 67.8%, and matches VoiceBench AlpacaEval 4.81. On Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5, Audio responds to 75% of interruptions and achieves continuation rates of 97%, 88%, 86% for backchannels, other-directed speech, and background speech, surpassing Gemini 3.1 Live and GPT-4o on these metrics.
AI.conclusion: The architecture demonstrates effective proactive, full-duplex multimodal dialogue with strong continuation and interruption handling, validating a unified timeline plus delegation framework as a scalable approach for integrated perception and interaction in both audio and visual modalities.

title: Learning Through Energy Refinement and Manifold Projection: A Cooperative EBM-AE Framework
summary:
Energy-Based Models (EBMs) provide a flexible framework for generative modeling by learning an energy landscape that assigns low energy values to realistic samples and higher energies to unlikely observations. Despite their theoretical appeal, training EBMs remains challenging due to the computational cost of Langevin sampling and the difficulty of efficiently exploring the learned data manifold. In this work, we propose a cooperative Energy-Based Model and Autoencoder (EBM-AE) framework that combines energy-based refinement with manifold projection. The proposed approach jointly trains an EBM with a denoising autoencoder and introduces an iterative EBM$\rightarrow$AE$\rightarrow$EBM sampling procedure in which Langevin dynamics and autoencoder projection alternately refine generated samples. Within this framework, the autoencoder acts as a manifold projection operator that regularizes sampling trajectories, while the EBM performs energy-based refinement toward low-energy regions of the learned distribution. Extensive experiments conducted on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that joint EBM-AE training substantially improves generation quality compared with a conventional autoencoder.
  Beyond unconditional generation, we evaluate the proposed framework on image inpainting tasks involving structured and random masks. The results show that manifold projection provides the majority of the reconstruction capability, whereas the final energy-based refinement becomes increasingly beneficial as the reconstruction problem becomes more challenging.
  Taken together, the results indicate that combining manifold projection and energy minimization provides an effective and interpretable framework for generation, reconstruction, and out-of-distribution detection, while offering new insights into the complementary roles of energy-based modeling and representation learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cooperative EBM-AE framework that jointly trains an energy-based model with a denoising autoencoder and uses an iterative EBM→AE→EBM sampling loop. Demonstrates improved MNIST generation over a plain autoencoder and shows that manifold projection dominates reconstruction in inpainting, with energy refinement aiding harder cases, suggesting complementary roles for energy-based modeling and representation learning.
AI.motivation: Address the training and sampling inefficiencies of EBMs (costly Langevin sampling and poor exploration of the data manifold) by leveraging a denoising autoencoder as a manifold projection to stabilize sampling and enhance generation and reconstruction.
AI.method: Jointly train an EBM and a denoising autoencoder. Use an iterative sampling procedure where Langevin dynamics and autoencoder projection alternate (EBM→AE→EBM). The autoencoder acts as a manifold projection operator; the EBM refines toward low-energy regions.
AI.result: On MNIST, the joint EBM-AE framework improves generation quality compared with a conventional autoencoder. In inpainting with structured and random masks, manifold projection accounts for most reconstruction, while the final energy-based refinement helps more challenging reconstructions. The framework supports generation, reconstruction, and out-of-distribution detection.
AI.conclusion: Combining manifold projection with energy minimization yields an effective and interpretable framework for generation, reconstruction, and OOD detection. The study provides insight into how energy-based modeling and representation learning can complement each other.

title: Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation
summary: We present an automated pipeline that converts NCERT textbooks into interactive video explanations that respond directly to user queries. A user uploads a PDF and asks a question; the system then generates a video-based explanation as output, handling both text and visual elements from the PDF for multi-modal retrieval and response generation. The pipeline combines a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model with generative multimedia components. The RAG stage is optimized for the structure of NCERT textbooks and performs best on content from those books. Given a user query, the RAG model retrieves relevant content from the PDF and generates a multi-scene script containing narrative explanations and structured visual prompts aligned with the textbook's explanatory style. These prompts are passed to a Stable Diffusion module, implemented layer by layer for interpretability and control, which generates contextually relevant images. The images are then processed by DynamiCrafter to produce animated sequences. Finally, a Google Text-to-Speech module generates synchronized narration, aligning speech with the visual scenes through time-based control. The result is a coherent video explanation integrating animation, narration, and textbook-aligned visuals, transforming static educational material into an engaging learning experience. By combining multi-modal document retrieval, generative visual models, animation frameworks, and speech synthesis, this pipeline demonstrates a scalable approach to delivering interactive, personalized digital education content.

AI.tldr: End-to-end pipeline converts NCERT PDFs into interactive video explanations via retrieval-augmented generation, diffusion-based visuals, animation, and TTS; aims for multi-modal, textbook-aligned, personalized explanations; focuses on modularity and scalability with potential evaluation and reliability challenges.
AI.motivation: Address the need for scalable, multimodal, interactive educational content that leverages static textbooks to create engaging explanations, improving accessibility and personalized learning at scale.
AI.method: An end-to-end pipeline where a user uploads a PDF and queries the content. A RAG model retrieves relevant text/pictures from the PDF and generates a multi-scene narrative aligned with the textbook style. Stable Diffusion (layer-by-layer) creates contextually relevant images. DynamiCrafter animates the images into sequences. Google Text-to-Speech provides synchronized narration, time-aligned with visuals. The approach emphasizes multi-modal retrieval and modular generation for scalability and interpretability.
AI.result: The abstract demonstrates a feasible, integrated system architecture and demonstrates the viability of the pipeline for producing textbook-aligned, multi-modal video explanations, though it does not report empirical learning outcomes or user-study results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline offers a scalable, modular framework for transforming static educational material into interactive digital content, with benefits in engagement and accessibility, but requires thorough evaluation of educational effectiveness, accuracy, and reliability.

title: A Novel Robot-Assisted Learning Pedagogy for Children with ASD
summary: Interaction paradigms used in robot-assisted autism intervention have historically employed robots as teachers, clinical assistants, or more-abled peers to promote a variety of social skills. These modalities often leverage the expertise of trained practitioners to ensure that child-robot interactions are productive or clinically grounded to yield positive therapeutic benefits for children across the autism spectrum. Yet, despite the fact that the majority of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) attend mainstream schools and spend 80% or more of their time in the general classroom [27], there is a paucity of research incorporating validated classroom teaching pedagogies into robot-assisted autism interventions. In this work, we introduce a novel teaching methodology for advancing social skills in school-aged children with ASD. We evaluate the effectiveness of a novel robot-assisted autism intervention which incorporates the learning-by-teaching pedagogy and explores the comparative benefits of employing a robot versus a human confederate for improved performance on a set of social skills tasks. Results show that 80% of study participants performed better in the robot condition (mean performance in the robot condition=63%, mean performance in the confederate condition=37%), irrespective of the scenario order. Further, 90% of all participants were significantly more engaged in the robot condition (mean engagement: robot=61%, confederate=32%) and, while the effect did not result in the confederate condition, analyses indicate that overall engagement in the robot condition contributed to improved performance. These results suggest that robots employed in a learning-by-teaching context may help enhance engagement and improve performance on a simple social skills task for children with ASD.

AI.tldr: Robot-assisted autism intervention using learning-by-teaching shows higher engagement and performance versus a human confederate.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether validated classroom teaching pedagogy (learning-by-teaching) can be effectively incorporated into robot-assisted autism interventions and to compare robot versus human confederates for improving school-aged children with ASD.
AI.method: Experimental study with a learning-by-teaching paradigm comparing a robot instructor to a human confederate on social skills tasks in school-aged children with ASD; outcomes include task performance and engagement, with order effects examined.
AI.result: Robot condition led to higher mean performance (63% vs 37%), higher engagement (61% vs 32%), with 80% of participants performing better in the robot condition and 90% more engaged; results reportedly independent of scenario order.
AI.conclusion: Learning-by-teaching robots may enhance engagement and improve performance on simple social skills tasks in children with ASD; supports integrating validated classroom pedagogy into robot-assisted interventions, though further work is needed to assess generalizability, scalability, and longer-term outcomes.

title: Beyond OCR Accuracy: Text-Centric VQA Under Image Degradation with Modular and End-to-End
summary: Text-centric Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires reading and reasoning over text embedded in images, a task made substantially harder when images suffer from real-world degradation such as motion blur, low resolution, or compression artifacts. While modular OCR-based pipelines and end-to-end vision-language models are both widely used for this task, their comparative robustness under degraded conditions remains underexplored. We present an empirical study comparing two modular pipelines with SA-DBNet, a custom detector architecture combining ResNet-18 with self-attention spatial modeling and deformable convolutions against an end-to-end vision-language baseline, evaluated on 4013 degraded images with 7000 question-answer pairs. Fine-tuned modular pipelines achieve up to 57.50% exact-match accuracy versus 38.00% for the end-to-end baseline, with domain-specific fine-tuning yielding a gain of up to 29.50 percentage points. Critically, we find that conventional OCR error metrics like Character Error Rate and Word Error Rate are unreliable predictors of downstream VQA performance, as semantic reasoning can compensate for recognition failures when contextual cues are present. These findings highlight the importance of task-aware evaluation for text-centric VQA systems under realistic visual conditions. Codes are available here

AI.tldr: Text-centric VQA under degradation favors modular OCR pipelines with SA-DBNet over end-to-end models; OCR error metrics (CER/WER) poorly predict VQA performance; domain-specific fine-tuning yields substantial gains; highlights need for task-aware evaluation.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of text-centric VQA under real-world image degradation and compare modular OCR-based pipelines against end-to-end vision-language models; examine whether OCR error metrics align with downstream VQA performance.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing two modular OCR-based pipelines (with SA-DBNet detector: ResNet-18 + self-attention spatial modeling + deformable convolutions) to an end-to-end V-L baseline. Evaluated on 4013 degraded images with 7000 QA pairs. Included fine-tuning, with domain-specific fine-tuning, and measured exact-match (EM) accuracy. Analyzed correlation between OCR metrics (CER/WER) and VQA performance.
AI.result: Modular pipelines achieve up to 57.50% EM vs 38.00% for the end-to-end baseline; domain-specific fine-tuning yields up to 29.50 percentage points improvement. OCR error metrics (CER/WER) are unreliable predictors of downstream VQA performance; semantic reasoning can compensate for recognition failures with contextual cues.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware evaluation is essential for text-centric VQA under realistic visual conditions. Modular OCR-based pipelines with domain-specific fine-tuning are more robust than end-to-end baselines on degraded imagery; relying on OCR error metrics alone is insufficient to gauge VQA capability.

title: Machine Learning in Fish Farming
summary: This chapter explores how machine learning (ML) is transforming aquaculture, with a particular focus on enhancing decision-making processes and improving operational efficiency. The chapter is structured to first introduce the challenges in aquaculture and the role of AI and then provide an overview of ML techniques in the context of aquaculture, followed by applications, emerging trends, future directions, and case studies. The focus is on real-world applications of ML techniques, including Random Forest, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), as well as emerging technologies such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and large language models (LLMs). Key applications include biomass estimation, species recognition, behavioural analysis, and environmental forecasting. The chapter also highlights the synergy between ML and the Internet of Things (IoT) for real-time monitoring and decision support. Ultimately, ML-driven innovations have the potential to revolutionise fish farming, leading to more efficient, sustainable, and productive practices in the aquaculture industry.

AI.tldr: ML transforms aquaculture decision-making and operations, enabling real-time monitoring and forecasting through RF, CNNs, RNNs, GNNs and LLMs; key applications include biomass estimation, species recognition, behavior analysis, and environmental forecasting, with IoT integration.
AI.motivation: Address challenges in aquaculture such as efficiency, sustainability, productivity, and the need for real-time decision support through AI.
AI.method: Literature/chapters review synthesizing ML techniques applied to aquaculture (RF, CNNs, RNNs, GNNs, LLMs), IoT integration, and real-world applications, emerging trends, and case studies.
AI.result: Provides a synthesized landscape of ML in aquaculture, highlighting effective methods, deployment examples, and potential impact on efficiency and sustainability; identifies trends and case studies.
AI.conclusion: ML-driven innovations have the potential to revolutionize fish farming by enabling smarter, data-driven management and sustainable practices.

title: Question's Gambit: The First Move Matters in Agentic Deep Search
summary: Deep research agents answer complex questions through iterative loops of searching, reading, and reasoning. Recent work on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as BrowseComp-Plus shows that well-configured lexical retrieval can surface high-quality evidence, yet agents may still fail to connect documents carrying evidence to the gold documents. We identify a deep research agent's first retrieval move as an important design decision for this setting. We introduce Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that decomposes the question into a set of clues, reformulates them into complementary searches, consolidates the retrieved results, and reranks the candidate pool before the agent begins its iterative search-and-reasoning process. This produces an opening context designed to support both clue aggregation and final-answer verification. We further evaluate on MultiHop-RAG to test whether these benefits transfer beyond BrowseComp-Plus to a more conventional multi-hop question structure. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus show that Question's Gambit improves retrieval recall and downstream agent accuracy over strong baselines, improving answer accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% with gpt-5.5 over Pi-Serini, the strongest reported agentic baseline. Our results confirm that effective agentic deep research depends not only on the tools available inside the loop, but also on the quality of the first move. We published our implementation publicly at https://github.com/radinhamidi/Question-s-Gambit.

AI.tldr: Introduces Question's Gambit, a first-move retrieval module that decomposes a question into clues, forms complementary searches, consolidates results, and reranks candidates to open the reasoning process; improves performance on BrowseComp-Plus and transfers to MultiHop-RAG.
AI.motivation: Address the critical role of the first retrieval move in deep-research agents and bridge the gap between retrieved documents and gold evidence, enabling stronger clue aggregation and final-answer verification.
AI.method: Propose Question's Gambit: decompose question into clues, reformulate into complementary searches, consolidate retrieved results, rerank candidate pool, and provide an opening context before iterative search-and-reasoning; evaluate on BrowseComp-Plus and MultiHop-RAG; compare against strong baselines; release code at GitHub.
AI.result: On BrowseComp-Plus, improved answer accuracy from 83.1% to 90.5% using gpt-5.5, surpassing Pi-Serini; also observed improved retrieval recall and overall agent performance; results suggest successful transfer to a conventional multi-hop structure (MultiHop-RAG).
AI.conclusion: Effective agentic deep research hinges on the quality of the first move in retrieval; the proposed Gambit enhances early evidence gathering and verification, reinforcing that the loop tools alone are insufficient without a strong opening.

title: Beyond Dead Reckoning: A Point of View on Camera--DAS--GNSS Continuity in Road Tunnels
summary: Road tunnels remove satellite visibility where connected and automated vehicles still require continuous, attributable, and integrity-bounded positioning. This Point of View argues that tunnel localization should be treated as infrastructure-assisted cross-modal track continuity, not as extrapolation from the last trusted satellite fix. A trusted portal satellite solution provides the global anchor, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) continuous motion evidence, cameras sparse identity and lane anchors, onboard sensing short-term dynamics, and edge computing association, fusion, integrity monitoring, and guarded reacquisition. Ground truth is reserved for offline calibration and validation. The article develops a falsifiable research and deployment agenda for progressing from synchronized multimodal evidence to validated, integrity-aware tunnel positioning continuity.

AI.tldr: A viewpoint arguing tunnel localization should be infrastructure-assisted cross-modal track continuity rather than extrapolation from the last GPS fix, proposing a global-anchor portal satellite, DAS motion evidence, sparse cameras, onboard sensing, and edge fusion with integrity monitoring to create verifiable tunnel positioning; ground truth reserved for offline calibration; and a falsifiable research/deployment agenda for integrity-aware continuity.
AI.motivation: Satellites lose visibility inside road tunnels; connected and automated vehicles require continuous, attributable, and integrity-bounded positioning even when GNSS is unavailable.
AI.method: Proposes a conceptual, architecture-level framework that fuses multimodal signals from a portal/global satellite anchor, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) motion evidence, sparse camera-based identity/lane anchors, and onboard sensing, with edge computing for association, fusion, integrity monitoring, and guarded reacquisition; ground truth is used offline for calibration/validation; emphasizes a falsifiable research and deployment agenda.
AI.result: As a viewpoint paper, it outlines a framework and a set of testable research questions rather than presenting empirical results; it aims to move from synchronized multimodal evidence to validated, integrity-aware tunnel positioning continuity.
AI.conclusion: Tunnel localization should be treated as infrastructure-assisted cross-modal track continuity, not extrapolation from the last trusted satellite fix; the article provides a falsifiable roadmap for research and deployment to achieve integrity-aware tunnel positioning.

title: Semantic Privacy Protection with Utility Preservation for 3D Point Clouds
summary: Point cloud data face serious semantic privacy risks during acquisition, transmission, and cross-institutional sharing. Existing methods mostly rely on geometric perturbation or destructive encryption, which can reduce the recognizability of the original class but often impair downstream usability. This paper proposes a class-transfer-based semantic encryption framework for point clouds, aiming to conceal original class information while preserving task utility and supporting authorized recovery. Specifically, we construct a unified latent space with a shared-backbone Normalizing Flow, and combine LoRA and FiLM to achieve parameter-efficient class-conditional adaptation. We further introduce diffusion-guided flow alignment to regularize the latent distribution, construct an energy-based category transition graph, and obtain an optimal class-transfer table through global matching. Then, a latent-space Neural ODE continuously evolves source-class latents into target-class latents, which are decoded into target-class point clouds through the inverse flow. We adopt attacker-oriented metrics, including New-Class Recognition Rate (NCRR), Original-Class Leakage Rate (OCLR), and Original Label Recovery Rate (OLRR), to evaluate privacy and utility. Experiments on classification and segmentation benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves controllable semantic transformation, effectively reduces original-class semantic leakage, preserves downstream learnability in the protected domain, and supports reliable authorized reconstruction.

AI.tldr: A class-transfer-based semantic encryption framework for point clouds that conceals original class information while preserving task utility and enabling authorized recovery. It uses a shared-backbone Normalizing Flow, LoRA/FiLM for class-conditional adaptation, diffusion-guided flow alignment, an energy-based transition graph, Neural ODE latent evolution, and inverse flow decoding to transfer source-class latents to target-class latents.
AI.motivation: Point clouds pose semantic privacy risks during capture, transmission, and cross-institutional sharing. Existing perturbation/encryption methods often hurt downstream usability. There is a need for controlled, class-level semantic concealment with guaranteed authorized reconstruction.
AI.method: Construct a unified latent space with a shared-backbone Normalizing Flow. Use LoRA and FiLM for parameter-efficient class-conditional adaptation. Apply diffusion-guided flow alignment to regularize latent distributions. Build an energy-based category transition graph and determine an optimal class-transfer table via global matching. Evolve source-class latents to target-class latents with a latent-space Neural ODE, then decode through the inverse flow to get target-class point clouds. Evaluate with attacker-oriented metrics NCRR, OCLR, and OLRR across classification and segmentation tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on classification and segmentation benchmarks demonstrate controllable semantic transformation, reduced original-class leakage, preserved downstream learnability in the protected domain, and reliable authorized reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical, controllable privacy-preserving approach for point clouds by combining probabilistic latent modeling, parameter-efficient adaptation, diffusion-based regularization, a transition graph for class mapping, and Neural ODE-driven latent morphing, with attacker-focused evaluation showing improved privacy-utility trade-offs.

title: Finite-Time Node Separation in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks with Persistent Gaussian Perturbations
summary: Persistent Gaussian perturbations have been shown to prevent asymptotic oversmoothing in recurrent Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by ensuring a positive stationary Dirichlet energy. However, this global energy bound does not guarantee that individual node representations remain distinct at finite depths. In this paper, we provide a complementary finite-time analysis of the same persistent-noise architecture. Let \(d\) denote the representation dimension and \(σ\) the noise standard deviation. We first prove an exact second-moment decomposition for the expected squared distance between any two node representations, yielding the universal lower bound \(2σ^2 d\) at every positive time step without contraction or stationarity assumptions. More precisely, conditional pairwise distances have a noncentral chi-square characterization: the noncentrality parameter is the deterministic message-passing separation normalized by \(2σ^2\). This yields dynamics-aware fixed-time and finite-horizon near-collision bounds that retain information discarded by the central worst-case analysis. The earlier central Gaussian bound is recovered as the worst-case zero-separation case. We additionally prove almost-sure pairwise noncollision, derive a uniform finite-horizon guarantee, and establish permutation equivariance in distribution for the stochastic dynamics and permutation-invariant graph outputs. Our results complement the asymptotic energy analysis of prior work and provide rigorous finite-time guarantees on node-level representation separation.

AI.tldr: Finite-time analysis of persistent Gaussian noise in recurrent GNNs shows exact second-moment separation lower bound and non-collision guarantees, complementing asymptotic energy bounds.
