AI.motivation: Fill the gap between global, asymptotic energy-based guarantees for persistent-noise GNNs and finite-depth, node-level separation by providing finite-time, distributional characterizations of pairwise distances.
AI.method: Derives an exact second-moment decomposition for expected squared distance between node representations under persistent Gaussian perturbations. Establishes that conditional pairwise distances follow a noncentral chi-square distribution with noncentrality equal to the deterministic message-passing separation normalized by 2σ^2. Uses this to obtain fixed-time and finite-horizon near-collision bounds, almost-sure noncollision, and permutation-invariance properties.
AI.result: Proves a universal lower bound of 2σ^2 d on the expected squared distance at every positive time step without contraction assumptions; identifies noncentrality parameter as separation/2σ^2; provides uniform finite-horizon guarantees and permutation equivariance in distribution.
AI.conclusion: The work complements prior asymptotic energy analyses by delivering rigorous finite-time guarantees on node-level representation separation in persistent-noise recurrent GNNs.

title: Safety Signals to Verify NetOps Agents with Action-Level Granularity
summary: Agentic Network Operations (NetOps) are an emerging paradigm promising to enable workload-aware, self-adjustable, and reliable autonomous networks. While agents have proven their value in incident summarization and telemetry signal extraction, their effectiveness as autonomous control-loop engines heavily relies on their long-horizon reliability. One such setting is the datacenter fabric, where an agent must respond to alarms and operator intents while abstaining from high-risk actions that may cause or extend downtime. Abstention, however, presupposes that an action's impact is known pre-execution, which necessitates a per-action ground truth that NetOps agent benchmarks do not provide. We construct such a ground truth for the network repair task of NetArena. A symbolic replay of the emulated network, validated against the environment at every turn, yields the exact value of every action. From the action-level value, we derive two pre-execution targets, namely whether an action reduces the repair distance (progress) and whether it increases it (harm). We show across 10 agent models, that agent verifiers leveraging internal signals predict both harm and progress more reliably than a baseline using observable signals only. Perspectively, we aim to use these signals as safety feedback to an agent harness to abstain from risky actions and protect the target system.

AI.tldr: Ground truth for NetOps action impact is constructed via symbolic replay of emulated networks, enabling pre-execution risk assessment. Internal-signal verifiers predict action harm and progress better than observable-signal baselines across 10 agent models, suggesting safety abstention could protect systems.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable long-horizon autonomous NetOps control by requiring a per-action ground truth of impact, thus supporting abstention from high-risk actions and improving datacenter reliability.
AI.method: Create a symbolic replay of the NetArena emulated network, validated at every step to obtain exact action values. Derive pre-execution targets: (1) progress—action reduces remaining repair distance; (2) harm—action increases it. Evaluate 10 agent models using verifiers that leverage internal signals; compare to a baseline that uses only observable signals.
AI.result: Across 10 agent models, verifiers that leverage internal signals predict both harm and progress more reliably than the observable-signal baseline, demonstrating improved pre-execution risk assessment.
AI.conclusion: Internal-signal-based safety feedback can serve as a safety harness to abstain from risky actions in NetOps agents, potentially reducing downtime and improving robustness; further work involves integrating these signals into live control loops and evaluating generalization to real networks.

title: An Adaptive Fixed-Time Line-of-Sight Guidance Scheme for 3D Path Following of Underwater Vehicles: Theory and Experiment
summary: Reliable path tracking is crucial for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating in dynamic and uncertain marine environments. However, traditional line-of-sight (LOS) guidance methods rely on asymptotic convergence, resulting in slow disturbance recovery and unpredictable tracking performance. Existing robust control methods typically require modifications to the underlying vehicle controller, limiting their practical application on commercial AUV platforms. This paper proposes a robust fixed-time adaptive LOS guidance framework for 3D path tracking for AUVs. By combining fixed-time stability theory with LOS guidance, this method guarantees path tracking convergence within a preset time range, with the convergence time independent of initial conditions. Furthermore, a fixed-time adaptive estimator is developed to rapidly compensate for time-varying sideslip disturbances caused by ocean currents. A time-varying look-ahead mechanism is also introduced to improve tracking performance on curved paths. Lyapunov analysis proves the fixed-time stability of the proposed framework, and numerical simulations and physical experiments demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art adaptive LOS methods, this framework exhibits superior tracking accuracy, convergence speed, and anti-interference capability. In simulation, the time-varying look-ahead variant reduced cross-track and vertical-track RMSE by 69.37\% and 67.46\%, respectively, during curved-path tracking. In field experiments with an Iver 3 AUV, the proposed fixed-time guidance reduced average tracking error by 56.35\% in straight-path evaluation and 27.59\% in curved-path evaluation compared with conventional adaptive LOS guidance.The proposed method provides a practical guidance-level solution for achieving reliable autonomous navigation of AUVs in complex marine environments.

AI.tldr: Fixed-time adaptive LOS guidance for 3D AUV path tracking providing preset-time convergence, disturbance compensation, and look-ahead; validated by simulations and field tests with significant accuracy and speed improvements.
AI.motivation: Address slow disturbance recovery and reliance on asymptotic convergence in LOS guidance; avoid altering vehicle controllers, enabling practical deployment on commercial AUVs.
AI.method: Integrates fixed-time stability with LOS guidance; develops fixed-time adaptive estimator for time-varying currents; introduces time-varying look-ahead; proves fixed-time stability via Lyapunov; uses simulations and field experiments.
AI.result: Fixed-time convergence within a preset window; substantial RMSE reductions on curved and straight paths; field test with Iver 3 shows meaningful error reductions; improved tracking accuracy, convergence speed, and anti-disturbance performance.
AI.conclusion: Offers a practical, guidance-level solution for reliable AUV navigation in dynamic marine environments, especially under currents, with validated performance gains over adaptive LOS methods.

title: DiVA: Enabling Interactive Digital Life Simulation via Video Models
summary: We present DiVA, a deeply interactive digital life simulator pioneering a new paradigm for long-term, open-ended interactive experiences within digital character worlds. DiVA's architecture pairs a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a router with a meticulously designed stacked video pipeline for seamless, multi-turn interactions with action and audio response. To maintain continuity and avoid degradation, we model generation as a three-part coupled system: waiting video, action video, and the transitions between them. These transitions are critically handled by our Anchored Video Continuation (AVC) module, which returns the character to stable states to prevent degradation. By encoding information from the preceding action video segment, AVC ensures smooth transitions, significantly reducing camera jitter and inconsistencies common in current video transition methods. This design also enables complex pose changes (e.g., sitting to standing) typically difficult for audio-driven models. These system designs together ensure high-fidelity identity, coherence, and dynamics for extended experiences. To validate our pipeline design, we comprehensively compare our system against alternatives by replacing our core generation module with mainstream long-video, continuation, and interpolation methods. We further analyze the necessity of the three-stage design, anchor-state selection, transition naturalness, spatial grounding, and the quality-latency trade-off, and we expand the comparison to additional long-form audio-driven avatar models. Results confirm DiVA is markedly superior in maintaining long-term visual quality and realism, validating its effectiveness as a sustainable, interactive simulation.

AI.tldr: A three-stage, AVC-stabilized long-form avatar video pipeline (waiting, action, transitions) powered by an MLLM router and a stacked video system, designed to preserve identity and continuity over long interactive sessions; evaluated against alternatives showing superior long-term visual quality and realism.
AI.motivation: Address degradation and instability in long-duration, open-ended interactive digital character experiences. Improve continuity, pose changes, and coherence across extended interactions.
AI.method: A three-part generation pipeline: waiting video, action video, and transitions controlled by an Anchored Video Continuation (AVC) module. An MLLM acts as a router to orchestrate multimodal inputs, with a stacked video pipeline to produce multi-turn interactions. AVC encodes information from preceding action segments to produce stable transitions and reduce jitter, enabling complex pose transitions and maintaining identity across time. Systematic ablations compare against mainstream long-video, continuation, and interpolation methods; analyses cover three-stage necessity, anchor-state selection, transition naturalness, spatial grounding, and quality-latency trade-offs, extended to other long-form audio-driven avatars.
AI.result: Empirical results show DiVA maintains long-term visual quality and realism better than alternatives, with reduced jitter, better pose changes, and stable identity over extended interactions; validating the architecture for sustainable, interactive simulation.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage design with AVC and a router-based MLLM, plus a stacked video pipeline, is effective for high-fidelity, long-duration, open-ended avatar experiences, offering improved continuity and realism critical for sustainable digital character worlds.

title: Minibatch persistency, eight years later: what batch reuse costs in steps and joules, and what it saves in data
comment: 36 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Pre-registered study (OSF Registries, embargoed); registration, harness and per-run archives in the supplementary material of the journal submission
summary: Minibatch persistency reuses data instead of reading it: rather than drawing a fresh minibatch at every optimizer step, it takes K consecutive steps on the same one. Absorbed into data echoing in 2019, it has carried one objection -- that reuse merely imitates a larger learning rate -- and no baseline tuned as carefully as the method itself. This paper runs the missing test. A pre-registered study trains a 49M-parameter Transformer on FineWeb-Edu at minibatch size B in {32, 128, 512}, 8 seeds per cell, tuning the learning rate separately for every batch size and every arm, against a reuse-free control that changes the sampling and nothing else. Each headline claim is a cost to reach a fixed loss, read on four axes: optimizer steps, fresh tokens, seconds, and joules at the socket. We then replicate on new seeds and a newer GPU generation, and put the three arms on one schedule in steps. The outcome of our study is that what minibatch reuse buys is neither speed nor energy but data, and only at large minibatch size: at B = 32 it reads more fresh tokens than the baseline, not fewer. On steps, seconds and joules it is at best free; and at B = 512, where it looks best, a registered control cannot separate the effect of reuse from the position on the learning-rate schedule at n = 8 seeds. The technique is therefore worth using where fresh data rather than compute is the binding cost: a corpus that runs out, a pipeline that pays per sample, a stream that cannot be rewound. Where the data can simply be read again, spaced epochs do as well or better.

AI.tldr: Minibatch persistency rarely improves training efficiency; it yields data advantages only at large batch sizes when data cost dominates, and cannot be clearly separated from learning-rate effects at those scales.
AI.motivation: To test a long-standing objection that minibatch reuse merely imitates a larger learning rate and to provide a fair, preregistered comparison across batch sizes and seeds.
AI.method: A preregistered study training a 49M-parameter Transformer on FineWeb-Edu with minibatch sizes {32, 128, 512}, 8 seeds per cell, tuning LR separately for each batch size/arm, against a reuse-free control that only changes sampling. The authors measure optimizer steps, fresh tokens, time (seconds), and energy (joules). They replicate with new seeds and newer GPUs and put all arms on a common schedule.
AI.result: Minibatch reuse yields data advantages only at large batch sizes and does not reliably reduce compute or energy use. At B=32, it tends to read more fresh tokens than the baseline; at B=512, the reuse effect cannot be disentangled from the LR schedule. Overall, reuse is beneficial mainly where data are the binding cost; otherwise, spaced epochs perform as well or better.
AI.conclusion: Minibatch reuse should be adopted conditionally: it can help when data access is costly or non-replayable, but does not provide universal speed/energy gains and may be confounded with learning-rate dynamics; spaced-epoch strategies are competitive when data can be re-read.

title: When does a scaling result justify a different allocation? A critical review of resource-allocation evidence for AI systems
summary: AI scaling studies increasingly evaluate systems that combine a pretrained model with retrieval, search, verification, tools, and interaction. Yet a higher score under a larger budget does not by itself show where additional resources are best spent. This critical integrative review asks when a reported scaling result supports a resource-allocation decision. It compares evidence across pretraining, test-time computation, retrieval, and agent evaluation, distinguishing the performance of a tested procedure from the best performance achievable under a resource limit. The synthesis shows that three mismatches recur across this evidence: success counted before an answer is chosen, information a deployed system will not have, and costs left out of the comparison. A capability surface expresses performance as a function of budgets, mechanisms, and available information. Worked analytical examples show how the evaluation metric, deployment volume, selection rule, and stopping policy can alter an allocation conclusion. A resource envelope provides a structured record of the task, development and run-time resources, information access, and procedure behind a reported score. Its application to a published comparison illustrates which conclusions the evidence supports and which deployment questions remain unresolved. The resulting framework specifies the comparisons needed to choose among feasible systems and motivates experiments on the transfer of allocation rules across tasks and operating conditions. It does not propose a universal scaling law or infer general intelligence from benchmark gains.

AI.tldr: A framework to evaluate AI scaling results by separating resource allocation decisions from reported scores, via a capability surface and resource envelope that link performance to budgets, mechanisms, and information access.
AI.motivation: To address when a scaling result meaningfully informs resource allocation, by uncovering mismatches between reported scores and the resources, information, and deployment context underlying them.
AI.method: Integrated literature review with formal constructs: a capability surface (performance vs budgets/mechanisms/info) and a resource envelope (task, resources, info access, procedure). Includes worked analytical examples and application to an existing comparison.
AI.result: Identifies recurring mismatches (pre-answer success, unavailable information, omitted costs). Proposes a structured evaluation framework that clarifies which comparisons are valid and what deployment questions remain unresolved; avoids universal scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: The framework guides choosing among feasible systems and motivates cross-task transfer of allocation rules; it does not claim general intelligence or a universal scaling law, but provides a structured basis for resource-aware evaluation.

title: A Personalized Dynamic Balance Evaluation Paradigm for Hip Exoskeleton-Assisted Walking under Unexpected Ground Perturbations
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Hip exoskeletons may improve recovery from unexpected gait perturbations, yet personalizing assistance remains difficult because balance is multidimensional and human-in-the-loop experiments are small-sample and noisy. We present a participant-specific composite balance cost that integrates seven biomechanical sub-metrics spanning margin of stability, center-of-mass dynamics, and whole-body angular momentum. The sub-metrics are converted to direction-aligned, dimensionless cost features, and nonnegative fusion weights are learned on the simplex. Coupled with an empirical-Bayes hierarchical model, the learned-composite selector estimates each tested condition's posterior probability of being best, P(best), and a high-probability candidate set with size $K_{0.8}$. The framework was evaluated with three participants walking at 1.1 m/s during unilateral belt-slip perturbations across 46 hip-assistance conditions. In the full-budget analysis (B = 4 repeats per condition), the selector concentrated 80% of the posterior probability within 1 to 5 of 46 conditions, compared with 2 to 12 for equal-weight fusion and 4 to 37 for principal component analysis fusion. This smaller candidate set could shorten personalization experiments and limit participants' exposure to repeated perturbations in future studies. Selected-condition trials showed lower observed composite costs than no-torque trials, with nominal p < 0.05 for P2 and P3. Leave-one-repeat-out refits yielded positive mean held-out rank correlations for all participants and moderate stability of the learned weights and candidate sets. These proof-of-concept results support participant-specific composite balance evaluation for candidate selection in perturbation-based human-in-the-loop experiments.

AI.tldr: Participant-specific composite balance cost using seven biomechanical sub-metrics, learned via simplex-constrained fusion; hierarchical Bayesian model estimates P(best) for perturbation conditions; evaluated on 3-participant belt-slip perturbations across 46 hip-assistance conditions; shows concentrated posterior on a small subset of conditions and improved performance for selected trials.
AI.motivation: Balance is multidimensional; personalizing hip exoskeleton assistance is difficult in small noisy studies; aim to streamline condition selection for perturbation-based human-in-the-loop experiments.
AI.method: Compute seven sub-metrics, convert to direction-aligned, dimensionless costs; use nonnegative fusion weights on the simplex to create a composite balance cost; apply empirical-Bayes hierarchical model to estimate P(best) and K0.8; evaluate across 46 conditions with 3 participants; compare for full-budget B=4 repeats; perform leave-one-repeat-out tests.
AI.result: 80% of posterior probability within 1-5 of 46 conditions; equal-weight and PCA fusion yield 2-12 and 4-37 respectively; selected trials show lower composite costs than no-torque trials; p<0.05 for P2 and P3; leave-one-repeat-out shows positive held-out rank correlations; weights and candidate sets show moderate stability.
AI.conclusion: Proof-of-concept supports participant-specific composite balance evaluation as a candidate selector in perturbation-based HIL experiments; potential to reduce experimental burden and exposure to perturbations.

title: TotalSynth: Robust Whole-Body Synthetic CT from MRI and CBCT
summary: Purpose: To develop and evaluate TotalSynth, a reusable pretrained framework for whole-body synthetic CT (sCT) generation from MRI and cone-beam CT (CBCT) images. Materials and Methods: In this retrospective technical study, the dataset was assembled between 2020 and 2026 from SynthRAD challenge data, four prostate cohorts, and BIC-MAC. After registration quality control, 1450 of 1800 public challenge pairs were retained; 350 were excluded for insufficient registration quality or major source/CT mismatch. The corpus also included 84 additional prostate MRI/CT and 60 external BIC-MAC MRI/CT cases. Three 5-fold model families were evaluated with image-domain, anatomy-aware, registration-based, and uncertainty metrics. Age and sex were not consistently available across public datasets. Results: The released MRI-to-CT model achieved an overall MAE of 67.49 HU, SSIM of 0.920, and PSNR of 29.28 dB. The CBCT-to-CT model achieved an overall MAE of 53.55 HU, SSIM of 0.939, and PSNR of 32.09 dB. The unified model maintained similar performance on MRI inputs (MAE, 67.68 HU) and CBCT inputs (MAE, 54.22 HU). On external BIC-MAC data, MRI-to-CT MAE was 100.91 HU without fine-tuning and 62.21 HU after fine-tuning. Conclusion: TotalSynth provides reusable MRI- and CBCT-based CT synthesis models with broad anatomical coverage, while external evaluation highlights the need for local validation and optional fine-tuning under domain shift.

AI.tldr: TotalSynth is a reusable pretrained framework for whole-body sCT generation from MRI and CBCT; demonstrates competitive accuracy across datasets with MAE ~54–68 HU, SSIM ~0.92–0.94, PSNR ~29–32 dB; external validation suggests domain shift requires local validation and optional fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Provide a universal, reusable sCT synthesis framework that works with MRI and CBCT inputs across diverse anatomical regions and datasets, enabling broader clinical integration.
AI.method: Three 5-fold model families (image-domain, anatomy-aware, registration-based) were evaluated on 1450 retained public challenge MRI/CBCT pairs plus 84 MRI/CT and 60 external BIC-MAC cases, with quality-control, using MAE, SSIM, PSNR and uncertainty metrics to assess performance and generalization on MRI and CBCT inputs.
AI.result: MRI-to-CT MAE 67.49 HU, SSIM 0.920, PSNR 29.28 dB; CBCT-to-CT MAE 53.55 HU, SSIM 0.939, PSNR 32.09 dB. Unified model: MRI inputs MAE 67.68 HU; CBCT inputs MAE 54.22 HU. External BIC-MAC MRI-to-CT MAE 100.91 HU (no fine-tune) and 62.21 HU (with fine-tuning).
AI.conclusion: TotalSynth delivers reusable MRI- and CBCT-based CT-synthesis models with broad anatomical coverage, but external evaluation highlights the need for local validation and optional fine-tuning under domain shift.

title: Exploring napping paradigm for Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 7th International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI 2026). To appear in Springer Communications in Computer and Information Science
summary: Biological organisms minimize free energy by balancing two competing demands on their internal world model: it must be accurate enough to predict sensory input, yet simple enough to generalize beyond it. Two mechanisms regulate this balance offline: sleep reduces complexity through gradual synaptic downscaling, while stochastic noise attenuates precision, relaxing the constraint sensory input imposes on synaptic reorganization. Engineered Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) leave this balance unaddressed, favoring instantaneous, noiseless weight normalization instead. This paper investigates the hypothesis that a biologically inspired micro-sleep paradigm, napping -- combining proportional weight scaling with continuous stochastic membrane activity -- can replicate the stability of normalization while shedding model complexity. We evaluate this in an unsupervised recurrent SNN trained via trace-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) on Gabor-preprocessed MNIST. We tune napping across three regularization regimes by sweeping its duration and membrane noise level, then compare the best configuration against weight normalization. Across all three regimes, well-tuned napping matches the accuracy of normalization: accuracy peaks at brief durations and low noise, then declines monotonically as either grows. Clustering diverges, with the strongest geometric separation arising at longer durations and higher noise -- the two terms of free energy pulling apart, accuracy rewarding data fit and structure rewarding the simpler representation that gradual, noisy downscaling induces. This gain carries a simulation cost normalization avoids, so napping is most compelling where representational structure, rather than raw classification efficiency, is the priority.

AI.tldr: Biologically inspired micro-sleep (napping) with proportional weight scaling and stochastic membrane activity can match weight-normalization performance in an unsupervised recurrent SNN on MNIST, while offering distinct representational structure; brief napping with low noise is best for accuracy, longer duration or higher noise increase clustering but reduce accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address how biological mechanisms like sleep and noise regulate the trade-off between accurate internal models and generalizable, simple representations in neural networks, and to test whether a biologically plausible micro-sleep regimen can preserve normalization benefits in engineered SNNs.
AI.method: Unsupervised recurrent SNN trained with trace-based STDP on Gabor-preprocessed MNIST. Introduce napping as a micro-sleep: proportional weight scaling plus continuous stochastic membrane activity. Sweep over three regularization regimes by varying napping duration and membrane noise; compare best-performing configuration against traditional weight normalization.
AI.result: Tuned napping achieves accuracy comparable to weight normalization across regimes. Accuracy peaks at short durations and low noise; increasing duration or noise degrades performance. Clustering diverges, with stronger geometric separation at longer durations and higher noise, indicating conflicting pressures from data fit versus simpler representations. The gains in representational structure come at a simulation cost relative to normalization, making napping advantageous when representation quality—not raw accuracy—is prioritized.
AI.conclusion: A biologically inspired micro-sleep paradigm can stabilize learning and maintain accuracy comparable to normalization while enabling richer representational structure. It is most compelling in scenarios where representational simplicity is less critical than capturing structured internal representations, accepting higher simulation cost.

title: Beyond Scene Description: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Non-visual Access to Virtual Worlds
summary: Virtual worlds now host classrooms, meetings, conferences, shops, and social venues, and nearly every interaction they expose assumes a user who can scan a three-dimensional scene, follow avatars, and read floating panels. Blind and visually impaired (BVI) users are left with assistive tools that each solve one task in isolation: naming an object, reading text, describing a scene, or planning a route. A live virtual room defeats that model: obstacles, speakers, gestures, chat, slides, and notifications arrive together, and a tool that narrates all of them trades a visual barrier for an auditory one. This paper presents MetaBlind, an architecture that distributes nonvisual access across eight specialized agents, spanning perception, navigation, social and object interaction, communication, safety and trust, memory, and personalization, and that places an Accessibility Orchestrator between those agents and the user. Agents publish candidate information into a shared accessibility context instead of speaking to the user directly. The orchestrator scores each candidate on safety relevance, goal relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, and estimated listening load, then releases only the items it judges relevant at that moment through speech, structured audio, or haptic output. We give the selection step a formal statement, specify the orchestration cycle as an algorithm, and define an evaluation protocol against a single-agent assistant. MetaBlind is reported at the design stage, with no prototype measurement or user study, and the protocol states which outcomes would support the design and which would refute it.

AI.tldr: MetaBlind proposes a multi-agent accessibility architecture for BVI users in live virtual worlds, orchestrated by an Accessibility Orchestrator that selectively conveys nonvisual information.
AI.motivation: To overcome fragmented nonvisual access tools by integrating perception, navigation, social/object interaction, communication, safety, memory, and personalization into a single orchestrated accessibility layer for dynamic virtual environments.
AI.method: Divide accessibility tasks among eight specialized agents; use a shared accessibility context; an orchestrator scores candidate information on safety, relevance, urgency, confidence, user relevance, and listening load; release selected items via speech, structured audio, or haptic output; formalize selection as a problem statement and algorithm; propose an evaluation protocol against a single-agent baseline.
AI.result: Design-stage report with no prototype or user study; provides a formal evaluation protocol and criteria to support or refute the design as evidence.
AI.conclusion: MetaBlind outlines a principled, evaluable approach toward integrated nonvisual access in AV environments, though empirical validation remains necessary.

title: Language-Guided Representation Learning for Robust Cross-Sensor Material Recognition
comment: Accepted for presentation at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Robots need touch to manipulate objects safely and reliably, as many properties, such as softness, texture, and contact stability, are hard to infer from vision alone. However, vision-based tactile sensors yield different observations of the same material due to variations in optics, elastomer properties, and illumination, leading to poor generalization when trained on a single or multiple sensors. We propose a language-guided distillation framework for learning sensor-robust tactile representations. Language encodes high-level semantic properties of touch (e.g., rough, soft, slippery) that remain invariant across sensing hardware, providing a natural sensor-agnostic supervisory signal. We construct a 39K-sample touch-language dataset with human-annotated material labels and train a tactile encoder to align sensor-specific tactile images with language embeddings in a shared semantic space. We evaluate our approach for few-shot learning and cross-sensor transfer and benchmark it on six existing tactile datasets. Our method achieves 95% accuracy in the 100-shot setting, improves cross-sensor transfer by an average of 13.3% accuracy, and yields up to 19% accuracy gains across six existing tactile datasets. These results demonstrate that language-guided distillation enables scalable and hardware-agnostic tactile representation learning. Code and dataset are available at https://mashood3624.github.io/Language_Tactile/

AI.tldr: Language-guided distillation aligns sensor-specific tactile images with language embeddings to learn sensor-agnostic tactile representations, enabling strong few-shot and cross-sensor generalization across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Vision-based tactile sensing varies across hardware (optics, elastomer, illumination), causing poor generalization. A hardware-agnostic supervisory signal could mitigate this by grounding tactile semantics in language.
AI.method: Construct a 39k-sample touch-language dataset with human-annotated material labels. Train a tactile encoder to map sensor images into a shared semantic space with language embeddings, enabling alignment with high-level touch properties (e.g., rough, soft, slippery). Evaluate via few-shot learning and cross-sensor transfer across six existing tactile datasets.
AI.result: Achieves 95% accuracy in the 100-shot setting. Cross-sensor transfer improves by an average of 13.3% accuracy. Up to 19% accuracy gains across six tactile datasets. Code and dataset released.
AI.conclusion: Language-guided distillation provides scalable, hardware-agnostic tactile representations that improve generalization across sensors and datasets; a practical approach for robust tactile perception.

title: Event-Level Emotion Recognition in the Wild Using Deep Facial Expression Analysis
comment: The paper has been submitted to IEEE conference
summary: Facial emotion recognition (FER) in real-world environments remains challenging due to unconstrained imaging conditions, including multiple faces, occlusions, pose variations, and complex lighting. Most existing studies focus on individual facial emotion classification and do not address the analysis of collective emotional states at the event level. This paper proposes an end-to-end pipeline for event-level emotion recognition from photographs. The approach detects faces in each image, classifies facial expressions using a deep convolutional neural network, and aggregates face-level emotion probabilities to estimate the overall emotional distribution of a public event. A comparative evaluation of several CNN architectures on the FER- 2013 and RAF-DB datasets demonstrates that transfer learning with EfficientNet-B2 trained on RAF-DB is more suitable for real-world RGB data. The proposed method is evaluated on a real-world event dataset containing 1658 images. Experimental results show stable emotion distributions across event subsets, confirming the effectiveness of event-level aggregation for emotion analysis in the wild.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end event-level emotion recognition pipeline aggregates face-level FER outputs to estimate overall emotional distribution in images; transfer learning with EfficientNet-B2 on RAF-DB yields robust performance in real-world RGB data.
AI.motivation: To analyze collective emotions at the event level under unconstrained conditions, addressing a gap where most FER work targets single-face emotion classification.
AI.method: Face detection per image, CNN-based facial expression classification, and aggregation of face-level probabilities to form an event-level emotion distribution. Comparative evaluation of CNN architectures using FER-2013 and RAF-DB; transfer learning with EfficientNet-B2 pre-trained on RAF-DB. Evaluation on a real-world event dataset of 1658 images.
AI.result: EfficientNet-B2 with RAF-DB transfer learning performs best for real-world RGB data. Event-level aggregation yields stable emotion distributions across event subsets, supporting effectiveness of the approach in the wild.
AI.conclusion: Event-level FER from photographs is feasible and robust when combining face detection, reliable expression classification, and aggregation; transfer learning with RAF-DB improves performance for real-world conditions.

title: Optimal Transport for Efficient, Unsupervised Anomaly Detection on Industrial Data
summary: Effective anomaly detection frameworks are a central pillar of the Industry 4.0 paradigm. In this paper, we introduce an Optimal Transport (OT)-based framework for anomaly detection, designed to detect deviations from normal behaviour in time-series sensor data. The OT-based method requires minimal user input and adapts to real-time data without the need for labelled training data. Our method effectively addresses existing limitations related to data labelling, generalisability, and scalability, demonstrating resilience against short-term fluctuations, noise, and data gaps - common challenges in industrial environments. Additionally, our method provides counterfactual explanations improving the auditability of the approach when deployed in industrial settings. The proposed method learns the mapping between normal and observed operating conditions through a sliding reference window that adapts to the dynamicity of the data. We evaluate our approach on three industrial datasets, from shipping, industrial HVAC systems, and publicly available benchmark data. The method was highly effective in identifying anomalies and reducing false positives, outperforming traditional methods, while maintaining computational efficiency and ease of configuration.

AI.tldr: OT-based, unsupervised anomaly detection for time-series in Industry 4.0 leveraging sliding reference window; robust to noise/gaps, real-time adaptation, counterfactual explanations; outperforms traditional methods on three industrial datasets; scalable and label-efficient.
AI.motivation: Address need for unsupervised, scalable anomaly detection in industrial sensor data with limited labeling, robustness to noise and data gaps, and explainability.
AI.method: Optimal Transport mapping between normal and observed conditions using a sliding reference window; no labeled data; handles nonstationarity; provides counterfactual explanations; designed for streaming data with real-time adaptivity; computationally efficient.
AI.result: High effectiveness in anomaly detection, reduced false positives; outperforms traditional methods; maintains efficiency and ease of configuration; validated on shipping, HVAC, and benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The OT-based framework is a promising, scalable, interpretable approach for Industry 4.0 anomaly detection, reducing labeling requirements and enhancing auditability.

title: OptoAgent: A Trustworthy Multi-Agent Framework for Opportunistic Vision Micro-Screening in Classroom Environments
summary: A child with reduced distance vision often does not know that anything is wrong. Children adapt, move closer, and rarely report the difficulty, so the problem can survive years of schooling before an adult notices. School screening addresses part of this, but it runs on a schedule, depends on staffing, and is separated from the classroom moments where the difficulty appears. Smartphone and web-based acuity tests have widened access, yet every one of them still needs somebody to start a test. We present SightSentinel, an architecture that turns a wall display a child already reads from into a recurring screening site. Ordinary educational content carries short calibrated optotype probes, and eight specialized agents divide the work. Perception agents recover viewing distance, recognition accuracy, approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, and interocular difference from each encounter. A quality agent discards observations taken under bad geometry, poor lighting, or inattention. A longitudinal agent accumulates only the surviving evidence against the child's own baseline, and an orchestrator reports a Vision Concern Score routed through a safety gate whose output range excludes diagnosis, refraction, prescription, and reassurance. The design question is whether many cheap, noisy, well-gated encounters can reach a referral decision that one scheduled test reaches late or misses. We state the formulation, the architecture, a four-stage validation protocol against clinical reference standards, and the conditions under which the approach should be rejected.

AI.tldr: SightSentinel embeds calibrated acuity probes into ordinary classroom content and uses a lightweight, multi-agent system on a wall display to continuously screen a child’s distance vision, aiming to produce timely referral decisions without relying on separate, scheduled tests.
AI.motivation: Many children have reduced distance vision that goes unnoticed due to adaptation and lack of reporting. School screening is infrequent and resource-intensive; smartphone/web tests require initiation. A classroom-integrated, automatic screening could improve early detection and referrals.
AI.method: An architecture that overlays short optotype probes onto wall-mounted reading content. Eight specialized agents handle perception tasks (viewing distance, recognition accuracy, approach behavior, gaze stability, response latency, interocular difference); a quality agent discards observations from bad geometry/lighting/inattention; a longitudinal agent aggregates surviving evidence against the child’s own baseline; an orchestrator emits a Vision Concern Score via a safety gate that prohibits diagnosis, refraction, or reassurance. The system relies on a feedback loop across repeated encounters to accumulate evidence and trigger referrals when needed. A four-stage validation protocol against clinical reference standards is proposed.
AI.result: The paper presents a validation plan consisting of four stages to compare SightSentinel's outputs to clinical reference standards and to specify conditions under which the approach should be rejected. Specific quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The approach raises the possibility that many inexpensive, noisy but well-gated encounters can substitute for a late or missed scheduled test, provided the system’s gating and longitudinal aggregation are robust. The paper outlines criteria for adoption and rejection and calls for rigorous multi-stage validation.

title: Belief-Adaptive Online Autonomy for Quadrotor UAV Navigation under GNSS Degradation in Urban Environments
summary: Reliable online autonomy is critical for quadrotor operation in urban airspaces, where global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) measurements suffer from multipath, blockage, and latency issues, introducing non-stationary, temporally correlated errors that degrade conventional GNSS-IMU fusion. This paper presents a belief-adaptive online autonomy framework that augments an extended Kalman filter (EKF) with explicit GNSS trust modelling, second-order online belief adaptation, and latency-aware out-of-sequence measurement handling. GNSS trust is represented as a latent belief state that modulates measurement weighting and multipath bias uncertainty, and is updated online using EKF consistency signals. Unlike reactive covariance tuning, the proposed approach enables proactive and stable sensor trust adaptation without prior environmental knowledge or offline training. Evaluation in simulated urban air mobility scenarios with correlated multipath, stochastic latency, and obstacle constraints demonstrates improved belief convergence, smoother trajectories, and reduced estimation and tracking errors compared to naive, adaptive, and first-order baselines. The framework preserves classical GNSS-IMU fusion structure and can be integrated directly into existing flight control pipelines, supporting robust online autonomy in GNSS degraded environments.

AI.tldr: A belief-adaptive EKF framework for GNSS-IMU fusion that online models GNSS trust to handle multipath and latency, improving estimation and trajectories in urban quadrotor autonomy without offline training.
AI.motivation: GNSS in urban airspaces suffers multipath, blockage, and latency, causing non-stationary, temporally correlated errors that degrade conventional GNSS-IMU fusion; a robust online method is needed.
AI.method: Augment EKF with latent GNSS trust state, second-order online belief adaptation, and latency-aware out-of-sequence measurement handling; GNSS trust modulates measurement weighting and multipath bias uncertainty and is updated online via EKF consistency signals; preserves classical GNSS-IMU fusion structure for direct integration into flight controllers; no offline training.
AI.result: Simulation-based evaluation in urban air mobility scenarios with correlated multipath, stochastic latency, and obstacle constraints shows improved belief convergence, smoother trajectories, and reduced estimation and tracking errors compared with naive, adaptive, and first-order baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework preserves GNSS-IMU fusion structure and enables robust online autonomy in degraded GNSS environments, with straightforward integration into existing flight control pipelines.

title: Physically Typed and Geometry-Aware Representations for Earth Foundation Models
summary: Earth-observation (EO) foundation models have become exceptionally effective at learning se mantic, high-dimensional geospatial embeddings, while modern weather and climate models have demonstrated that Earth-specific geometry, spherical operators, meshes, and hybrid physical solvers can materially improve prediction. Yet these two advances are not equivalent. A conventional latent embedding has no inherent physical transformation law, whereas scalar fields, tangent polar-vector fields, axial/pseudovector quantities, covectors, and higher-order tensors transform differently under rotations, reflections, and changes of local coordinate frame. This proposal asks whether a general purpose Earth foundation model should preserve those distinctions explicitly, or whether standard embeddings plus augmentation already learn everything that matters. The central contribution is therefore not a more complicated architecture by assumption, but a staged falsification program. A compute-conscious ERA5 dry run first compares conventional, augmentation-matched, typed equivariant, and Hodge/Helmholtz variants under spatial, temporal, orientation, and low-data shifts. Only if explicit geometric typing yields reproducible improvements does the program advance toward a multimodal Earth foundation model in which semantic embeddings coexist with physically typed fields. The proposed gap is narrower and more defensible than claiming that current models ignore geometry entirely: several systems already respect spherical domain geometry, and emerging work explicitly learns scalar/vector fields on spheres. The unresolved question is whether foundation-scale, multimodal, parity-aware field typing produces practical gains beyond those existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Staged falsification to test whether Earth foundation models should explicitly encode geometric field types beyond standard embeddings; compare conventional embeddings, augmentation-matched, typed equivariant, and Hodge/Helmholtz variants, across shifts, before committing to a typed multimodal Earth foundation model.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between semantic Earth-observation embeddings and physics-aware geometry; determine if explicit geometric typing yields practical gains beyond augmentation.
AI.method: Compute-conscious ERA5 dry run; compare conventional embeddings, augmentation-matched, typed equivariant, and Hodge/Helmholtz variants under spatial, temporal, orientation, and low-data shifts; use a staged falsification program to decide progression.
AI.result: Framework for evaluation proposed; no definitive empirical gains claimed yet; notes existing systems that respect spherical geometry and emerging work learning scalar/vector fields on spheres.
AI.conclusion: Whether foundation-scale, parity-aware geometric typing yields practical gains remains unresolved; if gains are demonstrated, advance toward a multimodal Earth foundation model where semantic embeddings coexist with physically typed fields.

title: Hardware-Aware Learned Representation Compression for Distributed In-Sensor Vision
comment: Under submission at IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computing
summary: In-sensor computing reduces the cost of transmitting high-resolution image data by performing early-stage processing near the sensor. However, the logic chip integrated with a CMOS image sensor (CIS) is tightly constrained in compute and memory, limiting conventional deep neural network partitioning. We present OASIS, a distributed in-sensor vision framework that uses a lightweight encoder to generate compact, task-relevant representations before off-chip transmission. The encoder is trained end-to-end using task, entropy, and reconstruction objectives, while the decoder is used only during training. OASIS supports two complementary deployment paths. The first applies 4-bit quantization and Huffman coding while preserving the spatial structure required by classification and dense-prediction tasks. The second uses Sobol-based hyperdimensional computing (HDC) to transform the encoder latent into a fixed-dimensional binary hypervector for associative-memory classification. For the SwinViT-based VWW model, mapping a $3\times3\times8$ latent to a 64-dimensional hypervector provides an additional $1.77\times$ communication reduction with less than one percentage point of accuracy loss relative to the 128-dimensional configuration, yielding an overall $18{,}816\times$ reduction compared with raw 8-bit image transmission. We implement the digital near-sensor pipeline on an AMD Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA and characterize it using direct board-level power measurements and Vivado post-implementation analysis, together with circuit-simulated CIS models and a 7-nm ASIC projection. Across visual wake-word classification, hand tracking, and eye tracking, OASIS reduces total system energy by approximately $2\times$-$4.5\times$ while maintaining competitive accuracy, demonstrating a practical hardware-algorithm co-design path for communication-efficient in-sensor vision.

AI.tldr: OASIS enables near-sensor vision by training a lightweight encoder to produce compact representations, offering two deployment paths (quantization/Huffman and Sobol-based hyperdimensional computing) that dramatically cut off-chip data while preserving accuracy; demonstrated on FPGA/ASIC projections with substantial energy savings and up to ~18,800× data reduction versus raw 8-bit image transmission.
AI.motivation: CIS pipelines face severe compute/memory constraints and incur high data movement costs when sending high-resolution imagery off-chip. A near-sensor, communication-efficient solution is needed that preserves task performance while reducing bandwidth and energy.
AI.method: Train an encoder end-to-end with task, entropy, and reconstruction objectives; the decoder is unused at inference. Two deployment paths: (1) 4-bit quantization with Huffman coding that preserves spatial structure for classification and dense-prediction tasks; (2) Sobol-based hyperdimensional computing (HDC) to map the latent to a fixed-dimensional binary hypervector for associative-memory classification. Evaluation on SwinViT-based VWW; a 3×3×8 latent mapped to a 64-dim hypervector yields 1.77× extra comm reduction over a 128-dim baseline.
AI.result: Achieves up to 18,816× reduction in data transmission compared with raw 8-bit images. The 64-dim hypervector setup provides an additional 1.77× reduction relative to a 128-dim latent while maintaining less than ~1 percentage point accuracy loss. FPGA implementation on AMD Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ validates power and timing; ASIC-level projections (7 nm) indicate viability. Across visual wake-word, hand tracking, and eye tracking tasks, total system energy is reduced by ~2×–4.5× with competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical hardware–algorithm co-design path for communication-efficient in-sensor vision, offering complementary deployment modes that suit different application constraints and showing substantial energy savings without compromising performance.

title: AI Deployment Accountability Engineering: A Vision for Accountable AI in Safety-Critical Socio-Technical Systems
comment: Appeared in ACM AI Summit 26, Atlanta, GA as a vision paper
summary:
Artificial intelligence systems are rapidly becoming critical components in healthcare, finance, public services, and other safety-critical domains. Yet the engineering practices used to evaluate these systems remain predominantly model-centric, emphasizing properties such as accuracy, robustness, fairness, and interpretability before deployment. These properties are necessary but insufficient once an AI system operates within an ever changing socio-technical environment characterized by distribution shifts, institutional constraints, human feedback loops, privacy requirements, and interactions among multiple AI agents.
  This vision paper introduces AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE), a proposed AI engineering subdiscipline concerned with establishing measurable, continuous, and actionable accountability for deployed AI systems. ADAE treats accountability as a deployment-layer property rather than solely as a property of an individual model. It seeks to determine whether an AI-enabled system continues to operate within acceptable risk limits, identify the contexts in which failures emerge, attribute failures across interacting technical and human components, translate technical failures into downstream consequences, and support timely intervention.
  We articulate a research agenda built around four interconnected pillars: structured discovery of context-dependent failure modes, privacy-preserving accountability measurement, system-level risk analysis for agentic AI, and translation of technical failures into operational, and institutional risks. The broader goal is to establish foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures for accountable AI deployment across safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: Proposes AI Deployment Accountability Engineering (ADAE): a deployment-layer discipline to continuously measure and manage accountability of AI systems in safety-critical settings, with four pillars: context-dependent failure discovery, privacy-preserving accountability measurement, system-level risk analysis for agentic AI, and translation of technical failures into operational/institutional risk.
AI.motivation: Model-centric evaluation (accuracy, robustness, fairness, interpretability) is insufficient for deployed AI in dynamic socio-technical environments; there is a need to monitor and manage accountability after deployment under distribution shifts, human feedback loops, privacy constraints, and multi-agent interactions.
AI.method: Vision/perspective paper that defines a new subdiscipline and outlines a four-pillar research agenda; aims to develop foundational principles, mathematical tools, and system architectures for accountable AI deployment.
AI.result: A high-level framework and research agenda rather than empirical results or validated methods.
AI.conclusion: Establish foundational principles, tools, and architectures to enable accountable AI deployment across safety-critical domains.

title: Primitive-Informed Sampling-Based MPC for Multi-Fingered Dexterous Manipulation
summary: We present a primitive-informed sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) framework for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation. Sampling-based MPC avoids the need for gradients through complex contact dynamics, but direct exploration of the high-dimensional joint space is inefficient and makes performance strongly dependent on the sampling distribution. Our framework biases sampling using low-dimensional manipulation primitives that encode coordinated finger motions, while simultaneously optimizing joint-level residuals to adapt these motions to the current hand-object configuration. Task-related rollout constraints reject infeasible trajectories during forward simulation, improving the effective use of the sampling budget. We evaluate the approach on a physical Allegro hand using a synchronized MuJoCo digital twin. Ablations show that both the primitive and residual are necessary for reliable continuous in-hand rotation, that increasing the sampling budget alone does not recover this coordination, and that rollout constraints substantially improve success rate. A primitive extracted from a single object remains effective across object sizes and under model mismatch, and the framework further supports grasping, object reorientation, and coordinated arm-hand reach-grasp-transport, using primitives extracted from both a simulation-trained policy and human hand-motion data.

AI.tldr: A primitive-informed sampling-based MPC framework for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation that biases sampling with low-dimensional coordination primitives while optimizing joint residuals; augmented by rollout constraints to reject infeasible trajectories.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based MPC struggles in high-dimensional, non-smooth contact spaces due to inefficient exploration and dependence on sampling distributions. Injecting domain knowledge via primitives and residual adaptation aims to improve reliability and generalization without gradients.
AI.method: Introduce low-dimensional manipulation primitives to bias the sampling process; jointly optimize joint-level residuals to adapt primitive motions to current hand-object configuration; apply task-related rollout constraints to prune infeasible trajectories during forward simulation; evaluate on a physical Allegro hand with a MuJoCo digital twin; perform ablations to isolate the effects of primitives, residuals, and rollout constraints; primitives derived from simulation-trained policies and human hand data; show cross-object generalization.
AI.result: Ablations show that both the primitive and the residual are necessary for reliable continuous in-hand rotation; simply increasing sampling budget does not recover coordination; rollout constraints substantially improve success rate; a primitive from a single object generalizes across object sizes and under model mismatch; the framework supports grasping, object reorientation, and coordinated arm-hand tasks, using primitives from both simulation data and human motion.
AI.conclusion: Primitive-informed sampling-based MPC with joint residual adaptation and rollout constraints offers robust, generalizable dexterous manipulation, reducing sensitivity to sampling distributions and enabling transfer across objects and tasks; the approach is effective with primitives extracted from diverse sources (simulation or human data) and validated on a physical hand with a digital twin.

title: SkyAnchor: Updating Metric-scale Aerial 3D Gaussian Scenes from Unposed Ground-View Sequences
summary: We study how to update a pre-built aerial scene with a newly captured, unposed ground-view sequence. The aerial scene already contains a reliable metric Structure-from-Motion (SfM) reconstruction and a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model, whereas the ground-view sequence is collected later to add street-level appearance but has unknown camera poses and global scale. Registering this sequence to the aerial SfM reconstruction is challenging because single-image cross-view localization is brittle and long trajectories are prone to drift. To address these challenges, we present SkyAnchor, which treats the existing aerial scene as a fixed scaffold for ground-view registration and scene update instead of jointly reconstructing aerial and ground imagery from scratch. It first localizes short groups of consecutive ground frames against geometrically verified aerial support, producing sparse anchor poses. It then recovers the full ground trajectory with anchor-constrained submaps, fixing the front and rear anchor poses during incremental registration and bundle adjustment. Finally, it inserts filtered ground Gaussians while preserving the aerial view, followed by lightweight joint refinement. Experiments on seven real aerial--ground scenes show accurate metric ground trajectories and updated 3D Gaussian scenes with strong aerial- and ground-view rendering quality.

AI.tldr: SkyAnchor updates an aerial scene with a newly captured, unposed ground-view sequence by anchoring ground frames to the aerial scaffold via anchor poses and anchor-constrained submaps, enabling accurate ground trajectories and consistent 3D Gaussian updates without full joint reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To efficiently fuse ground-view appearance into an existing aerial SfM and 3DGS while mitigating pose/scale ambiguity and drift inherent in cross-view registration of long sequences.
AI.method: 1) Localize short groups of ground frames against aerial support to obtain sparse anchors with geometric verification. 2) Recover full ground trajectory using anchor-constrained submaps; fix front and rear anchors during incremental registration and bundle adjustment. 3) Insert filtered ground Gaussians into the 3DGS while preserving aerial view, followed by lightweight joint refinement.
AI.result: Seven real aerial–ground scenes show accurate metric ground trajectories and updated 3D Gaussian scenes with strong rendering quality for both aerial and ground views.
AI.conclusion: SkyAnchor provides a practical, scaffold-based registration workflow that avoids end-to-end joint reconstruction, improving integration of ground-view data into existing aerial reconstructions with accurate metrics and high-quality rendering.

title: Linear Ensemble Sampling with Smaller Ensembles
summary: Ensemble sampling offers a practical approach to randomized exploration by maintaining a collection of models, but how small an ensemble can be while retaining strong regret guarantees remains unresolved. In particular, the existing guarantees use an ensemble size of $Θ(d\log T)$, leaving a logarithmic gap in the horizon $T$ relative to the intrinsic $Ω(d)$ ensemble-size barrier. We aim to narrow this gap by proposing an ensemble sampling algorithm that refreshes the ensemble only when the regularized Gram matrix changes substantially. This mechanism localizes the perturbation analysis to epochs with controlled Gram-matrix drift and reduces the sufficient ensemble size to $Θ(d\log d+d\log\log T)$, while preserving the state-of-the-art $\tilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt T)$ regret for ensemble sampling with arbitrary bounded arm sets. We further show that, when the arm set is finite of cardinality $K$, the proposed algorithm achieves the sharper regret bound $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T\log K})$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first ensemble-sampling guarantee that simultaneously recovers both canonical regret scalings known for randomized linear bandit algorithms: the $\tilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt{T})$ rate for arbitrary bounded arm sets and the $\tilde O (d\sqrt{T\log K})$ rate for finite arm sets. The algorithm also admits an anytime implementation without resetting past data, and experiments show that it remains competitive with baselines while using substantially smaller ensembles.

AI.tldr: Adaptive ensemble sampling with epoch-based Gram-matrix-triggered refresh reduces the required ensemble size while preserving key regret guarantees: Õ(d^{3/2}√T) for arbitrary bounded arms and Õ(d√(T log K)) for finite K; includes an anytime variant and empirical validation with smaller ensembles.
AI.motivation: Close the gap between the ensemble-size lower bound Ω(d) and the prior Θ(d log T) regret guarantees for ensemble sampling in linear bandits; unify canonical regret scalings within a single ensemble-sampling framework.
AI.method: Refresh the ensemble only when the regularized Gram matrix changes substantially, localizing perturbation analysis to epochs with controlled Gram-matrix drift. This yields a reduced ensemble size Θ(d log d + d log log T) while maintaining the state-of-the-art regret. Proves regret bounds for both arbitrary and finite arm sets and provides an anytime implementation without data resets.
AI.result: Regret guarantees: Õ(d^{3/2}√T) for arbitrary bounded arm sets; Õ(d√(T log K)) when the arm set is finite of size K. Demonstrates an anytime version and empirical results showing competitive performance with substantially smaller ensembles.
AI.conclusion: First ensemble-sampling analysis that simultaneously achieves the canonical regret scalings for randomized linear bandits, with practical benefits from smaller ensemble sizes and an anytime, reset-free implementation.

title: A note on goal-based hierarchical RL
summary:
The agent-centric general value function (ACGVF) construction of
  \citet{tasse2026goal} lets the agent make two decisions that are
  normally imposed by the environment or agent designer: which goal to
  pursue and when to declare a goal as finished (in addition to
  choosing the action). This is a very general framework that
  subsumes almost all prior work on reinforcement learning, control
  and planning, as well as more general formalisms proposed in the
  cognitive sciences. However, it assumes the environment is fully
  observed, i.e., that the observation is a sufficient statistic. In
  \citet{murphy2025rl}, a general agent design was proposed where the
  policy is based on an internal belief state $z_t$ and an internal
  goal; however, the goals were assumed to be externally provided. In
  this note, we unify and extend these two approaches using the
  formalism of hierarchical hidden Markov models (HHMM) \citep{murphy2001hhmm}.

AI.tldr: Agent-centric GVF generalizes decision-making to goal selection and termination; but assumes full observability; this note unifies with hierarchical hidden Markov models to incorporate internal beliefs and partial observability.
AI.motivation: Relax full observability and unify prior approaches (ACGVF and internal-belief-goal design) under a single probabilistic framework using HHMMs.
AI.method: Formulate the agent design as a hierarchical hidden Markov model that jointly captures action policy, internal belief state z_t, and internal goals, enabling integration of goal choice and termination with planning under partial observability.
AI.result: The note presents a unified HHMM-based framework that extends ACGVF and internally-goal-driven designs to partially observable settings; theoretical mapping and construction, with anticipated applicability but no empirical results in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: HHMM-based unification broadens the scope of agent-centric planning by explicitly modeling internal beliefs and goals across hierarchical levels, enabling more general decision-making under partial information; future work includes inference, learning, and scalable algorithms.

title: Real-World Reinforcement Learning with MPC Scaffolding for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising route to dexterous manipulation policies that can adapt directly from physical interaction, but learning is hindered by inefficient early exploration and costly failures. We propose a framework that uses sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) as scaffolding for real-world dexterous RL, providing structured prior experience and task-directed guidance during learning without human demonstrations or corrective actions. A small set of MPC trajectories is first used to populate an offline replay buffer and to pretrain the actor and critic. During online learning, MPC intermittently guides data collection while an off-policy Soft Actor-Critic learner trains from both prior MPC experience and newly collected physical interaction, with control gradually transitioning to the learned policy. On continuous in-hand rotation with a 16-DoF Allegro hand, the method reaches 100\% success in policy-only evaluation (5/5 trials) after 7 minutes of online RL, following initialization with 20 MPC trajectories collected on hardware in 12 minutes. Online training incurs about three object drops on average. After 20 minutes of online learning, the policy achieves more than five times the rotation speed of the MPC controller. It completes 1000 consecutive rotations over more than 110 minutes without a drop. Ablations show complementary benefits from MPC-based pretraining, retained MPC experience, and online MPC guidance. We further demonstrate rapid adaptation to different object geometries and successful goal-conditioned reorientation, showing that the framework enables efficient, low-intervention, real-world dexterous RL.

AI.tldr: MPC-guided real-world dexterous RL using offline MPC pretraining and online MPC-guided data collection with SAC, achieving rapid, high-success manipulation on a 16-DoF hand without demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous manipulation suffers from poor early exploration and costly failures; a framework providing structured prior experience and task-directed learning without human demonstrations is needed.
AI.method: Seed offline buffer with a small set of sampling-based MPC trajectories to pretrain actor/critic. During online learning, intermittently use MPC to guide data collection while an off-policy Soft Actor-Critic learns from both MPC experiences and new physical interaction, gradually transferring control to the learned policy. Retain MPC data in replay to preserve guidance.
AI.result: On a 16-DoF Allegro hand for in-hand rotation: policy-only evaluation reaches 5/5 success after 7 minutes of online RL (20 MPC trajectories collected on hardware in 12 minutes). Online training averages ~3 drops. After 20 minutes, policy rotates >5× faster than the MPC controller and completes 1000 consecutive rotations over 110+ minutes with no drop.
AI.conclusion: MPC scaffolding, via pretraining, retained MPC experience, and online MPC guidance, enables efficient, low-intervention real-world dexterous RL with rapid adaptation to object geometry and goal-conditioned tasks.

title: BLInD: Learning Driver Intent as a Distribution over Future Ego Trajectories
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
summary: We present BLInD (Blind Learned Intent Distribution), a compact network that maps recent vehicle-state history (e.g. speed, curvature, indicator, and vehicle type) to a top-k distribution of future ego trajectories, with no camera, LiDAR, map, or object-track inputs. We find that vehiclestate history alone is sufficient to learn a useful multimodal distribution over near-term ego trajectories, and its low-latency nature makes it well-suited for safety-critical deployment. We investigate two distribution architectures, autoregressive (AR) and flow-matching, and train on both mixed-platform opensource and Wayve datasets. Both generalize without datasetspecific adaptation; the flow-matching model achieves best topk ADE/FDE of 0.15/0.37 m on Wayve, 0.15/0.36 m on Waymo, and 0.28/0.59 m on nuScenes, with the AR model reaching comparable coverage. Integrating the distributions into an AEB trigger task, a strict all-candidates policy reduces false positives from 1.51% to 0.11% with AR (13.7x reduction, 94.9% TP) and to 0.06% with flow-matching (25.1x reduction, 98.7% TP) compared to a 1-CTRV policy with 100% true positive score. BLInD runs in 0.87 ms with the AR head and 2.9 ms with the flow-matching head on an NVIDIA DRIVE Orin ECU making it compatible with real-time deployment on automotive ECUs. While existing learned distribution models rely on scene context and blind vehicle-state models typically collapse to a single path, BLInD is learned, blind, and cross-domain simultaneously, a combination not demonstrated by prior work. These results show that such a distribution provides a controllable and plausible intent sampling interface for downstream systems, with AEB as one instantiation.

AI.tldr: BLInD is a compact, blind learned distribution model that maps recent vehicle-state history to a top-k set of near-term ego trajectories using autoregressive and flow-matching architectures. It achieves accurate, multimodal predictions without scene inputs and runs in real time, improving AEB decision quality and generalizing cross-domain across datasets.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether vehicle-state history alone can yield a useful multimodal distribution over near-term ego trajectories, enabling low-latency, safety-critical planning without reliance on cameras, LiDAR, maps, or object tracks.
AI.method: Two distribution architectures are trained on mixed-platform open-source and Wayve datasets using only vehicle-state history (speed, curvature, indicators, vehicle type). They generate a top-k distribution of futures (multimodal) and are evaluated for accuracy (ADE/FDE) and latency. The AEB integration uses a strict all-candidates policy to measure false positives and true positives.
AI.result: Flow-matching achieves the best top-k ADE/FDE (Wayve 0.15/0.37 m; Waymo 0.15/0.36 m; nuScenes 0.28/0.59 m). AR offers comparable coverage. Inference times are 0.87 ms (AR) and 2.9 ms (flow-matching) on NVIDIA DRIVE Orin. AEB triggers reduce false positives from 1.51% (baseline) to 0.11% (AR) and 0.06% (flow); both achieve high TP (94.9% and 98.7%). Generalizes across datasets without adaptation.
AI.conclusion: BLInD demonstrates that a compact, blind, cross-domain learned distribution over ego trajectories is feasible and useful for safety-critical systems, offering a controllable, plausible intent-sampling interface for downstream modules such as AEB.

title: Tabby: An Open Pretraining Recipe for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: In this report, we release Tabby, a long context probabilistic time series foundation model, together with a complete and open recipe of how it was built. Tabby adopts an encoder-only patch Transformer architecture and concentrates the contributions on the data and the training procedure. The pretraining corpus combines an extended real-world collection, GIFT-Eval-Pretrain+ and BLAST, with synthetic data from KernelSynth and CauKerV2, an online generator that composes temporal dynamics through randomly sampled structural causal models. Training couples a progressive convergence schedule, which yields reusable intermediate checkpoints, with a deep quantile supervision objective for intermediate layers. The resulting 145M parameter backbone supports contexts of up to 8,192 observations and serves forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, while a prompt-tuning module further improves in-distribution forecasting performance with the pretrained weights frozen. Tabby achieves competitive zero-shot forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval and the out-of-distribution TIME benchmark, while the same pretrained backbone also supports classification on the UCR Archive and zero-shot anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. We release training pipeline and model as open source at huawei-noah/trustworthyAI.

AI.tldr: Tabby is a 145M-parameter long-context time series foundation model (8k context) using an encoder-only patch Transformer, trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with progressive convergence and deep quantile supervision, enabling forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, plus a prompt-tuning module; achieves competitive zero-shot results and is open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Address the need for a versatile, long-context time series foundation model that can support forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, and that is reproducible via an open training recipe and data mix (real + synthetic).
AI.method: Encoder-only patch Transformer backbone (145M params) with context up to 8,192; pretraining on an expanded real-world corpus (GIFT-Eval-Pretrain+, BLAST) plus synthetic data (KernelSynth, CauKerV2) generated via an online temporal dynamics engine using random structural causal models. Training employs a progressive convergence schedule with reusable intermediate checkpoints and a deep quantile supervision objective for intermediate layers. A prompt-tuning module, with pretrained weights frozen, further improves in-distribution forecasting.
AI.result: The model yields a versatile backbone for forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, with competitive zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and TIME; the pretrained backbone also enables classification on the UCR Archive and zero-shot anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. The work accompanies an open-source release of training pipeline and model at Huawei's trust-worthyAI repository.
AI.conclusion: Tabby demonstrates that combining a moderately large, long-context Transformer with a data-centric training recipe and progressive supervision can produce a practical, multi-task time series foundation model that performs well out of the box on several benchmarks and supports efficient fine-tuning via prompt-tuning on frozen weights.

title: DynSTEER: Dynamic Stage-wise Trajectory Evaluation and Execution-time Review for Agents
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon task execution. However, current evaluation paradigms face three major limitations: terminal-only assessment ignores intermediate processes and struggles to localize errors efficiently and accurately, single-reference matching penalizes valid alternative solution paths, and post-hoc trajectory judging incurs high costs without the ability to halt failed runs early. To address these issues, we propose DynSTEER, a dynamic stage-wise trajectory evaluation framework for agents. DynSTEER segments rollouts into stages anchored by key completed actions, focusing evaluation on essential milestones with adequate context while enabling targeted strategy adjustments. It compiles a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views to respect diverse legitimate strategies without leaking ground truth. Furthermore, it adaptively routes evaluation queries across multi-tier judges and halts unrecoverable executions online to curb resource waste. Experiments demonstrate that DynSTEER improves evaluation discriminability across LLM agents by 85.2\% over native evaluation, separates all model pairs with statistical significance, and saves 34.51\% of execution steps on failed rollouts.

AI.tldr: DynSTEER offers dynamic stage-wise evaluation for long-horizon LLM agents, addressing terminal-only evaluation, single-path matching, and post-hoc cost via milestone-based, path-tolerant, multi-tier judgments with online halting.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation paradigms fail to localize errors, penalize legitimate alternative strategies, and waste compute; thus there is a need for incremental, robust evaluation with early stopping.
AI.method: Segment rollouts into stages anchored by key actions; construct a path-tolerant milestone graph from public task views; route evaluation queries across multi-tier judges; on-the-fly halt of unrecoverable runs; focus computation on critical milestones with sufficient context.
AI.result: Empirical results show 85.2% improvement in discriminability vs native evaluation; all model pairs are separable with statistical significance; 34.51% reduction in steps for failed rollouts.
AI.conclusion: DynSTEER yields more discriminative, fair, and resource-efficient evaluation; enables targeted strategy adjustment and early termination; the milestone graph supports diverse legitimate strategies and reduces wasted compute.

title: HydroMap: Probabilistic Water Surface Elevation Mapping for Semantic Scene Representation in Inland Waterways
summary: Autonomous surface vehicles operating in inland waterways require a persistent representation of both surrounding structures and the water surface.
