LiDAR-based simultaneous localization and mapping often produces sparse or missing water returns, leaving this operational surface absent from the reconstructed scene. We propose HydroMap, an odometry-decoupled framework that reconstructs water surface elevation from stereo observations and integrates it with the structural map. Per-frame water points form joint cell observations with propagated stereo and pose uncertainty, and successive observations are fused into a persistent probabilistic elevation map. Semantic map conversion then combines the elevation map with structural geometry in a unified 2.5D representation of water, boundaries, structures, and overhead regions. On the Pohang Canal and Leuven Vaart datasets, the elevation RMSE remains below 5 cm relative to LiDAR references expressed in the same map frame. The elevation and semantic maps are published at 2 Hz and 1 Hz, respectively. HydroMap thereby complements LiDAR maps with a persistent representation of the water surface for downstream navigation in inland waterways.

AI.tldr: HydroMap provides an odometry-decoupled framework that fuses stereo-derived water surface elevations with a structural map to create a persistent 2.5D representation for inland-waterway navigation. It achieves cm-level elevation accuracy (<5 cm RMSE) and publishes elevation and semantic maps at 2 Hz and 1 Hz, respectively, on canal datasets.
AI.motivation: LiDAR SLAM often yields sparse/missing water returns on inland waterways, leaving water surfaces underrepresented in maps. A persistent water-surface representation is needed for reliable navigation.
AI.method: HydroMap reconstructs water surface elevation from stereo observations decoupled from odometry. Per-frame water points are fused as joint observations with propagated stereo and pose uncertainty into a persistent probabilistic elevation map. Semantic map conversion then yields a unified 2.5D map of water, boundaries, structures, and overhead regions.
AI.result: Elevation RMSE remains below 5 cm relative to LiDAR references in the same map frame on Pohang Canal and Leuven Vaart datasets. Elevation and semantic maps are published at 2 Hz and 1 Hz, respectively.
AI.conclusion: HydroMap complements LiDAR maps by adding a persistent water-surface representation, enabling improved downstream navigation for inland waterways.

title: SGWIB:Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein Information Bottleneck for Video Highlight Detection
summary: Video highlight detection aims to identify temporally important segments that capture the most informative or engaging events in a video. Reliable prediction therefore requires not only discriminative segment representations but also preservation of the temporal relationships among neighboring and distant segments. The information bottleneck principle has proven effective for learning compact and task-relevant representations, yet it has not been explored for video highlight detection, and applying conventional formulations directly would overlook inter-segment relational structure and distort highlight relevant temporal organization during compression. We therefore introduce the Sliced Gromov-Monge Gap (SGMG), a structure aware regularizer that measures the excess relational distortion induced by a prescribed source-to-bottleneck mapping relative to an optimal sliced structural correspondence. Building on SGMG, we develop SGWIB, an information-bottleneck framework for single-modal video highlight detection that learns compact bottleneck representations while preserving inter-segment temporal structure. We further introduce Home-Away-Related Contextual Pseudo-Labels and a contextual disentanglement module that reduce sports-specific contextual bias by separating highlight oriented information from contextual patterns. Experiments on MrHiSum and MoSu show that SGWIB attains the best Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, mAP@50, and mAP@30 among the compared single-modal methods on both datasets. On MrHiSum, the visual model improves the strongest previous results by 0.031, 0.031, 0.87, and 0.75 on these four metrics, respectively. These results show that structure-aware information-bottleneck regularization combined with contextual disentanglement improves segment-level highlight prediction.

AI.tldr: Introduces SGMG as a structure-aware information bottleneck regularizer for video highlight detection, enabling SGWIB with contextual disentanglement to preserve temporal segment relationships and achieve state-of-the-art single-modal performance on MrHiSum and MoSu.
AI.motivation: Preserve temporal relationships among video segments while learning compact representations; conventional information bottleneck lacks inter-segment relational structure and distorts highlight-relevant temporal organization during compression.
AI.method: Propose Sliced Gromov-Monge Gap (SGMG) as a structure-aware regularizer; build SGWIB information-bottleneck framework for single-modal video highlight detection; introduce Home-Away-Related Contextual Pseudo-Labels and a contextual disentanglement module to reduce sports-specific contextual bias.
AI.result: SGWIB achieves the best Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, mAP@50, and mAP@30 among compared single-modal methods on MrHiSum and MoSu. On MrHiSum, the visual model improves previous best scores by 0.031, 0.031, 0.87, and 0.75 across the four metrics.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware information-bottleneck regularization combined with contextual disentanglement improves segment-level highlight prediction and outperforms prior single-modal methods on the tested datasets.

title: Data-Efficient Agentic Graph Domain Adaptation via Reliability-Aware Prototype Learning
summary: Agentic learning systems are often required to adapt after deployment by observing new data and reusing prior knowledge under limited supervision or feedback. For graph-structured prediction, Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA) naturally instantiates this setting by transferring knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled target graphs under distribution shifts. However, most GDA methods assume sufficient labeled source graphs, which becomes restrictive in data-efficient agentic settings where only limited source evidence can be retained. Under such constraints, source semantics become unreliable, leading to unstable source anchoring, uncertain target association, and fragile targetmarginal calibration. To address these challenges, we propose DEAG, a reliability-aware prototype learning framework for data-efficient agentic GDA. DEAG estimates class reliability from retained source support and embedding compactness, and constructs stable reusable source anchors by blending empirical prototypes with classifier directions. Guided by these anchors, DEAG performs prototype-aware soft target association and aligns confidence-weighted target centers with source semantics. A source-prior regularizer further sharpens target predictions while keeping the target marginal consistent with retained source evidence. Experiments on graph benchmarks with diverse domain shifts show that DEAG improves average adaptation performance over competitive GDA baselines under the same source-data budget.

AI.tldr: DEAG is a reliability-aware prototype learning framework for data-efficient graph domain adaptation (GDA) that improves cross-domain graph prediction under limited source data by using reliability-estimated prototypes, stable source anchors, prototype-aware target association, and a source-prior regularizer.
AI.motivation: Agentic learning with limited supervision requires robust GDA despite unreliable source semantics; existing methods fail under constrained source evidence leading to unstable anchors and miscalibrated targets.
AI.method: DEAG estimates class reliability from retained source support and embedding compactness; builds stable reusable source anchors by blending empirical prototypes with classifier directions; performs prototype-aware soft target association; aligns confidence-weighted target centers with source semantics; uses a source-prior regularizer to sharpen predictions while keeping target marginals consistent with retained source evidence.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on graph benchmarks with diverse domain shifts shows DEAG achieves higher average adaptation performance than competitive GDA baselines under the same source-data budget.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware prototype learning with stable anchors and target alignment enables robust, data-efficient GDA and improves average adaptation under limited source data.

title: Diffusion-Based Generation of Gait Trajectories
comment: International Conference on NeuroRehabilitation (ICNR2026), September 29-October 2, 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Generation of musculoskeletal gait trajectories conditioned on patient-specific parameters remains a key challenge for wearable robotics and rehabilitation. Assistive systems such as lower-limb exoskeletons require reference trajectories that adapt to individual morphology and therapeutic goals while preserving biomechanical realism. Traditional approaches rely on hand-crafted gait templates or optimization procedures that scale poorly across subjects and walking conditions. In this work, we explore conditional diffusion models for generating lower-limb joint-angle trajectories conditioned on gait parameters such as step length. We compare a baseline transformer diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer variant incorporating adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance. Experiments on a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles show that diffusion models can generate realistic periodic gait trajectories while enabling some controllability variation in gait characteristics, highlighting their potential for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics.

AI.tldr: Conditional diffusion models can generate patient-specific lower-limb gait trajectories, offering some controllable variation in gait parameters while maintaining biomechanical realism. A baseline transformer diffusion model is compared to a controllable diffusion transformer with adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance; trained on 4,590 gait cycles, showing promise for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics.
AI.motivation: Need for adaptable, biomechanically realistic reference trajectories for wearable robotics that generalize across subjects and walking conditions; traditional templates/optimizations are limited in scalability and personalization.
AI.method: Compare a baseline transformer diffusion model with a controllable diffusion transformer variant that uses adaptive normalization and classifier-free guidance. Train on a dataset of 4,590 gait cycles, conditioning on gait parameters such as step length to generate lower-limb joint-angle trajectories.
AI.result: Diffusion models produce realistic, periodic gait trajectories and enable controllable variation in gait characteristics. The controllable variant offers added control through adaptive normalization and guidance strategies.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based generative modeling is a promising approach for personalized gait synthesis in assistive robotics, with potential extensions to improve controllability, realism, and real-time applicability across diverse subjects and walking conditions.

title: Exact Feasibility Certification and Optimal Responsibility Allocation for Multi-Robot CBF Safety Filters
summary: Multi-robot Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety filters can become infeasible, but a failed quadratic program (QP) does not indicate why the conflict occurred or how to resolve it. To address this, we develop an exact feasibility certificate for multi-agent CBF filters with heterogeneous control-affine dynamics and convex input sets. The certificate quantifies a feasibility reserve by separating the demand imposed by safety constraints from the available actuator supply. This decomposition shows when CBF gain tuning or increased actuation can and cannot resolve infeasibility, and identifies the agents and interactions responsible for the conflict. We further propose an algorithm to optimally allocate shared safety constraints by maximizing the worst local feasibility margin, yielding a linear program for polyhedral input sets. In $320$ paired closed-loop simulations, the proposed allocation reduces infeasible control steps from roughly $50\%$ to $6.2\%$, and reduces safety-violating runs from $118/160$ to $24/160$. In addition, across $52$ infeasibility events, the certificate identifies an interaction whose relaxation restores feasibility in $94\%$ of cases.

AI.tldr: Exact feasibility certificate for multi-agent CBF safety filters with heterogeneous control-affine dynamics and convex input sets; decomposes feasibility into demand vs supply, enabling identification of conflicts and optimal allocation of shared safety constraints.
AI.motivation: In multi-robot safety filtering, QP-based CBFs can become infeasible without indicating the cause or remedy; there is a need to diagnose feasibility margins and provide actionable guidance.
AI.method: Derive an exact feasibility certificate that quantifies feasibility reserve by separating safety-demand from actuator-supply for heterogeneous, control-affine agents with convex input sets. Propose an algorithm to optimally allocate shared safety constraints by maximizing the worst local feasibility margin, yielding a linear program for polyhedral input sets.
AI.result: The approach reduces infeasible control steps from ~50% to 6.2% in 320 paired simulations, and safety-violating runs from 118/160 to 24/160; across 52 infeasibility events, the certificate identifies an interaction whose relaxation recovers feasibility in 94% of cases.
AI.conclusion: The feasibility certificate provides diagnostic insight, enabling targeted gain tuning or actuation increases, and identifies responsible agents/interactions; the allocation algorithm yields substantial practical improvements in multi-robot safety filtering.

title: Zero-Shot Cross-Material Ptychographic Phase Reconstruction Using Deep Learning
summary: Ptychographic phase reconstruction is commonly formulated as an iterative inverse problem, requiring repeated object-probe updates and resulting in substantial computational cost for large-scale 4D-STEM data. We present a direct local-to-global learning framework that reconstructs full-field phase maps from diffraction measurements without iterative refinement during inference. The proposed network predicts local wrapped-phase patches from individual diffraction patterns using a sine-cosine representation, and the predictions are assembled into a full-field reconstruction using calibrated scan positions and Gaussian-weighted stitching. To evaluate generalization beyond the training domain, the model is trained on one material and directly applied to another in a zero-shot setting without target-domain fine-tuning. Experiments on AuPd and MoS$_2$ demonstrate consistent cross-material transfer in both directions, with the proposed method achieving the best full-field MSE, PSNR, and MS-SSIM among the evaluated learning-based methods. Compared with the iterative ePIE approach, the proposed direct local-to-global pipeline reduces end-to-end reconstruction time by approximately 10x, demonstrating its potential for efficient and transferable ptychographic reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Direct local-to-global learning framework for ptychographic phase reconstruction: predicts local wrapped-phase patches from diffraction patterns with sine-cosine representation, stitches into full-field maps using scan positions and Gaussian weighting; achieves zero-shot cross-material transfer (AuPd, MoS2), best learning-based full-field metrics, and ~10x speedup over ePIE.
AI.motivation: Reduce computational cost of iterative ptychographic reconstruction on large-scale 4D-STEM data and enable rapid, transferable phase reconstruction without iterative refinement during inference.
AI.method: A neural network predicts local wrapped-phase patches from individual diffraction patterns using a sine-cosine phase representation. Local patches are stitched into a full-field reconstruction using calibrated scan positions and Gaussian-weighted blending. The model is trained on one material and evaluated in zero-shot transfer to another material without target-domain fine-tuning.
AI.result: Experiments on AuPd and MoS2 show consistent cross-material transfer in both directions. The method achieves the best full-field MSE, PSNR, and MS-SSIM among evaluated learning-based methods and reduces end-to-end reconstruction time by about 10x compared to the iterative ePIE approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed direct local-to-global learning pipeline provides efficient, transferable ptychographic reconstruction with strong cross-material generalization and substantial speed gains over traditional iterative methods.

title: Stabilizing Performative Feedback Loops with Minimal Model Deployments
summary:
When algorithmic predictions inform people's decisions, the models we deploy are performative and actively shape the data we see. This feedback loop between algorithms and their broader environments introduces a challenge in the mechanics of social prediction: If different predictive models induce different distributions, is it possible to efficiently learn a prediction rule that is optimal for the distribution that it induces? Formally, this solution concept is known as performative stability. A core challenge in learning a performatively stable predictor is that, unlike supervised learning where distributions are fixed, the learner must deploy different predictors and observe their induced distributions.
  The main contribution of our work is a new algorithmic procedure that, in the high-accuracy regime, finds a performatively stable model in nearly the minimum number of model deployments without making any assumptions regarding how predictions shape distributions. In particular, our procedure succeeds at finding a randomized performatively stable predictor using exponentially fewer model deployments than prior approaches. Our second main contribution is a structural result showing how this recent randomized notion of stability achieved by our algorithm can be derandomized into a single predictor satisfying the prior deterministic notion if one is willing to assume that the loss is well-conditioned and that performative effects are weak, as in early work in this area. On a technical level, our results come from building on an underexplored technical connection between performative stability and expected variational inequalities.

AI.tldr: A procedure to learn performatively stable predictors with near-minimal model deployments, via a randomized stability framework, and a derandomization result under mild assumptions using a variational-inequality connection.
AI.motivation: In performative prediction, predictions shape distributions; learning must account for feedback loops and distributional shift. The challenge is to find a predictor that is optimal for the distribution it induces, requiring efficient interaction (deployments). Prior work needs many deployments and assumes specific distribution-shaping models; a distribution-agnostic, sample-efficient method is desirable.
AI.method: Introduce a new algorithmic procedure that, in the high-accuracy regime, finds a performatively stable model with nearly minimal deployments. It leverages a randomized notion of stability and exploits a crucial link between performative stability and expected variational inequalities to drive learning.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves exponentially fewer model deployments than prior approaches to obtain a randomized performatively stable predictor. Additionally, a structural result shows that, under well-conditioned loss and weak performativity, the randomized stability can be derandomized into a single deterministic predictor, aligning with early deterministic notions of performative stability.
AI.conclusion: The work advances performative prediction by delivering a practically and theoretically efficient method for finding stable predictors and by bridging randomized and deterministic stability through a variational-inequality perspective.

title: Lightning Weave: Improving the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier of Reasoning Models through Capability Composition
summary: A core goal of efficient reasoning is to improve the accuracy-efficiency frontier. However, jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency can be challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors. Independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in accuracy and efficiency. We introduce Lightning Weave, a post-training framework that extracts and composes these independently learned capabilities in a single student through on-policy distillation. Each acquired capability is represented by the policy shift from the model before post-training to the resulting specialist. Lightning Weave combines aligned log-ratio shifts at shared student token states and uses Tilted-Target DOPD to convert the cached signals into a stable learning target. Each anchor pair scores the cached trajectories once, enabling subsequent student training without serving multiple live anchor models concurrently. Across diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave substantially improves upon the base students and achieves a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency frontier. On Qwen3.5-4B, it raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer response tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the anchor signals yields a strong empirical accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier. These results establish Lightning Weave as a new practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: Lightning Weave is a post-training framework that composes independently learned accuracy- and efficiency-focused capabilities into a single student via on-policy distillation, using policy-shift anchors and Tilted-Target DOPD, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency frontiers on math and code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency is challenging because the objectives favor different behaviors; independent post-training offers complementary strengths, but combining them in one model requires a principled, stable method.
AI.method: Represent each acquired capability as the policy shift from the base model to a specialist; align log-ratio shifts at shared token states; use Tilted-Target DOPD to convert signals into stable learning targets; score each anchor pair once per trajectory, enabling training from cached signals without running multiple live anchors; train a single student to blend capabilities by adjusting anchor strengths to trade accuracy for efficiency.
AI.result: Across diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave improves base students and yields a strong accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier; on Qwen3.5-4B, HMMT 2025 accuracy rises from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7% fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy rises from 41.7% to 54.2% with 9.6% fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: Lightning Weave provides a practical route to efficient reasoning through capability composition, enabling tunable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs; the approach establishes a state-of-the-art frontier and will have code released soon.

title: Comparing Trajectories from Positions Alone: Curvature-Based Time Alignment and Drift Error Metric
summary: In field robotics, acquiring independent large-scale reference trajectories more accurate than the evaluated estimates remains an open challenge. The domain is widely reliant on Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE), computed with automated tools, that rest on assumptions and evaluation parameters rarely made explicit. When unreported, the errors can be misleading and hinder fair comparisons. This paper introduces a trajectory-evaluation protocol for standardized and reliable accuracy assessment in state estimation, localization, and Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). The approach combines a novel temporal alignment method based on curvature signals with an error metric normalized by travelled distance. We explicitly account for temporal synchronization, sampling alignment, and extrinsic calibration, quantifying their influence through a sensitivity analysis. The proposed protocol contributes to more rigorous, reproducible, and standardized trajectory evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a standardized trajectory-evaluation protocol for state estimation, localization, and SLAM that uses curvature-based temporal alignment and distance-normalized errors, with explicit handling of synchronization, sampling, and extrinsic calibration through sensitivity analysis.
AI.motivation: Current ATE/RPE tools rely on opaque assumptions and unreported parameters, leading to misleading comparisons and poor reproducibility in field robotics trajectory evaluation.
AI.method: Introduce a trajectory-evaluation protocol combining (i) a curvature-signal based temporal alignment, (ii) an error metric normalized by travelled distance, and (iii) a sensitivity analysis that quantifies the effects of temporal synchronization, sampling alignment, and extrinsic calibration.
AI.result: The abstract claims improved rigor, reproducibility, and standardization in trajectory evaluation through the proposed protocol; no concrete experimental results are stated in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The protocol advances rigorous, reproducible, and standardized trajectory evaluation for state estimation, localization, and SLAM by addressing synchronization, sampling, and calibration factors.

title: Mind2Cloud: EEG-to-Point Cloud Generation with Two-Granularity Diffusion Decoding
comment: European Conference on Computer Vision -- ECCV 2026
summary: Reconstructing 3D objects from brain signals offers a promising avenue for understanding human visual cognition. While prior work has shown initial success using EEG signals for 3D reconstruction, existing methods typically employ a uniform diffusion decoder, overlooking the evolving semantic granularity of both EEG representations and the diffusion denoising process. In this paper, we propose Mind2Cloud, a novel EEG-to-point-cloud generation framework based on two-granularity diffusion decoding. The core of Mind2Cloud is a time-aware decoder that integrates a global Transformer branch and a local Point-Voxel CNN (PVCNN) branch across diffusion timesteps through a learnable fusion mask. Specifically, Transformer layers are incorporated into the early upsampling stages to capture global object structure under high uncertainty, while PVCNN modules are used in later stages to refine local geometric details. Inspired by the hierarchical nature of EEG-based visual representations, this design dynamically adapts its spatial granularity in accordance with the coarse-to-fine trajectory of diffusion denoising. We further introduce an adversarial refinement module to enhance geometric realism and semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on the EEG-3D dataset across all 12 subjects demonstrate that Mind2Cloud outperforms prior work in both geometric accuracy and semantic alignment, setting a new benchmark for EEG-to-point-cloud generation. Our source code is available at https://github.com/duasoi/Mind2Cloud.

AI.tldr: EEG-to-point-cloud generation with two-granularity diffusion decoding (Mind2Cloud) using a time-aware fusion of a global Transformer and a local PVCNN, plus adversarial refinement; achieves superior geometric and semantic accuracy over previous EEG-3D methods.
AI.motivation: Uniform diffusion decoders overlook evolving EEG representation granularity and diffusion denoising dynamics, potentially limiting geometric realism and semantic alignment in EEG-driven 3D reconstruction.
AI.method: Time-aware decoder with two branches: Transformer (global structure) in early upsampling; PVCNN (local geometry) in later stages; learnable fusion mask integrating branches across diffusion timesteps; coarse-to-fine granularity guided by denoising trajectory; adversarial refinement module for realism and semantic consistency; trained on EEG-3D dataset across 12 subjects; code release at GitHub.
AI.result: Outperforms prior work in geometric accuracy and semantic alignment across all 12 subjects; establishes a new benchmark for EEG-to-point-cloud generation.
AI.conclusion: Mind2Cloud advances EEG-to-3D reconstruction by aligning representation granularity with diffusion dynamics; demonstrates improved realism and semantics; source code available.

title: Multi-Modal Tumor Survival Prediction via Graph-Guided Mixture of Experts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have displayed impressive capabilities in handling tasks that require few demonstration examples, making them effective few-shot learners. Despite their potential, LLMs face challenges when it comes to addressing complex real-world tasks that involve multiple modalities or reasoning steps. For example, predicting cancer patients' survival period based on clinical data, cell slides, and genomics poses significant logistical complexities. Although several approaches have been proposed to tackle these challenges, they often fall short in achieving promising performance due to their inability to consider all modalities simultaneously or account for missing modalities, variations in modalities, and the integration of multi-modal data, ultimately compromising their effectiveness. This thesis proposes a novel approach for multi-modal tumor survival prediction to address these limitations. Taking inspiration from recent advancements in LLMs, particularly Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based models, a graph-guided MoE framework is introduced. This framework utilizes a graph structure to manage the predictions effectively and combines multiple models to enhance predictive power. Rather than training a single foundation model for end-to-end survival prediction, the approach leverages a MOE-guided ensemble to manage model callings as tools automatically. By leveraging the strengths of existing models and guiding them through a MOE framework, the aim is to achieve better performance and more accurate predictions in complex real-world tasks. Experiments and analysis on the TCGA-LUAD dataset show improved performance over the individual modal and vanilla ensemble models.

AI.tldr: A graph-guided mixture-of-experts (MoE) ensemble is proposed for multi-modal tumor survival prediction, treating existing models as tools and orchestrating them via MoE; it outperforms single-modality and vanilla ensemble baselines on TCGA-LUAD.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of existing multi-modal survival prediction methods, which struggle to leverage all modalities simultaneously, handle missing modalities, and integrate heterogeneous data; the work aims to efficiently integrate multiple models using a MoE framework guided by a graph.
AI.method: Introduce a graph-guided MoE framework that manages predictions with a graph structure and ensembles multiple pre-existing models as tools; the MoE guides model callings automatically instead of training a single end-to-end foundation model; applies to multi-modal cancer data (clinical, imaging, genomics) with missing modalities; evaluates on the TCGA-LUAD dataset.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves improved performance over individual modal baselines and vanilla ensemble models on TCGA-LUAD.
AI.conclusion: A graph-guided MoE ensemble enhances multi-modal tumor survival prediction by effectively integrating diverse modalities and orchestrating model calls, suggesting broader applicability to complex real-world tasks requiring multi-modal data integration.

title: Depth and Scale in the Sub-150M Regime: JugnuLM-53M vs JugnuLM-110M
summary: We scale our conventional sub-150M pretraining recipe from 53.5M to 109.7M parameters, holding the method fixed (Qwen3-style decoder with grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, and a z-loss; FineWeb-Edu data) and changing only the geometry to a deep-and-thin 23-layer x 576-hidden design. The larger model improves across the board -- BLiMP 78.1 -> 81.3, ARC-Easy 51.4 -> 52.5, WikiText-2 byte-perplexity 2.04 -> 1.95 -- and its 81.3% BLiMP essentially matches GPT-X2-125M (81.28) at about 12% fewer parameters. Notably the 110M model achieves this on fewer training tokens (about 8B vs 12B), so the gain is attributable to capacity and depth, not more data. Both models are deliberately conventional; this report is a clean scaling control and the baseline rung (R0) of an ablation study of what further improves models in this regime. An ablation ladder follows: value residuals (R1) and the Muon optimizer (R2) lift ARC-Easy by a cumulative +3.6 (52.5 -> 56.1) at a near-flat BLiMP and are kept; a diverse data blend (R3) and two logit-distillation settings (R4a/R4b) are not kept -- honest negatives. R3 pins ARC-Easy to FineWeb-Edu's educational filtering rather than raw diversity; distillation from a 1.7B teacher can reach the class-leading ARC-Easy (56.99, matching GPT-X2-125M) but only at a perplexity cost that dialing KD down then erases -- so R2 remains the best kept stack.

AI.tldr: Scaling a conventional decoder from ~54M to ~110M parameters with a deep-and-thin 23-layer, 576-hidden design yields consistent performance gains on linguistic benchmarks; ablations show value residuals and Muon optimizer help, while data diversification and logit distillation offer diminishing returns; capacity/depth drive gains more than data.
AI.motivation: Understand scaling behavior in the 100M-parameter regime for a conventional architecture and establish a baseline (R0) for subsequent ablations.
AI.method: Hold architecture (Qwen3-style decoder with grouped-query attention, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, QK-Norm, z-loss) and data (FineWeb-Edu); increase capacity by adopting a deep-and-thin 23-layer x 576-hidden design to 109.7M parameters; train with ~8B tokens; evaluate BLiMP, ARC-Easy, WikiText-2; perform ablations: R1 value residuals, R2 Muon optimizer; R3 diverse data blend; R4a/b logit distillation.
AI.result: Larger model improves BLiMP 78.1→81.3, ARC-Easy 51.4→52.5, WikiText-2 perplexity 2.04→1.95; at ~109–110M, performance matches GPT-X2-125M on BLiMP with ~12% fewer parameters; training tokens are ~8B vs 12B, so gains stem from capacity/depth, not data; R1+R2 raise ARC-Easy to 56.1 with near-flat BLiMP; R3 and R4 (diverse data and logit distillation) are not kept—honest negatives; distillation from a 1.7B teacher can reach ARC-Easy 56.99 but incurs perplexity costs, erasing gains when adjusted, so R2 remains the best stack.
AI.conclusion: In this 100M-scale regime, capacity and depth are the primary drivers of gains; a clean R0 baseline is strong, while selective ablations (notably value residuals and Muon optimizer) provide robust but task-dependent improvements; broader data diversification and distillation offer limited or offsetting benefits.

title: Two-Stage Personalized Gait Phase Estimation in Stroke Survivors During Exoskeleton-Assisted Walking: An Offline Feasibility Study
summary: This study evaluated personalized gait phase estimation for stroke survivors using functional inertial measurement unit (IMU) alignment and two-stage sequential adaptation of models pre-trained on healthy gait. The estimator used signals from a thigh-mounted IMU. Heel force-sensitive resistor measurements provided reference phase labels for offline adaptation and evaluation. Stage 1 established a distillation-regularized participant-specific model, and Stage 2 performed conditional refinement using low-rank adaptation. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), and Transformer models were evaluated in five stroke survivors walking with a powered knee exoskeleton using leave-one-subject-out hyperparameter selection and sequential test-then-adapt Stage 2 replay. Relative to the non-adapted baselines, Stage 1+2 reduced the mean participant-wise phase root mean square error by 84.2%, 77.0%, and 60.7%, respectively. The Transformer achieved the lowest final error (2.90 +- 1.13$% of the gait cycle) and heel-strike timing error (23.7 +- 4.5ms). Policy-specific ablations showed that every-cycle updates generally produced the lowest or near-lowest error, whereas conditional updating reduced the update frequency with small accuracy differences. After personalization, alignment produced model-dependent changes in phase error while preserving or improving heel-strike detection and reducing heel-strike timing error for the LSTM and Transformer. Concurrent embedded tests showed that the TCN and Transformer maintained 100-Hz inference during Stage 2 updates without deadline misses, whereas the LSTM missed the 10-ms deadline in 6.6% of inferences. All updates completed within 0.8s. These results support the offline feasibility and embedded computational timing of the proposed framework for exoskeleton-assisted walking.

AI.tldr: Two-stage personalized gait phase estimation for stroke survivors using thigh IMU and heel-force labels: distillation-regularized subject-specific fine-tuning followed by low-rank adaptation; Transformer yields the best final phase precision (~2.9% gait cycle) with ~24 ms heel-strike timing error; achieves high embedded throughput (100 Hz) with updates under 0.8 s; gains over non-adapted baselines up to ~84%.
AI.motivation: Address inter-subject variability in gait phase estimation for exoskeleton-assisted walking in stroke survivors by adapting healthy-models via alignment and efficient on-device updates.
AI.method: Pretrained LSTM/TCN/Transformer models on healthy gait; Stage 1 distillation-regularized participant-specific adaptation; Stage 2 conditional low-rank adaptation; data from thigh-mounted IMU with heel force-sensitive resistor as reference labels; leave-one-subject-out hyperparameter selection; sequential test-then-adapt Stage 2 replay; performance metrics: phase RMSE and heel-strike timing error; embedded evaluation at 100 Hz.
AI.result: Stage 1+2 reduced mean participant-wise phase RMSE by 84.2% (LSTM), 77.0% (TCN), and 60.7% (Transformer) relative to non-adapted baselines; Transformer achieved lowest final phase error = 2.90±1.13% gait cycle and heel-strike error = 23.7±4.5 ms. Every-cycle updates generally yielded the best accuracy; conditional updating reduced update frequency with minimal accuracy loss. Alignment after personalization caused model-dependent phase-error changes but preserved/improved heel-strike detection and reduced timing error for LSTM/Transformer. TCN and Transformer sustained 100 Hz inference during Stage 2 without deadline misses; LSTM missed 10 ms deadline in 6.6% of inferences. All updates completed within 0.8 s.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates offline feasibility and embedded real-time timing of the proposed two-stage adaptation framework for exoskeleton-assisted gait, with Transformer-based models offering the strongest performance and update strategies balancing accuracy and update load.

title: CirrGuide: A Deep Cascaded Framework for Liver Cirrhosis Segmentation and Severity Classification from T2-Weighted MRI
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 17th International Workshop on Machine Learning in Medical Imaging (MLMI 2026), held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026
summary: We present CirrGuide, a deep cascaded framework for cirrhotic liver segmentation and severity classification. Cirrhosis causes progressive structural changes in the liver and can lead to serious clinical complications, making severity assessment important for disease monitoring and treatment planning. However, severity classification is challenging because imaging patterns are often subtle, spatially variable, and similar across adjacent stages. CirrGuide addresses this by explicitly linking localization with classification. A ResNet50 encoder with an Attention U-Net decoder first predicts a soft cirrhotic liver mask, which is then used as an anatomical prior in a ResNet50-based classification branch. This branch combines global multi-scale features with mask-guided attention-pooled regional features to classify Mild, Moderate, and Severe cirrhosis. On the official CirrMRI600+ T2-weighted (T2W) 2D split, CirrGuide achieves 89.83% Dice and 84.14% mIoU for segmentation, 69.58% accuracy and 61.55% macro F1-score for severity classification. Compared with segmentation-only, classification-only, and multi-task baselines, CirrGuide improves both localization and severity classification, demonstrating the benefit of using predicted cirrhotic liver masks as anatomical priors for cirrhosis analysis.

AI.tldr: CirrGuide is a cascade deep learning framework that jointly segments cirrhotic liver and classifies cirrhosis severity by using the segmentation mask as an anatomical prior in a ResNet50-based classifier, improving localization and severity accuracy.
AI.motivation: Severity of cirrhosis is hard to assess from imaging due to subtle, spatially variable patterns that are similar across adjacent stages; leveraging explicit localization can guide classification.
AI.method: A ResNet50 encoder with an Attention U-Net decoder first outputs a soft cirrhotic liver mask. This mask serves as an anatomical prior in a second ResNet50-based classification branch that fuses global multi-scale features with mask-guided attention-pooled regional features to categorize Mild, Moderate, and Severe cirrhosis.
AI.result: On CirrMRI600+ T2-weighted 2D split: segmentation Dice 89.83%, mIoU 84.14%; classification accuracy 69.58%, macro F1-score 61.55%.
AI.conclusion: Using predicted liver masks as anatomical priors enhances both localization and severity classification, outperforming segmentation-only, classification-only, and multi-task baselines.

title: To do($x$) or not to do($x$): Medical Image Counterfactuals for Dataset Augmentation
summary: Medical image analysis is often hindered by biased datasets, which can lead to biased models and limited clinical applicability. A promising strategy for mitigating such biases is to augment training data with synthetic images. Counterfactual (CF) generation is one such strategy, though the term is used in two different senses: in some works, CFs are produced through causality-based interventions derived from structural causal models, whereas in others, they are produced by non-causal image edits or conventional conditional generative models, such as altering anatomy or adding pathologies. In this work, we study this distinction and evaluate its practical consequences for medical image augmentation. We compare three conditioning strategies: $\textit{Deterministic}$, which changes selected variables while holding the remaining variables fixed; $\textit{Undirected}$, which updates variables according to learned statistical associations without assigning causal directions; and $\textit{Causal}$, which propagates interventions along a directed causal graph. We analyse how these choices affect the resulting images, and explore when causally grounded methods improve dataset augmentation or bring limited benefit. In particular, we assess downstream performance and fairness, where fairness refers to reduced sensitivity to dataset biases across sensitive subgroups. Our experiments demonstrate that using a causal approach to synthetic training data generation can lead to tangible benefits, with these insights offering valuable guidance to machine learning practitioners for the effective design of data generation protocols.

AI.tldr: This work distinguishes causal vs. non-causal counterfactuals for medical image augmentation, comparing three conditioning strategies (Deterministic, Undirected, Causal) and evaluating their impact on downstream accuracy and fairness; results suggest causally grounded CF data generation can yield tangible benefits for performance and bias mitigation.
AI.motivation: Medical image analysis suffers from dataset biases that limit clinical applicability. Synthetic data via counterfactual generation offers a path to debiasing, but “counterfactual” has been used variably (causal interventions vs. non-causal edits). Understanding the practical consequences of these approaches is essential for effective data augmentation.
AI.method: The study defines three conditioning strategies for CF generation: Deterministic (variable edits with others fixed), Undirected (updates based on learned statistical associations without causal directions), and Causal (interventions propagated along a directed causal graph). It analyzes how these choices shape the generated images and assesses their effect on downstream performance and fairness across sensitive subgroups. Experimental evaluation benchmarks the strategies on relevant medical imaging tasks.
AI.result: A causal CF generation approach can yield tangible benefits in dataset augmentation, improving downstream performance and fairness in some settings. The findings offer practical guidance on when and how to design data generation protocols for better generalization and reduced bias.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating causally grounded counterfactual data generation can enhance medical image augmentation and fairness. Practitioners should carefully align CF generation with the underlying causal structure, as the choice of conditioning strategy substantially influences benefits and applicability.

title: Moral Rebel Agents: Decision-Making Under Conflicting Obligations
summary: Autonomous agents are typically obliged to follow user-assigned tasks. However, strict obedience may conflict with moral obligations that arise during execution. This paper investigates \textbf{moral rebellion}: the ability of an autonomous agent to deviate from a user-assigned task when morally justified. We formalize five agent architectures: an \textit{amoral agent} that pursues assigned tasks without considering moral obligations, and four forms of \textbf{moral rebel agency}: (1) \textit{utilitarian agents} that opportunistically maximize task outcomes; (2) \textit{deontic} agents that enforce normative constraints; (3) \textit{utilitarian-deontic} (UD) agents that combine deontic constraints with utilitarian reasoning; and (4) \textit{dutiful} agents that additionally preserve commitments to assigned tasks. We implement these architectures within a hierarchical task network planning framework and evaluate them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain that exposes trade-offs among assigned-task completion, opportunistic rescue, and norm compliance. Our empirical results show that the proposed agents exhibit distinct trade-offs among rescue results, assigned-task completion, and norm compliance. In particular, the preservation of task commitments emerges as an important dimension of moral rebellion, for which the UD and dutiful agents produce substantially different behaviors despite their shared utilitarian and deontological foundations. These findings highlight the importance of commitment-aware moral reasoning for autonomous agents operating in morally consequential environments.

AI.tldr: A study formalizes and compares five agent architectures—amoral, utilitarian, deontic, utilitarian-deontic (UD), and dutiful—within a hierarchical task network planning framework in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain to examine how task completion, rescue outcomes, and normative compliance trade off, highlighting commitment preservation as a key dimension distinguishing UD and dutiful agents.
AI.motivation: Addressing potential conflicts between user-assigned tasks and moral obligations in autonomous agents by systematically analyzing how different moral frameworks influence behavior, especially under commitments and normative constraints.
AI.method: Formalize five agent architectures, implement them in a hierarchical task network (HTN) planning framework, and evaluate them in a Mini Search-and-Rescue domain that exposes trade-offs among task completion, opportunistic rescue, and norm compliance.
AI.result: Agents display distinct trade-offs among rescue success, adherence to assigned tasks, and normative compliance. Commitment preservation emerges as a critical dimension of moral rebellion; UD and dutiful agents diverge in behavior despite shared utilitarian/deontological underpinnings.
AI.conclusion: Commitment-aware moral reasoning is important for autonomous agents operating in morally consequential environments; preserving commitments can significantly alter behavior even when utilitarian and deontological considerations are present.

title: From Learned-Mode AV-Traffic Pairing to Planner Decisions: A Marginal-Preserving Study on Argoverse 2
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 16th Workshop on Planning, Perception and Navigation for Intelligent Vehicles (PPNIV), held in conjunction with IEEE/RSJ IROS 2026
summary: Joint motion forecasts pair each autonomous-vehicle (AV) future with surrounding traffic, but actor-level metrics do not show whether that structure matters to a planner. We study this question with a marginal-preserving product control that removes AV-traffic pairing among the learned modes while retaining the fixed constant-velocity pair and holding trajectories, actor-level marginals before planner conditioning, candidates, the cost terms and weights, and fallback fixed. The intervention also changes candidate-conditioned concentration. Across twelve runs on 1,400 held-out Argoverse 2 scenarios, the intervention changes 3.0% of route-level offline selections at $τ=4$ m. Control-minus-joint recorded-trajectory regret is $-0.026$ and $-0.118$ at the two training sizes; crossed and seed-$t$ intervals span zero. At $τ=1$ m, relative costs change in 87.9% of route evaluations and route-level offline selections in 8.1%. Before concentration matching, descriptive outcome estimates favor the control. Most of this gap disappears along an approximate concentration-matching path; the remaining contrasts are $+0.112$ and $-0.047$, and both crossed intervals span zero. Actor-level forecast metrics remain identical. Pairing-strength and temperature sweeps show that the decision contrast grows with pairing removal and sharper conditioning. The intervention changes planner decisions even though actor-level metrics remain unchanged. The matching analysis, however, cannot separate any recorded-outcome effect of learned-mode AV-traffic pairing from the accompanying change in conditioned concentration.

AI.tldr: Marginal-preserving intervention removes AV–traffic pairing to test its effect on planner decisions; finds planner decisions shift despite unchanged actor-level forecasts, but concentration changes confound causal attribution; effect size increases with stronger pairing removal and sharper conditioning.
AI.motivation: Assess whether actor-level forecast structure (AV–traffic pairing) matters to planner-level decisions beyond their marginals.
AI.method: Marginal-preserving product control to disrupt AV–traffic pairing while preserving margins, using 12 runs over 1,400 Argoverse 2 cases. Compare control vs joint across route-level metrics (offline selections, regret, costs) at multiple tau values; examine concentration matching, and perform pairing-strength and temperature sweeps to study the contrast.
AI.result: Intervention changes 3.0% of route-level offline selections at τ=4 m. Control-minus-joint recorded-trajectory regret: -0.026 and -0.118 at two training sizes; at τ=1 m, relative costs change in 87.9% of route evaluations and 8.1% of route-level offline selections. Before concentration matching, descriptive outcomes favored the control; most gap fades along approximate concentration-matching path; remaining contrasts are +0.112 and -0.047 with both crossed intervals spanning zero. Actor-level forecast metrics remain identical. Pairing-strength and temperature sweeps show the decision contrast grows with pairing removal and sharper conditioning. The matching analysis cannot disentangle the AV–traffic pairing effect from changes in conditioned concentration.
AI.conclusion: There is a planner-level effect of removing AV–traffic pairing even when actor-level metrics remain unchanged, but concentration changes confound causal attribution; the observed effect largely arises through conditioning, and robust separation of pairing effects from concentration requires alternative identification strategies.

title: Quantum-Gated LiteSSD: A Parameter-Efficient Lightweight Hybrid Quantum-Classical Framework for Forward-Looking Sonar Object Detection
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026 Marine Vision as short paper
summary: Forward-looking sonar object detection is essential for underwater perception, yet deployment on embedded platforms requires highly compact models. To address this challenge, we explore quantum computing and introduce Quantum-Gated LiteSSD, a parameter-efficient hybrid quantum--classical detector that reformulates QuCNet-style multi-circuit quantum processing as an identity-centered channel-gating mechanism for spatial feature modulation. Experiments on the Marine Debris Watertank dataset and UATD forward-looking sonar benchmarks demonstrate an effective parameter--accuracy trade-off. The proposed detector achieves 90.84% $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ on Watertank with approximately $62\times$ fewer parameters than YOLO26s and $164.3\times$ fewer parameters than SSD-VGG16. On UATD, the model achieves 70.37% $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ with only 0.150M parameters, making it approximately $4.1\times$ smaller than SSGA-YOLO while retaining meaningful multi-class detection capability.

AI.tldr: A compact quantum-classical detector, Quantum-Gated LiteSSD, for forward-looking sonar that achieves competitive mAP50 with dramatically fewer parameters, enabling embedding on resource-constrained platforms.
AI.motivation: Underwater forward-looking sonar perception requires real-time, low-power inference on embedded hardware. Traditional CNNs are too large; the authors leverage quantum-inspired channel gating to achieve parameter-efficient spatial feature modulation.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum–classical detector that reformulates QuCNet-style multi-circuit quantum processing as an identity-centered channel-gating mechanism to modulate spatial features within a LiteSSD framework.
AI.result: On Marine Debris Watertank: mAP50 = 90.84% with ~62× fewer parameters than YOLO26s and ~164.3× fewer than SSD-VGG16. On UATD forward-looking sonar: mAP50 = 70.37% with 0.150M parameters, ~4.1× smaller than SSGA-YOLO, while supporting multi-class detection.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that a quantum-inspired, parameter-efficient hybrid detector can achieve competitive detection accuracy on specialized sonar benchmarks, suggesting viability for embedded deployment and motivating further exploration of quantum-inspired gating for spatial feature modulation.

title: LIMBO: Lifelong Inference-Time Memory and Budget Optimization for LLM Agents
comment: Accepted by the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI'26)
summary: As LLM agents become integrated into increasingly complex workflows, they must continually acquire new capabilities while retaining competence on previously learned tasks. Lifelong agents address this through experience replay, injecting past interactions into the prompt to leverage prior experience during inference. However, replay is not free: every replayed trajectory competes with retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and verification for the same limited prompt and compute budget, making effective resource allocation essential. Existing approaches allocate these resources using fixed replay policies, regardless of whether replay is beneficial for the current task. We identify this as inference-time memory allocation, a distinct problem class for lifelong agents, and introduce LIMBO: the first online framework to our knowledge that treats memory as a controllable inference-time resource and jointly optimizes memory strategy and inference budget for each incoming task. Unlike prior approaches that fix the replay policy or require model weights, teacher supervision, or offline retraining, LIMBO learns this allocation online in a single pass, explicitly balancing task performance and inference cost without modifying the underlying agent. Across three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves better cost-accuracy tradeoffs than state-of-the-art memory-augmented baselines and nearly matches all strongest such baselines at up to ~83% lower inference cost (~53% on average). LIMBO adapts its policy across models and environments without retraining, demonstrating that effective allocation can be learned online rather than manually specified.

AI.tldr: LIMBO treats replay memory as an inference-time resource and jointly optimizes per-task memory strategy and inference budget in a single online pass, enabling cost-aware lifelong LLM agents without retraining.
AI.motivation: Lifelong agents must learn new capabilities while retaining prior skills; fixed replay policies waste limited prompt and compute budgets; online, adaptive memory allocation is needed to optimize task performance under resource constraints.
AI.method: LIMBO is an online framework that allocates memory and inference budget per incoming task in a single pass, balancing performance and cost without modifying model weights, supervision, or offline retraining; memory is treated as a controllable inference-time resource.
AI.result: On LifelongAgentBench with three LLM backbones, LIMBO achieves better cost-accuracy tradeoffs than memory-augmented baselines and reaches up to ~83% lower inference cost (≈53% on average), adapting across models/environments without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Memory can be effectively allocated online as a controllable inference-time resource for lifelong agents, enabling efficient, model-agnostic operation without retraining and with robust cross-task adaptability.

title: Bayesian Intelligence from the Outside
summary: Inferring intelligence from observable behavior is a foundational challenge in artificial intelligence. We develop a theory of Bayesian intelligence for agents such as language models. Each prompt induces a possibly imperfect internal experiment; the agent updates a full-support prior by Bayes' rule and faithfully reports its posterior over the possible answers to the question. Repetitions draw fresh, independent outcomes from the same unobserved experiment at one fixed state. We show that the agent's behavior admits this explanation if and only if its reports are not fully contradictory, i.e., some state remains possible under every report across all prompts. Report frequencies and the sizes of positive probabilities impose no further restrictions. We further propose and characterize the behavioral implications of an intelligence order that makes the behavior of two agents consistent with one agent having access to a more informative experiment: there should exist a coupling of report distributions such that the more informative agent's report excludes every answer excluded by its counterpart. Finally, we show the difficulty of aggregating coarse reports from intelligent agents: unless the agent reports a belief about the complete state of the world, the optimal aggregation can assign arbitrary weights to states that have not been excluded. These results provide a basis for understanding when agents' behavior is intelligent and highlight the difficulty of rejecting Bayesian rationality.

AI.tldr: Bayesian intelligence: prompts induce internal experiments; reports consistent with Bayes updates if no report excludes all states; intelligence order via couplings; coarse reports hinder aggregation.
AI.motivation: Formalize when observable behavior from AI agents is consistent with Bayesian rationality and to study how to compare and aggregate such agents.
AI.method: A probabilistic model: a full-support prior over latent states; each prompt triggers an (potentially imperfect) internal experiment; agent updates by Bayes rule and reports the posterior over answers; repetitions sample independent outcomes from the same state; derive necessary and sufficient conditions for report-consistency; define an intelligence order via stochastic coupling; analyze aggregation of coarse reports.
AI.result: Characterizes exactly when an agent’s reports can be explained as Bayesian posteriors; report frequencies or positive probabilities carry no extra constraints. Introduces a coupling notion to compare information content between agents (one having a more informative experiment). Shows aggregation of coarse reports is ill-posed: without a complete state belief, optimal aggregation can arbitrarily weight non-excluded states.
AI.conclusion: Provides a rigorous criterion to identify intelligent (Bayesian) behavior and highlights challenges in ruling out Bayesian rationality, comparing agents by informational content, and aggregating partial reports in AI evaluations.

title: IMPACT-VLA: Interaction-aware Multimodal Propagation Attribution via Counterfactual Trajectories for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies perform robot manipulation tasks using multimodal inputs such as visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. However, it remains unclear at which execution stages each modality contributes to final task success and how input interventions propagate through subsequent states, observations, and actions. Existing attribution approaches primarily measure local sensitivity or temporally aggregated importance, limiting their ability to capture phase-dependent contributions and cross-phase dependencies. We propose Interaction-aware Multimodal Propagation Attribution via Counterfactual Trajectories for Vision-Language-Action Policies (IMPACT-VLA). IMPACT-VLA constructs behavioral phases from action transitions in a successful reference rollout, aligns them with policy query boundaries, and defines phase-modality blocks as attribution units. It then performs closed-loop counterfactual re-execution to quantify each block's contribution to final task success. We further analyze cross-phase non-additive interactions and trajectory propagation while distinguishing behavioral from functional recovery. Across 30 LIBERO robot manipulation tasks using OpenVLA-OFT, dominant-modality transitions occurred in 25 tasks (83.3%), and closed-loop attribution identified task-critical information more faithfully than Static Action Perturbation. Later-block marginal gains for negatively interacting pairs increased by approximately 3.3x under early-phase input replacement, while functional recovery could occur without behavioral recovery. These results reveal when multimodal inputs support task success and how their contributions become conditionally coupled during closed-loop execution.

AI.tldr: IMPACT-VLA introduces a phase-aware, counterfactual attribution framework for Vision-Language-Action policies, revealing when modalities dominate, cross-phase interactions, and the distinction between behavioral and functional recovery across 30 robot manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: To identify how each modality (vision, language, proprioception) contributes to task success across execution phases and how input interventions propagate through the closed-loop policy, addressing limitations of local sensitivity and aggregated importance.
AI.method: Build behavioral phases from a successful reference rollout, align these phase blocks with policy query boundaries, define phase-modality blocks as attribution units, and perform closed-loop counterfactual re-execution to quantify each block’s contribution. Analyze cross-phase non-additive interactions and trajectory propagation while distinguishing behavioral vs functional recovery. Evaluate on 30 LIBERO/ OpenVLA-OFT tasks and compare to Static Action Perturbation baselines.
AI.result: Dominant-modality transitions occurred in 25 of 30 tasks (83.3%). Closed-loop attribution outperformed Static Action Perturbation in identifying task-critical information. Later-block marginal gains for negatively interacting pairs increased ~3.3x under early-phase input replacement. Functional recovery could occur without behavioral recovery. Demonstrates phase-dependent contributions and cross-phase coupling of multimodal inputs during closed-loop execution.
AI.conclusion: IMPACT-VLA enables phase-aware, counterfactual attribution in VLA policies, revealing when and how multimodal inputs contribute to task success and how their effects propagate and couple across phases, with implications for designing robust multimodal controllers.

title: LPA-CWM: A Learned Physical Adjudicator for Motion Reasoning with Counterfactual World Models
comment: A quick overview is available at https://LPA-CWM.github.io
summary: Counterfactual world models (CWM) extract motion from pretrained video predictors by comparing factual and intervened predictions. However, responses generated under different target-frame masks vary in reliability, while uniform aggregation weights them equally. We formulate response aggregation as candidate reliability learning and propose LPA-CWM with a lightweight Learned Physical Adjudicator (LPA). Trained on dense MOVi-F trajectories, the 3.0M-parameter LPA compares visual context and response structure across an unordered candidate set to predict relative weights, while the CWM predictor and intervention generator remain frozen. The weighted responses undergo windowed localization and one paired re-evaluation to recover motion. We also introduce Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence (CMC), a ground-truth-anchored evaluation protocol that jointly measures localization, trajectory completeness, visibility, and continuity, counting missing predictions as failures on visible dynamic points. On the evaluated DAVIS and Kinetics subsets, LPA-CWM improves $\mathrm{DCA}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ over Uniform CWM by 60.0\% and 29.0\%, respectively, and also improves tracking accuracy under TAP-Vid First. A quick overview is available at https://LPA-CWM.github.io.

AI.tldr: Learned candidate reliability for counterfactual world models (CWM) using a lightweight Adjudicator; LPA-CWM weights responses to improve motion recovery; introduces CMC evaluation; achieves substantial gains on DAVIS/Kinetics and TAP-Vid First.
AI.motivation: Response reliability varies across target-frame mask interventions in CWM; uniform aggregation can misweight responses and degrade motion recovery.
AI.method: Train a 3.0M-parameter Learned Physical Adjudicator (LPA) on dense MOVi-F trajectories; LPA compares visual context and response structure across unordered candidate set; freeze CWM predictor and intervention generator; compute relative weights; perform windowed localization and one paired re-evaluation; introduce Completeness-aware Motion Correspondence for evaluation.
AI.result: On DAVIS and Kinetics, DCA_avg improves by 60.0% and 29.0% over Uniform CWM; also better tracking accuracy under TAP-Vid First.
AI.conclusion: LPA-CWM with CMC provides more reliable motion extraction in CWM by learning candidate reliabilities; the evaluation protocol offers a more comprehensive assessment of localization, completeness, visibility, and continuity.

title: T-SMART: Mechanism-Level Attribution for Tool-Augmented Time-Series Question Answering
comment: Accepted by the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI'26)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can struggle with time-series question answering (TS-QA), especially when numerical signals are serialized as text and require explicit computation. Tool-augmented approaches improve performance, but existing systems often intertwine language reasoning, computation, and perception, making it difficult to determine which components drive the gains. We present T-SMART, a neurosymbolic framework that separates these roles: a frozen LLM interprets questions and selects operations, deterministic tools perform numerical computation, and structured perception is invoked only when needed. Controlled paired ablations show that deterministic computation provides the dominant benefit, improving accuracy by 31.7 percentage points over direct LLM reasoning on serialized time series, while language understanding and perception offer smaller complementary gains. These results indicate that tool-augmented TS-QA benefits primarily from reliable numerical execution rather than additional language-model reasoning and provide a controlled framework for analyzing component contributions in neurosymbolic time-series systems.

AI.tldr: Deterministic numerical execution dominates gains in tool-augmented TS-QA; separating components shows most improvement comes from reliable computation rather than LLM reasoning or perception.
AI.motivation: To disentangle which components of tool-augmented time-series question answering—LLM reasoning, numerical tools, and perception—drive performance when time-series signals are serialized as text.
AI.method: Introduce T-SMART: a frozen LLM to interpret questions and select operations; deterministic tools perform numerical computation; structured perception invoked on demand; use controlled paired ablations to quantify each component's contribution.
AI.result: Deterministic computation yields a 31.7 percentage-point accuracy gain over direct LLM reasoning on serialized time series; language understanding and perception provide smaller complementary gains.
AI.conclusion: Reliable numerical execution is the primary driver of performance in tool-augmented TS-QA; the framework enables controlled analysis of component contributions in neurosymbolic time-series systems.

title: AppliedScientist: Automated Scientific Revision Through Iterative AI Reviewing
summary: Automated reviewing systems are increasingly evaluated based on the quality of the reviews they produce. Yet a review is only useful if acting on it leads to a measurable improvement in the paper. We present AppliedScientist, a closed-loop system that couples an autonomous AI scientist with an AI reviewer, and evaluate it by iteratively revising rejected papers from a range of research subfields. To mirror how human authors build on earlier drafts, the AI scientist has access to its previous versions during revision. To avoid bias from prior judgments, however, each review is generated independently, with the reviewer having no memory of earlier feedback or scores. We compare three revision settings: one initialized with the original venue reviews, one initialized with AI-generated reviews, and autonomous self-revision using the same fixed prompt in every round. Because the reviewer both guides and evaluates the revision, we also assess the human-initialized revisions using Stanford Reviewer as an independent evaluator. Reviewer-guided revision consistently improves more than fixed-prompt self-revision, and Stanford Reviewer also assigns higher scores to later revisions. AppliedScientist resolves 128 of 150 execution-related weaknesses (85.3%), but only 2 of 18 idea-related weaknesses (11.1%), suggesting that iterative revision is effective at improving experiments and implementation, but rarely changes concerns about novelty or significance.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop AI system (AppliedScientist) pairs an autonomous AI scientist with an AI reviewer to iteratively revise rejected papers. Reviewer independence across rounds plus three revision settings show reviewer-guided revision outperforms fixed-prompt self-revision; human evaluator (Stanford Reviewer) validates later revisions. Significant gains on execution/implementation weaknesses but limited impact on idea/novelty concerns.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether automated, closed-loop review-and-revise cycles yield meaningful improvements to papers, beyond just producing readable reviewer judgments; examine the extent to which revision guided by an AI reviewer can improve quality and what aspects (execution vs. novelty) are affected.
AI.method: Develop AppliedScientist that integrates an autonomous AI scientist with an AI reviewer. The scientist revises rejected papers, with access to earlier versions. Each review is generated independently (no memory) to avoid bias. Compare three revision settings: (1) starting from original venue reviews, (2) starting from AI-generated reviews, and (3) autonomous self-revision with a fixed prompt across rounds. For human evaluation, use Stanford Reviewer as an independent assessor on reviewer-guided revisions. Evaluate across multiple subfields; measure resolution of weaknesses and overall scores.
AI.result: Reviewer-guided revisions improve more than fixed-prompt self-revisions. Stanford Reviewer assigns higher scores to later revisions. AppliedScientist resolves 128 of 150 execution-related weaknesses (85.3%) but only 2 of 18 idea-related weaknesses (11.1%), indicating strong gains for experiments/implementation but limited impact on novelty or significance.
AI.conclusion: Iterative revision through a reviewer-guided loop effectively improves empirical and implementation aspects of papers, while concerns about novelty/impact are less amenable to revision. Systematic AI-assisted revision can enhance research quality when guided by an external reviewer signal.

title: Atomic Motion Coordinate for Language-Steerable and Force-Responsive Manipulation
summary: Can changing only the language instruction redirect a VLA policy's end effector, or does the visually driven motion prior dominate? We present Atomic Motion Coordinate, a geometry-grounded coordinate for steerable and force-responsive manipulation. Each arm owns thirteen signed translation, rotation, and hold atoms grounded from text and forward kinematics with vision withheld, and the coordinate is injected into every action-expert block via weighted codebook alignment. Contact history modulates the same coordinate through a bounded spherical residual that is recomputed from a fixed nominal latent to regenerate only the unexecuted horizon suffix. Across 7,520 offline horizon interventions, opposite-atom separation reaches 92.5/83.1% (single/dual) versus 39.1/24.0% for LA4VLA-style. Across 50 real-robot trials per task, AMC raises OOD fruit progress from 60.5% to 87.8%; force adaptation raises Plug/Vase from 59.0/71.5% to 78.5/75.2%.

AI.tldr: Introduces Atomic Motion Coordinate (AMC), a geometry-grounded, text- and vision-informed coordinate for steerable, force-responsive manipulation, injected into action-expert blocks and modulated by contact history; demonstrates strong atom-separation and improved real-robot performance over LA4VLA-style baselines.
AI.motivation: Resolve whether language-only instructions can redirect a visually driven policy or whether the motion priors dominate, by grounding motion coordinates in geometry and foregrounding a horizon-aware regeneration mechanism.
AI.method: Define AMC as thirteen signed atoms per arm (translation, rotation, and hold) grounded from text and forward kinematics with vision withheld. Inject AMC into action-expert blocks via weighted codebook alignment. Modulate the same coordinate with contact history using a bounded spherical residual computed from a fixed nominal latent to regenerate only the unexecuted horizon suffix. Evaluate on 7,520 offline horizon interventions and 50 real-robot trials per task, comparing against LA4VLA-style baselines.
AI.result: Opposite-atom separation: 92.5/83.1% (single/dual) for AMC vs 39.1/24.0% for LA4VLA-style. Real-robot gains: AMC raises OOD fruit progress from 60.5% to 87.8%; force adaptation improves Plug/Vase from 59.0/71.5% to 78.5/75.2%.
AI.conclusion: AMC demonstrates that a geometry-grounded, horizon-aware coordinate—coupled with a learnable, codebook-aligned integration into action-expert blocks—substantially improves reachability and adaptability in both OOD and force-sensitive tasks, while reducing reliance on language-specific redirection and outperforming LA4VLA-style approaches. The results indicate a dominant role for the motion prior when vision is withheld, with language as a supplementary steerable signal through the AMC embedding.

title: Adapting Open-Weight MLLMs to Generate Point Prompts for Electron Microscopy Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the BioImage Computing (BIC) Workshop at ECCV 2026
summary: Promptable models such as microSAM segment electron microscopy (EM) images from point prompts, but automation requires generating prompts without user input. We ask whether open-weight multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate them from natural-language requests by returning coordinates to a frozen segmenter. To that end, we convert masks from three mitochondria datasets into training examples, pairing images and instructions with centroid coordinates, then train LoRA adapters while freezing the MLLM backbone and microSAM. We find that Qwen3-VL reaches segmentation AP$_{50}$ $0.736$ after supervised fine-tuning and reward optimization, up from $0.247$ without adaptation, while automatic prompt generation (APG) achieves $0.773$. In addition, two other MLLMs improve, reaching or exceeding APG. When compared with a supervised centroid-heatmap detector that reaches AP$_{50}$ $0.904$ for this mitochondria task, Qwen3-VL more closely matches the annotated point set and instance counts. Moreover, training on two public datasets transfers to an unseen third, while training on all three transfers to an independent EM volume. Robustness tests show stable performance under unseen formulations of the natural-language request, while the coordinates can be reused by a second segmenter. To our knowledge, this is the first feasibility study of open-weight MLLMs as EM point generators, providing an inspectable, language-directed link between localization and mask decoding.

AI.tldr: Open-weight multimodal LLMs can generate EM segmentation prompts for a frozen segmenter by producing centroid coordinates; fine-tuning with LoRA on Qwen3-VL yields AP50 around 0.736–0.773, approaching—but not surpassing—a centroid-heatmap detector's 0.904; results transfer across datasets and EM volumes; robustness to NL prompt variations; first feasibility study linking localization and mask decoding via language-directed prompts.
AI.motivation: Assess whether open-weight MLLMs can autonomously generate precise localization prompts for a frozen segmentation model in electron microscopy, reducing user input and enabling natural-language control.
AI.method: Convert mitochondria masks from three datasets into training triplets: images, natural-language instructions, and centroid coordinates. Train LoRA adapters while freezing the MLLM backbone and microSAM. Evaluate multiple MLLMs (e.g., Qwen3-VL) with supervised fine-tuning and reward optimization. Compare against automatic prompt generation (APG) and a supervised centroid-heatmap detector. Test cross-dataset transfer (train on two datasets, test on the third) and transfer to an independent EM volume. Conduct robustness checks against varying NL formulations; assess whether generated coordinates can be reused by another segmenter.
AI.result: Qwen3-VL achieves AP50 of 0.736 after supervised fine-tuning and reward optimization; APG yields AP50 of 0.773. Other MLLMs improve as well, reaching or exceeding APG.
