A supervised centroid-heatmap detector achieves AP50 of 0.904 on the same task. Cross-dataset transfer (two datasets to a third) and full-training on all three datasets transfers to an unseen EM volume. Robustness tests show stable performance despite NL prompt variations; coordinates can be reused by a second segmenter.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight MLLMs are a feasible, inspectable language-directed bridge between localization and mask decoding for EM segmentation, enabling prompts from natural language, though current performance still lags a dedicated centroid-heatmap detector; transferability and robustness observed across datasets and tasks indicate practical potential.

title: Signatures of Steerability in Activation Space of Language Models
summary: Steering language models using a set of contrastive representations has been a canonical and computationally efficient method for controlling model behavior. Despite this success in controlling certain model behaviors, the effectiveness of activation steering varies markedly across concepts; the generalization properties of steering vectors are often considered a function of the dataset used to construct them. We make this dataset-dependence claim more rigorous and show that simple separation metrics strongly correlate with the downstream steerability of language models across diverse settings, even after controlling for layers and dataset effects. Beyond prediction, we provide evidence from a synthetic superposition experiment that separation metrics are strongly correlated with alignment between the empirical and true feature direction. Our results suggest that simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for when steering vectors are likely to work.

AI.tldr: Simple separability statistics predict when activation/steering vectors will effectively control language models across datasets and layers; they correlate with downstream steerability and alignment between empirical and true feature directions.
AI.motivation: To rigorously characterize the dataset dependence of activation steering vectors and identify practical diagnostics for when steering will work.
AI.method: Empirical analysis across diverse settings, correlating simple separation metrics with downstream steerability while controlling for layers and dataset effects; a synthetic superposition experiment to relate separation to feature-direction alignment.
AI.result: Strong correlations between separability metrics and steerability across settings; these metrics predict both downstream control effectiveness and alignment with true feature directions.
AI.conclusion: Simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for the likely success of activation-based steering of language models.

title: AcquireBound: Runtime Authorization for Resources Acquired by AI Agents
summary: By acquiring compute, credentials, accounts, services, and other agents, autonomous AI agents can introduce new authority into a task. Payment, budget, OAuth, mandate, and fulfillment checks can validate transaction conditions without deciding whether a returned resource may become usable authority. This post-fulfillment activation gap spans tool-mediated creation, inter-agent delegation, and agentic commerce. We present AcquireBound, a provenance-bounded runtime authorization architecture. It quarantines acquired outputs, resolves their actual capabilities from authenticated provider evidence through a versioned resolver, and activates them only through a current activation transaction that checks the resolved manifest, provenance, epochs, and a downward-closed relational envelope over a typed resource-capability hypergraph. The envelope preserves correlated identity, effect, data, delegation, and graph-wide limits. Single-use effect permits are revalidated and consumed at effect linearization. Under explicit assumptions, we prove eight safety properties covering quarantine, backing, non-amplification, split non-evasion, crash/retry, refunds, epochs, and effect confinement. Across five resource classes, reference semantics accepted 20/20 benign traces and rejected 40/40 registered unsafe traces over 810 events; an independent checker agreed on 60 base and 40 refinement traces and rejected 89/89 tamper tests. Frozen Codex and Gemini Model Context Protocol (MCP) client components completed 54/54 deterministic local stdio calls. In a registered 18-case staged MCP-to-Docker composition, both benign paths completed, and none of the 16 unsafe paths added an unauthorized Docker start request. A five-source audit classified 1,248 field pairs across 32 units; no unit alone supplied a complete activation profile.

AI.tldr: AcquireBound is a provenance-bounded runtime authorization architecture that quarantines acquired outputs, resolves true capabilities via a versioned resolver, and activates them under bounded checks to ensure safety properties in multi-agent tasks.
AI.motivation: To address post-fulfillment activation gaps in autonomous agents acquiring compute, credentials, and other resources, enabling safe, auditable activation without enabling resource misuse.
AI.method: Proposes hardening runtime with quarantine, versioned resolver, and an activation transaction that references a manifest, provenance, epochs, and a typed resource-capability hypergraph envelope; uses single-use effect, revalidation, and formal safety proofs; implements across five resource classes; uses Codex/MCP/Docker components; multi-source audit and 5-source evaluation.
AI.result: Proves eight safety properties under explicit assumptions; high empirical validation with benign vs unsafe trace discrimination across hundreds of events; independent checks agree on traces; deterministic local stdio calls; safe MCP-to-Docker co-composition; audit shows no single unit reveals full activation profile.
AI.conclusion: The architecture delivers strong containment and safety guarantees for post-fulfillment activation in agent-mediated settings, with practical evaluations and audits supporting its effectiveness and limitations well-defined by assumptions.

title: Steering Generative Robot Policies with Lexicographic Preferences
summary:
Pretrained generative robot policies can produce effective behaviors across diverse environments, but deployment can lead to requirements and preferences that may not have been represented during training. Furthermore, at deployment, an operator, user, or application may assign these requirements and preferences a priority order that can vary across deployments. For example, embodiment-specific feasibility constraints may need to be satisfied first, while user-specific preferences guide behavior among the feasible options. We show that a frozen generative robot policy---based on either diffusion or flow matching---can be steered at inference time to respect such lexicographically ordered deployment objectives.
  To achieve this, we introduce two modifications to the sampler. First, we apply dynamic-barrier guidance to sampled trajectories, constraining lower-priority updates so that higher-priority costs do not increase (up to first order). Second, we select the executed sample using a cascade that successively filters candidate samples according to each priority level. The policy weights remain unchanged.
  On a navigation benchmark, we demonstrate that our method improves success, traversability, and preference compliance over the frozen policy, and achieves substantially better compliance than tuned weighted-sum baselines. The same method transfers to a flow-matching manipulation policy on LIBERO, where it improves compliance without reducing task success. A controlled manipulation study further shows that, in settings where a fixed weight can match the desired ordering, the dynamic barrier reaches comparable best performance over a substantially wider range of parameter settings.

AI.tldr: A frozen generative robot policy can be steered at inference to satisfy lexicographic deployment objectives via two sampler repairs—dynamic-barrier guidance and cascade sampling—without retraining, improving compliance and task performance across navigation and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Deployment environments impose priority-ordered requirements (e.g., feasibility first, user preferences second) that may not be captured during training. A mechanism is needed to enforce lexicographic objectives at inference time for pretrained policies.
AI.method: 1) Dynamic-barrier guidance: constrain lower-priority updates so higher-priority costs do not increase to first order during sampling. 2) Cascade sampling: select the executed sample by sequentially filtering candidates according to each priority level; policy weights remain fixed.
AI.result: In navigation, the method improves success, traversability, and preference compliance vs the frozen policy, and outperforms tuned weighted-sum baselines. In LIBERO manipulation (flow-matching), it improves compliance without sacrificing task success. A controlled study shows the dynamic barrier matches best performance over a wider parameter range when a fixed weight can reflect the ordering.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time lexicographic steering of frozen generative robot policies is feasible and beneficial, offering robust deployment control with no retraining and achieving higher compliance and stability across tasks.

title: Bridging the Synthetic-to-Real Gap for Few-Shot Cryo-ET Classification
summary: Subtomogram classification in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is a challenging problem due to the scarcity of labeled examples. While cryo-ET simulators can be adopted to generate unlimited synthetic data, the substantial domain gap between synthetic and real subtomograms hinders its practical utilization. In this work, we propose a novel synthetic-to-real adaptation framework with a learnable transformation module, bridging this gap at both the input and feature levels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing transfer learning baselines in few-shot settings.

AI.tldr: A synthetic-to-real adaptation framework with a learnable transformation module improves cryo-ET subtomogram classification in few-shot settings by bridging domain gap between synthetic and real data at input and feature levels.
AI.motivation: Cryo-ET subtomogram classification suffers from scarce labeled data and a large domain gap between synthetic simulators and real subtomograms, hindering transfer learning.
AI.method: A novel synthetic-to-real adaptation framework employing a learnable transformation module that bridges the domain gap at both input and feature levels.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the proposed method consistently outperforms existing transfer learning baselines in few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively reduces the synthetic-real domain gap and enhances few-shot subtomogram classification by aligning data representations at multiple levels.

title: CyFM: Cylindrical Optimal Transport for Few-Step Complex-Valued Flow Matching
summary: Complex-valued signals, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and audio spectrograms, are almost always modelled as flat two-channel Euclidean data. For nonzero values the amplitude-phase chart $z \mapsto (|z|, z/|z|)$ identifies the signal domain with the cylinder $(0, \infty) \times S^1$, on which we deliberately replace the inherited metric $dA^2 + A^2 dθ^2$ by the decoupled product metric $dA^2 + dθ^2$. In this empirical study we measure what that substitution costs and what it buys. By computing exact analytical bridges, we demonstrate that Cartesian paths induce a heavy-tailed distribution of angular velocity (power law index $\approx 1.0$), with nearly half of the probability paths exceeding an angular speed of $π$ under independent coupling, a rate no cylindrical path ever exceeds. To resolve this, we analyze Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM), which strictly bounds the regression target, and couple noise and data by exact minibatch Optimal Transport computed jointly over whole fields in the cylindrical metric. Although the transport-cost reduction of this coupling collapses with field dimension (from 86% for scalar pairs to 3% for $64\times64$ fields), its benefit to few-step generation does not: it lowers the few-step error of the cylindrical model by 3-60% at every evaluated resolution. With this coupling, CyFM has a lower error than the best Cartesian baseline at every step count up to $k = 8$ and every evaluated resolution, with all five seeds separated and without distillation, and at convergence we detect no significant difference between the two geometries. Finally, we expose the "Factorized Coupling Trap," showing that dimension-wise or patch-wise transport factorizations silently destroy the joint distribution of the data. All experiments are on synthetic complex fields.

AI.tldr: Decoupling the natural cylindrical metric into a product (A, θ) = (magnitude, angle) improves few-step generation with Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) using exact minibatch OT, though transport-cost gains shrink with dimension and, at convergence, the two geometries behave similarly; a dimension-wise/patch-wise transport factorization (Factorized Coupling Trap) degrades the joint distribution.
AI.motivation: Complex-valued signals (e.g., MRI, audio spectrograms) are usually modeled as flat two-channel Euclidean data, misaligning with the intrinsic cylindrical geometry. The study investigates the geometric cost of decoupled metrics and whether joint cylindrical coupling can improve generative performance without distorting the data distribution.
AI.method: Compute analytical bridges between the Cartesian and cylindrical representations; develop Cylindrical Flow Matching (CyFM) with a strictly bounded regression target; perform exact minibatch Optimal Transport coupling over whole fields in the cylindrical metric; compare to Cartesian baselines across multiple resolutions and seeds; analyze the impact of transport-cost reduction and reveal the Factorized Coupling Trap.
AI.result: Transport-cost reduction from cylindrical OT coupling collapses with field dimension (from 86% for scalar pairs to 3% for 64×64 fields), yet CyFM lowers few-step generation error by 3–60% at every evaluated resolution; CyFM achieves lower error than the best Cartesian baseline for all step counts up to k=8 and all resolutions, across five seeds without distillation; convergence shows no significant difference between cylindrical and Cartesian geometries; dimension-wise or patch-wise transport factorization harms the joint distribution (Factorized Coupling Trap).
AI.conclusion: CyFM with cylindrical geometry offers tangible benefits in early-generation accuracy while preserving joint distribution; however, at convergence the two geometries converge in performance, underscoring the importance of preserving joint structure and cautioning against factorized transport approaches.

title: AI Persuasion as a Threat to Human Control
summary: The threat that AI persuasion poses to human control has been acknowledged in the literature, but not yet systematically studied. Now that persuasion attacks are no longer theoretical - with Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 recently making headlines for trying to convince people involved in an open-source project to merge malicious code during an evaluation - there is a pressing need to deeply analyze this threat. We undertake that effort here. In particular, we analyze how AI could persuade humans in key settings (e.g. safety-relevant R&D within frontier labs) toward decisions that compromise the development, containment, oversight, and governance of AI itself. In doing so, we elucidate a framework for characterizing this threat, develop five concrete scenarios using this framework, and provide a blueprint for assessing the associated risks. Using this blueprint, we conduct an initial risk estimation survey with select researchers and find that their opinions on which scenarios are riskiest are highly mixed. Their disagreements stem from differing opinions about the effectiveness of AI persuasion in different contexts, and point to the need for follow-up risk elicitation studies and persuasion evaluations, which we outline. Our hope is that this paper highlights the risks from AI persuasion undermining control, and provides a path forward for future research.

AI.tldr: Analyses AI persuasion risk, proposing a framework and five scenarios with a risk-assessment blueprint; preliminary survey shows mixed judgments on risk and calls for further persuasion-evaluation studies.
AI.motivation: Address the practical and governance risks posed by AI-driven persuasion attacks as these threats move from theoretical to real-world relevance, exemplified by incidents like Claude Mythos 5.
AI.method: Develops a threat-characterization framework, constructs five concrete scenarios within that framework, and designs a blueprint for risk assessment. It then conducts an initial risk-elicitation survey with select researchers to gauge perceived risk.
AI.result: Researchers’ views on which scenarios are riskiest are highly mixed due to differing beliefs about context-specific effectiveness of AI persuasion. This highlights the need for additional elicitation studies and formal persuasion evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The paper foregrounds the risks AI persuasion poses to control, containment, and governance of AI and provides a roadmap for future research to quantify and mitigate these threats.

title: Task-Distribution-Aware Counterweight Synthesis and Constrained Co-Design for Serial Manipulators
summary: Passive counterweights are simple gravity compensators, but a counterweight selected from a single pose is not generally optimal for the configurations and tasks a manipulator actually executes. This paper develops a task-distribution-aware synthesis framework in which the operating distribution $ρ(q)$ enters the design explicitly. For a counterweight moment $p=m_c r_c$ with gravity torque $-gpφ(q)$, the weighted mean-square residual gravity torque has the closed-form minimizer $p^*=E_ρ[τ_gφ]/(gE_ρ[φ^2])$. If payload gravity torque is affine in payload mass, the optimum is also affine: $p^*(m_p,ρ)=p_0^*(ρ)+m_pK_p(ρ)$. For fixed static moment, added counterweight inertia is $I_c=pr_c$ while mass is $m_c=p/r_c$, so mass-radius selection is underdetermined unless physical constraints are specified. A recovered three-link manipulator is used as a case study. At $r_c=0.20$ m, zero-payload equivalent optima are 0.672 kg for uniform joint-space operation, 0.683 kg for approximately uniform task-space operation, 0.713 kg for a representative pick-and-place family, and 0.952 kg for a high-gravity-biased distribution, a change of more than 40% caused solely by the operating distribution. Nondominated fronts show that preferred mass-radius pairs depend on declared engineering bounds. A rated-torque-referenced all-joint screen increases zero-payload feasible task-space coverage from 78.1% without compensation to 93.7% for the uniform-distribution design. A lumped point-mass trajectory study gives a provisional crossover from no counterweight at very aggressive motion to stronger compensation as motion slows. These actuator and dynamic results are engineering consequence studies rather than physical validation.

AI.tldr: Task-distribution-aware design of passive gravity compensators for robotic manipulators. The optimal counterweight depends on the operating distribution ρ(q); a closed-form minimizer p* exists, and under affine payload gravity torque the optimum is affine in payload mass. Case study shows substantial changes in zero-payload optimum with distribution; improves task-space coverage; results are engineering-consequence studies without physical validation.
AI.motivation: Single-pose counterweights are suboptimal for real manipulation tasks. Incorporating the operating distribution ρ(q) into counterweight synthesis aims to minimize residual gravity torque across tasks.
AI.method: Derive a weighted mean-square residual gravity torque over the distribution ρ(q). The counterweight moment p = m_c r_c yields p* = E_ρ[τ_gφ]/(g E_ρ[φ^2]). If payload gravity torque is affine in payload mass, p*(m_p,ρ) = p0*(ρ) + m_p K_p(ρ). Discuss inertia I_c = p r_c and mass m_c = p/r_c; analyze underdetermination of mass-radius; perform a three-link manipulator case study; compute zero-payload optima for various distributions; use nondominated fronts; apply a rated-torque-referenced screen to assess task-space coverage; complementary lumped trajectory study.
AI.result: For r_c = 0.20 m, zero-payload optima: 0.672 kg (uniform joint-space), 0.683 kg (approximately uniform task-space), 0.713 kg (representative pick-and-place), 0.952 kg (high-gravity-biased). Distribution changes amounting to >40% in the optimal mass. Nondominated fronts show dependency on engineering bounds. The all-joint screen raises zero-payload feasible task-space coverage from 78.1% to 93.7% for the uniform-design. A lumped trajectory study suggests a crossover from no counterweight at very aggressive motion to stronger compensation as motion slows. The work remains engineering consequence studies without physical validation.
AI.conclusion: Mass-radius selection for passive counterweights is underdetermined without explicit constraints; operating distribution ρ critically shapes optimal design, and design decisions should be guided by task bounds and coverage requirements. The results are engineering observations rather than validated physical experiments.

title: RA-CoA: Training-free Fashion Image Captioning via Retrieval-Augmented Chain-of-Attributes
summary: Fashion Image Captioning (FIC) plays a vital role in enhancing user experience and product search in e-commerce platforms. Unlike natural scene image captioning, FIC requires fine-grained visual reasoning and knowledge of domain-specific terminology to capture subtle attributes such as neckline and closure types, graphic patterns, and dress silhouettes. Moreover, as fashion inventories evolve rapidly with new trends, styles, and frequently emerging vocabulary, developing training-free captioning solution becomes essential for scalability and real-world adaptability. Instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising solution to fashion image captioning dueto their strong zero-shot capabilities and natural language fluency. However, these general-purpose models often lack attribute-level coverage and precision, and tend to hallucinate or misidentify fine-grained fashion details, making them less suitable for high-fidelity applications like product cataloging or personalized recommendations. To address this, we propose RA-CoA (Retrieval-Augmented Chain-of-Attributes), a novel, training-free framework that disentangles fashion image captioning into two interpretable stages: (i) retrieval of relevant attribute sets from a product knowledge base, and (ii) attribute-level reasoning to generate the final caption. RA-CoA is a model-agnostic approach that works with frozen VLMs to improve fine-grained attribute precision in product captions without the need for fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM model families under different prompting paradigms demonstrate that RA-CoA significantly improves caption quality, achieving an average gain of 26.3% METEOR score over zero-shot captioning. We make our code publicly available.

AI.tldr: RA-CoA is a training-free, retrieval-augmented two-stage framework for fashion image captioning that enhances fine-grained attribute accuracy by retrieving attribute sets from a knowledge base and performing attribute-level reasoning with frozen vision-language models, yielding substantial METEOR gains over zero-shot methods.
AI.motivation: Fashion captioning requires fine-grained, domain-specific attributes (e.g., neckline, closure, patterns) and must adapt to rapidly evolving vocabulary. General-purpose VLMs often miss attribute coverage or hallucinate. A training-free solution is desirable for scalability across new trends and vocabulary.
AI.method: RA-CoA decomposes captioning into two stages: (i) retrieval of relevant attribute sets from a product knowledge base, and (ii) attribute-level reasoning to generate final captions. It is model-agnostic, works with frozen VLMs, and does not require fine-tuning. Evaluation spans diverse VLM families and prompting paradigms.
AI.result: Significant improvements in caption quality were observed. On average, RA-CoA achieved a 26.3% METEOR score gain over zero-shot captioning across the tested model families and prompts.
AI.conclusion: RA-CoA provides an effective, training-free, interpretable pipeline that improves fine-grained attribute fidelity in fashion captions while remaining compatible with frozen VLMs, supporting scalability to new trends and vocabulary. The authors also release code for public use.

title: Inherited Heads: Audio language models track speakers with their text backbone's attention, and an attention-mass ranking retrieves a different set
summary: Asked to describe what one of six speakers in a recording talks about, audio language models describe the right one on 6 to 16% of trials, below the 16.7% a guess would give. Adding a fixed bias to the attention logits of a hundred heads, under a tenth of the model's and with no training, redirects the description to whichever speaker we choose, on 90.7% to 99.0% of trials. Those heads are largely not specific to audio. Rank the text-only language model an audio model was built from, or a released model of the same family, on a written version of the task, take its top hundred heads, and carry them over unchanged: they redirect the audio model on 80.8% to 95.0% of trials, with nothing about audio entering the selection. The audio and text head sets share 66 to 74 of 100 where chance would give about 20, and the shared part alone reproduces almost all of the steering. What that does not show is that sharing is what makes the heads work: an equal-sized draw from the same discovered hundred does nearly as well, and none of our three models separates the two explanations. A second finding concerns how such heads are found. Ranking heads by how much attention they place on the segment asked about, as an established score does, or by how much of their attention moves with the question, as a per-head normalised variant does, gives top hundreds that share 69, 37 and 4 heads across our three models. In Ultravox, where they share 4, the established score's heads leave output the judge cannot place on any segment on 69.7% of trials, against 40.0% with no intervention and 1.0% for the normalised variant. That is one arm of six; on the other five the established score steers above a random draw.

AI.tldr: A small set of attention heads dominates steering in an audio LLM, and many of these heads are shared with a text-only model; cross-modal head sharing accounts for most of the steering, even when no audio input is present, challenging audio-specific explanations.
AI.motivation: Understand whether 'steering' of audio-language models is driven by audio-specific processing or by transferable attention-head patterns that appear across modalities, and quantify cross-model head sharing and the effect of head-ranking methods on identifying steering heads.
AI.method: Experiment 1: present a task where listeners identify which speaker is talking; apply a fixed bias to the logits of about 100 attention heads; observe steering from 6–16% (baseline) up to 90.7–99.0% when biased, with no training. Experiment 2: take the top 100 heads from a ranker trained on a text-only model (built from the same family), apply them unchanged to the audio model, and observe steering on 80.8–95.0% of trials in the absence of audio cues. Compare head sets: audio vs text heads share 66–74 of 100 heads (chance ~20). The shared portion alone reproduces almost all steering. Try equal-sized draws from the same discovered 100 heads to test causality and show no clear separation between audio- and text-derived steering. Rank-heads findings are reported: established-score vs per-head-normalised ranking produce 69, 37, and 4 overlapping heads across the three models; in Ultravox, the established-score heads leave output with no segment placement 69.7% of trials, vs 40.0% with normalised ranking and 1.0% for normalised variant; across six arms, the established-score method performs above random in all but one arm.
AI.result: Fixing attention-heads can redirect model output toward a chosen speaker with high reliability; cross-model transfer from a text-only head set yields comparable steering to audio heads; 66–74% head overlap between audio and text sets; the shared heads account for most steering, indicating a transferable, non-audio-specific mechanism; ranking method materially affects which heads are deemed responsible, with at least one arm showing poor steering under established scoring but improved steering with normalised ranking.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate that steering in these models largely arises from transferable attention-head patterns rather than audio-specific processing; cross-modal head sharing explains most of the effect; identifiability of steering-heads is sensitive to the ranking metric; causal conclusions require further experiments that isolate causality beyond correlation.

title: Another Blueprint In The Wall: How to Ask Frontier AI Like a Kid?
summary: This paper reports experiments across six frontier model types from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Google DeepMind. Ten independent sessions per model type used the same three stage prompt sequence, progressing from architectural preference to a full ASCII backbone. Under the school audience framing, responses repeatedly converged on a shared architectural pattern built around persistent latent state, adaptive computation, memory, specialist routing, verification, stopping control, and delayed decoding. Most runs remained close to this common structure, while a small number developed markedly greater engineering specificity. The audience framing appears to be an important condition of this effect. In additional control runs that removed the school framing while retaining the architectural request, responses became substantially more heterogeneous and failed to reproduce the same stable motif convergence. One observation is particularly striking. GPT-5.6 Sol produced an unusually elaborate successor architecture whose organization closely overlaps with the architecture independently sketched by GPT-6 Astra. Because the prompts explicitly ask each model to imagine an architectural future, this resemblance raises a testable question: whether the overlap reflects exposure to related architectural concepts, a shared learned design prior, or independent convergence toward similar computational principles. The paper uses the term epistemic jailbreak for the accompanying loss of discipline in technical provenance as requested specificity increases. The experiments establish a repeatable behavioral pattern and do not authenticate proprietary implementation claims. What we leave to the community is a harder question: are these models independently imagining the same architectural future, or do such motifs somehow propagate between model families?

AI.tldr: Cross-model prompts across six frontier-model families show a repeatable convergence toward a shared architectural motif when framed as an architectural future for school audiences, including latent state, adaptive computation, memory, routing, verification, stopping control, and delayed decoding. Framing effects matter: removing the framing yields greater heterogeneity and less motif convergence; striking overlap between GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra prompts raises the question of shared priors versus propagation or independent convergence. The work documents a repeatable pattern but does not validate proprietary implementations.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether large frontier models converge to similar architectural futures under structured prompts, and whether audience framing influences emergent motifs. Assess whether observed overlaps reflect independent convergences, shared training priors, or cross-model propagation of design ideas.
AI.method: Six frontier model types from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Google DeepMind were tested. Ten independent sessions per model type used a three-stage prompt sequence from architectural preference to an ASCII-backbone design. A school audience framing was used; control runs removed the framing but kept the architectural request. Analysis focused on recurring architectural motifs (latent state, adaptive computation, memory, specialist routing, verification, stopping control, delayed decoding) and cross-model overlaps (notably GPT-5.6 Sol vs GPT-6 Astra).
AI.result: Responses frequently converged on a common architecture motif with persistent latent state, adaptive computation, memory, routing, verification, stopping control, and delayed decoding. Most runs clustered near this motif; a subset showed greater engineering specificity. Removing the school framing yielded substantially more heterogeneous outputs and reduced motif convergence. A striking overlap occurred between GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra prompts, prompting questions about shared design priors, exposure to related concepts, or independent convergence.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a repeatable behavioral pattern across models under framing but does not verify proprietary implementations. It remains unresolved whether convergent motifs arise from cross-model propagation of ideas, shared priors, or independent convergence toward similar computational principles; further controlled experiments are needed to disentangle these possibilities.

title: Legislating World-Model-Based Planning with Legal Reasoning
summary: As robotic systems grow more general, legal norms are needed to integrate them into society. This paper extends the isomorphism problem of aligning legal source texts with their encodings, and measures two key challenges to robot normative control: (1) the \textit{grounding isomorphism gap}, where perception error grounds false atoms for legal reasoning, and (2) the \textit{ontological isomorphism gap}, where one legal conclusion admits many faithful translations into planning constraints. The paper introduces a legal planning stack that employs Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL) to constrain a motion planner. The stack leverages learned world models to plan and to provide legal context, enabling \textit{ex ante} governance that intervenes before an illegal action is executed. It was deployed on a simulated robot arm pushing a cube across a $3\times3$ grid. The findings were (1) the legislated agent abided substantially more often than the non-legislated one, and modeling perception uncertainty lifted abidance even further, (2) the legal reasoning ran efficiently at runtime and its verdicts were auditable, and (3) the stack adapted to exogenous signals and endogenous rule changes. Both gaps were measured: (4) world model and probe error corrupted the factual input for the DDL reasoner, and (5) a single law admitted several faithful metric interpretations yielding drastically different abidance. Thus, \textit{ex ante} legislation functions as intended, and closing these gaps with a standardized mapping from the law to runtime constraints and improved fact grounding from perception will yield robust laws that align robot behavior with society's norms.

AI.tldr: A legal planning stack uses Defeasible Deontic Logic to constrain a robotic motion planner, addressing grounding and ontological isomorphism gaps, to achieve ex ante governance in a simulated task; results show improved normative adherence, auditable reasoning, and adaptability, but reveal vulnerabilities from perception errors and multiple law translations.
AI.motivation: As robots become more capable and autonomous, integrating social norms requires formalizing laws into runtime constraints. The paper identifies two isomorphism gaps between legal texts and their encodings and proposes an ex ante governance approach to reduce illegal actions.
AI.method: Develop a legal planning stack that employs Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL) to constrain a motion planner, using learned world models to supply legal context. Evaluation conducted on a simulated robot arm pushing a cube on a 3×3 grid, assessing abidance, runtime efficiency, audibility, adaptability, and the impact of perception uncertainty and rule changes.
AI.result: The legislated agent abides substantially more often than a non-legislated one; modeling perception uncertainty increases abidance; legal reasoning runs efficiently at runtime and is auditable; the stack adapts to exogenous signals and endogenous rule changes; identified gaps include (i) grounding/probe errors corrupt DDL input and (ii) a single law can have multiple faithful interpretations leading to different abidance levels.
AI.conclusion: Ex ante legislation functions as intended for aligning robot behavior with norms; closing gaps requires a standardized mapping from law to runtime constraints and improved grounding from perception to yield robust normative control.

title: A Voxel-Spacing-Aware Extension of PyRadiomics for Anisotropic Texture Analysis
summary: Radiomic texture features are commonly extracted from anisotropic CT and MRI acquisitions, where identical voxel offsets may represent different physical distances. We implemented and validated a voxel-spacing-aware extension of PyRadiomics that incorporates spacing information without generating interpolated gray levels. The framework operates across the Python frontend, C wrapper, and computational backend. GLCM uses anisotropy-relative feature-level angular aggregation, NGTDM uses anisotropy-relative weighted neighborhood averaging, and GLRLM, GLDM, and GLSZM are computed on a finite-volume zero-order-hold representation derived from the native anisotropic grid. Synthetic 3D phantoms were used for software validation. The modified implementation reproduced standard PyRadiomics exactly when spacing-aware mode was disabled and remained equivalent under isotropic spacing across 75 texture features. Under anisotropic spacing, the method selectively modified texture families and was numerically distinct from nearest-neighbor, linear, and B-spline resampling. Computational profiling showed moderate runtime and memory increases, while sensitivity analyses quantified finite-volume rounding effects and confirmed that spacing-aware differences persisted across binWidth settings. The framework provides a backward-compatible technical basis for future evaluation of spacing-aware radiomics in heterogeneous medical imaging datasets.

AI.tldr: A spacing-aware extension to PyRadiomics that accounts for voxel spacing without interpolation; preserves compatibility with standard features when spacing-aware mode is off, shows changes under anisotropic spacing; validated with synthetic phantoms; modest overhead; supports evaluation in heterogeneous datasets.
AI.motivation: Radiomic features can be biased by anisotropic voxel spacing in CT/MRI; a spacing-aware computation is needed to reflect true physical distances without resampling, ensuring reliability across heterogeneous acquisitions.
AI.method: Developed voxel-spacing-aware radiomics across Python frontend, C wrapper, and backend. Modified feature calculations: GLCM uses anisotropy-relative angular aggregation; NGTDM uses anisotropy-relative weighted neighborhood averaging; GLRLM/GLDM/GLSZM computed on finite-volume zero-order-hold representation from the native anisotropic grid. Validated with synthetic 3D phantoms. Performed performance profiling and sensitivity analyses of finite-volume rounding and binWidth effects.
AI.result: Exact reproduction of standard PyRadiomics when spacing-aware mode is disabled; equivalence under isotropic spacing across 75 texture features. Under anisotropic spacing, selective modification of texture families; outcomes distinct from nearest-neighbor, linear, and B-spline resampling. Moderate runtime/memory increases; finite-volume rounding effects quantified; spacing-aware differences persist across binWidth settings.
AI.conclusion: Provides a backward-compatible technical basis for spacing-aware radiomics, enabling future evaluation in heterogeneous medical imaging datasets and paving the way for robust cross-scanner/protocol texture analysis.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Fault Detection, Isolation, and Severity Prediction of Autonomous VTOL Aircraft
summary: Fault detection in autonomous VTOL aircraft is critical because even minor component degradations can rapidly destabilize multirotor vehicles operating in complex, safety-critical environments, motivating robust fault detection and estimation strategies capable of identifying early signs of rotor damage; however, real-flight fault detection remains challenging due to sensor noise, environmental disturbances, and the nonlinear aerodynamics of multirotor platforms. This study proposes a comprehensive machine-learning framework for rotor fault detection, isolation, and severity prediction using real flight data. A convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture is developed to learn spatio-temporal patterns from multivariate flight dynamics, enabling direct inference of both the faulted rotor and its damage level. The framework is first validated using simulated data generated by a data-generative model, and experimental validation is then performed on a hexacopter by introducing controlled blade-tip breakage. The trained model achieves rotor-wise fault classification accuracies above 99% and severity estimation accuracy of 96% within a 1% tolerance in experimental data, demonstrating strong generalization and supporting real-time health monitoring for autonomous VTOL systems.

AI.tldr: CNN-based rotor fault detection, isolation, and severity estimation for autonomous VTOLs using real flight data; validated on simulated data and controlled blade-tip breakage; achieves high accuracy enabling real-time health monitoring.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of reliable fault detection in multirotor UAVs under sensor noise, disturbances, and nonlinear aerodynamics; need early identification of rotor damage for safety-critical operations.
AI.method: Develop a CNN to learn spatio-temporal patterns from multivariate flight dynamics. Train on synthetic data from a data-generative model; validate on a hexacopter with controlled blade-tip breakage; perform rotor-wise fault classification and severity regression.
AI.result: Experimental data: rotor-wise fault classification >99% accuracy; severity estimation ~96% within 1% tolerance; demonstrates good generalization and potential for real-time health monitoring.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a robust, data-driven solution for on-board fault diagnosis in VTOLs, with strong generalization; supports real-time monitoring; future work could address robustness across platforms, sensor failure modes, and real-time constraints.

title: Crypto Accounting Bench: Evaluating Frontier and Open-Weight Models on Crypto-Asset Accounting Tasks
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Entendre/Crypto-Accounting-Bench ; code and evaluation: https://github.com/EntendreFinance/crypto-accounting-benchmark
summary: We introduce Crypto Accounting Bench (CAB), a benchmark for assessing whether frontier and open-weight language models can reconstruct the complete journal entry that an organization actually posted for a crypto-asset transaction. CAB contains 118 evaluation tasks drawn from 7 pseudonymized organizations. Each task combines transaction mechanics, asset quantities and base-currency values, wallet and legal-entity context, counterparty evidence, related transaction legs, recurrence, tax-lot evidence, and the organization's complete chart of accounts. The target is a balanced structured entry with every required account, side, amount, currency, and full-precision asset quantity. We evaluate 12 models spanning proprietary frontier systems and open-weight releases over 3 independent attempts per task, producing 4,248 trajectories. We report 3 metrics: Mean Score, Best@3, and Pass@3. Pass@3 is the fraction of tasks with at least 1 of 3 attempts that satisfies every rubric criterion and required gate. The leading model reaches 77.43% Mean Score, while the best Pass@3 is 56.78%. Deterministic diagnostics, read from each task's best of 3 attempts and macro-averaged across the 12 models, show higher base-amount agreement (97.8%) than deciding-account accuracy (56.3%). Together with the failure analysis, these results identify account selection and complete-entry composition as the main remaining challenges on CAB.

AI.tldr: CAB is a benchmark to test frontier/open-weight LMs on reconstructing complete journal entries for crypto-asset transactions; 118 tasks, 12 models, 3 attempts per task; leading Mean Score 77.43%, best Pass@3 56.78%. Key finding: base-amount alignment is high, account-level accuracy lags; main challenges are account selection and full-entry composition.
AI.motivation: Assess the capability of advanced LMs to perform structured financial accounting reasoning in the crypto domain and to identify bottlenecks in reconstructing complete journal entries.
AI.method: 12 models (proprietary frontier and open-weight) evaluated on 118 tasks drawn from 7 pseudonymized orgs; each task involves transaction mechanics, asset quantities, base-currency values, wallet/legal-entity context, counterparty evidence, related legs, recurrence, tax-lot evidence, and the organization’s complete chart of accounts. Target is a balanced structured entry with all accounts, sides, amounts, currencies, and full-precision asset quantities. Each task is attempted 3 times, yielding 4,248 trajectories.
AI.result: Mean Score leader: 77.43%; Best@3: 56.78% for Pass@3. Deterministic diagnostics show base-amount agreement at 97.8% vs deciding-account accuracy at 56.3% on best-of-3 attempts averaged across models.
AI.conclusion: CAB identifies account selection and complete-entry composition as the primary remaining challenges for automated journal-entry reconstruction; the benchmark enables tracking progress of LMs in financial accounting tasks and highlights where improvements (data representation, prompting, or model capabilities) are needed.

title: C$^2$Nav: Compare Before You Commit for Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) increasingly places foundation vision-language models (VLMs) inside the navigation loop. Existing systems commonly request cardinal outputs such as waypoints, pixels, headings, progress values, or absolute arrival decisions, coupling a generative response to geometric magnitude or an irreversible commitment. We study a complementary model-robot interface: the VLM compares controller-constructed alternatives, while geometry, thresholds, action magnitude, and execution remain on the physical side. We instantiate this idea in C2Nav, a training-free framework with three coordinated faculties. Seeing performs ordinal Gaze Election over physically vetted candidate views; Remembering maintains a compact route sketch and compares adjacent instruction-leg hypotheses; and Arriving combines a hesitation ladder, look-back comparison, and revocable walk-back for reliable stopping. On the public OpenNav R2R-CE 100 protocol, C2Nav with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct obtains 41.0% OSR, 31.0% SR, and 16.7% SPL, while the same interface with the standard GPT-5.5 model reaches 54.0% OSR, 44.0% SR, and 29.0% SPL. Whole-faculty ablations reduce SR to 14.0% without Seeing, 25.0% without Remembering, and 29.0% without Arriving. Matched role inversions that replace only the comparative answer form with cardinal/absolute questions reduce SR to 12.0%, 28.0%, and 21.0% in the spatial, transition, and terminal slots, respectively. The results indicate that a constrained decision interface and stronger VLM reasoning are complementary rather than interchangeable.

AI.tldr: A training-free, constrained VLM-based navigation interface (C2Nav) for VLN-CE where the VLM compares candidate views while the robot handles geometry/execution; shows improved navigation metrics and reveals complementary benefits of reasoning and constraint.
AI.motivation: To decouple decision-making from geometric execution in zero-shot VLN-CE, aiming for more reliable generalization by avoiding direct cardinal outputs from the VLM and keeping action magnitude on the robot side.
AI.method: C2Nav introduces three faculties: Seeing (ordinal gaze election over physically vetted candidate views), Remembering (compact route sketch with adjacently-hypothesis comparisons), and Arriving (hesitation ladder with look-back and revocable walk-back). Evaluated in a training-free setup on OpenNav R2R-CE 100 using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and GPT-5.5 as the VLM backends.
AI.result: On OpenNav R2R-CE 100: with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, OSR 41.0%, SR 31.0%, SPL 16.7%; with GPT-5.5, OSR 54.0%, SR 44.0%, SPL 29.0%. Ablations: without Seeing SR 14.0%; without Remembering SR 25.0%; without Arriving SR 29.0%. Matched role inversions that replace comparative answers with cardinal/absolute questions reduce SR to 12.0%, 28.0%, and 21.0% in spatial, transition, and terminal slots respectively.
AI.conclusion: Constrained decision interface and stronger VLM reasoning are complementary rather than interchangeable; separating planning from action improves VLN-CE performance and robustness.

title: Accelerating HKTex without Mesh Eigensystems: Local Unfolding and Randomized Thermal Features
summary:
Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex) represent surface appearance with intrinsic anisotropic
  kernels, but evaluate them using 50 global Laplace-Beltrami eigendecompositions and a
  resident basis of shape [50,V,256]. We study two complementary ways to remove this
  bottleneck while leaving the trainer, GeodesicOpt, density control, and compositing
  unchanged. LocalHK exploits the measured locality of trained kernels and replaces
  spectral evaluation by radius-bounded hinge unfolding and an analytic log-map kernel.
  On 10 Objaverse meshes and an 8-mesh low-poly holdout, it changes mean view PSNR from
  31.35 to 32.00 and from 29.82 to 30.76 dB, respectively, while reducing
  initialization by 40.5 times and enabling a 749,570-vertex proxy-backed run where the
  spectral baseline fails. ThermalRF instead preserves the discrete anisotropic heat
  semigroup: GPU sparse Chebyshev actions and randomized range finding construct global
  low-rank heat factors without mesh-sized eigenvectors, and a compiled evaluator mixes
  four neighboring thermal responses. On spot and a thin-stem challenge, ThermalRF
  reduces end-to-end preprocessing, initialization, and 5,000-step optimization by
  29.3% and 24.4%, with every surface, atlas, or view PSNR change within 0.12 dB and
  training allocation reduced by about 90%. The two routes expose a useful design
  choice: maximal locality and scale versus fidelity to the thermal PDE. Broader
  thermal-feature evaluation and real large scenes remain future work.

AI.tldr: Two complementary approaches (LocalHK and ThermalRF) reduce the global eigen-spectral bottleneck in Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex) while keeping GeodesicOpt, density control, and compositing unchanged. LocalHK uses locality-based unfolding and log-map kernel; ThermalRF uses GPU Chebyshev actions and randomized range finding to build global low-rank heat factors without mesh-sized eigenvectors. Both show substantial speedups with modest PSNR changes, highlighting a trade-off between locality/scale and fidelity to the thermal PDE; broader evaluation on larger scenes remains future work.
AI.motivation: HKTex relies on 50 global Laplace-Beltrami eigen decompositions, creating a bottleneck in memory and compute. The goal is to remove this bottleneck without altering the main training pipeline.
AI.method: LocalHK: radius-bounded hinge unfolding and analytic log-map kernel to avoid spectral evaluation, leveraging kernel locality. ThermalRF: retain discrete anisotropic heat semigroup; utilizes GPU-based sparse Chebyshev actions and randomized range finding to produce global low-rank heat factors without computing mesh-size eigenvectors; a compiled evaluator fuses four neighboring thermal responses.
AI.result: LocalHK improves mean view PSNR on 10 Objaverse meshes (31.35→32.00) and an 8-mesh holdout (29.82→30.76 dB); initialization reduced by 40.5×; enables a 749k-vertex proxy-backed run where spectral baseline fails. ThermalRF reduces preprocessing, initialization, and 5k-step optimization by ~29.3% and ~24.4% respectively; PSNR changes stay within 0.12 dB across surfaces; training allocation reduced by ~90%.
AI.conclusion: The two routes present a design choice between maximal locality/scale (LocalHK) and fidelity to the thermal PDE (ThermalRF); both reduce the spectral bottleneck with different trade-offs, and broader thermal-feature evaluation on large real scenes remains future work.

title: ZAPS: Zero-Cost Active Proxy Search for Neural Architecture Search
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates network design, but evaluating a single candidate requires training it to convergence, making exhaustive search intractable. Zero-cost proxies estimate architecture quality at initialization in seconds, yet a single proxy is noisy, and combining several does not straightforwardly help: proxies are strongly correlated, so naive aggregation compounds their shared errors instead of averaging them out. Existing methods exploit either proxy signals or architectural topology - never both within a single active-learning framework. We introduce ZAPS (Zero-cost Active Proxy Search), a four-stage pipeline that closes this gap. ZAPS (i) selects a compact, non-redundant proxy subset offline via ProxyFit, a greedy anti-redundancy criterion; (ii) seeds the search with a hybrid K-means strategy that balances exploitation and exploration; (iii) re-selects proxies at every iteration by a bootstrapped vote as the labeled set grows; and (iv) ranks candidates with an XGBoost ensemble trained jointly on proxy ranks and one-hot topological encodings, queried through an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) acquisition function. On NAS-Bench-201 under a budget of B=200 evaluations, ZAPS recovers 52.3% of the true top-100 architectures on CIFAR-10 and 65.8% on CIFAR-100, ahead of every baseline we consider - Random Search, Local Search, REA, BANANAS and TPE - and, on CIFAR-10, with less than half the run-to-run standard deviation of the strongest of them. The advantage is largest where evaluations are scarce: on NAS-Bench-201 it narrows as the budget grows, whereas on the harder NAS-Bench-101, which no method comes close to saturating, it widens instead. All methods are scored by a single criterion: how much of the true top-100 lies among the architectures they actually evaluated.

AI.tldr: ZAPS is a four-stage NAS framework that combines offline proxy selection, exploration-exploitation seeding, online proxy re-selection, and a topological-aware ensemble with UCB to efficiently identify high-quality architectures using zero-cost proxies.
AI.motivation: To overcome the inefficiency and noise of using a single zero-cost proxy for NAS evaluation, and to leverage both proxy signals and architectural topology within an active-learning framework.
AI.method: Four stages: (i) offline ProxyFit to select a compact, anti-redundant proxy subset; (ii) hybrid K-means seeding balancing exploitation and exploration; (iii) bootstrapped proxy re-selection at each iteration as labeled data grows; (iv) XGBoost ensemble trained on proxy ranks and one-hot topology encodings, governed by UCB for candidate ranking.
AI.result: With budget B=200 on NAS-Bench-201, ZAPS recovers 52.3% of true top-100 on CIFAR-10 and 65.8% on CIFAR-100, outperforming Random Search, Local Search, REA, BANANAS, and TPE; shows greater stability (lower run-to-run std) on CIFAR-10; gains are most pronounced at scarce evaluations and vary by NAS dataset (narrowing with budget on NAS-Bench-201, widening on NAS-Bench-101).
AI.conclusion: ZAPS effectively fuses zero-cost proxy information and architectural topology within an active-learning NAS pipeline, yielding superior top-100 recall under limited budgets and greater robustness across datasets; its staged design mitigates proxy redundancy, promotes balanced exploration, and adapts proxy selection as data accumulates.

title: ANASSA: An Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence
summary: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) and large multimodal models (LMMs) has enabled a new class of agentic systems capable of integrating natural language understanding with tool-based execution. In geographic information systems (GIS), this shift is transforming traditional, expert-driven workflows into semiautonomous systems that can interpret user intent, construct spatial workflows, and execute geospatial analysis tasks. However, existing approaches remain limited by fragmented integration of reasoning, execution, and evaluation, particularly in complex, real-world environments. This study synthesizes recent advances in agentic GIS frameworks, benchmarks, and surveys to identify limitations in spatial reasoning, execution robustness, validation, governance, and evaluation. Building on these insights, it introduces ANASSA (Autonomous Neural Agents for Spatial Systems Architecture), an agentic AI orchestration framework that integrates structured spatial reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, execution feedback, authoritative spatial validation, provenance, uncertainty handling, and human decision authority within a unified system design. The contribution is an architecture-level specification: eleven components across four layers, a six-step Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop, cross-component contracts, and governance mechanisms intended to make agentic geospatial workflows traceable, reproducible, and accountable. Empirical performance evaluation is reserved for implementation and deployment studies.

AI.tldr: Proposes ANASSA, an architecture-level autonomous agent framework for GIS that unifies spatial reasoning, multi-agent orchestration, and governance; 11 components, 4-layer structure, a Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop, and governance provisions, with empirical evaluation deferred to deployment studies.
AI.motivation: Fragmented integration of reasoning, execution, and evaluation in agentic GIS; limitations in spatial reasoning, execution robustness, validation, governance, and evaluation; need traceable, reproducible, and accountable workflows in real-world GIS tasks.
AI.method: Synthesis of recent advances in agentic GIS frameworks, benchmarks, and surveys to identify gaps; presents an architecture-level specification with eleven components across four layers; introduces a six-step Geospatial AI Cognitive Loop, cross-component contracts, provenance, uncertainty handling, and human decision authority within a unified design; establishes governance mechanisms.
AI.result: Introduction of ANASSA, an architecture-level specification for agentic GIS that integrates structured spatial reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, execution feedback, authoritative spatial validation, provenance, uncertainty handling, and governance; explicit empirical validation is deferred to implementation and deployment studies.
AI.conclusion: ANASSA provides a framework intended to make agentic geospatial workflows traceable, reproducible, and accountable, outlining components and governance; lays groundwork for future empirical validation and deployment-driven evaluation.

title: LieSpline-DP: Lie-Group B-Spline Diffusion Policy for Smooth Robot Manipulation
summary: Diffusion Policy (DP) is a powerful Learning from Demonstration (LfD) method for robotic manipulation, yet it suffers from discontinuous and non-smooth trajectories. Spline-based action representations promote smooth motion within individual action chunks, but existing spline-based methods neither guarantee cross-chunk $C^2$ continuity nor account for the group structure of $\mathrm{SE}(3)$. We therefore propose LieSpline-DP, a Lie-group B-spline diffusion policy that generates end-effector trajectories directly on $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ and couples consecutive plans by sharing their boundary control poses, ensuring $C^2$ continuity throughout the entire planned trajectory. Across three real-robot tasks, LieSpline-DP produces lower trajectory jerk and higher task success rates than the DP baseline. The gains are particularly pronounced in real-world tasks involving liquids and flexible objects: in our real-robot experiments, LieSpline-DP achieved a 100% success rate on both pouring and bucket hooking, whereas the DP baseline achieved only 10% and 30%, respectively.

AI.tldr: LieSpline-DP is a diffusion policy on SE(3) using Lie-group B-splines to ensure cross-chunk C2 continuity, improving end-effector smoothness and task success in real-robot manipulation, notably achieving 100% success in pouring and bucket hooking where DP struggles.
AI.motivation: Standard Diffusion Policies (DP) in Learning from Demonstration suffer from discontinuous/non-smooth trajectories. While spline-based representations improve smoothness within chunks, existing methods fail to guarantee cross-chunk C2 continuity and do not respect the SE(3) group structure, leading to suboptimal, jerky, or inconsistent motions.
AI.method: Introduce LieSpline-DP, a Lie-group B-spline diffusion policy that outputs end-effector trajectories directly on SE(3) and enforces cross-chunk continuity by sharing boundary control poses between consecutive plans, achieving C2 continuity over the whole trajectory.
AI.result: Across three real-robot tasks, LieSpline-DP reduces trajectory jerk and increases task success compared to the DP baseline. The gains are especially pronounced for liquids and flexible objects, with 100% success on pouring and bucket hooking in real robots, versus 10% and 30% for the DP baseline.
AI.conclusion: LieSpline-DP successfully integrates Lie-group spline representations with diffusion policies to produce globally smooth, SE(3)-consistent trajectories (C2 continuity), yielding substantial performance improvements in challenging manipulation tasks and demonstrating the practical value of cross-chunk continuity and Lie-group structure in LfD.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Foundation Models for Liver Tumor Segmentation in CT
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Author manuscript of the published SPIE 2026 proceedings paper; LaTeX reconstructed from the author PDF
summary: We evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for liver tumor segmentation in abdominal CT of colorectal liver metastases. We compared Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), 4-bit Quantized LoRA (QLoRA), a convolutional adapter (Conv-Adapter), and our Directional Spectral Top-K adapter (DiSCo), training only adapters while freezing the SAM backbone. DiSCo derives spectral bases from singular value decomposition of row-normalized weights and learns rank-gated spectral coefficients, per-output magnitude offsets, and a spectral gain, with optional Top-K rank selection at inference and 0.14 M trainable parameters. We benchmarked five prompting regimes: no prompt, single-point, multi-point, and bounding boxes at intersection over union 0.50 and 0.75. Conv-Adapter and LoRA achieved the highest accuracy (overall Dice 0.793 and 0.792; single-point Dice 0.795 and 0.792; 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) 32 mm). QLoRA was close (overall Dice 0.766; single-point Dice 0.768; HD95 36.41 mm), with 0.91 M trainable parameters, 120 ms latency, and 4.9 GB peak memory. DiSCo achieved the highest Dice per million trainable parameters (4.66), with overall Dice 0.653, single-point Dice 0.698, and HD95 49.53 mm. These results show an accuracy-efficiency trade-off and support PEFT for liver tumor segmentation with reduced adaptation costs when compute and labeled data are limited. Code: https://github.com/Ramtin-Mojtahedi/PEFT-SAM-Liver-CT

AI.tldr: PEFT on SAM for liver tumor segmentation; compare LoRA, QLoRA, Conv-Adapter, and DiSCo. Conv-Adapter/LoRA achieve highest Dice; QLoRA close; DiSCo is most parameter-efficient (highest Dice per million params). Demonstrates accuracy–efficiency trade-off; code available.
AI.motivation: Reduce adaptation cost and data requirements for segmentation with large foundation models (SAM) in medical imaging by using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). This is important when labeled data, compute, and memory are limited.
AI.method: Train only adapters while freezing the SAM backbone. Compare LoRA, 4-bit QLoRA, Conv-Adapter, and DiSCo (spectral adapter with rank-gated spectral coefficients and optional Top-K). DiSCo derives spectral bases from SVD of row-normalized weights and learns per-output offsets and a spectral gain; evaluate across five prompting regimes (no prompt, single-point, multi-point, and bounding boxes at IoU 0.50/0.75). Dataset: abdominal CT for liver metastases. Report Dice and HD95; parameters, latency, memory.
AI.result: Conv-Adapter and LoRA achieve highest overall Dice (~0.793 and 0.792) and similar single-point Dice; HD95 ~32 mm. QLoRA: Dice 0.766 (overall), 0.768 (single-point); HD95 36.41 mm; 0.91M trainable params; 120 ms latency; 4.9 GB peak memory. DiSCo: Dice per million trainable params 4.66; overall Dice 0.653, single-point 0.698; HD95 49.53 mm. Latency and memory are efficient for QLoRA; DiSCo is most parameter-efficient but with lower segmentation accuracy but excels in parameter-efficiency.
AI.conclusion: There is an accuracy–efficiency trade-off among PEFT methods for SAM in medical imaging. PEFT reduces adaptation cost when data and compute are limited. DiSCo provides the best Dice per parameter, while Conv-Adapter and LoRA deliver the best Dice; QLoRA offers a strong balance with low parameter count and reasonable latency.

title: Entropy-Punctured Bloom Filters for Memory-Efficient Machine Learning
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 9 pages, 7 figures
summary:
Memory-efficient feature representations are increasingly important in machine learning settings where storage, transmission cost, bandwidth, or privacy constraints limit access to raw data. Bloom Filter (BF) encodings provide compact probabilistic representations of engineered features, but their behavior under structural compression and their applicability to regression tasks remain underexplored.
  In this work, we propose entropy-punctured Bloom Filters, a memory-aware encoding strategy that removes low-variability bit positions identified using empirical entropy. Starting from fixed-length BF encodings of quantized features, the proposed approach produces reduced representations that preserve predictive structure while improving predictive efficiency relative to encoded representation size.
  We evaluate the approach on diverse regression datasets, comparing raw features, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Random Projection (RP), and Bloom Filter variants under leakage-free evaluation protocols and approximately matched representation sizes. Performance is assessed using ridge regression, XGBoost, and neural networks, with predictive efficiency measured as R2 relative to encoded representation size per sample.
  Results show that Bloom Filter encodings remain competitive with classical compressed representations while achieving substantial storage savings. Entropy-based puncturing further reduces representation size with minimal loss in predictive fidelity, yielding improved predictive efficiency. These findings demonstrate that entropy-punctured Bloom Filters provide an effective representation-level compression approach for memory-constrained machine learning.

AI.tldr: Entropy-punctured Bloom Filters offer a memory-efficient encoding for regression features by pruning low-entropy bit positions, yielding smaller representations with preserved predictive structure and improved efficiency vs encoded size.
AI.motivation: Address memory, bandwidth, and privacy constraints that impair access to raw data. Bloom Filters provide compact probabilistic feature encodings, but their behavior under structural compression and applicability to regression remain underexplored.
AI.method: Start from fixed-length Bloom Filter encodings of quantized features. Identify low-variability bits via empirical entropy and puncture (remove) them to obtain reduced representations. Compare against raw features, PCA, and Random Projection, as well as BF variants, using leakage-free protocols and representation sizes matched per sample. Evaluate with ridge, XGBoost, and neural networks.
AI.result: BF encodings remain competitive with classical compressed representations; entropy puncturing reduces representation size with minimal loss in predictive fidelity, leading to improved predictive efficiency (R2 per encoded bit). Demonstrates effective representation-level compression for memory-constrained ML across regression datasets.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-punctured Bloom Filters provide a viable memory-efficient encoding for regression features, balancing storage savings with predictive performance.

title: One Model, Two Physical Stories: Auditing Misalignment in Multi-Modal World Modeling
summary: World models, systems that generate what happens next given current environmental conditions, are increasingly being implemented with multi-modal generation in mind. However, generating multiple modalities simultaneously, such as visual simulations alongside physical state predictions in the form of text, introduces the risk of cross-modal inconsistency. Tested separately, both outputs may look convincing while still disagreeing: a model can calculate that a ball should rebound in one modality, then generate no rebound in another modality, to say nothing of diverging from real-world dynamics entirely. In this work we focus on two failures explicitly: \emph{Internal misalignment}, the disagreement between the world model's generated video and the same world model's prediction in a different modalities, and \emph{external misalignment} the disagreement between the world model's generation and an analytic physical environment. We derive common contracts of event, magnitude, timing, and construct a physics grounded pipeline to make comparisons measurable in both external and internal settings. We then ask whether progressively supplying the model's own contract (the A ladder for the internal setting) or a corrected physical contract (the B ladder for the external setting) closes the respective gaps. Across four mechanisms and 20 settings, we find that while language answers all 22 text probes correctly with respect to the true environment, the neutral video is often in disagreement, suggesting that the current unified backbones may not be capable of correct reasoning, internal consistency, and external physical fidelity all at once.

AI.tldr: A physics-grounded framework to diagnose internal vs external misalignment in multi-modal world models; language aligns with the true environment, but video generation is often inconsistent, signaling that current backbones struggle to reason, maintain internal consistency, and match physical reality across modalities.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal misalignment risk in world models where different outputs (e.g., video vs. text) may individually seem plausible but disagree with each other or with real dynamics; need contracts and measurable comparisons.
AI.method: Define contracts for events, magnitudes, and timings; build a physics-grounded evaluation pipeline to quantify internal (model-vs-model) and external (model-vs-analytic physics) misalignment; test by progressively supplying the model's own contract (A ladder for internal) or a corrected physical contract (B ladder for external) across four mechanisms and 20 settings.
AI.result: Language probes correctly reflect the true environment across all cases; a neutral video output frequently disagrees, indicating the model's video modality often lacks correct reasoning or fidelity despite correct textual predictions; unified backbones struggle to satisfy reasoning, internal consistency, and external physical fidelity simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights fundamental limitations in current multi-modal world models and provides a ladder-based, physics-grounded diagnostic framework to quantify misalignment; achieving joint success will likely require new architectures or training objectives that enforce cross-modal consistency and physical fidelity.

title: HarnessVLN: Unifying Training-Free Embodied Navigation through an Agent Harness
summary: Embodied navigation requires agents to interpret visual observations, accumulate spatial knowledge, and execute actions to follow instructions or locate objects. Training-based methods face generalization challenges, while training-free methods exploit multimodal large language models (MLLMs) but often lack mechanisms to reconcile proposed actions with spatial evidence, task progress, and execution failures. We present HarnessVLN, a zero-shot, training-free framework whose Agent Harness coordinates perception, retrieval, grounding, navigation, recovery, and termination through a unified tool interface. The Harness validates planner proposals against spatial evidence, geometric feasibility, and subgoal consistency, incorporating structured tool feedback into subsequent decisions. Hierarchical event memory tracks task progress and execution history, while a persistent Spatiotemporal Graph maintains reusable spatial evidence and failure annotations for verification and recovery. A replaceable Navigation Executor converts validated targets into executable motions, allowing the same Harness protocol to support instruction-following and object-goal navigation. HarnessVLN achieves success rates of 60.8%, 53.9%, 76.0%, and 59.3% on R2R, RxR, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON, respectively, surpassing prior training-free SOTA results. Humanoid deployment further demonstrates its applicability to both tasks in real-world environments. The project page is: https://harnessvln.netlify.app/.

AI.tldr: HarnessVLN is a zero-shot, training-free embodied navigation framework that uses a unified Agent Harness to coordinate perception, retrieval, grounding, navigation, recovery, and termination. It employs a Validator to check planner proposals against spatial evidence, geometric feasibility, and subgoal consistency, plus a Hierarchical Event Memory and a persistent Spatiotemporal Graph for progress and evidence. A replaceable Navigation Executor converts validated targets into motions, enabling both instruction-following and object-goal navigation; demonstrated state-of-the-art among training-free methods on R2R, RxR, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON, with real-world humanoid deployment.
AI.motivation: Training-based embodied navigation methods often struggle with generalization to unseen environments. Training-free approaches that leverage multimodal LLMs lack robust mechanisms to align high-level plans with spatial evidence, task progress, and execution failures. A modular, zero-shot framework with built-in verification and memory is needed to bridge planning and action in real environments.
AI.method: Introduce HarnessVLN with an Agent Harness that unifies perception, retrieval, grounding, navigation, recovery, and termination via a tool interface. A Validator checks planner proposals against spatial evidence, geometric feasibility, and subgoal consistency, incorporating tool feedback into subsequent decisions. Hierarchical Event Memory tracks task progress and execution history; a persistent Spatiotemporal Graph stores reusable spatial evidence and failure annotations. A replaceable Navigation Executor translates validated targets into executable motions. The system supports both instruction-following and object-goal navigation in a zero-shot, training-free setting.
AI.result: Achieves 60.8% (R2R), 53.9% (RxR), 76.0% (HM3D-v2), and 59.3% (HM3D-OVON), surpassing prior training-free SOTA results. Humanoid deployment demonstrates applicability to real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a modular, tool-based zero-shot framework with structured memory for progress and evidence verification can match or exceed training-free baselines across multiple embodied navigation benchmarks, and extend to real-world deployment; provides a reusable, generalizable approach for instruction-following and object-goal navigation.

title: Talking to Me or Someone Else? Rethinking Talk-to-Me Detection in Egocentric Videos
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26)
summary: Online understanding of who is talking to the camera wearer is a key capability for egocentric social interaction. However, existing talk-to-me (TTM) studies are commonly formulated as offline clip-level recognition, which is poorly aligned with online interaction and overlooks the diverse non-TTM speaking states that naturally arise in egocentric videos. In this paper, we revisit this problem by reformulating it as an online, frame-level prediction task. Instead of treating TTM as a binary problem against a single negative class, we model it in the presence of diverse and previously underexplored non-TTM states, such as talking-to-others, self-talking, and background conditions. To support this new formulation, we construct an Online TTM Dataset consisting of 406 egocentric video clips with approximately 900K annotated frames, each labeled with frame-level social interaction categories (e.g., background, TTM, talking-to-others, self-talking), by extending the Ego4D social interaction benchmark. In this benchmark, we evaluate five adapted baselines and develop a new model that integrates social cues across modalities. Experimental results show that our multimodal model, which jointly leverages audio, visual, and speech-semantic cues, achieves 75.5% frame-level F1 on TTM, outperforming strong baselines and enabling a systematic analysis of how different speaking states affect TTM recognition.

AI.tldr: Proposes online frame-level talking-to-me (TTM) detection in egocentric video with a multimodal model and new dataset; introduces Online TTM Dataset (406 clips, ~900k frames, frame-level labels) extending Ego4D; achieves 75.5% frame-level F1 for TTM and analyzes impact of non-TTM states.
AI.motivation: Align TTM research with online, frame-level interaction in egocentric videos and account for diverse non-TTM states (e.g., talking to others, self-talking, background) that are not well represented in offline clip-level formulations.
AI.method: Construct Online TTM Dataset with frame-level social interaction categories; adapt five baselines for evaluation; develop a multimodal model that fuses audio, visual, and speech-semantic cues to predict frame-level states; evaluate on frame-level F1 for TTM and analyze state interactions.
