AI.result: The multimodal model achieves 75.5% frame-level F1 on TTM, outperforming strong baselines; demonstrates the usefulness of incorporating diverse non-TTM states and multi-source cues; provides systematic analysis of how speaking states affect TTM recognition.
AI.conclusion: Online, multimodal frame-level modeling with a dedicated dataset substantially improves TTM recognition in egocentric videos and offers a framework to study the influence of various speaking states on social interaction understanding.

title: Data-free On-policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a standard component of frontier post-training pipelines, yet how much its training data actually contributes has gone largely unexamined. On the two teacher-student pairings most common in practice, we find OPD almost indifferent to its data: eight prompts already match a 17k-problem dataset, and three independently built datasets whose difficulty and teacher-student KL differ several-fold produce nearly indistinguishable training curves. Two causes account for this. First, the unit of data in OPD is the state a prompt leads to, not the prompt itself: a single prompt keeps exposing new teacher correction as sampling continues, while the marginal value of additional prompts collapses after eight. Second, replacing mathematics with competitive programming still recovers over ninety percent of the in-domain gain, indicating that OPD transfers the teacher's mode of reasoning rather than knowledge related to the data. We take this to its limit with Data-free On-policy Distillation (DF-OPD), in which the teacher writes its own training questions under a simple prompt -- no external data, no filtering -- leaving a system of just two policies. DF-OPD matches and even surpasses real data, and the questions it produces track the teacher's own post-training data on three key diagnostics of training dynamics, which other real datasets do not. Applied to multi-teacher distillation, where the (prompt, domain) pairs normally have to be derived from post-training data that is often out of reach, 1k self-generated questions close 98.5% of the available headroom, even surpassing the 96.6% reached with 7k real examples. Moreover, together these results invite a reassessment of the role data plays in OPD.

AI.tldr: OPD data contribute little to gains; the training signal is dominated by the state corrections (prompt-led states) rather than the quantity/nature of prompts. Data-free OPD (DF-OPD) can match or exceed real-data OPD by the teacher generating its own questions; in multi-teacher distillation, small self-generated datasets recover near-maximum headroom. Overall, results prompt rethinking the assumed role of data in OPD.
AI.motivation: To quantify how much labeled training data actually drives improvements in On-policy Distillation (OPD) and to test whether data can be replaced by self-generated prompts or questions, including a data-free variant.
AI.method: Empirical study of common OPD setups using two teacher-student pairs; analyze the marginal value of prompts vs. dataset size; substitute mathematics with competitive programming to test generalization of gains; develop Data-free OPD (teacher writes questions without external data); apply to multi-teacher distillation and compare headroom with real datasets; track training-dynamics diagnostics.
AI.result: The unit of data in OPD is the state reachable by a prompt, not the prompt itself: after ~eight prompts, marginal value of more prompts collapses. Eight prompts suffice to match a 17k-problem dataset. Replacing math with programming retains over 90% of in-domain gains, indicating transfer of reasoning mode rather than data content. DF-OPD matches or surpasses real data, with generated questions tracking the teacher’s post-training data on training dynamics diagnostics where real datasets do not. In multi-teacher distillation, 1k self-generated questions close 98.5% of headroom, surpassing 96.6% achieved with 7k real examples. These findings suggest rethinking OPD data’s role.
AI.conclusion: OPD gains largely arise from the teacher’s reasoning pattern and the state produced by prompts rather than the external data volume or content. Data-free or minimal data generation can achieve competitive gains, challenging the conventional emphasis on large curated training datasets in OPD.

title: El Agente Potente: High-Throughput Agentic Atomistic Simulations
comment: 64 pages, 16 figures, and 3 tables, including Supporting Information. Main text: 24 pages, 6 figures, and 1 table
summary: Foundational machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by achieving near-ab initio accuracy across large chemical spaces at a fraction of the computational cost. A central challenge in using these tools for high-throughput property calculations is translating high-level scientific intent into adaptive simulation campaigns without compromising workflow rigour. We introduce El Agente Potente, an agentic system that combines typed execution graphs with a complementary coding mode for MLIPs-driven atomistic simulations. Typed execution graphs provide structured and provenance-aware execution for standardized workflows, with large language models (LLMs) restricted to planning and routing while deterministic Python components perform scientific computation and validation. Complementing this structured execution, a coding agent constructs customized workflows for tasks requiring greater procedural flexibility while invoking existing Potente functions for supported calculations. We demonstrate El Agente Potente across computational materials discovery, molecular energy-landscape exploration, adsorption, and catalytic reaction workflows, together with systematic benchmarks of reproducibility and LLM token cost. These results establish typed execution graphs and code-based workflow construction as complementary mechanisms for agentic scientific computing, combining controlled, auditable execution with the flexibility required for customized atomistic simulations

AI.tldr: Introduces El Agente Potente, a hybrid agentic framework that couples typed execution graphs with a coding agent to manage MLIP-driven atomistic simulations, balancing structured, provenance-aware workflows with procedural flexibility.
AI.motivation: To enable high-throughput, adaptable, and reproducible MLIP-driven simulations by translating high-level scientific intent into workflow campaigns without sacrificing rigour.
AI.method: Use typed execution graphs for structured, provenance-aware workflows where LLMs handle planning/routing while deterministic Python components perform computation and validation; a coding agent constructs customized workflows for flexible tasks, invoking Potente functions for supported calculations.
AI.result: Demonstrates the approach across computational materials discovery, molecular energy-landscape exploration, adsorption, and catalytic reaction workflows; provides systematic benchmarks on reproducibility and LLM token cost, illustrating that typed graphs and code-based workflow construction are complementary for agentic scientific computing.
AI.conclusion: Typed execution graphs and code-based workflow construction together enable auditable, controlled execution with the flexibility required for customized atomistic simulations in MLIP-driven research.

title: PredTac: Learning Contact-Rich Manipulation with Predicted Touch
summary: Contact-rich manipulation benefits from tactile feedback, yet physical tactile sensors introduce hardware, calibration, synchronization, and maintenance costs that complicate policy learning and deployment. We formulate predicted touch as an alternative to measured tactile input and present PredTac, a framework that learns to infer tactile states from causal visual observations and robot states and uses the predicted touch as an explicit interface for policy learning and execution. A tactile predictor is first trained with tactile supervision and then used to provide contact information without requiring measured tactile input during downstream policy training or execution. We evaluate PredTac across three contact-rich manipulation tasks in simulation and on a real robot, and further examine how policy performance depends on the predicted contact content. In simulation goal-offset evaluations, predicted-touch policies achieve 27.0%, 52.0%, and 44.7% success on USB, Barbed-spike, and Valve, respectively, improving over the visual baseline by 8.0-13.7 percentage points. On the real robot, predicted-touch ACT achieves 70.0%, 50.0%, and 90.0% success on USB insertion, Barbed extraction, and Valve rotation, respectively, with a three-task mean of 70.0%, approaching measured-touch ACT at 72.2% and substantially outperforming visual ACT at 21.1%. Fixed-policy interventions further show that performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of predicted contact, with spatial rearrangement at fixed value distributions reducing Valve success by 10.7 percentage points. These results demonstrate that predicted touch can provide useful contact information for contact-rich manipulation without requiring tactile sensing as a policy input.

AI.tldr: PredTac learns to predict tactile state from vision and robot state to serve as a tactile interface for policy learning, enabling contact-rich manipulation without using measured tactile input; demonstrates competitive performance vs. visual baselines and is close to measured-tactile performance in both simulation and real robot trials.
AI.motivation: Tactile sensors provide rich contact information but incur hardware, calibration, and maintenance costs that hinder policy learning and deployment; a predicted touch interface can unlock tactile-like feedback without the sensors.
AI.method: A two-stage approach: (1) train a tactile predictor using tactile supervision to map causal visual observations and robot states to tactile states; (2) use the predicted touch as input to policy learning and execution, eliminating the need for measured tactile input during downstream tasks. Evaluated on three contact-rich manipulation tasks in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.result: Simulation: predicted-touch policies reach 27.0%, 52.0%, 44.7% success on USB, Barbed-spike, Valve—8.0–13.7 percentage points above visual baseline. Real robot (ACT): 70.0%, 50.0%, 90.0% on USB insertion, Barbed extraction, Valve rotation; three-task mean 70.0%, close to measured-touch ACT (72.2%) and well above visual ACT (21.1%). Fixed-policy analyses show performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of predicted contact; rearranging spatial distributions at fixed values reduces Valve success by 10.7 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Predicted touch provides a useful, practical substitute for tactile sensing in policy learning for contact-rich manipulation, achieving substantial gains over vision-only baselines and approaching the performance of actual tactile sensors; spatial structure of predicted contact is important for optimal performance.

title: SignMimic: Robust High-Quality Sign Language Motion Generation via Human-Shape-Oblivious Pose Transfer Guidance
summary:
We study the challenge of sign language video mimicking: given a driving video and a single reference frame, synthesize a video where the target signer reproduces the source
  motion while preserving identity and linguistic form. Prior pipelines entangle rigid motion, non-rigid deformation, and view-dependent completion in a monolithic generator,
  causing handshape drift and spatio-temporal instability. We present SignMimic, which (i) applies a TNet-based model to study SE(3) rigid canonicalization to stabilize global
  pose, (ii) performs non-rigid adaptation in a canonical space to preserve fine-grained articulators (hands/face) and coarticulation via NIF2D, and (iii) uses Pose-MAE-style
  completion before conditional video diffusion. This factorization injects geometric and linguistic priors, yielding shape and spatio-temporal consistency. On several large-scale
  datasets (ASL 50K, How2Sign, CSL News), SignMimic achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on video quality, identity similarity, and frame continuity while also achieving
  minimal loss when performing back translation (SLT) on generated videos. Ablations confirm the role of rigid canonicalization, non-rigid adaptation, and completion. Code, model
  checkpoints, and video examples will be released.

AI.tldr: SignMimic factorizes sign-language video synthesis into rigid canonicalization, non-rigid adaptation, and Pose-MAE completion, introducing geometric/linguistic priors to stabilize pose and articulation, and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: To address entanglement of rigid motion, non-rigid deformation, and view-dependent completion in monolithic generators that cause handshape drift and temporal instability, by injecting explicit geometric and linguistic priors.
AI.method: (i) TNet-based SE(3) rigid canonicalization to stabilize global pose; (ii) non-rigid adaptation in a canonical space to preserve fine-grained articulators and coarticulation via NIF2D; (iii) Pose-MAE-style completion before a conditional video diffusion model.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance in video quality, identity similarity, and frame continuity across ASL 50K, How2Sign, and CSL News; minimal loss in back translation (SLT) on generated videos; ablations validate the contributions of rigid canonicalization, non-rigid adaptation, and completion.
AI.conclusion: A factorized pipeline that leverages geometric and linguistic priors yields improved shape and spatio-temporal consistency for sign-language video synthesis; code/models will be released to facilitate replication.

title: Graph-Transformer Fraud Detection with Self-Supervised Pretraining and Conformal Risk Control
summary: Financial fraud in corporate transaction networks has grown more coordinated and harder to detect with rule-based engines and with classical learning models that treat each transaction in isolation. This paper presents GTFD, a graph-transformer fraud detector that fuses structural and temporal evidence from a corporation's payment graph. GTFD encodes the graph with a multi-head graph attention network, encodes ordered transaction sequences with a gated transformer, and combines both views through a cross-modal gating layer. A conformal risk-control head converts the fused representation into threshold-free anomaly scores with finite-sample coverage guarantees, and the network is trained with self-supervised link-mask pretraining plus adversarial augmentation so it remains stable under scarce labels and under adversarial perturbation. On a corporate transaction benchmark enriched with coordinated fraud rings, GTFD reaches an AUROC of 0.990, an F1-score of 96.1% (precision 96.3%, recall 95.9%), and an accuracy of 98.4%. It reduces the false-positive rate by about 29% relative to the strongest baseline while raising coordinated fraud-ring recall from 85.1% to 96.5%. Ablations attribute roughly 2.0 AUROC points to self-supervised pretraining and 1.9 AUROC points to the conformal head, and adversarial stress tests show GTFD retains 89.2% accuracy at perturbation magnitude 0.20 where the next-best model falls to 76.4%.

AI.tldr: A graph-transformer fraud detector (GTFD) fuses structural and temporal evidence from corporate payment graphs using a multi-head graph attention network and a gated transformer, with cross-modal gating and a conformal risk-control head for threshold-free anomaly scoring; trained with self-supervised link-mask pretraining and adversarial augmentation; achieves state-of-the-art results and robustness on a fraud-ring benchmark, with significant ablations showing contributions from pretraining and the conformal head.
AI.motivation: Fraud in corporate transaction networks is increasingly coordinated and difficult to detect with isolated rule-based or traditional models. There is a need to jointly model graph structure (who transacts with whom) and temporal transaction sequences, while maintaining reliable error guarantees and robustness under limited labels and adversarial perturbations.
AI.method: 1) Encode the payment graph with a multi-head graph attention network to capture structural relationships. 2) Encode ordered transaction sequences with a gated transformer to model temporal dynamics. 3) Fuse the two views through a cross-modal gating layer. 4) Use a conformal risk-control head to produce threshold-free anomaly scores with finite-sample coverage guarantees. 5) Train with self-supervised link-mask pretraining and adversarial augmentation to promote stability under scarce labels and perturbations.
AI.result: On a corporate benchmark with coordinated fraud rings, GTFD achieves AUROC 0.990, F1 96.1% (precision 96.3%, recall 95.9%), and accuracy 98.4%. False positives reduced by ~29% relative to the strongest baseline; coordinated-fraud-ring recall improves from 85.1% to 96.5%. Ablations assign ~2.0 AUROC to self-supervised pretraining and ~1.9 AUROC to the conformal head. Under adversarial perturbation (magnitude 0.20), accuracy remains 89.2% (vs 76.4% for the next-best).
AI.conclusion: The integration of graph structure, temporal sequence modeling, and conformal risk control yields superior fraud detection performance and robustness to perturbations, with substantial gains attributed to self-supervised pretraining and the conformal head; the approach is effective for detecting coordinated fraud rings in corporate payment networks.

title: Self-Orchestrating Language Models: Leveraging Semantic Dependence for Efficient Inference
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities, but their deployment presents significant efficiency challenges. Autoregressive decoding imposes substantial inference latency and under-utilizes hardware accelerators in low batch size regimes. Discrete diffusion models can generate in parallel but struggle to match autoregressive quality without many diffusion denoising steps. Long-context reasoning creates memory bottlenecks that strain even state-of-the-art accelerators.
  My thesis is that language models can direct their own inference execution strategy by annotating semantic dependence -- which tokens depend on which others -- in their generation. I call such models self-orchestrating language models. For each system, I design a runtime that acts on these annotations to parallelize autoregressive decoding, evict intermediate context, or derive denoising orders, achieving Pareto-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs.
  I demonstrate this approach through three self-orchestrating systems. First, PASTA uses semantic dependence to parallelize autoregressive decoding, training the model to annotate which output chunks can generate independently. Second, TIP uses semantic dependence to evict intermediate reasoning steps from the KV cache, reducing memory consumption while preserving accuracy. Third, Planned Diffusion uses semantic dependence to derive a denoising order for discrete diffusion, autoregressively generating a plan that specifies which chunks to denoise in parallel.

AI.tldr: Self-orchestrating LMs annotate semantic dependencies to guide inference, enabling three systems (PASTA, TIP, Planned Diffusion) that parallelize autoregressive decoding, evict KV-cache context, and plan diffusion denoising order, achieving Pareto-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Tackling core inefficiencies in LLM inference: autoregressive latency and underutilized hardware at small batch sizes, diffusion quality vs. step count, and memory bottlenecks from long-context reasoning; enable models to steer their own execution via semantic annotations.
AI.method: Train LMs to annotate token-level dependencies that specify which output chunks or reasoning steps can be processed in parallel, which context can be evicted, and what denoising order to follow. Implement a runtime that uses these annotations to orchestrate computation. Three instantiations: PASTA (parallel autoregressive decoding using chunk-level dependencies), TIP (evict intermediate reasoning steps from the KV cache to save memory), Planned Diffusion (derive a denoising plan for parallel steps in discrete diffusion).
AI.result: Conceptual and system-level demonstration across three self-orchestrating modalities, reporting Pareto-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs; concrete empirical results are not provided in the abstract but claims efficient inference improvements.
AI.conclusion: Self-orchestrating LMs offer a general framework for directing inference strategy through semantic annotations, enabling efficient deployment across latency- and memory-bound regimes via end-to-end runtime orchestration.

title: X-WBC: A Cross-Embodiment Foundation Model for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
summary: Scaling humanoid whole-body control toward general-purpose deployment requires large human motion corpora and training experience shared across robot bodies. Existing methods usually train one policy per robot, leaving motion experience isolated across embodiments. We introduce X-WBC, a cross-embodiment foundation framework that separates relatively shared human motion semantics from embodiment-specific physical execution. Human-centered command tokens align full human motion, robot reference motion, and sparse VR observations. A causal Transformer learns reusable temporal structure from mixed multi-robot rollouts, while lightweight robot-specific modules map the shared representation to each robot's proprioception and action space. Across nine simulated embodiments, external motions, and four real robots, experiments show that joint training improves tracking, the aligned representation supports consistent control across command sources, and the learned policy remains competitive beyond the training corpus. These results support heterogeneous humanoids as joint data sources and establish cross-embodiment joint training as a practical route toward whole-body control foundation models.

AI.tldr: Cross-embodiment foundation model for humanoid whole-body control that learns a shared motion representation from mixed robot data via a causal Transformer and per-robot adapters.
AI.motivation: To scale WBC across multiple humanoid embodiments by sharing large-scale human-motion semantics while respecting embodiment differences; current practice trains a policy for each robot, isolating motion experience.
AI.method: Introduce human-centered command tokens that align human motion, robot reference motion, and sparse VR observations. A causal Transformer learns reusable temporal structure from mixed multi-robot rollouts, while lightweight robot-specific modules map the shared representation to each robot's proprioception and action space.
AI.result: Across nine simulated embodiments, external motions, and four real robots, joint training improves tracking, the aligned representation supports consistent control across command sources, and the learned policy remains competitive beyond the training corpus.
AI.conclusion: Cross-embodiment joint training with heterogeneous humanoids supports a practical path toward whole-body control foundation models.

title: 3D Gait-Based Autism Classification Using Attention-Enhanced Deep Learning with Cross-Fold Statistical Stability Analysis
summary: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition whose early diagnosis remains challenging because conventional clinical assessments are often subjective, time-consuming, and require expert evaluation. Gait provides a promising non-invasive behavioral biomarker for auto- mated ASD screening; however, existing studies have primarily relied on single-dataset evaluations, convolutional architectures, and descriptive summaries of cross-validation performance without formally assessing fold-to-fold stability. This study addresses these gaps with an attention-enhanced Transformer framework for ASD classification, evaluated on two structurally different 3D gait feature representations: precomputed statistical gait descriptors and raw biomechanical ground-reaction- force measurements. Under five-fold cross-validation, the proposed framework achieved 99.00% accuracy, 99.02% precision, 99.00% recall, 99.00% F1-score, and 99.00% specificity on the public Kinect-based benchmark, exceeding the performance of the compared state-of-the-art methods. On the independent private force-plate dataset, it achieved mean values of 95.00% accuracy, 93.81% precision, 96.67% recall, 95.13% F1-score, and 93.33% specificity.

AI.tldr: Attention-enhanced Transformer for ASD classification using gait features; cross-dataset evaluation shows near-perfect results on Kinect data and strong results on force-plate data.
AI.motivation: Develop an objective, non-invasive ASD screening tool leveraging gait as a behavioral biomarker and address gaps in prior work (single-dataset focus, CNNs, and lack of fold stability assessment).
AI.method: Proposes an attention-enhanced Transformer framework evaluated on two 3D gait feature representations: (1) precomputed statistical gait descriptors and (2) raw biomechanical ground-reaction-force measurements; assessed with five-fold cross-validation on a public Kinect-based gait dataset and tested on an independent private force-plate dataset.
AI.result: Kinect dataset: 99.00% accuracy, 99.02% precision, 99.00% recall, 99.00% F1, 99.00% specificity. Force-plate dataset: 95.00% accuracy, 93.81% precision, 96.67% recall, 95.13% F1, 93.33% specificity.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based Transformer architectures can robustly classify ASD from gait across different representations and datasets, indicating cross-dataset generalization potential; however, real-world generalization and confounding factors require further validation.

title: CoArena: Evaluating Computer-Use and Multi-Agent Systems in Real Time
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables, 4 algorithm listings. All figures are drawn in TikZ/pgfplots from the source. Project page: https://coarena.ai
summary: Static benchmarks for computer-use agents fix a task set at release and score every system against it once. That makes them reproducible, and it lets them drift from what they should measure: a fixed task set ages, leaks into training corpora, and cannot follow how people actually use agents from week to week. CoArena measures use directly. Real users submit tasks; two systems, each a single model or a multi-agent pipeline behind the same tool interface, execute the same task concurrently in identical sandboxed desktops; users judge the two outcomes without knowing which system produced them; and a public leaderboard is refit from those judgments. The central contribution is a formal account of what makes such an evaluation real-time. We define real-time as five measurable properties, each with an equation and a worked example: continuous task arrival, live concurrent execution, online rating updates, freshness with contamination resistance, and bounded feedback latency from a failed run to a reusable training environment. The rating methodology follows in full: the Bradley-Terry pairwise model, its likelihood with weighted observations and ties, the penalized maximum-likelihood estimator, and the streaming update applied when a single vote arrives (a stochastic-gradient step on the same likelihood, recovering Elo). It gives confidence intervals from the observed information and a cluster-robust sandwich, rank bands from a parametric bootstrap, the rule by which a new system enters the board, and the convergence rate of the estimate. Vote quality is treated with inter-judge agreement statistics, redundant judging, and explicit handling of ties and abstentions. A five-system example with 211 votes is carried from the vote matrix to ratings, intervals, and rank bands. Every number is derived from stated inputs or labeled illustrative; none is a measurement of a deployed system.

AI.tldr: CoArena presents a real-time, user-driven evaluation framework for computer-use agents, with live task submission, online ratings via Bradley–Terry, uncertainty measures, and a demonstrated five-system example.
AI.motivation: To address the drift and misalignment of static benchmarks with real user usage by evaluating agents on real, concurrent tasks submitted by users, with live updates and a public leaderboard.
AI.method: Users submit tasks; two systems (single models or multi-agent pipelines) compete on identical sandboxed desktops; users judge outcomes blind to system identity; a public leaderboard is refitted from judgments. The paper defines five real-time properties (continuous task arrival, live concurrent execution, online rating updates, freshness with contamination resistance, bounded feedback latency) with equations and worked examples. Rating uses the Bradley–Terry pairwise model with weighted observations and ties, penalized MLE, and streaming SGD (recovering Elo). Provides confidence intervals via observed information and a cluster-robust sandwich; rank bands via parametric bootstrap; rules for new-system entry and convergence rate. Vote quality assessed via inter-judge agreement, redundant judging, and handling of ties/abstentions. Includes a five-system example with 211 votes, deriving ratings, intervals, and rank bands; all numbers are from inputs or labels; not measurements of a deployed system.
AI.result: Formalizes a real-time evaluation pipeline with five measurable properties, a complete matchmaking and updating procedure, and uncertainty quantification. Demonstrates the method on a five-system, 211-vote example, producing ratings, intervals, and rank bands from synthetic but labeled data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework delivers a principled, real-time, user-driven evaluation that yields dynamic rankings with quantified uncertainty, suitable for public leaderboards and ongoing comparison of agents as new tasks arrive.

title: Domain Generalization for Smartphone-Based Human Activity Recognition: A Systematic Analysis of Components and Interactions
summary: Smartphone-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) models often degrade under distribution shifts caused by changes in users, devices, sensor placements, environments, and acquisition protocols. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this problem by learning from source domains without access to target data. Existing DG methods span training objectives, representation initialization, and architectural modifications, but these components are typically evaluated in isolation despite operating at different stages of the learning pipeline. We present a large-scale controlled benchmark of DG for smartphone-based HAR, comprising more than 410,000 experiments across four model architectures, thirteen training objectives including Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), five initialization strategies, four architectural configurations, and two shift scenarios: cross-dataset and cross-position. Results show that individual DG components provide limited and highly conditional gains. Alternative objectives rarely outperform ERM consistently, self-supervised initialization helps in specific settings, and architectural modifications, particularly Dynamic Domain Generalization, provide the clearest standalone improvements. Joint configurations, however, frequently outperform their individual components and exhibit complementary and sometimes super-additive interactions, although gains remain model- and shift-dependent. Class-level analysis shows that the strongest configurations mainly improve difficult, shift-sensitive decision boundaries. Finally, oracle checkpoint analysis reveals substantial unrealized performance: source-validation selection recovers only 53% and 26% of the available oracle gain in cross-dataset and cross-position settings, respectively. Overall, effective HAR domain generalization requires jointly designing DG components and robust model-selection strategies.

AI.tldr: Jointly designed DG components outperform isolated ones in smartphone HAR; Dynamic Domain Generalization provides the clearest standalone gains, while other objectives and initializations offer limited, condition-specific improvements. Joint configurations yield complementary and sometimes super-additive gains, but gains are model- and shift-dependent; robust model selection is crucial. Oracle analysis reveals substantial unrealized potential.
AI.motivation: Domain Generalization for smartphone-based HAR is challenged by distribution shifts from users, devices, sensor placements, environments, and protocols. Prior work typically evaluates DG components in isolation, complicating understanding of their interactions within the learning pipeline. A large-scale, controlled benchmark across multiple architectures, objectives, initializations, and shift scenarios is needed to quantify component interactions and practical gains.
AI.method: A large-scale benchmark comprising >410k experiments across four model architectures, thirteen training objectives (including Empirical Risk Minimization, ERM), five initialization strategies, four architectural configurations, and two shift scenarios (cross-dataset and cross-position). The study analyzes (i) individual DG components, (ii) joint configurations, (iii) class-level effects, and (iv) oracle checkpoint improvements via validation vs. oracle gains.
AI.result: Individual DG components offer limited, highly conditional gains. Alternative objectives rarely outperform ERM in a consistent manner; self-supervised initializations help only in specific settings; architectural changes, especially Dynamic Domain Generalization (DDG), yield the most reliable standalone improvements. When combined, DG components frequently outperform any single component, showing complementary and sometimes super-additive interactions, though results depend on model and shift. Class-level analysis indicates strongest gains on difficult, shift-sensitive decision boundaries. Oracle checkpoint analysis shows validation-based selection recovers only 53% (cross-dataset) and 26% (cross-position) of the full oracle gain, signaling substantial unrealized potential.
AI.conclusion: Effective HAR domain generalization requires jointly designing DG components and robust model-selection strategies, rather than relying on isolated improvements. Practitioners should favor joint configurations with attention to the shift scenario and implement robust model selection to realize potential gains.

title: A Vision Based Framework Integrating Attention and Action Cues for Interpretable Cognitive Workload Assessment in Human Robot Collaborative Assembly
summary: The introduction of human-robot collaboration (HRC) in industrial assembly operations is revolutionizing the manufacturing landscape. In this evolving environment, operators are required to seamlessly coordinate their manual tasks with real-time task information and robotic behaviors. These demands fluctuate during operation, yet conventional workload assessments depend on body-worn physiological sensors that complicate practical deployment. Here, we present a vision-based attention--action framework for continuous and interpretable workload-related assessment in HRC assembly. The framework combines RGB-D observations with robot states and calibrated task-related areas to construct a temporally confirmed representation of operator behavior. This representation identifies where task demand is concentrated and explains how it develops when attention and action diverge, the task context changes, or the operator hesitates. We evaluated the framework in a three-level collaborative gearbox assembly experiment with ten participants, using subjective ratings and synchronized physiological signals as independent references. Raw NASA-TLX ratings confirmed increasing perceived workload across conditions, with significant effects on overall workload and its mental and temporal dimensions. The vision-derived HRC-CWL output was significantly associated with ECG-derived features in seven of nine participants with complete correlation data. Synchronized interaction episodes further showed temporal correspondence between detected hesitation and physiological activity. Real-time deployment demonstrated that the framework can operate without requiring operators to wear additional sensors. These findings support HRC-CWL as an interpretable behavioral proxy for cognitive ergonomics analysis and adaptive robot assistance, rather than a direct psychophysiological measure of workload.

AI.tldr: A vision-based attention-action framework (HRC-CWL) for continuous, interpretable workload estimation in human-robot collaboration (HRC) assembly, using RGB-D data, robot states, and task-area cues to provide a sensor-free proxy of cognitive workload, validated against subjective and physiological references.
AI.motivation: Conventional workload assessments rely on wearable physiological sensors, which complicate deployment in real-time HRC environments. There is a need for non-intrusive, continuous, and interpretable workload metrics to support adaptive robot assistance.
AI.method: Developed a vision-based attention–action framework that fuses RGB-D observations, robot states, and calibrated task-related areas to produce a temporally confirmed representation of operator behavior. The framework identifies where demand concentrates, and how it evolves when attention and action diverge, task context changes, or hesitation occurs. Evaluation used a three-level collaborative gearbox assembly with ten participants, comparing to NASA-TLX ratings and synchronized physiological signals. Real-time deployment demonstrated sensor-free operation.
AI.result: NASA-TLX showed increasing perceived workload with significant effects on overall workload and its mental and temporal dimensions. The vision-derived HRC-CWL correlated with ECG-derived features in seven of nine participants with complete data. Synchronized interaction episodes aligned hesitation with physiological activity. The framework operates in real time without additional sensors.
AI.conclusion: HRC-CWL serves as an interpretable behavioral proxy for cognitive ergonomics analysis and adaptive robot assistance, rather than a direct psychophysiological measure of workload.

title: Bi-Level Routing and Sparse Spatial Attention based Multi-View BEV 3D Object Detection for Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted to 2026 9th International Conference on Computer Information Science and Application Technology (CISAT). 4 pages, 1 figure
summary: Bird's Eye View (BEV)-based multi-view 3D object detection suffers from challenges of computational complexity, multi-scale feature extraction, and efficiency of dense 2D-to-BEV view transformation. To address these problems, this paper proposes an improved BEV 3D object detection algorithm Sparse-BEVNet. Firstly, a Bi-Level Routing Attention (BRA) mechanism is introduced into the image feature extraction network to reduce the computational burden of the backbone. Second, Cascaded Group Attention (CGA) is employed in the feature fusion module, which enhances deep interaction across features of different hierarchical levels without introducing additional computational overhead. Furthermore, a Sparse Spatial Cross-Attention mechanism is adopted to replace the conventional dense view projection pipeline. Experimental results on the public nuScenes dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 45.2% and a nuScenes Detection Score (NDS) of 54.5%, corresponding to 3.6% and 2.8% improvements relative to the baseline model, respectively.

AI.tldr: Sparse-BEVNet introduces Bi-Level Routing Attention (BRA) in the backbone, Cascaded Group Attention (CGA) in feature fusion, and Sparse Spatial Cross-Attention to replace dense projection, addressing BEV-based 3D detection efficiency and multi-scale feature fusion. It achieves improvements on nuScenes (mAP 45.2%, NDS 54.5%) over a baseline.
AI.motivation: BEV-based multi-view 3D object detection suffers from high computational complexity, multi-scale feature extraction challenges, and inefficient dense 2D-to-BEV view projection. There is a need for more efficient backbones and cross-scale attention mechanisms to reduce compute while preserving or improving accuracy.
AI.method: 1) Bi-Level Routing Attention (BRA) integrated into the image feature extractor to cut backbone computation. 2) Cascaded Group Attention (CGA) in the fusion module to enable deeper cross-scale interactions without extra cost. 3) Sparse Spatial Cross-Attention replacing the traditional dense view projection pipeline with a sparser, likely learnable mechanism.
AI.result: On the nuScenes dataset, the method yields mAP of 45.2% and NDS of 54.5%, corresponding to 3.6% and 2.8% improvements over a baseline model, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BRA, CGA, and Sparse Spatial Cross-Attention jointly improve efficiency and accuracy for BEV-based multi-view 3D object detection, demonstrating effective performance gains on nuScenes.

title: Bayesian optimization with kernel ensembles and disagreement-based acquisition for source localization and acoustic inversion
summary: Joint source localization and geoacoustic inversion requires optimizing an objective built from an expensive normal mode propagation model. Bayesian optimization (BO) with a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate can obtain accurate parameter estimates within a limited number of forward model evaluations, but its performance depends on the choice of kernel family. With few observations in a seven-dimensional search space, no single kernel can be expected to perform consistently well across individual inversions. To reduce this dependence, we use a weighted ensemble of GPs with different kernel families, allowing the surrogate to adapt to the observed objective without committing to one kernel in advance. The ensemble is combined with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function that determines where the expensive objective should be evaluated next. Experiments on simulated and measured SWellEx-96 data show that the resulting method achieves the lowest mean final objective among the considered BO strategies and reduces parameter estimation error on most coordinates. Ablation results further show that the ensemble provides robustness to kernel choice, while the acquisition function accounts for most of the optimization gain.

AI.tldr: A weighted ensemble of Gaussian processes with diverse kernels, combined with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function, improves Bayesian optimization for joint source localization and geoacoustic inversion in a high-dimensional, expensive objective, achieving lower final objectives and reduced parameter error compared to single-kernel BO.
AI.motivation: To reduce sensitivity of BO to kernel choice in limited-data, high-dimensional geoacoustic inversions, where forward models are expensive.
AI.method: Construct a weighted ensemble of GP surrogates with different kernels; integrate into BO with an optimum-conditioned acquisition function to select next evaluation; test on simulated and real SWellEx-96 data.
AI.result: The ensemble-BO achieves the lowest mean final objective among studied BO strategies and reduces parameter estimation errors on most coordinates; ablations show kernel ensemble improves robustness and that the acquisition function drives most optimization gains.
AI.conclusion: Ensembling GP kernels and using an optimum-conditioned acquisition function yields robust, data-efficient BO for complex geoacoustic inversion tasks.

title: GGUF-Metadata Prediction of Single-Sequence llama.cpp Throughput Across Three Systems
comment: 27 pages: 5-page manuscript with 4 figures, followed by a 22-page supplementary results appendix. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: We predict single-sequence model throughput from GGUF metadata using roofline-shaped predictors with quantization-specific scale factors fitted on reference models. The scored cohort comprises 318 phase-depth measurements from 53 host-file configurations on two Apple M4 Max systems and an NVIDIA RTX 5080. On host-specific held-out sets of four, five, and two configurations, an active-parameter decode model obtains 13.1%, 14.4%, and 36.1% mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), versus 49.4%, 55.3%, and 51.9% when charging total parameters. Leave-one-host-out coefficients fitted on the other two systems yield 11.6%, 16.8%, and 36.0% test MAPE. A low-bit model ladder changes ordering across runtime stacks. The P2 prefill baseline gives 18.7%, 22.2%, and 108.2% test MAPE. GGUF structure helps on all three systems, but fitted efficiencies are not universal.

AI.tldr: Roofline-based throughput prediction for single-sequence models using quantization-specific scales; active-parameter decoding reduces MAPE across hosts; GGUF helps but efficiency transfer is not universal; low-bit ladders alter runtime ordering; P2 prefill baseline often underperforms.
AI.motivation: Develop accurate, host-aware throughput models for single-sequence models by leveraging GGUF metadata and quantization-aware scaling to predict performance across diverse hardware and runtime stacks.
AI.method: Fit roofline-shaped predictors with quantization-specific scales on reference models. Use 318 phase-depth measurements from 53 host-file configurations on two Apple M4 Max systems and an NVIDIA RTX 5080. Evaluate with host-specific held-out sets using an active-parameter decode model; compare to a total-parameter charging baseline. Perform leave-one-host-out evaluation. Examine the effects of a low-bit model ladder and a P2 prefill baseline. Assess GGUF structure impact and transferability of fitted efficiencies.
AI.result: Active-parameter decode yields 13.1%, 14.4%, 36.1% MAPE on host-held-out sets versus 49.4%, 55.3%, 51.9% for total-parameter baseline. Leave-one-host-out MAPE: 11.6%, 16.8%, 36.0%. P2 prefill baseline: 18.7%, 22.2%, 108.2%. Low-bit ladder changes runtime ordering. GGUF structure improves performance across all systems, but fitted efficiencies are not universal.
AI.conclusion: Quantization-aware, host-adaptive predictors enhance throughput estimation. GGUF aids consistency but transferability of fitted efficiencies is limited; active-parameter decoding substantially reduces error, yet extreme cases (e.g., P2 prefill) reveal data-system interaction complexity.

title: Distributed Safe Cooperative Vector Field for Trajectory Curvature Constrained Multi-Robot Systems
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Best Student Paper Award at the 9th Chinese Conference on Swarm Intelligence and Cooperative Control (CCSICC 2025)
summary: Trajectory curvature constraints are inherent in practical multi-robot systems due to the limited turning capabilities of the robots. Without properly accounting for these constraints, robots may fail to accomplish assigned tasks, and their trajectories may diverge from the intended paths. This paper proposes a distributed safe cooperative vector field approach for multi-robot systems subject to trajectory curvature constraints. The proposed approach is composed of a cooperative vector field and a safety-oriented collision avoidance vector field, aiming to address the problems of cooperative motion and safe collision avoidance in multi-robot path-following tasks. A safety-oriented collision avoidance vector field with adaptively adjustable reactive boundary is developed to accommodate the kinematic curvature constraints of robots, thereby ensuring the physical feasibility of collision avoidance maneuvers. The proposed vector field requires only a single virtual variable from each neighboring robot to achieve cooperative motion and ensure both obstacle avoidance and inter-robot collision avoidance. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through both simulations and real-world experiments on an actual multi-robot platform.

AI.tldr: A distributed vector-field framework for multi-robot path following with trajectory curvature constraints, combining a cooperative field and a safety collision-avoidance field with adaptive boundaries; validated in simulation and real experiments.
AI.motivation: To address feasibility and safety challenges introduced by finite turning radii in multi-robot path-following, ensuring cooperative motion and obstacle/inter-robot collision avoidance with minimal inter-robot communication.
AI.method: Develop two vector fields: a cooperative vector field for coordinated motion and a safety-oriented collision-avoidance vector field with an adaptively adjustable reactive boundary that respects kinematic curvature constraints. The approach communicates via a single virtual variable from each neighbor, enabling distributed coordination and safe maneuvers under curvature limits. Validation includes simulations and real-world experiments on a multi-robot platform.
AI.result: Demonstrates effective safe cooperative motion under curvature constraints, with the adaptive reactive boundary maintaining feasibility and safety in both inter-robot and obstacle avoidance across simulated and real-world tests.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distributed vector-field framework enables physically feasible, safe cooperative motion for multi-robot systems subject to trajectory curvature constraints, with low communication requirements and practical applicability.

title: MorphoStyle: Motion Style Transfer with Morphology Control
summary: Human motion may be viewed as a combination of action content, style, and body morphology. Existing motion style transfer methods transfer a reference style onto a content motion while assuming a canonical body, whereas shape-aware motion generators adapt motion to a target shape without explicit style control. This separation of motion style and shape (morphology) makes it difficult to generate stylized motions for non-canonical bodies; naively combining a style transfer module with a shape-aware generator often leaks action content from the style reference and disrupts shape-consistent kinematics. We present MorphoStyle, a framework for shape-aware motion style transfer that is built on a shape-conditioned Finite-Scalar-Quantization Variational Auto-Encoder (FSQ-VAE). The key contribution is to pose the desired style transfer as modular latent disentanglement comprising: (i) a contrastive style encoder that extracts content-decoupled style embeddings; (ii) a text-guided style-routing mechanism that locates style-relevant joints in a text-motion feature space; and (iii) a manifold preserving style modulator that injects discriminative style embeddings in content features as a temporally-gated low-rank offset. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MorphoStyle outperforms competing baselines in terms of both shape control and motion style transfer, while simultaneously providing quantitative shape control. For more details, please see project website: https://github.com/funkdub/MorphoStyle.

AI.tldr: MorphoStyle enables shape-aware motion style transfer across non-canonical bodies by combining a shape-conditioned FSQ-VAE with modular latent disentanglement: a contrastive style encoder, a text-guided style routing mechanism, and a manifold-preserving style modulator.
AI.motivation: Existing motion style transfer methods assume a canonical body or lack explicit style control, making it difficult to transfer style to non-canonical morphologies without leaking content or breaking shape-consistent kinematics.
AI.method: MorphoStyle uses a shape-conditioned Finite-Scalar-Quantization Variational Auto-Encoder (FSQ-VAE) with modular latent disentanglement: (i) a contrastive style encoder for content-decoupled style embeddings, (ii) a text-guided style-routing mechanism to locate style-relevant joints in a text–motion feature space, and (iii) a manifold-preserving style modulator that injects discriminative style embeddings into content features as a temporally-gated low-rank offset.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show MorphoStyle outperforms competing baselines in both shape control and motion style transfer, while providing quantitative shape control.
AI.conclusion: MorphoStyle provides effective shape-aware motion style transfer through modular latent disentanglement, enabling stylized motions for non-canonical bodies with preserved kinematics and explicit shape control.

title: Biquaternionic Space with Complex-valued Attention for Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Temporal knowledge graph embedding (TKGE) models infer missing facts in knowledge graphs that evolve over time. Many existing models use a single geometric space, which can limit their ability to represent diverse relational patterns, or treat entity representations as static. We propose Biquaternionic Space with Complex-valued Attention (BSCA), a TKGE model that combines circular and hyperbolic rotations within a unified biquaternionic framework. A complex-valued attention mechanism adaptively fuses time-conditioned and relation-conditioned entity representations, allowing them to vary with temporal and relational context. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show competitive performance across datasets, with the largest improvement on GDELT: BSCA achieves an MRR of 52.1\%, compared with 38.1\% for the strongest baseline in our comparison.

AI.tldr: BSCA introduces a biquaternionic space integrating circular and hyperbolic rotations for TKGE, with a complex-valued attention to fuse time- and relation-conditioned entity representations; achieves strong results, notably on GDELT.
AI.motivation: Address limitation of single geometric spaces and static entity representations in TKGE, enabling richer relational dynamics across time.
AI.method: Biquaternionic framework combining circular/hyperbolic rotations; complex-valued attention to fuse time-conditioned and relation-conditioned entity embeddings; temporal dynamics via time-conditioned vectors; apply across five datasets.
AI.result: Competitive performance across five benchmarks; largest gain on GDELT with MRR 52.1% vs 38.1% baseline.
AI.conclusion: BSCA is effective for dynamic relational reasoning in TKGE, leveraging geometry and attention to capture diverse patterns; promising for future exploration of quaternionic representations and attention-based fusion in temporal graphs.

title: Externalizing Requirement-to-Repair Artifacts as Observable Traces for LLM-Based Program Repair
comment: Accepted at REALM Workshop, EMNLP 2026. Code: https://github.com/ForeverMJ/THEMIS
summary: Repository-level repair requires not only correct patches but also inspectable records that explain how issue requirements are translated into code changes and post-edit evidence. We contribute THEMIS, a stage-aware repair workflow that externalizes this requirement-to-repair process through semantic interpretation, a runtime requirement-code graph, graph-derived Developer guidance, retained repair rationale and patches, and post-edit audit records. A retrospective audit of 300 SWE-bench Lite cases demonstrates that these artifacts provide broad support for cross-stage inspection: a complete Developer rationale is available for 288 cases, and 214 cases (71.3%) retain a complete audited field set connecting the selected stages. The retained records further enable systematic measurement of cross-stage correspondence: target symbols recur in 62.6% of Developer rationales and in 62.8% of patches, rising to 75.8% when related symbols are included. In a paired 100-case comparison, the relational workflow resolves 19 cases versus 9 for the direct same-input condition; because the two conditions also differ in Analyzer output, graph-derived distillation, and Judge records, we report this as preliminary, workflow-level evidence rather than a causal effect of the graph component. Together, these results show that THEMIS makes otherwise implicit requirement-to-repair transitions inspectable, enabling systematic examination of how repair decisions persist, align, and evolve across stages.

AI.tldr: THEMIS provides a stage-aware, auditable repair workflow that externalizes requirement-to-repair reasoning via semantic graphs and post-edit records; retrospective study shows broad cross-stage traceability and preliminary workflow-level benefits.
AI.motivation: Improve inspectability and auditability of repository repairs by exposing how issue requirements translate into code changes across stages, enabling measurement of cross-stage correspondence.
AI.method: Introduce THEMIS with semantic interpretation, a runtime requirement-code graph, graph-derived Developer guidance, retained repair rationale and patches, and post-edit audit records. Evaluate on 300 SWE-bench Lite cases and a paired 100-case study, measuring completeness of rationales/audits, symbol recurrence, and cross-stage consistency across conditions.
AI.result: High completeness of records: 288/300 cases have complete Developer rationale; 214/300 (71.3%) retain a complete audited field set. Target symbols recur in 62.6% of rationales and 62.8% of patches (75.8% when related symbols counted). In a paired 100-case comparison, relational workflow resolves 19 cases versus 9 for the direct same-input condition, but differences in Analyzer output, graph-derived distillation, and Judge records temper causal claims; results are preliminary workflow-level evidence.
AI.conclusion: THEMIS makes implicitly defined requirement-to-repair transitions inspectable and supports systematic cross-stage analysis of how repair decisions persist, align, and evolve. The findings are promising but not yet causal; further controlled studies are needed to isolate the graph component's effect.

title: Low Clearance Hinge Joint Mechanism Based on 3D Printing on Sheet Fabrication Methodology
summary: This paper presents a low-clearance hinge joint mechanism based on the 3D printing on sheet fabrication method. This approach simplifies the fabrication of hinge mechanisms and overcomes limitations of conventional origami manufacturing by eliminating the need for adhesives commonly used during assembly, making it suitable for robots at the tens-of-centimeters scale. The advantages and disadvantages of three types of hinge joint mechanisms are compared, and a hinge joint that can be designed with low clearance for various facet thicknesses is selected. Based on the selected hinge joint, the twisting angle and bending force are analyzed, leading to the implementation of a clearance of 0.1 mm. Torsional resistance is experimentally evaluated to measure the torque required for twisting caused by plastic deformation and clearance. The results show that the torque associated with plastic deformation is sufficient to constrain the undesired degrees of freedom of the hinge joint, while the torque required for twisting due to clearance is minimal. Based on the analyzed data, the proposed hinge joint mechanism is applied to a 3-degree-of-freedom delta robot manipulator, demonstrating precise motion with low clearance.

AI.tldr: Low-clearance hinge joints fabricated by sheet-based 3D printing; adhesive-free, suitable for tens-of-centimeter robots; 0.1 mm clearance; plastic-deformation torque constrains undesired DOF while clearance torque is minimal; demonstrated on a 3-DOF delta robot.
AI.motivation: Address fabrication complexity and adhesive limitations in hinge mechanisms for sheet-based robotics; enable reliable, low-clearance joints at mid-scale.
AI.method: Compare three hinge types; select a low-clearance design compatible with varying facet thickness; implement 0.1 mm clearance; analyze twisting angle and bending force; experimentally measure torsional resistance due to plastic deformation and clearance; apply to 3-DOF delta robot.
AI.result: Plastic-deformation torque suffices to constrain undesired DOF; clearance-induced torque is minimal; delta robot achieves precise motion with low clearance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hinge joint enables adhesive-free, low-clearance operation in sheet-fabricated robotics and is effective for mid-scale delta manipulator applications; further work could examine durability, wear, and scalability.

title: What Input Resolution Is Required for Bird Species Identification, and What Is Its Latency Cost on an Edge Device? A Study of 14 Input Resolutions and Six Architectures with On-Device Measurements
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. On-device measurements on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (JetPack 6.2, TensorRT 10.3). Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22697995
summary: Bird-strike mitigation at wind farms requires identifying distant birds that span only tens of pixels, so the classifier's input resolution N is a design variable, not a fixed specification. We study it with a factorial design over 14 side lengths N (16 to 224), six architectures, two training and evaluation regimes and 30 random seeds -- 2,520 checkpoints and 5,040 evaluations -- plus latency measured on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano. Four results. (1) The selected N depends on the target: 0.90 is met on validation by ResNet50 at N=112 in an estimated 1.85 ms (0.8980 on test) and 0.95 by DINOv2-L at N=144 in 12.70 ms; changing the model buys more accuracy than raising N (+5.93 versus +2.33 points at N=112). (2) The benefit of lowering N depends on the assumed preprocessing path: N=224 -> 80 saves 13.5% when each individual is decoded from its own file but 46.2% when the detector decodes the 4K frame once; the Pareto set grows from 20 to 23 configurations. (3) Accuracy must be measured on the deployed engine: half precision costs ViT-S/16 alone 4 to 7 points at N>=96 while the CNNs stay within 0.1 points, and with selection held at validation the choice differs at 26 of 176 targets. A broken FP16 engine can run faster than a correct one, undetectable from latency; admitting 14 ViT-S/16 FP32 configurations moves the recommendation over the 0.931-0.938 band and under the 10 ms budget. (4) ViT-L-scale models fit this device, but activations exceed the FP16 range; splitting the graph at transformer-block boundaries confines FP32 to the affected segments, making the deployed DINOv2-L chain 1.85x faster than the single-engine build. We also quantify how the regime-difference sign stabilises with seed count; a sensitivity split removing some forms of group sharing preserves all 14 non-trivial signs at the selection boundary.

AI.tldr: Input resolution N is treated as a design variable for bird-strike detection on edge devices, with a large factorial study showing model choice and deployment path often dominate accuracy and latency gains; practical recommendations depend on target and preprocessing path, with FP16 behavior and graph-splitting strategies affecting deployed throughput.
AI.motivation: Mitigate bird strikes by detecting distant, small birds in real-time; understand how input resolution interacts with architecture, training regimes, and deployment to guide edge-device choices.
AI.method: A factorial design across 14 input sizes (N=16–224), six architectures, two training/evaluation regimes, and 30 seeds (2,520 checkpoints, 5,040 evaluations). Latency measured on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano. Analyzed four core findings and conducted seed-sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: (1) N chosen depends on target: for validation, ResNet50 at N=112 yields 0.90 (1.85 ms) and test 0.898; DINOv2-L at N=144 yields 0.95 (12.70 ms); changing model yields larger accuracy gains than raising N (+5.93 vs +2.33 at N=112). (2) N savings depend on preprocessing: N=224->80 saves 13.5% with per-object decoding, 46.2% when decoding the 4K frame once; Pareto set grows from 20 to 23 configurations. (3) Deployed engine matters: half precision costs ViT-S/16 by 4–7 pp for N>=96; CNNs stay within ~0.1 pp; with validation selection, 26 of 176 targets differ; a broken FP16 engine can be faster undetectably; switching to FP32 (14 ViT-S/16 configs) moves recommendations across the 0.931–0.938 band and under 10 ms. (4) ViT-L-scale fits device but activations exceed FP16; graph-splitting at transformer-block boundaries confines FP32 to affected segments, making DINOv2-L 1.85x faster than single-engine. (5) Regime-difference sign stabilizes with seeds; sensitivity split that removes some group-sharing maintains all 14 non-trivial signs at the selection boundary.
AI.conclusion: Deployments should be driven by the actual running engine and target constraints rather than architecture alone; reducing input resolution can yield large latency savings but depends on preprocessing path and precision; encoding FP16/FP32 limitations and graph-partition strategies critically influence throughput and the optimal configuration; architecture choice (e.g., ViT-L vs CNNs) must be vetted against device FP16 range and potential speedups from partitioned deployments.

title: Learning Source Acquisition Policies by Offline Planning
summary: Predicting under an acquisition budget requires choosing feature groups whose value can depend on later queries. O-MPAC transfers finite-horizon risk-cost targets from complete training records into a shared source-action scorer. At inference time, the scorer uses partial observations and source metadata, re-scores after each query, and applies a hard cost mask. We analyze how tied teacher targets and the remaining planning horizon affect the learned decisions. Uniform supervision over tied minima preserves the target distribution under source relabeling. In a five-seed routing experiment, it achieves 0.965 accuracy under both original and context-last orders. On six real tasks, validation selects H1 without action cross-entropy in all thirty splits. O-MPAC has the highest mean budget-integrated accuracy on five tasks against source-adapted GDFS, DIME, AACO+NN and a static policy.

AI.tldr: O-MPAC enables budgeted feature acquisition by transferring finite-horizon risk-cost targets into a shared scorer that re-scores with partial observations and hard cost masking; it analyzes the effect of tied teacher targets and planning horizon, and demonstrates strong performance on routing and real tasks, outperforming several baselines.
AI.motivation: Predicting under a constrained acquisition budget where querying feature groups incurs costs and information arrives over time. The goal is to maintain target distributions under relabeling and achieve high accuracy with limited queries.
AI.method: Train a shared source-action scorer by transferring finite-horizon risk-cost targets from complete training records. At inference, use partial observations and source metadata, re-score after each query, and apply a hard cost mask. Study the impact of tied teacher targets and horizon length; show that uniform supervision over tied minima preserves the target distribution under source relabeling. Evaluate on five-seed routing (0.965 accuracy) and six real tasks (H1 validation, no action CE in splits). Compare against source-adapted GDFS, DIME, AACO+NN, and a static policy.
AI.result: O-MPAC achieves 0.965 accuracy in routing under both original and context-last orders. Across six real tasks, validation selects H1 with no action cross-entropy in all 30 splits. It obtains the highest mean budget-integrated accuracy on five tasks versus the listed baselines.
AI.conclusion: O-MPAC effectively leverages a shared scorer to plan within an acquisition budget, with uniform supervision over tied targets preserving label distributions and outperforms established baselines on both synthetic routing and real tasks.

title: Geometric Flow enhanced Graph Coarsening
summary: Recently, researchers have proposed a graph pooling operation, akin to the pooling process in conventional convolutional neural networks (CNN), aimed at reducing the computation cost of Graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs). While most GCNN-based methods treat graph pooling as a node clustering problem and propose learning a cluster assignment matrix, existing clustering-based pooling methods tend to focus solely on the rough topology information of graphs, neglecting the exploitation of higher-order mutual connections among neighbors. In terms of message passing on graph, the ease of information passing on edges reflects the closeness between neighboring nodes, which significantly relies on the interconnectivity among neighbors. In this study, we address this gap by considering such local connection information and introducing a novel graph pooling method named RicciPool. We introduce discrete graph curvature, particularly Ollivier-Ricci curvature, as a measure of higher-order connectivity around an edge. Subsequently, we construct an Ollivier-Ricci flow formula to reweigh edge weights, leveraging the crucial information provided by Ricci curvature, particularly vital for extracting clusters in graphs. Building upon this foundation, we utilize the spectral clustering technique to learn a new cluster assignment matrix. Experimental results on multiple bioinformatics protein datasets and social networks underscore the effectiveness of our proposed method.

AI.tldr: RicciPool: A graph pooling method that leverages Ollivier-Ricci curvature to reweight edge weights via an Ollivier-Ricci flow, followed by spectral clustering to learn a new cluster assignment matrix, demonstrating effectiveness on bioinformatics and social networks.
AI.motivation: Address the neglect of higher-order mutual connections in prior clustering-based graph pooling methods by incorporating local connectivity information through discrete graph curvature.
AI.method: Compute Ollivier-Ricci curvature on graph edges, apply an Ollivier-Ricci flow to reweight edge weights, then use spectral clustering to learn a new cluster assignment matrix for pooling.
AI.result: Experimental results on multiple bioinformatics protein datasets and social networks show the method effectively preserves graph structure and improves pooling performance compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: RicciPool demonstrates that incorporating higher-order connectivity via Ricci curvature into pooling enhances cluster quality and GCNN efficiency.

title: Planning in the Backbone: DiffAdapterVLA for Native Continuous Trajectory Generation with Driving VLMs
summary: Pretrained driving vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual, route, language, and driving context into rich driving priors, yet their representation objectives remain separated from continuous driving planning. Existing methods typically begin trajectory generation only after the VLM has formed a final condition, leaving depth-wise condition computation outside the stepwise formation of trajectory state. We introduce DiffAdapterVLA, which realizes Planning in the Backbone: it injects explicit trajectory tokens into selected VLM late layers, bringing trajectory state into backbone forward computation, where it co-evolves with driving conditions at different depths. Lightweight layer-wise DiffAdapters organize this computation into recursive trajectory refinement, while asymmetric joint attention preserves directed guidance from the condition stream to trajectory planning. By placing planning within existing backbone computation rather than relying on an independent trajectory planner, DiffAdapterVLA adapts only lightweight trajectory modules to turn existing driving priors into efficient continuous planning capability. NAVSIM results show that it achieves high-quality closed-loop planning with low end-to-end latency using few trainable parameters, and demonstrate that jointly evolving trajectory state and depth-wise driving conditions in VLM late-layer computation effectively realizes continuous trajectory planning.

AI.tldr: DiffAdapterVLA enables planning in the backbone of pretrained driving vision-language models by injecting trajectory tokens into late layers with lightweight DiffAdapters, enabling recursive trajectory refinement and depth-aware conditioning; achieves low-latency, parameter-efficient continuous planning (NAVSIM).
AI.motivation: Current driving VLMs integrate visual, route, language, and context but treat planning as a separate module; trajectory generation typically unfolds after final conditioning, leaving depth-wise condition computation outside stepwise trajectory formation.
AI.method: Insert trajectory tokens into selected late layers of the VLM backbone. Use lightweight layer-wise DiffAdapters to enable recursive trajectory refinement and maintain asymmetric joint attention that channels guidance from the condition stream to trajectory planning. Planning thus occurs within the backbone forward pass, co-evolving trajectory state and depth-wise conditions with minimal additional parameters.
AI.result: NAVSIM evaluates the approach on high-quality closed-loop planning with low end-to-end latency and few trainable parameters, showing effective continuous trajectory planning by jointly evolving trajectory state with depth-wise conditions in late-layer computations.
AI.conclusion: Planning embedded in the backbone is an efficient way to convert driving priors into continuous planning capabilities, with lightweight adapters enabling parameter-efficient adaptation of existing VLM priors into real-time planning.

title: SPARK: Representation-Level KV Memory Alignment for Safer Vision-Language Models
summary:
Vision-language models (VLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that distribute harmful intent across text and images, making unimodal safety mechanisms insufficient. We investigate whether this vulnerability can be mitigated directly in the multimodal key-value (KV) memory formed during prefill, without modifying model parameters at inference time. We introduce SPARK, a two-stage framework for targeted KV-memory repair. Stage 1 uses a disposable diagnostic adapter to identify harm-associated directions in multimodal key and value representations. Stage 2 projects out these directions, learns a lightweight residual repair, and anchors repaired keys with an image-structural prior to preserve visual grounding. Rather than applying the intervention uniformly, SPARK mixes repaired and original memory using a head-wise coefficient g_h* determined by intervention-relevant subspace energy E_h, requiring no explicit harm classifier at inference.
  Across LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Chameleon-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and InternVL2-4B, SPARK reduces multimodal attack success while preserving general capability. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, image-only jailbreak attack success falls to 4.7%, while MMMU remains within 0.6 points of the undefended model (47.8 vs. 48.4) with near-baseline language quality. On MM-SafetyBench, attack success decreases from 39.2% to 12.4%. Even under white-box adaptive joint prompt-image attacks, attack success is limited to 20.3%, compared with 54.6% for the undefended model. These results suggest that multimodal jailbreak behavior can be substantially mitigated by selectively repairing intervention-relevant KV subspaces at prefill, particularly when harmful evidence is carried by the visual modality.

AI.tldr: SPARK mitigates multimodal jailbreaks by repairing multimodal key-value memory during prefill via a two-stage, selective KV-subspace intervention; it reduces attack success across models while preserving language capabilities and without runtime parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models aggregate harms across text and images; unimodal safety is insufficient as jailbreak signals can be distributed across modalities within the model's KV memory.
AI.method: Stage 1: use a disposable diagnostic adapter to identify harm-associated directions in multimodal key/value representations. Stage 2: project out these harmful directions, learn a lightweight residual repair, and anchor repaired keys with an image-structural prior to preserve visual grounding. The repair is mixed with original memory using head-wise coefficients g_h* determined by intervention-relevant subspace energy E_h; inference-time harm classifier is not required. Evaluated across LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Chameleon-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, InternVL2-4B.
AI.result: On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, image-only jailbreak success drops to 4.7%; language quality (M-MMU) remains near baseline (47.8 vs 48.4). On MM-SafetyBench, attack success decreases from 39.2% to 12.4%. Under white-box adaptive joint prompt-image attacks, attack success is 20.3% vs 54.6% for undefended. Across models, SPARK reduces multimodal attack success while preserving general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Selective prefill KV subspace repair can substantially mitigate multimodal jailbreak behavior, particularly when harmful evidence is carried by the visual modality, without modifying model parameters at inference.

title: Nonparametric Variance-Penalized Actor-Critic: Statistical Inference for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Variance penalization is a principled approach to risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) that explicitly trades expected return for policy stability. Existing methods require a dedicated second critic to estimate return variance online, adding architectural complexity and compounding estimation error during learning. We propose a nonparametric variance-penalized actor-critic (VPAC) framework that replaces the variance critic with statistically grounded online estimators based on bootstrapping and random scaling, techniques drawn from the statistical inference literature for stochastic approximation. These estimators require no auxiliary network, maintain a single-critic architecture, and produce variance penalties that are bounded by construction, enabling clean convergence analysis. We establish almost-sure convergence for both a variance-penalized Q-learning algorithm and a two-timescale actor-critic variant via the ordinary differential equation (ODE) method, requiring only that variance estimates remain bounded rather than consistent. Empirically, we evaluate across discrete and continuous stochastic environments, demonstrating that the proposed methods match or exceed the variance reduction achieved by the existing dual-critic VPAC baseline while eliminating the overhead of a second critic. We further validate on a high-temperature superconductor (HTS) manufacturing case study, where VPAC-RS (Random Scaling) achieves a 74% reduction in steady-state critical current variability and a 63% reduction in episode return standard deviation, translating directly to improved yield consistency. Our results establish nonparametric statistical inference as a practical and theoretically sound alternative to auxiliary critics for risk-sensitive RL.

AI.tldr: Nonparametric variance estimation replaces the second critic in risk-sensitive RL, enabling a single-critic VPAC with bootstrapping and random scaling; proven convergence; empirically effective and leads to strong performance gains without extra network overhead.
AI.motivation: Reduce architectural complexity and estimation error in variance-penalized RL by removing the dedicated variance critic, while maintaining principled risk-sensitive objectives and convergence guarantees.
