Dproj provides a direct diagnostic of semantic-memory integrity and helps isolate memory-driven from navigation/calibration failures; the method shows strong empirical gains but may incur computational overhead and relies on accurate semantic likelihoods.

title: Learning Continuous Source Responses For Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: Advances in image generation have made synthetic images increasingly difficult to distinguish from real photographs, raising concerns about the trustworthiness of visual media. Existing AI-generated image detectors often perform well on in-domain data, but their robustness and cross-generator generalization remain limited. These limitations are commonly attributed to overfitting to shortcut cues. Although many methods seek to suppress shortcut learning, most retain binary classification as the training task without reconsidering how the task itself shapes the learned representations. We introduce CuRe, a framework for learning Continuous Source Responses that revisits authenticity detection from the perspective of the training task. CuRe reformulates backbone adaptation as regression of real-generated mixing ratios, providing finer supervision that encourages the model to capture authenticity-related variation beyond binary endpoint separation. We further select a compact source-response subspace to suppress nuisance variation and limit the final classifier's access to potential shortcut cues. Across ten public benchmarks, CuRe achieves an average balanced accuracy of 89.7%, exceeding the second-best method by 5.2 percentage points. Further experiments demonstrate consistent generalization gains across visual backbones and strong robustness to common image degradations. Code is available at https://github.com/manic-cui/CuRe

AI.tldr: CuRe reframes detection as regression on real/generated mixing ratios to learn continuous authenticity representations, improving cross-generator generalization and robustness.
AI.motivation: Detectors often overfit to shortcut cues and rely on binary endpoints, leading to poor cross-generator robustness. A training task that captures authenticity-related variation beyond binary separation is needed.
AI.method: Formulate backbone adaptation as regression of real-generated mixing ratios; select a compact source-response subspace to suppress nuisance variation and limit access to shortcut cues, enhancing generalization across backbones.
AI.result: Average balanced accuracy of 89.7% across ten benchmarks, outperforming the second-best method by 5.2 percentage points; shows strong cross-generator generalization and robustness to degradations.
AI.conclusion: Continuous supervision via mixing-ratio regression improves authenticity detection and generalization; code available at the provided GitHub URL.

title: Should All Noises Be Treated Equally: Impact of Input Noise Variability on Neural Network Robustness
summary: Geophysical data collected from active field sites are often contaminated by complex and heterogeneous noise, obscuring weak seismic events, and complicating automated interpretation. Although deep learning offers promising solutions for seismic processing, its performance is highly sensitive to the nature of training noise, especially under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. This study investigates the influence of noise parameters, such as type, scale, and complexity on the performance, generalization and robustness of neural networks in two geophysical tasks: first break picking and denoising. We simulate seismic-while-drilling data and apply controlled input source noise augmentation using stochastic generators to vary the noise characteristics. Different neural networks are trained on fixed noise types and scales, then evaluated across both seen and unseen noise scenarios. We incrementally increase the complexity of the noise by introducing compound noise mixtures and assess the performance of the model under increasingly challenging OOD conditions. This yields a robustness matrix that captures the generalizability of each model relative to its training configuration. Results indicate that larger noise scales boost generalization, and that effective alignment between noise type, task complexity, and architecture is key for maximizing generalization gains. In addition, training with compound noises mitigate weaknesses associated with single-noise training, acting as an additional implicit regularizer to improving robustness. These findings highlight key factors influencing model resilience in noisy geophysical environments and offer guidance for developing deep learning models that generalize effectively across diverse and unpredictable noise conditions.

AI.tldr: Training noise characteristics decisively shape deep learning generalization in seismic tasks; using diverse/compound noise during training enhances robustness and OOD performance, with larger noise scales further improving generalization; aligning noise type with task and model architecture is beneficial.
AI.motivation: To understand how the type, scale, and complexity of training noise affect generalization and robustness of neural networks in seismic processing under out-of-distribution conditions, across two tasks (first-break picking and denoising).
AI.method: Simulate seismic-while-drilling data and apply controlled input-source noise augmentation via stochastic generators to create varied noise types and scales. Train networks on fixed noise configurations (type/scale), then evaluate on both seen and unseen noise. Incrementally increase noise complexity by introducing compound noise mixtures and assess performance under increasingly challenging OOD scenarios. Construct a robustness matrix linking model performance to training configuration.
AI.result: Findings show that larger noise scales improve generalization; effective alignment between noise type, task complexity, and architecture is key for maximizing gains. Training with compound noises mitigates weaknesses of single-noise training and acts as an implicit regularizer, enhancing robustness across diverse noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: Noise-aware training strategies that employ diverse or compound noise, matched to the task and architecture, yield more resilient DL models for seismic processing, enabling better generalization in unpredictable noisy geophysical environments.

title: Four Ledgers, Not One Score: Responsible Communication of LLM-Judge Calibration in Biomedical ML
comment: 6 pages, 0 figures, 3 tables. A public reproducibility artifact accompanies the paper
summary: Synthetic perturbations appear to offer inexpensive calibration data for LLM evaluators in biomedical ML, where expert review is scarce. Yet a planted mutation key is neither a detector output nor automatically human ground truth. We formalize four distinct ledgers: planted perturbations, independent detector outputs, source-linked human dispositions, and human-added discoveries. We then audit the evaluation design, scoring code, read paths, and current human records of a private synthetic Japanese care-handoff workflow. The factory stored 69 planted error cards across 47 targets. Final review covers 22 targets and contains 22 confirmed imported proposals, 9 rejected proposals, and 79 human-added cards; only 3 reviewed targets are double annotated. Passing imported plant keys to a generic detector scorer yields 22/(22+9)=0.710 and 22/(22+79)=0.218. A direct audit identity shows that these values are proposal-confirmation yield and submitted-ledger composition, not judge precision and recall, because no independent detector realization was preserved for the audited proposals in the available records. The audit also finds source-name collisions, row shadowing, forced severity, vacuous ratio defaults, and unsupported zero-support field weights. We contribute a provenance-aware claim audit, a storage contract, and a minimum calibration gate for responsibly communicating biomedical ML capability claims. This single-workflow forensic case is an existence proof of a failure mode, not an estimate of its prevalence: existing human work supports an exploratory audit of synthetic proposals, but not LLM-judge operating characteristics, clinical validity, corpus prevalence, or robust inter-annotator agreement.

AI.tldr: A forensic audit of synthetic perturbation-based LLM evaluation in biomedical ML reveals that planted perturbations and audited proposals do not yield true judge performance metrics; identifies flawed evaluation ledgers and systemic issues; proposes provenance-aware audit, storage contract, and calibration gate; demonstrates a failure mode rather than prevalence.
AI.motivation: Assess whether synthetic perturbations provide reliable calibration data for LLM evaluators in biomedical ML and illuminate auditability gaps and misinterpretations in evaluation claims.
AI.method: Audit of a private synthetic Japanese care-handoff workflow. Defined four ledgers: planted perturbations, independent detector outputs, source-linked human dispositions, and human-added discoveries. Tallied 69 planted error cards across 47 targets; final review covered 22 targets with 22 confirmed imported proposals, 9 rejected proposals, and 79 human-added cards. Computed detector-scorer yields from imported plant keys; checked read paths and provenance; identified data-quality issues (source-name collisions, row shadowing, forced severity, vacuous defaults, zero-support weights).
AI.result: Found that the reported yields reflect proposal-confirmation rate and ledger composition, not actual judge precision/recall since no independent detector realization was preserved for audited proposals. Revealed multiple provenance and data-quality problems. Generated a provenance-aware claim audit, a storage contract, and a minimum calibration gate. Demonstrates a single-forensic-case failure mode rather than prevalence.
AI.conclusion: The study provides existence proof of a failure mode in synthetic-perturbation evaluation of biomedical LLMs. It argues for improved auditing, provenance tracking, and governance to responsibly communicate biomedical ML capabilities.

title: StereoPatch: Patch-Aligned RGB-Depth Fusion for Spatial Perception in Robot Manipulation
summary: Recent advances in robot imitation learning have produced visuomotor policies that predict actions directly from visual observations. Yet visually similar scenes can require different actions as target position, object height, or contact geometry changes. Pretrained RGB features may map these geometrically distinct states to similar policy inputs, while simply adding depth requires the policy to learn RGB-depth correspondence from the same limited demonstrations used to learn control. We introduce StereoPatch, a patch-aligned RGB-depth representation that binds registered metric geometry directly to the RGB patches used for action prediction. On a shared 2-D patch grid, asymmetric cross-attention incorporates depth information into the corresponding RGB features before action decoding. The resulting StereoPatch Tokens provide a geometry-aware visual representation that can condition general visuomotor policies without changing their underlying learning objectives. Across six real-robot tasks, StereoPatch achieves higher closed-loop success than appearance-only, geometry-only, raw RGB-D, and late-fusion baselines. Additional experiments across three simulation suites evaluate compatibility across visuomotor policy architectures, spatial generalization, and operating limits. Results suggest that resolving control-relevant geometric ambiguity benefits from aligning depth directly with the visual features used for action prediction, rather than supplying it as an independent modality. Project page: https://aus.bot/research/stereopatch/.

AI.tldr: StereoPatch links depth to RGB patches with cross-attention to produce geometry-aware tokens, improving visuomotor policy performance across robots and simulators.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies can misinterpret geometrically distinct states that look visually similar; depth as an independent modality or RGB-D fusion may not resolve this without reworking learning objectives. Aligning metric geometry with the RGB features used for action prediction aims to reduce geometric ambiguity.
AI.method: Create a patch-aligned RGB-depth representation on a shared 2-D patch grid. Use asymmetric cross-attention to inject depth information into corresponding RGB features before decoding actions, producing StereoPatch Tokens that condition policies without altering their objectives.
AI.result: Six real-robot tasks show higher closed-loop success than appearance-only, geometry-only, raw RGB-D, and late-fusion baselines. Additional simulation experiments demonstrate compatibility across architectures, improved spatial generalization, and operating limits. The approach suggests geometry-aware depth integration outperforms treating depth as a separate modality.
AI.conclusion: Aligning depth directly with visual features used for action prediction resolves control-relevant geometric ambiguity and generalizes across architectures and environments without changing learning objectives.

title: Mobile CT Services for Rural, Regional, and Remote Areas: Current Practice and Future Integration with Telehealth and Regulatory-Authorised AI
summary: Computed tomography (CT) plays an essential role in clinical workflow to improve patient outcomes. However, access to CT imaging and specialist interpretation remains limited, particularly in rural, regional, remote (RRR), and other resource-limited settings. Recent advances in mobile CT, telehealth, and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to extend advanced imaging services to populations in RRR settings. This review examines: 1) mobile CT systems deployed in trucks, trailers, ambulances, and other mobile platforms; 2) telehealth technologies supporting CT-based healthcare; and 3) AI for CT that has received regulatory authorisation or is currently deployed in clinical practice. Applications are evaluated across four clinical functions: screening and diagnosis, patient monitoring, risk prediction, and intervention or therapeutic decision support. The review covers neurological, thoracic, cardiovascular, abdominal, oncological, musculoskeletal, and interventional imaging, with particular attention to stroke, cancer, and other image-guided treatment. Other factors such as regulatory status, deployment status, and estimated technology readiness (TRL) level are compared. Current evidence indicates that mobile CT, telehealth, and AI for conventional CT are individually relatively mature, but fully integration of these technologies remains less widely deployed and validated in the clinical settings. Key barriers include regulatory variation, domain shift, connectivity requirements, cost, workflow integration, cybersecurity, and limited evidence of patient-level benefit. Future research should prioritise prospective, multicentre evaluation of integrated CT systems in real-world and underserved clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A scoping review of mobile CT, telehealth, and AI-enabled CT in resource-limited settings, assessing deployment, readiness (TRL), and regulatory status across clinical domains; finds maturity in components but limited real-world integration; calls for prospective multicentre evaluation.
AI.motivation: Improve access to CT imaging where access is limited by geography and resources; leverage mobile platforms, telehealth, and AI to extend imaging services and inform care.
AI.method: Narrative scoping review of mobile CT deployments (mobile platforms), telehealth CT support, and AI-based CT with regulatory status; evaluation by four clinical functions and multiple organ systems; comparison across regulatory/deployment/TRL.
AI.result: Independently, mobile CT, telehealth, and AI are relatively mature; integrated systems are not widely deployed or validated; key barriers include regulatory differences, domain shift, connectivity, cost, workflow integration, cybersecurity, and limited patient-level benefit evidence.
AI.conclusion: Prioritize prospective, multicentre evaluation of integrated CT systems in real-world, underserved settings.

title: GNN4PPM: Multi-Target Predictive Process Monitoring with Relational Graph Convolutional Networks
comment: Accepted for presentation at the BPM 2026 Forum. The final version will appear in the Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing (LNBIP) post-proceedings
summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) aims at predicting at runtime and as early as possible the future states of a process execution. Common tasks include predicting the next event, the time to completion of a trace, and outcomes. Existing approaches typically consider an event from the perspective of the executed activities along with their timestamps and case identifiers. This leads to the disadvantage that in real-life settings, there is much more information recorded in the event log that is not captured or completely ignored when performing prediction tasks. We introduce GNN4PPM, an approach that predicts all next events along with their complete data payload at once. We represent event information in a heterogeneous knowledge graph that captures the event log as an RDF semantics, and train the embeddings with a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN). Our approach is promising in comparison to existing solutions, and experiments with state-of-the-art solutions prove the accuracy and applicability of GNN4PPM in complex settings.

AI.tldr: GNN4PPM predicts all next events and their complete data payloads by modeling an event log as a heterogeneous RDF-based knowledge graph and applying Relational Graph Convolutional Networks (R-GCN).
AI.motivation: Current predictive process monitoring (PPM) approaches mostly focus on events defined by activities with timestamps and case IDs, ignoring richer information captured in logs. This limits predictive accuracy and completeness.
AI.method: Represent the event log as a heterogeneous knowledge graph with RDF semantics and train embeddings using an R-GCN to predict the next events along with their full data payloads.
AI.result: Experiments show competitive accuracy and applicability compared to state-of-the-art methods, indicating effectiveness in complex settings.
AI.conclusion: A graph-based, RDF-driven representation can effectively leverage richer event-log information to improve PPM tasks, with GNN4PPM delivering accurate, comprehensive next-event predictions.

title: Horizon-specific Expert Fusion for Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
summary: Short-term photovoltaic power forecasting requires models to represent regular solar cycles and weather-driven fluctuations whose importance changes with the forecast horizon. This study develops a hierarchical ensemble that combines temporal neural models, historical analogs, state climatology, and gradient-boosted trees. Solar geometry and numerical weather forecasts describe the expected generation conditions, while horizon-specific convex weights combine complementary predictions. A separate calibration step uses available historical forecast errors to account for recent bias. The framework is evaluated on public PVDAQ data at 15--240-minute horizons and on three GEFCom2014 solar zones at hourly horizons up to four hours. On PVDAQ, the ensemble achieves a daylight capacity-normalized mean absolute error of 4.315%, reducing error by 4.11% relative to full-feature LightGBM and by 6.03% relative to fine-tuned Chronos-2 under identical calibration. Expert-removal experiments identify redundancy within the ensemble. Across three training seeds on GEFCom2014, learned fusion improves upon equal weighting but performs comparably to LightGBM. The results support horizon-specific combination as a useful forecasting strategy while showing that its advantage over strong individual models depends on the dataset and evaluation period.

AI.tldr: A horizon-aware hierarchical ensemble improves short-term PV forecasts by fusing diverse models with physics and data-driven components; gains are dataset-dependent but show promise for horizon-specific fusion.
AI.motivation: Forecast accuracy for solar power is governed by regular diurnal/seasonal cycles and weather-driven fluctuations whose relative importance changes with forecast horizon; leveraging multiple model families and horizon-specific fusion could capture both types of dynamics.
AI.method: Construct a hierarchical ensemble combining temporal neural models, historical analogs, state climatology, and gradient-boosted trees. Use solar geometry and numerical weather forecasts to describe expected generation conditions; apply horizon-specific convex weights to fuse predictions; include a calibration step from historical forecast errors to correct recent bias. Evaluate on PVDAQ (15–240 min horizons) and GEFCom2014 solar zones (hourly up to 4 h). Examine redundancy via expert-removal; compare learned fusion to equal weighting and to LightGBM/Chronos-2 baselines under calibration.
AI.result: On PVDAQ, daylight capacity-normalized MAE = 4.315%, reducing error by 4.11% vs full-feature LightGBM and 6.03% vs Chronos-2 under calibration. Expert-removal suggests redundancy in the ensemble. On GEFCom2014 (three seeds), learned fusion beats equal weighting but is comparable to LightGBM; horizon-specific fusion yields benefits but depend on dataset and evaluation period.
AI.conclusion: Horizon-specific combination is a useful forecasting strategy for short-term PV power, capable of harnessing complementary predictions from diverse models. However, its advantage over strong single models is dataset- and period-dependent, with redundancy indicating potential simplification opportunities.

title: DIDO: Distilling Interaction-Centric Dynamics into One-Step Denoising for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) use video generation models to predict future visual dynamics for robotic manipulation, but iterative denoising introduces additional latency for closed-loop control. We empirically find that visual content converges at different rates during denoising. Static background structure forms early, whereas the gripper and manipulated object remain blurry after the first step, with their interaction dynamics emerging only through subsequent denoising. Consequently, naively truncating a multi-step video model to one step preserves scene structure but loses the interaction-centric dynamics most critical for manipulation. To address this issue, we propose DIDO, which distills the converged dynamics of a multi-step video model into a single denoising step. DIDO combines distribution matching distillation with interaction-centric representation guidance. Beyond compressing multi-step generation into one forward pass, DIDO explicitly models the gripper, manipulated object, and their interaction using supervised bounding-box visual reasoning tokens. Additionally, DIDO aligns the target object's representations across multiple model layers with features from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder. This interaction-centric guidance helps the distilled model preserve both the relevant entities and their future dynamics in a single step, while substantially reducing inference latency. DIDO achieves an average success rate of 99.0\% on LIBERO, 76.6\% on LIBERO-Plus, and 92.0\% on RoboTwin, while also demonstrating effective transfer to long-horizon and generalization tasks in real-world robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: DIDO distills converged dynamics of a multi-step World Action Model into a single denoising step, reducing latency while preserving interaction dynamics between gripper and manipulated objects through interaction-centric guidance and cross-layer feature alignment; achieves strong task success and transfers to real-world manipulation.
AI.motivation: Iterative denoising in video-based WAMs incurs latency and can erode interaction-centric dynamics. Early frames capture static background, while gripper/object interactions emerge later; truncating to one step loses critical dynamics for manipulation.
AI.method: DIDO uses distribution matching distillation combined with interaction-centric representation guidance. It introduces supervised bounding-box visual reasoning tokens for the gripper, manipulated object, and their interaction, and aligns target object representations across model layers with features from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder to preserve interaction dynamics in a single forward pass.
AI.result: Average success rates: LIBERO 99.0%, LIBERO-Plus 76.6%, RoboTwin 92.0%. Demonstrates effective transfer to long-horizon and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Distilling converged dynamics into one-step inference preserves essential interaction dynamics while substantially reducing latency, enabling robust manipulation performance and better generalization.

title: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA for Multi-Task Medical Vision-Language Learning
comment: MICCAI FLARE26 Task3 Challenge Report, 18 pages, 6 figures
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) allow a single model to perform clinical image analysis tasks ranging from diagnosis classification to report generation. However, joint adaptation is challenged by heterogeneous output formats, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced training data. Hence, we present \textbf{Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA}, a framework built on MedGemma-1.5-4B. The framework uses a shared-specific Mixture-of-LoRA architecture comprising one shared LoRA and six task-specific expert LoRAs, together with a two-stage training procedure. In Stage 1, we jointly train the shared LoRA and all task-specific expert LoRAs on all tasks. In Stage 2, we first freeze the backbone, the shared LoRA, and all non-target experts, and refine one task expert at a time. Classification and regression then receive an additional modality-balanced continuation, in which smaller modality groups are repeated to match the largest group. In the FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, the proposed method achieves 0.85 balanced accuracy for classification, 0.48 micro-F1 for multi-label classification, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanYL03/MICCAI-FLARE-2026-Challenge-Task3-2D.

AI.tldr: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA for medical VLMs with a shared LoRA and six task-specific experts, enabling joint then task-specific fine-tuning to handle heterogeneous outputs and imbalanced data; shows strong FLARE 2026 Task 3 results.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous output formats, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced training data hinder joint adaptation of medical vision-language models across tasks.
AI.method: A shared-specific Mixture-of-LoRA architecture with one shared LoRA and six task-specific expert LoRAs on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Stage 1 jointly trains the shared and all task experts; Stage 2 freezes backbone, shared LoRA, and non-target experts and refines one task expert at a time; an additional modality-balanced continuation repeats smaller modality groups to match the largest group during classification/regression.
AI.result: On FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, achieves 0.85 balanced accuracy (classification), 0.48 micro-F1 (multi-label), 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 MAE (regression).
AI.conclusion: The proposed Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA demonstrates effective task-specific specialization with improved multi-task performance on a standardized medical imaging benchmark; code is available.

title: Selecting k Paths with the Minimum Longest Path Length in the Stochastic Semi-Bandit Setting
summary: When performing parallel data transmission through a network using multiple paths, it is practically important to minimize the maximum transmission time among the selected paths. This study addresses an online problem in which $k$ paths from an origin vertex to a destination vertex must be selected at each time step within a network represented as a directed graph. Here, the number of paths going through each edge in each parallel data transmission is limited to its capacity, and the time required for transmission is determined stochastically. We formulate the semi-bandit problem of selecting a set of paths to minimize the maximum traversal time among the selected paths and propose an algorithm to solve it.

AI.tldr: Online semi-bandit optimization for selecting k parallel s-t paths to minimize the maximum stochastic traversal time under edge capacity constraints.
AI.motivation: In parallel data transmission, selecting multiple paths with per-edge capacity limits to reduce worst-case delay is practically important; delays are stochastic.
AI.method: Formulate as an online semi-bandit problem for selecting a set of k paths each step; propose an algorithm to solve the problem under stochastic traversal times and capacity constraints.
AI.result: An algorithmic framework is proposed to tackle the semi-bandit path-selection problem with the objective of minimizing the maximum traversal time among chosen paths.
AI.conclusion: Addresses online multi-path selection with capacity constraints and stochastic delays; provides an algorithmic approach for minimizing maximum path delay in parallel data transmission.

title: The average-farmer illusion in language-model simulations of agricultural decisions
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly used as synthetic people in surveys and social simulations, yet their apparent realism is often judged from population averages or distributional similarity. We tested what such evidence actually establishes by comparing Claude, Codex and Kimi under four prespecified prompt designs with matched farmer decisions from China and four African countries. Some configurations reproduced observed means and adoption rates. However, their person-level predictions were weak; their decisions clustered around typical values and policy-relevant extremes were largely missing. Most strikingly, a simple generator fitted only to the observed marginal dis- tribution, and given no information about any farmer, achieved greater distributional similarity than every language-model configuration. Prompt additions produced conditional gains rather than uni- versal improvement: results varied with model, outcome, population and validation target. We call this the average-farmer illusion: a synthetic population can look realistic while failing to repro- duce who does what or how behaviour varies. We provide a claim-matched validation framework and reusable modular prompts that turn prompt construction into an auditable experimental process. Population-level resemblance should therefore be treated as the start of validation, not as evidence of individual simulation.

AI.tldr: Language-model agents can mimic population statistics but fail at individual-level behavior; a simple marginal-distribution generator can rival or outperform LMs; call for a validation framework and auditable prompts to avoid the 'average-farmer illusion' where realistic means do not imply realistic individual actions.
AI.motivation: Question whether population-level realism from language-model agents truly yields accurate individual behavior and heterogeneity in survey-like tasks; identify risks of relying on distributional similarity as validation.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of three LMs (Claude, Codex, Kimi) under four prompt designs against matched farmer decisions from China and four African countries; include a simple generator fitted to the observed marginal distribution as a baseline; assess means, adoption rates, and individual-level predictions; introduce claim-matched validation framework and modular prompts.
AI.result: Some configurations reproduce observed means and adoption rates, but individual-level predictions are weak with clustering around typical values and with few policy-relevant extremes captured; the marginal-distribution generator often matches distribution better than any LM; prompt design yields conditional, not universal, improvements across models/outcomes/populations; introduces the ‘average-farmer illusion.’
AI.conclusion: Population-level resemblance is only the starting point for validation. Do not treat distributional similarity as evidence of accurate individual behavior; adopt a claim-matched validation framework and reusable modular prompts to auditablely test LMs as synthetic populations.

title: An Information-Space Perspective to Scene Graph Sufficiency for Robotic Task Planning
comment: In review for IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Planning in complex environments requires task specifications grounded in representations that capture objects, relations, and affordances; scene graphs meet this need, but their size in large environments hinders efficient planning. While task-aware pruning and hierarchical abstractions have been explored, a general, task-centric formalization of what constitutes a sufficient scene graph for planning remains open. This paper provides such a formalization by modeling planning over scene graphs within an information-spaces framework through the definition of scene graph transition systems and relevant action semantics for navigation and manipulation. We then introduce derived scene graphs via information mappings that merge and prune nodes and induce quotient transition systems augmented with motion primitives to capture higher-level actions over merged graph nodes. Sufficiency is characterized by two conditions: (i) the information mapping yields a deterministic quotient, and (ii) the task is well-posed over derived traces, ensuring plans found on the derived model are feasible on the maximal system. We illustrate the framework using a task over an example environment, showing both sufficient and insufficient reduced scene graphs.

AI.tldr: Formalize sufficiency of reduced scene graphs for planning using an information-spaces framework.
AI.motivation: Scene graphs capture objects, relations, and affordances but explode in large environments; a task-centric formalization of sufficient graphs is needed to enable efficient planning.
AI.method: Define scene graph transition systems with action semantics for navigation and manipulation; construct derived scene graphs via information mappings that merge/prune nodes, yielding quotient transition systems with motion primitives for higher-level actions; state sufficiency via two conditions: deterministic quotient and well-posedness of the task over derived traces.
AI.result: Provides a general framework and criteria for sufficiency; demonstrates with an example environment showing both sufficient and insufficient reduced scene graphs.
AI.conclusion: Sufficient reduced scene graphs enable planning that remains feasible on the full system; the approach clarifies and validates when pruning/abstraction preserves plan feasibility.

title: Beyond Natural Images: Rethinking AI-Generated Image Detection in Documents
summary: AI-generated image detection has attracted increasing attention, but existing evaluations mainly focus on natural images, leaving AI-generated document images largely underexplored. This omission is concerning because documents often appear in sensitive real-world scenarios, such as invoices, expense reports, certificates, and medical records. In this paper, we first construct a controlled diagnostic benchmark, AIGDoc-Pilot, and reveal that existing detectors suffer substantial performance degradation on AI-generated document images, with the mean AUC dropping by more than 7%. Based on this, we further reveal two document-specific properties behind this gap: generation artifacts exhibit strong spatial inconsistency across local regions, and text density significantly affects real-synthetic separability, where text-dense regions offer stronger discriminative evidence. Motivated by these findings, we construct AIGDoc, a larger document-centric dataset containing diverse real-world documents and AI-generated counterparts produced by multiple advanced generation and editing models. Extensive experiments on AIGDoc demonstrate that existing detectors still struggle to reliably identify AI-generated documents, while document-based training partially narrows the gap. Together, these results offer valuable insights for developing dependable and generalizable detectors in document-centric scenarios. The code and datasets will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: AI-generated document image detection lags behind natural-image detectors; new benchmarks reveal sizable performance drops and document-specific cues; a larger, diverse dataset shows detectors still struggle; document-focused training helps but is not sufficient; code/datasets to be released.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations on AI-generated image detection focus on natural images, but documents appear in sensitive real-world contexts (invoices, certificates, medical records). There is a risk that detectors trained on natural images generalize poorly to document imagery.
AI.method: Construct AIGDoc-Pilot, a controlled diagnostic benchmark to assess detectors on AI-generated document images; identify two document-specific properties behind the performance gap: (1) generation artifacts show strong spatial inconsistency across local regions; (2) text density affects real-synthetic separability, with text-dense regions offering stronger cues. Develop AIGDoc, a larger, diverse document-centric dataset with real documents and AI-generated counterparts from multiple generation/editing models. Conduct extensive experiments showing detectors fail to reliably identify AI-generated documents; document-based training partially narrows the gap.
AI.result: Detectors experience substantial degradation on AI-generated document images, with mean AUC dropping by more than 7% on AIGDoc-Pilot. Document-specific cues are identified. On AIGDoc, detectors still struggle, though document-centric training provides partial improvement.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer insights for building dependable, generalizable detectors in document-centric scenarios; the authors plan to release code and datasets publicly upon acceptance, enabling broader validation and development.

title: Pathwise Individual Rationality in Federated Learning: A Mechanism-Architecture Co-Design
summary:
Participation in federated learning (FL) comes at a cost. Clients trade off privacy, communication, and compute costs for potentially greater gains in model efficacy. This paper explores this tradeoff under the aegis of individual rationality (IR) versus autarky, the basic game-theoretic requirement that the federation provide utility no worse than local training. Using the above as the design target, we examine pathwise performance of FL, as a per-round bound on cumulative surplus, not just as an asymptotic equilibrium guarantee under different models of client data distribution heterogeneity. Along this path, clients can remain below their local-training baseline for hundreds of rounds. The natural remedy is to cap each client's per-round contribution so that this shortfall stays bounded, and we prove that it backfires, collapsing learning even at low-to-modest heterogeneity.
  We then propose a novel design that combines short-term participation guarantees with personalized model evaluation, while maintaining fair incentives. We provide a theoretical basis for this new approach and empirically demonstrate that clients can avoid short-term losses without harming overall performance, even under moderate data distribution heterogeneity; under severe heterogeneity, the design shows promising outcomes for clients compared to their local baseline at some cost in accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes incentive design in federated learning under individual rationality and autarky, shows that capping per-round contributions harms learning, and proposes a design that guarantees short-term participation with personalized evaluation. It provides theoretical guarantees and empirical results showing benefits under moderate data heterogeneity and potential trade-offs under severe heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Federated learning involves privacy, communication, and compute costs. To ensure participation, models must be IR-friendly and meet autarky. Analyzing pathwise, per-round surplus reveals that naive constraints can backfire, necessitating incentive-compatible, robust designs.
AI.method: Pathwise analysis of cumulative surplus under different client data heterogeneity models; evaluation and refutation of per-round contribution caps; development of a new design that couples short-term participation guarantees with personalized model evaluation; theoretical justification and empirical experiments demonstrating incentives alignment and performance under varying heterogeneity.
AI.result: Finding: cap-based per-round constraints can collapse learning even at low-to-moderate heterogeneity. The proposed design supports short-term participation without harming overall performance under moderate heterogeneity, and offers some accuracy gains over local baselines under severe heterogeneity at a cost in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: An incentive-compatible FL design that balances short-term guarantees with personalized evaluation preserves global performance under realistic heterogeneity; when heterogeneity is severe, clients may still benefit relative to local training at some accuracy cost. The work provides a theoretical basis and empirical validation for pragmatic participation guarantees in FL.

title: BusMA: A Bus Communication Substrate for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-Agent (MA) systems are effective at solving complex tasks that demand planning, tool use, and the synthesis of evidence from multiple sources. Existing systems typically adopt Hierarchical Manager-Worker (HMW) or Router-based Message Passing (RMP) structures as their communication protocol. However, these designs restrict agent autonomy: Worker agents cannot directly consult specific "peers", and misrouted messages can propagate errors. Inspired by bus architectures in computer systems, we propose BusMA, a communication framework that allows any agent to address other agents through a shared channel, i.e., the Bus. It consists of agent registration, message routing, and shared memory management components. Worker agents, each equipped with tools, have their own local memory and can reason, act (tool usage), and communicate by posting shared messages with specific intents. We introduce four intents: discussion, challenge, guidance, and request for explanation, which support fine-grained communication among agents. A Chair agent monitors the shared memory to coordinate interactions and facilitate convergence among Workers. To evaluate the effectiveness of BusMA, we conduct extensive experiments with two frontier LLMs across 13 tasks spanning visual reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and knowledge retrieval demonstrate that BusMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HMW and RMP methods.

AI.tldr: BusMA introduces a bus-based multi-agent communication framework enabling direct addressing via a shared channel, with a Chair to coordinate, four intents for fine-grained interaction, and tools-equipped workers; it outperforms HMW and RMP baselines on 13 tasks using two frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: Current hierarchical (HMW) and router-based (RMP) MA communication restrict agent autonomy and risk misrouting; a shared bus aims to decouple agents, improve routing precision, and enhance convergence and collaboration.
AI.method: Design and implement BusMA with: (i) agent registration, (ii) message routing, (iii) shared memory management; workers have tools, local memory, reasoning, action, and can post shared messages with intents (discussion, challenge, guidance, explanation); a Chair agent monitors memory to coordinate and drive convergence; evaluate on 13 tasks across visual reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and knowledge retrieval using two frontier LLMs.
AI.result: Empirical results show BusMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HMW and RMP baselines across the 13 tasks and two frontier LLMs.
AI.conclusion: BusMA provides a scalable, autonomous, bus-based communication paradigm for MA systems, improving coordination and task performance through direct peer addressing, shared memory, and structured intents; the Chair role facilitates convergence among workers.

title: Flow-Matched Motion Priors: Online Optimal-Transport Rewards for Imitation Learning
summary: Learning a motion prior requires a reward that guides a policy from its current behavior toward demonstrated motion. Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) provide such a reward with a discriminator. However, adversarial objectives can become uninformative when policy and expert supports are far apart. A naive use of optimal transport (OT) averages matched expert successors into a barycentric target. Averaging across gait phases can weaken the target's joint motion. We introduce Flow-Matched Motion Priors (FMP), an online scalar reward learned from paths connecting current rollout histories to an expert motion bank. Entropic OT supplies the coupling. Before each policy update, we train a neural potential with flow matching (FM) along the rollout-to-expert paths, endpoint-gradient supervision, and relative-value calibration. The actor receives only physical observations and the reward remains a scalar, as in AMP. Controlled reward-model experiments show substantially better generalization beyond the fitting rollout than value-only or endpoint-only fitting. On Unitree G1, matched 50-million-transition experiments compare FMP with AMP, a barycentric OT reward, and nested ablations under demonstration and fixed-pose initialization. FMP produces stable forward walking at 0.727 m/s from demonstration resets and 0.338 m/s from a fixed default pose. In the fixed-pose condition, it incurs 129 falls versus 243 for the endpoint-only control. Against a static score-gradient teacher, dynamic FM reduces score-increment error at interpolation fractions 0.25 and 0.50 while using 29% less offline fitting time.

AI.tldr: Flow-Matched Motion Priors (FMP) introduce a scalar reward learned via entropic optimal transport flow matching along rollout-to-expert paths to address limitations of adversarial priors and barycentric OT. This yields better generalization and data efficiency for robotic locomotion, with favorable real-robot results compared to AMP and endpoint-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) suffer from uninformative rewards when policy and expert supports are distant, and naive barycentric OT can blur target motion across gait phases. There is a need for a reward mechanism that remains informative and data-efficient across diverse rollout states and initialization.
AI.method: FMP trains a neural potential to define a scalar reward by performing flow matching along paths from current rollout histories to an expert motion bank, using entropic OT to couple rollout and expert trajectories. Before each policy update, endpoint-gradient supervision and relative-value calibration refine the potential. The actor operates on physical observations, retaining a scalar reward analogous to AMP.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows improved generalization beyond the fitting rollout compared to value-only or endpoint-only fitting. On Unitree G1, 50M-transition experiments compare FMP against AMP, a barycentric OT reward, and ablations. FMP achieves stable forward walking (0.727 m/s with demonstration resets; 0.338 m/s with fixed-pose initialization). In the fixed-pose condition, FMP records 129 falls vs 243 for endpoint-only control. Against a static score-gradient teacher, dynamic FM reduces score-increment error at interpolation fractions 0.25 and 0.50, while using 29% less offline fitting time.
AI.conclusion: FMP offers a scalable, information-rich, scalar reward framework for motion priors by leveraging entropic OT flow matching and path-based supervision. It improves generalization and data efficiency relative to AMP and barycentric OT, and demonstrates competitive, robust locomotion performance on a real robot under varied initializations.

title: Rethinking Camouflage Image Generation towards a Training-Free Paradigm
summary: Camouflage image generation (CIG) aims to synthesize realistic camouflaged images by blending foreground objects into concealment-compatible background contexts. Achieving this objective requires jointly satisfying three coupled requirements: foreground preservation to retain target integrity, semantic compatibility to select plausible concealment contexts, and appearance assimilation to reduce visual discrepancies. Recent approaches predominantly rely on task-specific training on camouflage datasets to address these requirements, incurring substantial computational cost and limiting generalization beyond the training domain. To address these limitations, we formulate training-free CIG as a concealment-oriented paradigm that preserves the target while reducing its perceptual separability from the synthesized surroundings, rather than maintaining its visual prominence, without parameter updates. We instantiate this paradigm with FreeCam based on a frozen inpainting diffusion framework to preserve the foreground. Within this framework, a Contextual Reasoning Module exploits frozen multimodal priors to infer an environment favorable to concealment, thereby promoting semantic compatibility, while an Intrinsic Appearance Module extracts low-level color and texture cues from the foreground to guide background synthesis toward appearance assimilation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FreeCam achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and camouflage effectiveness without task-specific training, while its generated images provide synthetic supervision for camouflaged object detection and reduce target detectability under general object detectors.

AI.tldr: Training-free camouflage image generation (FreeCam) uses a frozen inpainting diffusion framework with two modules to preserve the foreground and promote concealment: a Contextual Reasoning Module leveraging frozen priors for semantic compatibility and an Intrinsic Appearance Module guiding appearance assimilation, achieving state-of-the-art results without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Conventional CIG methods rely on task-specific training on camouflage datasets, which is computationally costly and limits generalization beyond the training domain.
AI.method: Propose a training-free concealment-oriented paradigm implemented as FreeCam within a frozen inpainting diffusion framework. A Contextual Reasoning Module uses frozen multimodal priors to infer disguise-friendly environments, while an Intrinsic Appearance Module extracts low-level color/texture cues from the foreground to steer background synthesis; no parameter updates are performed.
AI.result: FreeCam achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and camouflage effectiveness without task-specific training; it also provides synthetic supervision for camouflaged object detection and reduces target detectability under general object detectors.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of training-free, concealment-oriented CIG by leveraging frozen priors and modular design to balance foreground preservation, semantic compatibility, and appearance assimilation, avoiding task-specific training while delivering high-quality camouflaged images.

title: Diagnosing Temporal Misalignment in Multichannel Time-Series Classification with Minimum Description Length
summary: Multichannel time-series classification commonly assumes synchronized sensor streams, although latency, clock drift, and preprocessing can introduce relative delays during data collection or after deployment. Existing synchronization solutions are often hardware-specific and difficult to apply retrospectively. Consequently, synchronization problems may remain undetected while classification performance is suboptimal. We introduce a classifier- and label-free diagnostic based on minimum description length (MDL). Our method applies candidate temporal shifts to sensor groups and measures how efficiently one group can be encoded through a representation of the remaining channels. An increased codelength indicates that the shift destroys shared temporal structure, whereas the minimum identifies the alignment most strongly supported by the data. Unlike learned synchronization methods, the diagnostic requires neither retraining nor a trusted aligned reference and can therefore test both training and deployment data for misalignments. Experiments on two controlled synthetic tasks and nine real-world datasets show that the metric exposes alignment structure and can recover accuracy under induced deployment drift. A whole-dataset audit further identifies stable nonzero MDL optima in established benchmarks including FordChallenge, Opportunity, PAMAP2, and UCIActivity, revealing potential systematic offsets that conventional model evaluation does not expose. Our method thus provides a general-purpose tool for detecting, understanding, and correcting temporal misalignment throughout the time-series learning pipeline. Our code is available under https://github.com/sbuschjaeger/mdl-temporal-misalignment.

AI.tldr: MDL-based diagnostic detects and corrects temporal misalignment across multichannel time-series streams without retraining or aligned references.
AI.motivation: Multichannel time-series classification assumes synchronized streams, but latency, clock drift, and preprocessing can introduce delays. Traditional synchronization methods are hardware-specific and retrospective alignment is hard, potentially masking misalignments that harm performance.
AI.method: Apply candidate temporal shifts to sensor groups and evaluate how efficiently one group can be encoded from the remaining channels using minimum description length (MDL). A longer codelength indicates loss of shared structure; the MDL minimum identifies the strongest-supported alignment. The approach is classifier- and label-free and requires no retraining or trusted aligned reference, enabling testing on both training and deployment data.
AI.result: Experiments on two synthetic tasks and nine real-world datasets show the MDL metric reveals alignment structure and can recover accuracy under deployment drift. A whole-dataset audit identifies stable nonzero MDL optima in benchmarks (FordChallenge, Opportunity, PAMAP2, UCIActivity), suggesting potential systematic offsets not exposed by conventional evaluation. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a general-purpose tool for detecting, understanding, and correcting temporal misalignment throughout the time-series learning pipeline.

title: Enabling Creative Exploration for Vibe Design Agents
summary: Vibe design agents turn natural-language briefs into rendered interfaces and frontend code. Yet a useful design agent should do more than produce one valid page: it should help users explore coherent alternatives. Increasing token-level temperature is a blunt solution because it varies aesthetic decisions and syntax-sensitive code at the same time. We instead separate exploration from implementation through an inference architecture that makes design direction an explicit intermediate decision. Inspired by Verbalized Sampling, a pre-pass proposes structured design specifications with typicality scores, an external selector samples one, and the downstream generator realizes the selected specification together with the original request under fixed settings. We apply this approach to UI themes and visual-asset prompts. Across 168 prompts, with 1,255 paired comparisons per temperature for each intervention, theme sampling broadens observed selection coverage and screenshot variation, while LLM-judge preferences vary across interventions, prompt complexity, and viewport. In an online experiment with more than 300,000 tasks, the observed code-export increase remains statistically uncertain, while fewer negative feedback events coexist with more correction interactions and modest operational costs. Together, these findings identify structured design specifications as a practical control point for exploring alternative UI concepts while keeping downstream generation settings fixed.

AI.tldr: Structured design-direction sampling separates exploration from implementation in Vibe design agents, enabling multiple coherent UI concepts without changing downstream generation settings; empirical evidence shows broader concept coverage and user-preference variability, though code-export impact is uncertain.
AI.motivation: To overcome reliance on high-temperature sampling for exploring design alternatives, and to produce more coherent, varied UI concepts while keeping generation rigor and safety fixed.
AI.method: Introduce an inference architecture with a pre-pass producing structured design specifications with typicality scores; an external selector samples one specification; downstream generator renders the chosen spec together with the original user request under fixed settings; applied to UI themes and visual-asset prompts; evaluation across many prompts and large-scale tasks.
AI.result: Theme sampling broadens observed selection coverage and screenshot variation. LLM-judge preferences vary by intervention, prompt complexity, and viewport. In online tasks, code-export gains are statistically uncertain, but fewer negative feedback events and more corrections, with modest costs.
AI.conclusion: Structured design specifications offer a practical control point to explore alternative UI concepts while keeping downstream generation settings fixed; the approach yields more diverse design exploration with variable preferences and uncertain code-export benefits.

title: Tracking the Ground: Online Lidar Identification of Robot-Induced Soil Deformation in Agricultural Environments
comment: This paper has been submitted for possible publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Agriculture faces many challenges, and robotic systems can play an important role in addressing them by improving the efficiency and sustainability of field operations. Among these challenges, preserving soil health is a critical concern, as vehicle-soil interactions can degrade the soil structure and produce unwanted surface deformation. A key step toward soil-aware robotics is to explicitly account for how vehicle traffic deforms the ground, yet soil state is typically not treated as a variable. We address this gap by proposing a framework to quantify traffic-induced soil deformation and estimate its evolution online from lidar observations. The method relies on a reduced-order parametric model that represents the soil behavior via physically interpretable parameters, yielding a continuously updated and observable representation of soil state. Experiments conducted in different soil conditions demonstrate the ability of the approach to capture deformation induced by the robot. By making soil response measurable and interpretable during operation, the proposed framework establishes a basis for soil-aware robotic operation, in which the estimated state can be exploited to adapt robotic behaviors in order to reduce soil degradation.

AI.tldr: A reduced-order, physically interpretable model estimates traffic-induced soil deformation online from lidar, enabling soil-aware robotic control.
AI.motivation: Soil health is threatened by vehicle-induced deformation; traditional robotics treat soil state as implicit. A real-time, interpretable soil state model is needed to guide adaptive, low-impact operations.
AI.method: Develop a reduced-order parametric soil model with observable parameters; fuse lidar-derived observations to update the model online; validate across varied soil conditions to capture deformation due to robot traffic.
AI.result: The framework yields continuously updated soil state representations that reflect deformation patterns caused by the robot; experiments across soil types demonstrate the method's ability to capture traffic-induced soil changes via lidar.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for soil-aware robotics by making soil response measurable and interpretable online, enabling adaptive behaviors to reduce soil degradation.

title: Contour-Guided Spectral Routing for Robust Real-Time Pedestrian Detection
summary: Real-time pedestrian detection in driving scenes is constrained by three coupled failure modes: tiny targets lose discriminative evidence, occlusion weakens geometric support, and weather or illumination changes distort appearance statistics. We formulate the detector through a unified \emph{contour-guided spectral routing} view rather than treating frequency processing, attention, and boundary reasoning as independent add-ons. The detector routes information in a prescribed order: spatial evidence is first augmented with global spectral context, deep representations then exchange spatial and spectral cues, and cross-scale fusion is finally conditioned on boundary--semantic disagreement. This ordering yields a compact representation pipeline in which low-frequency context stabilizes global structure while high-frequency evidence protects small-object contours. We further retain a wavelet-subband training transformation that perturbs low- and high-frequency coefficients independently, targeting appearance shifts caused by fog, rain, snow, and low illumination. The formulation exposes a single routing variable at each stage and distinguishes reusable signal transforms from the task-specific policy that decides where each signal is injected. On CityPersons, the proposed detector obtains 70.4 AP$_{50}$ and 44.2 AP$_{50:95}$, compared with 68.1 and 42.2 for RT-DETR, while the full wavelet-augmented configuration reaches 71.1 and 44.6.

AI.tldr: A contour-guided spectral routing detector with wavelet-based frequency perturbations improves real-time pedestrian detection under challenging conditions, achieving higher CityPersons AP than RT-DETR (with additional gains from full wavelet augmentation).
AI.motivation: Three coupled failure modes in driving scenes—tiny targets, occlusion, and appearance changes due to weather/illumination—are not well addressed by separating frequency processing, attention, and boundary reasoning. The work proposes a unified routing framework that jointly leverages spatial, spectral, and boundary cues to stabilize detection across scales and conditions.
AI.method: A four-stage, contour-guided spectral routing pipeline: (1) augment spatial evidence with global spectral context; (2) enable exchange between spatial and spectral representations; (3) perform cross-scale fusion conditioned on boundary–semantic disagreement; (4) apply a wavelet-subband training transformation that perturbs low- and high-frequency coefficients independently. A single routing variable governs each stage, separating reusable signal transforms from the task-specific policy that decides injection points. This yields a compact representation where low-frequency context stabilizes global structure and high-frequency evidence preserves small-object contours.
AI.result: On CityPersons, the detector achieves 70.4 AP50 and 44.2 AP50:95, surpassing RT-DETR at 68.1 and 42.2; with full wavelet augmentation, results improve to 71.1 and 44.6.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contour-guided spectral routing with wavelet-based perturbations yields robust real-time pedestrian detection by stabilizing global structure with low-frequency cues and protecting small-object contours with high-frequency evidence, achieving superior CityPersons performance and offering a unified framework that decouples signal transforms from task-specific routing decisions.

title: SH-WRNN: Implicit Spherical Harmonics Weight Field Routing Neural Networks for Asymmetric Edge Intelligence
summary: Deep learning architectures remain rigidly built upon traditional fully connected layers. While networks scale up, few challenge this foundational root. In this work, we reshape this paradigm by transforming the core synapse weight matrix from static, discrete parameters into a differentiable, continuous field governed by spherical harmonics functions. We introduce the Implicit Spherical Harmonics Weight Field Routing Neural Network (SH-WRNN), which constrains weight matrices within a continuous parametric field instead of optimizing millions of localized discrete weights. When retrieving the weight matrix of the current layer, connection parameters are localized using latitude and longitude on a rectangular plane mapped from the continuous field. The latitudinal coordinate is specified by activated neurons from the previous layer, while the longitudinal coordinate is determined by keys generated from previous layer activations via matrix multiplication. By evaluating intersections on this map, the network dynamically extracts its connection weights on-the-fly. Empirical validation on MNIST demonstrates that under compact configurations of (32, 10, 10) and (32, 3, 10), SH-WRNN achieves robust accuracies of 91.05% and 81.54% within a single training epoch. Furthermore, we propose an asymmetric Surface Baking scheme. Upon convergence, the continuous weight field is baked once into a static parametric surface. By eliminating analytical spherical harmonics calculations during inference and reducing dynamic matrix extraction to high-speed localized memory slicing, this scheme achieves asymmetric algorithmic acceleration with negligible accuracy degradation. This paradigm shift bypasses GPU memory-bandwidth monopolies, opening a novel path to reshape the advantages of CPU computing. Code is available at https://github.com/jzb1111/SphericalHarmonyRoutedNeuralNetWork.

AI.tldr: Proposes SH-WRNN: a neural network where the weight matrix is a differentiable spherical-harmonics-based field rather than a fixed set of parameters, with on-the-fly weight retrieval via latitude/longitude coordinates mapped from activations; shows MNIST results with compact configurations and introduces Surface Baking to convert the field into a static surface for faster inference.
AI.motivation: Alleviate rigidity and memory-bandwidth bottlenecks of traditional fully connected layers by replacing static weight matrices with a continuous, differentiable weight field controlled by spherical harmonics, enabling more compact representations and potential CPU-friendly inference.
AI.method: Replace weight matrices with an implicit continuous weight field parameterized by spherical harmonics. For a given layer, retrieve connection weights by mapping the previous-layer activations to a latitudinal coordinate and by generating a longitudinal coordinate from keys obtained via a matrix product of previous activations; intersections on the mapped field determine the weights. Training updates the field parameters. Evaluate on MNIST with compact configurations (32,10,10) and (32,3,10); introduce Surface Baking to bake the continuous field into a static parametric surface at convergence, removing harmonic calculations at inference and using memory slicing for speed.
AI.result: MNIST results: 91.05% accuracy for configuration (32,10,10) and 81.54% for (32,3,10) within a single training epoch. Surface Baking yields asymmetric acceleration with negligible accuracy loss, enabling faster CPU-based inference.
AI.conclusion: SH-WRNN demonstrates that weight matrices can be effectively represented as differentiable continuous fields, enabling dynamic, on-the-fly weight retrieval and potential CPU-friendly acceleration via Surface Baking, challenging conventional reliance on static weight storage and GPU bandwidth. Code available.

title: ER-EDF: A Psychology-Grounded Emotion Regulation Framework for Speech Empathetic Dialogue Generation in Large Audio-Language Models
summary: Empathetic response generation in spoken dialogue systems requires both accurate emotion perception and appropriate emotion regulation. Grounded in psychological theories such as the Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation theory, effective empathy depends not only on inferring a user's affective state but also on regulating how it is expressed in responses. However, recent large audio-language models (LALMs) largely treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal, lacking explicit regulatory mechanisms, which often leads to affect mirroring rather than calibrated support. We propose ER-EDF, a psychology-grounded framework that explicitly decouples emotion perception and emotion regulation in LALMs. Perception tracks the user's emotional state, while regulation determines how this state should guide empathetic response generation. The framework is model-agnostic and integrates seamlessly into existing LALMs. We further construct a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset and introduce empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching. Experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show that ER-EDF consistently improves empathetic response quality in both automatic and human evaluations, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation in spoken empathetic dialogue systems, paving a new direction for psychologically grounded empathetic AI.

AI.tldr: ER-EDF is a psychology-grounded, model-agnostic framework that decouples emotion perception from regulation in large audio-language models to improve empathetic spoken dialogue responses; it includes a dataset and empathy-aware metrics and shows consistent gains across five LALMs and two datasets.
AI.motivation: Current LALMs treat emotion as a direct conditioning signal, which leads to reflection-like affect mirroring and insufficient calibrated support. Psychological theories (Perception-Action Model and emotion regulation) motivate separating emotion perception from regulation to achieve better empathetic responses.
AI.method: Propose ER-EDF architecture that explicitly separates perception (emotional state tracking) and regulation (how the state guides response generation); model-agnostic integration into existing LALMs; construct a spoken empathetic dialogue dataset; introduce empathy-aware evaluation metrics beyond lexical matching; conduct experiments over five LALMs and two datasets.
AI.result: ER-EDF yields consistent improvements in empathetic response quality across automatic and human evaluations, demonstrated across multiple LALMs and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling emotion perception and regulation is essential for psychologically grounded empathetic AI; ER-EDF provides a scalable, model-agnostic framework that encourages a new direction in empathetic dialogue systems and paves the way for better calibrated empathetic responses.

title: Volumetric Harmonic Field Navigation for Quadrotors
summary: Quadrotor navigation in cluttered 3-D environments requires global guidance while local motion remains subject to collision and motion limits. Harmonic potentials provide dense guidance from a global boundary value problem, but coupling a volumetric harmonic field to constrained physical quadrotor motion remains an open experimental problem. We couple a precomputed volumetric harmonic field with a constrained predictive planner that queries the field at predicted positions instead of extracting a global reference path. In Structured 3-D tests, harmonic guidance yields larger minimum clearance and lower RMS jerk than matched Dijkstra guidance, at the cost of longer paths; the same pattern remains when both methods use the same passage. Long maze tests span routes far beyond one prediction horizon, and Crazyflie trials validate physical execution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first physical quadrotor demonstration of volumetric harmonic field navigation. The results show that globally constructed harmonic guidance can directly support local constrained motion generation on a physical quadrotor.

AI.tldr: Volumetric harmonic fields guide a quadrotor via a constrained predictor, outperforming Dijkstra in clearance and jerk with longer paths; demonstrated in 3-D tests, long mazes, and Crazyflie experiments; first physical demo of volumetric harmonic navigation.
AI.motivation: Enable robust global-to-local navigation for quadrotors in cluttered 3-D spaces by leveraging volumetric harmonic potentials and a planner that respects dynamic constraints.
AI.method: Precompute volumetric harmonic field; use a constrained predictive planner that queries the field at predicted positions instead of extracting a global path; compare to Dijkstra-based guidance; tests include structured 3-D environments, long-maze routes, and physical Crazyflie trials.
AI.result: Harmonic guidance achieves larger minimum clearance and lower RMS jerk than Dijkstra guidance (same passage), at the cost of longer trajectories; success maintained over horizons beyond a single prediction horizon; physical validation on a quadrotor.
AI.conclusion: Globally constructed harmonic guidance can directly support local constrained motion generation on a physical quadrotor.

title: Newton Deep Unfolding for Compressed Sensing
summary: Compressed sensing (CS) reconstructs images from highly limited measurements, but existing deep unfolding methods are typically driven by first-order optimization and weakly exploit the optimization states generated during reconstruction. To address these limitations, we propose a Newton deep unfolding network (NDU-Net), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first deep unfolding framework that leverages second-order optimization for CS reconstruction. Specifically, NDU-Net introduces a Newton update (NU) module to estimate Newton-type update directions and generate optimization states that characterize the current reconstruction process. Furthermore, a Newton-guided multi-scale prior (MP) module is designed to incorporate these optimization states into multi-scale feature restoration, thereby enabling the learned prior to adapt to the current reconstruction stage. Experimental results under different CS ratios confirm that our proposed NDU-Net achieves promising reconstruction performance and exhibits enhanced robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/DNU-Net.

AI.tldr: Introduces NDU-Net, a Newton-based deep unfolding framework for compressed sensing that uses a Newton update module to estimate second-order directions and a Newton-guided multi-scale prior to adapt restoration to the current reconstruction stage, achieving improved robustness across CS ratios.
AI.motivation: Existing deep unfolding methods primarily rely on first-order optimization and do not effectively exploit optimization states during reconstruction, potentially limiting accuracy and robustness in CS tasks.
AI.method: Proposes a Newton update (NU) module to estimate Newton-type update directions, generating optimization states; introduces a Newton-guided multi-scale prior (MP) module that uses these states to guide multi-scale feature restoration, enabling the prior to adapt to the reconstruction stage.
AI.result: Experimental results across varying compressed sensing ratios show improved reconstruction performance and enhanced robustness compared to baseline methods; a public code implementation is provided.
AI.conclusion: NDU-Net demonstrates that incorporating second-order optimization information via Newton-based updates and state-aware priors can enhance CS reconstruction quality and robustness, establishing a new direction for deep unfolding methods.

title: Know When to Stop, Where to Restart: Accelerating Multi-Turn Agentic On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a standard approach for transferring capabilities from large teachers to compact students. Its cost, however, is dominated by autoregressive student rollouts and scales poorly in multi-turn agentic settings. Existing acceleration methods truncate or relocate the supervision signal according to fixed, offline budgets, despite substantial variation in teacher-signal reliability both within and across trajectories. Our empirical analysis on $τ^2$-bench reveals a clear structure in this variation: informative supervision is concentrated in the prefix of each turn, and, most importantly for multi-turn agentic training, the cross-turn loss of teacher endorsement is temporally locked to the student's first erroneous action rather than accumulating gradually over turns. Building on these findings, we propose STRIDE (Stop-and-Restart on-policy Distillation acceleration), which combines two complementary techniques: adaptive early stopping, which terminates a rollout once the cumulative teacher log-probability falls below an out-of-distribution threshold, and a prefix buffer, which caches high-quality prefixes and restarts generation at the weakest correct turn. Together, these mechanisms induce a data-driven curriculum that progressively extends coverage to later turns. On $τ^2$-bench retail, our method matches full-trajectory OPD and exceeds the 30B teacher at a $3.73\times$ speedup, surpasses the baseline itself at $2.34\times$, and retains a $4.51\times$ speedup under cross-domain multi-teacher training. As a supplementary generalization test beyond the agentic setting, STRIDE outperforms full OPD on AIME 2025 at a $5.10\times$ speedup and on AIME 2024 at a $3.08\times$ speedup; averaged across the two evaluations, both fixed-budget truncation baselines remain below full OPD.

AI.tldr: STRIDE accelerates on-policy distillation by combining adaptive early stopping with a prefix buffer, creating a data-driven curriculum that expands coverage across turns. It matches full OPD performance while delivering substantial speedups across multi-turn and cross-domain tasks.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation remains costly due to autoregressive rollouts; fixed offline budgets for acceleration fail to account for variable teacher-signal reliability within and across trajectories. There is a systematic structure in supervisory signal: high-quality information concentrates in the prefix of each turn, and cross-turn loss aligns with the first incorrect action rather than accumulating over turns.
AI.method: STRIDE integrates two components: (1) adaptive early stopping that terminates rollouts when the cumulative teacher log-probability falls below an out-of-distribution threshold, and (2) a prefix buffer that caches high-quality prefixes and restarts generation at the weakest correct turn. Together, they form a data-driven curriculum that gradually extends coverage to later turns.
AI.result: On τ^2-bench retail, STRIDE matches full OPD and achieves 3.73× speedup over the 30B teacher; it surpasses the baseline at 2.34× and retains 4.51× speedup under cross-domain multi-teacher training. Generalization tests show STRIDE outperforming full OPD on AIME 2025 (5.10×) and AIME 2024 (3.08×); averaged across tasks, fixed-budget truncation baselines stay below full OPD.
AI.conclusion: STRIDE provides a principled, data-driven acceleration for on-policy distillation that preserves performance while delivering substantial speedups, including in cross-domain and generalization settings.

title: OpenAI4S: Code as Action, Science as Sessions
