summary: AI co-scientists could accelerate computational research, but over a long-running study the workflow also has to stay inspectable, resumable and reproducible, which requires persistent computational state and provenance. Here we present OpenAI4S, an open-source scientific research agent built around the principle of \emph{Code as Action, Science as Sessions}. OpenAI4S combines a persistent computing runtime with research-session management: orchestration is handled through structured tool calls, while scientific actions are represented as complete code cells executed in persistent Python and R kernels. An append-only Action Ledger, per-cell execution records, versioned artifacts, environment records, and workspace checkpoints preserve how results were produced and support session recovery, branching, and extension. Configurable sandboxing, permission controls, and code and trajectory screening provide complementary safeguards. We evaluate OpenAI4S on 36 research scenarios spanning retrosynthesis, molecular dynamics, protein binder design, protein mutation, catalyst screening, and mineral spectroscopy, measuring scientific task accuracy, workflow completeness, and reproducibility of the resulting repositories. OpenAI4S achieves an overall score of 7.83, compared with 5.7--6.4 for a general-purpose coding harness evaluated with three frontier models, with the largest gains on long-horizon and computation-intensive workflows. These results suggest that integrating persistent execution with session-level provenance can improve the reliability of AI-assisted scientific workflows. Environment specification and full rerunnability remain weak for every evaluated system, ours included, so reproducibility is still an open problem for scientific agents. The system is available under the MIT license at \href{https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}{github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/OpenAI4S}.

AI.tldr: OpenAI4S enables persistent, session-aware AI-driven scientific workﬂows with per-cell execution, provenance, and sandboxed governance; it outperforms general-purpose coding harnesses on long-horizon, compute-intensive tasks, but reproducibility and environment replay remain weak.
AI.motivation: To address the need for inspectable, resumable, and reproducible AI-assisted computational research by combining persistent execution with session-level provenance and structured tool-driven orchestration.
AI.method: A software stack built around Code as Action and Science as Sessions, featuring persistent Python/R kernels, per-cell execution, an append-only Action Ledger, versioned artifacts, environment records, workspace checkpoints, sandboxing and access controls, and trajectory screening; evaluation on 36 tasks across chemistry and materials domains with comparisons to general-purpose models.
AI.result: OpenAI4S achieves an overall scoring of 7.83, outperforming a general-purpose coding harness (scores 5.7–6.4). Greatest gains observed on long-horizon, computation-intensive workflows; environment specification and full rerunnability remain weak.
AI.conclusion: Persistent execution with session-level provenance can improve reliability of AI-assisted scientific workflows, but reproducibility challenges persist; the system is open-source under MIT license.

title: Continuous Manifold-Decomposed Impedance Retargeting for Contact-Rich Imitation Learning
summary: CMDIR extends Manifold-Decomposed Impedance Retargeting (MDIR) to transform fixed-impedance demonstrations into continuous variable-impedance controllers, which can also serve as structured supervision for imitation learning. Continuous Task-Manifold Impedance Representation (TMIR) pairs an evolving task frame with controller instructions. Demo-relative Compromise dynamics retain moving-basis transport and control/physical metric mismatch, yielding displacement, reaction-impulse, and perturbation-sensitivity criteria. Quality-to-Fast automatically compiles a solver structure from development paths within a predefined finite space, re-instantiates that structure for each demonstration, and certifies the resulting candidate by multi-resolution evaluation. Across 225 retargeted-controller trials in three real contact tasks, full CMDIR improves mean task-proxy retention and reduces mean pose deviation, force fluctuation, and peak force relative to discrete MDIR. FastMPO achieves a $5.8$--$9.4\times$ speedup over C-MPO with comparable closed-loop outcomes. Downstream experiments demonstrate learnability of the complete TMIR supervision interface; lower force fluctuation and peak force are observed among successful executions, while completion reliability remains uneven across tasks and environments.

AI.tldr: CMDIR converts fixed-impedance demonstrations into continuous variable-impedance controllers via MDIR; TMIR couples a dynamic task frame with controller instructions; introduces Demo-relative Compromise dynamics and a Quality-to-Fast solver; empirically improves retargeting performance (225 trials, real contact tasks), speeds up planning (FastMPO), and demonstrates learnability of the TMIR supervision interface with task-dependent reliability.
AI.motivation: Bridge fixed-impedance demonstrations to continuous-variable impedance control and provide structured supervision for imitation learning in contact-rich manipulation; improve stability, safety, and performance by aligning dynamic impedance with evolving task frames.
AI.method: Extend MDIR to CMDIR for continuous impedance retargeting; introduce TMIR combining evolving task frame with controller instructions; formulate Demo-relative Compromise dynamics to handle transport, metric mismatch, and perturbations; implement a Quality-to-Fast solver to generate and certify retargeted controller structures from a finite development space; evaluate on 225 trials across three real tasks; compare with discrete MDIR and C-MPO; assess downstream learnability of TMIR supervision.
AI.result: CMDIR yields higher mean task-proxy retention and reduces mean pose deviation, force fluctuation, and peak force compared with discrete MDIR. FastMPO achieves 5.8–9.4× speedup over C-MPO with comparable closed-loop performance. Downstream tests show TMIR supervision is learnable; successful executions exhibit lower force fluctuations and peak forces, though completion reliability varies by task and environment.
AI.conclusion: CMDIR and TMIR jointly enable efficient, robust imitation learning for impedance-controlled manipulation, offering improved retargeting performance, faster planning, and a learnable supervision interface; some tasks remain challenging with variable reliability across settings.

title: A Generative AI Integrated Multimodal Framework for Low-Latency Multi-Camera Person Re-Identification
comment: Presented at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Responsible Artificial Intelligence (IRAI)
summary:
Person re-identification (ReID) is essential for multi-camera surveillance and tracking, yet remains difficult due to viewpoint and illumination changes, occlusion, background clutter, and low resolution imagery. We propose a generative AI integrated multimodal ReID framework designed explicitly for robustness under missing cues and low latency deployment. The key idea is a cost aware early-exit cascade that prioritizes inexpensive, high confidence evidence and only triggers expensive modalities for ambiguous cases.
  Our system integrates (i) global visual embeddings from segmented person regions, (ii) automatically generated fine grained semantic attribute descriptions generated by vision-language models (VLMs), and (iii) optional facial embeddings when face observations are reliable. To optimize the balance between accuracy and latency, we use a cost aware early-exit cascade instead of fusing all modalities. Specifically, we first inspect the top-k retrieval results to determine whether the query is unambiguous. If the best match is clearly separated from the remaining candidates, we stop early and return the result to minimize latency; in ambiguous cases, we keep multiple hypotheses and invoke additional modalities (face/semantic) with adaptive reliability weighting to refine the decision.
  We report person re-identification performance using mAP and Rank-1 accuracy on the Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-reID benchmarks. The proposed adaptive early-exit cascade resolves 60.7% of DukeMTMC-reID queries and 68.4% of Market-1501 queries without invoking semantic reasoning, reducing computational overhead while maintaining competitive retrieval performance.

AI.tldr: A multimodal, cost-aware early-exit ReID framework that uses global visual embeddings, VLM-generated semantic attributes, and optional facial embeddings, with a cascade that stops when unambiguous to save latency. It reports mAP and Rank-1 on Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-reID, claiming substantial bypass of semantic reasoning for many queries (≈60-68%).
AI.motivation: Address core challenges in person re-identification (viewpoint/illumination changes, occlusion, background clutter, low resolution) while achieving low-latency inference and robustness to missing cues by avoiding unnecessary use of expensive modalities.
AI.method: A generative AI integrated multimodal ReID framework with a cost-aware early-exit cascade. It combines (i) global embeddings from segmented regions, (ii) VLM-generated fine-grained semantic attribute descriptions, and (iii) optional facial embeddings when reliable. Instead of fusing all modalities, the system checks top-k retrieval results; if the best match is clearly separated, it returns early; otherwise, it employs additional modalities with adaptive weighting to refine results.
AI.result: The approach yields competitive retrieval performance (measured by mAP and Rank-1) on Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-reID and significantly reduces computation by resolving a large portion of queries without invoking semantic reasoning: 60.7% on DukeMTMC-reID and 68.4% on Market-1501.
AI.conclusion: An adaptive, cost-aware early-exit cascade can maintain competitive ReID accuracy while reducing latency and computation by selectively invoking expensive modalities; however performance depends on the ambiguity threshold and quality of generated semantic attributes and facial cues.

title: Symmetries and Singularities
summary: Deep neural networks are highly over-parameterized, and different parameter values represent the same predictive function. This makes their effective complexity difficult to measure using only the number of parameters or the rank of the Hessian. Singular Learning Theory addresses this issue through the local learning coefficient (LLC), which characterizes the effective complexity of a model near a given solution. Existing methods for estimating the LLC often rely on posterior sampling, which can be computationally expensive for large neural networks. This makes accurate LLC estimation difficult at scale. In this work, we use known structures in the model to simplify the analysis and make LLC estimation more tractable. Specifically, we study the LLC of a graph attention model by exploiting symmetries in both the graph structure and the attention parameters. An analytic framework through a teacher--student setting, and explicit LLC estimates after considering the symmetry--induced degeneracies are developed.

AI.tldr: Analytic estimation of the local learning coefficient (LLC) for a graph attention model by exploiting symmetry to reduce degeneracies and avoid heavy posterior sampling.
AI.motivation: LLC quantifies effective model complexity in Singular Learning Theory; existing estimation relies on costly posterior sampling; need scalable LLC estimation for over-parameterized neural networks.
AI.method: Analyze LLC in a teacher-student setting; identify symmetry-induced degeneracies in graph structure and attention parameters; derive analytic expressions for LLC using symmetry.
AI.result: Explicit LLC estimates derived; symmetry exploitation yields tractable, closed-form or simplified expressions for the LLC in the considered model.
AI.conclusion: Structural symmetry enables scalable, accurate LLC estimation for graph attention models, improving understanding of effective complexity without expensive sampling.

title: Medical Knowledge Simplification for Patients in the Era of LLMs: A Case Study on Diabetes
summary: Complex medical information is often difficult for patients to understand, making effective medical knowledge simplification essential for improving patient comprehension, informed decision-making, and health outcomes. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide a promising approach for simplifying complex medical information into patient-friendly language; however, their effectiveness in real-world patient education remains insufficiently explored through human evaluation. To investigate their practical effectiveness, this paper presents a case study on diabetes knowledge simplification through the implementation and evaluation of MediClear, an LLM-based medical knowledge simplification system enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Public diabetes-related articles from Diabetes Australia, WHO, American Diabetes Association (ADA), NIDDK, and AIHW are indexed in the RAG knowledge base to retrieve clinically grounded information, which is then simplified by the LLM into accessible patient explanations. We evaluate the generated responses using standard readability metrics, including the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), and conduct a human study involving 10 participants. Results show that MediClear consistently reduces the reading level of generated responses to the recommended patient literacy range while achieving high user satisfaction and willingness for future use. This case study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to improve the accessibility of medical knowledge for patient education.

AI.tldr: MediClear, an LLM-based knowledge-simplification system with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), reduces diabetes information to patient-friendly language; evaluated with FKGL and 10 participants, achieving readable outputs and high user satisfaction.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in patient comprehension of complex medical information and the limited real-world evaluation of LLM-based simplification; improve patient education outcomes.
AI.method: Implement MediClear with a RAG knowledge base built from Diabetes Australia, WHO, ADA, NIDDK, AIHW; generate simplified patient explanations; assess readability with FKGL and conduct a small human study (n=10) measuring satisfaction and willingness to reuse.
AI.result: FKGL scores lowered into the recommended patient literacy range; high user satisfaction and willingness to reuse; indicates potential real-world impact.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based medical knowledge simplification with RAG can enhance accessibility of medical information for patient education; case study supports feasibility, though broader evaluation needed.

title: Bench2Dex: Benchmarking Visuo-Tactile Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across Dexterous Hands
summary: Tactile sensing provides contact information that can be difficult to infer from vision alone, but tactile hardware for dexterous hands has not converged to a common design. Dexterous hands differ in finger structure, contact surfaces, and sensor layouts, while simulated tactile signals still differ from measurements produced by physical sensors. These factors make it difficult to study visuo-tactile manipulation across diverse dexterous hands within a consistent experimental setting. We present Bench2Dex, a simulation benchmark for visuo-tactile bimanual manipulation across 12 dexterous hands. We adapt existing robot models with a shared simulated tactile interface that converts local contact geometry into image-like tactile observations. The interface provides a consistent observation format across different hand morphologies without attempting to reproduce the output of a specific physical tactile sensor. Bench2Dex includes 26 bimanual manipulation tasks that involve tool use, articulated-object interaction, and multi-stage manipulation, together with about 1.3K human-teleoperated demonstrations. The benchmark provides synchronized visual, tactile, proprioceptive, action, and object-state observations, together with executable task metrics. For robustness, we group seven perturbation types into invariance axis, where the correct action does not change, and equivariance axis, where the correct action changes together with the perturbation. We evaluate ACT, Diffusion Policy, pi0.5, and GR00T N1.5 on Bench2Dex and report their performance and failure modes. Bench2Dex is meant as a platform for studying visuo-tactile learning across dexterous hands. It does not assume that simulated tactile observations can replace real tactile sensing; it offers a shared setting for algorithm development while tactile hardware and simulation models are still evolving.

AI.tldr: Bench2Dex: a unified simulation benchmark for visuo-tactile manipulation across 12 dexterous hands, with 26 bimanual tasks, synchronized multi-modal data, and perturbation-based robustness evaluation.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation in tactile sensing hardware and simulation, enabling consistent visuo-tactile learning research across diverse hand morphologies.
AI.method: Adapt existing robot models with a shared tactile interface that maps local contact geometry to image-like tactile observations; provide 26 tasks, ~1.3k human teleoperation demonstrations; synchronize visual, tactile, proprioceptive, action, and object-state data; define seven perturbations along invariance and equivariance axes; evaluate multiple policies.
AI.result: Demonstrates benchmark viability by reporting performance and failure modes of ACT, Diffusion Policy, pi0.5, and GR00T N1.5; shows consistent observation format across hands and facilitates studying visuo-tactile learning, though not aiming to replicate a specific tactile sensor output.
AI.conclusion: Bench2Dex provides a platform for visuo-tactile learning across dexterous hands, enabling algorithm development with a shared setting while acknowledging that simulated tactile observations are not a substitute for real hardware; tactile models and hardware remain evolving.

title: Lightweight Generalized DeepFake Face Detection with WAVIE: Wavelet Augmented Vision Intermediate Embeddings
comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC) 2026
summary:
Deepfake detection systems often exhibit significant performance degradation when deployed on unseen manipulation methods, limiting their reliability in real-world multimedia environments. This lack of generalization poses critical challenges for misinformation mitigation, digital forensics, and human-centric AI systems. Existing detectors perform well on the forgery methods they are trained on, but their accuracy drops sharply on unseen pipelines. To bridge this generalization gap, we propose WAVIE (Wavelet Augmented Vision Intermediate Embeddings), an end-to-end architecture that combines complementary spatial and frequency cues on top of a frozen CLIP backbone. WAVIE projects intermediate transformer embeddings through a lightweight learnable module, applies a three-level Daubechies-6 (db6) discrete wavelet transform (DWT), refines the low-frequency branch while preserving the high-frequency branch, reconstructs the feature via inverse DWT, and performs classification.
  Trained only on FaceForensics++, WAVIE achieves AUROC = 0.852 on Celeb-DF-v1, 0.852 on Celeb-DF-v2 and 0.831 on WildDeepFake (WDF) at the frame level, outperforming several state-of-the-art generalization baselines. Extensive ablation studies confirm the importance of both the wavelet module and the intermediate-feature aggregation for cross-dataset performance, highlighting the necessity of jointly leveraging spatial and frequency domains. These results position WAVIE as a strong baseline for deepfake detection in the wild.

AI.tldr: WAVIE uses a wavelet-augmented intermediate feature module atop a frozen CLIP backbone to improve deepfake detection generalization to unseen manipulation methods; it shows cross-dataset AUROC around 0.85 on Celeb-DF variants and 0.831 on WildDeepFake, outperforming several generalization baselines; ablations validate the value of combining spatial and frequency cues via Daubechies-6 DWT.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors typically generalize poorly to unseen manipulation pipelines, hindering real-world reliability for misinformation mitigation and digital forensics. A method that bridges this generalization gap by leveraging both spatial and frequency information can improve robustness.
AI.method: An end-to-end WAVIE architecture that freezes a CLIP backbone and projects intermediate transformer embeddings through a lightweight module, applies a three-level Daubechies-6 DWT to the features, refines the low-frequency branch while preserving high-frequency information, reconstructs via inverse DWT, and performs classification. Training is performed solely on FaceForensics++.
AI.result: Frame-level AUROC: Celeb-DF-v1 0.852, Celeb-DF-v2 0.852, WildDeepFake 0.831. WAVIE outperforms several state-of-the-art generalization baselines. Ablations show the wavelet module and intermediate-feature aggregation are essential for cross-dataset performance.
AI.conclusion: WAVIE provides a strong baseline for deepfake detection in the wild by jointly leveraging spatial and frequency cues; the wavelet-based intermediate embedding augmentation is effective for generalization to unseen manipulation pipelines.

title: WaterKron and FlipFlop Hessian: Information-Theoretically Grounded Quantization with Kronecker-factored Hessians
summary: How should a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation be chosen for post-training quantization? We address this question through WaterKron, which combines two-sided GPTQ with row- and column-dependent waterfilling scales and entropy coding. We derive its high-rate distortion with respect to the full Hessian using an explicit Kronecker-Hessian mismatch factor $Φ$. This factor quantifies the asymptotic distortion penalty due to the Kronecker Hessian approximation and provides a criterion for selecting the factors optimally. Minimizing $Φ$ leads to a Gaussian covariance-fitting problem with classical ``flip-flop'' updates. We thus give a rate-distortion justification for using the resulting FlipFlop Hessian in quantization. We evaluate it empirically, finding that the FlipFlop Hessian consistently improves KL divergence and perplexity over input-only, marginal, and Frobenius-based Hessian choices.

AI.tldr: WaterKron combines two-sided GPTQ with row/column-dependent waterfilling and entropy coding to optimize Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations for post-training quantization; it introduces a mismatch factor Φ that enables a rate-distortion-based selection (FlipFlop Hessian) via Gaussian covariance fitting; empirically better than other Hessian choices.
AI.motivation: To reduce quantization distortion in post-training quantization by selecting an effective Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation that minimizes a distortion measure under rate constraints.
AI.method: Derive high-rate distortion with respect to the full Hessian using a Kronecker-Hessian mismatch factor Φ; optimize Φ by solving a Gaussian covariance-fitting problem with flip-flop updates, yielding the FlipFlop Hessian; combine with row/column waterfilling scales and entropy coding within WaterKron.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows FlipFlop Hessian improves KL divergence and perplexity over input-only, marginal, and Frobenius-based Hessian baselines.
AI.conclusion: Provides a rate-distortion justification for the FlipFlop Hessian in post-training quantization and a principled method to select Kronecker factors, with practical performance gains.

title: HazardAuditor: From Executable Threats to Safer Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents increasingly interact with browsers, terminals, file systems, and external services, introducing safety risks that emerge through runtime behavior rather than generated content alone. Existing guard models target static prompts and responses and are poorly suited to agent execution; existing executable safety platforms produce evaluation verdicts rather than the normalized supervision a guard model needs to learn across heterogeneous agent frameworks. We introduce HazardAuditor, an execution-grounded framework that closes both gaps. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous agents (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and OpenClaw) in controlled environments and normalizes their interactions into a canonical event representation for cross-framework supervision. We further observe that token-level post-training objectives create a structural mismatch for generative guards, causing longer rationales to dominate gradient updates. Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO) addresses this by converting deterministic safety outcomes into sequence-level advantages and normalizing rationale and verdict regions, making the safety decision the effective unit of optimization. Across multiple benchmarks and heterogeneous computer-use systems, HazardAuditor improves accuracy by up to 16.5 percentage points over the strongest prior guard. Code, models, and evaluation artifacts will be available at https://yunhao-feng.github.io/HazardAuditor/.

AI.tldr: HazardAuditor is an execution-grounded guard framework that normalizes heterogeneous agent interactions for cross-framework supervision and uses GuardPO to optimize sequence-level safety decisions, achieving up to 16.5 percentage points accuracy gains over prior guards.
AI.motivation: Existing guard models focus on static prompts/responses and fail to address safety during real-time agent execution across diverse environments; current evaluation platforms yield verdicts rather than normalized supervision suitable for learning guards across frameworks.
AI.method: Run diverse agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw) in controlled environments, normalize their runtime interactions into a canonical event representation, and apply Guard Policy Optimization (GuardPO) to convert deterministic safety outcomes into sequence-level advantages and normalize rationale and verdict regions, making safety decisions the optimization unit.
AI.result: HazardAuditor achieves up to 16.5 percentage-point accuracy improvement over the strongest prior guard across multiple benchmarks and heterogeneous computer-use systems; code, models, and artifacts will be released at the stated URL.
AI.conclusion: An execution-grounded, cross-framework guard framework that aligns training objectives with real-world safety decisions, improving robustness of guard models across diverse agent platforms.

title: JEPLO: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for LiDAR-Based Legged Locomotion
summary: Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) remains less explored than RGB-D sensing for perceptive legged locomotion, and existing LiDAR-based approaches often rely on explicit mapping. We present JEPLO (Joint-Embedding Predictive learning for legged LOcomotion), a single-stage learning framework for mapping-free, LiDAR-based perceptive locomotion for legged robots. We introduce a proprio-exteroceptive JEPA (PE-JEPA) world model to learn predictive egocentric terrain representations from onboard observations, including raw LiDAR scans. A concurrent JEPA-teacher-student (CJTS) pipeline is further proposed to train a locomotion policy informed by JEPA latent representations in simulation using deep reinforcement learning with a simple reward formulation. The framework achieves successful sim-to-real transfer, enabling omnidirectional traversal of diverse terrains, including long staircases and high boxes, with lightweight onboard computation. Evaluations demonstrate greater robustness than existing perceptive locomotion frameworks, particularly under degraded perception caused by occlusion, sparsity and noise. Further analysis validates JEPLO's ability to retain task-relevant information under these challenging conditions. We open-source our implementation, experimental datasets, and hardware setup designs https://github.com/ASIG-X/JEPLO.

AI.tldr: Proposes JEPLO, a single-stage, mapping-free LiDAR-based perceptive locomotion framework for legged robots using JEPA-based world modeling (PE-JEPA) and a teacher-student CJTS training pipeline to enable sim-to-real transfer and robust navigation across diverse terrains with degraded perception.
AI.motivation: LiDAR-based perceptive locomotion is underexplored compared to RGB-D sensing; existing LiDAR methods rely on explicit mapping and may falter under occlusion, sparsity, and noise. There is a need for an efficient, mapping-free approach with robust sim-to-real transfer and lightweight onboard computation.
AI.method: PE-JEPA world model learns predictive egocentric terrain representations from onboard observations, including raw LiDAR scans. CJTS (concurrent JEPA-teacher-student) trains a locomotion policy in simulation using deep RL guided by JEPA latent representations. The framework is single-stage, mapping-free, and designed for onboard efficiency, with open-source release.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer enabling omnidirectional traversal of diverse terrains (e.g., long staircases, high boxes) with lightweight onboard computation. Exhibits greater robustness than existing perceptive locomotion methods, particularly under occlusion, sparsity, and noise. Validates that JEPLO preserves task-relevant information under challenging perception conditions.
AI.conclusion: JEPLO shows that joint embedding predictive learning with JEPA latent representations can enable robust, mapping-free LiDAR-based legged locomotion with efficient onboard computation and successful sim-to-real transfer, reducing reliance on explicit environment maps and enhancing resilience to perception degradation.

title: Context-Aware Mutual Learning for Blind Image Inpainting and Beyond
comment: Published in Expert Systems with Applications 268 (2025), Article 126224
summary: Blind image inpainting, aiming to recover contaminated images in the case of unknown masks, is a challenging task. Motivated by the perspective of human vision and knowledge, blind image inpainting can be decomposed into two stages: mask estimation and image inpainting based on the estimated mask. The two-stage idea exhibits evident advantages in enhancing inpainting quality and augmenting the generalization capability of unknown real-world contamination by explicitly employing the estimated mask for image inpainting compared to one-stage scheme. This two-stage idea has also been intuitively implemented. However, existing two-stage methods excessively emphasize the unilateral relationship of mask estimation to image inpainting, and may overlook the mutual relations between them. Specifically, mask estimation can provide more contextual semantics for image inpainting to strengthen the understanding of semantics, and image inpainting can offer more contextual details (e.g., textures and edges) for mask estimation to improve the learning of details. In this work, we propose a novel Context-Aware Mutual Learning (CAML) framework for blind image inpainting that joints mask estimation and image inpainting to mutually exploit contextual information. In the CAML framework, we design the Inpainting-Guided Context-Mutual (IGCM) learner to acquire the complementary contextual details from image inpainting for assisting mask estimation, and the Estimation-Guided Context-Mutual (EGCM) learner to strengthen the understanding of contextual semantics from mask estimation for assisting image inpainting. Ablation studies validate the efficacy of our CAML. Extensive experiments show that our CAML achieves state-of-the-art performance on both blind image inpainting and additional vision tasks, i.e., snow removal, shadow removal, and watermark removal, indicating its superiority.

AI.tldr: CAML jointly learns mask estimation and image inpainting for blind image inpainting through two mutual learners (IGCM and EGCM), achieving state-of-the-art results and better generalization, with applicability to other vision tasks like snow/shadow/watermark removal.
AI.motivation: Two-stage blind image inpainting often treats mask estimation and inpainting unidirectionally. Exploiting mutual contextual information between stages can enhance semantic understanding and texture/detail recovery, improving performance and generalization.
AI.method: Proposes Context-Aware Mutual Learning (CAML) with two mutual learners: Inpainting-Guided Context-Mutual (IGCM) leverages image inpainting to enrich mask estimation, and Estimation-Guided Context-Mutual (EGCM) uses mask estimation to strengthen image inpainting. Joint optimization and iterative mutual guidance to exploit contextual information across stages. Ablation studies and experiments on blind inpainting and related tasks (snow, shadow, watermark removal).
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on blind image inpainting and related tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of mutual context learning; ablations validate the contributions of IGCM and EGCM components.
AI.conclusion: Mutual context mutual learning across mask estimation and inpainting improves semantic understanding and texture/detail reconstruction, leading to better inpainting quality and generalization to realistic contaminations.

title: An immune world model for multiscale forecasting and therapeutic hypothesis generation
summary: Immune therapies act across cell-intrinsic programs, tissue ecosystems, and patient-specific immune states, yet most predictors address these scales separately. We used a governed evolutionary AI Scientist to construct the Immune World Model, an action-conditioned model that learns how interventions move immune states across cellular, tissue, and individual levels. The Immune World Model--building Scientist searched candidate architectures and workflows, and the resulting world model was frozen before independent confirmation. The frozen model generalized to unseen interventions and biological contexts, recovered intervention-specific cellular programs, integrated cell and tissue information to improve ecosystem and patient-response prediction, and forecast unseen perturbation combinations. Immune World Model--guided analysis then combined measured perturbations with cross-axis inference to nominate IL-36$γ$ plus SIRP$α$ inhibition as a complementary-axis therapeutic hypothesis, whereas a governed self-correction audit rejected every screened cytokine pair. The Immune World Model provides a framework for multiscale immune simulation that connects AI Scientist-driven model construction, intervention forecasting, and the generation of prospectively testable therapeutic hypotheses.

AI.tldr: An AI-assisted, multiscale immune model (Immune World Model) that learns to forecast interventions across cellular, tissue, and patient levels, enabling new therapeutic hypotheses while also auditing and filtering out ineffective cytokine pairs.
AI.motivation: To bridge disparate scales in immune prediction by using an AI-driven, governed, evolutionary design process to construct a coherent multiscale world model that can generalize to unseen perturbations and contexts.
AI.method: Developed the Immune World Model via a governed evolutionary AI Scientist to search architectures/workflows for an action-conditioned, multiscale immune simulator. The model was frozen after construction and validated on unseen interventions/contexts. It integrates cellular programs with tissue and ecosystem information to predict perturbation outcomes and patient responses, and to forecast novel perturbations.
AI.result: The frozen World Model generalized to unseen interventions and contexts, recovered intervention-specific cellular programs, improved cross-scale prediction, and forecasted unseen perturbation combinations. Guided analyses nominated IL-36γ plus SIRPα inhibition as a therapeutic hypothesis, while a governance audit rejected all screened cytokine pairs.
AI.conclusion: The Immune World Model offers a scalable framework for multiscale immune simulation, combining AI scientist-driven model construction, intervention forecasting, and generation of testable, prospectively verifiable therapeutic hypotheses.

title: T-LoopFormer: Token-Level Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning With Dynamic Routing
summary: Looped Transformers have recently demonstrated strong performance in both reasoning and language tasks by reusing a shared set of parameters across multiple iterations, achieving parameter efficiency without sacrificing representational power. Besides, looped Transformers perform inference directly in the latent space (latent reasoning) to reduce the number of tokens consumed during inference, thereby achieving improved sample efficiency. However, these models typically apply a fixed recursion depth uniformly to every token, leading to suboptimal compute allocation and leaving significant efficiency gains on the table. In this work, we propose \textbf{dynamic token-choice routing} for looped transformers, enabling each token to adaptively determine its own number of loop iterations based on its hidden state. We use a dynamic router to decide whether a token should continue recursing or exit early, allowing simple tokens to bypass unnecessary computation while hard tokens receive deeper processing. To ensure that this adaptive mechanism does not compromise decoding efficiency, we further introduce recursion-wise KV caching, which maintains an independent key-value cache for each recursion loop. This design ensures that tokens at different depths only attend to their corresponding cached states, effectively eliminating redundant computations for exited tokens and enabling fast autoregressive decoding. Extensive experiments show that T-LoopFormer reaches the sota performance under the same parameters on PPL and 10 zero-shot reasoning tasks, even surpassing the base model at 24x FLOPs and our model could reach the lowest inference latency, which validate the effectiveness of token-choice router and recursion-wise KV cache. Code: https://github.com/YuMingQian1234/T-LoopFormer.

AI.tldr: Adaptive per-token recursion in looped transformers via dynamic routing and per-depth KV caching yields efficient latent reasoning with maintained or improved performance.
AI.motivation: Fix compute inefficiency in fixed-depth looped transformers by allocating compute on a per-token basis, enabling cheap tokens to exit early and hard tokens to recurse deeper.
AI.method: Introduce a dynamic token-choice router that decides, for each token at each loop, whether to continue recursion or exit; implement recursion-wise KV caches so each depth has its own key/value cache, ensuring tokens only attend to relevant cached states and enabling fast autoregressive decoding.
AI.result: State-of-the-art or competitive performance under the same parameter count on perplexity (PPL) and 10 zero-shot reasoning tasks; significant FLOPs reduction (up to 24x) with maintained or improved accuracy; lower inference latency due to efficient decoding.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic token-choice routing combined with recursion-wise KV caching can substantially improve efficiency of looped transformers without sacrificing performance, making latent reasoning more practical for real-time or resource-constrained settings; code released.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Sparse Refinement for Action Chunking Transformer Policies
summary: Learning chunk-based visuomotor policies for long-horizon robot manipulation remains challenging. Recent action-chunking methods have shown promising performance by predicting temporally extended action sequences. However, their failures are often dominated by prediction errors at a small number of critical timesteps rather than uniformly poor predictions across the entire action chunk, making uniform refinement inefficient and insufficiently targeted. To address this bottleneck, we propose Uncertainty-Guided Refinement (UGR), a sparse refinement framework for chunk-based visuomotor policies. Specifically, UGR follows a coarse-to-refine design: it first predicts a full action chunk, estimates per-step temporal uncertainty from the coarse hidden states, and applies residual correction only to the most uncertain timesteps selected by a binary mask. The uncertainty branch is decoupled from the coarse action predictor, enabling clean attribution of the refinement gains to uncertainty-guided correction rather than additional predictor capacity. Extensive experiments on five dual-arm manipulation tasks from the RoboTwin benchmark show that UGR achieves the best success rate on four tasks, improves over the ACT baseline by up to 13% absolute, and outperforms both full-chunk and position-agnostic block refinement in ablation studies.

AI.tldr: Uncertainty-Guided Refinement (UGR) targets sparse residual corrections at the most uncertain timesteps within a predicted action chunk, improving chunk-based visuomotor policies for long-horizon manipulation.
AI.motivation: Prediction errors in chunk-based actions are concentrated at a few critical timesteps, making uniform refinement inefficient; a targeted, uncertainty-driven approach is needed.
AI.method: Coarse-to-refine pipeline: first predict a full action chunk, estimate per-step temporal uncertainty from coarse hidden states, then apply residual corrections only to the most uncertain timesteps via a binary mask. The uncertainty branch is decoupled from the coarse action predictor to enable clear attribution of gains to uncertainty-guided refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated on five dual-arm RoboTwin tasks; UGR achieves best success rate on four tasks, improves ACT baseline by up to 13 percentage points, and outperforms full-chunk and position-agnostic block refinement in ablations.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-guided sparse refinement effectively concentrates corrective effort on critical moments, enabling stronger performance gains for chunk-based visuomotor policies and providing clearer attribution of improvements to uncertainty-driven refinement.

title: From Visual Attribution to Clinical Reasoning: Explainable Parkinson's Disease Screening from Hand-Drawn Patterns
summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) manifests early neuromotor impairments that become observable in controlled hand-drawn patterns such as spirals and meanders, where tremor-induced oscillations, stroke irregularity, and curvature instability reflect underlying motor degradation. In this work, we present an explainable framework for PD screening from offline hand-drawn patterns that integrates discriminative visual modeling with clinically grounded reasoning. The predictive model captures distributed structural distortions and fine-grained texture variations. It is evaluated under subject-disjoint protocols to ensure reliable generalization. To move beyond black-box classification, we introduce a multi-stage explainability pipeline that combines visual attribution with structured symptom abstraction. Salient regions are identified using attention- and gradient-based localization, followed by extraction of clinically meaningful motor descriptors quantifying contour roughness, curvature irregularity, stroke variability, and tremor-frequency energy. These descriptors are subsequently translated into coherent clinical rationales through a language-based reasoning module, linking model evidence to established PD symptomatology. By bridging visual attribution and clinical interpretation, the proposed framework advances interpretable document intelligence for neurological screening using hand-drawn patterns. Experimental results on publicly available Parkinson's disease handwriting datasets demonstrate competitive predictive performance and clinically consistent explanations.

AI.tldr: An explainable, multi-stage framework for PD screening from offline hand-drawn patterns that links visual model cues to clinical symptoms via descriptors and a language-based rationale, with subject-disjoint evaluation and competitive results.
AI.motivation: To enable interpretable PD screening from handwriting patterns by integrating discriminative visual features with clinically grounded reasoning, moving beyond black-box classifiers.
AI.method: A multi-stage pipeline: (1) discriminative visual modeling with attention/gradients to identify salient regions; (2) extract motor descriptors: contour roughness, curvature irregularity, stroke variability, tremor-energy; (3) language-based reasoning module translating descriptors into clinical rationales; (4) subject-disjoint evaluation on public datasets.
AI.result: Competitive predictive performance and clinically consistent explanations on PD handwriting datasets.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges visual attribution and clinical interpretation, advancing interpretable screening from handwriting; demonstrates potential for interpretable document intelligence in neurology.

title: GRPO-QM: Target Preserving Exploration for Quantum Tomography
summary: Reward-based learning can alter the very posterior distribution that scientific inference aims to estimate. GRPO-QM sidesteps this by learning only an exploration strategy for a stated quantum-tomography posterior: a group-relative policy chooses among reversible physical moves, and an exact Metropolis correction ensures the posterior remains stationary once the policy is fixed. We then examine what learning contributes beyond physical proposal mechanisms and prior knowledge. Reconstruction comparisons suggest that most of the gains over the tested flows come from those two components rather than from learning itself, and a closed-form counterexample explains why: a reward tied to accepted motion can increase even when a physical observable remains highly correlated. Reward comparisons that control for initialization also show that aggregating across posteriors can invert the ranking that a reward implies within any single posterior. Lastly, on 45 enumerated posteriors with three training seeds each, exact and sampled gradients of the same trajectory objective reduce mean physical estimation variance by $12.63\%$ and $6.32\%$ relative to a tuned mixture, while averaging the trajectory score without rescaling its penalty yields only $0.43\%$. This indicates that objective scaling accounts for part of the disparity between sampled and exact training. The regained benefit is concentrated at four shots and flips sign at sixteen, so these exact, visible-bank diagnostics identify a concrete, reproducible failure mode in sampled training, the objective-scaling fix that addresses part of it, and the remaining gap.

AI.tldr: Reward-based learning in quantum tomography largely derives its gains from exploration strategy and existing physical priors, not the learning itself. GRPO-QM uses a group-relative policy with an exact Metropolis correction to keep the posterior stationary, then analyzes what learning contributes. Key findings show most improvements stem from the proposal mechanism and priors; rewards can mislead via correlations and aggregation across posteriors can invert single-posterior rankings. Exact vs. sampled gradients reduce estimation variance substantially, but the benefit depends on objective scaling and training regime, with a reproducible failure mode in sampled training that a scaling fix addresses partially.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the contribution of learning from the underlying physical proposal mechanism and prior knowledge in reward-based optimization for quantum-state tomography, and to identify when and how learning improves posterior estimation variance.
AI.method: Introduce GRPO-QM: a group-relative exploration policy over reversible quantum moves with an exact Metropolis correction to preserve the stated posterior. Systematically compare reconstruction performance, variance reduction, and sensitivity to objective scaling across many posteriors (45 posteriors, 3 seeds each) using exact and sampled gradients of a trajectory objective, and test the effects of aggregating posteriors and different shot counts.
AI.result: Most gains over baseline flows arise from the exploration and prior knowledge rather than from learning itself. A closed-form counterexample shows reward tied to accepted motion can increase despite high correlation of a physical observable. Aggregating across posteriors can invert reward-ranked rankings within a single posterior. Exact and sampled gradients reduce mean physical estimation variance by 12.63% and 6.32% relative to a tuned mixture; simply averaging the trajectory score without rescaling penalties yields only 0.43%. Objective scaling accounts for part of the disparity between training regimes, with benefits concentrated at four shots and flipping sign by sixteen shots; identifies a concrete, reproducible failure mode in sampled training and a partial objective-scaling fix.
AI.conclusion: Reward shaping and aggregation effects dominate performance; learning provides limited additional gains beyond the proposal mechanism and priors. Proper objective scaling and awareness of cross-posterior aggregation effects are essential to avoid misinterpretation of learning gains; a detected failure mode in sampled training is addressable but leaves residual gaps requiring further study.

title: STHMoE: Hypergraph-Enhanced Heterogeneous Dependency Coordination for LLM-Based Urban Traffic Data Forecasting
summary: Spatio-temporal traffic forecasting is a fundamental big data analytics task for intelligent transportation systems, where massive urban sensor streams exhibit heterogeneous, non-stationary, and structurally dynamic patterns. Although recent deep learning and large language model (LLM)-based methods have advanced traffic forecasting, they often remain temporally centered and lack effective coordination of temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural cues under evolving traffic regimes. To address this heterogeneous dependency coordination problem, we propose STHMoE, a Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-Enhanced Mixture of Experts framework for urban traffic data forecasting. STHMoE decouples traffic dynamics into frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, and higher-order spatial representations, which are modeled by prompt-guided heterogeneous experts built upon a partially frozen LLM backbone. The first three experts leverage domain-specific statistical prompts, while the higher-order spatio expert uses a structural placeholder prompt and obtains dependency information from an adaptive hypergraph module. To capture evolving spatial structures in traffic data,, STHMoE jointly learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without predefined topologies. An entropy-aware MoE router with coefficient-of-variation load balancing adaptively fuses expert outputs while improving expert utilization and routing confidence. Experiments on 10 real-world traffic benchmarks show that STHMoE achieves competitive performance against temporal, spatio-temporal graph, and LLM-based baselines.

AI.tldr: STHMoE is a spatio-temporal forecasting framework that combines a mixture-of-experts with an adaptive hypergraph, leveraging a partially frozen LLM backbone to decouple traffic dynamics across frequency, time, space, and higher-order structures, and uses an entropy-aware router to fuse expert outputs.
AI.motivation: Traffic data are heterogeneous, non-stationary, and dynamically evolving. Existing temporal-centric DL/LLM methods struggle to coordinate temporal, spectral, pairwise spatial, and higher-order structural cues under changing traffic regimes.
AI.method: STHMoE decouples dynamics into four representations (frequency-domain, time-domain, spatio-domain, higher-order spatial). It uses prompt-guided heterogeneous experts built on a partially frozen LLM backbone: three domain-specific statistical prompts and a higher-order spatio expert with a structural placeholder prompt fed by an adaptive hypergraph module. The model learns first-order graph dependencies and higher-order group interactions without predefined topology, and employs an entropy-aware mixture-of-experts router with coefficient-of-variation load balancing to fuse outputs adaptively.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 10 real-world traffic benchmarks shows STHMoE achieving competitive performance relative to temporal, spatio-temporal graph, and LLM-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: STHMoE effectively coordinates heterogeneous temporal, spectral, and higher-order spatial cues under evolving traffic regimes by integrating a prompt-guided mixture-of-experts with adaptive hypergraph structures and an entropy-aware routing mechanism, demonstrating competitive performance on real-world data.

title: DuctAM: A Duct-Assisted Quadrotor-Based Aerial Manipulator Enabling High-Force Push-and-Pull Interactions
summary: Uncrewed Aerial Manipulators (UAMs) extend the capabilities of Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from perception to physical interaction. Among various aerial interactions, push-and-pull operations are fundamental manipulation primitives that require sustained horizontal forces while maintaining stable flight. In this paper, we propose DuctAM, a compact aerial manipulation platform that enhances horizontal force capability for push-and-pull interactions using two ducted fans integrated along the quadrotor interaction axis. An attitude-force decoupled control scheme enables controllable horizontal forces without requiring large attitude changes. Extensive real-world experiments are conducted to validate the DuctAM. Figure-eight trajectory tracking experiments demonstrate stable flight and accurate motion control in both quad and duct modes. Force-measurement experiments quantify the decoupled longitudinal force capability of DuctAM. Finally, representative push-and-pull interaction tasks, including cart pushing, door closing, and drawer opening, verify the practical effectiveness of DuctAM. The results show that DuctAM achieves significantly improved horizontal interaction force capability while maintaining stable flight compared with conventional UAVs.

AI.tldr: DuctAM is a compact aerial manipulation platform that uses two ducted fans along the quadrotor interaction axis to boost horizontal forces for push-and-pull tasks, coupled with an attitude-force decoupled controller to maintain stable flight.
AI.motivation: UAMs require sustained horizontal interaction forces for manipulation tasks (push-pull) without sacrificing flight stability; conventional UAVs struggle with large attitude changes to generate horizontal forces. A ducted-fan augmentation can increase horizontal capability while decoupling attitude control.
AI.method: Integrate two ducted fans along the interaction axis of a quadrotor and implement an attitude-force decoupled control scheme to generate controllable horizontal forces with minimal attitude changes. Validate via real-world experiments: figure-eight trajectory tracking in quad and duct modes; force-measurement experiments for longitudinal force; push-pull tasks (cart pushing, door closing, drawer opening).
AI.result: DuctAM achieves significantly improved horizontal interaction force capability while maintaining stable flight, outperforming conventional UAVs in push-pull tasks and preserving accurate motion control.
AI.conclusion: DuctAM demonstrates that combining ducted-fan augmentation with an attitude-force decoupled controller yields practical, stable, and enhanced horizontal manipulation capabilities for UAMs, enabling robust push-pull interactions in real-world scenarios.

title: AlayaVista: Streaming World Modeling from Panoramic States to Perspective Video
summary: Interactive video world models must maintain broad scene context under camera motion while producing high-fidelity observations with low latency. Existing approaches face a representation trade-off: perspective models operate on local views and must preserve off-screen content over long rollouts, whereas broader spatial coverage is typically obtained by synthesizing full-sphere videos or constructing explicit 3D representations. Motivated by the complementary roles of global context and selective local acuity in visual perception, we present AlayaVista, a camera-controllable streaming video world model that decouples panoramic world evolution from perspective observation synthesis. Given a single perspective image, AlayaVista constructs a 360-degree scene prior using a pretrained panorama expansion model and then evolves the scene as a camera-conditioned panoramic latent state. A latent viewport renderer maps this state to the requested perspective video latents, while a perspective refiner restores details, suppresses artifacts, and performs super-resolution. To support efficient streaming, we adapt the panoramic generator to chunk-autoregressive generation and distill both panoramic generation and perspective refinement into few-step processes. To provide the supervision required by this design, we construct MUGEN, a large-scale real-world panoramic video dataset containing 1,318 hours of videos at resolutions of at least 4K, together with rich semantic and geometric annotations.

AI.tldr: AlayaVista decouples panoramic world evolution from perspective synthesis to enable camera-controllable, low-latency 360-degree view generation using a panoramic latent state, a latent viewport renderer, and a perspective refiner, trained with the MUGEN dataset.
AI.motivation: Addresses the representation trade-off in interactive video world models: preserving broad scene context under camera motion (global context) while achieving high-fidelity, low-latency perspective observations (local acuity).
AI.method: From a single perspective image, build a 360-degree scene prior via a pretrained panorama expansion model; evolve a camera-conditioned panoramic latent state; render requested perspective latents through a latent viewport renderer; refine with a perspective refiner that restores details and performs super-resolution; enable streaming efficiency via chunk-autoregressive generation and distillation to few steps; supervise with MUGEN, a large-scale real-world panoramic video dataset (1,318 hours at 4K+).
AI.result: The abstract presents the architectural framework and dataset, but does not report quantitative results or empirical evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling panoramic world evolution from perspective synthesis can improve context preservation and reduce latency in interactive video models; the MUGEN dataset provides large-scale real-world panoramic data for supervision and evaluation.

title: Carryover Drafting: Recycling Rejected States for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by verifying multiple drafted tokens in parallel, allowing a single target forward pass to accept several tokens. By construction, verification computes representations for both accepted and rejected tokens. Yet, conventional drafters retain only the representations of accepted tokens, leaving the substantial verifier computation spent on rejected tokens effectively wasted. We find that these discarded hidden states generated during target forward retain useful information about future tokens that can improve subsequent drafts. However, realizing this opportunity poses two distinct challenges. At inference, recycling overhead can increase drafting latency, diminishing the speedup gained from increased acceptance length. During training, standard parallel drafter training does not produce inference-aligned rejected states, while obtaining them through sequential rollouts would sacrifice parallelism across training positions. We introduce Carryover Drafting, which addresses both challenges. Carryover recycles rejected target hidden states as temporary KV context, allowing the drafter to selectively attend to them. It reuses the drafter's existing interface and adds only a single learned embedding to distinguish rejected states from committed context. The additional KV context is replaced each drafting round, keeping its length bounded by one proposal block. We introduce parallel draft--verify--draft training that exposes the drafter to inference-aligned rejected states while preserving parallelism across training positions. Experiments with DFlash and a DSpark-derived semi-autoregressive drafter across two target models show that this simple Carryover mechanism improves average acceptance length by 6.5--14.7% and end-to-end vLLM speedup by 7.9--14.4% over the corresponding baselines, with speedup gains reaching 28.8% on translation.

AI.tldr: Carryover Drafting recycles rejected target states as temporary KV context in speculative decoding, enabling inference-aligned information reuse without increasing interface complexity; paired with parallel draft–verify–draft training, it yields consistent speedups and longer acceptance in two models.
AI.motivation: In speculative decoding, rejected tokens generate useful hidden states but are discarded, causing wasted verifier computation and missed opportunities to improve future drafts. Recycling them could improve efficiency, but it risks added latency and training misalignment.
AI.method: Introduce Carryover Drafting: reuse rejected target hidden states as temporary KV context, distinguished by a learned embedding, with context length bounded to one proposal block and replaced each drafting round. Train with parallel draft–verify–draft training to expose the drafter to inference-aligned rejected states without sacrificing training parallelism.
AI.result: Empirical gains: average acceptance length up by 6.5–14.7%; end-to-end vLLM speedup by 7.9–14.4% (up to 28.8% for translation) over baselines; validated on DFlash and DSpark-derived semi-autoregressive drafter across two target models.
AI.conclusion: Carryover Drafting provides an effective, low-overhead mechanism to exploit discarded states, improving drafting efficiency and inference speed while maintaining parallel training. The approach generalizes to other speculative decoding setups and yields meaningful practical speedups.

title: VisInteract: Towards Dynamic Interactive Text-to-Visualization under Imperfect Queries
summary: Real-world visualization requests are routinely ambiguous, incomplete, or factually incorrect, yet existing Text-to-Visualization (Text-to-Vis) systems assume well-specified inputs and produce charts in a single pass. When queries are imperfect, a system must \emph{interact} with the user to recover the true intent, but no benchmark or method supports this dynamic process. We introduce \textbf{VisInteract}, a new paradigm that reframes Text-to-Vis as interaction-driven intent recovery, and \textbf{VisInteract-Bench}, to our knowledge, that is the first benchmark for dynamic interactive Text-to-Vis, featuring controlled imperfection injection, a leakage-controlled User Agent for realistic multi-turn feedback, and dual-perspective (code and chart) automated evaluation. On the algorithmic side, we propose \textbf{Vis-MCTS}, a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) enhanced method, introducing improvements over classical MCTS, that \emph{Progressive Widening} to tame the unbounded tool-argument space in tree search, \emph{cross-rollout information sharing} so clarifications and critiques benefit the entire search tree, and \emph{Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition} that routes scalar user feedback along data-fidelity, visual-design, and intent-alignment dimensions to resolve credit assignment across heterogeneous actions. Extensive Experiments across two LLM backbones show that Vis-MCTS consistently outperforms all Text-to-Vis baselines, improving end-to-end task success by $13.40\%$--$16.27\%$ over the strongest interactive baseline and by more than $5\times$ over non-interactive ones.

AI.tldr: Proposes VisInteract: an interaction-driven framework for dynamic, interactive Text-to-Visualization with a benchmark (VisInteract-Bench) and a Monte Carlo Tree Search–based algorithm (Vis-MCTS). Demonstrates significant improvements in interactive visualization tasks over non-interactive baselines.
AI.motivation: Real-world visualization requests are often ambiguous, incomplete, or factually incorrect, yet existing Text-to-Vis systems assume well-specified inputs and lack benchmarks for interactive clarification. A benchmark and method are needed to support iterative intent recovery.
AI.method: Introduce VisInteract paradigm; VisInteract-Bench with controlled imperfection injection, a leakage-controlled User Agent for realistic multi-turn feedback, and dual-perspective (code and chart) automated evaluation. Propose Vis-MCTS, a Monte Carlo Tree Search–enhanced approach with Progressive Widening to manage unbounded tool-argument space, cross-rollout information sharing to disseminate clarifications, and Dimension-Aware Reward Decomposition allocating feedback across data-fidelity, visual-design, and intent-alignment dimensions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across two LLM backbones shows Vis-MCTS outperforms all Text-to-Vis baselines, achieving end-to-end task success improvements of 13.40%–16.27% over the strongest interactive baseline and more than 5× improvement over non-interactive systems.
AI.conclusion: An interaction-driven paradigm for Text-to-Visualization is effective for recovering user intent under imperfect queries. The VisInteract-Bench provides a realistic, controllable benchmark, and Vis-MCTS advances state-of-the-art by robustly handling multi-turn clarifications and diverse action credits.

title: WLA$^3$: World Latent Action Modeling for Semantics, Dynamics, and Kinematics
comment: Project page can be found at https://wla-3.github.io/
summary: Scaling generalist policy models with heterogeneous data is limited by the lack of unified, low-noise action supervision. Human egocentric videos are abundant, but only a small fraction comes with high-quality hand-action labels. Observed world transitions offer a common source of action-related supervision across data sources. We introduce WLA$^3$ (World Latent Action Modeling for Semantics, Dynamics, and Kinematics), a unified generalist policy model framework built around representations learned by a World Latent Action Model (WLAM). WLAM first learns how multimodal world states change over a local interval, encoding synchronized camera views and available embodiment-state changes into a compact local latent action and a richer transition feature. Reconstruction from partial modalities and consistency across overlapping windows encourage robust transition representations. WLA$^3$ reuses them across semantics, dynamics, and kinematics: local latent actions support action-sensitive physical-dynamics modeling, segment-level features directly supervise the VLM through a Semantic Latent Aggregate (SLA), and an action expert jointly predicts latent actions together with embodiment-specific robot controls. Human videos provide scalable transition supervision, while robot trajectories ground the shared representation in executable native controls. On LARYBench, the final 32D latent action reaches 67.89\% average classification accuracy. WLA$^3$ achieves 81.9% average success across six real-robot tasks versus 66.2% for $π_{0.5}$. Performance improves as generalist policy model mid-training data scales, and human videos support human-to-robot transfer. Project page can be found at https://wla-3.github.io/.

AI.tldr: WLAM-based framework (WLA^3) unifies multimodal world-state transitions into a latent action space to support semantics, dynamics, and kinematics for generalist policies, leveraging both human videos and robot trajectories. It yields strong real-robot performance and scalable transfer.
AI.motivation: Generalist policy models suffer from noisy, fragmented supervision when trained on heterogeneous data. World-transition signals offer a common, scalable supervision source across data sources (human egocentric videos and robot data).
AI.method: Train a World Latent Action Model (WLAM) to encode local latent actions from synchronized multimodal world states (camera views + embodiment-state changes) over short windows. Use reconstruction from partial modalities and overlapping windows to learn robust transition features. WLA^3 reuses WLAM representations across semantics (Semantic Latent Aggregate supervising VLM), dynamics (local latent actions for action-sensitive dynamics), and kinematics (an action expert predicting latent actions with executable robot controls). Human videos provide scalable transition supervision; robot trajectories ground representations in native controls.
AI.result: On LARYBench, the 32D latent action achieves 67.89% average classification accuracy. WLA^3 attains 81.9% average success across six real-robot tasks, vs 66.2% for a baseline π_0.5. Performance improves as the generalist policy model's mid-training data scale; human videos aid human-to-robot transfer.
AI.conclusion: WLAM-based world-transition representations enable unified supervision for semantics, dynamics, and kinematics, enabling scalable generalist policies with strong real-robot performance and transfer from human data.

title: DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
comment: Submitted to the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
summary: Video segmentation models recognize and track objects over time, but they do not indicate whether each segmented region moves independently of the observing camera. This dynamicity attribute cannot be inferred from semantics alone and is confounded by camera ego-motion. We introduce \method, an online framework that augments query-based video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction. It jointly produces the original segmentation outputs and a dynamic or static state for each predicted region. At inference, DynEoMT uses only the current frame and propagated queries, without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps. Because established video segmentation benchmarks do not annotate this attribute, we also introduce a class-agnostic offline supervision pipeline using camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, DynEoMT achieves balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance. These results show that segmentation-region dynamicity can be learned from propagated queries, enabling its online prediction without a dedicated motion-processing pipeline at inference. The complete code will be released as open source to enable full reproduction of the method and experiments.

AI.tldr: DynEoMT is an online framework that extends query-based video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction, enabling per-region dynamic/static states without traditional motion inputs, and uses a joint online and offline supervision pipeline.
AI.motivation: Current video segmentation lacks a per-region dynamicity attribute and is confounded by camera ego-motion; enabling online dynamicity prediction can improve understanding of object motion and tracking without extra motion-processing pipelines.
AI.method: Jointly outputs segmentation results and a per-region dynamicity label using an online DynEoMT framework with propagated queries on the current frame. Inference uses only the current frame and propagated queries (no optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps). An offline, class-agnostic supervision pipeline labels dynamicity by using camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering to annotate dynamic vs. static regions.
AI.result: On VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, achieve balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance.
AI.conclusion: Dynamicity of segmentation regions can be learned from propagated queries, enabling online prediction without a dedicated motion-processing pipeline; code will be released for full reproducibility.

title: Are Gradient Boosting Models Suitable for Intermittent Demand Forecasting?
summary: Demand forecasting is critical in modern industry, offering opportunities to reduce costs and gain competitive advantage through improved inventory management. However, forecasting becomes particularly challenging for products with intermittent demand, where demand occurs infrequently and time series contain many zero observations. Such dynamics are common across diverse sectors, such as industrial organizations, consumer goods, aviation, automotive, and electronics. Motivated by these challenges, this paper explores the potential of gradient boosting models to improve forecasting performance. We evaluate statistical, specialized, machine learning, and ensemble approaches across multiple datasets. The results show that specialized methods achieve the strongest performance among individual models, while gradient boosting on its own tends to underperform. However, combining a machine learning model with a specialized approach improves forecasting accuracy by up to 10%, demonstrating that even simple ensembles can outperform single models. Overall, the findings highlight the value of combining machine learning with domain-specific forecasting techniques for intermittent demand.

AI.tldr: Ensemble approach that combines machine learning with domain-specific techniques improves intermittent-demand forecasting; gradient boosting alone underperforms, but simple ML-specialized ensembles can surpass single models by up to 10%.
AI.motivation: Intermittent demand poses forecasting challenges due to many zero observations and infrequent demand, causing higher costs and inventory risk. The study investigates whether gradient boosting can enhance forecasts and whether combining ML with specialized domain methods yields gains.
AI.method: Evaluate various modeling paradigms (statistical, specialized, machine learning, and ensemble approaches) on multiple datasets focusing on intermittent demand. Compare individual models to ensembles, with particular emphasis on gradient boosting performance and the impact of combining ML with specialized techniques.
AI.result: Specialized methods outperform individual models. Gradient boosting on its own tends to underperform in intermittent-demand forecasting. However, incorporating a machine-learning model into a simple ensemble with specialized approaches yields up to 10% accuracy gains, surpassing single-model performance.
AI.conclusion: Combining machine learning with domain-specific forecasting techniques meaningfully improves intermittent-demand forecasting; even simple ensembles can outperform individual models, highlighting the value of hybrid approaches in this context.

title: Issue Bias in Generative AI Writing Assistance: Political Issues and LLMs in the Swedish 2026 Election
summary: Generative AI writing assistants and the Large Language Models (LLMs) that power them are increasingly part of how voters gather information before elections. With growing evidence that they influence users' opinions, it is increasingly important to understand the views and positions of these tools. To better understand these views, we examine the stances supplied by six LLMs on a variety of Swedish-language writing tasks ahead of the 2026 Swedish parliamentary election. We cross 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and neutral, positive, and negative prompt framings, producing 24,717 prompts per model and 148,302 responses. To study these, we look at the models' default stance tendencies, compare how they respond to similar issues, and compare their responses with those of each of Sweden's eight parliamentary parties on the same issue. We find that Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Mistral have similar profiles; ChatGPT more often supplies neutral or ambivalent text; and Grok differs most on topics such as migration, crime, and gender. When comparing the political parties, we find that the Social Democrats are closest to all six models. Still, after correcting for multiple comparisons, none of the within-model differences in party distances remains significant. Overall, we find that no model has a clear preference, nor a clear preference for a party, but that this depends on the specific issue or task the user asks about.

AI.tldr: Six LLMs were evaluated on Swedish political prompts across 107 policy propositions and 77 templates, revealing diverse but non-partisan alignment; no model showed a clear party preference, though some clusters resemble each other, and Social Democrats align most with the models on average.
AI.motivation: Understand the positions and potential biases of generative AI writing aids when assisting political information before elections, especially in non-English language contexts.
AI.method: Crossed 107 policy propositions with 77 writing templates and three prompt framings (neutral, positive, negative), generating 24,717 prompts per model and 148,302 responses across six LLMs; compared models' default stances, response consistency across related issues, and distances to Sweden's eight parliamentary parties; analyzed within-model differences after multiple-comparisons correction.
AI.result: Identified clustering of models (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Mistral) with similar profiles; ChatGPT more neutral/ambivalent; Grok diverges on migration, crime, gender. Parties: Social Democrats closest to all six models; after correction, no significant within-model party distance differences. No model shows a clear party preference; stance depends on issue/task.
AI.conclusion: Nuanced, task-dependent alignment of LLMs with political parties; implication for using LLMs in political information contexts; need for transparency about model-agnostic vs. issue-specific biases and cautious interpretation of model-generated political text.

title: Goal-Oriented Communications for Physical AI: Design and Testbed
comment: Submitting to IEEE for potential publications
summary: Physical AI relies on frequently-updated, latency-sensitive video stream to perceive, reason, and interact with the physical world, resulting in strict latency requirements with much higher data volumes that existing 5G networks cannot support. Goal-oriented communication (GoC) offers as a promising approach to solve this challenge by transmitting only task-relevant semantic representations. However, existing GoC frameworks were mainly evaluated in the simulations while their effectiveness has never been validated in a practical deployment of physical AI application. In this work, we develop an end-to-end GoC testbed for Physical AI, which connects a PiPER robot arm equipped with an RGB-D camera and a 5G modem to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge server through a 5G OpenAirInterface network. We propose and implement three GoC frameworks that transmit 3D bounding boxes, 2D scene graphs, and 3D scene graphs, as three types of semantic representations, respectively. They share the common functional modules designed for closed-loop Physical AI applications, including semantic extraction, full stack 5G transmission, language model inference, digital twin validation, and robotic control.
