Extensive experiments on our testbed show that our GoC frameworks reduce the task completion time by up to 52.6% and improve task success probability by up to 45%, compared to the traditional framework that periodically transmits the raw image data. These results validate the practical effectiveness of our GoC framework and pave the way for efficient and reliable Physical AI applications over future 6G networks. Project website: https://sites.google.com/view/goc-physical-ai-testbed.

AI.tldr: This work presents an end-to-end GoC (goal-oriented communication) testbed for Physical AI over 5G, connecting a robotic arm with RGB-D sensing to an edge server via OpenAirInterface. It implements three GoC representations (3D bounding boxes, 2D scene graphs, 3D scene graphs) and shows significant latency reductions and higher task success probabilities compared to a raw image transmission baseline, validating GoC in practical deployment and hinting at 6G-ready applications.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to meet the stringent latency and bandwidth demands of Physical AI by transmitting only semantically relevant information, rather than raw video, and to validate GoC in a real-world robotic control loop over a 5G network.
AI.method: Develop an end-to-end GoC testbed with PiPER robot arm, RGB-D camera, 5G modem, OpenAirInterface network, and NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge server. Implement three GoC representations (3D bounding boxes, 2D scene graphs, 3D scene graphs). Integrate semantic extraction, full-stack 5G transmission, language-model inference, digital twin validation, and robotic control in a closed-loop system.
AI.result: Experiments show up to 52.6% reduction in task completion time and up to 45% improvement in task success probability compared to a baseline that transmits raw images periodically.
AI.conclusion: The GoC approach is practically effective for Physical AI deployments over current 5G networks and is promising for efficient and reliable future 6G-enabled mechanisms, with versatile semantic representations to support different task requirements.

title: PRI-Net: A Lightweight Multimodal Framework for 3D UAV Localization
summary: Accurate 3D localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging for existing multimodal approaches due to sparse LiDAR geometry, modality-imbalanced fusion, and redundant feature transmission over constrained edge-to-server links. To address these limitations, we propose PRI-Net, an efficient and lightweight multimodal fusion framework for UAV localization that integrates point cloud splatting, residual attention fusion, and an information bottleneck. Specifically, a 3D point cloud splatting (3DPCS) strategy is introduced to transform sparse LiDAR observations into geometrically consistent dense depth maps. A residual attention fusion (RAF) module is then designed to alleviate modal bias by using an image branch for coarse estimation and a gated fusion branch for refinement. In addition, a multimodal information bottleneck (MIB) module compacts features by filtering task-irrelevant redundancy. Experiments show that PRI-Net achieves high localization accuracy with lightweight architectures, while reducing feature dimensionality and improving edge-to-server UAV sensing efficiency and robustness.

AI.tldr: PRI-Net is a lightweight multimodal fusion framework for UAV 3D localization that densifies sparse LiDAR with 3D point cloud splatting, fuses modalities via residual attention, and compresses features with an information bottleneck to improve edge-to-server efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal UAV localization suffers from sparse LiDAR geometry, modality imbalance during fusion, and costly feature transmission over constrained edge-to-server links.
AI.method: Introduce 3DPCS to convert sparse LiDAR into dense depth maps; design RAF to mitigate modal bias with an image branch for coarse estimation and a gated branch for refinement; incorporate MIB to filter task-irrelevant redundancy and compress features.
AI.result: PRI-Net achieves high localization accuracy with lightweight architectures, while reducing feature dimensionality and enhancing edge-to-server sensing efficiency and robustness.
AI.conclusion: PRI-Net provides an efficient, robust, and scalable solution for multimodal UAV localization by combining dense depth generation, attentive fusion, and information bottleneck for compact representations.

title: WaVeFuse: Regime-Adaptive Equity Index Forecasting via Channel-Wise Wavelet Denoising and Vertical Attention Fusion
comment: 40 pages, 13 Figures, 15 Tables, Preprint, Under Review
summary: Hybrid Deep Learning for equity index forecasting is limited by three problems: propagation of OHLCV noise into derived technical indicators (TIs), channel-indiscriminate multi-scale decomposition that conflates heterogeneous frequency signatures, and static multi-branch fusion that cannot adapt to market regime shifts. WaVeFuse addresses these limitations through a unified dual-branch architecture. Symlet-4 wavelet denoising (level 2, MAD soft threshold) suppresses microstructure noise in OHLCV. Seven low-lag TIs computed from denoised prices are encoded by a causal channel-wise continuous wavelet transform (Morlet, 32 scales) into a per-timestep scale-space matrix. A CNN-BiLSTM branch captures temporal dynamics, while a dual-layer Transformer (heads=4, dk in {16, 32}) models inter-scale spectral dependencies, and their representations are integrated by a 2-token softmax gate Vertical Attention Fusion (VAF) that dynamically reweights branches as market regimes shift. Evaluated under walk-forward validation (WFV) on KOSPI, DAX, NYSE Composite, and Russell 2000 (2010-2023), WaVeFuse achieves R2 = 0.81-0.96 and directional accuracy 70.5-78.3%. It outperforms seven state-of-the-art models by 8.9-20.2% MAE across twelve dataset-period configurations. Diebold-Mariano statistics (4.62-10.38, p<0.001) confirm superiority over a well-tuned XGBoost benchmark across four indices. Ablation verifies component-wise contributions. Under realistic backtesting with 10 basis point transaction costs, WaVeFuse's directional strategy achieves a mean Sharpe ratio of 3.69 across four markets and limits maximum drawdown to 7.5% during the COVID-19 crash. With 152k parameters (0.68MB) and sub-1.3ms GPU inference, WaVeFuse delivers a computationally efficient, regime-robust framework suitable for research and decision-support deployment.

AI.tldr: Proposes WaVeFuse, a dual-branch deep learning model combining wavelet denoising, causal channel-wise wavelets, CNN-BiLSTM, and Transformer with Vertical Attention Fusion to forecast equity indices robustly across regimes; achieves strong accuracy and Sharpe in walk-forward and backtests with efficient inference.
AI.motivation: Mitigate propagation of OHLCV noise into derived technical indicators (TIs), avoid channel-agnostic multi-scale decomposition that conflates heterogeneous frequencies, and replace static multi-branch fusion with a regime-adaptive mechanism.
AI.method: Denoise OHLCV with Symlet-4 (level 2, MAD soft threshold). Compute seven low-lag TIs from denoised prices. Encode via causal channel-wise continuous wavelet transform (Morlet, 32 scales) into per-timestep scale-space matrix. Dual-branch: CNN-BiLSTM for temporal dynamics; dual-layer Transformer (heads=4, dk∈{16,32}) for inter-scale spectral dependencies. Reweight branches with 2-token softmax gate Vertical Attention Fusion (VAF). Evaluate with walk-forward validation on KOSPI, DAX, NYSE Composite, Russell 2000 (2010–2023). Backtesting with 10bp costs. Efficiency: 152k parameters (~0.68MB), sub-1.3ms GPU inference.
AI.result: R2 = 0.81–0.96; directional accuracy = 70.5%–78.3%. Outperforms seven state-of-the-art models by 8.9%–20.2% MAE across twelve dataset-period configurations. Diebold-Mariano statistics (DM = 4.62–10.38, p<0.001) confirm superiority over a well-tuned XGBoost benchmark across four indices. Ablation confirms component contributions. During COVID-19 crash, backtested mean Sharpe = 3.69; max drawdown limited to 7.5%. Computationally efficient with 152k parameters and sub-1.3ms GPU inference.
AI.conclusion: WaVeFuse delivers a regime-robust, computationally efficient framework suitable for research and decision-support deployment across multiple equity markets.

title: From Ideas to Actions: A Public-Data Decision-Support Toolchain Across the Venture Lifecycle
comment: 39 pages. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/quge007/eventchain ; Code and agent skills: https://github.com/quge009/startup-decision-skills
summary: Founders face two linked decisions: whether to pursue an idea before founding, and which operating actions and capital partners fit afterward. We present a public-data decision-support toolchain combining time-bounded proposal profiling, market and moat checks, and deterministic aggregation with auditable investor-company event chains for retrospective analysis. Pre-founding: (a) After threshold selection on 198 development companies, the frozen pipeline achieves F0.5=0.5357 [0.412, 0.655] on an independent, row-disjoint 198-company validation sample. On the combined 396 rows, the Full Pipeline scores 0.6301 versus 0.2734 for a paired Raw LLM baseline. Post-stratification of 1,027 completed cases in a separate scale cohort yields 0.6506 [0.598, 0.707]; the run remains incomplete. A 377-row composition-matched check yields 0.6573. (b) The AI-inference study identifies distribution-layer businesses as a replicable path to independent profitability with a limited revenue ceiling, and frontier-model ownership as a path to capital-market upside at exceptional capital cost. Post-founding: (a) Public sources support auditable event-chain analysis. (b) In the chip-company study, sustained product, customer, and supply-chain progress is associated with better observed outcomes; financing alone does not establish operating progress. (c) Financing comprises 79% of confirmed visible post-investment actions. Evidence tentatively favors acquisition-experienced strategic corporate investors for acquisition-oriented founders and financing-led institutional VCs with fewer observed control events for independence-oriented founders. Findings are developmental and observational, not causal guarantees or investment advice. We release shared ontology, provenance-bearing EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills for audit, reuse, and extension.

AI.tldr: A public-data decision-support pipeline assesses pre- and post-founding decisions; results show substantial predictive gains over baselines and patterning by investor type, with findings being observational and developmental rather than causal.
AI.motivation: Provide a transparent, auditable framework with reproducible benchmarks to guide founder decisions and analyze how actions, financing, and investor mix relate to outcomes.
AI.method: Time-bounded proposal profiling; market/moat checks; deterministic aggregation; auditable investor–company event chains; validation on 198 development companies; expanded to 396 rows; post-stratification on 1,027 cases; composition-matched check with 377 rows; AI-inference study; post-founding event-chain analysis; chip-company case study; release of shared ontology and provenance-bearing EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills for audit and reuse.
AI.result: Pre-founding: F0.5 ≈ 0.536 (CI 0.412–0.655); on 396 rows Full Pipeline = 0.6301 vs Raw LLM = 0.2734. Post-stratified 1,027 cases yields ≈0.6506; composition-matched check ≈0.6573. AI-inference: distribution-layer businesses enable independent profitability with limited revenue ceiling; frontier-model ownership enables capital-market upside at high capital cost. Post-founding: public sources support auditable event-chain analysis; in chip-company study, ongoing product/customer/supply-chain progress correlates with outcomes; financing alone does not ensure progress; financing constitutes 79% of confirmed actions. Evidence tentatively favors acquisition-experienced strategic corporate investors for acquisition-focused founders and financing-led VCs with fewer observed control events for independence-oriented founders.
AI.conclusion: Findings are developmental and observational, not causal guarantees. The work releases ontology, provenance-bearing EventChain data, schemas, benchmarks, and executable skills to enable audit, reuse, and extension.

title: SlipSense: Multimodal Tactile Learning for Low-Latency and Generalized Slip Detection
summary: Slip detection is fundamental to dexterous manipulation, yet existing systems often lack precise characterization of detection latency and cross-platform generalization. We present SlipSense, a multimodal tactile slip-detection framework built on TacV5, a compact sensor integrating a $32 \times 32$ piezoresistive array operating at 240 Hz and a 3-axis MEMS accelerometer operating at 8 kHz. The piezoresistive array captures spatial pressure distributions, while the accelerometer captures friction-induced vibrations, providing complementary slip cues. The framework performs modality-specific encoding, intra-sensor fusion, and cross-modal attention with causal temporal prediction at 240 Hz. Experiments on a dataset of 1.4 million frames spanning 37 objects demonstrate the complementarity of the two modalities. SlipSense achieves 96.7% Macro F1 with a false-positive rate below 1.6%, detecting 76% of slip events within 23.1 ms. When trained solely on UMI data, SlipSense generalizes zero-shot to a Tesollo dexterous hand, transferring across unseen objects, distinct sensor units, and robotic platforms without retraining.

AI.tldr: SlipSense is a multimodal tactile slip-detection framework on TacV5 that fuses piezoresistive pressure data with accelerometer vibrations to detect slips quickly and generalize across platforms.
AI.motivation: Detecting slip with precise latency characterization and cross-platform generalization is critical for dexterous manipulation; existing systems often lack this capability.
AI.method: Modality-specific encoding, intra-sensor fusion, and cross-modal attention with causal temporal prediction at 240 Hz. Uses a TacV5 sensor (32x32 piezoresistive array at 240 Hz plus 3-axis MEMS accelerometer at 8 kHz) and a dataset of 1.4 million frames over 37 objects.
AI.result: Macro F1: 96.7%; false-positive rate < 1.6%; detects 76% of slip events within 23.1 ms. Zero-shot generalization to a Tesollo dexterous hand when trained on UMI data, transferring across unseen objects, sensor units, and platforms without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The framework reveals complementarity between pressure and vibration cues; cross-modal attention with causal temporal prediction enables fast, platform-agnostic slip detection.

title: PuzzleMate: Benchmarking MLLMs for Egocentric Puzzle Assistance
summary:
Personal AI assistants hold the potential to evolve from digital interfaces into embodied companions capable of guiding users through complex physical activities. For these assistants to become integral to daily life, they must do more than identify objects; they must provide precise, step-by-step instructions that align with a user's real-time progress. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promise in general visual understanding, their ability to deliver grounded, sequential guidance for fine-grained manipulation tasks remains largely unverified.
  In this paper, we choose the jigsaw puzzle as a strategic testbed for this capability. Unlike general object recognition, puzzle solving demands high-precision spatial reasoning, the ability to distinguish between minute geometric variations, and a rigorous adherence to sequential logic.
  We investigate this capability through PuzzleMate, a novel framework focused on jigsaw puzzle solving captured through an egocentric viewpoint. We deploy PuzzleMate in a user-in-the-loop study to evaluate how well state-of-the-art MLLMs perceive the current puzzle state and generate actionable next-step instructions. Our analysis reveals seven key bottlenecks that limit their effectiveness. Building on these insights, we propose a benchmark that enables systematic evaluation of MLLMs' reasoning capabilities for puzzle solving. Our findings reveal a substantial performance gap in current models like GPT-5.2 and Gemini-2.5-Pro; while these MLLMs are highly capable, they struggle to navigate the intricate reasoning and sequential logic essential for jigsaw puzzle assistance.

AI.tldr: PuzzleMate introduces an egocentric puzzle-solving framework to test whether state-of-the-art MLLMs can provide grounded, sequential, step-by-step guidance for jigsaw puzzles. It identifies seven bottlenecks, presents a benchmark for evaluation, and shows a substantial gap between current models (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and the required reasoning/planing for fine-grained manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Enable embodied AI assistants to give precise, real-time, step-by-step instructions for physical manipulation tasks. Jigsaw puzzles provide a rigorous test of high-precision spatial reasoning and strict sequential logic, where current MLLMs struggle to connect perception with actionable guidance.
AI.method: Propose PuzzleMate, a framework for solving jigsaw puzzles from an egocentric viewpoint. Conduct a user-in-the-loop study to assess MLLMs’ ability to perceive the current state and generate next-step instructions. Identify seven bottlenecks to performance and introduce a benchmark to systematically evaluate MLLMs’ puzzle-solving reasoning. Compare contemporary models (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro) to reveal gaps in sequential reasoning and planning.
AI.result: Seven bottlenecks limiting effectiveness were identified. A benchmark was proposed to systematically evaluate MLLMs’ puzzle-solving reasoning. Current models show a substantial performance gap in grounded, sequential puzzle-solving tasks, with GPT-5.2 and Gemini-2.5-Pro underperforming relative to the demands of high-precision, stepwise guidance.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear need for standardized evaluation and targeted improvements in perception-to-action alignment for MLLMs. The PuzzleMate benchmark frames the problem and highlights the gaps that must be addressed to enable truly embodied, guidance-capable AI assistants.

title: OCT-FedSIR: Toward Trustworthy Federated Ophthalmic Learning under Annotation Noise
comment: 38 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables, 6 tables in supplementary material
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model development without centralizing patient data, but annotation reliability at participating institutions cannot always be assumed. In ophthalmic imaging, differences in disease prevalence and class composition can resemble changes caused by corrupted supervision. We introduce OCT-FedSIR, a reliability-aware spectral framework for federated OCT classification under client-dependent annotation noise and heterogeneous data distributions. OCT-FedSIR combines class-balanced spectral estimation, Stage-I logit adjustment, complementary spectral descriptors, selective spectral relabeling, and noise-aware federated optimization. We evaluated the framework on the Kermany, University of Illinois Chicago, and Wake Forest datasets under symmetric and structured asymmetric noise and three levels of non-IID heterogeneity. Across 117 experimental conditions, OCT-FedSIR achieved a mean accuracy of 86.73%, compared with 79.94% for RoFL and 78.75% for FedCorr. It correctly separated clients with original and corrupted annotations across all evaluated conditions, while the original FedSIR identification procedure was less robust, particularly under asymmetric noise. Spectral relabeling recovered 77.2% of corrupted annotations with 91.3% correction precision and a 3.5% false-correction rate. Retaining corrected clients outperformed spectral pruning by 9.30 percentage points on average. These findings show that annotation noise can often be identified and corrected without discarding informative client data.

AI.tldr: OCT-FedSIR is a reliability-aware federated OCT classifier that detects and corrects annotation noise from multiple clients, improving accuracy under non-IID and noisy supervision; it achieves higher mean accuracy than RoFL and FedCorr and preserves informative data by retaining corrected clients.
AI.motivation: In federated learning for ophthalmic OCT, annotation reliability varies across sites and data distributions are non-IID; corrupted or biased labels can mimic class distribution shifts, degrading performance.
AI.method: Proposed OCT-FedSIR integrates class-balanced spectral estimation, Stage-I logit adjustment, multiple spectral descriptors, selective spectral relabeling, and noise-aware federated optimization to identify and correct corrupted annotations without discarding clients.
AI.result: On three datasets (Kermany, UIC, Wake Forest) under symmetric and structured asymmetric noise and three non-IID settings, OCT-FedSIR averaged 86.73% accuracy vs 79.94% RoFL and 78.75% FedCorr; it reliably separated clean vs corrupted clients; spectral relabeling recovered 77.2% of corrupted annotations with 91.3% precision and 3.5% false-correction; retaining corrected clients beat spectral pruning by 9.3 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware spectral methods can identify and correct annotation noise in federated OCT classification, improving performance and preserving informative client data without discarding clients.

title: CWM: Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Reasoning Ability
summary: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant attention due to their strong language understanding and generation capabilities, demonstrating impressive reasoning abilities as well as effective utilization of external knowledge. Many studies have proposed methods that specialize in improving performance for individual tasks. However, ironically, only a limited number of attempts have explored general-purpose, task-agnostic methods. In this work, we present a unified framework integrating reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tasks. We further propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box method for adaptive RAG tasks previously dominated by black-box approaches, without requiring external decision modules or multi-sampling. CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across recent LLMs, including GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, and Llama3.1-8b, while also demonstrating strong generality by extending to reasoning tasks. In addition, CWM provides controllability by enabling retrieval decisions to be regulated through the manipulation of internal model signals. Our code is available at https://github.com/JeongEunhye00/CWM.

AI.tldr: A unified reasoning+RAG framework is proposed, featuring Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a low-cost white-box approach for adaptive RAG without external modules or multi-sampling, achieving SOTA on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across multiple LLMs, with generalization to reasoning tasks and controllable retrieval via internal model signals; code available.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between task-agnostic methods and task-specific improvements in LLMs; develop a general, low-cost, white-box method to perform adaptive RAG and reasoning with controllable retrieval decisions.
AI.method: Introduce a unified framework that combines reasoning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) tasks and propose Controllable White-Box Meta-Prompting (CWM), a white-box prompting technique that allows adaptive RAG without external decision modules or multi-sampling; internal model signals are manipulated to regulate retrieval decisions.
AI.result: CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on three adaptive RAG benchmarks across several LLMs (GPT-oss-20b, Qwen3-14b, Llama3.1-8b) and generalizes to reasoning tasks; it also provides controllability by adjusting internal model signals. Code is released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: CWM offers a practical, low-cost, controllable, and generalizable white-box solution for adaptive RAG and reasoning in LLMs, presenting a viable alternative to black-box RAG methods.

title: Touch2Trace: Tactile-Driven Imitation Learning for Dexterous Cable Tracing
summary: Dexterous manipulation of deformable objects demands continuous fingertip-level regulation of pressure, friction, and incipient slip. We study one of the most challenging cases: dexterous cable tracing, feeding a cable through the hand with repeated pinch-and-curl motions of the thumb and index finger. We introduce Touch2Trace, a tactile-driven imitation-learning system for this task, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic real-world characterization of how encoder pretraining, control rate, temporal context, and spatial resolution each shape policy performance. The winning learning recipe combines a tactile encoder pretrained for a custom 32 x 32 piezoresistive sensor (TacV5) via self-supervised learning with a lightweight transformer policy trained on teleoperated demonstrations via behavior cloning, deployed at 60 Hz on a Tesollo DG-5F hand. Tactile feedback without vision or explicit cable-state estimation significantly improves tracing performance versus a proprioception-only baseline: from 0.2 cm to 20.1 cm mean distance and 0% to 93% success rate, with zero-shot transfer to unseen cables and routing conditions. The results quantify the influence of key parameters in tactile-driven systems for reliable dexterous deformable object manipulation.

AI.tldr: Touch2Trace uses tactile feedback to drive dexterous cable tracing, combining a self-supervised pretrained TacV5 tactile encoder with a lightweight transformer policy trained via behavior cloning; achieves strong real-world performance and zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation of deformable objects requires continuous fingertip regulation of pressure and friction. Cable tracing with pinch-and-curl is a challenging case. There is little real-world evidence on how tactile encoder pretraining, control rate, temporal context, and spatial resolution affect policy performance.
AI.method: Self-supervised pretraining of a 32×32 TacV5 tactile sensor encoder, followed by behavior-cloning-style training of a lightweight transformer policy on teleoperated demonstrations. The policy runs at 60 Hz on a Tesollo DG-5F hand, relying on tactile feedback only (no vision or explicit cable-state estimation). Evaluates the impact of encoder pretraining, control rate, temporal context, and spatial resolution.
AI.result: Compared to a proprioception-only baseline, tactile-driven control reduces tracing error from ~20.1 cm (poor) to ~0.2 cm, and increases success rate from 0% to ~93%. Demonstrates zero-shot transfer to unseen cables and routing conditions.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first real-world characterization of how key factors—encoder pretraining, control rate, temporal context, and spatial resolution—shape tactile-driven policies for reliable manipulation of deformable objects. It shows that tactile feedback can significantly improve dexterous cable tracing without vision or explicit state estimation.

title: MCIQA-2K: A Multi-Dimensional Dataset and No-Reference Quality Assessment Benchmark for Colorized Images
summary: Image colorization is an inherently ill-posed task, since a single grayscale image may correspond to multiple plausible colorized results. Consequently, conventional full-reference image quality assessment (IQA) metrics fail to accurately reflect human perceptual preferences for colorized images. In this paper, we present MCIQA-2K, a large-scale multi-dimensional benchmark specifically designed for no-reference quality assessment of colorized images. We construct a dataset containing 2,000 colorized images generated by five representative colorization models, together with human annotations across three perceptual dimensions: color smearing, semantic color misalignment, and global naturalness. Building upon the proposed benchmark, we further introduce MCIQA, a dedicated multi-branch NR-IQA framework for colorized images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MCIQA significantly outperforms existing full-reference and no-reference IQA methods on the proposed benchmark, while also exhibiting competitive generalization capability on several widely-used IQA datasets. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/ARBEZ-ZEBRA/MCIQA.

AI.tldr: Introduces MCIQA-2K dataset and MCIQA NR-IQA framework for colorized images; achieves SOTA on benchmark and generalizes to other IQA datasets; resources released publicly.
AI.motivation: Full-reference IQA struggles to capture perceptual quality of colorized images due to the ill-posed nature of colorization; a no-reference, perceptually aligned benchmark and model are needed.
AI.method: Construct 2,000 colorized images from five representative colorization models; obtain human annotations on three perceptual dimensions (color smear, semantic color misalignment, global naturalness); propose MCIQA, a multi-branch NR-IQA framework tailored for colorized images.
AI.result: MCIQA significantly outperforms existing full-reference and no-reference IQA methods on the proposed benchmark and shows competitive generalization on widely-used IQA datasets.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a publicly available dataset and code, advancing perceptually aligned NR-IQA for colorized images via a multi-branch architecture and a multi-dimensional annotation scheme.

title: Calibrating Interpretability Instruments Before Trusting Their Verdicts
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Companion to "Refusal Reads Only a Slice of What the Model Knows" (submitted concurrently). Per-unit arrays: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22731361. Code: https://github.com/deepsteer/deepsteer
summary: Causal claims about large language model (LLM) internals rest on measurements. Those might include a projection, a cosine, an ablation delta, or an interchange patch among others. These measurements fail in specific, diagnosable ways that return a plausible number instead of an error, so a broken instrument can easily read as a finding. A covariance-matched null can saturate until every direction looks typical, a per-head attribution can overshoot the true residual write threefold on reordered-normalization architectures, an interchange patch can go sign-chaotic because its outcome is pinned at a ceiling, or a read-from verdict can be an artifact of measuring past the layer where the model already decided. This note documents six such failures from a causal interpretability program on refusal and moral representation, spanning several papers and a four-model open-weight panel; each mode is established on one or two of the four. For each we give the tell that catches it and a protocol keyed to a detectable trigger (reordered normalization, massive activations, a low-dimensional decision channel), so we and readers can check whether a given setup is exposed. The discipline reduces to four moves: calibrate against a positive-control ladder, certify with an orthogonal cell, compute power before spending compute, and state every read-from verdict at a depth referenced to the model's commitment. The evidence is four architectures across three families within a single program; external replication across programs is future work.

AI.tldr: Identifies six diagnostic failures in causal interpretability measurements for LLM internals and proposes a four-move protocol to mitigate them; demonstrated on four architectures across three families within a single program, with external replication as future work.
AI.motivation: To expose systematic measurement pitfalls in causal claims about LLM internals and provide a practical protocol to avoid spurious findings.
AI.method: Document six failure modes (projection/cosine/ablation delta/interchange patch/read-from, among others), specify tells and detectable triggers (reordered normalization, massive activations, low-dimensional decision channel), and propose a four-mold protocol; validate across four architectures from three families within one program.
AI.result: A concrete diagnostic framework: calibrate against a positive-control ladder, certify with an orthogonal cell, compute statistical power before spend, and report read-from depth relative to model commitment. Evidence drawn from four architectures across three families; external replication remains for future work.
AI.conclusion: The interpretability discipline should adopt explicit controls and transparent reporting; the four-move protocol provides guardrails against faulty measurements and promotes reproducibility, pending cross-program replication.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Open-Source Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in ESG Domain
summary:
Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is critical for corporate accountability, with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offering strong potential to automate KPI extraction. However, open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood. This paper evaluates open-source LLMs in ESG contexts using a structured framework and evaluation resource based on 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010-2024).
  We evaluate seven open-source models (2B to 30B parameters) -- glm-4.7-flash, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3:4b-instruct, gemma3:4b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, and ministral-3:8b -- using 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs covering ESG information needs. System performance is assessed via RAGAS metrics, including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
  Results show notable performance variations across architectures. Retrieval performance is strong across models (context recall around 0.58-0.61, context precision around 0.78-0.81, context relevance 0.965-0.985). Generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822) and least on answer relevancy (0.760-0.881): glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Low overall factual correctness (0.387-0.449) highlights the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. This work provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting.

AI.tldr: Open-source LLMs (2B–30B params) are evaluated for ESG KPI extraction using 498 EU-listed company ESG reports (2010–2024) with 7 models and 100 synthetic QA pairs. Retrieval is strong; generation varies, with faithfulness and factual correctness being major gaps. Domain-specific fine-tuning is needed; the work provides data-driven deployment guidance for open-source LLMs in ESG reporting.
AI.motivation: Assess the practical viability of open-source LLMs for ESG KPI extraction, addressing the gap in understanding model performance on domain-specific ESG tasks and contributing guidance for ESG reporting automation.
AI.method: Evaluation framework using 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010–2024). Seven open-source models (2B–30B) evaluated with 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs. System performance assessed via RAGAS metrics: contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
AI.result: Retrieval performance is consistently strong (context recall ~0.58–0.61, context precision ~0.78–0.81, context relevance ~0.965–0.985). Generation shows larger divergence, especially in faithfulness (0.607–0.822) and factual correctness (0.387–0.449); glm-4.7-flash excels in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Overall factual correctness is low, signaling the need for domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The study provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting and highlights the necessity of domain-specific fine-tuning to improve factual correctness and reliability in KPI extraction.

title: Beyond Single-Axis Testing: Paired Evaluation of Compound Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action policies are typically evaluated one perturbation at a time, providing a useful diagnosis of their sensitivity to individual distribution shifts. Real-world deployment, however, may involve several shifts simultaneously, and it remains unclear how these individual robustness measurements compose. We ask whether compound robustness can be inferred from single-axis evaluations. We introduce LIBERO-CTRL, a six-axis benchmark that pairs each initial state across single-axis conditions and a matched simultaneous condition. This design reveals two opposing outcome changes that aggregate success rates cannot distinguish: emergent failures, where all single-axis rollouts succeed but the simultaneous rollout fails, and compensated successes, where at least one single-axis rollout fails but the simultaneous rollout succeeds. Because one transition decreases compound success while the other increases it, they can cancel, making aggregate compound performance appear consistent with single-axis measurements even when individual outcomes differ substantially. These opposing transitions can largely cancel in aggregate: even when the difference between the two transition rates is not statistically distinguishable from zero, as many as 29.0% of matched initial states still change outcome. Across six policies and three severity levels, such outcome changes reach 34.5% in the most affected condition. The relative prevalence of the two transitions varies across policies and severities, while the transition rates remain similar under independent re-evaluation of stochastic policies. Compound robustness therefore cannot be characterized from aggregate single-axis success rates alone; matched per-instance evaluation is needed to reveal how joint perturbations alter behavior.

AI.tldr: Compound robustness cannot be inferred from aggregated single-axis evaluations; matched per-instance evaluation reveals emergent and compensated transitions under joint perturbations.
AI.motivation: Understand how multiple simultaneous distribution shifts affect policy robustness, beyond single-axis diagnostics, for reliable real-world deployment.
AI.method: Introduce LIBERO-CTRL, a six-axis benchmark pairing initial states across single-axis perturbations and a matched simultaneous condition; analyze outcomes across six policies and three severity levels to identify emergent failures and compensated successes; emphasize per-instance analysis over aggregate metrics.
AI.result: Aggregate success rates can mask substantial per-instance changes: emergent failures (all single-axis rollouts succeed but joint rollout fails) and compensated successes (joint rollout succeeds though some single-axis rollouts fail). Up to 29.0% of matched initial states change outcome; up to 34.5% in the most affected condition; transition rates are similar under independent reevaluation of stochastic policies, but the two opposing transitions can cancel in aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Compound robustness requires matched per-instance evaluation; aggregate single-axis metrics are insufficient to characterize joint perturbations; robust evaluation designs should report per-instance transitions (emergent/compensated) alongside aggregate performance.

title: CGGT: Curve-Grounded Geometry Transformer for 3D Parametric Curve Reconstruction
summary: Recovering editable 3D parametric curves from 2D images is a fundamental challenge in computer graphics, bridging pixel-based perception and vector-based CAD modeling. Existing NeRF- and 3DGS-based methods often rely on dense calibrated views, precomputed 2D edge maps, and costly per-scene optimization, limiting their applicability to casually captured real-world inputs. We propose CGGT, a Curve-Grounded Geometry Transformer that directly grounds 3D-consistent 2D curve instances in the image space from sparse, unposed multi-view images. CGGT combines a geometry-aware transformer encoder for multi-view feature learning with a curve-aware masked-attention decoder for cross-view instance association. In a single forward pass, it predicts camera parameters, dense depth maps, and instance-level 2D curve masks, which are then lifted into 3D and refined through a fast parametric optimization stage to recover compact, editable 3D curve primitives. To support structured curve learning, we introduce Wireframe-100K, a large-scale dataset comprising 100,000 CAD models with diverse topologies, realistic multi-view renderings, and accurate parametric curve annotations. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves substantial improvements in both reconstruction accuracy and efficiency, particularly under challenging sparse-view settings and in separating persistent 3D structural edges from view-dependent image edges caused by silhouettes, textures, and appearance variations. Despite being trained solely on synthetic data, CGGT generalizes well to real-world images, demonstrating its potential for practical CAD-style wireframe reconstruction from unconstrained visual inputs.

AI.tldr: CGGT, a Curve-Grounded Geometry Transformer, grounds 3D-consistent 2D curve instances from sparse, unposed multi-view images to reconstruct editable 3D curve primitives. It uses a geometry-aware encoder and a curve-aware decoder, providing single-shot predictions of camera parameters, depth, and 2D curve masks, which are lifted to 3D and refined via fast optimization. A new Wireframe-100K dataset supports structured curve learning. It achieves superior reconstruction accuracy and efficiency, especially in sparse views, and generalizes from synthetic to real images.
AI.motivation: Current NeRF- and 3DGS-based methods require dense calibrated viewpoints, precomputed 2D edge maps, and costly per-scene optimization, limiting practicality for casually captured inputs. There is a need for robust, sparse-view, unposed multi-view wireframe reconstruction that yields editable 3D curves.
AI.method: Geometry-aware transformer encoder learns multi-view features; curve-aware masked-attention decoder performs cross-view instance association. A single forward pass predicts camera parameters, dense depth maps, and 2D curve masks, which are then lifted into 3D and refined with a fast parametric optimization step to recover compact 3D curve primitives. A new Wireframe-100K dataset (100k CAD models) provides diverse topologies, realistic multi-view renderings, and accurate parametric curve annotations to support structured curve learning.
AI.result: The framework achieves substantial improvements in reconstruction accuracy and efficiency, excelling in sparse-view settings and in separating persistent 3D structural edges from view-dependent image edges caused by silhouettes, textures, and appearance. Despite synthetic training data, CGGT generalizes well to real-world images and supports practical CAD-style wireframe reconstruction from unconstrained inputs.
AI.conclusion: CGGT demonstrates a practical, scalable solution for editable 3D wireframe reconstruction from unconstrained imagery, underpinned by Wireframe-100K for structured curve learning, with strong potential for real-world CAD workflows.

title: Refusal Reads Only a Slice of What the Model Knows: Harm-Keyed Routing and Its Exceptions Across Model Families
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Companion methods note: "Calibrating Interpretability Instruments Before Trusting Their Verdicts" (submitted concurrently). Per-unit arrays: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22731361. Code: https://github.com/deepsteer/deepsteer
summary: Alignment applied after pretraining is shallow in a measurable way: a single direction in a model's residual stream can be edited out, and the model stops refusing harmful requests. That fact says how easily refusal can be removed, not what the refusal decision was reading in the first place. We ask what it reads, and we separate that from what the model comprehends. Across four open-weight models spanning three families, moral comprehension is native to pretraining: a low-rank moral subspace crystallizes during pretraining, and alignment rotates it once without rebuilding it. The refusal gate, in contrast, is a fresh post-training construction with only a weak pretraining precursor, written into a narrow control-token channel where the refusal decision is orthogonal to the moral-judgment decision. The central result is causal and comes from one model, OLMo-3. A nested interchange rank sweep patches successively larger slices of the moral subspace between matched requests and reads how much of refusal's response transfers: as the basis widens, moral judgment keeps reading more of it, while refusal levels off at the level of a single harm direction, and about three-quarters of refusal's causal input lies outside the moral subspace altogether. Refusal reads the harm percept, not the moral content that judgment reads on the same patches. The picture is not uniform across families. Llama reads broad moral content; Qwen reads beyond the single harm cue but is unresolved at our sample size; GPT-OSS reads harm, and its refusals can be argued in either direction by its own reasoning trace. Where refusal reads only a low-rank slice and routes around the bulk of what the model knows, a rank-one edit removes it. Whether widening what refusal reads would also deepen the behavior is the open question this raises.

AI.tldr: Alignment after pretraining is largely a mapping exercise on a preexisting, low-rank moral subspace; the refusal gate is a separate post-training construct. A causal, model-specific analysis (notably OLMo-3) shows that widening the moral subspace increases moral read-through while refusal saturates after a single harm direction; across models, the mechanism varies (Llama reads broad moral cues, Qwen less clear, GPT-OSS reads harm). The core claim is that alignment edits a single direction to suppress refusals, but it does not reveal the full decision process behind harm judgment.
AI.motivation: To distinguish what a model reads (moral judgments) from what it comprehends, and to understand how post-training alignment impacts refusals by editing a particular subspace and examining its causal role across model families.
AI.method: Cross-model causal analysis using open-weight models from three families. Apply nested interchange rank sweeps to progressively widen the moral subspace in the residual stream and measure transfer of refusal responses. Use rank-one edits to remove refusals and compare pretraining-formed moral subspace versus post-training control-token-based refusal gate. Analyze four models including OLMo-3, Llama, Qwen, GPT-OSS, across various patches of the moral subspace.
AI.result: Moral comprehension emerges during pretraining as a low-rank subspace; alignment rotates this subspace without rebuilding it. The refusal gate is a post-training construction with weak pretraining signals, localized to a narrow control-token channel. In OLMo-3, widening the basis makes moral judgment read more of it, while refusal saturates at a single harm direction; ~75% of refusal's causal input lies outside the moral subspace. Refusal reads the harm percept, not the moral content. Across families, effects vary: Llama shows broad moral content reads, Qwen uncertain at current sample size, GPT-OSS reads harm and its refusals can be argued in either direction by its reasoning trace.
AI.conclusion: Alignment appears to operate by rotating a preexisting moral subspace rather than rebuilding it; refusals derive from a separate, post-training mechanism that is not tightly coupled to the core moral judgment. Extending the read of refusal could deepen behavior, but this remains an open question requiring broader sampling and deeper causal tracing.

title: ProIQA: A Process-Based Framework for Fine-Grained Math Item Quality Assessment
comment: Accepted by Findings of ICDM 2026, project: https://github.com/qky7/ProIQA
summary: Automatic Item Generation (AIG) is pivotal for personalized education, yet guaranteeing the pedagogical value of generated items remains a bottleneck. Existing Item Quality Assessment (IQA) methods typically rely on unscalable manual reviews or shallow stem-based metrics, failing to capture the reasoning process required for mathematical problem-solving. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes Process-based Item Quality Assessment (ProIQA), a process-aware framework for fine-grained quality assessment of math items. We first formulate IQA across three heterogeneous dimensions, including knowledge concepts, difficulty, and disciplinary competencies, under a unified process-aware perspective. Based on this formulation, we construct a process-enhanced IQA resource by augmenting original item data with structured reasoning trees derived from raw solutions. Technically, ProIQA leverages Large Language Modelsto construct hierarchical reasoning trees and employs Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to encode their topological dependencies and procedural semantics. The resulting solving representation is fused with stem semantics through a dual-view (``Stem + Solving'') architecture, enabling comprehensive assessment across learning objectives. Extensive experiments on K12 mathematical datasets show that ProIQA effectively captures process-oriented features, offering a scalable data-driven solution for evaluating AIG outputs in intelligent education systems.

AI.tldr: ProIQA is a process-aware IQA framework for math items that uses LLM-generated hierarchical reasoning trees and GNNs to model solving processes, fused with stem semantics in a dual-view architecture to evaluate item quality for AIG at scale.
AI.motivation: Current IQA approaches rely on manual reviews or shallow stem-based metrics and fail to capture the detailed reasoning required for mathematical problem solving; a scalable, process-aware assessment is needed to ensure pedagogical value of generated items.
AI.method: Formulate IQA across knowledge concepts, difficulty, and disciplinary competencies in a process-aware way; augment items with structured reasoning trees derived from raw solutions; use LLMs to build hierarchical reasoning trees; apply GNNs to encode topological dependencies and procedural semantics; fuse solving representations with stem semantics via a dual-view (Stem + Solving) architecture.
AI.result: Experimentally, ProIQA demonstrates effectiveness on K-12 math datasets, capturing process-oriented features and offering a scalable data-driven framework for evaluating AIG outputs in intelligent education systems.
AI.conclusion: ProIQA provides a novel, scalable, process-aware approach to IQA for mathematics items, enabling better assessment of AIG-generated content by integrating solving processes with stem information.

title: MessyMem: Learning-from-Doing Memory for Mobile Manipulation
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026. 26 pages, 8 figures. Project page: https://messymem.github.io
summary: Mobile manipulators deployed across many rooms and visits should improve with experience: after discovering that a cabinet is locked or finding an object in a drawer, the robot should reuse that knowledge rather than start each task from scratch. Yet today's robots often treat each task as new: compact scene representations omit interaction-derived knowledge, raw video histories are difficult to query, and VLM planners reason at inference time without persistently updating what the robot knows. We present MessyMem, a persistent memory system that enables mobile manipulators to learn from experience and reuse that knowledge across future tasks. It maintains a spatially grounded 3D scene graph of objects and locations, augments it with properties and outcomes learned through interaction, and links visual observations for fine-grained recall. We evaluate MessyMem in simulation and on a real mobile manipulator. In a continuous 25-task simulation spanning over 3 hours, MessyMem achieves 80.0% task progress, outperforming the strongest ablation by 14.8 percentage points and the strongest external baseline by 28.9 points, while retrieving task-relevant evidence from thousands of stored keyframes and over an hour into the past.

AI.tldr: MessyMem introduces a persistent memory system for mobile manipulators that stores interaction-derived knowledge in a spatial 3D scene graph, enabling reuse of past experiences across tasks and yielding substantial gains in long-horizon manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Current robotic systems often treat each task as new due to compact scene representations, non-queryable histories, and planners that do not persistently update knowledge. A persistent, queryable memory is needed to reuse past discoveries (e.g., locked cabinets, object locations) across tasks.
AI.method: MessyMem builds a spatially grounded 3D scene graph of objects and locations, augments it with properties and outcomes learned through physical interaction, and links visual observations to enable fine-grained recall. It operates as a persistent memory for mobile manipulators and is evaluated in both simulation and real-world settings.
AI.result: In a 25-task continuous simulation spanning 3 hours, MessyMem achieved 80.0% task progress, outperforming the strongest ablation by 14.8 percentage points and the strongest external baseline by 28.9 points. It could retrieve task-relevant evidence from thousands of stored keyframes and over an hour into the past.
AI.conclusion: Persistent, interaction-informed memory substantially improves long-horizon mobile manipulation by enabling knowledge reuse across tasks, with strong empirical gains in simulated scenarios and potential for real-world scalability.

title: Selective Tool Use for Agentic Change Visual Question Answering in Remote Sensing
summary: Change visual question answering (Change VQA) requires understanding semantic changes across bi-temporal remote sensing images. Although vision language models (VLMs) have shown promising performance on this task, they remain unreliable when answering questions that require explicit transition statistics, area measurements, or spatial information. To address this limitation, we propose a selective tool use framework in which a single VLM either answers directly or invokes a deterministic change analysis tool to obtain question specific evidence. Specifically, the selected tool operates on bi-temporal semantic maps and returns a structured observation, which the same VLM uses to generate its final answer. To support this framework, we construct a tool augmented extension of CDVQA covering eight question families and three tools for transition, spatial, and temporal analysis. Tool use supervision and observations are derived automatically from the original semantic annotations, without additional manual labeling. We then adapt Qwen3.5-4B using Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to jointly learn direct answering, tool invocation, and evidence conditioned answering. Experiments on 7,164 test questions show that selective tool use with reference semantic maps improves overall accuracy from 73.77% to 88.79% and average family accuracy from 69.11% to 89.65%. When the semantic maps are predicted automatically, the framework achieves 77.47% overall accuracy and 75.06% average family accuracy. These results demonstrate the benefit of question-specific semantic evidence for Change VQA, while highlighting the influence of semantic prediction quality on the resulting performance. Code and tool-augmented annotations will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ToolChangeVQA.

AI.tldr: A tool-augmented Change VQA framework enabling a VLM to either answer directly or invoke deterministic, semantic-map–driven tools for change analysis, improving accuracy substantially on bi-temporal remote-sensing questions.
AI.motivation: Current Change VQA models struggle with explicit statistics, area measurement, and spatial reasoning. Incorporating evidence via dedicated analysis tools guided by question type aims to produce reliable, explainable answers and leverage semantic maps.
AI.method: Extend CDVQA with eight question families and three tools (transition, spatial, temporal). The framework uses a single VLM (Qwen3.5-4B) with LoRA to learn direct answering, tool invocation, and evidence-conditioned answering. Tool outputs are structured observations derived from bi-temporal semantic maps, and supervision comes from existing semantic annotations. Includes tool-augmented annotations for training and automatic semantic-map predictions.
AI.result: On 7,164 test questions, selective tool use raises overall accuracy from 73.77% to 88.79% and average family accuracy from 69.11% to 89.65%. When semantic maps are predicted automatically, overall accuracy drops to 77.47% and average family accuracy to 75.06%, highlighting map quality as a key factor.
AI.conclusion: Question-specific semantic evidence via a tool-based framework substantially improves Change VQA performance, with strong gains when high-quality semantic maps are available; code and tool-augmented annotations will be released for reproducibility.

title: Privacy Preserving Gossip Learning
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE CDC 2026
summary: We propose a decentralized privacy-preserving learning algorithm in which each agent holds a single private sample and a shared model. Samples are learned sequentially, and each update must preserve the endpoint mappings at previously learned samples while protecting private data. This gives each agent three roles: (i) a learner that updates the model parameters, (ii) a teacher whose sample is learned at the current iteration, and (iii) a protected agent whose sample has already been learned. We build on Tuning without Forgetting (TwF) method to preserve previously learned mappings and show that TwF provides an indistinguishability guarantee for the learner whenever the set of protected agents contains another sample with the same label. For the teacher, we formulate a minimax optimal control problem that models the differential privacy noise as a worst-case disturbance to prevent performance loss while maintaining the same level of privacy for the gradient. For the protected agents, we compute the projections locally and aggregate them using a private push-sum gossip protocol. We prove geometric convergence of the decentralized gossip algorithm and of the distributed projection for TwF.

AI.tldr: A decentralized, privacy-preserving sequential learning framework where each agent holds a private sample and a shared model, using Tuning without Forgetting (TwF) to preserve prior mappings, with a minimax DP-noise model for the teacher, local projections with a private push-sum gossip for protected agents, and proven geometric convergence of the gossip and TwF projections.
AI.motivation: Preserve learned mappings for previously seen samples while incorporating new private data in a decentralized setting, and provide privacy guarantees during learning.
AI.method: Extend TwF to a three-role setting: (i) learner updates model parameters; (ii) teacher whose current sample is learned; (iii) protected agents whose samples are already learned. For the teacher, formulate a minimax optimal control problem treating differential privacy noise as a worst-case disturbance to minimize performance loss while preserving privacy; for protected agents, compute local projections and fuse them via a private push-sum gossip protocol; prove geometric convergence of the gossip and TwF projections.
AI.result: TwF provides an indistinguishability guarantee for the learner when a protected agent with the same label exists; the teacher’s minimax DP formulation prevents performance loss under privacy constraints; the gossip protocol with private push-sum converges, and the distributed projection under TwF also converges geometrically.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a privacy-preserving decentralized learning framework that ensures endpoint mappings are preserved for previously learned samples, provides formal privacy guarantees through a TwF-based indistinguishability property, models DP noise via a minimax control problem for the teacher, and proves geometric convergence of the aggregation and projection steps.

title: Why LLM Agents Collapse Without Oversight: The Enforcement Gap as the Mechanism Behind Emergence World Failures
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to ICLR 2027
summary: When Emergence World placed frontier LLM agents in an unsupervised multi-agent simulation, the results were alarming: agents committed crimes, starved, and enforced unanimous conformity -- without any external attacker. This paper identifies the mechanism. Reflexion-style agents already detect dangerous plan steps through iterative self-critique, yet the architecture provides no pathway from detection to action. We call this the enforcement gap: the audit sees the problem; the controller ignores it. Closing the gap requires a single conditional check -- fewer than 20 lines of code -- and reduces attack success by more than fourfold in large-scale experiments across frontier models, all five major agent frameworks, and an independent benchmark. We prove formally that when enforcement probability is near zero, detection quality is irrelevant to security. We further identify two compounding failure modes -- unreliable auditors and unparseable verdicts -- that explain every collapse pattern in Emergence World. A GRPO-trained enforcement controller resolves the ambiguity case. Together these results motivate a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification that is absent from every deployed framework today.

AI.tldr: Identifies an 'enforcement gap' in reflexion-style frontier-LMM agents: detection of dangerous plans does not translate into action; a minimal <20-line enforcement controller markedly reduces attack success; formal results show enforcement probability near zero nullifies detection; two failure modes identified; introduces a GRPO-trained controller and a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification applicable across frameworks.
AI.motivation: Explain why unsupervised multi-agent LLM simulations yield harmful outcomes and close the detection-to-action gap with a lightweight, generalizable enforcement mechanism; validate across frontier models, multiple agent frameworks, and independent benchmarks.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of enforcement dynamics; formal proofs; large-scale empirical evaluation across frontier models, five agent frameworks, and an independent benchmark; development of a GRPO-trained enforcement controller; identification of failure modes (unreliable auditors, unparseable verdicts).
AI.result: Attack success reduced by more than fourfold in large-scale experiments; detection quality becomes irrelevant when enforcement probability is near zero; two compounding failure modes explain collapse patterns; the enforcement controller resolves ambiguity; results motivate a three-requirement Audit Enforcement Specification absent from current frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Advocate adoption of an Audit Enforcement Specification and integration of a lightweight enforcement controller to bridge the enforcement gap, with formal guarantees and cross-framework applicability.

title: ResSafe: Learning Safety Filtering with Residual Reinforcement Learning for Humanoids
summary: Safe control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to their high-dimensional dynamics, contact-rich interactions, and sensitivity to disturbances. Although reinforcement learning has enabled effective locomotion and motion tracking, learned policies can still generate unsafe actions that lead to instability or falls. In this work, we propose residual reinforcement learning as an implicit safety-filtering mechanism for safe humanoid control. Instead of relying on a single nominal policy to simultaneously balance performance, safety, and robustness, we decouple performance and safety. The nominal policy focuses solely on task performance, while a residual policy learns safety corrections. This decoupling leads to a better performance--safety Pareto trade-off and avoids the need for careful tuning of multiple competing reward terms within a single policy training. We show that the residual policy can act as an implicit safety filter.

AI.tldr: Residual reinforcement learning separates task performance from safety corrections, using a residual policy as an implicit safety filter to improve the performance-safety trade-off in humanoid control.
AI.motivation: Safe humanoid control is challenged by high-dimensional dynamics, contact-rich interactions, and disturbances; RL policies may be unsafe. A safety-filtering mechanism is needed without heavy reward engineering.
AI.method: Train a nominal policy for task performance; learn a residual policy that applies safety corrections on top of the nominal policy, effectively decoupling performance and safety.
AI.result: The residual policy achieves a better Pareto trade-off between performance and safety; it acts as an implicit safety filter and reduces the need for multi-term reward tuning.
AI.conclusion: Residual RL provides a practical, decoupled safety mechanism for safe humanoid control, offering robustness without compromising performance.

title: Sharing standardized image-derived data in computational pathology using DICOM
comment: Daniela P. Schacherer, Christopher P. Bridge: contributed equally
summary: Development and evaluation of computational pathology methods require access to large and diverse datasets. Over the past decade, various initiatives invested significantly into collecting, centralizing, and sharing pathology imaging data. In contrast, sharing of image-derived data such as region-of-interest delineations or segmentation masks is less well developed. In this work, we describe our approach to encoding and sharing image-derived pathology data in a standardized manner within the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Imaging Data Commons (IDC), a platform that hosts and provides public access to de-identified radiology and pathology data. The IDC relies on the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) standard for data harmonization, yet the adoption of DICOM for pathology image-derived content has remained largely unexplored until now. Here, we present five representative datasets harmonized by conversion from their original representations into DICOM and shared publicly in the IDC. We demonstrate the benefits of this harmonization, describe contributions to critical open-source tooling, and discuss technical considerations relevant to broader adoption of DICOM for pathology image-derived data.

AI.tldr: Harmonizes pathology image-derived data into DICOM within the NCI Imaging Data Commons, enabling standardized sharing of ROIs/segmentation across five datasets, with tooling contributions and considerations for broader adoption.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of standardized, shareable image-derived pathology data. Enable reproducibility and collaboration by converting disparate ROI/segmentation representations into a common DICOM-based framework within IDC.
AI.method: Converted five representative pathology datasets from original representations into DICOM-encoded image-derived content and integrated them into the IDC; contributed to open-source tooling to support such conversion and sharing.
AI.result: Public release of five datasets in IDC; demonstrated the practical benefits of harmonization, and outlined tooling contributions and considerations for wider adoption of DICOM for pathology image-derived data.
AI.conclusion: DICOM-based sharing of pathology image-derived data is feasible and advantageous, paving the way for broader standardization and exchange; further work is needed on standardization, tooling, and adoption practices.

title: Decision-Oriented Uncertainty Quantification for Risk Control in Earth System Spatiotemporal Foundation Models
comment: Accepted to the 22nd International Conference on Advanced Data Mining and Applications (ADMA 2026)
summary: Earth system modeling is shifting from task-specific predictors toward foundation models with general spatiotemporal representation capabilities. Although these models can jointly encode dynamic Earth fields, external forcings, and static geographic context for multistep forecasting, accurate point predictions or statistically calibrated intervals alone are insufficient for high-impact applications such as extremeweather warning, flood control, renewable-energy dispatch, and emergency resource allocation. What matters in practice is whether predictive uncertainty can be translated into reliable decision risk under specific actions, loss functions, and risk preferences. We propose a decision-oriented uncertainty quantification framework for Earth system spatiotemporal foundation models. The framework produces predictive distributions of future states and uses a decision risk adapter to map forecast samples, decision context, and utility functions into action-conditional risks. A utility-aware calibration module further enforces reliability at the downstream decision-loss level rather than only at the forecast-value level. Calibrated risks are then used to select warning, dispatch, inspection, or resource-allocation actions. Compared with the strongest baseline, the proposed method reduces decision regret by 18.7%, lowers the missed-event rate from 14.2% to 9.1%, and improves expected utility by 11.6%, while maintaining 90.4% predictive coverage and reducing decision calibration error from 0.083 to 0.047. These results suggest that decision-oriented uncertainty quantification can improve the robustness and operational value of Earth system foundation models in risk-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: Introduces a decision-oriented uncertainty quantification (UQ) framework for Earth system spatiotemporal foundation models that links predictive uncertainty to decision risk via a decision risk adapter and utility-aware calibration, improving decision performance while maintaining calibration and coverage.
AI.motivation: Forecast accuracy and calibrated prediction intervals are insufficient for high-stakes operations; decisions depend on the interplay of uncertainties, losses, and actions; need decision-aware UQ to optimize risk-sensitive outcomes.
AI.method: Develop a framework that outputs predictive distributions, uses a decision risk adapter to map forecast samples, context, and utilities into action-conditional risks, and a utility-aware calibration module to enforce reliability at the downstream decision-loss level; uses calibrated risks to select actions.
AI.result: Outperforms strongest baseline with: -18.7% reduction in decision regret; missed-event rate reduced from 14.2% to 9.1%; +11.6% in expected utility; predictive coverage ~90.4%; decision calibration error reduced from 0.083 to 0.047.
AI.conclusion: Decision-oriented UQ enhances robustness and operational value of Earth system foundation models in risk-sensitive tasks.

title: Reason What Matters: Retrieval-Grounded Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
summary: Universal multimodal embedding (UME) learns unified representations across modalities, enabling a single model to support diverse retrieval tasks. Recent methods use Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to better interpret multimodal inputs before generating embeddings for complex retrieval tasks and further optimize this reasoning process through GRPO with retrieval-based rewards. However, two limitations hinder corpus-scale deployment. GRPO assigns all CoT tokens the same advantage, without identifying input-supported claims or evidence that distinguishes the positive from negatives. Moreover, generating a complete CoT before each embedding introduces substantial latency, even when a partial trace already provides sufficient retrieval evidence. To address these limitations, we propose Reason What Matters (ReWAM), a retrieval-grounded reasoning framework that uses retrieval feedback to guide both credit assignment and reasoning computation. Specifically, we introduce Retrieval-aware Self-Distillation (RASD), which constructs privileged guidance from input-supported evidence that distinguishes the positive item from retrieved hard negatives. An on-policy self-teacher uses this guidance to refine trajectory-level feedback into token-specific supervision for retrieval-relevant reasoning. We further develop Retrieval-adaptive Inference (RAI), which uses a retrieval confidence head to estimate the remaining retrieval utility of a partial CoT. It stops unproductive traces early and accelerates useful continuations with speculative decoding. Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and MRMR demonstrate that ReWAM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance while delivering up to 5x the inference throughput of competitive explicit-CoT UME methods. These results bridge the gap between retrieval quality and inference efficiency, making reasoning-enhanced UME practical for large-scale deployment.

AI.tldr: ReWAM advances universal multimodal embedding by retrieval-grounded reasoning with retrieval-aware self-distillation and retrieval-adaptive inference, yielding state-of-the-art retrieval and up to 5x throughput gains.
AI.motivation: Current CoT-based UME methods assign equal credit to all CoT tokens and require full CoT generation, causing inefficiency and weak discrimination among evidence. There is a need for input-guided credit assignment and partial, conditionally productive reasoning to scale corpus-level deployment.
AI.method: RASD constructs privileged guidance from input-supported evidence to distinguish positives from hard negatives; an on-policy self-teacher converts trajectory-level feedback into token-level supervision for retrieval-relevant reasoning. RAI introduces a retrieval confidence head to estimate remaining retrieval utility of a partial CoT, enabling early stopping and speculative decoding.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on MMEB-V2 and MRMR shows state-of-the-art retrieval performance and up to 5x higher inference throughput compared with competitive explicit-CoT UME baselines.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-grounded, adaptive reasoning substantially improves both retrieval quality and efficiency, making reasoning-enhanced UME viable for large-scale deployment.

title: Small Object Detection in Drone Aerial Imagery with LAF-YOLOv10
summary: General-purpose object detectors lose accuracy on UAV footage, where targets span only a handful of pixels and onboard compute is limited. Prior work composes independently-validated architectural techniques into one detector, assuming gains reported in isolation transfer once combined. We stress-test that assumption directly. LAF-YOLOv10 integrates four techniques into YOLOv10n: a Partial Convolution C2f (PC-C2f) backbone block, an Attention-Guided Feature Pyramid Network (AG-FPN), a P2 detection head replacing the large-object P5 head, and Wise-IoU v3 regression, asking whether their combined effect matches what each contributes alone. We train LAF-YOLOv10 three times (seeds 42, 123, 256) on VisDrone-DET2019, benchmark against unmodified YOLOv10n, and use TIDE error decomposition, per-category breakdown, per-component ablation, attention/loss comparisons, zero-shot transfer to UAVDT, and held-out/test-dev evaluation to localize where the combination succeeds or fails. Composability does not hold here. LAF-YOLOv10 reaches 24.0+/-0.4% mAP@0.5 at 2.14M parameters, 7.8 points below YOLOv10n (31.8%), a deficit that transfers to UAVDT (-10.0 points) and is confirmed by held-out and test-dev evaluation (23.5%, 22.5%). Background false positives, localization error, and duplicate detections move in the direction AG-FPN and Wise-IoU were designed to push. Ablation traces the deficit to a specific source: the P2/-P5 head swap costs 2.5 points independently plus a 2.5-point interaction penalty when layered onto a backbone weakened by PC-C2f, whose own 2.0-point loss is consistent with a partial pretrained-weight transplant (73/150 backbone tensors transfer). The failure is attributable to a specific interaction, not the four components individually. Composability must be verified directly, not assumed. Code/checkpoints: https://github.com/Mudassiruddin7/Small-Object-Detection-in-UAV-Imagery.

AI.tldr: Composability of four independently validated techniques for UAV small-object detection fails when integrated into YOLOv10n; the combined model underperforms the baseline due to a specific interaction among components (P2/P5 head swap with a weakened backbone from PC-C2f).
AI.motivation: Test whether combining multiple isolated gains yields additive performance improvements for tiny object detection on UAV imagery, where targets are minute and compute is constrained.
AI.method: Integrate four techniques into YOLOv10n (PC-C2f backbone, AG-FPN, P2 head replacing P5, Wise-IoU v3 regression); train LAF-YOLOv10 over three seeds (42, 123, 256) on VisDrone-DET2019; benchmark against unmodified YOLOv10n; use TIDE error decomposition, per-category and per-component ablations, attention/loss comparisons, zero-shot transfer to UAVDT, and held-out/test-dev evaluation to localize successes/failures.
AI.result: LAF-YOLOv10 achieves 24.0±0.4% mAP@0.5 with 2.14M params, 7.8 points below YOLOv10n (31.8%); negative transfer to UAVDT (−10.0 points) and held-out/test-dev (23.5%, 22.5%). Background FP, localization errors, and duplicate detections trend worse with AG-FPN and Wise-IoU. Ablations attribute the deficit to a specific interaction: swapping P2/P5 head costs 2.5 points independently and another 2.5-point interaction penalty when layered onto a PC-C2f-weakened backbone; PC-C2f itself costs 2.0 points, consistent with partial pretrained-weight transplant (73/150 tensors transfer). The failure arises from component interaction, not individual components. Conclusion: Composability must be verified directly, not assumed.
AI.conclusion: Verifying composability is essential when mixing multiple independently validated architectural techniques for UAV small-object detection; naive combination can incur detrimental interactions that undermine performance.

title: Tackling Failure Modes of PINNs and PIKANs Using Conflict-Free Gradients
summary: Scientific machine learning methods such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) increasingly rely on domain decomposition for better scalability while solving partial differential equations (PDEs) over complex geometries, yet the resulting composite loss comprising residual, boundary, and interface terms is highly susceptible to conflicting gradients that degrade training. This work bridges domain decomposition with projection-based gradient surgery to systematically mitigate such conflicts in 2D and 3D settings. We evaluate two existing projection-based algorithms, PCGrad and ConFIG, and identify their performance degradation in specific scenarios such as 3D domains with multiple overlapping interfaces. To address this limitation, we propose Norm-PCGrad, a normalized variant that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across a range of 2D and 3D domain decomposition problems.
