Across the benchmarks considered, Norm-PCGrad consistently achieves the lowest relative $L_2$ error compared to training without gradient surgery as well as to existing algorithms such as PCGrad and ConFIG, while incurring negligible additional computational overhead. To improve computational efficiency of domain decomposition frameworks such as Extended PINN (XPINN), we propose replacing vanilla PINNs in selected subdomains with separable architectures such as Separable PINN (SPINN), reducing the computational cost from quadratic (or cubic) to linear. We additionally demonstrate that gradient surgery extends to physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs), yielding substantial accuracy improvements for 3D domain decomposition and confirming the generality of the proposed approach across network architectures.

AI.tldr: Norm-PCGrad with domain-decomposition PINNs improves optimization by mitigating gradient conflicts; shows state-of-the-art accuracy in 2D/3D, with SPINN for efficiency and applicability to PIKANs.
AI.motivation: Domain-decomposition PINNs suffer from conflicting gradients among residual, boundary, and interface losses, hindering training stability and accuracy; need robust gradient mitigation for scalable, complex geometries.
AI.method: Evaluate existing gradient-surgery methods PCGrad and ConFIG; introduce Norm-PCGrad (normalized projection-based Gradients); apply SPINN in selected subdomains to reduce computation; extend gradient surgery to PI-Kernel ANNs (PIKANs); test across 2D/3D benchmarks; assess computational overhead.
AI.result: Norm-PCGrad achieves lowest relative L2 error across 2D/3D benchmarks compared to no-gradient-surgery and to PCGrad/ConFIG, with negligible overhead; SPINN reduces cost from quadratic/cubic to linear; gradient surgery extends to PIKANs with substantial accuracy gains in 3D; overall improved robustness and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Normalized projection-based gradient surgery yields state-of-the-art performance for domain-decomposition PINNs across architectures; efficiency gains via separable networks; approach generalizes to PIKANs, suggesting broad applicability to physics-informed ML with composite losses.

title: Evaluation Metrics for Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly formalized as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which an agent maximizes expected reward while keeping its expected cumulative cost below a specified safety bound. Existing safe RL benchmarks predominantly report whether an algorithm is safe on average, following this expectation-based guarantee. We argue that this convention is insufficient to reliably characterize an algorithm's true safety: it fails to capture how often and how severely the safety bound is violated, whether this holds consistently across tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior is representative of behavior of the final converged policy. Therefore, we introduce (i) evaluation metrics for safe RL that address each of these concerns and in addition allow for aggregation across tasks and safety bounds. We furthermore define (ii) a safety tier system to systematically categorize and compare algorithms in terms of safety and reliability at both training and for a final policy. Using this framework, we provide (iii) an empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks. Our results show that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal information the other metrics cannot. We therefore recommend reporting all three jointly, rather than compressing this information into a single value, as is common practice. We provide SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support the reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.

AI.tldr: Proposes a comprehensive evaluation framework for safe RL, introducing new metrics, a safety tier system, and SafeRLEval to assess safety beyond average guarantees.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation in safe RL relies on expectation-based safety, which obscures how often/severely safety bounds are violated, inconsistency across tasks/bounds, and training-time versus final policy behavior.
AI.method: (i) Define evaluation metrics addressing violation frequency/severity and cross-task/bound aggregation; (ii) introduce a safety tier system to categorize algorithms by safety and reliability; (iii) perform empirical safety evaluations across multiple safety navigation tasks; (iv) release SafeRLEval as an open-source evaluation suite.
AI.result: Aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task-/bound-specific results reveal information not captured by a single aggregate value; training-time and final-policy safety can diverge; three-report approach recommended; availability of SafeRLEval for future research.
AI.conclusion: Adopt multi-metric, distributional, and task-/bound-specific reporting to reliably characterize safety; use the safety tier system for systematic comparison; standardize evaluation with SafeRLEval.

title: A Building as a Repository: KIR, a Typed Intermediate Representation for Agent-Authored Building Information Models
comment: 13-page paper and 10-page supplement; 8 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/5vbkgsghhh-hash/kir
summary: Autonomous agents that author building information models need more than access to a host API. They need a representation of what they intended, what a compiler decided on their behalf, what was refused, what was observed after execution and what remains unknown. We present KIR, a typed intermediate representation in which a building is authored as a program held in a versioned repository and lowered to host applications as build targets. KIR is organised around seven ways in which a generator writing into a stateful, partially observable host goes silently wrong, and gives each a representation in data: ambiguous selectors become typed refusals with candidates; defaults keep their provenance; obligations that will not be checked are named before execution; vacuous witnesses are rejected statically; a lost transaction response becomes the state UNCONFIRMED with a verify-before-retry rule; the reverse path obeys a census invariant; and decisions are bound by digest to the state they were made against. On a pinned snapshot with 83 operation contracts and Revit as the only backend, offline experiments refuse 29 of 42 stress-test programs with diagnostic codes and no uncaught exception, name 38 of 377 witness obligations as unwitnessable, admit 31 of 100 combinations of execution, witness and acceptance states under seven stated invariants, and find no vacuous witness in 219 certificate runs; a 60-storey tower is 11,263 characters as KIR against 3,709,235 characters of emitted C#. Native Revit runs are reported from project records and kept separate from reproduced results. A controlled comparison with agents that write host code directly is specified but not yet executed; it is the principal open question.

AI.tldr: KIR is a typed intermediate representation for authoring building information models as programs; it encodes intent, compiler decisions, refusals, observations, and unknowns within a versioned repository; demonstrates diagnostic structure and significant compression against a Revit backend; principal open question: comparison with agents that write host code directly.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, provenance-rich representation for agents interacting with stateful, partially observable hosts (e.g., building information models), enabling diagnosis, debugging, and verification of the synthesis process.
AI.method: Proposes KIR organized around seven silent failure modes of a generator writing into a stateful, partially observable host; defines data representations for: ambiguous selectors turning into typed refusals with candidates; defaults preserving provenance; obligations that will not be checked named before execution; vacuous witnesses rejected statically; a lost transaction response labeled UNCONFIRMED with a verify-before-retry rule; a census invariant for the reverse path; and decisions bound by digest to the state they pertain to. Evaluation on a pinned snapshot with 83 operation contracts invoking Revit as the only backend, yielding: offline experiments refusing 29 of 42 stress-test programs with diagnostic codes and no uncaught exception; naming 38 of 377 witness obligations as unwitnessable; admitting 31 of 100 combinations of execution, witness and acceptance states under seven invariants; finding no vacuous witness in 219 certificate runs; and a 60-storey tower described by 11,263 characters in KIR versus 3,709,235 characters of emitted C#. Native Revit runs are reported from project records and kept separate from reproduced results. A controlled comparison with agents that write host code directly is specified but not yet executed; it remains the principal open question.
AI.result: Empirical results show KIR’s ability to encode programs and their provenance under seven failure modes, yielding diagnostic codes for refusals and invariants; substantial compression relative to emitted host code (11,263 chars in KIR vs 3.7M chars of C# for a 60-storey tower); multiple metrics indicating partial success across refusals, unwitnessables, and execution/invariant combinations; back-end-specific results limited to Revit; no uncaught exceptions in reported runs; native Revit results are separate from reproduced results.
AI.conclusion: KIR offers a provenance-rich, constraint-aware representation that exposes where and why a synthesis may fail silently; it demonstrates compression and diagnostic advantages but its comparative effectiveness against generators that produce host code directly remains untested and requires broader back-end validation and more experiments.

title: Semantic Fibers and Cross-Gram Interference: A Calculus of Safety Drift in Overcomplete Representations
summary:
A deployed language model may refuse a harmful request in English yet comply with its faithful translation, revealing a cross-lingual safety failure that cannot be characterized reliably by output behavior alone. We formalize this phenomenon through an audited equivalence relation and show that, for a declared quotient, representation, metric, feature dictionary, scoring head, threshold, and contrast model, the resulting safety drift admits an exact linear-algebraic characterization. Specifically, the drift is a cross-Gram functional of the within-fiber contrast; its worst admissible value is a support function, while margin invariance is characterized by an annihilator condition.
  We introduce an intrinsic calibrated exposure measure, governed by the leverage duality $χ^2=1/\ell-1$, which separates observed drift into three diagnostically distinct regimes: a reader fault removable by recalibration, an exact correction that is too ill-conditioned to be reliable, and a representation-level collision that no readout-only intervention can remove. Thus, identical observed exposure can lead to fundamentally different remediation verdicts. The framework also extends to cone-valued safety heads. An untied order-swap identity provides a diagnostic for the linear control interface; its calibration-state residual predicts a distinct three-control composition error on unseen states and targets, achieving median Spearman correlation $0.964$, compared with $0.269$ for a static cross-Gram baseline. etc.....

AI.tldr: A formal framework for cross-lingual safety drift in language models using an audited equivalence relation and linear-algebraic invariants; it introduces an exposure-based diagnostic that partition drift into three regimes, plus a highly predictive diagnostic for linear control interfaces, suggesting principled remediation limits.
AI.motivation: To understand and diagnose cross-lingual safety failures where safe behavior in one language does not translate to other languages, beyond analysis of raw outputs.
AI.method: Define an audited equivalence relation for declared quotients (representation, metric, feature dictionary, scoring head, threshold, and contrast model). Model safety drift as a cross-Gram functional of the within-fiber contrast; characterize worst-case drift as a support function; describe margin invariance via an annihilator condition. Introduce an intrinsic calibrated exposure measure governed by leverage duality χ^2=1/ℓ−1. Extend framework to cone-valued safety heads. Propose an untied order-swap identity as a diagnostic for the linear control interface. Use calibration-state residuals to predict a three-control composition error on unseen states and targets; report high Spearman correlation (median 0.964) relative to a static cross-Gram baseline (0.269).
AI.result: Provides an exact linear-algebraic characterization of cross-lingual safety drift and a diagnostic taxonomy—reader-fault removable by recalibration, exact-but-ill-conditioned correction, and representation-level collision with readout-limited remediation. Demonstrates a high-correlation diagnostic predictor for control composition errors across unseen states, and extends to cone-valued safety heads.
AI.conclusion: Drift in cross-lingual safety is analyzable via an audited equivalence framework with an exposure-based taxonomy; some drifts are remediable by calibration, others require representation-level fixes beyond readout, and the approach yields strong diagnostic correlations, suggesting principled approaches to safety in multilingual deployments.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Pretrained Language Models for Time-Series Forecasting
summary: We study the adaptation of pretrained language models to univariate time-series forecasting through a parameter-efficient transfer learning framework, with the goal of understanding which design choices drive effective cross-modal transfer. While language models operate on discrete textual tokens, time series consist of continuous numerical observations with temporal dependencies. To bridge this modality gap, we project fixed-length time-series patches directly into the embedding space of a pretrained GPT-2 backbone, bypassing textual tokenization and treating the Transformer as a generic sequence encoder. Through controlled ablation studies on seven benchmark datasets spanning energy, weather, traffic, and finance, we analyze the effects of (i)~representation strategy (continuous embeddings versus textual serialisation), (ii)~adaptation regime (frozen backbone versus partial or full fine-tuning), (iii)~architectural components such as adapters, pooling strategies, and prediction heads, and (iv)~input context length. Continuous patch-based embeddings consistently outperform textual prompting and randomly initialised backbones. The adapted pipeline attains MASE within the range of specialised forecasting architectures while updating less than 1\% of total model parameters. Results further indicate that freezing the pretrained backbone and training lightweight projection and adapter modules provides a favourable accuracy--efficiency trade-off with stable behaviour across varying context lengths.

AI.tldr: Pretrained GPT-2 can be repurposed for univariate time-series forecasting via continuous patch embeddings; freezing the backbone with lightweight adapters yields competitive performance at <1% trainable parameters; continuous embeddings outperform textual serialization and random backbones across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Leverage large language models for cross-modal transfer to numerical time-series forecasting in a parameter-efficient way.
AI.method: Project fixed-length time-series patches into the GPT-2 embedding space to bypass tokenization; compare continuous embeddings vs textual serialization; explore frozen, partial, and full fine-tuning; incorporate adapters, pooling strategies, and prediction heads; evaluate across seven datasets (energy, weather, traffic, finance) and varying context lengths.
AI.result: Continuous patch-based embeddings outperform textual prompts and randomly initialized backbones; the adapted pipeline attains MASE comparable to specialized forecasting architectures while updating <1% of parameters; freezing the backbone with lightweight projection and adapters provides favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off with stable behavior across context lengths.
AI.conclusion: Continuous patch embeddings enable effective cross-modal transfer for time-series forecasting; key design choices (representation, adaptation regime, adapters) significantly influence performance, offering a scalable, parameter-efficient forecasting framework.

title: Reverse Spatio-Temporal Disease Progression Modelling
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at SASHIMI 2026, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026
summary: Deep learning-based spatio-temporal disease progression models commonly overlook the incubation period of progressive diseases, limiting the use of those models in early interventions, which are vital for not easily reversible diseases such as Alzheimer's. This is because, the existing deep learning based longitudinal disease-progression models are almost always run forward: from an observed baseline they predict future decline. In many clinical settings, however, imaging begins only after pathology is suspected or already visible, the earlier, healthier patient-specific reference was never acquired. To address this, we propose to study reverse disease progression prediction: given later diseased anatomy, reconstruct the unobserved healthier anatomy that preceded it. We use a two-stage model in which a frozen 3D vector-quantised autoencoder defines a compact discrete latent space, while a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) learns continuous-time dynamics in that space. A recurrent encoder reads late observations in reverse temporal order, initialises the latent state, and the ODE is integrated backwards across the trajectory. On a controlled Morpho-MNIST benchmark with a sinusoidal perturbation, our model successfully recovered the unseen previous states from later observations of the non-monotonic trajectory. On longitudinal brain MRIs from Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, at the task to recover the previous unseen trajectory towards healthy states of the patients from observed later diseased states, our model outperforms the baselines that uses copy-nearest and mean-observed, with positive disease-reversal scores in every diagnostic stratum. We hope that our work can provide insights and tools towards discovering the incubation periods from single-shot scans, and developing early interventions of diseases based on imaging.

AI.tldr: Introduces reverse disease progression modeling using a frozen VQ-VAE and Neural ODE to reconstruct prior healthy states from later diseased imaging; demonstrates on Morpho-MNIST and ADNI with improved recovery over baselines.
AI.motivation: Clinical imaging often captures patients after pathology onset; forward-time progression models cannot recover the unseen healthier states, limiting early intervention insights. Estimating incubation periods from imaging could enable earlier interventions for non-reversibly progressive diseases like Alzheimer's.
AI.method: Two-stage model: (1) a frozen 3D vector-quantised autoencoder defines a compact discrete latent space; (2) a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation learns continuous-time dynamics in that latent space. A recurrent encoder reads late observations in reverse temporal order, initializes the latent state, and the ODE is integrated backwards across the trajectory. Evaluation on Morpho-MNIST with sinusoidal perturbation and on longitudinal brain MRIs from ADNI; baselines include copy-nearest and mean-observed; performance metric is disease-reversal scores.
AI.result: On Morpho-MNIST, the model successfully recovers unseen previous states from later observations of non-monotonic trajectories. On ADNI MRI data, it outperforms baselines in recovering prior trajectories toward health, with positive disease-reversal scores in every diagnostic stratum.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a pathway to estimate incubation periods from single-scan data and to inform early interventions, though further validation and generalization to diverse diseases are needed.

title: Interpolation Is Not Invariance: Pair Count Is Not Coverage in Transformation Audits
summary:
Counting equivalent pairs is a common way to report transformation-audit coverage, but it can substantially overstate the constraints imposed by an audit: pairs generated from the same semantic object are correlated, and complete orbit graphs contain algebraically redundant edges. We therefore distinguish four complementary quantities---edge count $m$, effective contrast rank $s$, population support rank $r$, and graph spectral gap $η$---and characterize their roles in audit coverage and deployment reliability. Under a rank-$r$ Gaussian contrast model, a population-invariant calibrated reader exists exactly when the anchor has a component in $\ker T$. When an audit has rank $s < r$, its unobserved risk is $R^\star/U$, with $U \sim \operatorname{Beta}((r-s)/2,s/2)$; when $s \ge r$, exact calibrated interpolation is infeasible. The same distinction appears in orbit topology: a spanning tree imposes the same exact-null constraints as a complete graph, while a sharp graph Poincare inequality propagates edge-level drift to an entire orbit at a cost proportional to $1/η$. Cyclic audits can additionally yield zero pair-level leave-one-out error without holding out any semantic object.
  To address these failures, we derive exact block-Woodbury leave-one-orbit-out updates and introduce a source-disjoint deployment gate over finitely many candidate readers. The gate retains the original reader unless uncertainty bounds certify lower drift within a prescribed clean-utility budget. etc..

AI.tldr: The paper refines transformation-audit coverage by separating correlated pair effects from true constraints via four metrics (edge count m, effective contrast rank s, population support rank r, spectral gap η); it provides theoretical characterizations under a rank-r Gaussian contrast model, a calibrated-reader condition, risk expressions, and topology-driven constraints, plus exact update methods and a gating mechanism to improve deployment reliability.
AI.motivation: Counting equivalent pairs often overstates audit constraints because pairs from the same semantic object are correlated and orbit graphs contain redundant edges. A more robust, decomposition-based framework is needed to quantify coverage and guide reliable deployment.
AI.method: Define four quantities: edge count m, effective contrast rank s, population support rank r, and graph spectral gap η. Analyze under a rank-r Gaussian contrast model. Derive conditions for a population-invariant calibrated reader (exactly when the anchor has a component in ker T). For s<r, obtain the unobserved risk distribution R*/U with U~Beta((r−s)/2, s/2); for s≥r, exact calibrated interpolation is infeasible. Map results to orbit topology: spanning trees impose the same exact-null constraints as complete graphs; graph Poincare inequality links edge drift to orbit-wide drift with cost ~1/η. Cyclic audits can yield zero pair-level leave-one-out error without leave-out semantic objects. Provide exact block-Woodbury leave-one-orbit-out updates and introduce a source-disjoint deployment gate to manage uncertainty with a clean-utility budget.
AI.result: A theoretical framework that clarifies how m, s, r, and η govern audit coverage and reliability; precise conditions for calibrated readers; explicit risk distributions; connections between graph topology and null constraints; practical computational updates (block-Woodbury) and a deployment gate to control drift.
AI.conclusion: The framework reduces overstatement of audit constraints by disentangling correlation structure from genuine coverage limits, offering rigorous metrics and operational tools (updates and deployment gate) to enhance reliability of transformation audits; it also identifies clear limitations when s≥r and points to directions for empirical validation.

title: MAPS: Memory-Aware Predictive Scheduling Framework for Large Language Model Serving
summary: The surge of large language model (LLM) applications on personal devices imposes massive, bursty workloads on cloud serving infrastructure. While prefill-decode disaggregation improves throughput and scalability, memory-bound decode instances often suffer from persistent load imbalance, as output lengths are unknown when requests arrive at the cloud. To address this, we propose MAPS, a Memory-Aware Predictive Scheduling framework tailored for disaggregated LLM serving. MAPS performs device-assisted speculative output length prediction overlapped with cloud-side prefilling, incurring negligible latency overhead. To handle generation uncertainty, MAPS applies uncertainty-aware calibration to derive output-length upper bounds with target coverage, enabling safe scheduling decisions. Building on these bounds, MAPS employs a hierarchical global-local scheduling strategy to mitigate inter-decoder queue buildup and intra-decoder head-of-line blocking. Extensive experiments on two real-world workloads and two LLMs show that MAPS significantly outperforms three state-of-the-art systems, reducing average end-to-end latency by 42.6 and tail latency by up to 84.8.

AI.tldr: MAPS is a memory-aware predictive scheduling framework for disaggregated LLM serving that uses device-assisted length prediction, uncertainty-aware bounds, and hierarchical scheduling to reduce latency and tail latency.
AI.motivation: Burst workloads from personal-device–driven LLM use saturate cloud serving; memory-bound decode instances suffer from load imbalance because the output length is unknown at request arrival. A safe, accurate prediction and scheduling mechanism is needed.
AI.method: MAPS combines device-assisted speculative output-length prediction overlapped with cloud-side prefill, uncertainty-aware calibration to derive output-length upper bounds with target coverage, and a hierarchical global-local scheduling strategy to reduce inter-decoder queue buildup and intra-decoder head-of-line blocking.
AI.result: Experiments on two real-world workloads and two LLMs show MAPS outperforms three state-of-the-art systems, reducing average end-to-end latency by 42.6% and tail latency by up to 84.8%.
AI.conclusion: MAPS effectively mitigates memory-bound scheduling challenges in disaggregated LLM serving and delivers substantial latency improvements through predictive length bounds and hierarchical scheduling.

title: Direct Conditional Transition Sampling for Diffusion Inverse Problems
summary: Training-free diffusion inverse solvers typically choose between local measurement guidance and costly clean-space posterior updates. Independent posterior refresh can improve global correction by sampling a clean conditional and re-noising it, but its practical realization requires probability-flow ODE integration and clean-space Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). We propose Direct Conditional Transition Sampling (DCTS), a direct stochastic-flow approximation to the same ideal refresh target. Rather than explicitly drawing a clean sample, DCTS estimates the measurement-conditioned clean mean along a short inner path and transports Gaussian source noise directly to the next noisy state. A denoiser-compatible sufficient statistic and a covariance-scaled operator update enable this conditional-mean estimation. Experiments on four inverse problems demonstrate that DCTS achieves competitive reconstruction quality with up to $16.8\times$ speedups over competing methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes Direct Conditional Transition Sampling (DCTS), a training-free diffusion-inverse solver that mimics an ideal posterior refresh by estimating a conditional mean along a short inner path and transporting Gaussian noise to the next state, yielding faster reconstruction with competitive quality.
AI.motivation: To enable effective global correction in diffusion-based inverse solvers without expensive probability-flow ODE integration or clean-space MCMC, thus reducing computation while preserving reconstruction quality.
AI.method: Direct Conditional Transition Sampling (DCTS): estimate the measurement-conditioned clean mean along a short inner path and transport Gaussian source noise directly to the next noisy state. It uses a denoiser-compatible sufficient statistic and a covariance-scaled operator update to perform conditional-mean estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on four inverse problems show that DCTS achieves competitive reconstruction quality with up to 16.8× speedups over competing methods.
AI.conclusion: DCTS offers a practical, fast alternative to full posterior refresh in diffusion inverse solvers, delivering substantial speedups with maintained (competitive) reconstruction quality.

title: AgentKV: Phase-Aware KV Eviction for Agentic LLMs
summary: Agentic serving can consume orders of magnitude more tokens than chatbot workloads, stressing both KV-cache capacity and decode-time bandwidth. Most KV-eviction methods score cached keys against representative queries drawn from the most recent tokens, assuming future attention resembles recent attention. We show that agentic generation violates this assumption: future queries form a mixture over think, act, tool, and others phases, and principal-angle analysis shows these components occupy measurably different query subspaces, so recency representatives systematically undervalue keys that upcoming phases will need. We propose AGENTKV, which maintains a small query buffer per phase and scores cached keys against their union. We further implement AGENTKV in a persistent multi-turn serving path that carries compressed KV state across turns and compacts retained KV pages online. Across two models, six task domains, and three KV budgets each, AGENTKV improves task score by 5.5 points on average over R-KV and 5.3 over Tri-attention. Relative to upstream full-KV SGLang, AGENTKV improves output-token throughput by up to 1.80x. Code: https://github.com/LiuTaowen-Tony/agentkv.

AI.tldr: AGENTKV introduces per-phase KV caches for agentic generation, improving eviction relevance and throughput. It maintains per-phase query buffers (think, act, tool, others), scores cached keys against their union, and uses a persistent multi-turn path with online KV compaction. Empirical results show +5.5 task-score vs R-KV and +5.3 vs Tri-attention; up to 1.80x throughput vs full-KV SGLang across models/domains/budgets.
AI.motivation: Agentic generation tasks stress KV-cache capacity and decode-time bandwidth, and existing eviction methods rely on recency assuming future attention resembles recent attention. In agentic workflows, future queries form a mixture of phases with distinct subspaces, causing recency-based eviction to undervalue keys needed in upcoming phases.
AI.method: Introduce AGENTKV with small per-phase query buffers and a union-based key-scoring strategy. Implement in a persistent multi-turn serving path that carries compressed KV state across turns and performs online compaction of retained KV pages. Evaluate across two models, six task domains, and three KV budgets.
AI.result: AGENTKV achieves an average task-score improvement of 5.5 points over R-KV and 5.3 over Tri-attention across the tested settings. Relative to upstream full-KV SGLang, it increases output-token throughput by up to 1.80x. Code is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Per-phase, union-based key scoring effectively aligns eviction decisions with the heterogeneous future queries of agentic generation, yielding notable gains in task performance and throughput. The approach adds per-phase state and online KV management but demonstrates robust improvements across models and domains.

title: RSIAgent: Autonomous Exploration for Recursive Self-improvement in New Environments
summary: Digital agents must often adapt to new environments whose interfaces, tools, and failure modes are not fully captured by pretrained models. We introduce \textbf{RSIAgent}, a training-free multi-agent framework for recursive self-improvement through autonomous memory construction. RSIAgent coordinates curriculum, actor, and verifier agents to continually explore the environment, validate outcomes, and retain environment-specific knowledge, including reusable causal relationships between actions, conditions, and consequences. It further adopts a \textbf{broad-then-deep} exploration strategy, combining parallel broad recursive self-exploration for discovering diverse environment structures with focused deep self-exploration for uncovering hard cases, hidden constraints, boundary conditions, and previously unknown causal dependencies. The resulting memory is frozen and can be directly reused for downstream tasks without updating model parameters. Experiments on OSWorld-v2 and Agent's Last Exam show that RSIAgent substantially improves strong open-source models, enabling Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3 to outperform frontier closed-source models including GPT-6.

AI.tldr: RSIAgent is a training-free multi-agent framework for recursive self-improvement via autonomous memory construction. It uses a curriculum, actor, and verifier to explore and memorize environment-specific knowledge, employing broad-then-deep exploration and freezing memory for downstream tasks, improving open-source models to surpass frontier closed-source systems like GPT-6.
AI.motivation: Pretrained models often fail to adapt to new environments with unseen interfaces, tools, and failure modes. There is a need for environment-specific, reusable knowledge and causal relationships that can be leveraged without retraining.
AI.method: RSIAgent coordinates three agents (curriculum, actor, verifier) to drive continual exploration, validate outcomes, and retain knowledge. It adopts a broad-then-deep exploration strategy to discover diverse environment structures and hard cases, resulting in a frozen memory that can be reused for downstream tasks without parameter updates.
AI.result: Experiments on OSWorld-v2 and Agent's Last Exam show that RSIAgent substantially improves strong open-source models, enabling Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3 to outperform frontier closed-source models including GPT-6.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free, memory-centric framework enables recursive self-improvement in digital agents, delivering reusable environment-specific knowledge and causal dependencies that enhance downstream model performance without updating model parameters.

title: Open-UniMo: Towards Unified Motion-Language Understanding and Generation in the Open World
summary: Unified motion generation and understanding is crucial for embodied AI systems that can both synthesize and interpret human actions in open-world environments. Existing motion-language models often treat motion as an auxiliary modality of a language model, leading to text-dominated representations and limited cross-modal interaction. Moreover, the next-token prediction paradigm is not naturally suited to long motion sequences, where autoregressive generation may accumulate prediction errors. To address these challenges, we propose Open-UniMo, a unified Large Motion-Language Model (LMLM) trained on million-scale open-world motion-language data. Open-UniMo promotes modality parity by extending Qwen's vocabulary of about 150K text tokens with 64K motion tokens, enabling motion and language to share a unified token space. We further introduce motion-consistent Chain-of-Thought reasoning as an intermediate representation to bridge language semantics and motion dynamics. Open-UniMo is trained with a two-stage pipeline, where supervised fine-tuning establishes CoT-guided bidirectional motion-language mapping and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves semantic alignment while mitigating cumulative errors in autoregressive motion-token generation. To support comprehensive evaluation, we propose Open-MoBench, a VLM-guided benchmark for assessing text-to-motion (T2M) generation, motion-to-text (M2T) understanding, and bidirectional consistency. Extensive experiments show that Open-UniMo achieves state-of-the-art performance on both conventional metrics and Open-MoBench. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that M2T understanding is not primarily limited by motion-token vocabulary size; instead, coupling M2T with the learnable T2M generation path yields stronger cross-modal representations, demonstrating that generation can facilitate understanding in AR-based motion-language modeling.

AI.tldr: Open-UniMo unifies motion and language in a single Large Motion-Language Model by expanding the vocabulary to share text and motion tokens, applying Chain-of-Thought for bidirectional mapping, and using Group Relative Policy Optimization to curb errors; evaluated on Open-MoBench with state-of-the-art results and insightful ablations showing generation aids understanding.
AI.motivation: Overcome text-dominated, modality-aspect limitations in motion-language models and address error accumulation in autoregressive motion generation for long sequences in open-world settings.
AI.method: Two-stage training: (1) supervised fine-tuning with CoT-guided bidirectional motion-language mapping; (2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve semantic alignment and reduce error accumulation. Extend Qwen vocabulary by 64K motion tokens to create a shared token space between motion and language. Propose Open-MoBench as a VLM-guided benchmark for T2M, M2T, and bidirectional consistency.
AI.result: Open-UniMo achieves state-of-the-art performance on conventional metrics and Open-MoBench. Ablations show M2T understanding is not merely limited by motion-token vocabulary; coupling M2T with a learnable T2M generation path yields stronger cross-modal representations and demonstrates that generation can facilitate understanding in autoregressive motion-language models.
AI.conclusion: Open-UniMo advances unified motion-language modeling by enabling modality parity, introducing CoT-guided alignment and GRPO to mitigate generation errors, and providing a comprehensive benchmark (Open-MoBench) to evaluate T2M, M2T, and bidirectional consistency; generation benefits understanding in AR-based motion-language modeling.

title: SeqMaestro: From nucleotide sequences to biological hypotheses through interpretable machine learning
summary: Nucleotide sequence analysis is central to problems spanning regulatory genomics, evolutionary biology, and phenotype prediction. Classical bioinformatics methods extract interpretable sequence properties such as motifs and k-mer composition, but their flexibility is limited. In contrast, modern deep learning models can learn powerful predictive representations directly from raw sequences, yet their internal representations and decision mechanisms are difficult to inspect. Interpretable machine learning methods (e.g., sparse linear models and decision trees) provide human-understandable representations of predictive relationships but are not designed to operate directly on nucleotide sequences. Here, we introduce SeqMaestro, a machine learning framework that proposes biological hypotheses from nucleotide sequences using interpretable models. Our solution is centered around a two-layer interface that connects nucleotide sequences with the broader ecosystem of interpretable machine learning. SeqMaestro uses this interface to fit diverse combinations of interpretable models, feature representations, and extraction strategies, leveraging variability across transparent models to identify robust biological signals and richer predictive relationships than feature importance alone can provide. The system also supports data transformation and cleaning, model fitting, hyperparameter tuning, reliability analysis, and synthesis of results into a contextualized written report. By providing these capabilities through a no-code workflow, SeqMaestro is designed to make interpretable sequence analysis accessible to researchers without requiring extensive programming or machine learning expertise. SeqMaestro thereby provides an accessible route from nucleotide sequences to biological hypotheses.

AI.tldr: SeqMaestro provides a no-code framework that enables interpretable ML on nucleotide sequences by coupling a two-layer interface to diverse feature representations and models, integrating data cleaning, fitting, tuning, reliability analysis, and report generation to propose biological hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Address the interpretability gap of deep learning and the rigidity of classical methods by enabling interpretable sequence analysis directly on DNA/RNA data, accessible to researchers without ML expertise.
AI.method: A two-layer interface links nucleotide sequences to an ecosystem of interpretable machine learning models (e.g., sparse linear models, decision trees) and feature representations. The framework supports data transformation/cleaning, model fitting, hyperparameter tuning, reliability analysis, and synthesis of results into a contextualized, no-code report.
AI.result: Identifies robust biological signals and richer predictive relationships than reliance on feature importance alone, and outputs a contextualized written report to support hypothesis generation.
AI.conclusion: SeqMaestro provides an accessible route from sequence data to biological hypotheses by enabling flexible, interpretable sequence analysis through a no-code workflow.

title: SkillLift: Learning Dense Rubrics from Sparse Oracles for Efficient Skill Evolution
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on persistent skills, i.e., reusable procedural prompts, to adapt without weight updates. Existing skill self-evolution methods directly revise skill text based on execution feedback, but each oracle evaluation requires a full agent rollout, creating a supervision bottleneck that confines search to failure-patching updates. Our key insight is that ranking is a smoother supervision target than absolute outcome regression: identifying which skill is better requires fewer oracle evaluations than predicting exact scores. Building on this insight, we propose SkillLift, which decouples skill search from oracle cost by learning an oracle-aligned rubric as a structured evaluation space. We formalize this as a bilevel optimization problem solved via alternating optimization: an inner loop uses the frozen rubric as a cheap surrogate to guide skill revision at no oracle cost, while an outer loop invokes a small number of oracle rollouts to re-align the rubric via rank correlation, amortizing oracle cost and stabilizing text-space updates. Experiments on complex agent task benchmarks show that our method outperforms existing auto-skill methods with 40--70\% less token cost compared to frontier evolving methods. Codes are available at https://github.com/WalteR-MittY-pro/SkillLift.

AI.tldr: SkillLift uses a bilevel, oracle-aligned ranking rubric to cheaply evolve LLM-based agent skills, cutting supervision cost while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: To reduce the supervision burden of self-evolving persistent agent skills by replacing regression on absolute scores with ranking-based supervision, using a learnable rubric aligned with oracle feedback.
AI.method: Proposes SkillLift with a bilevel optimization: inner loop uses a frozen, cheap rubric surrogate to guide skill revisions without oracle calls; outer loop performs a small number of oracle rollouts to realign the rubric via rank correlation, thus amortizing oracle cost and stabilizing text-space updates.
AI.result: On complex agent task benchmarks, SkillLift outperforms existing auto-skill methods and achieves 40–70% lower token cost relative to frontier-evolving approaches.
AI.conclusion: A ranking-based supervision framework with a learnable rubric effectively decouples skill search from oracle cost, enabling more efficient and stable auto-skill evolution.

title: ESAFusion: LiDAR--4-D Radar Fusion via Local Geometric Complementation and Multiscale Adaptive Interaction for 3-D Object Detection
summary: LiDAR--4-D radar fusion combines accurate spatial geometry with motion and reflectivity cues from radar, offering a promising solution for 3-D object detection in complex driving environments. However, sparse radar observations and differences in spatial sampling between the two modalities complicate reliable cross-modal complementation. Moreover, the relative importance of modalities and feature scales varies across spatial regions, making adaptive fusion challenging. To address these challenges, we propose ESAFusion, an evidence-aware and scale-adaptive framework that combines local geometric complementation with multiscale adaptive interaction. Specifically, we introduce an Evidence-Aware Radar Selection (ERS) module to suppress radar clutter using motion and observation-quality evidence while retaining foreground confidence for subsequent fusion. Then, the Pillar-Level Complementary Encoder (PCE) improves cross-modal complementation under mismatched spatial sampling using local geometric support from neighboring LiDAR pillars. We further design an Intra- and Inter-Scale Adaptive Fusion (ISAF) module to adaptively adjust the contributions of different modalities and feature scales in bird's-eye-view (BEV) space. Extensive experiments on the View-of-Delft (VoD) dataset show that ESAFusion achieves the highest mean average precision (mAP) among the compared methods, reaching 74.60% in the Entire Annotated Area and 88.89% in the Driving Corridor. It also attains the highest average precision (AP) for Cyclist among these methods in both regions while running at 19.23 FPS. Evaluations on VoD-Fog further demonstrate robustness under progressively degraded LiDAR observations. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/SenJieHu549/ESAFusion.

AI.tldr: ESAFusion is a LiDAR–4D radar fusion framework for 3D object detection that uses evidence-aware radar selection, pillar-level complementation, and intra-/inter-scale adaptive fusion to address sparse radar, sampling mismatch, and region-wise modality importance, achieving state-of-the-art results on VoD with robustness to fog.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal fusion of LiDAR and radar is challenged by sparse radar observations, misaligned spatial sampling, and variable modality importance across BEV regions; existing methods struggle to suppress clutter and adapt fusion scales.
AI.method: Evidence-Aware Radar Selection (ERS) filters radar signals using motion and observation-quality cues; Pillar-Level Complementary Encoder (PCE) leverages neighboring LiDAR pillar geometry for cross-modal complementation under sampling differences; Intra- and Inter-Scale Adaptive Fusion (ISAF) dynamically weights modalities and feature scales in BEV.
AI.result: On the View-of-Delft (VoD) dataset, ESAFusion attains mAP 74.60% in Entire Annotated Area and 88.89% in Driving Corridor, with top AP for Cyclist; runs at 19.23 FPS; robust under VoD-Fog degradation; code to be released.
AI.conclusion: ESAFusion advances LiDAR–radar fusion with evidence-aware and scale-adaptive design, yielding strong detection performance and robustness, suitable for real-time deployment; publicly available code.

title: Cross-Block Conditioning in Deep Boltzmann Machines for Statistical Data Fusion
summary: Statistical data fusion combines two panels that share a block of covariates but observe disjoint outcome blocks, and in its traditional form no row observes both outcomes at once. That rules out the discriminative criterion one would rather train a Deep Boltzmann Machine with, since multi-prediction training needs ground truth for whatever it holds out. We propose observed-block multi-prediction, which restricts the multi-prediction objective to targets drawn from what each row actually observes. It is well defined for any missingness pattern and reduces to the original criterion when rows are complete. Having a discriminative criterion that survives the setting lets us ask whether the joint model is needed at all, by separating what it contributes into a representation part and an inference part. On two consumer panels, on grids over sample size and covariate width spanning 35 cells and 875 runs, the fine-tuned DBM is the best of fifteen methods in every cell; but almost none of that advantage comes from generative pre-training, which is confined to the smallest sample size on one dataset and absent on the other. It comes from conditioning on one outcome block when predicting the other. This term amounts to +0.19 and +0.07 percentage points, is positive in all 35 cells, and, unlike every other contribution we measure, neither decays as the panels grow, nor requires a second hidden layer, nor requires more inference. Permuting one outcome block to destroy its association with the other removes the gain entirely, which is what the account predicts. The margins are small. But a small effect that does not decay is a different object from one that does, because it rests on evidence that no model mapping covariates to outcomes can accept.

AI.tldr: Observed-block multi-prediction for data fusion with panel data where outcomes are observed in disjoint subsets. The discriminative criterion is well-defined for any missingness and, in a grid search on two consumer panels, a fine-tuned Deep Boltzmann Machine (DBM) using this criterion outperforms 14 alternatives in all 35 settings. Gains mainly come from conditioning on one outcome block when predicting the other, not from generative pre-training; the gain persists with panel growth and disappears if the blocks are permuted to destroy association, indicating the effect cannot be captured by simple covariate-to-outcome mappings.
AI.motivation: Traditional statistical data fusion with disjoint outcome blocks lacks a suitable multi-prediction objective because some rows lack ground truth for held-out outcomes. The authors seek a discriminative criterion that remains defined under arbitrary missingness and to test whether a joint generative model is necessary by decomposing the model into representation and inference components.
AI.method: Introduce observed-block multi-prediction: restrict the multi-prediction objective to targets available for each row. Apply to Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) and compare 15 methods across two consumer panels over grids of 35 cells (sample size × covariate width) and 875 runs. Evaluate contributions from generative pre-training and cross-block conditioning, and test robustness by permuting one outcome block to break association.
AI.result: The DBM with observed-block multi-prediction is best among 15 methods in every cell (35 cells). Almost all of its advantage is not due to generative pre-training, which is minimal or absent across datasets, but due to conditioning on one outcome block when predicting the other. This cross-block effect yields +0.19 and +0.07 percentage points in the two panels, positive in all cells, does not decay with increasing sample size or covariate width, and does not require a second hidden layer or more inference. Permuting one block to destroy association eliminates the gain.
AI.conclusion: A discriminative, missingness-aware objective can yield durable gains tied to cross-block conditioning, not to generative pre-training. The non-decaying, block-connected margin provides evidence for a representation–inference separation and suggests that a full joint generative model may not be necessary for this data-fusion task.

title: When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary
summary:
AI agents increasingly execute long-running workflows that externalize effects through independently supplied tools. Under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state may be inconsistent with the workflow's intended resolution: required effects may be missing or duplicated, aborted effects may survive, and committed effects may depend on provisional state that is later withdrawn. Advanced transaction models address related failures, but assume that lower-level operations expose the semantics they depend on: whether an effect occurred, whether it can be compensated, staged, or safely reordered. Shared agent-tool interfaces usually do not.
  We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies. From the catalog we derive the boundary capabilities required to exclude each anomaly in general, and four points where black-box tool invocation alone cannot provide a general guarantee. We then ask how much of this is expressible in a widely used shared tool interface, measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by registered Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The fields are widely emitted but provide only coarse call-level hints, and none of the required capabilities is fully expressible. These results motivate reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary.

AI.tldr: Proposes an effect-history model and an eight-anomaly catalog to reason about external effects in AI agent workflows; finds existing shared tool interfaces (MCP) are insufficient to express necessary guarantees; argues for transactional contracts at the tool boundary.
AI.motivation: As AI agents orchestrate long-running workflows with retries, speculation, concurrency, and partial failures, external state can drift from intended resolution; need formalism to detect and prevent anomalies.
AI.method: Develop an effect-history model separating external events from observed runtime state; derive eight recurring external-effect anomalies; map required boundary capabilities to exclude anomalies; identify four points where black-box tool invocation can't guarantee; empirically measure expressiveness of MCP's standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools.
AI.result: Eight anomalies identified; boundary capabilities necessary; MCP vocabulary is coarse and cannot express the required guarantees; high-level evaluation shows none of the required capabilities are fully expressible; needs reusable transactional contracts.
AI.conclusion: Tool-boundary transactional contracts are necessary to ensure reliability; current interfaces insufficient; propose standards for transactional contracts between agents and tools.

title: TTDF: A Two-Stage Framework for Reliable Surgical Phase Transition Detection
comment: Accepted at the COLAS Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Reliable workflow transition detection is important for context-aware surgical assistance and downstream decision support. However, online surgical phase recognizers primarily focus on frame-wise accuracy and temporal consistency, rather than the reliability of workflow transition events. Directly converting phase changes into events is unreliable: temporal jitter and workflow-illegal switches produce false or duplicate events, while persistent, workflow-consistent candidates may remain incorrect. To address this limitation, we formulate reliable workflow transition detection as a distinct event-level task operating on outputs of a frozen online phase recognizer. We propose the Two-Stage Transition Detection Framework (TTDF), a causal framework that progressively filters transition candidates. Transition Candidate Extraction (TCE) first applies a minimum-duration requirement and a workflow-graph constraint to remove false candidates caused by temporal jitter and phase transitions not allowed by the workflow graph. Specifically, a candidate is retained only if the predicted target phase persists for a minimum duration and the ordered phase pair belongs to the workflow graph's allowed transition set. TCE thereby produces a high-recall candidate set without additional training. Transition Candidate Verification (TCV) suppresses remaining false candidates using phase-posterior shifts and visual-change cues from frozen DINOv2 features. Events are assessed using a phase-pair-aware one-to-one matching protocol. Experiments on Cholec80 show that TTDF reduces false transition emissions while preserving recall and controlling decision delay.

AI.tldr: TTDF is a two-stage, causal framework that refines online phase predictions into reliable workflow transition events by first extracting high-recall transition candidates under duration and graph constraints, then suppressing false candidates using phase-posterior shifts and visual-change cues from frozen features, achieving fewer false transitions with preserved recall and controlled delay on Cholec80.
AI.motivation: Online surgical phase recognizers optimize frame-level accuracy and temporal consistency but do not guarantee reliable transition events; jitter, illegal switches, and persistent but incorrect candidates lead to unreliable event-based decisions. There is a need for a robust, event-level detection mechanism that leverages unfrozen or frozen models without additional training.
AI.method: Two-Stage Transition Detection Framework (TTDF) applied to outputs of a frozen online phase recognizer. Transition Candidate Extraction (TCE) enforces a minimum-duration requirement and workflow-graph constraints to filter out jitter-induced and illegal transitions, yielding a high-recall candidate set without extra training. Transition Candidate Verification (TCV) uses phase-posterior shifts and visual-change cues from frozen DINOv2 features, combined with a phase-pair-aware one-to-one matching protocol, to suppress remaining false candidates and decide final events.
AI.result: On the Cholec80 dataset, TTDF reduces false transition emissions while preserving recall and maintaining controlled decision delay.
AI.conclusion: TTDF offers a practical, causal, no-training-needed solution for reliable event-level workflow transition detection from online phase predictions, leveraging workflow graphs and frozen visual features; it demonstrates improved reliability on Cholec80 and may generalize to other surgical workflows or domains requiring robust event detection.

title: Cloud Workflow Scheduling Based on Graph Attention-Driven Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
comment: Paper submitted to IEEE Internet of Things Journal
summary: Dynamic cloud workflow scheduling must balance deadline satisfaction, container utilization, and energy consumption while dealing with stochastic task-execution speeds, placement-dependent communication, and coupled task and container decisions. Workflows are naturally modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), but conventional vector- or matrix-based states do not fully capture their dependency topology. To better represent task urgency and structural relationships, we assign predicted sub-deadlines to tasks and use a multi-head graph attention network (GAT) to extract dependency information from the evolving DAGs. Based on these representations, we develop a Graph Attention-Driven Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (GA-HRL) framework and model the scheduling process as an event-driven hierarchical semi-Markov decision process (SMDP). Workflow arrivals and task completions trigger scheduling events. At each scheduling event, the Task Scheduling (TS) agent first processes the currently ready tasks by assigning them to admissible existing containers or requesting new ones. The requested containers are then processed by the Container Scheduling (CS) agent for host placement before the environment advances. The two agents are trained alternately using separate Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Experiments on the 2018 Alibaba cluster trace show that GA-HRL maintains competitive workflow success rate and, in settings where success is comparable, generally achieves higher container utilization and lower energy consumption. Under the largest speed variation, it trades a small success-rate margin for substantially lower energy. Simulation code is available at: https://github.com/zongjin130/GA-HRL.

AI.tldr: GA-HRL for dynamic cloud workflow scheduling uses a graph attention network to capture DAG structure and an event-driven hierarchical SMDP with two PPO-trained agents (task scheduling and container scheduling) to optimize deadlines, utilization, and energy; evaluated on Alibaba trace with favorable trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Conventional vector/matrix states inadequately capture task dependencies and placement-dependent communications in DAG-based cloud workflows, limiting effective scheduling decisions for deadline satisfaction, utilization, and energy.
AI.method: Represent task urgency via predicted sub-deadlines; extract dependency information with a multi-head graph attention network on evolving DAGs. Develop Graph Attention-Driven Hierarchical RL (GA-HRL) and model scheduling as an event-driven hierarchical semi-Markov decision process. At scheduling events, Task Scheduling (TS) assigns ready tasks to admissible containers or requests new ones, then Container Scheduling (CS) selects host placement for requested containers. Environment advances after container placement. Train TS and CS alternately with separate PPO updates.
AI.result: On the 2018 Alibaba cluster trace, GA-HRL achieves competitive workflow success rates while attaining higher container utilization and lower energy consumption in most settings. In scenarios with large speed variation, it sacrifices a small degree of success rate to achieve substantially lower energy use. Source code for simulations is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Integrating DAG structure via graph attention with a hierarchical RL framework enables effective trade-offs among deadlines, utilization, and energy in dynamic cloud workflows, validated on real traces and accompanied by open-source simulation code.

title: Who Teaches Which Token? Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation for Scientific Reasoning
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) is becoming the standard way to integrate specialist capabilities into one model: train experts with RL, then distill them into the student on its own rollouts. Existing recipes assign supervision at the sequence level - each prompt goes to one domain teacher and every token receives the same weight - which implicitly assumes that a teacher is uniformly useful across a response. We find instead that useful teacher signal is sparse and heterogeneous along a reasoning trajectory, which raises a finer question: who should teach which token? Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation (VG-OPD) answers it by verification: the counterfactual gain of an expert on a specific answer criterion licenses that expert to teach, its disagreement with the student localizes the supervision, and criterion importance sets its weight; the gated KL enters GRPO as an additive token-level advantage. Instantiated for scientific reasoning with RL-trained capability experts, VG-OPD attains the best overall performance on seven benchmarks for 4B and 8B students, ranking first on five at both scales, with the largest gains on knowledge-intensive scientific reasoning tasks. Further analysis shows that the gains come from localizing verified supervision rather than from adding teachers or distillation loss: misplacing the same supervision budget is the single most damaging change, and indiscriminate distillation drags RL below its own floor where gated distillation lifts it.

AI.tldr: VG-OPD introduces verifier-gated, token-level supervision in multi-expert on-policy distillation, localizing teaching signals by expert utility and criterion importance; it outperforms uniform-sequence supervision on 7 benchmarks for 4B/8B students, especially in knowledge-intensive scientific reasoning.
AI.motivation: To address the assumption that a single teacher is uniformly useful across a response in multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD), by revealing that useful supervision is sparse and heterogeneous along reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: Propose Verifier-Gated Multi-Expert On-Policy Distillation (VG-OPD). Use verification: the counterfactual gain of an expert on a specific answer criterion licenses that expert to teach; use the student–expert disagreement to localize supervision; set weights with criterion importance; integrate gated KL into GRPO as an additive token-level advantage.
AI.result: VG-OPD achieves the best overall performance on seven benchmarks for both 4B and 8B students, ranking first on five tasks at both scales, with the largest gains on knowledge-intensive scientific reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Gains stem from localizing verified supervision rather than simply adding teachers or distillation loss; misplacing the same supervision budget is highly detrimental, and indiscriminate distillation can degrade RL performance below its baseline, while gated distillation lifts it.

title: SCOUT-SLAM: Structurally-Coupled Dual Uncertainty-Aware 3DGS SLAM in the Wild
summary: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM (3DGS-SLAM) has gained significant momentum in simultaneous localization and 3DGS scene reconstruction. In real-world scenarios with rapid camera motion and cluttered dynamic environments, existing methods rely on the stability of the underlying scene reconstruction to model uncertainty. This leads to a circular dependency between camera tracking accuracy and reconstruction quality: reconstruction instabilities degrade uncertainty modeling, which affects accurate camera tracking and static scene reconstruction. To address this, the paper proposes SCOUT-SLAM, a structurally-coupled dual-uncertainty framework in which both uncertainties are estimated from a shared base network. A low-rank adaptation of this network, trained on multi-view feature consistency, estimates a tracking uncertainty that does not depend solely on the reconstruction quality. A spatially-adaptive prior modulates the network's training objective so that reconstruction instability does not inflate uncertainty on static regions, keeping the shared representation intact for both branches. Evaluations on dynamic benchmarks (TUM RGB-D, Bonn Dynamic, Wild-SLAM MoCap) demonstrate that SCOUT-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art camera tracking accuracy and artifact-free static scene reconstruction.

AI.tldr: SCOUT-SLAM; a structurally-coupled dual-uncertainty framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM that jointly estimates tracking uncertainty and reconstruction quality using a shared base network with low-rank adaptation and a spatially adaptive prior; achieves state-of-the-art tracking and artifact-free static reconstruction on dynamic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In dynamic/rapid-motion scenes, reconstruction instability and tracking errors create a feedback loop, degrading uncertainty estimation and localization. A unified, robust uncertainty mechanism is needed that does not rely solely on reconstruction quality.
AI.method: Introduce a shared-base network for dual-uncertainty estimation; apply low-rank adaptation trained on multi-view feature consistency to estimate tracking uncertainty independent of reconstruction quality; incorporate a spatially-adaptive prior to limit the influence of reconstruction instability on static-region uncertainty; evaluate on dynamic benchmarks.
AI.result: SCOUT-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art camera tracking accuracy and artifact-free static scene reconstructions on TUM RGB-D, Bonn Dynamic, and Wild-SLAM MoCap benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A structurally-coupled dual-uncertainty framework effectively decouples tracking and reconstruction uncertainties, improving robustness in dynamic environments for 3DGS-SLAM.

title: High-Probability Nash Regret for Decentralized Learning in Markov $α$-Potential Games: Episodic and Fully Online Asynchronous Algorithms with Applications to Markov Congestion Games
summary: We study decentralized learning of Nash equilibria (NE) in infinite-horizon discounted Markov games under bandit feedback, focusing on Markov $α$-potential games. We develop KL-projected natural policy gradient (NPG) algorithms in two settings: an episodic setting with frozen policies during sampling and a fully online setting in which players receive a single realized cost sample per time step and update their policies asynchronously along a continuing trajectory. We establish finite-time high-probability NE regret bounds of order $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$ and $\widetilde O(T^{-2/15})$ for the episodic and fully online settings, respectively, up to fixed approximation terms. Crucially, our bounds eliminate the distribution-mismatch coefficient, which can scale prohibitively with the size of the state space, while accommodating potential approximation, estimation-oracle bias, and transition sensitivity. We further identify a state-wise potential structure that yields sharper guarantees with additive dependence on the potential approximation error $α$. We specialize the framework to independent-resource Markov congestion games (IMCGs), establish their approximate-potential and transition-sensitivity properties, and construct decentralized estimation oracles from realized costs. As an application, we introduce strategic online job scheduling on stochastic machines and obtain a scalable decentralized algorithm for learning stable dispatching policies. Overall, our results provide the first finite-time high-probability NE regret guarantees for fully online asynchronous decentralized learning in Markov $α$-potential games, remove distribution-mismatch coefficients from the regret bounds, accommodate fixed estimation-oracle bias, and provide scalable decentralized learning with finite-time guarantees for IMCGs.

AI.tldr: KL-projected natural policy gradient for decentralized NE learning in infinite-horizon Markov α-potential games with bandit feedback; provides finite-time high-probability NE regret bounds in episodic and fully online settings, removes distribution-mismatch coefficients, and applies to IMCGs with scalable decentralized estimation and job-scheduling applications.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of learning Nash equilibria in decentralized, infinite-horizon Markov games under bandit feedback. Prior work suffers from distribution-mismatch and loose finite-time guarantees; the paper aims to achieve tight, distribution-mismatch-free regret bounds and scalable decentralized learning in α-potential games.
AI.method: Develop KL-projected natural policy gradient (NPG) algorithms for two settings: (i) episodic with frozen policies during sampling, and (ii) fully online with asynchronous updates and single-cost samples. Prove finite-time high-probability NE regret bounds, remove distribution-mismatch terms, and allow approximation/estimation-bias and transition sensitivity. Identify state-wise potential structure for sharper bounds, and specialize to independent-resource Markov congestion games (IMCGs) with decentralized estimation oracles. Apply to strategic online job scheduling on stochastic machines.
AI.result: Finite-time high-probability NE regret bounds of order ~T^{-1/4} (episodic) and ~T^{-2/15} (fully online) up to fixed approximation terms; distribution-mismatch coefficient removed; bounds accommodate potential approximation error α, estimation bias, and transition sensitivity; state-wise potential yields additive dependence on α; IMCGs satisfy approximate-potential/transition-sensitivity properties; construction of decentralized estimation oracles; scalable algorithm for decentralized policy learning; application to online job scheduling.
AI.conclusion: Presents the first finite-time high-probability NE regret guarantees for fully online asynchronous decentralized learning in Markov α-potential games; eliminates distribution-mismatch terms; supports fixed estimation bias and scalable learning in IMCGs; demonstrates practical decentralized strategies for job scheduling on stochastic machines.

title: Can AI systems have free will?
summary: While there has been much discussion of whether AI systems could function as moral agents or acquire sentience, there has been very little discussion of whether AI systems could have free will. I sketch a framework for thinking about this question, inspired by Daniel Dennett's work. I argue that, to determine whether an AI system has free will, we should not look for some mysterious property, expect its underlying algorithms to be indeterministic, or ask whether the system is unpredictable. Rather, we should simply ask whether we have good explanatory reasons to view the system as an intentional agent, with the capacity for choice between alternative possibilities and control over the resulting actions. If the answer is "yes", then the system counts as having free will in a pragmatic and diagnostically useful sense.

AI.tldr: A pragmatic framework for ascribing free will to AI by treating it as an intentional agent with choices and control, rather than relying on metaphysical properties or indeterminism.
AI.motivation: To provide a workable, diagnostic criterion for free will in AI by extending Dennett's intentional stance, avoiding appeals to mystery or unpredictability.
AI.method: Propose evaluating whether we have good explanatory reasons to view an AI system as an intentional agent with capacity for choice among alternatives and control over actions; if so, attribute free will in a pragmatic sense.
AI.result: A practical criterion for AI free will: systems that function as intentional agents with choice and control can be said to have free will in a pragmatic, diagnostic sense, independent of underlying indeterminism or unpredictability.
AI.conclusion: Free will can be ascribed to AI systems in a pragmatic sense when they meet criteria of intentional agency and control, offering a useful diagnostic framework rather than a metaphysical claim.

title: PhysBrain 1.5: From Vision-Language Models to Physical Foundation Models
summary: We present PhysBrain 1.5, a unified model for understanding physical environments, generating actions, and predicting future states. Motivated by the physical loop of observation, interaction, and environmental change, we bring these capabilities into a common learning framework. Starting from a general vision--language model, we encode language responses, end-effector motion, and dense visual targets as discrete sequences and jointly optimize them with autoregressive next-token prediction. Pre-training draws its embodied supervision entirely from human interaction videos, using task-centered episodes to pair semantic and spatial context with recovered motion and subsequent observations. We then adapt the model through supervised fine-tuning on a mixture of human demonstrations, robot trajectories, and simulated experience. Across 28 embodied understanding benchmarks, our 8B model achieves an average score of 72.5, setting a new open-source state of the art and performing on par with leading proprietary models such as GPT-6-Astra and Gemini 3.6 Flash. It achieves the best open-source results on 14 benchmarks while retaining general multimodal capabilities. Beyond these understanding evaluations, qualitative examples show the model's ability to produce end-effector trajectories and predict future scenes through spatially aligned RGB, depth, and robot-mask outputs.

AI.tldr: PhysBrain 1.5 is an 8B unified multimodal model that learns perception, action generation, and future-state prediction in a single sequence-based framework, achieving open-source SOTA across 28 embodied benchmarks and enabling end-effector control and future-scene prediction.
AI.motivation: Address the physical loop of observation, interaction, and environmental change by unifying understanding, action generation, and prediction within a shared learning framework, leveraging a vision-and-language foundation.
AI.method: Encode language responses, end-effector motion, and dense visual targets as discrete sequences and optimize via autoregressive next-token prediction. Pre-train using embodied supervision from human interaction videos with task-centered episodes linking semantic/spatial context to recovered motion and subsequent observations. Fine-tune with a mix of human demonstrations, robot trajectories, and simulated data. Evaluate on 28 embodied benchmarks; provide end-effector trajectories and future-scene predictions using spatially aligned RGB, depth, and robot-mask outputs.
AI.result: 8B PhysBrain achieves an average score of 72.5 across 28 benchmarks, establishing a new open-source state of the art and matching leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-6-Astra, Gemini 3.6 Flash). It attains the best open-source results on 14 benchmarks and demonstrates qualitative capabilities such as generating end-effector trajectories and predicting future scenes.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a versatile, open-source embodied AI that jointly models language, perception, action, and prediction within a unified framework. It shows strong open-source performance and general multimodal capabilities, though details on data distribution, tokenization choices, and real-world generalization remain areas for further scrutiny.

title: Evaluating Contextual Bias in CNN Image Classification: Evidence from Agricultural Benchmark Datasets
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are typically evaluated using held-out classification accuracy, an approach that presupposes predictions are based primarily on the intended object of interest rather than incidental surrounding context. We test this assumption in CNN-based agricultural image classification by comparing model performance on original images with performance on background-dominated patches extracted from the same images across eight publicly available agricultural benchmark datasets and four widely used CNN architectures. Background-dominated patches were classified above dataset-specific random chance for six of the eight datasets, and substantially above chance for four of them, indicating that contextual information contributes to model predictions for the majority of datasets evaluated. For these four datasets, we further evaluated whether this behavior reflected genuine class-discriminative information or was primarily attributable to class imbalance using macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 together with class-balanced test subsets. The results show that contextual reliance does not admit a single explanation: class imbalance accounts for a substantial portion of the observed signal for some datasets and architectures, whereas above-chance contextual classification persists after balancing for others. Together with previous evidence from curated object recognition and cancer pathology imaging, these findings support the growing view that contextual bias is a recurring characteristic of CNN-based image classification rather than a phenomenon confined to a single application domain. More broadly, this work provides a systematic framework for quantifying contextual bias across heterogeneous image datasets by combining dataset-specific random-chance baselines, contextual bias categorization, macro-averaged evaluation, and class-balanced robustness analysis.

AI.tldr: CNNs in agricultural image classification leverage contextual cues; background-only patches can be predicted above chance, indicating contextual bias across datasets and architectures. The study provides a framework to quantify this bias.
