The main limitation of this study is the dataset's class imbalance, and while weighted training helped mitigate this, further research and additional data are needed to guarantee model generalizability. Future studies should also explore the influence of genetic variations, environmental factors, and clinical differences on model performance across diverse populations.

AI.tldr: A semi-supervised transcriptomic biomarker study for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) uses deep learning and SHAP-based XAI to diagnose across disease stages. It selects 15 genes via SelectKBest, achieving 90.74% accuracy; 20 genes yield the lowest loss (0.3187). DNAJB14 emerges as the top influential gene with functional validation showing its inhibition reduces malignant traits. Main limitation is class imbalance; more data and diverse populations are needed for generalizability.
AI.motivation: To develop a transparent, DL-based diagnostic framework for HCC that leverages transcriptomic biomarkers across disease stages, while addressing class imbalance and ensuring interpretability via SHAP; also to validate potential biomarkers functionally.
AI.method: Construct a transcriptomic biomarker dataset via semi-supervised learning from three source datasets. Conduct multiple deep learning experiments with differing feature extraction techniques and gene sets. Use SelectKBest for feature selection (15 or 20 genes). Apply a weighted training approach to mitigate class imbalance. Use SHAP-based XAI to interpret model decisions. Perform functional validation showing DNAJB14's role in HCC phenotypes and effect of its inhibition.
AI.result: Best-performing model achieved 90.74% accuracy with 15 genes. The model with the lowest loss (0.3187) used 20 genes. SHAP identified DNAJB14 as the most influential gene. Functional validation indicated DNAJB14 contributes to malignant properties and its inhibition reverses migration, invasion, colony, and sphere formation. Main limitation is dataset class imbalance; weighted training helped, but generalizability requires more data and exploration of genetic/environmental/clinical factors across populations.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of DL+XAI for HCC diagnosis and biomarker discovery. DNAJB14 is highlighted as a key biomarker with functional relevance. Generalizability needs additional diverse data and consideration of population-specific factors.

title: CrossDistill: Balancing Quality and Diversity via Trajectory-Level Hybrid Few-Step Distillation
summary: Few-step distillation accelerates diffusion models but must balance diversity and fidelity: trajectory-based distillation preserves mode coverage, while distribution matching sharpens samples but can reduce diversity. We show that this tension can be exploited in a noise-regime-dependent way: high-noise steps largely determine global modes, whereas low-noise steps refine local details. We propose CrossDistill, a trajectory-level hybrid distillation framework that splits the sampling trajectory at a crossover point, applies a trajectory-preserving objective on the high-noise interval and a distribution-matching objective on the low-noise interval, and couples the two stages through the crossover state. In contrast to loss-level mixing, and complementarily to training-time two-stage recipes, CrossDistill explicitly assigns complementary objectives along the noise axis, so that global branching is preserved before local statistics are sharpened. CrossDistill is a noise-level scheduling policy: PCM and DMD are plug-in instantiations, while the noise partition, crossover coupling, and objective ordering are the key design elements. Experiments on text-to-video diffusion models and qualitative image-to-video results show that CrossDistill expands the few-step quality-diversity frontier, retaining seed-level variation while achieving competitive visual fidelity.

AI.tldr: CrossDistill is a noise-aware, trajectory-level hybrid distillation that splits the sampling path into high-noise (trajectory-preserving) and low-noise (distribution-matching) phases, coupling them at a crossover state to widen the few-step quality-diversity frontier while preserving seed variation.
AI.motivation: Few-step diffusion distillation faces a fidelity-diversity trade-off: trajectory-based objectives preserve mode coverage but blur details, while distribution-matching sharpens samples but can reduce diversity. An adaptive, noise-aware approach could leverage the strengths of both.
AI.method: CrossDistill introduces a trajectory-level hybrid framework that splits the sampling trajectory at a crossover point along the noise schedule. It applies a trajectory-preserving objective on the high-noise interval and a distribution-matching objective on the low-noise interval, with coupling through the crossover state. PCM (trajectory-preserving and distribution-matching plug-ins) are instantiated as the two objectives; the key design elements are noise partition, crossover coupling, and objective ordering. This approach differs from loss-level mixing and complements training-time two-stage recipes.
AI.result: Empirical results on text-to-video diffusion models and qualitative image-to-video outputs show CrossDistill expands the few-step quality-diversity frontier, maintaining seed-level variation while achieving competitive visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly assigning complementary objectives along the noise axis via a noise-level scheduling policy improves the speed-versus-diversity trade-off in diffusion distillation. CrossDistill provides a modular, plug-in framework (PCM/DMD) with key design knobs—noise partition, crossover coupling, and objective ordering—for broad applicability.

title: Not All Prompts Are Equal: Exploration-Guided Prompt Scaffolding for Multimodal Reinforcement Post-Training
summary: Training prompts in online reinforcement learning (RL) differ substantially in how informative they are for the current policy: some are already saturated while others are too difficult to yield reliable learning signals, yet both receive equal rollout budget under standard training. We propose an exploration-guided prompt scaffolding framework that adapts the training prompt distribution dynamically throughout RL post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Central to our approach is the $\textit{Exploration Potential Score} (EPS)$, a lightweight rollout-based proxy for prompt utility derived from KL-regularized policy improvement theory, computable directly from on-policy rollout statistics without additional overhead. Rather than discarding low-utility prompts, we use a teacher model to generate scaffolded rewrites that preserve the original task intent while making subsequent training more informative, reframing teacher supervision as training-data refinement rather than output imitation. Integrated with GRPO on Geo3K and MMK12, our method consistently outperforms the baseline on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks, achieving up to 9.7\% relative improvement in-domain and gains of 11.5\% on MathVision and 11.1\% on MMMU-Pro.

AI.tldr: Introduces an Exploration Potential Score (EPS) to guide dynamic, exploration-aware prompt training for online RL with multimodal LLMs; uses a teacher to generate scaffolded rewrites, reframing supervision as training-data refinement; achieves consistent gains on Geo3K/MMK12 and other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Prompt utility during RL post-training is heterogeneous; standard equal-budget rollout wastes effort on saturated or too-difficult prompts. A data-driven, adaptive approach is needed to maximize informative learning signals.
AI.method: EPS is a lightweight rollout-based proxy for prompt utility derived from KL-regularized policy improvement theory, computable from on-policy rollouts without extra overhead. Low-utility prompts are transformed by a teacher into scaffolded rewrites that preserve task intent, turning supervision into data refinement rather than output imitation. The approach integrates with GRPO on Geo3K and MMK12.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over baselines on in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, with up to 9.7% relative in-domain gain and 11.5% (MathVision) and 11.1% (MMMU-Pro) gains on respective benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, exploration-guided prompt scaffolding using EPS and teacher-based data refinement enhances online RL post-training for multimodal LLMs, offering gains across diverse benchmarks.

title: EEG-Xplain: Decoding Neural Black-Boxes of EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models such as BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGMamba have achieved remarkable performance in neural signal decoding, but their black-box nature limits clinical trust and neuroscientific validation. We propose a unified attribution framework for interpreting EEG foundation models across heterogeneous architectures. The framework integrates gradient-, perturbation-, and activation-based explanation methods to analyze model behavior in spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions. Spatially, it identifies critical EEG channels and visualizes their distributions using topographic maps. Temporally, it highlights decision-relevant signal segments through attribution heatmaps. In the frequency domain, it quantifies the contributions of canonical EEG rhythms via spectral perturbation analysis. To assess explanation reliability, we introduce a population-level evaluation combining Area Over the Perturbation Curve (AOPC) and cross-method consistency analysis. The framework further leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform structured attribution outputs into natural-language reports, bridging low-level neural representations and high-level semantic reasoning. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including Mumtaz2016 and TUAB, demonstrate that the generated explanations are consistent with established neurophysiological markers, validating meaningful neural representations while exposing potential dependencies on artifacts and spurious patterns. The proposed framework provides a standardized approach for evaluating the interpretability, reliability, and physiological plausibility of EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: A unified attribution framework for EEG foundation models (gradient, perturbation, activation methods) across spatial, temporal, and frequency domains, with population-level evaluation and LLM-generated natural-language reports. Validated on Mumtaz2016 and TUAB; demonstrates alignment with neurophysiological markers but reveals artifact/spurious-pattern dependencies; aims to standardize interpretability and reliability of EEG models.
AI.motivation: Address the black-box nature of EEG foundation models and enable clinical trust and neuroscientific validation by providing a unified, multi-dimensional attribution framework that aggregates explanations across architectures and dimensions.
AI.method: Combine gradient-, perturbation-, and activation-based explanations to analyze spatial (topographic channel importance), temporal (decision-relevant segments via attribution heatmaps), and frequency (spectral perturbation) aspects. Use population-level evaluation with AOPC and cross-method consistency. Visualize with topographic maps and attribution heatmaps. Employ LLMs to translate structured attribution outputs into natural-language reports.
AI.result: Explanations align with established neurophysiological markers, indicating meaningful neural representations; framework reveals dependencies on artifacts and spurious patterns; offers a standardized approach for evaluating interpretability, reliability, and physiological plausibility of EEG foundation models.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a standardized, multi-faceted approach to interpret EEG foundation models, bridging low-level neural representations and high-level reasoning, and enabling more robust validation and reporting of neural plausibility.

title: From Visual Feedback to Textual Reviews: A Multi-Agent Vision-Language Framework for Image-Grounded Review Assistance
summary: Visual feedback in the form of user-uploaded images and videos is becoming increasingly common in e-commerce platforms because it provides authentic evidence of product quality, defects, packaging conditions, and real-world usage. However, visual feedback alone often lacks the contextual explanations and subjective opinions necessary for informed decision-making, while many users provide limited textual feedback due to the effort required to compose detailed reviews. To bridge this gap, we introduce image-grounded review assistance, a novel task that aims to generate editable review drafts from user-uploaded product images. Unlike conventional image captioning, which focuses on objective visual description, the proposed task requires product-specific understanding, sentiment estimation, and evidence-driven review composition under challenging real-world conditions, including degraded image quality, excessive zoom-in, target ambiguity, and partial product visibility. We propose a multi-agent vision-language framework consisting of four specialised roles: product grounding, visual sentiment estimation, visual evidence generation, and review synthesis. The framework employs explicit intermediate representations, including product entities, predicted ratings, and evidence summaries, to improve interpretability and visual grounding. Experiments on a curated subset of the Amazon Reviews Electronics dataset demonstrate the feasibility of generating coherent, product-aware, and sentiment-aware review drafts from visual feedback. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to formulate image-grounded review assistance as a multi-agent vision-language reasoning problem, providing a practical step toward AI-assisted review authoring in e-commerce systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes image-grounded review assistance using a four-agent vision-language framework to generate editable, product-aware review drafts from user images; demonstrates feasibility on a subset of Amazon Electronics.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap between visual feedback and textual reviews; enable informative reviews despite limited user-written text; handle real-world image challenges (degraded quality, zoom-in, ambiguity).
AI.method: Four specialized agents: product grounding, visual sentiment estimation, visual evidence generation, and review synthesis; explicit intermediate representations (product entities, predicted ratings, evidence summaries); multi-agent reasoning with interpretable outputs that ground text in visual evidence and product knowledge.
AI.result: Feasibility demonstrated; ability to generate coherent, product-aware, and sentiment-aware review drafts; improved interpretability and grounding through explicit intermediate representations; first to formulate image-grounded review assistance as multi-agent vision-language reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a novel task and framework for AI-assisted review authoring in e-commerce; paves the way for broader evaluations, user studies, and robustness to real-world visual conditions.

title: What Does an LLM Learn from Reinforcement Learning? A Mechanistic Interpretability Perspective with Fixed-SAE Track
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely utilized in large language model training to improve targeted capabilities, yet how RL reshapes a model remains poorly understood. Prior attempts to explain how RL works largely offer behavioral perspectives, leaving open what RL gives a model at the representation level: can RL create genuinely novel features, and which existing features does it enhance or suppress? Recent developments in mechanistic interpretability suggest sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a promising lens to decompose internal activations into human-interpretable features; however, they cannot be directly applied to tracking change across training. In this work, we introduce Fixed-SAE Track, a framework that trains one shared SAE per considered layer on activations pooled across the base model and all RL checkpoints, holding every feature direction fixed so that representation shifts are rigorously defined through the activations of interpretable SAE latents, including the detection of emerging novel features. Validated across multiple datasets and RL algorithms, we find that RL-induced drift is small, gradual, concept specific, and concentrated in late layers, mainly enhancing the sampling rates of a small set of ladder tokens, formatting scaffolding such as step breaks and answer delimiters, rather than reshaping problem content. Steering these features into the base model recovers around 80% of RL's performance gain, suggesting that RL primarily elicits capabilities the model already possesses, much as steering does. We further design a synthetic benchmark with features known by construction to test whether RL can instill genuinely novel features. We believe Fixed-SAE Track provides a principled approach to tracking representation shifts and offers representational evidence for understanding how reinforcement learning changes the inner representation of LLMs.

AI.tldr: Fixed-SAE Track tracks representation changes during RL by training a fixed sparse autoencoder per layer across the base model and all RL checkpoints, enabling precise measurement of feature-level drift. It finds small, late-layer, concept-specific changes that mainly enhance a small set of tokens/formatting cues rather than reshaping content; steering these features recovers ~80% of RL gains. A synthetic benchmark assesses the ability to cultivate genuinely novel features.
AI.motivation: There is a gap in understanding how RL modifies internal representations of LLMs. Behavioral explanations dominate, but it is unclear what new features RL creates and which existing features are leveraged or suppressed. Fixed-SAE Track leverages mechanistic interpretability to quantify representation shifts across training.
AI.method: Train one shared sparse autoencoder (SAE) per selected layer using activations pooled across the base model and all RL checkpoints, keeping all SAE feature directions fixed to define representation shifts through latent activations. Detect emerging novel features via changes in latent activations. Validate on multiple datasets and RL algorithms. Include a synthetic benchmark with known features to test for genuinely novel features.
AI.result: RL-induced representation drift is small, gradual, concept-specific, and concentrated in late layers. It predominantly boosts sampling rates of a limited set of ladder tokens and formatting scaffolding (e.g., step breaks, answer delimiters) without reshaping problem content. Steering these features back into the base model recovers about 80% of RL’s performance gain. A synthetic benchmark demonstrates the method’s ability to test for genuinely novel features.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-SAE Track offers a principled framework to track representation shifts during RL and provides representational evidence that RL largely leverages preexisting capabilities rather than inventing broad new features. It also enables targeted benchmarking for genuinely novel features.

title: NoteVQA: Benchmarking VLMs on Real-Life Questions from Human Communities
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly power consumer-facing AI search, yet evaluating them on the diversity of everyday visual questions remains challenging. Existing benchmarks often target predefined capabilities, such as multi-hop retrieval or long-form synthesis, whereas users ask photo-grounded questions spanning a long tail of everyday scenarios. Despite advances in VLMs, users on Xiaohongshu, a mainstream Chinese image-sharing platform, continue to turn to other people for help with everyday visual questions. Motivated by this behaviour, we curate NoteVQA from these questions, yielding 252 items across 12 topical categories and 7 user intents. Each item includes a concise reference distilled from expert community responses and a human-audited interleaved reference answer that combines textual explanations with supporting visual evidence. We evaluate both short-answer correctness and interleaved-answer quality. To support the latter, we introduce AgenticInterleave, a single-agent ReAct framework for retrieval-supported answer generation, together with IVR-12, a 12-dimensional rubric for assessing the content, presentation, and image quality of interleaved references and model outputs. Across 10 frontier VLMs, the highest short-answer accuracy is 52.8\%, while adding agentic search to Qwen3.5-397B-A17B improves accuracy by only 2.0\%. For interleaved answers, the same model running AgenticInterleave scores 3.52 under IVR-12, compared with 4.65 for the human-audited references, with the largest gap in content quality. These results highlight the challenges that everyday visual questions pose for current VLMs in both answer accuracy and the quality of visually grounded explanations.

AI.tldr: NoteVQA provides 252 real-world, photo-grounded questions sourced from Xiaohongshu with expert-derived references and human-audited interleaved answers, plus a retrieval-guided framework (AgenticInterleave) and a 12-dimension rubric (IVR-12) to evaluate visual QA systems. Across 10 frontier VLMs, short-answer accuracy peaks at 52.8% with modest gains from agentic search; interleaved explanations lag behind human references, highlighting persistent challenges in everyday visual question answering and visually grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking VLMs on everyday, photo-grounded questions remains underexplored. Existing datasets focus on predefined capabilities, failing to capture the long-tail, real-world visual queries users ask on social platforms. The work aims to (i) collect a realistic VQA dataset (NoteVQA) from Xiaohongshu, (ii) provide concise textual + visual references, and (iii) study not only answer correctness but the quality of visually grounded, interleaved explanations via a retrieval-assisted framework and a standardized rubric.
AI.method: Construct NoteVQA from user questions (252 items, 12 topical categories, 7 user intents). Each item includes a concise expert-derived reference and a human-audited interleaved reference answer combining text with supporting visuals. Develop AgenticInterleave (single-agent ReAct) for retrieval-supported answer generation and IVR-12 rubric to assess interleaved outputs. Evaluate 10 frontier VLMs; measure short-answer accuracy and interleaved-answer quality.
AI.result: Highest short-answer accuracy across models: 52.8%. Adding agentic search to Qwen3.5-397B-A17B yields a 2.0 percentage-point improvement. For interleaved answers, AgenticInterleave scores 3.52 (IVR-12) vs 4.65 for human references, with the largest gap in content quality.
AI.conclusion: Everyday visual questions remain challenging for current VLMs, both for direct answers and for visually grounded, explanatory interleaves. The NoteVQA dataset and IVR-12/AgenticInterleave framework enable a more nuanced evaluation of real-world VQA capabilities and point toward improvements in retrieval integration and content quality of explanations.

title: Zero-shot video highlight detection based on text descriptions and synthetic images
summary: Detecting video highlights, the most informative or engaging moments in a video, is important for applications such as video summarization and content recommendation. We propose a zero-shot framework that combines CLIP, large language models (LLMs), and diffusion models. Given lightweight video metadata, such as a title or category, an LLM generates textual descriptions of likely highlight events. These descriptions are further converted into synthetic visual prototypes using a diffusion model. Textual and visual representations are matched to video frames using CLIP, enabling frame-level highlight detection without highlight annotations or dataset-specific training. Experiments on TVSum and SumMe demonstrate strong zero-shot performance, with particularly favorable results on TVSum. The proposed approach provides an effective framework for metadata-conditioned zero-shot video highlight detection.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot video highlight detection leveraging metadata: LLMs convert lightweight metadata into textual highlight events, diffusion creates visual prototypes, then CLIP aligns text and visuals to video frames to detect highlights without annotations or training on the target dataset. Strong zero-shot results on TVSum and SumMe, especially TVSum.
AI.motivation: Eliminate dependence on annotated highlight datasets by using multimodal foundation models to interpret lightweight metadata and detect highlights in a zero-shot setting.
AI.method: Pipeline: input lightweight video metadata (e.g., title, category). An LLM generates textual descriptions of likely highlight events. A diffusion model synthesizes corresponding visual prototypes. CLIP matches textual descriptions and synthetic visuals to video frames to produce frame-level highlight scores, enabling zero-shot highlight detection without dataset-specific training.
AI.result: Demonstrates strong zero-shot performance on TVSum and SumMe, with particularly favorable results on TVSum.
AI.conclusion: The approach confirms the feasibility of metadata-conditioned zero-shot video highlight detection using a combination of LLMs, diffusion models, and CLIP, offering a practical, training-free solution for video summarization and recommendation.

title: Sensory Precision Inference for Multimodal Arbitration under Uncertainty
comment: This work has been accepted for publication in the International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI2026) proceedings. This is the Submitted Manuscript before any peer review. The reviewed and edited version will be available on Springer Nature Link
summary: Autonomous agents operating on multisensory data cannot assume that all sensory modalities remain consistently informative. In real environments, sensory streams are frequently corrupted by noise, missing data, or inter-modal incongruence, requiring adaptive arbitration between competing sensory hypotheses. While active inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty-guided inference, the role of dynamically inferred sensory precision in generative multimodal arbitration under sensory conflict remains comparatively underexplored. We propose a multimodal perceptual inference model in which latent beliefs and modality-specific sensory precisions are jointly updated through iterative free-energy minimization. In our proposed model, sensory precision dynamics not only reflect sensory uncertainty but actively shape the evolution of latent beliefs during multimodal conflict. In addition, we introduce a learned prior over sensory precisions that induces structured, class-dependent precision patterns and influences cross-modal inference dynamics. We evaluate the model using a synthetic multimodal MNIST dataset combining visual, auditory, and tactile representations of digit classes under controlled sensory noise and inter-modal incongruence. Results show that dynamic precision inference improves reconstruction robustness under corrupted sensory evidence, supports coherent latent inference from reduced sensory evidence, and enables stable arbitration between conflicting modalities. Furthermore, learned precision priors generate interpretable precision structures that shape inference dynamics and cross-modal latent structure. These findings support sensory precision inference as a mechanistic control process for adaptive multimodal belief formation under uncertainty, highlighting precision dynamics as a computational mechanism for robust and interpretable multisensory integration.

AI.tldr: Dynamic inference of modality-specific precision in an active-inference framework improves robustness and interpretability of multimodal perception under noise and cross-modal incongruence.
AI.motivation: Multisensory environments often provide unreliable or conflicting signals. Existing active inference work largely treats precision statically, limiting adaptive arbitration. A joint, iterative update of latent beliefs and sensory precisions could enable principled, uncertainty-guided cross-modal fusion.
AI.method: A multimodal generative model where latent beliefs and modality-specific precisions are updated via iterative free-energy minimization. The model includes a learned prior over precisions that yields structured, class-dependent patterns and influences cross-modal inference. Evaluation on a synthetic multimodal MNIST dataset combining vision, audio, and tactile representations under controlled noise and incongruence.
AI.result: Dynamic precision inference improves reconstruction robustness under corrupted evidence, yields coherent latent inference from reduced sensory evidence, and stabilizes arbitration between conflicting modalities. Learned precision priors produce interpretable precision structures that shape inference dynamics and cross-modal latent structure.
AI.conclusion: Precision dynamics function as a mechanistic control for adaptive multisensory belief formation, providing robust and interpretable multimodal integration under uncertainty.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Robustness, Cost, and Governance Trade-offs for Vision-Language Models in Templated Document Extraction
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to extract structured fields from business documents, yet most evaluations report accuracy on clean benchmarks and offer little guidance to practitioners choosing an approach for a given task complexity. We address this gap with a measurement-grounded study and an open-source release. Across eleven systems (three commercial, two reasoning, five open-source VLMs in pretrained and fine-tuned form, and a non-LLM OCR->regex floor) scored on a 750-document held-out pool of synthetic checks, fine-tuning on 3K samples lifts the best open-source VLMs above F1 0.98-above every zero-shot commercial system on this task-while GPT-5 leads the commercial pool on F1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 collapses on Date. To turn these measurements into actionable choices, we introduce a practitioner-oriented selection framework that maps a task profile (quality, latency, governance, volume) to a recommended approach via filtering and total-cost minimization, illustrated on a hypothetical mid-volume document-extraction scenario.

AI.tldr: Measurement-grounded evaluation of 11 vision-language model systems for structured field extraction from synthetic checks; fine-tuned open-source VLMs achieve F1 > 0.98, surpassing zero-shot commercial models; GPT-5 tops commercial F1; Claude Sonnet 4.5 fails on Date; introduces a practitioner-oriented framework mapping task profile to model choice via filtering and total-cost minimization, with an open-source release.
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack guidance beyond clean benchmarks; need measurement-based recommendations that account for task quality, latency, governance, and volume for real-world document-extraction tasks.
AI.method: Assess 11 systems (3 commercial, 2 reasoning, 5 open-source VLMs in pretrained and fine-tuned forms, plus a non-LLM OCR→regex baseline) on a held-out pool of 750 synthetic checks. Fine-tune on ~3k samples. Evaluate with F1. Develop a practitioner-oriented selection framework that maps task profiles (quality, latency, governance, volume) to recommended approaches via filtering and total-cost minimization. Demonstrate with a hypothetical mid-volume scenario.
AI.result: Fine-tuning lifts the best open-source VLMs above F1 0.98, outperforming all zero-shot commercial systems on this task. GPT-5 leads the commercial pool on F1, while Claude Sonnet 4.5 collapses on the Date field.
AI.conclusion: Provides a cost-aware, task-profile–driven framework for selecting models in business document extraction, accompanied by an open-source release to assist practitioners.

title: RAIN: Region-Aware Inversion Network for Semantic Watermark Extraction
summary: Semantic watermarks for diffusion models embed ownership information into the generative process while preserving perceptual quality, but Gaussian-Shading extraction conventionally requires multi-step diffusion inversion to recover the initial noise. Recent one-step methods show that this cost can be reduced substantially. We study this problem through extended flow matching and conditional regression. The key observation is that, near the high-SNR image endpoint, recovering a useful noise statistic given by the first-step output of the extended flow matching in the high-SNR regime is much simpler than reconstructing the full inverse trajectory, and Gaussian Shading only requires the recovered latent to remain in the correct watermark decision region. Based on this observation, we propose a lightweight, prompt-free extractor that decomposes endpoint recovery into an image-like anchor and a noise-oriented residual, which increases the capability of the model to utilize GPU parallel computation. The resulting method avoids iterative inversion and repeated evaluation of a diffusion-scale U-Net, providing an efficient one-step extraction pipeline with a concise theoretical interpretation. The computational cost of extracting noise is lower than that of both OSI and FARI. The github repo is there: https://github.com/TheLovesOfLadyPurple/RAIN-lightweight-NN-for-one-step-semantic-watermark-extraction

AI.tldr: Lightweight one-step extraction of Gaussian-Shading watermarks for diffusion models using an endpoint decomposition (image-like anchor + noise residual) via extended flow matching and conditional regression, enabling GPU-friendly, non-iterative extraction with lower cost than OSI/FARI.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational burden of extracting semantic watermarks from diffusion-model outputs. Multi-step diffusion inversion is costly; existing one-step methods promise gains but need efficient, scalable solutions that preserve watermark integrity.
AI.method: Propose a prompt-free extractor that splits the endpoint noise recovery into an image-like anchor and a noise-oriented residual, based on extended flow matching and conditional regression. Near the high-SNR image endpoint, recovering the first-step latent is simpler than reconstructing the full inverse trajectory. The approach decouples endpoint recovery from iterative diffusion-scale U-NET evaluations, enabling a lightweight, GPU-friendly, one-step extraction pipeline with a theoretical interpretation.
AI.result: An efficient one-step extraction pipeline for Gaussian-Shading watermarks with lower computational cost than OSI and FARI, and a concise theoretical interpretation. A GitHub repo is provided for implementation details.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a practical and faster alternative to existing iterative methods for semantic watermark extraction, leveraging end-point statistics and endpoint decomposition. It promises improved throughput and parallelization, though its robustness across models, watermark types, and potential adversarial attacks remains to be fully validated.

title: Branched Optimal Transport Amortization
summary: Methods of Branched Optimal Transport (BOT) mimic the economy and efficiency of natural tree-like structures, such as those found in rivers and biological systems. These methods are widely applicable for designing efficient networks in society, from river basins and blood vessels to mail and gas distribution systems. However, they remain understudied in the context of designing deep generative models, particularly at a large scale. Standard continuous-time generative models, such as the flow matching approach, fail to capture the inherent hierarchical and branching patterns present in real-world data. Current models provide no mechanism for flows to merge or share pathways to minimize total transport cost. Inspired by the "economy of scale" principle in BOT, we introduce a novel, scalable branched flow-matching algorithm designed to solve the branched optimal transport problem in high dimensions. Our method adapts the Benamou-Brenier continuous-time optimal transport formulation to learn branched generative flows. These flows allow probability mass to aggregate along common pathways before branching out to diverse targets. Parametrized by neural networks, our method effectively learns complex branched generative processes. We demonstrate its effectiveness on challenging high-dimensional tasks in biology and image generation.

AI.tldr: Scalable branched flow-matching for branched optimal transport in high-dimensional generative modeling, enabling mass merging along shared pathways before branching to targets.
AI.motivation: Capture hierarchical, branching structure in real data and overcome limitations of flow-based generative models that cannot merge or share pathways; exploit economy of scale in BOT for efficient transport in high dimensions.
AI.method: Adapt Benamou-Brenier continuous-time OT to learn branched generative flows; neural-network parameterization; allow mass aggregation along common pathways before branching; optimize transport cost with branching constraints; scalable to high dimensions.
AI.result: Empirically effective on challenging high-dimensional tasks in biology and image generation; demonstrates modeling of branching structures and improved efficiency over standard continuous-time flows.
AI.conclusion: Provides a scalable framework for learning branched generative processes using BOT, enabling hierarchical generation and broader application in deep generative modeling.

title: New Conditions for Philosophers to Catch the Wave of Citizen Deliberation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence in advance
summary: Powerful technologies labeled ``AI''-without sufficient epistemic caution-are already reshaping political and private life, bringing both new dangers and new opportunities for citizen participation. These range from electoral and legislative engagement to the most ambitious form: political co-creation through citizens' assemblies. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support such processes through moderation, translation, facilitation, summarization, and writing assistance. But this potential remains largely unrealized. The Democratic Commons project takes a fundamentally interdisciplinary approach-from philosophy to computer science-to evaluate LLMs against five proposed democratic principles. At its core, the project is driven by the question of political bias: under what conditions can LLMs be used democratically within forms of citizen participation that are them- selves still largely experimental? Addressing these socio-technical questions requires grounding in political theory and, more broadly, in philosophy-disciplines that provide the normative frameworks without which the democratic evaluation of AI systems cannot be mean- ingfully conducted.

AI.tldr: A project (Democratic Commons) benchmarks LLMs against five democratic principles to assess their suitability in citizen participation, focusing on political bias and socio-technical conditions; aims to develop normative, interdisciplinary evaluation rather than report results.
AI.motivation: Ensure AI tools used in democratic contexts are epistemically cautious and legitimate; address political bias and democratic legitimacy in citizen participation; bridge philosophy and computer science to provide normative criteria for AI in democracy.
AI.method: Interdisciplinary evaluation framework combining philosophy/political theory and computer science; assesses LLM capabilities (moderation, translation, facilitation, summarization, writing assistance) against five democratic principles; focuses on conditions under which LLMs can be used democratically in experimental citizen participation processes.
AI.result: No empirical results are reported in the abstract; the project aims to establish an evaluative framework and criteria for democratic AI deployment, with emphasis on political bias and normative grounding.
AI.conclusion: Grounding in political theory and philosophy is essential to meaningfully evaluate AI in democratic contexts; without normative frameworks, the democratic assessment of AI systems remains incomplete.

title: What Makes a 3D Scene Editable? A Factorized Benchmark of Fidelity, Locality, Consistency, and Preservation
summary: Neural 3D scene editing is often evaluated by semantic alignment alone, although a convincing result may alter unrelated content or become inconsistent across views. We introduce EditBench3D, a representation-agnostic benchmark that treats editing as controlled information replacement. It evaluates four complementary properties: instruction fidelity, spatial locality, cross-view consistency, and preservation of non-target content. The protocol combines visibility-aware 3D target supports, paired descriptions, held-out cameras, and five edit families covering appearance, material, geometry, and object-level changes. We evaluate eight representative NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, hybrid, and proxy-based editors on 240 scene-edit pairs. The study shows that semantic fidelity is only weakly associated with the other editing properties, and that no single method is optimal across all dimensions. Explicit Gaussian editors offer a strong overall balance, whereas direct proxy manipulation provides the most conservative edits at the cost of open-ended fidelity. These findings support reporting editability as a multi-objective profile rather than a single semantic score.

AI.tldr: EditBench3D: a representation-agnostic, multi-objective benchmark for 3D scene editing that assesses instruction fidelity, spatial locality, cross-view consistency, and non-target preservation across eight editors and 240 scene-edit pairs.
AI.motivation: Semantic fidelity alone is insufficient to judge 3D editing; edits can affect unrelated content or break multi-view consistency.
AI.method: Protocol uses visibility-aware 3D targets, paired descriptions, held-out cameras, and five edit families across appearance, material, geometry, and object-level changes; evaluates eight editors (NeRF-based, 3D Gaussian Splatting, hybrid, proxy-based) on 240 pairs.
AI.result: Strong misalignment between semantic fidelity and other properties; no single editor excels across all metrics; Gaussian editors offer balanced performance; proxy-based edits are conservative but limited open-ended fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Recommend reporting edits with a multi-objective profile rather than a single semantic score; EditBench3D reveals complementary dimensions and helps compare editors across multiple criteria.

title: Ensemble-Conditioned Molecular Design
comment: Code available at: https://github.com/rssrwn/ensemble-cond-design datasets and checkpoints available at: https://zenodo.org/records/22485204
summary: Molecular design is typically approached as a problem of finding molecules which can adopt a single bioactive conformation. In reality, molecules occupy a distribution over conformations, and many of the properties which determine whether a candidate is viable depend on that distribution rather than on any single conformer. We reframe molecular design as an optimisation of both the modes and properties of molecules' conformational ensembles, where modes can be represented as shapes, pharmacophore profiles or protein pockets, and properties are aggregate scalars computed over the whole distribution. To realise this we introduce ensemble-conditioned guidance, a framework which conditions 3D molecular generative models on both axes simultaneously. Mode conditions are composed adaptively at inference by combining the vector fields produced under each condition. Conditions may be targeted or avoided, mixed across modalities and combined in arbitrary numbers, allowing a wide range of design tasks to be expressed with a single trained model. We introduce adaptive symmetry learning to allow conditions from different reference frames to be composed, and extend our generative framework to enable flexible-size generation. We evaluate on new benchmarks for multi-mode conditioning and ensemble property optimisation, and apply the framework to two practical drug discovery tasks, dual-target binder design and active-state-selective agonist design, where in both cases conditioning on the additional state improves the desired outcome over single-state conditioning.

AI.tldr: Proposes ensemble-conditioned guidance for 3D molecular generation, optimizing conformational ensembles via multi-modal conditioning and adaptive symmetry, enabling flexible-size generation and improved multi-task drug design (dual-target and active-state selective).
AI.motivation: Molecular properties arise from conformational ensembles, not single conformers, so design should optimize the distribution of states rather than a single conformation.
AI.method: Introduce ensemble-conditioned guidance that conditions 3D generative models on both conformational modes (shapes, pharmacophore profiles, protein pockets) and distribution-level properties. Modes are adaptively composed at inference by combining vector fields from each condition. Adaptive symmetry learning enables composition of conditions from different reference frames. Enables flexible-size generation. Evaluate on new benchmarks for multi-mode conditioning and ensemble property optimization; apply to dual-target binder design and active-state-selective agonist design.
AI.result: Conditioning on the additional state improves outcomes over single-state conditioning in both practical tasks; new benchmarks demonstrate capabilities of multi-mode conditioning and ensemble property optimization.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-conditioned generation offers a unified, flexible framework to optimize molecular conformational distributions, enabling complex design tasks across multiple modes and states with a single trained model.

title: Predicting build orientation for SLM dental parts: a comparison of rotation representations and direct vector regression
summary: Build orientation for selective laser melting (SLM) manufacturing of dental parts is usually chosen manually by technicians. We treat orientation prediction as supervised machine learning of the part's up-axis from technician-labeled production data, and test which rotation representations produce the best results. Using $n\approx2400$ patient-specific dental parts, we trained a ResNet-50 multi-view image backbone and a PointNeXt-S point-cloud backbone, both pretrained and fine-tuned end-to-end, on 13 up-axis representations spanning six classical $SO(3)$ parameterizations and seven representations defined directly on the unit sphere $S^2$. We report the geodesic angular error between predicted and ground-truth up-axis on a test set, with and without test-time augmentation (TTA) over $K=21$ known rotations. With TTA, the octahedral map achieves the lowest mean angular error ($10.6^\circ$, ResNet-50). The three lowest-error results overall are direct $S^2$ representations, though this may reflect label noise in the unsupervised in-plane component of the $SO(3)$ targets rather than a topological advantage. von Mises-Fisher collapses to a near-constant prediction when trained with PointNeXt-S but not with ResNet-50. TTA reduces mean angular error by 31-73 % across almost every representation and backbone. Overall, test-time augmentation over a small set of known rotations is the most consistent driver of accuracy, whereas the best-performing representation is strongly backbone-dependent.

AI.tldr: Supervised learning to predict dental part orientation for SLM by learning the part's up-axis from technician labels, comparing 13 rotation representations across six SO(3) parameterizations and seven S^2 representations using ResNet-50 and PointNeXt-S, with test-time augmentation (TTA). TTA substantially improves accuracy; direct S^2 representations often perform best, with backbone-dependent results; von Mises-Fisher collapses under PointNeXt-S; overall, TTA is the most consistent performance driver.
AI.motivation: Automate and improve accuracy of orientation selection in selective laser melting for dental parts, and systematically compare rotation representations and backbones to identify robust configurations and the benefit of test-time augmentation.
AI.method: Train supervised models to predict the part up-axis from labeled production data using 13 rotation representations (six SO(3) parameterizations and seven S^2 representations). Backbones: ResNet-50 multi-view images and PointNeXt-S point clouds; pretrained then end-to-end fine-tuned. Evaluate geodesic angular error on a test set with and without test-time augmentation over K=21 known rotations.
AI.result: With test-time augmentation, octahedral-map representation yields the lowest mean angular error (10.6° with ResNet-50). The three lowest errors overall come from direct S^2 representations. Von Mises–Fisher representation collapses to near-constant predictions with PointNeXt-S but not with ResNet-50. TTA reduces mean angular error by 31–73% across most representations and backbones. Conclusion: TTA is the most consistent driver of accuracy; the best representation is strongly backbone-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Test-time augmentation significantly boosts orientation-prediction accuracy in SLM for dental parts, and the optimal rotation representation depends on the chosen backbone; direct S^2 representations can outperform others, though topology-related labeling noise may influence results.

title: ThreshGuide: Class-Aware Labeled-Guided Thresholding for Semi-Supervised 3D Abdominal Multi-Organ Segmentation
summary: Pseudo-labeling is a strong paradigm for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, yet its effectiveness is highly sensitive to confidence thresholding. In abdominal multi-organ segmentation, a fixed global threshold is particularly suboptimal because organ classes differ substantially in size, appearance, and learning difficulty. In this work, we propose ThreshGuide, a class-aware threshold adaptation framework that uses labeled data to guide pseudo-label selection on unlabeled data. Built upon a standard teacher-student architecture, the teacher model evaluates labeled samples during training to estimate class-aware threshold targets by maximizing an error-aware F\b{eta} criterion that balances precision and coverage. These targets are then smoothed with an exponential moving average (EMA) and used to filter unlabeled voxels in a class-dependent manner. Experiments on FLARE2022 and AMOS2022 show that ThreshGuide performs competitively overall, yielding clear improvements specifically on hard-to-learn organs.

AI.tldr: Class-aware thresholding for pseudo-labeling in semi-supervised medical segmentation (ThreshGuide) improves hard-to-learn organs by adapting thresholds per class via labeled data and EMA-smoothed targets in a teacher-student framework; shows improvements on FLARE2022 and AMOS2022, particularly for small/complex organs.
AI.motivation: Global fixed thresholding in pseudo-labeling is suboptimal due to inter-class variability in size, appearance, and learning difficulty; a class-aware, data-guided thresholding approach can balance precision and coverage across organ classes.
AI.method: Extend teacher-student with class-aware threshold targets estimated by the teacher on labeled data by maximizing an error-aware F-beta criterion balancing precision and coverage. Targets are smoothed with exponential moving average (EMA) and applied to filter unlabeled voxels in a class-dependent manner.
AI.result: Competitive performance overall with clear improvements on hard-to-learn organs; validated on FLARE2022 and AMOS2022 datasets.
AI.conclusion: ThreshGuide demonstrates that per-class, data-guided threshold adaptation can mitigate issues of fixed global thresholds in semi-supervised medical segmentation, yielding better performance for challenging organs; approach leverages labeled data to guide pseudo-label selection and EMA smoothing to stabilize targets.

title: $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ Representation Learning: An Intrinsic Mixed-Curvature Space with Higher Curvature Capacities and Deeper Order-Aware Composition
summary: Mixed-curvature representation learning seeks to capture rich geometric structures that cannot be adequately modeled by a single curvature regime. Existing approaches largely rely on product manifolds, which require manually specifying how different curvature spaces are combined and separate their curvature contributions across factors. We introduce the $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ space, a representation geometry defined by the simple $\det(A)=1$ constraint and a left invariant Schatten-$p$ Finsler structure. Despite this minimal construction, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ exhibits pointwise negative, zero, and positive flag curvature around a common flagpole, while its mixed-curvature and curvature-coupling capacities are asymptotically maximal relative to the intrinsic geometric upper bound. Beyond geometry, its noncommutative group structure provides inherent order sensitivity, and its non-nilpotent Lie algebra admits nonzero nested Lie brackets at arbitrary depth, enabling deep order-aware composition. Empirically, $\mathbb{SL}(n)$ consistently outperforms a broad range of representation manifold baselines across graph benchmarks at different scales. It reduces average distortion over the strongest baselines by $44.3\%$ on KEGG and $40.5\%$ on HumanCyc, and improves Hits@20 by $42.8\%$ on OGBL-PPA. Experiments on Flickr30k-Order further support its ability to capture higher order dependencies from ordered composition. Together, these results show how a seemingly simple structural constraint can yield unexpectedly rich geometry, capacity, and composition within a unified representation space.

AI.tldr: Proposes the SL(n) space defined by det(A)=1 with a left-invariant Schatten-p Finsler structure to model mixed-curvature geometry in a unified representation space, achieving strong curvature versatility and leading empirical gains across graph and order-sensitive tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of product manifolds in mixed-curvature representation learning by introducing a minimal, unified geometric space that yields diverse curvature regimes and enables deep, order-aware composition.
AI.method: Define the SL(n) representation space via the det(A)=1 constraint and a left-invariant Schatten-p Finsler metric; analyze curvature properties (flag curvature) and the Lie algebra (noncommutative, non-nilpotent, nested brackets); evaluate on graph benchmarks (KEGG, HumanCyc, OGBL-PPA) and ordered-data tasks (Flickr30k-Order).
AI.result: SL(n) exhibits pointwise negative, zero, and positive flag curvature around a common flagpole; its mixed-curvature and curvature-coupling capacities are asymptotically maximal. Empirically, it reduces average distortion by 44.3% on KEGG and 40.5% on HumanCyc, and improves Hits@20 by 42.8% on OGBL-PPA; Flickr30k-Order results support higher-order dependency capture.
AI.conclusion: A seemingly simple determinant constraint yields rich geometry, enhanced capacity, and powerful order-aware composition within a unified representation space, achieving strong cross-domain performance.

title: Data storytelling meets interpretable machine learning: Decoding AI decisions for non-experts without revealing sensitive data and model details
summary: AI-driven automated decision-making requires both predictive performance and interpretability. Recent advances in interpretable machine learning (IML) provide tools for explaining model predictions, but the technical complexity of these explanations may hinder accessibility to non-experts. To address this challenge, this study integrates data storytelling with IML to enhance the explainability of AI-generated decisions for a broader audience. Following the design science research (DSR) paradigm, this study proposes a formal definition of data storytelling in IML, introduces the DIST Pyramid to align data storytelling with IML, and presents the I-P-O Model to describe their interactions. It further develops an architecture to explain AI decisions through distinct "What-if" and "Why-not" event-generation processes. The architecture also employs data desensitization to protect sensitive input data. To validate the approach, a case study is conducted with the Boston Housing dataset, using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values and large language models (LLMs) to generate data stories with And-But-Therefore (ABT) structures. An empirical evaluation shows that 76.4% and 74.3% of respondents rated the "What-if" and "Why-not" data stories as more comprehensible, with significantly higher accessibility scores than traditional SHAP visualizations. The paper concludes with the presentation of a narrative interpretation framework that integrates IML and data storytelling, thereby expanding the research scope as well as the practical applicability of AI decision-making.

AI.tldr: A DSR-driven framework that merges data storytelling with interpretable ML to improve explainability; introduces DIST Pyramid and I-P-O Model; uses What-if/Why-not narrative generation with SHAP + LLMs; validated on Boston Housing; higher comprehensibility and accessibility vs SHAP visuals; contributes a narrative interpretation framework.
AI.motivation: To broaden accessibility of IML explanations to non-experts by combining storytelling with explanations, addressing complexity of IMl outputs and protecting data privacy.
AI.method: Design Science Research (DSR) approach; formal definitions of data storytelling in IML; DIST Pyramid; I-P-O Model; architecture with What-if/Why-not event-generation; data desensitization; case study using Boston Housing; SHAP values and LLMs to generate ABT-styled data stories; empirical evaluation with user respondents.
AI.result: What-if and Why-not stories rated as more comprehensible by 76.4% and 74.3% of respondents; significantly higher accessibility scores than traditional SHAP visualizations.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a narrative interpretation framework that integrates IML with data storytelling, expanding both theoretical scope and practical applicability of AI decision-making.

title: MoVT: Video-Augmented Motion Tokenizer for Text-to-Motion Generation
summary: Text-driven 3D human motion generation models face significant challenges in responding to diverse and unconstrained textual prompts, primarily due to the limited availability of 3D motion training data. To address this, we introduce MoVT, a novel framework that effectively leverages the extensive range of human action videos to enhance text-to-motion generation. At the core of our approach is the cross-modal augmented motion tokenizer, which projects discrete 3D motion tokens into the 2D domain. This projection allows us to enrich the motion codebook with complex, real-world motion patterns derived from videos. The enriched discrete tokens are then mapped back to the 3D domain, resulting in aligned 3D and 2D codebooks with an enhanced capacity to represent intricate motions. These enhanced codebooks are integrated into a generative masked transformer, which predicts masked motion token indices in a modality-agnostic manner. This enables the use of text-index pairs, generated from the 2D codebook and annotated motion videos, to further enhance the generator. Extensive empirical evaluations show that MoVT performs favorably against prior state-of-the-art methods across multiple key metrics.

AI.tldr: MoVT introduces a cross-modal framework that enriches 3D motion tokens using 2D video data, via a cross-modal augmented motion tokenizer and a masked transformer, to improve text-to-motion generation beyond state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: The main barrier for text-to-3D motion generation is limited 3D motion data; abundant 2D action videos offer rich, real-world motion patterns that can be leveraged to augment 3D motion representations.
AI.method: A cross-modal augmented motion tokenizer projects discrete 3D motion tokens into the 2D domain to enrich a 3D/2D aligned codebook with complex motions from videos. The enriched tokens are mapped back to 3D and used in a generative masked transformer that predicts masked motion token indices in a modality-agnostic manner, leveraging text-index pairs from the 2D codebook and annotated videos to guide generation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show MoVT outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple key metrics across several benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating 2D video-derived motion patterns into a cross-modal tokenizer and a masked transformer yields a more expressive, text-driven 3D motion generator, improving quality and diversity compared to previous approaches.

title: Beyond Numerical Time Series: A Unified Benchmark for Multimodal Forecasting with Heterogeneous Context
summary: Most time series forecasting benchmarks remain numerical-centric and provide limited support for evaluating contextual information that shapes real-world temporal dynamics. Existing multimodal benchmarks also suffer from limited data and context coverage, fragmented evaluation settings, and overreliance on aggregate evaluation. In this paper, we propose \textbf{MUSE-Bench}, a unified benchmark for multimodal time series forecasting with heterogeneous context. It comprises fourteen datasets across eight domains and six types of context: metadata, events, holidays, news, images, and numerical covariates. We evaluate diverse forecasting paradigms, including statistical, data-specific, foundation, multimodal, and general-purpose LLM forecasting methods under shared non-overlapping forecast windows, common target observations, and consistent point and probabilistic metrics. Extensive experiments yield three main findings. First, numerical time series foundation models dominate the overall ranking, while Aurora, the evaluated multimodal foundation model, trails the leading numerical TSFMs but outperforms all evaluated data-specific models. Second, ablations show that external context improves the four evaluated context-aware models, whereas incorrect or temporally misaligned context degrades performance. Third, general-purpose LLMs perform poorly as direct forecasters, and LLM-guided refinement does not yield consistent improvements. MUSE-Bench enables systematic evaluation of how forecasting models utilize context and provides a foundation for future multimodal forecasting research.

AI.tldr: MUSE-Bench introduces a unified multimodal time series forecasting benchmark with 14 datasets across 8 domains and 6 context types (metadata, events, holidays, news, images, numerical covariates). It evaluates diverse forecasting paradigms and finds numerical TS foundation models dominate, context helps some models while misaligned context hurts, and general-purpose LLMs are weak as direct forecasters; the benchmark enables systematic multimodal forecasting research.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of existing time series benchmarks that are numerically focused and lack diverse, contextual information; provide a unified, extensible platform to evaluate how different models leverage heterogeneous context in forecasting.
AI.method: Assemble 14 datasets spanning 8 domains; incorporate six context types (metadata, events, holidays, news, images, numerical covariates); evaluate multiple forecasting paradigms (statistical, data-specific, foundation, multimodal, general-purpose LLMs) under shared forecast windows, common targets, and consistent point/probabilistic metrics.
AI.result: Numerical time series foundation models outperform others; Aurora (multimodal foundation model) trails leading numerical TSFMs but beats all data-specific models. External context improves context-aware models; incorrect or misaligned context degrades performance. General-purpose LLMs are weak forecasters; LLM-guided refinement lacks consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: MUSE-Bench provides a robust, systematic framework to evaluate context usage in multimodal forecasting and establishes a foundation for future multimodal forecasting research.

title: Are LLMs Good Financial User Simulators? A Preliminary Study
comment: The complete version will be open and the paper is under review in AAAI
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but their ability to reproduce evolving individual financial decisions remains unclear. We present a preliminary study in a controlled paper-trading environment with 120 volunteers. Participants used non-redeemable virtual funds under real-time market conditions; no real brokerage accounts, real-money positions, or real transaction records were accessed. Given only information available before a prediction cutoff, a simulator predicts the participant's next-trading-day action, traded security, and transaction quantity. We evaluate temporally aligned rolling predictions and compare settings with and without point-in-time market information. Market context improves action and ticker prediction in the controlled ablation, while transaction sizing remains difficult. We also observe systematic behavioral compression: models overproduce hold actions, underpredict sell decisions, and simplify multi-security transactions. These results provide an initial empirical characterization and motivate larger-scale evaluation of individual, temporal, and portfolio-level behavioral fidelity.

AI.tldr: Preliminary evaluation of LLMs as user simulators for paper-trading decisions: market context improves action/ticker prediction; transaction sizing is still hard; observed behavioral compression (more holds, fewer sells, simpler multi-security trades).
AI.motivation: Assess whether LLM-based user simulators can faithfully reproduce evolving individual financial decisions in a controlled trading environment.
AI.method: 120 volunteers used non-redeemable virtual funds in a real-time market setting. No real accounts or real-money data. A simulator, given information available before a prediction cutoff, predicts the next-trading-day action, traded security, and quantity. Temporal rolling predictions were evaluated, with ablation comparing settings with and without point-in-time market information.
AI.result: Inclusion of market context improves action and ticker prediction in the ablation; transaction sizing remains difficult. Systematic behavioral compression observed: models overproduce hold actions, underpredict sell decisions, and simplify multi-security transactions.
AI.conclusion: This work provides an initial empirical characterization of LLM-based trading behavior simulators and motivates larger-scale evaluation of individual-level temporal fidelity and portfolio-level behavioral fidelity.

title: Refinement-based Flow Policy Optimization
summary: Flow-based policies offer an expressive representation for online reinforcement learning, but conventional flow matching requires samples drawn from the distribution to be modeled. This poses a challenge when the desired action distribution is defined only implicitly by a Q-function, since directly sampling actions from the resulting distribution is generally intractable. We propose Refinement-Based Flow Policy Optimization (RFPO), a novel framework for training a flow policy in online reinforcement learning by alternating between Q-guided sample refinement and self-target flow matching. RFPO first generates actions from Gaussian noise using the current flow policy and then uses a finite-step stochastic refinement procedure to move them toward an energy-based distribution induced by the Q-function. Each refined action is then paired with its corresponding initial noise sample and used as a fixed target for flow-matching training. By repeatedly refining its own outputs and learning from the resulting targets, RFPO incorporates Q-guidance into the policy without requiring direct samples from the target distribution, while retaining the capacity to represent multiple action modes. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the distributional dynamics induced by RFPO. Across six continuous-control tasks, RFPO matches or outperforms a standard Gaussian-policy baseline on almost every task. Experiments on six synthetic two-dimensional target distributions with diverse geometries demonstrate that RFPO captures complex multimodal structure without mode collapse.

AI.tldr: RFPO introduces a refinements-based training loop for flow policies in online RL by alternating Q-guided action refinement with self-target flow matching. Actions are sampled from the current flow, refined toward a Q-induced energy distribution, and then used as fixed targets to train the flow, enabling multimodal policy representation without sampling from the target distribution.
AI.motivation: Flow-based policies require samples from the target distribution, but when the target is implicitly defined by a Q-function this sampling is intractable. RFPO seeks to inject Q-guidance into a flow policy without needing direct targets.
AI.method: Generate actions from Gaussian noise via the current flow; perform a finite-step stochastic refinement toward an energy-based distribution induced by the Q-function; pair each refined action with its initial noise; use this pair as a fixed target in a flow-matching objective; iterate to align the policy with Q-guided refinements. The approach includes a theoretical analysis of RFPO’s distributional dynamics.
AI.result: Empirically, RFPO matches or exceeds a Gaussian-policy baseline on six continuous-control tasks and captures complex multimodal target distributions in synthetic 2D experiments without mode collapse.
AI.conclusion: RFPO provides a practical and theoretically grounded framework to incorporate Q-guidance into flow policies without direct sampling from the target distribution, preserving multimodality and achieving strong empirical performance.

title: Design of a Deep Learning Credit Risk Early Warning System Integrating Multi-source Heterogeneous Data
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Published in Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Machine Intelligence and Digital Applications (MIDA 2026), Xi'an, China, April 24-26, 2026. ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3801438.3804860
summary: Advancements in data fusion and real-time analytics technologies have opened new avenues for addressing complex domain challenges. Financial risk early warning systems often suffer from inefficiency due to information silos and monitoring delays. This paper proposes a credit risk early warning system based on heterogeneous information fusion. The system employs a model architecture integrating deep neural networks and attention mechanisms to extract multidimensional features from diverse data sources such as transaction behaviors and social networks, thereby establishing an early identification mechanism for corporate and individual credit risks. System testing demonstrates that this approach significantly enhances the accuracy and timeliness of risk warnings, outperforming traditional rule-based engine solutions. The findings offer innovative insights for early intervention in financial risks, holding practical significance for safeguarding financial stability.

AI.tldr: A heterogeneous information fusion framework for credit risk early warning using deep neural networks and attention to integrate transactions and social network data, achieving higher accuracy and faster warnings than rule-based systems.
AI.motivation: Finance faces inefficiencies due to silos and delays in risk monitoring; early, accurate detection of credit risk at both corporate and individual levels is critical to stability.
AI.method: A multimodal architecture fusing diverse data sources via deep neural networks and attention mechanisms to extract multidimensional features; builds an early warning mechanism for credit risk at both corp and individual levels.
AI.result: Empirical testing indicates significant gains in warning accuracy and timeliness; outperforms traditional rule-based engines.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the value of heterogeneous information fusion and modern ML for proactive financial risk management; offers practical implications for financial stability through early interventions.

title: G-ray: Ray-Level Relative Geometric Position Encoding in Multi-View Vision Transformers under Camera Heterogeneity
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, 14 tables. Supplementary material included in the appendix. Project page: https://g-ray-project.github.io/
summary: We study relative position encoding for multi-view vision Transformers under camera heterogeneity, including varying fields of view (FoVs) or projection models. Existing rotary relative position encodings commonly use image-plane positional coordinates, producing projection-dependent relative phases and inconsistent geometric cues for cross-projection attention. We introduce G-ray, a ray-level relative position encoding whose rotary phases are parameterized by camera-local ray angles. The same camera-local ray pair induces the same relative phase across projections, providing projection-invariant positional consistency. G-ray can be used directly or integrated with existing encodings, retaining complementary geometric cues without additional learned parameters. We validate G-ray in three host encodings, RoPE, GTA, and RayRoPE, across 3D reconstruction and novel-view synthesis (NVS). Across three heterogeneous 3D reconstruction benchmarks at 50 views, G-ray leads all six averaged metrics and reduces mean pointmap relative error by 45.8% over MapAnything, with calibration supplied to both. Trained exclusively on homogeneous pinhole images, the 3D reconstruction model handles mixed pinhole and non-pinhole inputs without retraining and remains competitive on homogeneous pinhole 3D reconstruction protocols. For NVS, GTA and RayRoPE improve with G-ray under joint viewpoint and FoV variation. The project's webpage is available at https://g-ray-project.github.io/.

AI.tldr: G-ray provides a projection-invariant, ray-level relative-position encoding for multi-view Vision Transformers, compatible with existing rotary encodings, improving robustness to camera heterogeneity (FoV and projection models) with no extra learnable parameters.
AI.motivation: Rotary relative position encodings often rely on image-plane coordinates, causing projection-dependent phase and inconsistent geometry for cross-projection attention under varying cameras. A projection-invariant encoding is needed to unify geometry across views.
AI.method: Introduce camera-local ray angles to parameterize rotary phases, ensuring the same camera-local ray pair yields the same relative phase across projections. G-ray can be used directly or integrated with RoPE, GTA, or RayRoPE without additional learned parameters.
AI.result: Evaluated on three heterogeneous 3D reconstruction benchmarks at 50 views; G-ray achieves the best aggregated metrics and reduces mean pointmap relative error by 45.8% over MapAnything (with calibration). Models trained on homogeneous pinhole data generalize to mixed pinhole/non-pinhole inputs without retraining; in NVS, GTA and RayRoPE improve when combined with G-ray under joint viewpoint and FoV variation.
AI.conclusion: G-ray offers projection-invariant, geometry-preserving relative-position cues for multi-view Transformers, is complementary to existing encodings, and yields robust improvements under camera heterogeneity without adding learnable parameters.

title: Omni-Streaming Thinking
summary: Streaming omni-modal models must decide what and when to answer from the video chunks and synchronized audio observed so far. Visual cues often support an interpretation before an utterance or sound event is complete. If that interpretation enters memory as a fact, later reasoning can keep relaying it even after audio contradicts it. We call this failure premature cross-modal commitment. We propose Omni-Streaming Thinking (OST), which generates structured outputs that include evidence observed so far, forecasts of future evidence, and claims based on this evidence. Each claim is initially marked as pending and linked to a future verification interval. Audio and visual evidence are stored separately, and OST checks a claim against the evidence from the specified modality at the end of the verification interval. When contradictory evidence is detected, a refutation process reduces the influence of the claim and its dependent states, and then guides a state update using the new evidence. An answer gate decides whether the answer-critical claims meet the conditions for giving a response. Using a frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct backbone with lightweight adaptation, OST outperforms the strongest open baselines on five streaming and audio-visual benchmarks by more than 10% relative on average. We also introduce OST-DiagBench, which holds video fixed and edits audio to test agreement, absence, contradiction, coexistence, and subtitle-speech conflict. OST reaches d-prime = 2.95, compared with at most 1.38 for open baselines, while reducing vision-induced auditory hallucinations.

AI.tldr: OST introduces a structured, evidence-based streaming multimodal reasoning framework that postpones cross-modal commitments and verifies claims over time, yielding >10% relative gains on five benchmarks and reducing vision-induced auditory hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Prematurely committing to a visual interpretation before audio evidence is complete can cause persistent, incorrect beliefs when later audio contradicts them. A principled mechanism to track evidence and verify claims over time is needed for robust streaming AV reasoning.
AI.method: OST maintains separate audio and visual evidence; generates claims with pending status linked to verification intervals; at interval end, checks claims against modality-specific evidence; a refutation process reduces influence of contradicted claims and guides state updates; an answer gate decides when to respond. Implements on a frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct backbone with lightweight adaptation; evaluated on five streaming AV benchmarks. Also introduces OST-DiagBench, with video fixed and manipulated audio to test agreement, absence, contradiction, coexistence, and subtitle-speech conflict.
AI.result: OST outperforms strongest open baselines by more than 10% relative on average across five streaming AV benchmarks. It achieves d-prime = 2.95 on OST-DiagBench (vs. up to 1.38 for baselines) and reduces vision-induced auditory hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Structured, evidence-driven streaming reasoning (OST) robustly mitigates premature cross-modal commitments, improves answer reliability in streaming AV tasks, and provides a diagnostic framework (OST-DiagBench) to evaluate audiovisual consistency.

title: EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents
summary: Data agents aim to fulfill natural-language instructions over heterogeneous data, including tables, files, and databases. However, data agents face a challenging agent-data gap: heterogeneous data resides outside the agent, while the agent can access it (e.g., column names and file paths) only through generic tools. Existing approaches either let agents directly explore raw data sources or inject manually constructed semantic layers into prompts. However, neither scales well to large heterogeneous data sources nor adapts to different agent behaviors. In this paper, we introduce EvoOntology, a self-evolving ontology layer for data agents.
