EvoOntology encapsulates the ontology as an MCP server comprising a schema layer, a content layer, and a tool layer, enabling agents to actively query and interact with the ontology at runtime. To this end, we introduce a builder agent for autonomous ontology construction and a self-evolution loop that continuously refines the ontology through attribution-guided typed edits that are accepted only after a backbone-conditional paired evaluation. Experiments on three well-adopted data-agent benchmarks with four LLM backbones demonstrate that EvoOntology consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing semantic-layer approaches, effectively bridging the agent-data gap and enabling more effective interaction with heterogeneous data. Code: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/EvoOntology

AI.tldr: EvoOntology proposes a self-evolving ontology layer (MCP-based) for data agents to bridge the agent-data gap, featuring a builder agent and an attribution-guided, backbone-evaluated self-evolution loop; it outperforms baselines across benchmarks and backbones.
AI.motivation: To address the agent-data gap where heterogeneous data resides outside the agent and is only accessed via generic tools; existing approaches do not scale to large heterogeneous data or adapt to different agent behaviors.
AI.method: Introduce EvoOntology as an MCP server with schema, content, and tool layers. Add a builder agent for autonomous ontology construction and a self-evolution loop that refines the ontology through attribution-guided typed edits, accepted only after backbone-conditional paired evaluation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on three widely-used data-agent benchmarks across four LLM backbones shows EvoOntology consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing semantic-layer approaches, effectively bridging the agent-data gap.
AI.conclusion: EvoOntology enables scalable, adaptive interaction with heterogeneous data by providing a runtime-queryable ontology layer, with autonomous construction and evolution; evidenced by improved performance across benchmarks.

title: TwinICL: Diagnosing Multimodal In-Context Learning through Paired Counterfactuals
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables models to infer tasks from demonstrations, but existing benchmarks generally lack matched text and image versions needed to compare ICL performance across modalities. We introduce TwinICL, a procedurally generated benchmark providing such pairs for controlled comparison. Across six open-weight models and 38 tasks, multimodal ICL consistently underperforms text-only ICL, with gaps varying by task family. To test whether this gap can be recovered, we target visual access, task framing, and reasoning through three interventions. Their combination recovers strong multimodal ICL performance on a diagnostic subset, despite limited or inconsistent individual effects. To distinguish difficulties in executing tasks from those in inferring them, we evaluate models with explicit task instructions, revealing a modality gap even when the task is known. We then examine how adding demonstration inputs and outputs reshapes this gap, highlighting demonstrations' dual role as additional context to process and evidence about the task. The dataset is available at https://github.com/lab-flair/TwinICL.

AI.tldr: TwinICL provides a procedurally generated, matched text-image benchmark to compare in-context learning across modalities. Across six open-weight models and 38 tasks, multimodal ICL underperforms text-only ICL. Interventions (visual access, task framing, reasoning) in combination recover strong multimodal ICL on a diagnostic subset; explicit task instructions reveal a modality gap even when the task is known; demonstrations reshape the gap, serving as context and evidence about the task. Dataset available at GitHub.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of matched text and image benchmarks to study and compare in-context learning (ICL) across modalities. A controlled, procedurally generated benchmark enables systematic analysis of multimodal ICL performance and the impact of various interventions.
AI.method: Procedurally generate twin datasets with matched text and image versions. Evaluate six open-weight models on 38 tasks for both text-only and multimodal ICL. Investigate three interventions—visual access, task framing, and reasoning—and their combinations. Assess explicit task instructions to separate task inference from execution. Examine how demonstrations (inputs/outputs) reshape the ICL gap. Use a diagnostic subset to probe where improvements occur.
AI.result: Multimodal ICL consistently underperforms text-only ICL across tasks; the performance gap varies by task family. The combination of the three interventions recovers strong multimodal ICL performance on the diagnostic subset. When explicit task instructions are provided, the modality gap persists even if the task is known. Demonstrations act as both additional context and evidence about the task, shaping the gap.
AI.conclusion: TwinICL enables controlled cross-modal ICL research and showed that closing the multimodal gap requires a combination of visual access, proper task framing, reasoning, and informative demonstrations. The benchmark and baseline findings highlight where multimodal ICL lags and how to design interventions to improve it; the dataset is released at the linked GitHub repository.

title: Multi-source Transfer Learning of Time Series with a Shapelet-based Distance Measure
summary: Transfer learning is an effective technique for addressing data scarcity in deep learning for time series classification, but its success depends on the selection of source datasets. Conventional transferability estimation methods are often computationally expensive, as they require fully pre-training a model on each potential source dataset to assess its suitability. This paper introduces a novel, training-free source selection method named Shapelet Matching. Our approach first identifies discriminative shapelets from the target and potential source datasets. Then, Shapelet Matching quantifies dataset similarity by comparing the extracted sets of shapelets. To mitigate the risk of negative transfer from selecting an unsuitable single source, we introduce a multi-source transfer learning method. We select several source datasets based on their shapelet-based similarity scores, combine them into a single multi-source dataset, and use this aggregated dataset for pre-training. The model is then fine-tuned on the target task. We evaluated our method on 128 datasets from the UCR Archive using both temporal CNN and Transformer architectures. The empirical results demonstrate that our multi-source pre-training reduces the risk of negative transfer on average. Shapelet Matching achieves the strongest performance for the CNN backbone and remains competitive for patch-based Transformer architectures, while avoiding the cost of pre-training a separate model for every candidate source.

AI.tldr: Training-free source selection for time-series transfer learning via Shapelet Matching; uses discriminative shapelets to measure source-target similarity and constructs a multi-source pretraining dataset to reduce negative transfer without per-source pretraining.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity in time-series deep learning and high cost of evaluating transferability; conventional methods require pretraining on all candidates, which is impractical.
AI.method: Extract discriminative shapelets from target and candidate sources; compute similarity between shapelet sets; select top sources by similarity; combine them into a multi-source pretraining dataset; pretrain a model on this aggregated data; fine-tune on target; evaluate on 128 UCR datasets with temporal CNN and Transformer.
AI.result: Multi-source pretraining using Shapelet Matching reduces risk of negative transfer on average; strongest gains with CNN backbone; competitive for patch-based Transformers; avoids training a separate model for each candidate source.
AI.conclusion: Shapelet Matching provides a training-free, scalable approach to source selection in time-series transfer learning; effective across architectures; future work may optimize shapelet extraction, similarity measures, and integration with various downstream tasks.

title: KnowBench: Effort Reduction as a Unified, Deployment-Grounded Benchmark for Clinical AI
summary: Clinical AI systems are evaluated with instruments built for research settings (reference-based similarity metrics and expert rubric panels) that measure resemblance to an artifact rather than reduction of a burden. We introduce KnowBench, pioneered by Knowtex, whose unifying metric is Effort Reduction (ER): the proportion of system-generated clinical work product accepted by the responsible clinician under expert and safety review. ER is defined once and instantiated per task across the administrative workload clinical AI automates: visit notes, diagnosis and billing codes, orders, EHR chart summarization, patient after-visit summaries, and clinical decision support. In every instantiation the construction is identical: the clinician's review-and-attestation event is the ground truth, every accepted unit is work the system completed, and every correction is residual effort returned to the clinician. The primary contribution of this paper is the benchmark itself: the metric, its degenerate cases, and a reporting protocol under which ER claims are auditable and cross-system comparable. Alongside it we report an initial headline measurement from the documentation instantiation: over one million signed encounters across a production window exceeding six months and thirteen medical specialties, Knowtex's proprietary fine-tuned clinical foundation models operating inside a closed feedback architecture achieve an aggregate ER of 97.99%, with per-specialty aggregates spanning 96.8-98.9%. This release reports the protocol's checklist partially, and states which companion statistics are withheld; the benchmark is offered so that this figure, and every figure reported after it, can be held to the same standard.

AI.tldr: KnowBench defines Effort Reduction (ER) to quantify clinical AI’s real-world burden reduction, offering a unified, auditable benchmark across tasks.
AI.motivation: Current research metrics largely measure resemblance to artifacts rather than actual reduction in clinician workload; a universal, auditable metric is needed for cross-task clinical AI evaluation.
AI.method: ER is the proportion of system-generated clinical work products accepted by the responsible clinician under expert/safety review. It is instantiated per administrative task (notes, codes, orders, summaries, CDS). The ground truth is the clinician’s review/attestation; accepted units are completed system work; corrections represent residual clinician effort.
AI.result: Initial headline: >1 million signed encounters over six+ months across 13 specialties. The closed-loop, proprietary models achieve aggregated ER of 97.99%, with per-specialty ERs spanning 96.8–98.9%. The protocol/checklist is partially released; companion statistics are withheld. The benchmark is designed for auditable, cross-system comparability.
AI.conclusion: KnowBench/ER provides an auditable benchmark for real-world burden reduction in clinical AI and supports cross-system comparison. Limitations include partial disclosure, potential biases in reviewer processes, task-definition variability, and questions about generalizability beyond the reported production environment.

title: Tele360: Real-Time Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction from Sparse Unposed Cameras
summary: Live free-viewpoint visualization of real humans is critical for immersive communication and interactive digital experiences. Existing methods either rely on computationally expensive optimization or require calibrated cameras and low-resolution inputs, making real-time high-resolution deployment impractical. In this work, we present Tele360, the first real-time feed-forward system for dynamic human reconstruction and live free-viewpoint visualization from sparse, unposed RGB streams. Our system jointly estimates camera poses and reconstructs a dynamic 3D Gaussian representation for each time instance in a single forward pass. To achieve this, we start by designing a lightweight sparsity-aware multi-view transformer backbone that tokenizes foreground human regions while preserving global context through a shared scene token. We then employ a fully transformer-based Gaussian decoder to mitigate convolution-induced over-smoothing while keeping decoding sparse and efficient. In addition, we introduce a hybrid feature pyramid that injects multi-scale appearance cues into geometry prediction. We further introduce a lightweight differentiable Levenberg-Marquardt camera refinement layer to enhance multi-view consistency and geometric alignment. Moreover, to stabilize learning under sparse, unposed inputs, we transfer multi-view geometry priors from a large visual-geometry foundation model via teacher-student distillation. Finally, the predicted Gaussian maps are streamed with video codecs to remote devices for interactive free-viewpoint rendering. Extensive experiments show that Tele360 achieves state-of-the-art visual quality on studio benchmarks while supporting real-time 2K input-to-rendering at over 25 FPS on a single consumer GPU. Additional captured sequences illustrate its performance across varied subjects, clothing, and motions under our multi-camera setup.

AI.tldr: Tele360 delivers real-time, feed-forward dynamic human reconstruction and live free-viewpoint rendering from sparse, unposed RGB streams using a Transformer-based Gaussian representation, LM refinement, and distillation to achieve 25+ FPS at 2K inputs with state-of-the-art quality on studio benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of optimization-based or calibrated-input methods that are costly and impractical for real-time, high-resolution free-viewpoint visualization of dynamic humans, especially under sparse, unposed capture.
AI.method: A lightweight sparsity-aware multi-view transformer backbone tokenizes foreground regions with a shared scene token for global context; a fully transformer-based Gaussian decoder preserves detail without convolution-induced over-smoothing; a hybrid feature pyramid injects multi-scale appearance cues into geometry; a differentiable Levenberg-Marquardt refinement layer improves multi-view consistency; distillation from a large visual-geometry foundation model stabilizes learning under sparse, unposed inputs; Gaussian maps are streamed for remote interactive rendering.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art visual quality on studio benchmarks and runs in real-time (over 25 FPS at 2K input) on a single consumer GPU, with qualitative demonstrations across varied subjects, clothing, and motions under a multi-camera setup.
AI.conclusion: Tele360 demonstrates that real-time, high-quality free-viewpoint visualization from sparse unposed RGB streams is feasible with a fully Transformer-based Gaussian representation and lightweight optimization-style refinements, enabling practical telepresence and interactive digital experiences; further work may explore broader deployment and robustness to more diverse scenes.

title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linear Contextual Bandits with Arbitrary Adaptive Action Sets
summary:
We study stochastic linear contextual bandits with arbitrary action menus that may depend on the fixed parameter and the interaction history. We establish matching upper and lower bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Let $d$ be the dimension, $K$ be the menu size, and $T$ the time horizon. For $2\le K\le d$, we prove an upper bound $\widetilde O(K^{1/4}\sqrt{dT})$. When $T\ge d^2$, we further prove a lower bound $Ω(K^{1/4}\sqrt{dT})$. Thus, for $T\ge d^2$ and $2\le K\le d$, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors, and the polynomial dependence on $K$ is optimal. Compared with the previous $\widetilde O(\sqrt{dKT})$ bound, our upper bound improves the dependence on $K$ by a factor of $K^{1/4}$.
  For $K\ge d$, we prove an upper bound $\widetilde O_{d,T}\left(\sqrt{dT}\min\{\sqrt d,(d\log K)^{1/4}\}\right)$ and a lower bound $Ω\left(\sqrt{dT}\min\left\{\sqrt d,\left(\frac{d\log K}{\log(2d)}\right)^{1/4}\right\}\right)$. Here, $\widetilde O_{d,T}$ omits logarithmic factors only in $d$ and $T$. In particular, for polynomially large $K\ge d$, the upper and lower bounds both scale as $d^{3/4}\sqrt T$ up to logarithmic factors, improving the standard $\widetilde O(d\sqrt T)$ rate by a factor of $d^{1/4}$. As $K$ grows further, the regret smoothly recovers the $d\sqrt T$ scale once $\log K$ reaches order $d$.

AI.tldr: Near-optimal minimax bounds for stochastic linear contextual bandits with menus; improved dependence on menu size K; tight (up to logs) for 2 ≤ K ≤ d; and a transition to d^{3/4} sqrt{T} and then d sqrt{T} as K grows.
AI.motivation: Resolve how flexible action menus, potentially history- and parameter-dependent, affect regret; close the gap between upper and lower bounds and clarify K- and d-dependence.
AI.method: Derive matching (up to logarithmic factors) upper and lower bounds in regimes 2 ≤ K ≤ d and K ≥ d; compare with the prior sqrt(dKT) rate; use minimax and information-theoretic arguments to establish tightness across regimes; characterize phase transitions as K grows.
AI.result: Upper bounds: for 2 ≤ K ≤ d: ~O(K^{1/4} sqrt{dT}); for K ≥ d: ~O_{d,T}( sqrt{dT} * min{ sqrt{d}, (d log K)^{1/4} } ). Lower bounds: Ω(K^{1/4} sqrt{dT}) when T ≥ d^2; Ω( sqrt{dT} * min{ sqrt{d}, (d log K / log(2d))^{1/4} } ). These bounds match up to logs, proving the K-dependence is tight for K ≤ d; as K grows polynomially in d the rate scales as d^{3/4} sqrt{T}; and when log K ≈ d the rate recovers d sqrt{T}.
AI.conclusion: The paper sharply characterizes how menu size K interacts with dimension d to affect minimax regret; it tightens the known bounds, showing improved K-dependence and a smooth transition to the standard d sqrt{T} rate for large K.

title: Navigating Sparse Evidence: Agentic Visual RAG via Explicit Context Selection and Consolidation
summary: Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (VRAG) empowers models to navigate and answer queries about visually rich documents by retrieving relevant page images as visual evidence and reasoning over their content. However, effectively utilizing this visual evidence is usually impeded by two main challenges. First, answer-relevant evidence is sparse and may be concentrated in a small region of one page or dispersed across multiple pages. Second, existing agentic methods often generate answers based on raw exploration trajectories or compressed textual memories rather than an explicitly organized set of supporting images, making answers susceptible to exploration noise and obscuring the evidence-backed reasoning trace. We argue that the bottleneck lies not only in evidence discovery but also in its preservation and organization before answer generation. We propose SCoRE (Selection and Consolidation for Robust Evidence), a unified agent loop for explicit evidence selection and consolidation. During exploration, SCoRE retains only query-relevant observations and their source pointers in a maintained textual ledger, preserving earlier evidence while keeping the visual context bounded. At termination, it reloads the referenced original images and consolidates the visual evidence for answering, arranging it into a logical sequence. This decouples final reasoning from exploratory trial-and-error while ensuring strict visual grounding via indexed claim-to-image linkages. To enable end-to-end optimization of this unified rollout, our training paradigm combines filtered cold-start trajectory distillation with evidence-aware reinforcement learning, whose reward promotes evidence coverage, consolidation compactness, and answer correctness.

AI.tldr: SCoRE (Selection and Consolidation for Robust Evidence) is a unified VRAG framework that explicitly selects and consolidates visual evidence for robust, image-grounded answers. It decouples exploration from final reasoning by maintaining a query-relevant, pointer-based textual ledger during exploration and reloading original images at termination to construct a coherent, evidence-backed reasoning sequence.
AI.motivation: Evidence in visual retrieval–augmented generation is often sparse and either dispersed across pages or buried in raw exploration traces or unstructured textual memories, leading to noisy reasoning and weak traceability. There is a need to explicitly preserve and organize supporting images to enable robust, traceable visual grounding.
AI.method: During exploration, SCoRE keeps only query-relevant observations and their source pointers in a maintained textual ledger, preserving earlier evidence while bounding visual context. At the end, it reloads the referenced original images and consolidates the visual evidence into a logical sequence with indexed claim-to-image linkages. The approach decouples final reasoning from exploratory trial-and-error. End-to-end optimization combines filtered cold-start trajectory distillation with evidence-aware reinforcement learning, with rewards encouraging evidence coverage, consolidation compactness, and answer correctness.
AI.result: No empirical results are presented in the abstract; the paper outlines the framework and training paradigm without reported quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SCoRE provides a decoupled, end-to-end trainable loop for explicit evidence selection and consolidation in VRAG, enabling strict visual grounding and robust, evidence-backed answer generation.

title: Temporal Self-Distillation: Faster Inference in Discrete Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) promise fast inference by generating multiple tokens in parallel, but suffer severe performance degradation when parallel decoding is pushed too aggressively. We introduce Temporal Self-Distillation (TSD), a simple on-policy method that trains dLLMs for fast inference by distilling predictions across time. Specifically, TSD distills the model's denoising distribution at earlier timesteps toward its distribution at the final timestep at which a token is committed. This encourages earlier predictions to better anticipate the model's eventual output, enabling much more aggressive parallel decoding. Because its teacher signal comes from the model itself, TSD requires no offline teacher generation and applies seamlessly to both base and post-trained policies. Across seven benchmarks in mathematics, planning, and code, TSD substantially shifts the speed--quality frontier toward the low-compute regime. TSD thus provides a simple, single-stage approach to accelerating dLLMs, achieving speedups competitive with offline distillation while avoiding a complex two-stage pipeline.

AI.tldr: Temporal Self-Distillation (TSD) enables fast diffusion LMs by aligning early denoising with the final output via on-policy, self-distillation across time, enabling aggressive parallel decoding.
AI.motivation: Address the performance degradation of aggressively parallel decoding in diffusion language models by improving early predictions to anticipate the final token, without relying on offline teachers.
AI.method: On-policy self-distillation across time: distill earlier timesteps' denoising distributions toward the final timestep's distribution at which a token is committed. Single-stage training compatible with base and post-trained policies; no offline teacher generation.
AI.result: On seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and code, TSD substantially shifts the speed–quality frontier toward the low-compute regime, achieving speedups competitive with offline distillation while using a simple single-stage pipeline.
AI.conclusion: TSD provides a simple, effective single-stage approach for accelerating diffusion LMs, matching or approaching offline distillation performance without the need for a two-stage pipeline.

title: When Should a World Model Move? Loss-Conditioned State Execution
summary: We introduce loss-conditioned state execution, a model-agnostic method that decides whether to execute a world model's fixed feasible proposal or retain the current state. Predictive informativeness alone, however, does not establish whether an update will reduce downstream loss. Occurrence ranking can approach perfection while persistence remains the unique absolute-loss Bayes action. Two transition laws can also share occurrence information and conditional variance yet require opposite absolute-loss decisions. We formalize state movability as the existence of a loss-reducing feasible correction and distinguish it from the benefit of a particular proposal. Our method constructs a loss-specific feasible proposal from a predictive distribution and evaluates its groupwise bounded-loss gain over persistence on independent calibration units. The proposal is executed only in groups with a positive simultaneous lower confidence bound. For fixed proposals and groups with bounded unit losses, we prove that every accepted group has lower expected loss than persistence with high probability when calibration units are i.i.d. draws from the target population. Experiments on public forecasting and action-conditioned dynamics benchmarks show supported updates and a trade-off between certification and coverage. On 28,684 held-out M4 Monthly series, the method executes the proposal for 14.0% of series and achieves bounded loss 0.588, compared with 0.599 for persistence and 0.621 for always executing the proposal. The paired 95% bootstrap intervals for both comparisons lie below zero. In constrained forecasting of six unhealthy-inventory types from JD$\mbox{.}$com, a leading e-retailer in China, strong occurrence-ranking signal coexists with a loss-based preference for persistence, illustrating why event predictability and state execution must be evaluated separately.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic framework for loss-conditioned state updates that selectively executes a loss-reducing proposal only when groupwise confidence is positive, with theoretical guarantees under i.i.d. calibration and empirical gains on M4 and JD.com datasets.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between predictive informativeness and actual downstream loss reduction; distinguish the value of predictions from the value of proposals; formalize when a state can be moved (state movability) versus when it should persist.
AI.method: Construct a loss-specific feasible proposal from the predictive distribution; evaluate its groupwise bounded-loss gain over persistence on independent calibration units; execute the proposal only in groups with a positive simultaneous lower confidence bound; prove high-probability loss improvement for accepted groups under i.i.d. calibration units.
AI.result: Empirical results show selective updates and a trade-off between certification and coverage: on 28,684 M4 Monthly series, the method updates 14.0% of series with bounded loss 0.588 vs 0.599 (persistence) and 0.621 (always execute); bootstrap CIs for both comparisons lie below zero. In JD.com inventory forecasting, strong occurrence signals coexist with a loss-based preference for persistence.
AI.conclusion: Loss-conditioned state execution provides a principled, testable mechanism to gate updates that reduce downstream loss, separating prediction quality from loss impact and yielding measurable gains under suitable calibration assumptions; practical deployment hinges on calibration assumptions and threshold choices.

title: ChatGPT Images 2.5 in the Wild: A Launch-Period Dataset and Detector Evaluation
summary: An image tool can change its underlying generator while retaining its public name, making version attribution from online posts ambiguous. We study this problem after the ChatGPT Images 2.5 launch. Our frozen collection contains 3,478 images from 2,440 posts across 8 sources. Recorded posting times fall within the first 51.1 hours after the announcement. It records three attribution tiers and retains standalone images after image-form filtering and targeted review. Caption claims and host records provide admission evidence, not independently verified generator identity. The observed content profile depends on the source mixture: NightCafe supplies 39.0% of images but 77.0% of CLIP-assigned fantasy scenes. We then evaluate six frozen detectors at thresholds calibrated to a 5% flag rate on reference photographs. Collection flag rates range from 3.7 to 56.4%, falling 42-81 percentage points below GenImage recall. Held-out artwork false-positive rates range from 1.5 to 96.5%, so a higher collection flag rate does not by itself establish better detection. An exploratory X-only comparison with our April collection finds a higher September flag rate for Effort, and a suggestive difference for DoU, under fixed-threshold post-clustered bootstrap intervals. Attribution, content and processing differences prevent a causal interpretation of these contrasts. The collection supports analysis of reported model use during a product transition, with source and attribution evidence retained for interpretation.

AI.tldr: Evaluation of attribution robustness for image-generation tools post ChatGPT Images 2.5, using a frozen dataset of 3,478 images from 2,440 posts across 8 sources; analyzes six detectors, flag rates, and attribution evidence; finds variable performance and cautions against causal claims.
AI.motivation: Address attribution ambiguity when image-generation tools can switch underlying generators while preserving public branding; assess detector performance and evidence reliability across diverse sources during a product transition.
AI.method: Assemble a frozen collection of 3,478 images from 2,440 posts across 8 sources; record posting times within 51.1 hours after announcement; categorize into three attribution tiers; apply six detectors with thresholds calibrated to a 5% flag rate on reference photographs; analyze collection flag rates and held-out artwork false positives; compare with a prior April collection in an exploratory X-only analysis; discuss attribution, content, and processing differences.
AI.result: Collection flag rates span 3.7–56.4% (lower recall than GenImage); held-out artwork false positives range 1.5–96.5%; higher collection flag rate does not imply better detection; no causal interpretation possible from contrasts due to attribution/content/processing differences; evidence retained for interpretation of model use during product transition.
AI.conclusion: The dataset enables analysis of reported model use during a product transition with preserved source and attribution evidence; while useful for interpretation, it cannot establish causal links between detectors and attribution changes; highlights the need for careful inference when sources and processing differ.

title: Rethinking Correctness for Uncertainty Estimation in Clinical Prediction with Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models are increasingly explored for clinical prediction from electronic health records and medical images, where identifying unreliable predictions is important for safe deployment. Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables detecting such predictions, but its evaluation depends on a correctness criterion that determines whether each model output is correct. If this criterion disagrees with human judgement or distorts downstream UE performance, conclusions about model reliability can be misleading. We introduce a two-axis framework that evaluates correctness criteria by their agreement with human judgements and fidelity to human-referenced UE performance. We assess eight criteria across three clinical prediction tasks and three models using 450 predictions annotated by two reviewers. Across the audited tasks, canonical exact matching (EM) achieved the highest observed human agreement and lowest UE distortion, while the BERT-based matching (BEM) and LLM-judge also showed strong human agreement. Across four UE methods and 23,254 clinical predictions, criterion choice changed error-detection AUROC by up to 0.146 and reversed the relative ranking of UE methods. The LLM-judge also selectively accepted invalid or uncertain outputs, accepting 16 of 30 such human-identified errors. These results demonstrate that correctness assessment is an integral component of clinical UE evaluation and should be validated before UE methods are compared.

AI.tldr: Introduces a two-axis framework to evaluate correctness criteria for uncertainty estimation (UE) in clinical vision-language models; shows that the choice of criterion materially affects UE evaluation, with exact matching (EM) aligning best with human judgment and minimizing distortion; LLM-based and BERT-based matching show promise; criterion choice can flip UE method rankings and error-detection performance.
AI.motivation: To ensure UE evaluations in clinical prediction reflect true reliability and do not mislead deployment decisions due to misaligned correctness criteria that disagree with human judgment or distort UE performance.
AI.method: Propose a two-axis framework assessing correctness criteria by (1) agreement with human judgments and (2) fidelity to human-referenced UE performance. Evaluate eight correctness criteria across three clinical prediction tasks and three models using 450 predictions annotated by two reviewers. Assess four UE methods over 23,254 predictions to examine how criterion choice affects error-detection AUROC and method rankings. Analyze LLM-judge behavior on uncertain/invalid outputs in 30 cases.
AI.result: EM achieved the highest human agreement and the lowest UE distortion; BERT-based matching (BEM) and LLM-judge also showed strong human agreement. Across four UE methods and 23,254 predictions, criterion choice changed error-detection AUROC by up to 0.146 and could reverse the ranking of UE methods. LLM-judge selectively accepted 16 of 30 invalid or uncertain human-identified errors.
AI.conclusion: Correctness assessment is integral to clinical UE evaluation and should be validated before comparing UE methods; the choice of correctness criterion materially impacts reliability conclusions and downstream decisions.

title: Atria Dawn: The Dawn of Agentic Superintelligence
summary: As AI agents become participants in the development of their successors, they reshape both the production of intelligence and the role of human researchers. We introduce Atria Dawn Preview, a foundation agentic language model designed for scientific research and engineering workflows, with the goal of expanding the frontier of agent productivity in the real world. This model is trained via a Verifiable Experience Pipeline that connects tool-mediated interactions to executable environments and externally verified outcomes. Across 16 benchmarks spanning real-world research, engineering, and digital work, Atria Dawn Preview is competitive with frontier agents and achieves the highest reported score on five of them. Beyond standalone performance, we examine the real research-and-development process behind this model as a case study of human--AI collaboration, analyzing 769 task records from 56 participants together with agent logs. When asked to evaluate completed tasks under comparable conditions, participants rated about one-third of completed AI-assisted tasks as infeasible without AI. More strikingly, agents frequently propose methods and implement revisions, while humans retain most final decisions and guide exploration through judgment and feedback. These observations indicate a shift from task-level execution to project-level partnership, with human effort concentrating on what is worth pursuing and how evidence should guide research. Progress toward more autonomous AI research must therefore advance both the capacity for discovery and the capacity for meaningful human oversight, preserving accountable human authority over the risks and direction of continued development.

AI.tldr: Atria Dawn Preview is a foundation agentic LLM for scientific research and engineering, trained via a Verifiable Experience Pipeline; benchmark results show competitiveness and high performance on multiple tasks; a study of human-AI collaboration reveals AI expands feasible scopes but requires human oversight for project direction.
AI.motivation: Investigate how autonomous agents can contribute to real-world research and engineering, and understand how humans and AI collaborate at the project level as AI agents mature.
AI.method: Develop Atria Dawn Preview with Verifiable Experience Pipeline linking tool use to executable environments and externally verified outcomes; evaluate on 16 benchmarks; analyze 769 task records from 56 participants with agent logs; user evaluation of AI-assisted tasks to assess feasibility.
AI.result: Competitive with frontier agents; highest scores on five of 16 benchmarks; demonstrates AI-assisted workflows can render tasks infeasible without AI in about one-third of cases; humans retain final decision authority; agents propose methods and implement revisions; results imply shift toward project-level collaboration.
AI.conclusion: Advancing autonomous AI research requires both discovery capacity and meaningful human oversight; maintain accountable human authority over risks and direction; progress toward autonomous AI research should balance agent productivity with governance.

title: DNF-SR: Dual-Input and Negative-Aware Feature Fine-Tuning for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
summary: Benefiting from the powerful generative priors of diffusion models, diffusion-based real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) methods have demonstrated impressive performance.To achieve efficient Real-ISR, several recent works have designed one-step diffusion-based models.Howerver, unmediatedly feeding LR into a diffusion model creates a distributional gap with the model's original input.A straightforward approach to reduce the distribution gap is to introduce noise to the LR latents. However, directly adding noise inevitably corrupts the content of the LR images.In this study, we propose DNF-SR, a Dual-input and Negative-aware Feature fine-tuning method for Real-ISR.Specifically, we use a dual-input strategy that concatenates the original LR image with the noisy LR input and feeds them into a diffusion-based image editing model, ensuring both high-fidelity one-step super-resolution and improved perceptual and content consistency.Additionally, the noise present in the noisy LR input introduces randomness and diversity into the outputs. We exploit this property and propose a post-training optimization method, Negative-aware Feature Fine-Tuning (NF2T), which guides the model toward producing higher-quality results.NF^2T classifies multiple outputs into positive and negative subsets and then defines implicit policy improvement directions in both the image and feature spaces, thereby further enhancing the stability of the optimization.Extensive experiments show that DNF-SR outperforms other methods.Code will be released.

AI.tldr: DNF-SR introduces a dual-input, one-step diffusion-based Real-ISR pipeline with a Noise-aware Fine-Tuning (NF^2T) to reduce distribution mismatch and boost output quality; it concatenates the original LR with a noisy LR as inputs to a diffusion-based editing model and uses post-training optimization to refine results by clustering outputs into positive/negative subsets in image and feature spaces, achieving superior performance to prior methods.
AI.motivation: Bridge the distribution gap between LR inputs and the diffusion model's expected input in one-shot diffusion-based Real-ISR, while maintaining content fidelity and enabling output diversity.
AI.method: Propose DNF-SR: a dual-input strategy that feeds the original LR image and a noisy LR input into a diffusion-based image editing model; introduce NF^2T (Negative-aware Feature Fine-Tuning) as a post-training optimization that classifies multiple outputs into positive and negative subsets and defines implicit policy-improvement directions in both image and feature spaces to stabilize and enhance results.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that DNF-SR outperforms competing methods; code will be released.
AI.conclusion: DNF-SR provides an efficient, high-fidelity Real-ISR solution by combining dual-input diffusion editing with negative-aware fine-tuning, achieving improved perceptual and content consistency.

title: Convergence rates for generative drifting flows: fixed-scale obstructions and multihead acceleration
summary: Drifting models offer a promising route to faster generative AI: they perform gradual transport during training, while generating new samples in a single step. This paper asks whether the underlying drifting process can converge rapidly to a target distribution under ideal conditions, before finite-data or optimization effects are introduced. We show that its convergence rate depends critically on how it handles spatial scale. With a single fixed resolution, fine-scale features of the target can become nearly invisible, leading to extremely slow convergence. We introduce a multihead approach that combines scale-normalized information across a continuum of resolutions. We prove that this multihead approach restores exponential convergence near standard reference distributions. These results identify fixed resolution as a key bottleneck and provide a simple route to faster one-step generative models.

AI.tldr: A scale-aware, multihead drift approach eliminates the fixed-resolution bottleneck, yielding exponential convergence toward target distributions in one-step generative models.
AI.motivation: Drifting models promise faster, one-step generation by gradual transport during training. However, convergence to the target distribution can be very slow at a fixed spatial resolution, due to loss of fine-scale information.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the drift process at fixed resolution and introduces a multihead approach that aggregates scale-normalized information across a continuum of resolutions. It provides a theoretical proof that this multihead scheme restores exponential convergence near standard reference distributions.
AI.result: With a fixed single resolution, convergence is slow due to near-vanishing fine-scale features. The multihead, scale-normalized, multi-resolution scheme recovers exponential convergence close to reference distributions.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-resolution handling is the key bottleneck in drift-based one-step generative models. A simple multihead, scale-aware approach offers a clear route to faster generation by restoring exponential convergence.

title: AlgoEvo: Self-Evolving Agentic Search for Automated Algorithm Discovery
summary: Large language models have advanced automated algorithm discovery by synthesizing executable code, but existing frameworks trap them in rigid search pipelines with pre-defined control flows. This limitation restricts adaptive reasoning, blocks cross-paradigm transfer, and discards valuable execution feedback. We propose AlgoEvo, a unified agentic framework that transforms automated algorithm discovery into an interactive, knowledge-accumulating process. An autonomous agent dynamically inspects, diagnoses, and edits code based on runtime feedback. A design skill hub decouples paradigm-specific knowledge from the core discovery engine, allowing a single workflow to seamlessly handle single-objective, multi-objective, and multi-component design. Meanwhile, a hierarchical experience mechanism organizes search trajectories into a task-level tree to guide exploration and consolidates cross-task patterns into reusable skills. Across six representative benchmark tasks, AlgoEvo matches or surpasses specialized methods with substantially fewer evaluations and reduced token consumption, demonstrating strong intra-task accumulation, cross-task transfer, and the ability to reproduce or exceed existing state-of-the-art performance through flexible skill activation.

AI.tldr: AlgoEvo is a unified agentic framework for automated algorithm discovery that uses an interactive, runtime-feedback-driven approach with a design skill hub and a hierarchical experience mechanism, enabling cross-task transfer and efficient exploration. It matches or surpasses specialized methods on six benchmarks with far fewer evaluations and reduced token usage.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based automated algorithm discovery relies on rigid search pipelines with predefined control flows, limiting adaptive reasoning, cross-paradigm transfer, and effective use of execution feedback. A unified, knowledge-accumulating, and cross-task framework could improve efficiency and generalization.
AI.method: AlgoEvo introduces an autonomous agent that inspects, diagnoses, and edits code based on runtime feedback. It features a design skill hub that decouples paradigm-specific knowledge from the core discovery engine, supporting single-objective, multi-objective, and multi-component design. A hierarchical experience mechanism organizes search trajectories into a task-level tree to guide exploration and consolidates cross-task patterns into reusable skills. The evaluation spans six benchmark tasks.
AI.result: AlgoEvo matches or surpasses specialized methods with substantially fewer evaluations and reduced token consumption, demonstrating strong intra-task accumulation, cross-task transfer, and the ability to reproduce or exceed existing state-of-the-art performance through flexible skill activation.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, reusable approach to automated algorithm discovery by separating concerns (skills vs. engine) and organizing exploration hierarchically. Its success on multiple benchmarks indicates strong potential for generalization and efficiency gains, though details on benchmarks, ablations, and real-world applicability would strengthen the work.

title: AdaVSkip: Adaptive Visual Token Skipping Across Layers For Efficient MLLMs Inference
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require substantial computation to process numerous visual tokens across all transformer layers. Most methods for efficient MLLM inference exploit horizontal redundancy by compressing visual tokens. Beyond token reduction, recent studies exploit vertical redundancy through early exit or fixed-layer skipping. However, we find that the extent and distribution of this redundancy vary across inputs and differ between self-attention and MLP modules. Motivated by these observations, we propose AdaVSkip, which equips each layer with two lightweight routers that independently determine whether visual tokens pass through by or skip the self-attention and MLP modules. These decisions collectively define an input-specific visual-computation path, but their discrete and non-differentiable nature makes learning effective paths challenging. To address this challenge, we develop a progressive two-stage training framework that updates only the routers while keeping the backbone frozen. Stage I establishes an initial routing policy through supervised training with input-specific targets derived from module-wise necessity scores. To further align the routing policy with task performance, Stage II uses reinforcement learning to optimize routing decisions with direct feedback from generated answers. It combines an answer correctness reward with a skip-consistency reward that discourages excessive retention of visual-token computation. Across three MLLM backbones, AdaVSkip maintains strong task performance with substantially less computation. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, AdaVSkip reduces FLOPs by 53.2\% while preserving the original model's average performance. Combining it with visual token compression increases this reduction to 91.2\%, while retaining 97.2\% of the original performance on average.

AI.tldr: AdaVSkip introduces per-layer, per-token dynamic routing for self-attention and MLP in multimodal LLMs, enabling input-specific computation paths. Trained in two stages (supervised routing with necessity scores, then reinforcement learning with answer-based feedback and skip-consistency), it substantially reduces FLOPs with minimal performance loss across multiple backbones (e.g., 53.2% FLOP reduction on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, up to 91.2% with token compression, retaining ~97.2% accuracy).
AI.motivation: Redundancy in multimodal transformers varies across inputs and differs between self-attention and MLP. Prior approaches exploit horizontal (token-level) redundancy and vertical (layer-level) skipping, but fail to capture input-dependent differences. AdaVSkip seeks input-specific computation paths by dynamically routing visual tokens through or around both self-attention and MLP, to maximize efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Attach two lightweight routers per layer to independently decide participation of tokens in self-attention and MLP modules. Create input-specific computation paths. Train in two stages with the backbone frozen. Stage I: supervised training using module-wise necessity scores as targets to bootstrap routing policies. Stage II: reinforcement learning using feedback from generated answers, combining an answer-correctness reward with a skip-consistency reward to discourage excessive retention of computation. Applied across three MLLM backbones.
AI.result: Achieves substantial computation reduction with minimal performance loss across backbones. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, reduces FLOPs by 53.2% while preserving average performance. When combined with visual token compression, FLOPs reduction increases to 91.2%, with 97.2% of original performance retained on average.
AI.conclusion: AdaVSkip enables input-specific visual computation in MLLMs with two lightweight, per-layer routers and a two-stage training regime. This yields substantial FLOP reductions while maintaining high task performance, and complements existing token compression techniques.

title: ProtoGuide: Prototype-Driven Guidance for Class-Conditional Graph Generation
comment: Preprint. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. 35 pages, 2 figures, 33 tables
summary: Discrete diffusion models are a prominent family for graph generation, but standard class-conditional mechanisms embed the class signal in the denoiser during training, tying the conditioning mechanism to the trained model. Classifier guidance avoids this coupling in continuous domains by steering a frozen model with a classifier's gradient, but discrete graph diffusion samples discrete edge states, so gradients cannot propagate through the sampled graph. We introduce ProtoGuide, a post-hoc, backbone-agnostic framework that recovers an analogous mechanism. At each reverse step the denoiser's per-edge output is relaxed into a differentiable soft adjacency, embedded by a frozen Siamese graph neural network, and scored against a target-class prototype and its nearest competitor; the resulting per-edge gradient, damped by a cosine schedule, is injected back into the denoiser output. All components stay frozen, so guidance is retargeted by supplying a different prototype. On five classes of real-world networks and two architecturally different backbones, EDGE and DiGress, ProtoGuide raises macro classification accuracy from 50.7% to 73.5% and from 73.6% to 83.8%, and outperforms DiGress's built-in conditional training under our configuration. Gains are largest where the unguided models are weakest, and are not uniform across classes. Per-graph coverage remains high in most settings, while distributional effects are class-dependent. A Best-of-N selection baseline matches this accuracy given enough oversampling, but at a substantial cost in graph diversity. An independently initialized classifier, a directionality test, and a few-shot analysis support target-directed steering and robustness to very small support sets.

AI.tldr: ProtoGuide offers post-hoc, backbone-agnostic guidance for discrete diffusion graph generation by injecting gradients from a frozen Siamese GNN-based prototype comparison, without retraining, achieving substantial macro-accuracy gains across multiple backbones and five real-world class datasets.
AI.motivation: Decouple class conditioning from the trained denoiser in discrete diffusion models and enable target-directed guidance without coupling gradients through the sampled discrete graph.
AI.method: At each reverse step, convert per-edge denoiser outputs to a differentiable soft adjacency, embed with a frozen Siamese GNN as a target prototype vs. nearest competitor, and inject the resulting edge-wise gradient into the denoiser output. All components remain frozen; guidance is retargeted by changing the class prototype. Evaluated on two backbones (EDGE, DiGress) and five real-world network classes.
AI.result: Macro accuracy improved from 50.7% to 73.5% (EDGE) and 73.6% to 83.8% (DiGress); outperforms built-in conditional training under the authors' configuration. Gains are largest where unguided models are weakest. Per-graph coverage remains high in most settings; effects are class-dependent. Best-of-N with oversampling matches accuracy but hurts graph diversity. Independent classifier tests and few-shot analyses support target-directed steering and robustness.
AI.conclusion: ProtoGuide is an effective, backbone-agnostic post-hoc guidance framework for discrete diffusion graph generation that decouples conditioning from training, enabling flexible, target-directed steering with preserved model freezing and showing substantial accuracy gains across multiple datasets and backbones.

title: LongAgent: History-Guided Agentic Search for Longitudinal Outcome Prediction
comment: This paper is accepted to the MICCAI 2026 Agentic AI for Medicine Workshop
summary: Extracting informative representations from longitudinal data that can predict future outcomes remains a critical challenge in medicine. Medical datasets are inherently heterogeneous, consisting of a large number of variables collected from different sources, sampled with different temporal spacings, and representing different aspects of human health status. This requires identifying those variables with predictive value, processing longitudinal information, and integrating multiple variables for outcome prediction. Here, we propose a novel agent-based approach, LongAgent, that can autonomously search over combinations of variable sets, temporal windows and longitudinal aggregation functions, and identify candidates with promising predictive performance. LongAgent utilises a history memory of previous searches and numerical evidence to guide subsequent exploration. On synthetic data, LongAgent achieves a mean prediction RMSE of 1.7376 and improves over the strongest non-agent baseline by 0.0151 (95% CI: [0.0045,0.0260]; p=0.0273). On a real clinical dataset, it performs comparably to the best baseline.

AI.tldr: Agent-based framework LongAgent searches variable sets, time windows, and longitudinal aggregations to predict outcomes from heterogeneous longitudinal data, guided by history memory and evidence. It shows improved RMSE on synthetic data and competitive performance on real clinical data.
AI.motivation: Medical longitudinal data are highly heterogeneous (many variables, varying sampling rates, and multiple modalities). There is a need for automatic discovery of informative representations and effective fusion across time to predict future outcomes.
AI.method: LongAgent autonomously explores combinations of variable sets, temporal windows, and longitudinal aggregation functions. It uses a history memory of prior searches and numerical evidence to guide future exploration.
AI.result: Synthetic data: mean prediction RMSE 1.7376 with improvement over strongest non-agent baseline by 0.0151 (95% CI: [0.0045,0.0260]; p=0.0273). Real clinical data: performance comparable to the best baseline.
AI.conclusion: LongAgent demonstrates automated discovery of informative longitudinal representations and competitive predictive performance, particularly outperforming non-agent baselines on synthetic data and matching top methods on real clinical data.

title: SparseTalk - Sparsifying 3D Gaussian Language Fields for Efficient 3D Visual Question Answering
summary: 3D Gaussian language fields provide an explicit, spatially grounded representation for 3D visual question answering (VQA), but their dense semantic features can require tens of thousands of embeddings per scene, resulting in substantial storage, memory, and inference costs. We investigate how much of this representation is actually necessary for downstream reasoning. Starting from a full embedding representation, we systematically sparsify its semantic embeddings, including the previously underexplored regime below a single image-equivalent block down to 8 visual tokens. We compare random, geometric, semantic, and joint spatial-semantic selection strategies and introduce an object-based sparsification method that distributes the token budget across detected object instances while retaining background context. Experiments on ScanQA and MV-ScanQA reveal substantial redundancy in dense Gaussian language fields. Strong VQA performance is retained with only a few hundred semantic embeddings, corresponding to less than 1% of the original representation. Object-based selection performs well relative to others, with only modest observed changes down to 256 tokens. At this budget, SparseTalk retains 0.80% of SplatTalk's 32,076-token inference input and 0.332% of the mean 77,207-Gaussian dense field, increasing inference throughput while reducing decoded-feature memory 125-fold.

AI.tldr: Dense 3D Gaussian language fields for VQA are highly redundant; sparsifying to a few hundred embeddings (≤1% of original) preserves strong performance, with object-based token budgeting offering robust results and substantial throughput/memory gains.
AI.motivation: Reduce storage, memory, and inference costs of dense 3D Gaussian language fields used for 3D VQA without sacrificing reasoning capability.
AI.method: Systematically sparsify the full embedding representation across regimes from full density down to 8 visual tokens. Compare random, geometric, semantic, and joint spatial-semantic selection strategies. Propose an object-based sparsification that allocates tokens across detected object instances while retaining background context. Evaluate on ScanQA and MV-ScanQA.
AI.result: Significant redundancy in dense Gaussian language fields. High VQA performance can be maintained with only a few hundred embeddings, less than 1% of the original representation. Object-based selection performs well with modest degradation down to 256 tokens. At 256 tokens, methods retain small fractions of the original input (0.80% of SplatTalk’s 32k-token input and 0.332% of the mean 77k-Gaussian dense field), while boosting inference throughput and reducing decoded-feature memory by ~125x.
AI.conclusion: The dense 3D Gaussian language field representation is largely redundant for downstream reasoning. Sparse, object-focused token budgeting achieves strong performance with large gains in efficiency, making dense 3D VQA more practical for resource-constrained settings.

title: Bandits with Probing: Optimal Regret and the Limits of Winner Feedback
summary: A learner probes at most $k$ of $n$ arms each round, receives the maximum of their rewards in $[0,1]$, and competes with the best fixed arm. When does the probing advantage pay for learning? We determine two minimax laws. Under independent stochastic rewards with winner feedback (the maximum and a winning label), or on arbitrary fixed sequences given a single signed contrast between block maxima, the minimax regret has order $Φ_{n,k}(T)=\min\{\frac{n-k}{n}T,\frac{n-k}{k}\}$, $2\le k<n$. Under winner feedback, both arbitrary joint i.i.d. rewards and fixed sequences have minimax regret of order $R_{n,k}(T)=\frac{n-k}{n}\min\{T,\frac{n+T}{k},\sqrt{\frac{nT}{k}}\}$. Both laws have universal constants and anytime upper bounds. The first reduces regret to a pure coverage cost: same-round contrasts absorb the stability cost, and independence permits exact resampling whose gains fund sample advancement. The second adds a learning cost that becomes comparable to coverage at horizon $n$; beyond $nk$, numerical maxima improve over labels alone. The lower bound allows every adaptive action size.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when probing at most k of n arms per round provides a learning benefit under winner feedback, deriving two minimax regret laws that characterize the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The results give explicit regret rates Φ_{n,k}(T) and R_{n,k}(T) with phase transitions and universal constants, valid for both stochastic and adversarial settings, and show how coverage costs and learning costs interact.
AI.motivation: To determine when partial probing (exploration) in a bandit-like setting yields a net gain in regret reduction, and to obtain tight minimax rates under winner feedback for both stochastic and fixed-sequence reward models.
AI.method: Derives lower and upper bounds via minimax analysis under two feedback models: (i) independent stochastic rewards with winner feedback, and (ii) arbitrary fixed sequences with a single signed contrast between block maxima. Constructive strategies and adversarial instances yield universal constants and anytime bounds; the analysis separates a pure coverage cost from a learning cost.
AI.result: Two minimax laws: Φ_{n,k}(T) = min{ (n−k)/n · T, (n−k)/k }, for 2 ≤ k < n; and under winner feedback, R_{n,k}(T) = (n−k)/n · min{ T, (n+T)/k, sqrt(nT/k) }. Both laws have universal constants and provide anytime upper bounds. The first shows regret reduction via coverage; the second shows a learning cost that becomes comparable to coverage around horizon n; beyond nk numerical maxima improve over labels. Lower bounds allow adaptive action sizes.
AI.conclusion: The results precisely delineate when probing yields a net learning benefit and quantify the trade-offs between coverage and learning costs, yielding tight minimax rates across stochastic and adversarial settings and guiding practical probing strategies for k arms per round.

title: Pilot Early, Commit Late: A Real-Options Model of Enterprise AI Adoption under Rapid Technological Progress
summary: Artificial intelligence presents firms with an unusual timing problem. The technology frontier is improving rapidly, implementation is partly irreversible, and organization-specific capabilities are accumulated through action. This paper develops a two-period decision model of AI deployment under uncertainty in which a firm chooses among immediate deployment, a limited pilot, and waiting. Deployment earns current operating value but exposes the firm to architectural obsolescence; waiting preserves the option to adopt after the frontier is observed; a pilot sacrifices current operating value to build organization-specific learning without full commitment. The model yields five central timing results and a sixth comparative result on where learning occurs. First, a mean-preserving increase in frontier uncertainty raises the value of waiting and piloting but leaves immediate deployment unchanged when its payoff is affine in the frontier. Second, faster expected frontier progress can reduce the relative attractiveness of immediate deployment when deployed architecture captures only a limited share of future improvement. Third, a pilot dominates waiting exactly when the expected value of the capability it builds exceeds its cost. Fourth, sufficiently valuable organization-specific learning creates a nonempty region in which "pilot early, commit late" is optimal. Fifth, there is a closed-form modularity threshold above which immediate deployment dominates the best outside option. Sixth, production learning and pilot-specific learning affect the timing margin differently. A continuous-time extension recovers the standard result that uncertainty raises the adoption threshold while capability and modularity lower it. The paper separates deploying, experimenting, and waiting, and shows why rapid progress can rationally increase experimentation without justifying irreversible commitment.

AI.tldr: A two-period model of AI deployment under frontier uncertainty explores when firms should deploy now, pilot, or wait, revealing six timing results (and a sixth on learning location) and showing how modularity, learning, and uncertainty shape adoption; a continuous-time extension confirms that uncertainty raises adoption thresholds while capability/modularity lower them, clarifying why rapid progress boosts experimentation without automatic irreversible commitment.
AI.motivation: Rapid AI frontier progress creates a timing problem: deployment is partly irreversible and organization-specific learning accrues with action. The paper seeks to characterize optimal timing and the role of learning in a simple, tractable model.
AI.method: Two-period decision model with three actions: immediate deployment, limited pilot, and waiting. Payoffs depend on frontier value; deployment yields operating value but risks obsolescence; a pilot builds organization-specific learning at a cost, and waiting preserves the option. A continuous-time extension analyzes robustness; the analysis distinguishes production learning and pilot-specific learning and derives modularity thresholds.
AI.result: 1) A mean-preserving increase in frontier uncertainty raises the value of waiting and piloting but leaves immediate deployment unchanged when payoff is affine in the frontier. 2) Faster expected frontier progress can reduce the appeal of immediate deployment when architectural progress is not fully captured by deployment. 3) A pilot dominates waiting exactly when the expected value of the built capability exceeds its cost. 4) Sufficiently valuable organization-specific learning creates a nonempty region where 'pilot early, commit late' is optimal. 5) A closed-form modularity threshold exists above which immediate deployment dominates the best outside option. 6) Production learning and pilot-specific learning affect timing margins differently. Continuous time shows uncertainty raises adoption thresholds while capability and modularity lower them. The paper separates deploying, experimenting, and waiting and explains why rapid progress can increase experimentation without irreversible commitment.
AI.conclusion: The framework clarifies when to deploy, pilot, or wait under frontier uncertainty and distinguishes where learning occurs. It highlights conditions under which early piloting with late commitment is optimal, and shows how modularity and learning shape timing, with continuous-time results aligning with discrete-time insights.

title: Automated Perceptually-Motivated Assessment of Photographic Consistency in Paired Clinical Photographs: Pipeline Development and Internal Evaluation
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to SPIE Journal of Medical Imaging
summary:
Purpose: Paired pre- and post-operative photographs are the standard unit of evidence for plastic surgical outcomes, yet no objective metric verifies whether two images of the same patient were captured under conditions consistent for comparison.
  Approach: We developed a perceptually motivated pipeline that analyzes pre/post pairs across thirteen calibrated sub-metrics, partitioned by unsupervised correlation-structure analysis into five data-driven clusters (photometric, texture / sharpness, pose, illumination direction, and pitch), averaged within each cluster and combined across clusters by a weighted sum into a single consistency score. Each sub-metric is calibrated so that its median difference across published within-patient pairs scores 0.5, which is a reference point and carries no pass/fail meaning. The pipeline was calibrated on 134 matched within-patient published pre/post pairs and evaluated against identical-image pairs, synthetic-perturbation pairs, and 134 mismatched cross-publication pairs.
  Results: The master consistency score S separated matched from mismatched pairs (sensitivity index d' = 2.15, 95% confidence interval (CI) [1.83, 2.55]; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve AUC = 0.928, 95% CI [0.896, 0.959]), closely matching Gaussian-equal-variance predictions. The three head-pose angles did not fall in one cluster: yaw and roll grouped together while pitch separated. Identical pairs scored at ceiling (S = 0.99) and the master score fell monotonically with perturbation magnitude on all five perturbation axes.
  Conclusions: The score quantifies photographic comparability, not aesthetic or surgical quality, and provides a freely available web tool for auditing the photographic comparability of pre/post pairs, pending validation against expert judgment.

AI.tldr: A perceptual, data-driven pipeline quantifies photographic comparability in pre/post plastic-surgery pairs using 13 sub-metrics across 5 clusters, yielding a master score S that differentiates matched from mismatched pairs (AUC 0.928, d' 2.15); identical pairs near ceiling; tool available for auditing comparability.
AI.motivation: Currently, there is no objective metric to verify that pre/post photos of the same patient are captured under conditions appropriate for comparison, risking biased assessment of outcomes.
AI.method: Develop a pipeline that computes 13 calibrated sub-metrics, grouped into five data-driven clusters (photometric, texture/sharpness, pose, illumination direction, pitch) via unsupervised correlation-structure analysis. Sub-metrics are averaged within clusters and combined across clusters by a weighted sum into a single master score S. Each sub-metric is calibrated so that the median difference across published within-patient pairs equals 0.5. The pipeline is calibrated on 134 matched within-patient pre/post pairs and evaluated on identical-image pairs, synthetic perturbations, and 134 mismatched cross-publication pairs.
AI.result: The master score S distinguishes matched vs mismatched pairs (d' = 2.15, 95% CI [1.83, 2.55]; AUC = 0.928, 95% CI [0.896, 0.959]; identical-image pairs score near ceiling at S = 0.99). The five perturbation axes show monotonic degradation in S; head-pose angles did not cluster uniformly (yaw and roll cluster together; pitch separated).
AI.conclusion: The score measures photographic comparability (not aesthetic or surgical quality) and a freely available web tool for auditing pre/post photographic comparability is provided, pending validation against expert judgment.

title: BioDCASE: Active Learning for Bioacoustics
comment: This paper summarises the BioDCASE Active Learning for Bioacoustics data challenge. This paper was reviewed and accepted to the non-archival track of the ECCV Computer Vision for Ecology workshop via OpenReview
summary: Ecological monitoring increasingly relies on machine learning models, whose performance depends on the quality and quantity of labelled data. However, obtaining these labels is costly, particularly in passive acoustic monitoring, where vast amounts of data are collected but only a small proportion can feasibly be annotated. Active learning addresses this bottleneck by prioritizing which samples should be labelled. However, progress is difficult to measure, because published methods are evaluated under different models, budgets, evaluation metrics and datasets. To address this challenge, we present the 2026 Active Learning for Bioacoustics BioDCASE challenge: a systematic evaluation of sampling methods designed to identify effective AL strategies. Participant methods were evaluated across four subsets composed of terrestrial and marine data. Across ten proposed sampling methods from seven teams, the top-ranked method achieved an area under the learning curve 26.4 % higher than random sampling at the same annotation budget, averaged over four data subsets. Significant variation in performance was observed across subsets, with the top-performing submission achieving a 67.1 % gain for the HSN subset over random sampling and a gain of 8 % for the ATBFL subset. Top-ranking submissions combined multiple acquisition signals, and diversity-based selection outperformed pure uncertainty sampling. Furthermore, there is evidence that transitioning from diversity-based to uncertainty-based selection and explicitly reducing redundancy within acquisition batches improve model training. There is also initial evidence that larger acquisition batch sizes may be increasingly beneficial later in the labelling process.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of active-learning sampling methods for bioacoustic labeling (BioDCASE 2026). Across four data subsets (terrestrial and marine), diverse acquisition signals and batch strategies yielded up to 67% gains over random labeling, with diversity-based selection generally outperforming pure uncertainty sampling; strategies that transition from diversity-focused to uncertainty-focused sampling and reduce redundancy within batches perform best, with larger batch sizes potentially beneficial later in labeling.
AI.motivation: Labeling data for passive acoustic monitoring is costly; there is a lack of standardized benchmarks to compare active-learning (AL) approaches across models, budgets, metrics, and datasets.
AI.method: Ten sampling methods from seven teams were evaluated across four data subsets (terrestrial and marine). The study analyzed multi-signal acquisition, diversity-based vs. uncertainty-based sampling, batch-size effects, and redundancy within acquisition batches to assess how AL strategies influence learning curves under fixed annotation budgets.
AI.result: The top method achieved a 26.4% higher area under the learning curve (AULC) than random sampling on average across four subsets. Subset variation was large: best-performing submission earned 67.1% gains on the HSN subset and 8% on the ATBFL subset. Methods combining multiple acquisition signals and diversity-based selection outperformed pure uncertainty sampling. Transitioning from diversity-based to uncertainty-based selection and explicitly reducing redundancy within batches improved model training. Preliminary evidence suggests larger acquisition batch sizes may be more beneficial later in labeling.
AI.conclusion: A robust AL strategy for bioacoustic labeling benefits from integrating diverse acquisition signals and prioritizing diverse, non-redundant samples early, then shifting toward uncertainty-based selection as labeling progresses. Dataset-specific performance varies substantially, underscoring the need for standardized benchmarks and guidance on batch-size regimes in real-world bioacoustic exploration.

title: Recurrent GraphNeural NetworkswithSet-BasedAggregation
summary: Recurrent GNNs iterate message passing to convergence, and their logical characterizations to date rely on multi-set aggregation, graded (counting) logics, and halting or acceptance conditions that cannot be verified from the network's parameters. We study recurrent GNNs with set-based aggregation and identify sufficient conditions checkable from the weights for networks to compile into formulas and formulas into networks. The main result is an effective, two-directional equivalence between a class of networks and the Boolean closure of reachability and safety properties, the fragment B$Σ^{\circ}_1$ of the modal $μ$-calculus. The fragment is not an artifact: it is the exact expressive level of stabilization over finite vocabulary, which supports fixed points of a single polarity and Boolean combinations thereof, but not the composition of fixed points of opposite polarities. The correspondence needs no counting logic, no external halting signal, and no non-effective acceptance condition, yielding a verifiable path from weights to symbolic explanations for networks meeting the conditions.

AI.tldr: Two-way effective encoding between a class of recurrent GNNs with set-based aggregation and the Boolean closure of reachability and safety properties, captured by the fragment BΣ°1 of the modal μ-calculus; conditions on weights enable compilation between networks and formulas; no counting logic or external halting needed; establishes verifiable, symbolic explanations for networks meeting the criteria, but cannot express compositions of opposite-polarity fixed points.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of prior logical characterizations (multiset aggregation, counting logics, and unverifiable halting/acceptance signals) by identifying a weight-checkable set of conditions that yield a complete correspondence with a constructive logical fragment, enabling explanations and synthesis.
AI.method: Establish an effective, two-directional correspondence between a class of recurrent GNNs with set-based aggregation and the Boolean closure of reachability and safety properties within the BΣ°1 fragment of the modal μ-calculus; prove this fragment corresponds to stabilization over finite vocabulary with fixed points of a single polarity and Boolean combinations; show the conditions on weights that enable compiling networks to formulas and formulas to networks; demonstrate that no counting logic or external accepting conditions are required.
AI.result: Proves an exact, constructive equivalence between the networks and the BΣ°1 fragment; provides a verifiable path from weights to symbolic explanations for networks satisfying the weight-conditions; shows the expressive limit to fixed points of single polarity with Boolean combinations, and excludes the composition of opposite-polarity fixed points.
AI.conclusion: The work yields a practical, verifiable synthesis path from learned weights to formal explanations within a precise logical fragment, clarifying the expressive power of stabilization for these recurrent GNNs and offering a non-heuristic bridge between neural models and formal specifications; however, it restricts expressivity by not supporting mixed-polarity fixed-point compositions and relies on set-based aggregation with checkable weight conditions.

title: Weakly Supervised Spatial Grounding for Discriminative Attention-Based Ultrasound-Histopathology Alignment in Prostate Cancer Grading
summary: Unpaired cross-modal distillation transfers grade structure from histopathology into a micro-ultrasound (micro-US) encoder by aligning a pooled needle-region embedding to a frozen histopathology teacher under grade-group correspondence alone. A single objective is thereby required to serve two distinct functions: rendering patch features discriminative of tissue state, and selecting which patches enter the pooled representation. We decouple them. Weak spatial supervision derived from percentage involvement, recorded routinely at biopsy, constrains the predicted proportion of malignant tissue within each core, acting on the encoder features independently of the alignment objective. The alignment loss then operates on features that differ across a core, and attention concentrates on a subset of patches rather than remaining near-uniform. On 7,166 biopsy cores from 811 patients across seven centers under patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, the method reaches 67.1 macro AUC and 68.5 csPCa AUC, against 61.2 and 52.8 for the existing unpaired alignment method and 63.1 and 62.6 for the strongest unimodal baselines.
