AI.result: Patient-level balanced accuracy 0.958, macro-F1 0.963, ROC-AUC 0.990 across four folds; consistent improvements over HRUS baselines and cross-modal alternatives.
AI.conclusion: MRI-derived supervision substantially improves ultrasound-based ALS assessment while preserving low-cost, MRI-free inference, supporting clinical deployment in resource-limited settings.

title: Data-driven Prediction of Satellite-observed Avalanche Activity from Snowpack Simulations
comment: Proceedings paper for ISSW2026. 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: Avalanche forecasting requires knowledge of snowpack conditions and recent avalanche activity, but field observations are sparse across large mountain regions. We explore whether SNOWPACK simulations can predict avalanche activity mapped by synthetic aperture radar (SAR). We compiled five winters of Sentinel-1 avalanche detections across Norway and parts of Sweden, alongside SNOWPACK simulations forced by numerical weather predictions on a 20 x 20 km grid at different elevations and predefined slope angles. A transformer used five days of SNOWPACK outputs to predict the following day's SAR-detected Avalanche Activity Index (SAR-AAI). This index weights larger debris more heavily, spreads detections across possible occurrence dates and normalises by modelled runout area. The model was trained on four winters and evaluated on one validation winter. Regional mean predicted and reference SAR-AAI correlated at r = 0.803 after averaging over complete six-day periods. The model followed broad changes in time and space but produced smoother predictions and underestimated the strongest activity. Agreement at the 20 km cell scale was weaker (r = 0.549) after the same averaging. These results come from a single training run without evaluation on an untouched winter. Satellite observations also contain missed and false detections and uncertain timing. The results therefore do not establish operational forecast skill, but suggest that regional SNOWPACK simulations contain information about broad variations in satellite-observed avalanche activity.

AI.tldr: SNOWPACK simulations combined with a transformer can predict SAR-detected avalanche activity at a regional scale, achieving r≈0.80 for regional means but weaker at 20 km cell scale (r≈0.55). Not yet operational due to data limitations and single training run.
AI.motivation: Addresses the paucity of field observations for avalanche forecasting by leveraging physics-based snowpack simulations and satellite observations to predict avalanche activity.
AI.method: SNOWPACK forcing from numerical weather predictions on a 20x20 km grid (varying elevations and slopes) across five winters in Norway/ Sweden; a transformer uses five days of SNOWPACK outputs to forecast the following day’s SAR-Avalanche Activity Index (SAR-AAI); SAR-AAI weights larger debris, spreads detections across probable dates, and normalizes by runout area; trained on four winters and evaluated on one validation winter; performance averaged over six-day periods.
AI.result: Regional mean predicted SAR-AAI correlated with reference SAR-AAI r=0.803; smoother predictions and underestimation of strong activity; 20 km cell scale r=0.549; SAR data include missed/false detections and timing uncertainty; not demonstrated as operational skill; based on a single training run without testing on an unseen winter.
AI.conclusion: Regionally, SNOWPACK simulations contain information about broad variations in avalanche activity detectable by SAR, suggesting potential for assimilation or hybrid forecasting, but robust operational skill requires more rigorous validation (multiple winters, unseen data, and SAR uncertainty handling).

title: Learning from Reliable Negatives: Confidence-Anchored Test-Time Adaptation for GUI Grounding
summary: Graphical User Interface (GUI) grounding is essential for autonomous agents to map natural language instructions to precise screen coordinates. However, existing supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning methods are constrained by the high cost of annotation, creating a scalability bottleneck. In this paper, we introduce a label-free test-time training paradigm driven by two key insights: (1) confidence patterns in coordinate tokens are a better indicator than full-sequence confidence, and (2) in sparse GUI coordinate spaces, negative samples offer more reliable learning signals than potentially noisy positive ones. We first propose Confidence-Anchored Learning (CAL), which utilizes coordinate-token confidence to filter pseudo-labels and assign distance-based binary rewards. Building on this, we develop Confidence-Anchored Negative Learning (CANL), which exclusively optimizes the model using negative samples to bypass the risks of incorrect positive samples. Experimental results demonstrate that CANL-7B achieves 92.1% on ScreenSpot-V2. On more challenging ScreenSpot-Pro, CANL-7B reaches 33.8%, an 8.9% absolute improvement over the base model. Our findings establish coordinate-token confidence as a powerful alternative to manual annotations for scalable GUI agent development.

AI.tldr: Proposes label-free test-time training for GUI grounding via Confidence-Anchored Learning (CAL) and Confidence-Anchored Negative Learning (CANL). CAL uses coordinate-token confidence to filter pseudo-labels and assign distance-based rewards; CANL trains only on negative samples to avoid noisy positives. CANL-7B achieves 92.1% on ScreenSpot-V2 and 33.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro (8.9% absolute gain).
AI.motivation: High annotation costs in supervised fine-tuning and RL for GUI grounding create scalability bottlenecks. Recognizes that coordinate-token confidence patterns can better indicate correct coordinates than full-sequence confidence, and that negative samples can provide stronger learning signals in sparse GUI coordinate spaces.
AI.method: CAL (Confidence-Anchored Learning) filters pseudo-labels using coordinate-token confidence and assigns distance-based binary rewards. CANL (Confidence-Anchored Negative Learning) further restricts training to negative samples to avoid erroneous positives, enabling label-free, test-time adaptation.
AI.result: Empirical results show CANL-7B attaining 92.1% on ScreenSpot-V2 and 33.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro, with an 8.9 percentage-point improvement over the base model on the latter. These findings indicate coordinate-token confidence as a viable substitute for manual annotations in scalable GUI agent development.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate-token confidence enables scalable GUI grounding without manual labels. Negative learning (CANL) provides robustness in sparse coordinate spaces, delivering competitive or superior performance with reduced labeling requirements.

title: Rotation-Based Subspace Tracking for Robust Kernel PCA on Streaming Data
summary: Machine learning models process large amounts of data, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a widely used technique to reduce the dimensionality of the data and extract useful features. In practice, datasets often change over time (data drift) and/or arrive one sample at a time (streaming data), making it infeasible to process the entire dataset at once in batch mode. Real-world data also often contains nonlinear patterns, which traditional PCA cannot extract. Kernel PCA addresses this by implicitly mapping samples into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Raw data also often contains outliers, which can have an outsized effect on the estimated subspace unless the algorithm is made robust. However, existing online robust kernel PCA algorithms are designed to converge to a subspace that is assumed to be fixed, and gradient-descent-based updates lose their effectiveness at tracking further changes once this initial alignment is achieved. This paper introduces a rotation-based update mechanism, which updates the subspace estimate by rotating it toward each new incoming feature vector in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, rather than relying on gradient descent alone. We present two complementary rotation strategies, and show that the extent of rotation can be moderated by a robust influence function to mitigate the effect of outliers. Through experiments on synthetic streaming data with a known ground-truth subspace, we show that per-sample rotations converge faster than gradient descent alone, demonstrating an effective mechanism for dynamically tracking a nonlinear subspace in streaming data.

AI.tldr: Introduces a rotation-based online robust kernel PCA update to dynamically track nonlinear subspaces in streaming data, achieving faster convergence than gradient-descent-based methods and improved robustness.
AI.motivation: In streaming settings with data drift and outliers, online methods are needed to continuously track a nonlinear subspace; traditional PCA and gradient-descent-based online kernel PCA may be slow to adapt and sensitive to outliers.
AI.method: Proposes a rotation-based update mechanism in RKHS that rotates the current subspace toward each new feature vector. Two complementary rotation strategies are presented, with a robust influence function to attenuate outliers. Updates occur per-sample rather than via standard gradient descent, enabling dynamic tracking.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic streaming data with a known ground-truth subspace show per-sample rotations converge faster than gradient-descent updates, demonstrating improved adaptation to changing nonlinear subspaces.
AI.conclusion: The rotation-based updates provide a faster, robust mechanism for online kernel PCA in streaming contexts, effectively tracking nonlinear subspaces under data drift and outliers.

title: Hypergraph-Regularized Gramian Volumes for Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Volume-based multimodal retrieval jointly scores a text query with a candidate's video, audio, and subtitle embeddings. While this approach captures higher-order within-candidate alignment, the score remains candidate-local, and semantically related training samples primarily serve as contrastive negatives. This work introduces Hypergraph-Regularized Gramian Volumes (HyVol), a training-time module that incorporates these semantic relations prior to evaluating the original volume loss. Document hyperedges connect the observed modalities of each candidate, whereas semantic hyperedges link candidates whose detached captions are mutual top-k neighbors. A shallow gated hyper-graph network applies residual corrections to the modality embeddings. Presence masks exclude unavailable streams from message passing, and identity padding preserves the determinant of the observed Gram submatrix without feature imputation. As refinement operates on embeddings rather than scores, the same construction applies to both Gram and HyperGram. We remove the hypergraph after training, leaving the backbone-only architecture, original scoring function, and retrieval cost unchanged. We train both backbones on a 150K-clip subset of VAST-27M and evaluate zero-shot performance on six benchmarks. Under the paired protocol, HyVol improves R@1 across all five retrieval benchmarks, with video-to-text gains reaching +8.3 on MSR-VTT and +7.6 on VATEX. Under missing-modality masking, the V2T margin remains positive in all experimental settings, although the T2V margin becomes slightly negative in four.

AI.tldr: HyVol introduces a training-time hypergraph regularization for volume-based multimodal retrieval to incorporate semantic relations among candidates, improving cross-modal alignment; achieves substantial gains in R@1 on MSR-VTT and VATEX; the hypergraph is removed after training so inference remains unchanged.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of candidate-local scoring in volume-based retrieval and to leverage semantic relations among candidates (via detections such as top-k caption neighbors) by injecting prior information during training through a hypergraph-based regularization.
AI.method: Build document hyperedges over the observed modalities of each candidate and semantic hyperedges connecting candidates whose captions are mutual top-k neighbors. Apply a shallow gated hyper-graph network to compute residual corrections to modality embeddings, with presence masks for missing streams and identity padding to preserve Gram submatrix determinants. The regularization operates on embeddings (both Gram and HyperGram) and is removed after training, leaving the original backbone, scoring, and retrieval cost unchanged. Train on 150K clips from VAST-27M; evaluate zero-shot on six benchmarks.
AI.result: Under the paired protocol, HyVol improves R@1 across all five retrieval benchmarks, with video-to-text gains of +8.3 on MSR-VTT and +7.6 on VATEX. Under missing-modality masking, the V2T margin remains positive in all settings, though the T2V margin becomes slightly negative in four.
AI.conclusion: HyVol provides a training-time semantic regularization to enrich multimodal embeddings for volume-based retrieval without altering the downstream inference pipeline, yielding consistent gains in zero-shot performance; some modality-translation asymmetries under missing modalities suggest room for further improvement.

title: Same path, different: a mechanistic comparison of looped and stacked transformer encoders on 12-lead ECG
summary: Recurrent Transformers reusing their weights rather than stacking $L$ distinct layers are becoming widely adopted due to their parameter efficiency [1,2,3]. However, the exact representational and dynamical differences between looped and stacked architectures remain uncharacterized. This paper presents a controlled study on the example of bViT model [1] applying one weight-tied block $L$ times. We train two models: bViT and standard ViT [4] on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) classification tasks from the PTB-XL dataset under identical training protocols. Despite an $8.9\times$ parameter reduction, bViT achieves accuracy parity with ViT. Geometric similarity metrics demonstrate that both architectures construct comparable latent representations in an equivalent canonical order. Crucially, their dynamics differ: bViT exhibits smaller step sizes and inter-patient sensitivity, as well as near-neutral behavior away from the data manifold, whereas ViT exhibits collapsing dimensionality of representations and out-of-distribution feature expansion.

AI.tldr: Weight-tied recurrent transformers (bViT) can match ViT performance on ECG classification with ~9x fewer parameters; latent representations align under a common canonical order, but the dynamics differ: bViT shows smaller step sizes and greater robustness to inter-patient variation with near-neutral behavior off the data manifold, whereas ViT exhibits dimensionality collapse and expansion of out-of-distribution features.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in understanding how looped (weight-tied) transformers compare to stacked architectures, especially in domain-specific tasks with limited data. The study tests whether parameter sharing preserves representations and how dynamics differ in a controlled setting.
AI.method: Train two models (bViT with a weight-tied block applied L times and standard ViT) on PTB-XL 12-lead ECG classification under identical training protocols. Use 8.9x parameter reduction in bViT. Evaluate accuracy, latent representations via geometric similarity metrics in an equivalent canonical order, and dynamics (step sizes, inter-patient sensitivity, off-manifold behavior).
AI.result: bViT achieves parity with ViT in accuracy despite substantial parameter reduction (8.9x fewer params). Geometric similarity metrics show comparable latent representations when aligned to a canonical order. Dynamically, bViT has smaller step sizes and lower inter-patient sensitivity, with near-neutral behavior away from the data manifold, while ViT exhibits dimensionality collapse and expansion of out-of-distribution features.
AI.conclusion: Weight-tied recurrent transformers can replicate ViT performance with large parameter savings, and share similar latent geometry, but display distinct dynamical properties that may influence generalization and robustness, particularly regarding off-manifold behavior and OOD feature handling.

title: Concept-Grounded Reasoning with Prompt-Driven Localization for Interpretable Structured Report Generation
summary: Medical imaging modalities such as ultrasound and X-ray are widely used in clinical practice, where diagnosis follows a structured, evidence-driven workflow aligned with standardized criteria. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise for automated medical report generation, most existing systems rely on end-to-end multimodal fusion without modeling clinically defined intermediate attributes, leading to limited grounding and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose CORAL (COncept-grounded ReAsoning with Localization), a multimodal framework that integrates spatial grounding and concept-level supervision into a unified reasoning process. CORAL employs a prompt-driven medical segmentation model to localize lesions and predicts multi-class clinical attributes through a Concept Bottleneck module. The resulting textual concept tokens are combined with mask-modulated visual features within an MLLM to enable structured report generation and diagnostic prediction. Experiments on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, concept consistency, and report quality over strong general-purpose and medical MLLMs, indicating that concept-grounded reasoning better aligns generation with clinical decision processes.

AI.tldr: A concept-grounded, localization-aware framework (CORAL) improves multimodal medical report generation by grounding reasoning in clinically defined attributes and lesion localization, boosting accuracy and interpretability on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray.
AI.motivation: Limitations of end-to-end multimodal LLMs: lack of clinically meaningful intermediate attributes leads to weak grounding and interpretability; need structured, explainable reasoning aligned with clinical criteria.
AI.method: Use a prompt-driven medical segmentation model for lesion localization; a Concept Bottleneck (CB) module to predict multi-class clinical attributes; textual concept tokens fed with mask-modulated visual features into an MLLM for structured report generation and diagnostic prediction.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, concept consistency, and report quality on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray datasets compared to strong general-purpose and medical MLLMs.
AI.conclusion: Concept-grounded reasoning with localization enhances grounding, interpretability, and alignment with clinical decision processes in multimodal medical report generation.

title: End-to-End Verifiable and Robust Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning enables multiple parties to train a shared model without centralizing raw data with the help of an aggregator, but introduces integrity risks once participants or infrastructure are not fully trustworthy. Two requirements are particularly important: robustness to poisoned or Byzantine client updates, and verifiability of the aggregator so that clients or third parties can audit the reported aggregation without learning individual updates. Existing work has largely treated these goals separately, and efficient public verifiability for robust, outlier-excluding aggregation remains limited. We present a verifiable federated learning protocol that makes a robust aggregation pipeline publicly auditable. Our design combines cryptographic commitments with non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to certify both (i) cosine-similarity-based outlier exclusion and (ii) aggregation over the selected set, without revealing individual client updates to verifiers. In experiments under representative poisoning attacks, our method maintains high accuracy, with an average accuracy loss below 4\% across the evaluated configurations, while keeping verification overhead practical: proof artifacts can be generated and verified within minutes at the scale studied. In summary, our results show that robust outlier exclusion and public verifiability can be jointly achieved in a federated learning setting.

AI.tldr: A verifiable federated learning protocol that combines cryptographic commitments and non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to enable public verifiability of robust, outlier-excluding aggregation without revealing client updates; demonstrates accuracy preserved under poisoning with practical verification overhead.
AI.motivation: Address integrity risk in FL: need robustness to Byzantine updates and verifiability of aggregation; existing work treats goals separately; joint solution scarce.
AI.method: Cryptographic commitments + non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to certify (i) cosine-similarity-based outlier exclusion and (ii) aggregation over the selected set; maintains privacy of individual updates; public verifiability.
AI.result: Under poisoning attacks, average accuracy loss < 4% across evaluated configurations; verification overhead: proof artifacts generated and verified within minutes at the scale studied.
AI.conclusion: Robust outlier exclusion and public verifiability can be jointly achieved in federated learning.

title: Query-Conditioned Spherical Centroid Aggregation for Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Multimodal retrieval integrates video, audio, subtitles, and text; however, recent geometric aggregators, such as Gramian volumes, hyperbolic volumes, and spectral objectives, treat all modalities symmetrically. Under a unified evaluation protocol, their joint scores frequently lag behind the strongest single-modality pathway by 1.9 to 27.6 R@1. Controlled analyses attribute this outcome to uniform modality influence. This work introduces Spherical Centroid Aggregation with Learned Adaptive Relevance (SCALAR), a query-conditioned aggregator that assigns relevance-based weights to each available modality before computing a spherical centroid. SCALAR accommodates arbitrary modality subsets and is trained on masked, reduced-arity views using rank-8 LoRA adapters. Across five benchmarks, SCALAR achieves positive aggregation gain on four, reaching +4.0 R@1, while none of the evaluated prior aggregators is positive on more than one. A uniform-weight ablation reproduces the degradation observed with symmetric aggregation. With only 4.8 million trainable parameters, SCALAR attains the highest text-to-video R@1 on three and performs within seed variation of the best result on a fourth. Under test-time modality dropout, SCALAR's representation-stage score surpasses the released GRAM checkpoint at every evaluated masking rate and benchmark by 3.2 to 10.9 R@1. Finally, as modalities are removed, rerankers trained exclusively on complete modality sets increasingly converge toward their video-only pathways, diminishing these representation-level gains and underscoring a limitation of standard two-stage retrieval pipelines.

AI.tldr: SCALAR: a query-conditioned, adaptive-weight aggregator for multimodal retrieval that computes a spherical centroid over relevant modalities, using rank-8 LoRA adapters, yielding consistent gains over symmetric aggregators across five benchmarks with a small param footprint.
AI.motivation: Rectify the failure of symmetric/uniformly weighted multimodal aggregators, which typically underperform the best single modality and underutilize modality subsets.
AI.method: Propose SCALAR, a query-conditioned aggregator that assigns learned relevance weights to available modalities before forming a spherical centroid. Supports arbitrary modality subsets, trained on masked, reduced-arity views via rank-8 LoRA adapters. Includes test-time modality dropout and representation-stage scoring to compare against end-to-end baselines.
AI.result: Positive aggregation gains on 4 of 5 benchmarks (up to +4.0 R@1); uniform-weight baseline degrades performance; SCALAR with ~4.8M parameters achieves leading text-to-video R@1 on three benchmarks and matches the best within seed variation on a fourth; test-time masking outperforms GRAM checkpoint across masking rates; modalities removal collapses rerankers toward video-only paths, indicating limits of two-stage pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, lightweight, query-conditioned aggregation with SCALAR yields robust gains over symmetric aggregation, demonstrates modality-subset robustness, and highlights limitations of current two-stage retrieval pipelines.

title: Beyond Noise: Understanding and Overcoming Temperature Effects in Analog DNN Inference
comment: Published at the ECML PKDD Conference 2026, at the 7th Workshop on IoT, Edge, and Mobile for Embedded Machine Learning
summary: The energy efficiency of analog computing makes it one of the most promising candidates for deploying resource-intensive machine learning workloads on constrained platforms such as mobile and embedded devices. However, analog accelerators are inherently susceptible to noise and non-idealities arising from physical component variations, whose behavior is further sensitive to environmental factors. These effects can significantly degrade inference accuracy. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive experimental study on a representative example of analog hardware to investigate the impact of temperature. We first characterize the behavior of stochastic and systematic non-idealities across a range of operating temperatures. Following this, we compare a set of simulation-based and hardware-based mitigation strategies aimed at improving robustness against temperature-induced performance degradation. Our results suggest that temperature-induced degradation is driven primarily by systematic non-idealities rather than stochastic noise alone. Noise-aware training improves robustness, while hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration provide the strongest accuracy retention across varying thermal conditions.

AI.tldr: Temperature-driven accuracy degradation in analog ML hardware is largely due to systematic non-idealities, not just stochastic noise; among mitigation approaches, noise-aware training helps, but hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration provide the strongest robustness across varying temperatures.
AI.motivation: To improve energy-efficient analog computing for ML on constrained devices by understanding how temperature affects non-idealities and by evaluating mitigation strategies.
AI.method: Experimental study on a representative analog hardware platform. Characterizes stochastic and systematic non-idealities across a range of operating temperatures. Compares simulation-based and hardware-based mitigation strategies (e.g., noise-aware training, hardware-in-the-loop training, temperature-aware calibration).
AI.result: Finds that temperature-induced degradation is primarily driven by systematic non-idealities rather than stochastic noise alone. Noise-aware training improves robustness; hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration yield the strongest accuracy retention across temperature variations.
AI.conclusion: Robust analog ML performance under varying thermal conditions can be achieved with calibration- and training-based strategies, with hardware-in-the-loop training and temperature-aware calibration offering the most effective protection against temperature-induced degradation.

title: Robust Multi-Model Fitting through Learning Neighbor Regions
summary: Multi-model fitting involves fitting multiple models accurately in a noisy environment. It is the basis for computer vision tasks such as scene reconstruction and mixed reality. However, its performance is often limited by insufficient feature utilization, inefficient optimization, model overlap, and the non-differentiable pipelines. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a robust coarse-to-fine framework called Learning Neighbor Regions (LNR). Recognizing that substantial computational resources are wasted on numerous bad minimum sets, we propose the coarse-level module. This module utilizes a neural network to extract and analyze geometric feature of both local point-wise relationships and global contextual information in minimum sets, outputting confidence to pre-select a small number of good minimum sets, thereby enhancing overall efficiency before solving hypotheses. To address model overlap, LNR encodes neighbor region features for each hypothesis in its fine-level module. These region features consist of geometric features of neighboring data points, which can be used by multiple regions simultaneously. This design allows the neural network to individually refine and score each hypothesis. Importantly, LNR is trained to learn directly from data point features rather than from the hypothesis parameters, thus avoiding differentiating the sampling process and the model solvers. Extensive experiments on four classic multi-model fitting tasks demonstrate that LNR achieves state-of-the-art performance. The analysis suggests that LNR can be easily adapted to various robust multi-model fitting tasks.

AI.tldr: A robust coarse-to-fine framework LNR for multi-model fitting that uses neural networks to preselect good minimum sets and refine hypotheses via region features, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Improve multi-model fitting under noise by better feature utilization, optimization efficiency, and handling model overlap; reduce computation by preselecting good minima and leveraging neighbor region features.
AI.method: A coarse-level module uses a neural network to analyze geometric features of local and global relationships in minimum sets to output confidence, preselecting a subset of good minima; a fine-level module encodes neighbor region features for each hypothesis, comprised of geometric features of neighboring data points that can be shared by multiple regions; hypotheses are refined and scored via learned region features; training is based on data-point features rather than differentiating sampling and solvers.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four classic multi-model fitting tasks show state-of-the-art performance; LNR is easily adaptable to various robust multi-model fitting tasks.
AI.conclusion: LNR provides a data-driven coarse-to-fine framework that improves efficiency and accuracy by focusing on good minima and leveraging shared region features, mitigating model overlap and non-differentiable pipelines.

title: The Misery of Mechanistic Interpretability: A Formal Perspective
comment: Keywords: artificial intelligence; safety; interpretability; large language models; formal methods; verification; certification; robustness; sparse autoencoder; transcoder
summary: Mechanistic interpretability has become the dominant lens for understanding frontier language models, as their inner workings are complex and inherently black boxes. To gain insights into these models, interpretable replacement networks (IRNs) are trained at all layers, exposing interpretable features through sparsely activated neurons. However, the faithfulness of an IRN is usually evaluated only empirically on clean data, and we show that even semantically minor input perturbations flip the dominant IRN features-and thus the human-understandable interpretation-across five open-weight model families (GPT-2 small, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B, R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B). We propose the first formal verification framework for the faithfulness of an IRN, where reachability analysis certifies a sound upper bound of the faithfulness gap in adversarial scenarios. Moreover, we show that verification-aware training of IRNs substantially tightens this certified bound, restoring a feature-level interpretation that safety auditors can act on. Together, these results give, to the best of our knowledge, the first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability of large language models.

AI.tldr: Formal verification framework for IRN faithfulness in LLMs using reachability analysis; shows perturbations flip IRN features across multiple models; verification-aware training tightens bounds and restores interpretable features, offering first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between empirical faithfulness of interpretable replacement networks (IRNs) and the need for formal, verifiable guarantees, enabling safer auditing of model internals.
AI.method: Propose a reachability-analysis based verification framework that certifies a sound upper bound on the faithfulness gap under adversarial input perturbations; evaluate across multiple open-weight models; introduce verification-aware training to tighten the bound.
AI.result: Certified bounds on IRN faithfulness gaps; tightened bounds through verification-aware training; restoration of feature-level interpretability; claims of the first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability in large language models.
AI.conclusion: Presents the first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability via IRNs, enabling more reliable interpretability and safer auditing of frontier LMs.

title: End-to-End Cell Detection via Instance-aware Graph Modeling
summary: Accurate cell detection and classification are crucial for pathological analysis, directly affecting diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning. To capture complex cellular interactions beyond visual appearance within the tumor microenvironment, several approaches have employed graph neural networks to model spatial and relational patterns among cell nuclei, yielding promising results. However, these methods typically adopt a two-stage paradigm of visual extraction followed by relational modeling, which necessitates separate tuning for each stage, thereby increasing pipeline complexity and hindering end-to-end joint optimization. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end framework for cell detection and classification that jointly models patch-level visual representations and instance-level interactions, which incorporates a dynamic graph construction module and an instance-aware graph network. Specifically, the graph construction module dynamically builds the graph structure using learnable queries derived from patch-level features as cell instance representations, with adjacency defined by integrating feature similarity and spatial distances. The instance-aware graph network performs adaptive instance filtering and feature reorganization, aggregating them over the cell graph into a topological latent state for a selective state-space transition driven by visual cues, fusing appearance and relational evidence. When evaluated on multiple datasets with different staining protocols for cell and nucleus detection, our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in both detection and classification performance. The code will be released at https://github.com/RuochenLiu23/IGM.

AI.tldr: End-to-end cell detection and classification with a dynamic, instance-aware graph framework that jointly models patch-level visuals and cell–cell interactions for robust performance across varied staining protocols.
AI.motivation: To capture tumor microenvironment cell interactions and enable joint optimization of detection and relational reasoning, avoiding the complexity of two-stage pipelines.
AI.method: Introduce a dynamic graph construction module that uses learnable queries from patch-level features as cell representations; define adjacency by feature similarity and spatial distance; employ an instance-aware graph network for adaptive instance filtering and feature reorganization, aggregating over the graph to a topological latent state with a selective state-space transition guided by visual cues, fusing appearance and relational evidence in an end-to-end framework.
AI.result: On multiple datasets with different staining protocols, the method significantly outperforms baselines in both detection and classification. Code will be released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: An end-to-end graph-based approach can effectively fuse appearance and relational information for cell detection and classification, achieving superior performance and reduced pipeline complexity compared to two-stage methods.

title: Specifying Reward Functions for RL Without Environment Sampling
summary: Enabling human stakeholders to specify reward functions that lead to their desired outcomes is a key challenge in deploying reinforcement learning agents. Preference-based methods such as online RLHF can reduce the burden of manual reward design, but they require repeatedly training policies, sampling trajectories from the real world, and eliciting feedback, making them impractical in settings where environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. We introduce Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification (EARS), a method for learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction. Our approach uses a structured LLM-mediated process to construct a small set of expressive reward features from a task description and the environment observation space, then strategically samples imagined trajectories in this feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over the imagined trajectory pairs. We evaluate on three long-horizon domains: pandemic lockdown regulation design, insulin administration for diabetes patients, and autonomous vehicle control on a highway. We compare EARS to baselines that also enable reward specification without environment interaction--namely, methods that directly prompt an LLM to generate a reward function. When learning from either ground-truth preference labels or preferences labeled by a LLM, EARS designs reward functions that are more aligned with the ground truth reward function that produced the preferences or LLM context than these baselines. These results suggest that preference-based reward specification remains effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible.

AI.tldr: Learn reward functions from preferences without environment interaction using an LLM-guided feature space and imagined trajectories (EARS), outperforming LLM-based rewards in alignment on three long-horizon domains.
AI.motivation: Preference-based reward design is essential but costly when interacting with real environments; desire to remove need for real trajectories in RLHF-like settings.
AI.method: Construct expressive reward features via structured LLM process from task description and observation space; sample imagined trajectories in feature space; infer feature weights from preferences (human or LLM).
AI.result: EARS produces reward functions more aligned with ground-truth rewards than baselines that use direct LLM-generated rewards; validated on pandemic regulation design, insulin administration, and highway autonomous driving; robust to preference source.
AI.conclusion: Preference-based reward specification can be effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where real trajectories are expensive or unsafe.

title: Diffusion Trajectory Modeling for Semantic Correspondence
summary: Diffusion models generate images through an iterative diffusion process, and recent studies have demonstrated that the intermediate feature maps produced during this process contain rich visual representations, leading to their adoption across a variety of downstream tasks. However, most existing approaches are limited to either using a single feature map at a specific timestep or aggregating feature maps across multiple timesteps. We observe that intermediate representations in the diffusion process form meaningful trajectories along the time axis. In particular, the representation of each spatial patch evolves progressively throughout the generative process, encoding semantics that are difficult to capture from static snapshots alone. This observation motivates the need to treat diffusion representations as temporally structured trajectories rather than static snapshots. To this end, we propose Diffusion Trajectory Modeling (DTM), a framework that interprets the temporal evolution of each spatial patch as a trajectory and leverages it for semantic correspondence. By effectively modeling patch-wise trajectories generated across multiple timesteps, DTM captures correspondence cues that prior methods are not designed to capture. We further demonstrate empirically that spatially corresponding patches form similar trajectory patterns throughout the diffusion process, suggesting that the temporal axis of diffusion carries semantic information. Experiments on SPair-71k, SPair-U and AP-10K show that DTM achieves strong performance, presenting a new perspective for exploiting diffusion representations from a trajectory-centric viewpoint.

AI.tldr: Trajectory-based diffusion representations (DTM) model patch-wise temporal evolutions as trajectories to improve semantic correspondence, achieving strong results on SPair-71k, SPair-U, and AP-10K.
AI.motivation: Intermediate diffusion feature maps exhibit meaningful temporal evolution; static snapshots or single-timestep features miss semantic cues contained in the trajectory across timesteps.
AI.method: DTM treats the temporal evolution of each spatial patch as a trajectory across multiple diffusion timesteps and uses these trajectories to establish semantic correspondences between images.
AI.result: Empirically, patch-wise trajectory patterns are similar for semantically corresponding patches, enabling improved semantic matching; DTM achieves strong performance on SPair-71k, SPair-U, and AP-10K.
AI.conclusion: Spatial diffusion representations carry semantic information along the temporal axis; a trajectory-centric view reveals new cues for downstream tasks and offers a new perspective beyond static feature snapshots.

title: The Token Before the Value Is the Key: How Hybrid Architectures Organize Induction Circuits
summary: Hybrid language models can improve capability as well as efficiency, raising the question of how architectural complementarity becomes learned computation. We examine the established induction roles of Carrying predecessor information, Matching a source by content, and Copying its value. How are these position-sensitive and content-based computations allocated across heterogeneous layers? We introduce layer-type-agnostic paired probes that track Carrying and Matching through a common block-update interface. In recurrent--global and local--global hybrids, Carrying concentrates in efficient layers and Matching in global receivers. The measured local contribution concentrates on lag one: the token immediately before the historical value. Changing predecessor support through lag-one masking, convolution removal, or early learning-rate reduction can relocate Carrying and Matching between stages. Source-key restoration and fixed-value selection trace the receiver's dependence on the prepared source. These interventions also change natural-text recall, with outcomes depending on configuration and target. Varying local windows and induction-enriched training text changes the early development of functional Carrying and Matching, connecting architectural priors and training evidence to formation timing. Together, the probes and interventions shift the explanatory focus upstream: the organization of Matching follows how Carrying is learned. The token before the value provides a concrete link between a hybrid's architecture, circuit development, and recall. Code is available in https://github.com/ckpassenger/bind-match-copy/tree/main.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how carrying, matching, and copying computations distribute across layers in hybrid language models using layer-type-agnostic probes. It finds carrying concentrates in efficient layers and matching in global receivers (lag-one focused). Interventions (masking, convolution removal, learning-rate changes) can relocate these roles; source-key restoration and fixed-value selection reveal dependence on the prepared source. Training text and local windows shape early development of these functions. Concludes that the organization of matching follows how carrying is learned, linking architecture, circuit development, and recall; code available.
AI.motivation: To understand how architectural priors and training data shape distributed computations in hybrid language models, clarifying how position-sensitive (carrying/matching) and content-based (copying) operations are allocated across heterogeneous layers.
AI.method: Introduce layer-type-agnostic paired probes that track Carrying and Matching through a common block-update interface. Study recurrent-global and local-global hybrids. Use lag-one analysis to identify local contributions (token immediately before historical value). Apply interventions: lag-one masking, convolution removal, early learning-rate reduction to relocate Carrying and Matching. Employ source-key restoration and fixed-value selection to trace dependence on prepared sources. Vary local windows and conduct induction-enriched training text to observe effects on development. Assess recall in natural text and link findings to architectural and training factors. Provide open-source code.
AI.result: Carrying concentrates in efficient layers while Matching concentrates in global receivers in both recurrent-global and local-global hybrids. Local contribution is dominated by the lag-one token. Interventions such as lag-one masking, removing convolutions, or reducing learning rates can shift Carrying and Matching between stages. Source-key restoration and fixed-value selection reveal receiver dependence on the prepared source. Interventions and training variations modify natural-text recall and influence the early development of Carrying and Matching. Overall, the study shifts explanatory focus upstream to how Carrying learning shapes the subsequent organization of Matching and links architecture, circuit development, and recall (with the token before the value serving as a concrete bridge).
AI.conclusion: The organization of Matching follows how Carrying is learned, suggesting that architectural priors and early training dynamics jointly determine the allocation of these core computations in hybrid LMs. The token immediately preceding the historical value provides a concrete link between architecture, circuit development, and recall. The authors provide code to enable replication and further study.

title: CapsuleMotion: A Lightweight Real-Time Visual Motion Predictor for Capsule Endoscopy
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables, accepted at the 22nd Annual International Conference on Body Sensor Networks (BSN2026)
summary: Video Capsule Endoscopy (VCE) is a non-invasive medical examination that allows for the observation of the small intestine, which is otherwise difficult to access. A fundamental challenge persists in the form of their limited size in order to still be swallowable. The resulting restricted battery capacity, however, contradicts with the power-intensive nature of image capture and transmission. Therefore, we propose CapsuleMotion, a patient-specific dynamic capsule behavior that utilizes the available energy in a goal-oriented manner to increase the likelihood of a complete screening of the gastrointestinal tract. By investigating and combining metrics from the on-device image compression, CapsuleMotion predicts the motion between two successive frames. The camera's frame rate will be modified in accordance with the predicted magnitude of motion. Furthermore, prior to entering the small intestine, the capsule operates in a low power mode with a significantly reduced frame rate. In this mode, the LocalizationNet is employed to determine the current organ, provided that motion was predicted. The proposed framework is evaluated on the Rhode Island VCE dataset and deployed on an ultra-low power single-core RISC-V demonstrator with an integrated hardware accelerator. CapsuleMotion demonstrated the capability to reduce electric energy consumption by up to 20.66% in comparison with conventional capsules that lack a dynamic frame rate. Additionally, the accuracy of detecting the entry point of the small intestine has been improved.

AI.tldr: CapsuleMotion uses on-device image compression metrics to predict inter-frame motion and adapt the capsule's frame rate; includes a low-power mode and LocalizationNet-based organ detection; demonstrates energy savings and improved small intestine entry detection on VCE data, implemented on a low-power RISC-V platform.
AI.motivation: VCE faces stringent power constraints due to small kapsule size and high energy cost of image capture/transmission; dynamic frame-rate control aims to maximize GI tract coverage within energy limits.
AI.method: On-device image compression metrics predict motion between successive frames; frame rate is adjusted according to predicted motion magnitude; a low-power mode before entering the small intestine reduces frame rate; LocalizationNet determines the current organ when motion is predicted; evaluated on the Rhode Island VCE dataset; deployed on a ultra-low-power single-core RISC-V demonstrator with a hardware accelerator.
AI.result: Energy consumption reduced by up to 20.66% compared with conventional capsules; improved accuracy in detecting the entry point of the small intestine.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, patient-specific frame-rate and low-power strategies enabled by on-device motion prediction can substantially reduce energy usage while preserving or improving diagnostic performance, demonstrated on realistic VCE hardware.

title: Bayesian Optimisation Using Product-of-Experts Gaussian Process Models with Uncertainty Calibration
summary: Bayesian optimisation (BO) typically relies on a single global Gaussian process (GP) model as its surrogate model. However, GP regression has cubic computational complexity in the number of training data points, limiting its applicability to large-scale optimisation problems. The product-of-experts Gaussian process model with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c) mitigates this limitation by combining multiple local GP experts, enabling improved uncertainty quantification, reduced computational cost, and preservation of global correlations. Despite these desirable properties, the use of GP-pro-c in BO has not been thoroughly studied. This paper introduces BO-pro-c, a Bayesian optimisation algorithm that uses GP-pro-c as its surrogate model, and evaluate its performance across a diverse range of BO settings. Experimental results suggest that BO-pro-c maintains competitive optimisation performance while achieving a 0.9% reduction in simple regret and a 39.4% reduction in computational overhead relative to a BO algorithm based on a single global GP model.

AI.tldr: Introduces BO-pro-c, a Bayesian optimisation framework using a product-of-experts GP with uncertainty calibration as the surrogate, yielding competitive optimisation with notable computational savings over single global GP BO.
AI.motivation: Addresses cubic scaling of single GP regression in BO by using multiple local GP experts that provide uncertainty calibration, enabling scalable BO while preserving global correlations.
AI.method: Integrates GP-pro-c as the surrogate model in the BO loop and evaluates its performance across diverse BO settings, comparing against a BO baseline based on a single global GP.
AI.result: BO-pro-c delivers competitive optimisation performance with a 0.9% reduction in simple regret and a 39.4% reduction in computational overhead compared with the single-global-GP BO baseline.
AI.conclusion: GP-pro-c is a viable scalable surrogate for Bayesian optimisation, offering improved uncertainty handling and reduced computational cost, meriting further exploration across larger BO problems.

title: BSC-Net: A Small-Branch-Sensitive Structural Continuity Network for Coronary Vessel Segmentation and Quantitative Angiographic Analysis
summary: Vessel segmentation in X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is a fundamental step for quantitative coronary analysis and subsequent assessment of coronary artery disease. However, accurate vessel segmentation remains challenging because of imaging noise, complex bifurcations, and the overlap of vessels and background structures, which can lead to disrupted vascular connectivity and missed small branches. In this work, we propose BSC-Net, a ResNet-U-Net-based framework tailored to improve small-vessel representation and repair vascular structural continuity. BSC-Net enhances small-vessel representation through targeted sampling and improves vascular structural continuity by integrating long-range contextual modeling and Edge-Informed Loss (EIL). BSC-Net was validated on two public XCA datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in coronary vessel segmentation with Dice and IoU scores of 77.8%/90.6% and 64.5%/83.0%, respectively. Furthermore, based on the obtained vessel segmentation, we performed automated quantitative coronary analysis and derived clinically relevant morphological and hemodynamic parameters, including stenosis ratio, time-to-peak, and relative propagation velocity. These results demonstrate that BSC-Net produces accurate vessel segmentation results with preserved vascular continuity for quantitative coronary assessment, enabling reliable downstream analysis and clinical evaluation of coronary artery disease.

AI.tldr: Proposes BSC-Net, a ResNet-U-Net framework to improve small-vessel representation and vascular continuity in X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) segmentation, using targeted sampling, long-range contextual modeling, and Edge-Informed Loss; achieves state-of-the-art Dice/IoU on two public datasets and enables automatic quantitative analysis (stenosis, time-to-peak, propagation velocity).
AI.motivation: Accurate XCA vessel segmentation is challenging due to imaging noise, complex bifurcations, and overlap with background structures, leading to disrupted connectivity and loss of small branches. Improved small-vessel representation and continuity are needed for reliable quantitative coronary analysis.
AI.method: A ResNet-U-Net based architecture (BSC-Net) that enhances small-vessel representation via targeted sampling, incorporates long-range contextual modeling, and uses Edge-Informed Loss (EIL) to preserve vascular edges and continuity. Validated on two public XCA datasets with metrics such as Dice and IoU.
AI.result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in coronary vessel segmentation with Dice of 77.8% and IoU of 90.6% on one metric pair, and Dice 64.5% and IoU 83.0% on the other, enabling automated quantitative coronary analysis and extraction of clinically relevant parameters (stenosis ratio, time-to-peak, relative propagation velocity).
AI.conclusion: BSC-Net yields accurate vessel segmentation with preserved vascular continuity, enabling reliable downstream quantitative coronary assessments for CAD.

title: Multi-View Molecular Representation Learning with Hierarchical Graphs and Contextualized Fingerprints
comment: The paper has been accepted as a Full Research Paper at CIKM '26. Source code is available at https://github.com/knhc1234/HiFi-Mol
summary: Molecular property prediction requires representations that generalize from limited labeled data to structurally novel compounds. Existing molecular pretraining methods often rely on a single view: graph-based approaches model atom-bond topology but provide limited fragment-level supervision, whereas fingerprint descriptors encode chemical patterns but are typically used as fixed auxiliary features. We propose HiFi-Mol, a multi-view framework that separately pretrains a hierarchical graph encoder and a contextualized fingerprint encoder before downstream integration. The graph branch uses fragment-aware masking with multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations, while the fingerprint branch tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and applies masked language modeling to learn contextualized embeddings. During fine-tuning, HiFi-Mol combines projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings for downstream prediction. Evaluated on MoleculeNet benchmarks under the scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves a 2.77% improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Further analyses reveal that fragment-aware masking improves graph representation quality, and classification results demonstrate dataset-dependent strengths of the individual graph and fingerprint variants, confirming that the two views provide complementary predictive signals.

AI.tldr: HiFi-Mol is a multi-view pretraining framework for molecular property prediction that combines a hierarchical graph encoder with a contextualized fingerprint encoder, using fragment-aware masking and multi-resolution supervision on graphs and masked language modeling on fingerprint tokens. It achieves state-of-the-art average ROC-AUC gains on MoleculeNet scaffold splits and shows complementary signals between views.
AI.motivation: To improve generalization from limited labeled data to structurally novel compounds by leveraging complementary information from graph-based topology (substructure awareness) and traditional fingerprint patterns (contextualized patterns). Existing single-view pretraining may miss signals present in the other view.
AI.method: Pretrain two separate encoders: (1) a hierarchical graph encoder with fragment-aware masking and multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations; (2) a contextualized fingerprint encoder that tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and uses masked language modeling to learn contextual embeddings. During fine-tuning, combine projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings for downstream prediction.
AI.result: On MoleculeNet benchmarks with scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves a 2.77% absolute improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Analyses show fragment-aware masking improves graph representations, and classification results indicate dataset-dependent strengths of the graph and fingerprint views, supporting complementary predictive signals.
AI.conclusion: Two-view pretraining provides complementary signals that enhance classification performance under scaffold splits, with fragment-aware graph pretraining and contextualized fingerprint embeddings contributing to improved generalization to novel compounds.

title: MarKey: Marginal Utility Guided Greedy Keyframe Selection for Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video understanding remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) because densely encoding long frame sequences is computationally expensive, while uniform sampling under a limited visual budget can miss sparse yet decisive evidence. Recent training-free keyframe selection methods have enabled more efficient inference and yielded promising performance gains. However, many existing methods score frames largely in isolation without explicitly considering how each candidate complements the currently selected subset, potentially resulting in redundant selections and incomplete evidence coverage. To address this limitation, we propose MarKey, a training-free framework that formulates keyframe selection as subset-aware greedy optimization. At each iteration, MarKey scores each candidate using a tractable surrogate that jointly accounts for query relevance, marginal coverage gain, and context-dependent redundancy, and selects the frame with the highest utility. To make this iterative subset-aware evaluation efficient, MarKey uses a compact set of representative anchors to approximate full-video coverage and a bounded window of previously selected frames to limit context-dependent comparisons. Experiments on six benchmarks spanning holistic video understanding, human-centric video understanding, and open-ended video understanding demonstrate that MarKey consistently outperforms existing methods. Further analyses show robust gains across different MLLM backbones, model scales, and frame budgets.

AI.tldr: MarKey is a training-free, subset-aware keyframe selection method for long videos that uses a greedy, context-aware surrogate with anchors and a sliding window to efficiently select informative frames for multimodal LLMs, achieving consistent gains across tasks and backbones.
AI.motivation: Long-video understanding is hampered by computationally expensive dense frame sequences. Uniform sampling can miss sparse yet decisive evidence. Existing training-free keyframe methods score frames independently, risking redundancy and incomplete evidence coverage.
AI.method: Formulates keyframe selection as a subset-aware greedy optimization. At each iteration, evaluate a surrogate for each candidate that combines query relevance, marginal coverage gain, and context-dependent redundancy, then pick the highest-utility frame. Efficiency is achieved with a compact set of anchors to approximate full-video coverage and a bounded window of previously selected frames to limit context. The approach is training-free.
AI.result: Empirical validation on six benchmarks covering holistic, human-centric, and open-ended video understanding shows MarKey consistently outperforms existing methods. Analyses indicate robust gains across various MLLM backbones, model scales, and frame budgets.
AI.conclusion: MarKey delivers a scalable, training-free solution for subset-aware keyframe selection that improves long-video understanding by balancing relevance, coverage, and redundancy, with demonstrated cross-task and cross-model robustness.

title: Where to Compute and How to Interact: Operator-Readable Adaptation with Gauge-Aware Transport
summary: Adaptive meshes enable neural operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) to allocate spatial samples and computation according to local physical structures. Existing approaches, however, mainly address where to compute, with less attention to how information should interact after node relocation. Mesh adaptation changes local sampling scales, neighborhood structures, and geometric contexts, so representations formed at different nodes may not be directly comparable. Direct aggregation can therefore entangle physical variation with discretization-induced representation variation. Because allocation and interaction are jointly optimized through the same output objective, their individual roles are also difficult to distinguish from final errors alone. We introduce operator readability, requiring an adaptive operator to account for and test why computation is allocated to particular locations and how representations interact under the resulting nonuniform discretization. Based on this principle, we propose the Gauge-Aware Adaptive Mesh Neural Operator (GA-AMNO). Physics-informed adaptive allocation answers where to compute, while geometry-conditioned low-rank Gauge transport maps source features into target representation contexts before aggregation, answering how to interact. This makes mesh-to-solver information exchange inspectable and intervenable. We establish sufficient conditions for representation-consistent aggregation and analyze approximate transport errors and continuity under topology-preserving mesh deformations. Experiments on five PDE benchmarks demonstrate improved predictive accuracy, while controlled interventions and geometric-mismatch analyses verify the roles of allocation and interaction and show that Gauge transport improves cross-discretization representation compatibility under strong geometric mismatch.

AI.tldr: GA-AMNO separates where to compute (adaptive allocation) from how to aggregate (geometry-conditioned Gauge transport) in adaptive mesh neural operators, enabling inspectability and better cross-discretization performance.
AI.motivation: Address the entanglement between discretization-induced representation variation and physical variation in adaptive mesh neural operators; current methods focus on allocation but not on how representations interact across nonuniform meshes.
AI.method: Physics-informed adaptive allocation to decide where to compute, and geometry-conditioned low-rank Gauge transport maps that map source features into target representation contexts before aggregation, making mesh-to-solver information exchange inspectable.
AI.result: Establishes sufficient conditions for representation-consistent aggregation; analyzes approximate transport errors and continuity under topology-preserving mesh deformations; experiments on five PDE benchmarks show improved accuracy; controlled interventions and geometric-mismatch analyses confirm roles of allocation vs interaction and show Gauge transport improves cross-discretization compatibility under strong geometric mismatch.
AI.conclusion: Proposes operator readability as a design principle and GA-AMNO as a scalable, interpretable adaptive-mesh operator that separates allocation and interaction for transparent, more accurate PDE solving across nonuniform discretizations.

title: ViCo-SAM3: Vision-Conditioned Alignment for Open-Vocabulary Camouflaged Object Segmentation
summary: Open-vocabulary camouflaged object segmentation (OVCOS) aims to segment unseen camouflaged objects under text guidance. We observe that SAM3 still suffers from a pronounced semantic gap between global textual semantics and fine-grained pixel-level visual cues in OVCOS. Meanwhile, fully fine-tuning the text encoder introduces heavy parameter overhead and risks overfitting to training categories, which compromises open-vocabulary representation flexibility. To address these issues, we propose ViCo-SAM3, a Vision-Conditioned alignment framework designed for OVCOS. Specifically, we introduce vision-conditioned (ViCo) module, which dynamically modulates text embeddings with global visual context, enabling textual representations to adapt to the current image content and thereby effectively bridging the semantic gap between vision and text. Building on this, we further design a vision-conditioned cross-modal binding (ViCoBind) module to enhance cross-modal interaction and semantic alignment between visual and textual representations. Without bells and whistles, ViCo-SAM3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OVCamo benchmark and demonstrates strong generalization.

AI.tldr: ViCo-SAM3 introduces Vision-Conditioned alignment for open-vocabulary camouflaged object segmentation, using ViCo to modulate text embeddings with global visual context and ViCoBind for stronger cross-modal binding, built on SAM3. It achieves state-of-the-art results on OVCamo while maintaining open-vocabulary flexibility by avoiding heavy text-encoder fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: There is a pronounced semantic gap between global textual semantics and fine-grained pixel-level visual cues in open-vocabulary camouflaged object segmentation (OVCOS). Fully fine-tuning the text encoder incurs heavy parameter overhead and risks overfitting to training categories, reducing open-vocabulary generalization.
AI.method: Introduce ViCo-SAM3: a Vision-Conditioned alignment framework. The ViCo module dynamically modulates text embeddings with global visual context to adapt textual representations to the current image. The ViCoBind module reinforces cross-modal interaction and semantic alignment between visual and textual representations. The framework extends the SAM3 baseline without requiring full text-encoder fine-tuning.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OVCamo benchmark and demonstrates strong generalization.
AI.conclusion: Vision-conditioned alignment effectively bridges the gap between vision and text for OVCOS, enabling robust open-vocabulary segmentation without heavy text-encoder fine-tuning and showing strong generalization.

title: FedLTLib: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Federated Long-Tail Learning
summary: Driven by the escalating demand for privacy-preserving computing, Federated Learning (FL) has witnessed remarkable progress, becoming a cornerstone technology for bridging distributed data silos in mobile edge networks. However, in real-world mobile computing environments, data is generated by heterogeneous mobile devices with varying user behaviors, leading to a significant Long-Tail Distribution. Unlike idealized balanced datasets, data in the wild manifests an acute imbalance where a minority of head classes dominate the sample space while a vast number of tail classes, often representing rare but critical edge-case events, are extremely scarce. This data heterogeneity, which we formally characterize as "Double Heterogeneity", referring to the superposition of global class imbalance and local statistical skew, precipitates severe performance deterioration on tail classes, thereby spurring the vital research direction of Federated Long-Tail Learning (FL-LT). To standardize evaluation and accelerate research in this field, we introduce FedLTLib, a comprehensive benchmark tailored for FL-LT. Addressing the critical issues of inconsistent experimental configurations and unfair comparisons in prior work, FedLTLib establishes a standardized evaluation framework. The platform not only incorporates diverse benchmark datasets reflecting mobile data characteristics but also implements 13 state-of-the-art FL algorithms (4 traditional FL algorithms and 9 FL-LT algorithms). By leveraging FedLTLib, researchers can perform fair and reproducible evaluations of algorithm robustness and generalization capabilities under a unified experimental protocol, ultimately advancing the deployment of robust intelligence in mobile computing ecosystems.

AI.tldr: FedLTLib introduces a standardized benchmark for Federated Long-Tail Learning (FL-LT) with 13 algorithms across mobile-data–like datasets, enabling fair, reproducible evaluation under double heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: In FL with heterogeneous devices and user behaviors, data exhibit global class imbalance and local skew, causing severe tail-class performance drops. Prior work lacks a standardized, fair evaluation framework for FL-LT.
AI.method: Propose FedLTLib, a platform with diverse mobile-data benchmark datasets and a unified evaluation protocol, implementing 13 algorithms (4 traditional FL, 9 FL-LT) to enable fair comparisons and robust/generalization assessment.
AI.result: The platform enables fair and reproducible evaluation of FL-LT algorithms under a unified protocol, facilitating robust benchmarking and progress toward deployable mobile-intelligent systems.
AI.conclusion: FedLTLib fills a gap in FL-LT research by standardizing evaluation, enabling fair comparisons, and accelerating the development of robust privacy-preserving FL for mobile ecosystems.

title: A Conservative OCR-Enabled Workflow for R214 Sodium Screening of South African Packaged Foods
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 10th IEEE ICTAS 2026; to appear in the conference proceedings. 7 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables
summary: Using food package images to monitor sodium and salt content against South Africa's R214 sodium limits is challenging when screening decisions require product identity, nutrition facts panel evidence, reporting basis, and category-specific thresholds. This study presents a conservative image-based workflow that combines region detection, optical character recognition (OCR), product identity and sodium evidence extraction, R214 category assignment, deterministic threshold comparison, and independent vision language model comparison. The evaluation used 442 packaged food products and 3 929 full package images from a real-world South African food packaging dataset. A YOLO26s small detector generated 4 195 region crops, and strict post-processing produced one sodium evidence row per product. The integrated workflow produced 290 OUTSIDE R214 SCOPE, 139 REVIEW, seven SCREEN-PASS, and six SCREEN-FAIL outcomes. The independent Qwen2.5-VL 7B vision language model workflow produced 387 OUTSIDE R214 SCOPE, 31 REVIEW, twenty SCREEN-PASS, and four SCREEN-FAIL outcomes. The workflows agreed on exact R214 category assignment for 415 of 442 products (93.9%) and on whether the assigned category was within R214 scope for 416 of 442 products (94.1%). Final screening outcome agreement was 307 out of 442 products, or 69.5%. Manual verification on 60 products showed lower strict outcome agreement than regulated status agreement, while all manual INSUFFICIENT DATA cases were kept out of SCREEN-PASS and SCREEN-FAIL by both automated workflows. The findings show that conservative image-based screening can organise package evidence, identify clear cases, and assign uncertain cases to REVIEW rather than forcing SCREEN-PASS or SCREEN-FAIL decisions.

AI.tldr: An image-based, conservative workflow assesses whether packaged foods meet South Africa's R214 sodium limits using region detection, OCR, evidence extraction, and a vision-language model; evaluated on a real-world dataset; achieves high category agreement with a cautious decision process, routing uncertain cases to REVIEW rather than PASS/FAIL; two parallel systems (YOLO-based and Qwen2.5-VL) show similar performance.
AI.motivation: Detecting sodium content from packaging is challenging due to the need for product identity, nutrition facts panel evidence, reporting basis, and category-specific thresholds. The study aims to provide a robust, scalable, image-based screening workflow that minimizes erroneous PASS/FAIL decisions by explicitly handling uncertainty.
AI.method: A conservative image-based workflow using region detection (YOLO26s small detector) to generate region crops, OCR to extract sodium evidence, rules to assign product identity and sodium evidence, deterministic threshold comparisons against R214 categories, and an independent vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL 7B) to cross-check outcomes. Post-processing yields one sodium evidence row per product. Evaluation used 442 packaged products and 3,929 images from a real-world SA packaging dataset, producing outputs: 290 OUTSIDE R214 SCOPE, 139 REVIEW, 7 SCREEN-PASS, 6 SCREEN-FAIL (YOLO-based); 387 OUTSIDE R214 SCOPE, 31 REVIEW, 20 SCREEN-PASS, 4 SCREEN-FAIL (VL-based).
AI.result: The two workflows agreed on exact R214 category for 415/442 products (93.9%) and on whether the category was within R214 scope for 416/442 products (94.1%). Final screening outcome agreement was 307/442 (69.5%). Manual verification on 60 products showed lower strict outcome agreement than regulated status agreement; all manual INSUFFICIENT DATA cases were kept out of SCREEN-PASS and SCREEN-FAIL by both automated workflows.
AI.conclusion: Conservative image-based screening can structure evidence, identify clear cases, and route uncertain cases to REVIEW rather than forcing PASS/FAIL decisions, supporting scalable, accountable screening with two independent baselines.

title: Principal-timestep Restricted Init via Sparse Matrix-decomposition in Flow-matching
summary: Flow-matching diffusion models have recently emerged as a strong paradigm for high-fidelity visual generation. However, their prohibitively high fine-tuning cost limits scalability to downstream tasks. While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) combined with spectral initialization has demonstrated accelerated convergence and improved performance in autoregressive language models by better aligning gradient directions, we find that it fails to deliver similar gains in diffusion fine-tuning, often yielding marginal or even negative improvements over vanilla LoRA.We attribute this discrepancy to a fundamental mismatch between LoRA's low-rank parameterization and the intrinsically high-rank gradients induced by the flow-matching objective. In particular, stochastic timestep sampling introduces directionally heterogeneous gradient signals across training steps, leading to misaligned updates under low-rank constraints.To address this issue, we propose Prism-LoRA,a Principal-timestep Restricted Init via Sparse Matrix-decomposition framework that improves gradient alignment during fine-tuning. Our method consists of two key components: (i) principal timestep selection, which restricts initialization gradients to a subset of dominant timesteps to suppress effective gradient rank, and (ii) principal channel filtering, which removes task-irrelevant channels, enabling the one-step spectral initialization gradient to better align with the long-horizon optimization trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves both convergence speed and final performance across multiple diffusion fine-tuning benchmarks, including subject-driven generation, controllable generation, and deblurring, achieving not only performance improvement but also earlier stages of convergence over baseline LoRA and other spectral-init methods.

AI.tldr: Prism-LoRA improves diffusion fine-tuning by aligning low-rank updates to high-rank gradient signals via principal timestep selection and channel filtering, yielding faster convergence and improved final performance over LoRA and spectral-init baselines.
AI.motivation: LoRA with spectral initialization underperforms for diffusion fine-tuning due to high-rank gradient signals and stochastic timestep sampling, causing misaligned updates under low-rank constraints.
AI.method: Propose Prism-LoRA: 1) principal timestep selection restricting initialization gradients to dominant timesteps to suppress effective gradient rank, 2) principal channel filtering removing task-irrelevant channels to align one-step spectral initialization gradient with long-horizon optimization.
AI.result: Empirical results show Prism-LoRA consistently improves convergence speed and final performance across diffusion fine-tuning tasks (subject-driven generation, controllable generation, deblurring) compared to baseline LoRA and spectral-init methods.
AI.conclusion: Prism-LoRA mitigates the mismatch between low-rank parameterization and high-rank diffusion gradients, enabling faster and better fine-tuning; the approach yields robust gains across multiple downstream diffusion tasks.

title: AnchorGUI: Asymmetric Memory for Dual-Scale Learning in GUI Navigation
comment: Published in ECCV 2026. 41 pages including supplementary material
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable autonomous GUI navigation, but agents still struggle to process and learn from dense, continuous visual histories. This bottleneck hinders both immediate error correction within a single episode (intra-trial) and experience distillation across multiple attempts (cross-trial). We trace these challenges to an empirical informational asymmetry in GUI navigation: while expected transitions can often be compressed into lightweight textual summaries, unexpected outcomes benefit from preserved screenshots as causal evidence for accurate diagnosis. Building on this insight, we propose AnchorGUI, a unified framework driven by the Cognitive State Anchor (CSA). The CSA acts as a per-step primitive that actively compares expected and observed transitions, converting passive multimodal trajectories into explicit prediction-error signals. These signals orchestrate a dual-scale learning mechanism via an asymmetric memory.
