For intra-trial correction, a sliding window selectively retains visual evidence for detected mismatches, providing immediate, visually-grounded feedback. For cross-trial distillation, this asymmetric memory focuses the computationally expensive credit assignment search space on likely failure steps. Experiments across four benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our approach. On AndroidWorld, AnchorGUI achieves a 57.3% success rate with a $2.4\times$ token reduction per step. Furthermore, cross-trial distillation reaches 69.2% success (+11.9% gain), significantly outperforming standard reflection methods while maintaining sub-linear context scaling.

AI.tldr: AnchorGUI uses a Cognitive State Anchor to convert prediction errors into an asymmetric memory system for GUI navigation, enabling efficient intra-trial error correction with selective visual evidence and cross-trial credit assignment distillation; it yields improved success and data efficiency across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Dense, continuous visual histories in vision-language model (VLM) driven GUI agents hinder both immediate intra-trial corrections and cross-trial knowledge distillation. An informational asymmetry—compressible expected transitions textually vs. need for visual evidence for unexpected outcomes—drives the need for a new framework that can retain relevant visuals where needed.
AI.method: Introduce a per-step Cognitive State Anchor (CSA) that compares expected vs observed transitions to generate prediction-error signals. Employ an asymmetric memory with a sliding window for intra-trial visual evidence to provide immediate feedback and reserve computationally expensive credit assignment search for likely failure steps during cross-trial distillation. The approach enables dual-scale learning and includes a five-belt mechanism of prediction-error-driven updates across episodes.
AI.result: On AndroidWorld, AnchorGUI achieves 57.3% success with 2.4× token reduction per step. Cross-trial distillation reaches 69.2% success (+11.9% gain), outperforming standard reflection methods while maintaining sub-linear context scaling.
AI.conclusion: AnchorGUI effectively mitigates informational asymmetry in GUI navigation by combining prediction-error signals with an asymmetric memory, improving both immediate error correction and cross-trial knowledge distillation, with strong empirical gains on multiple benchmarks.

title: Backward SDEs-based Diffusion for Physics-Constrained Generation
summary: Pretrained score-based diffusion models provide strong unconditional priors, yet enforcing measurement or physics consistency in inverse problems is often handled by heuristic guidance, intermittent projections, or task-specific conditional training, with limited guarantees of feasibility at the end of inference. We propose terminal-conditioned inversion for score-based SDE priors. Given a frozen Score-SDE prior and a task-defined terminal feasibility specification, we construct an associated backward stochastic differential equation whose adapted solution defines a principled inverse map from the terminal requirement to a prior state at a chosen noise level. Under standard regularity conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the adapted solution and obtain terminal consistency by construction. We further develop a practical neural BSDE solver that composes arbitrary pretrained diffusion priors with domain constraints without modifying the score-defined coefficients, producing an anchored prior state that enables neighborhood sampling for uncertainty characterization. Experiments on toy datasets validate stable terminal-conditioned inversion and distributionally consistent neighborhood sampling. As a real-world case study, we apply the framework to sparse-view CT reconstruction and achieve improved reconstruction quality over representative training-free baselines while satisfying strict measurement feasibility under the prescribed terminal specification. Project is available in: \href{https://laplacelab.github.io/BSDEDiffusion/}{https://laplace.center/icmlbsdeI/}

AI.tldr: Terminal-conditioned inversion for score-based diffusion priors via a backward SDE, yielding a principled inverse map from terminal feasibility to a prior state at a chosen noise level; a neural BSDE solver composes pretrained priors with domain constraints without altering the score coefficients, enabling anchored priors and uncertainty-aware neighborhood sampling; validated on toy data and sparse-view CT with improved reconstruction and strict feasibility.
AI.motivation: Score-based diffusion models provide strong unconditional priors, but enforcing physical/measurement consistency is often heuristic and lacks end-of-inference feasibility guarantees. A principled, terminal-conditioned inversion would ensure feasibility at inference completion while leveraging pretrained priors.
AI.method: Fix a frozen Score-SDE prior and a user-defined terminal feasibility specification. Construct an associated backward SDE (BSDE) whose adapted solution defines an inverse map from the terminal constraint to a prior state at a chosen noise level. Prove existence and uniqueness under standard regularity; assure terminal consistency by construction. Develop a neural BSDE solver that plugs arbitrary pretrained diffusion priors into domain constraints without modifying the score-defined coefficients, producing an anchored prior state. This enables neighborhood sampling for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Toy-dataset experiments validate stable terminal-conditioned inversion and distributional neighborhood sampling. In sparse-view CT reconstruction, the method achieves improved reconstruction quality over representative training-free baselines while maintaining strict measurement feasibility under the terminal specification.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled framework for terminal-consistent inversion with score-based SDE priors, enabling uncertainty-aware sampling without retraining or altering diffusion coefficients, and demonstrates practical gains in a real-world CT task. The accompanying project page offers implementation details.

title: BVB: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding via Programmatic Reconstruction in Blender
summary: Multimodal agents can create complex videos in software such as Blender by coding without relying on diffusion models. Yet video understanding benchmarks still evaluate models mainly through question answering. If an agent truly understands a video, it can reconstruct it programmatically. We introduce BVB, Blender-VideoBench, a benchmark that tests this ability by asking agents to reconstruct real-world videos as animated Blender scenes. To ensure fair comparison, each agent programs the reconstruction through a lightweight harness, Mini-BVB, in an identical sandbox under a shared cost limit. The benchmark renders each reconstruction from its animated camera and evaluates it on two axes: (1) Dual VQA measures how many spatiotemporal facts the reconstruction preserves. (2) Latent Similarity measures how closely the reconstruction matches the source video perceptually. Our overall score, a square-root mean, favors balanced performance. We evaluate 51 configurations from 10 model families and analyze semantic retention, perceptual similarity, reasoning effort, and cost. The best model reaches 88.6 Latent Similarity but retains only 53.7% of the source-correct spatiotemporal answers. Additional reasoning improves visual similarity but does not close this gap in factual accuracy. In a blind study with 15 raters and five configurations, Latent Similarity correlates strongly with human preference. These results show that programmatic reconstruction is a viable test of agentic video understanding, and that semantic retention remains the main challenge.

AI.tldr: BVB (Blender-VideoBench) tests whether multimodal agents can reconstruct real-world videos as animated Blender scenes via a lightweight harness, evaluating semantic retention and perceptual similarity; shows partial success with strong correlation between latent similarity and human preference, but semantic retention remains the main challenge.
AI.motivation: Challenge the QA-centric evaluation of video understanding by proposing a programmatic, reconstructive criterion that measures an agent's ability to translate observed video into executable, animated scenes, enabling a zero-shot, cost-bounded, fair comparison.
AI.method: Create BVB benchmark where agents reconstruct real videos into Blender scenes, using a Mini-BVB harness in a controlled sandbox under a shared cost limit. Render reconstructions from a fixed camera and evaluate with two axes: (1) Dual VQA for spatiotemporal fact retention; (2) Latent Similarity for perceptual fidelity. Aggregate via a square-root mean score. Evaluate 51 configurations across 10 model families; use blind raters to assess human preference.
AI.result: Best model achieves 88.6 Latent Similarity but preserves only 53.7% of source-correct spatiotemporal answers. Although reasoning improves visual similarity, it does not close the gap in factual accuracy. Latent Similarity correlates strongly with human preference in a blind study with 15 raters across 5 configurations.
AI.conclusion: Programmatic reconstruction is a viable test of agentic video understanding and highlights semantic retention as the primary challenge for translating observed video into executable scenes.

title: Knowledge-Enriched Structured EHR Features for 30-Day Hospital Readmission Prediction on MIMIC-IV
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at SDSC 2026 Mid-Atlantic
summary: Recent approaches to 30-day hospital readmission prediction rely on pre-trained language models applied to discharge summaries. Although these methods achieve strong performance, they depend on the availability of clinical notes, incur substantial computational costs, and yield representations that lack interpretability. We propose a knowledge-enriched feature representation that augments structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) data with four medical knowledge sources: disease ontology mapping, procedure classification, drug ingredient vocabulary, and organ system laboratory aggregation, without using clinical notes. Each feature dimension corresponds to a named clinical concept, yielding a sparse and interpretable patient representation. The approach is evaluated with six classifiers on a MIMIC-IV v2.2 cohort. Under 20-fold cross-validation, the best configuration achieves an AUROC of 0.743. This performance is comparable to that of previously reported methods on this dataset, including both those using only structured data and those incorporating clinical notes, while requiring considerably less computational cost. Interpretability analysis shows that demographics, organ system labs, drug ingredient features, and first-level ontology disease categories drive prediction, while deeper hierarchy levels contribute negligibly. These findings indicate that knowledge-enriched structured features offer a competitive and efficient alternative to embeddings from clinical notes for 30-day readmission prediction.

AI.tldr: Knowledge-enriched features built on structured EHR data, augmented with disease ontology, procedures, drug ingredients, and organ-system labs, yielding an interpretable, sparse representation for 30-day readmission prediction. Achieves AUROC 0.743 on MIMIC-IV v2.2, competitive with note-based methods while reducing cost and improving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of discharge-note–based approaches (reliance on unstructured notes, high computational cost, and limited interpretability). Propose a structured-data–driven, knowledge-enriched representation to enable efficient, interpretable prediction.
AI.method: Construct a sparse feature space where each dimension corresponds to a named clinical concept. Augment structured EHR data with four knowledge sources: disease ontology mapping, procedure classification, drug ingredient vocabulary, and organ-system laboratory aggregation. Evaluate six classifiers on MIMIC-IV v2.2 using 20-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: Best AUROC of 0.743. Performance is comparable to methods using structured data alone or with clinical notes, but with substantially lower computational cost. Interpretability analysis shows drivers include demographics, organ-system labs, drug ingredient features, and first-level disease ontology categories; deeper ontology levels contribute little.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-enriched structured features can rival embeddings derived from clinical notes for 30-day readmission prediction, offering competitive accuracy with improved interpretability and reduced computation.

title: CatchMonitor: a machine learning system for automated fish discard quantification
summary: We report on the continued development of CatchMonitor, resulting in a prototype computer vision system designed to automatically quantify discarded fish from video footage collected from Remote Electronic Monitoring (REM) systems on fishing trawlers. The analysis of trawler surveillance footage is a challenging problem due to the real-world conditions on board fishing vessels. Building on our prior work we improve the accuracy of species identification through the application of semi-supervised learning. We utilise a simple and robust object tracking approach, upon which we build our prototype discard quantification system. Finally we analyse the variability of manual discard quantification performed by multiple expert human analysts, using it as a benchmark against which we compare the performance of our system.

AI.tldr: Prototype CatchMonitor for automated discard quantification from REM video using semi-supervised species identification and robust tracking; benchmarked against inter-expert variability.
AI.motivation: Automate and improve accuracy of quantifying discarded fish on fishing vessels to support fisheries monitoring and management, under challenging real-world on-board conditions.
AI.method: Extend prior work by applying semi-supervised learning for species identification; adopt a simple, robust object-tracking framework; build a prototype discard-quantification pipeline; assess performance against variability in manual quantification by multiple expert analysts.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved species-identification accuracy; provides a functional prototype for discard quantification; validates performance by comparing to inter-expert variability.
AI.conclusion: Semi-supervised species identification combined with robust tracking enables automated discard quantification from REM footage; the approach shows promise and establishes a human-analyst variability benchmark as a reference for system performance.

title: Assembling the CREW: A Collaborative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Automated Related Work Generation
summary: Automatic Related Work Generation (RWG) significantly reduces the human time and effort required to author the Related Work Section (RWS) of a research paper. However, prior methods leveraging multi-agent Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on a predefined workflow, where each agent is responsible for a specific step in the entire process. This rigid, static inter-agent coordination limits the adaptive collaboration required to synthesize complex scientific literature. To address this limitation, we propose CREW (Collaborative Reinforcement Learning for Related Work Generation), a novel framework where LLM agents bypass heuristic pipelines to dynamically coordinate by autonomously selecting actions, such as Retrieve, Disseminate, Compose, and Critique, driven by a policy optimized via Independent Proximal Policy Optimization (IPPO). Extensive experiments on a standard RWG benchmark demonstrate that our approach yields substantial quality improvements over strong existing baselines, while significantly reducing token costs. Code is available at https://github.com/YenPBao/CREW-Collaborative-MARL.git

AI.tldr: CREW introduces a dynamic, multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for Related Work Generation, where LLM agents autonomously select actions (Retrieve, Disseminate, Compose, Critique) under an Independent Proximal Policy Optimization policy, improving quality and reducing token costs over static pipelines.
AI.motivation: Prior RWG methods rely on rigid, predefined multi-agent workflows, which hamper adaptive collaboration among agents needed to synthesize complex literature. A dynamic coordination mechanism can better align tasks to content and context.
AI.method: Agents operate without a fixed pipeline, selecting actions through a policy optimized via Independent Proximal Policy Optimization (IPPO). Core actions include Retrieve, Disseminate, Compose, and Critique, enabling flexible collaboration to build the Related Work section.
AI.result: On a standard RWG benchmark, CREW achieves substantial quality improvements over strong baselines and significantly reduces token costs, demonstrating effective adaptive coordination among agents.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, collaborative RL with IPPO enables more effective RWG by letting agents autonomously coordinate steps, reducing reliance on rigid pipelines and lowering token usage while enhancing output quality; code is publicly available.

title: SyntheticDoc: A Large Synthetic Dataset for Document Unwarping and Illumination Correction
comment: D. Woortmann and T. Magne -- Equal contribution. Accepted at ECCV 2026 (Spotlight). 20 pages
summary: Deep learning models have become the standard tool for document rectification and illumination correction, yet their performance is fundamentally bound by their training data. For nearly a decade, the community has heavily relied on Doc3D, a pioneering but increasingly limited document unwarping dataset in terms of scale and quality. To address this bottleneck, we introduce SyntheticDoc, a massive, high-quality dataset designed to push the boundaries of document unwarping. SyntheticDoc is composed of 1,000,000 high-resolution procedurally generated training samples, alongside extensive validation and test sets. Each sample is paired with rich, pixel-perfect annotations, including UV maps, normal maps, albedo and shading. To ensure physical accuracy and photorealism, the paper geometries are generated via a physics-based simulator and rendered using a path tracer. To demonstrate the benefit of our dataset, we train a simple baseline model on SyntheticDoc and report on its performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods on both document unwarping and illumination correction tasks. Our dataset is available at https://igl.ethz.ch/projects/SyntheticDoc/ and the code used to generate it at https://github.com/tanguymagne/SyntheticDoc .

AI.tldr: SyntheticDoc: a 1M-sample high-quality synthetic dataset for document unwarping and illumination correction; includes UV/normal/albedo/shading annotations; physics-based rendering; baseline shows benefits over state-of-the-art; dataset and code released.
AI.motivation: Address the data bottleneck and limited scale/quality of Doc3D; improve generalization and realism for document rectification tasks.
AI.method: Procedurally generate 1,000,000 high-resolution samples; physics-based simulator; path-traced rendering; provide rich pixel-perfect annotations (UV maps, normal maps, albedo, shading); train a simple baseline model; compare with SOTA on unwarping and illumination correction.
AI.result: Baseline model trained on SyntheticDoc demonstrates competitive or improved performance relative to state-of-the-art on both tasks; validation/test sets; dataset and code released.
AI.conclusion: SyntheticDoc effectively mitigates data limitations, enabling improved performance and providing a resource for future research; promotes photorealism in document rectification research.

title: Solving Finite-sum Coupled Compositional Optimization via Multi-block-Single-probe Estimator
summary: Traditional variance reduction methods (e.g., SPIDER, SARAH, STORM) have been extensively investigated for improving the convergence rates of stochastic optimization. These techniques typically maintain a sequence of estimators for a single function (or gradient) across iterations. However, what if we need to track multiple functions, but can only access stochastic samples of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ functions at each iteration? This scenario arises in an important emerging family of finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (FCCO) problems of the form $\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(g_i(\mathbf{w}))$, where each $g_i$ is accessible only through a stochastic oracle. The key challenge is to track $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})=(g_1(\mathbf{w}), \ldots, g_m(\mathbf{w}))$ over time, where $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})$ has $m$ blocks but only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ blocks can be probed for their stochastic values at each step. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Multi-block-Single-probe Variance Reduction (MSVR) estimator to efficiently trace $\mathbf g(\mathbf{w})$ under partial block sampling. Building on the MSVR estimator, we develop several algorithms for FCCO problems, achieving improved sample complexities for non-convex, convex, strongly convex, and Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) objectives. We further obtain an improved dependence on $m$ when the outer function gradients $\nabla f_i$ are linear. Empirical studies on multi-task deep AUC maximization further demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed estimators.

AI.tldr: Introduces a multi-block single-probe variance reduction (MSVR) estimator for finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (FCCO) that tracks m stochastic blocks with only O(1) probes per iteration, leading to improved sample complexities across convex/non-convex regimes and better m-dependence when outer gradients are linear; validated on multi-task deep AUC maximization.
AI.motivation: In FCCO problems of the form (1/m) sum f_i(g_i(w)) where each g_i is accessible stochastically, existing variance-reduction methods track a single function's gradient; a practical scenario demands tracking many blocks with limited per-iteration access, motivating MSVR.
AI.method: Develop MSVR estimator to maintain and update multi-block estimates with single-probe sampling; integrate into algorithms for FCCO; analyze convergence across non-convex, convex, strongly convex, and PL objectives; leverage linearity of outer-gradients to improve m-dependence.
AI.result: Achieves improved sample complexities for FCCO across several objective classes; better dependence on m when gradients ∇f_i are linear; empirical experiments on multi-task deep AUC support effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: MSVR enables efficient variance reduction in FCCO under partial block sampling, broadening applicability to large-scale multi-block stochastic optimization; potential impact for multi-task learning and related problems.

title: Assessing nnU-Net Generalization across Brain Tumor Populations in BraTS-GoAT 2026
summary: BraTS-GoAT evaluates tumor segmentation across heterogeneous populations. We trained a conventional 3D nnU-Net on 1,351 labeled cases using five-fold cross-validation and 1,000 epochs per fold. The final predictor averaged all folds and applied test-time mirroring. On pooled official validation, global DSC values were 0.7805, 0.8288, and 0.8854 for enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), and whole tumor (WT). Under matched fold-0 inference, mean regional Dice decreased from 0.9058 on source out-of-fold (OOF) cases to 0.8310 on pooled validation (difference--0.0747). Mirroring gave small single-fold gains but no clear ensemble benefit; a residual-encoder alternative reached 0.8282 mean Dice. In labeled OOF predictions, failure cases had substantially smaller reference ET volumes; after adjustment for ET and WT volume, lower Dice remained associated with more disconnected ET components and a smaller fraction of ET contained in the largest component.

AI.tldr: BraTS-GoAT trains a 3D nnU-Net on 1,351 labeled cases with five-fold CV; achieves competitive DSC on ET/TC/WT on pooled validation; cross-fold inference shows performance drop; mirroring/ensemble provide limited gains; residual-encoder performs similarly; failures relate to ET volume/connectivity.
AI.motivation: Assess segmentation robustness across heterogeneous populations and real-world variability; quantify performance drop from source-out-of-fold to pooled validation; dissect factors driving errors.
AI.method: Train conventional 3D nnU-Net on 1,351 labeled cases; five-fold cross-validation; 1,000 epochs per fold; final predictor via fold averaging; test-time mirroring; evaluate on pooled official validation; examine fold-0 matched inference; compare to residual-encoder; analyze OOF predictions; adjust for ET and WT volumes; assess ET connectivity.
AI.result: Global DSC on pooled validation: ET 0.7805, TC 0.8288, WT 0.8854. Fold-0 inference: 0.9058 OOF → 0.8310 pooled (−0.0747). Mirroring yielded small gains; ensemble no clear benefit. Residual-encoder: 0.8282 mean Dice. In labeled OOF, failures linked to smaller ET volumes; after adjusting for ET/WT volume, lower Dice associated with more disconnected ET components and smaller ET in largest component.
AI.conclusion: Cross-population segmentation is feasible with nnU-Net but performance degrades when generalizing to pooled validation; volumetric and connectivity characteristics of ET influence Dice; test-time augmentation offers limited gain; alternative encoder (residual) not markedly better; attention to ET volume/connectivity essential for robust evaluation.

title: A Language-Guided Multimodal Foundation Model for Zero-Shot and Multi-Task Brain Signal Analysis
comment: 38 pages, 7 main figures and 20 supplementary figures; includes Supporting Information. Code: https://github.com/mingzhi-c/metis-brain-signal-foundation-model
summary: Brain signal analysis is essential for both neuroscience research and clinical diagnostics, yet current approaches face critical limitations. End-to-end models require task-specific retraining and exhibit limited generalization, while pre-trained models lack semantic depth and still depend on extensive fine-tuning. Meanwhile, general-purpose multimodal foundation models, though powerful in other domains, struggle to interpret brain signals due to representational misalignment and lack of domain knowledge. This study introduces a multimodal foundation model for zero-shot and multi-task brain signal analysis (METIS) through a unified language-signal alignment framework. METIS is pretrained on the largest and most diverse brain-signal corpus to date, comprising over 70,000 h of recordings from more than 11,000 subjects across 20 datasets. In a comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across 12 datasets, METIS outperformed the leading generalist model by over 20.9% in average accuracy. Remarkably, without any fine-tuning, METIS's performance matches or exceeds that of supervised, task-specific models. Furthermore, METIS demonstrates exceptional data efficiency and strong generalization, achieving an average AUROC advantage of over 16.0% in few-shot settings and 15.9% in cross-dataset transfer. This work establishes a new paradigm for general-purpose brain signal analysis, paving the way for next-generation neurotechnology.

AI.tldr: METIS is a multimodal foundation model for zero-shot and multi-task brain-signal analysis using language-signal alignment, pretrained on the largest diverse brain-signal corpus to date, achieving strong zero-shot and few-shot performance without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current end-to-end brain-signal models require task-specific retraining and struggle to generalize; pre-trained models lack semantic depth and still depend on fine-tuning; general-purpose multimodal models face representational misalignment with brain signals and lack domain knowledge.
AI.method: METIS is a multimodal foundation model trained with a unified language-signal alignment framework on a large, diverse brain-signal corpus (~70k hours, 11k subjects, 20 datasets). It emphasizes zero-shot and multi-task capabilities across 12 datasets.
AI.result: In zero-shot evaluation across 12 datasets, METIS outperformed the leading generalist model by >20.9% on average accuracy and matched or exceeded supervised task-specific models without fine-tuning. In few-shot settings, METIS achieved an average AUROC advantage >16.0%; in cross-dataset transfer, ~15.9% AUROC advantage.
AI.conclusion: METIS demonstrates a new paradigm for general-purpose brain-signal analysis, enabling robust zero-shot and few-shot performance and paving the way for next-generation neurotechnology.

title: PIVOT: Physics-Grounded Verification for AI-Generated Audio-Video Detection
summary: As generative models continue to advance, AI-generated content (AIGC) is becoming increasingly realistic, weakening the artifact cues commonly exploited by existing detectors. Nevertheless, faithfully reproducing the physical behavior of real-world events remains challenging for current generators. We therefore explore detecting AIGC by assessing whether the depicted event satisfies measurable constraints derived from physical laws. We introduce PIVOT, a physics-grounded AIGC detector, instantiated here for audio-video clips, that estimates physical quantities from video and audio, selects physical laws relevant to each clip, and verifies their measurable constraints. Beyond a real/fake decision, PIVOT returns supporting evidence that records the verification outcome, relevant time window, and supporting quantities for each applicable law. Although instantiated and evaluated here on audio-video data, the framework can, in principle, extend to other AIGC modalities whenever the physical quantities required for verification can be estimated reliably. We also introduce PhysForensics-Bench, comprising paired real and generated audio-video clips from nine event-centric scene families and two recent audio-video generators. On PhysForensics-Bench, PIVOT achieves 70.30% accuracy and 64.29% F1 score on Real+Seedance, and 72.16% accuracy and 65.82% F1 on Real+VEO. In comparison, direct inspection with Gemini 3.1 Pro obtains 53.96% accuracy and 60.09% F1 on Real+Seedance, and 57.22% accuracy and 63.44% F1 on Real+Veo. These results demonstrate the practical promise of physical-consistency verification as a structured and inspectable source of evidence that complements artifact-based AIGC detection.

AI.tldr: Physics-consistency detector for AIGC in audio-video (PIVOT) using measurable physical laws; introduces PhysForensics-Bench; shows higher accuracy/F1 than Gemini baselines; framework extensible to other modalities; emphasizes explainable evidence.
AI.motivation: Current detectors rely on artifact cues that degrade as generators improve; physics-based verification provides independent, interpretable evidence by checking compliance with physical laws.
AI.method: Estimate physical quantities from video/audio, select relevant laws per clip, verify measurable constraints, output evidence including time window and quantities; evaluated on PhysForensics-Bench with real/generated pairs and compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro.
AI.result: PIVOT achieves ~70.3% accuracy and 64.3% F1 on Real+Seedance; ~72.2% accuracy and 65.8% F1 on Real+VEO; outperforming Gemini baselines (e.g., 53.96% accuracy, 60.09% F1 on Real+Seedance); provides structured evidence for each verified law.
AI.conclusion: Physics-grounded verification is a promising, inspectable complement to artifact-based detectors and can extend to other modalities where physical quantities can be estimated; introduces a dataset (PhysForensics-Bench) to benchmark such methods.

title: Sylvas: Synergistic Learning Value based Device Scheduling in Federated Continual Learning
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Federated continual learning (FCL) enables shared global models to continuously adapt to distributed and non-stationary data streams, making it important for Internet of Things applications such as intelligent transportation, industrial monitoring, and unmanned systems. Under spatio-temporal data distribution dynamics and label scarcity, a key challenge is how to quantify the contribution of each edge device to global learning performance and schedule the most valuable devices under resource constraints for timely model updating. This article presents Sylvas, a synergistic learning value based device scheduling framework for FCL at the wireless edge. Sylvas evaluates the learning value of distributed data from two perspectives: distributional value, which characterizes the contribution of device data to global model learning from a spatio-temporal distribution perspective, and label value, which captures the quantity and reliability tradeoff of pseudo-labeled data. By integrating these factors into a synergistic learning value metric, Sylvas schedules devices with high learning value while satisfying communication and computation resource constraints. Case studies demonstrate that Sylvas supports timely model adaptation under spatio-temporal distribution dynamics and effectively exploits unlabeled data.

AI.tldr: Sylvas is a learning-value-based device scheduling framework for federated continual learning (FCL) at the wireless edge. It jointly scores devices by their distributional contribution to the global model and the value of pseudo-labeled data, and schedules high-value devices under resource constraints to enable timely model updates in non-stationary, labeled-scarce environments.
AI.motivation: In FCL with spatio-temporal data shifts and limited labels, there is a need to quantify each edge device's contribution to the global model and to select the most valuable devices for participation given bandwidth and computation limits.
AI.method: Define two learning-value components: distributional value assessing the device's data contribution to the spatio-temporal distribution of the global model, and label value assessing the quantity and reliability of pseudo-labeled data. Combine these into a synergistic learning-value metric to schedule devices that maximize learning gains while respecting communication/computation constraints.
AI.result: Case studies indicate Sylvas enables timely model adaptation under distribution shifts and efficiently leverages unlabeled data, improving the effectiveness of FCL at the wireless edge.
AI.conclusion: Sylvas provides a principled, resource-aware scheduling mechanism for FCL by quantifying and combining distributional and label values, enabling better utilization of edge data and unlabeled samples under dynamic conditions.

title: What a gated sensing pipeline never looks at: bandwidth reduction and the misses behind it
comment: 13 pages, 6 tables, no figures. Reports a superseded detection result alongside the corrected run that replaces it; Table 6 carries every scored run of every staged flight
summary: An airborne sensor on a contested link cannot send video, so the appealing move is to send findings instead and report the ratio between the two. We evaluate a gated sensing pipeline that does this, combining learned object detection and image-text comparison with deterministic scheduling, gating, evidence accumulation and transmission rules. On staged footage with the semantic stage live it sends 38,736 bits over 211 s, a reduction of 41,977x, and names 1 of 4 staged events with no false report. That detection has since been superseded: a correction to how the tracker measures speed removed the measurement artefact the normality model had been learning from, and the flight no longer warms. Under the corrected code the pipeline names 1 of 7 staged events across four flights, and we report both. On a control flight where nothing was staged it reports nothing, a reduction of 155,830x: the largest number in the study and the least informative, because a reduction ratio measures the scene. The mechanisms that produce the reduction also decide which observations ever reach a decision, so the two cannot be reported apart. We give a tick-level trace of one flight (3,187 rows) that places each of three missed events at the stage where it stopped progressing: one produced no track, one failed the structural place test at 0.129, and one passed 539 structural ticks but reached only 3.192 against a boundary of 3.807. We also report one instance of a known failure mode, an online normality model absorbing the object it will later judge, measured against the threshold that object then failed. The evidence is one detection and six misses across four staged flights, beside one clean control, and we treat it as a case study. We give the reproduction protocol and generated results, identify which supporting artifacts are not distributed, and state which experiments did not run.

AI.tldr: A gated sensing pipeline reduces data transmission by reporting detections and reasoning instead of streaming video, while maintaining limited event naming accuracy; but performance depends on code artefacts and decision rules, making the reduction inseparable from evidentiary decisions.
AI.motivation: In contested-link scenarios, video cannot be sent; need bandwidth-efficient, verifiable reporting of relevant events with traceable decision processes.
AI.method: A pipeline that combines learned object detection and image-text comparison with deterministic scheduling, gating, evidence accumulation, and transmission rules; evaluated on staged flights and a control flight; includes tick-level traces, reproduction protocol, and artifact disclosure.
AI.result: On staged footage: 38,736 bits transmitted over 211 s, 41,977x data reduction, correctly names 1 of 4 staged events with no false report. After a tracker-speed artefact correction, names 1 of 7 events across four flights; control flight reports nothing. Maximum reported reduction reaches 155,830x. A tick-level trace highlights where three missed events stalled; one known failure mode involves an online normality model absorbing the object. Overall evidence is one detection and six misses across four staged flights; reproduction protocol and artifacts are provided, with some artifacts not distributed and some experiments not run.
AI.conclusion: The data-reduction gains are intrinsically tied to the decision mechanism; reductions cannot be reported separately from evidentiary decisions. The study highlights artefact sensitivity, partial reproducibility, and the need for complete disclosure of supporting artifacts for robust generalization.

title: Transfer Learning for Socioeconomic Estimation in Forced-Displacement Settings
summary: Progress in inclusive household surveys has strengthened socioeconomic evidence for forcibly displaced populations, providing indispensable benchmarks on living conditions and welfare. However, these surveys remain resource-intensive and periodic, while conditions can change between rounds, particularly in settings affected by fragility, conflict, and violence. More frequently updated, spatially granular complementary evidence is therefore needed to identify where socioeconomic conditions may be changing between survey rounds and to inform operational prioritization. Earth observation and machine learning offer a scalable source of spatially explicit socioeconomic information. However, tools developed for general populations have not been systematically adapted and evaluated in forced displacement settings, where living conditions, settlement patterns, and displacement impacts may differ substantially. We address this gap by adapting a multimodal spatiotemporal vision transformer, pretrained on Demographic and Health Survey data from approximately 1.2 million households across 36 African countries, to forced displacement and host community settings in South Sudan, Cameroon, and Zambia. We develop and evaluate the updated, adapted model using socioeconomic indices derived from UNHCR FDS and RMS data. Our results show that satellite-derived geospatial covariates explain up to 66% of the variation in socioeconomic outcomes in camp-intersecting grids, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.37 index points, and 41% in non-camp-intersecting areas, with an MAE of 5.41. The framework complements and adds value to periodic household surveys by filling critical spatial and temporal data gaps with regularly updated, model-based socioeconomic estimates. These estimates sustain insight between survey rounds and support timely humanitarian prioritization and field verification.

AI.tldr: Adapts a multimodal spatiotemporal vision transformer pretrained on DHS data to forced displacement settings, using satellite covariates to predict socioeconomic outcomes in South Sudan, Cameroon, and Zambia. The approach yields substantial explained variation between survey rounds, offering frequent, spatially granular estimates to guide humanitarian prioritization.
AI.motivation: Periodic household surveys for forcibly displaced populations are costly and infrequent. There is a need for regularly updated, spatially granular evidence to detect socioeconomic changes between rounds and to optimize operational responses in fragile settings.
AI.method: Fine-tune/adapt a multimodal spatiotemporal vision transformer pretrained on DHS data (~1.2M households across 36 African countries) to forced displacement and host settings (South Sudan, Cameroon, Zambia). Use satellite-derived geospatial covariates to predict socioeconomic indices derived from UNHCR FDS and RMS data. Evaluate performance in camp-intersecting vs non-camp-intersecting grids.
AI.result: Spatial covariates explain up to 66% of variation in camp-intersecting grids (MAE 4.37 index points); 41% in non-camp-intersecting areas (MAE 5.41). The framework supplements periodic surveys by providing regularly updated, model-based socioeconomic estimates, aiding timely humanitarian prioritization and field verification.
AI.conclusion: The adapted model demonstrates meaningful predictive power in displaced settings and can fill data gaps between survey rounds, enhancing spatial-temporal insight for humanitarian action. Performance differences between camp and non-camp areas suggest context-specific calibration and ongoing validation are needed.

title: A Unified Vision-Language Model for PSMA PET/CT Report Generation, Visual Question Answering, and Lesion Segmentation
summary: Accurate PSMA PET/CT interpretation is central to prostate cancer management, yet existing PET/CT AI models typically address isolated tasks. We propose a unified PSMA PET/CT vision-language model for report generation, visual question answering, and lesion segmentation. The framework adopts an LLaVA-style architecture, comprising a PET/CT vision encoder, an MLP-Mixer projection module, a LoRA-tuned large language model, and a 3D segmentation branch. Training followed a four-stage strategy: vision encoder pretraining, projection-layer alignment, VLM fine-tuning, and final multitask tuning. Language tasks used 5,747 PSMA PET/CT datasets with paired reports, while segmentation used the PSMA subset of AutoPET. The model outperformed PET2REP and a CT-based baseline across standard report-generation metrics, improved performance across VQA question types, and achieved higher Dice and lesion-level overlap F1 than SegAnyPET and nnUNet. These results support the feasibility of a unified framework for structured, interactive, interpretable PSMA PET/CT analysis with voxel-level grounding within a single multitask model architecture.

AI.tldr: A unified PSMA PET/CT vision-language model handles report generation, VQA, and lesion segmentation within a single multitask architecture, outperforming task-specific baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome the fragmentation of AI tools in PSMA PET/CT interpretation and deliver an interpretable, voxel-grounded multitask system.
AI.method: A four-component model: (1) PET/CT vision encoder, (2) MLP-Mixer projection module, (3) LoRA-tuned large language model, and (4) a 3D segmentation branch. Training in four stages: vision encoder pretraining, projection-layer alignment, VLM fine-tuning, and final multitask tuning. Datasets: 5,747 PSMA PET/CTs with paired reports for language tasks; PSMA AutoPET subset for segmentation.
AI.result: The model surpasses PET2REP and a CT-based baseline on report generation benchmarks, improves VQA performance across question types, and achieves higher Dice and lesion-level F1 than SegAnyPET and nnUNet on segmentation.
AI.conclusion: A unified multitask framework for PSMA PET/CT analysis with voxel-level grounding is feasible and can unify structured reporting, interactive querying, and precise lesion segmentation within a single model.

title: MoveBench: A Benchmark for Global-Scale Wildlife Movement Forecasting
summary: Understanding and predicting wildlife movement is critical for ecology and conservation. While trajectory forecasting has advanced for human and vehicle movement, wildlife trajectories present distinct challenges: they are unconstrained in space, highly stochastic, and influenced by environmental conditions. We introduce MoveBench, the first large-scale benchmark for probabilistic wildlife movement forecasting, containing 2.6M GPS locations from 800+ individuals across 110 species in 127 countries, paired with 1.6B environmental raster tiles capturing 160 covariates known or hypothesized to influence movement. We propose a probabilistic evaluation protocol for movement trajectory forecasts, addressing limitations of point-prediction metrics for inherently stochastic phenomena. Through comprehensive empirical evaluation of four method families across multiple temporal and spatial scales, we reveal that: (1) existing predictive methods generalize better to future timepoints than to unseen individuals, (2) deep learning approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines, and (3) environmental covariate selection significantly impacts performance. MoveBench enables standardized evaluation of movement forecasting methods and provides a foundation for methodological advances on this ecologically important task.

AI.tldr: MoveBench introduces the first large-scale probabilistic wildlife movement forecasting benchmark, with 2.6M GPS points from 800+ individuals across 110 species in 127 countries and 1.6B environmental tiles (160 covariates). It also defines a probabilistic evaluation protocol for stochastic trajectories and reports that (i) generalization is easier across future timepoints than to new individuals, (ii) deep learning does not consistently beat simple baselines, and (iii) covariate selection crucially affects performance.
AI.motivation: Wildlife movement forecasting is inherently stochastic and environmentally driven, but there is no standardized, probabilistic benchmark to evaluate methods across diverse species, scales, and environments. A large, shared dataset with an evaluation protocol is needed to enable fair comparisons and methodological progress.
AI.method: Construct MoveBench, a large-scale wildlife movement dataset paired with environmental covariates; formulate a probabilistic evaluation protocol for trajectory forecasts; empirically assess four method families across multiple temporal and spatial scales.
AI.result: Empirical study shows limited superiority of deep learning over simple baselines, stronger generalization to future timepoints than to unseen individuals, and substantial impact of environmental covariate selection on predictive performance. MoveBench standardizes evaluation and supports methodological development for ecological forecasting.
AI.conclusion: MoveBench provides a comprehensive, scalable benchmark and probabilistic evaluation framework that enables rigorous comparison and advancement of wildlife movement forecasting methods across diverse species and environments.

title: VideoScout: Learning Agentic Active Exploration with Adaptive Reasoning Pacing for Long Video Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on short video understanding yet remain limited on long videos due to the limited visual context window. Prevailing approaches rely on uniform frame sampling or recent coarse-to-fine agentic zooming, both of which struggle to localize sparse, decisive evidence in sufficiently long videos. We formulate long video understanding as a \textbf{Sequential Evidence Acquisition (SEA)} problem, in which an agent reads the video turn by turn along the temporal axis, deciding at each turn how fast to watch, what evidence to retain, when to revisit uncertain segments, and when to stop and answer. Inspired by this view, we propose \textbf{VideoScout}, a multi-turn reasoning agent that instantiates the SEA paradigm through adaptive reasoning pacing. Specifically, by dynamically controlling the viewing pace, VideoScout enables efficient traversal of long videos within a bounded visual context window, allowing the agent to access more video content while balancing content analysis depth with reading efficiency. To train VideoScout, we construct VideoScout-66K, a set of over 66K high-quality exploration turns from 10K answer-verified trajectories, and adopt a two-stage pipeline: cold-start supervised fine-tuning teaches the agent per-turn output format, while the Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization (DAPO) algorithm performs trajectory-level reinforcement learning with a composite reward that jointly considers answer accuracy, output format compliance, and the temporal alignment between the agent's viewing progress and the teacher's answer timing measured by intersection-over-union (IoU). Extensive experiments on long video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our 7B model achieves strong performance compared with existing trained 7B agentic models.

AI.tldr: A 7B multimodal agent VideoScout enables sequential evidence acquisition for long videos by adaptive pacing, achieving strong performance on long-video tasks with a 66K-turn dataset and a two-stage training pipeline.
AI.motivation: Long videos exceed typical visual context windows; efficient long-sequence reasoning requires adaptive, turn-by-turn evidence collection to locate decisive cues.
AI.method: Propose VideoScout as a multi-turn SEA-based agent with dynamic viewing pace to traverse long videos within a bounded visual window. Train on VideoScout-66K with cold-start supervised fine-tuning for per-turn outputs, followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning using the Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization (DAPO) with a composite reward (answer accuracy, output-format compliance, and IoU-alignment between viewing progress and teacher timing).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on long video understanding show the 7B VideoScout competing well against existing trained 7B agentic models.
AI.conclusion: SEA-inspired adaptive pacing enables efficient long-video understanding within a limited visual context, validated by the proposed dataset and two-stage training framework and leading to strong performance with a 7B model.

title: Sharp Rates and a One-Line Correction for Spectral Representation Learning
summary: A self-supervised encoder is trained once, frozen, and reused through lightweight probes on tasks nobody named at training time; the practitioner's question is when the off-the-shelf features are good enough and when they need fixing. Canonical correlation analysis, HGR maximal correlation, and the population optimum of the spectral contrastive loss all return the top-$k$ singular subspace of a cross-view dependence operator, justified by isotropy: if the task prior has no directional preference, that subspace is universally optimal. We show isotropy is the wrong hypothesis. The prior enters the transfer risk only through the task covariance $Λ=\mathbb{E}[ΔΔ^\top]$, and only through its compression onto the operator's leading singular directions; what matters is not whether $Λ$ is isotropic but whether its preferred directions are ordered consistently with the operator's spectrum. We prove matching two-sided rates---worst-case regret is exactly $1-1/κ(Λ)$, refines to $1-A_k$ for an alignment coefficient $A_k$, localizes to the top-$2k$ subspace, becomes second order under a spectral gap, and is improvable by no task-agnostic representation---and show why alignment is generic: incoherent preferences cancel in high dimension, and $T$ diverse tasks force $α=\widetilde O(\sqrt{d_x/T})$, a quantitative account of why task diversity, not symmetry, makes self-supervised features transfer. The governing statistics cost $O(kd_x^2)$, and when they signal misalignment a one-line reweighting of the positive-pair term provably restores exact optimality. The result is a diagnostic that answers the practitioner's question from a small labelled budget and refuses when the task bank cannot support the width requested; on controlled data it takes a regret of $0.86$ down to $0.003$, and on a CIFAR-100 encoder it correctly predicts that no correction is needed.

AI.tldr: Isotropy is not the right prior for transfer with frozen self-supervised features. The paper characterizes when off-the-shelf features transfer well by examining alignment between the task covariance Λ and the spectrum of the cross-view operator. It provides exact regret bounds, localization to top subspaces, and a task-alignment diagnostic; a simple reweighting recovers optimality. Empirically, it shows small regret reductions on controlled data and that a CIFAR-100 encoder often needs no correction.
AI.motivation: Understand the limits of off-the-shelf self-supervised features and quantify when they suffice without fine-tuning, challenging the common isotropy assumption.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of a cross-view dependence operator, using canonical correlation, maximal correlation, and spectral contrastive loss frameworks. Derives two-sided regret bounds depending on Λ and the operator spectrum, introduces alignment coefficient A_k, proves localization to top-2k, second-order behavior under spectral gaps, and proposes a simple reweighting of the positive-pair term to regain optimality. Provides computational cost O(k d_x^2) and diagnostics based on labeled budget T.
AI.result: Exact worst-case regret is 1 - 1/κ(Λ); refined to 1 - A_k; results localize to the top-2k subspace and are second-order with a spectral gap; alignment is generic in high dimensions; task diversity (number of tasks T) drives α = Õ(√(d_x/T)); diagnostic with one-line reweighting restores optimality. Empirical demonstrations include controlled data with large regret reduction (0.86 to 0.003) and CIFAR-100 encoder predicting no correction needed.
AI.conclusion: Transfer performance of self-supervised encoders is governed by alignment between task covariance and the operator spectrum, not by isotropy. The paper provides a practical diagnostic and a simple corrective step, emphasizing the role of task diversity and alignment over symmetry.

title: ModaLens: Measuring Image Sensitivity in Report-Conditioned Medical VLMs
summary: A radiology report can already answer a clinical question, so it is hard to tell whether a vision-language model also uses the image. ModaLens, a paired image-swap audit, measures how report availability changes image sensitivity: MedGemma-27B on 3,199 paired MIMIC-CXR cases from 293 patients, all 14 questions per case (13 finding-specific and one composite), each image replaced by one from another study, usually of the same patient, with question and report fixed. Under an explicit answer instruction, the model's generated answer changes on 4.26 percent of trials with the report and 20.94 percent without it, a paired increase of 16.7 points (patient-clustered 95 percent CI 15.6 to 17.7), so report availability reduces image-swap sensitivity under this protocol; the original prompt with a lowercase first-token readout gives 4.70 percent against 17.07 percent, and substitutions also move continuous answer scores where the binary prediction does not change. The labels are derived from reports, which limits conclusions about visual correctness; the direction replicates in two further model lineages. Code, the exact prompts and a run record for every number are at https://github.com/criticaldata/MODALENS.

AI.tldr: ModaLens shows that in a paired image-swap audit, radiology-report availability reduces a vision-language model's sensitivity to image swaps when answers are instructed, but not when using a lowercase-first-token readout; results replicated across model lineages, implying reliance on textual cues rather than true image understanding in this setup.
AI.motivation: Disentangle whether vision-language models rely on images or only on accompanying text by measuring how swapping the image (while keeping the report/question fixed) changes model outputs.
AI.method: Modeled via ModaLens: 3,199 paired MIMIC-CXR cases from 293 patients, 14 questions per case (13 findings + 1 composite). Each image swapped with another study's image (often the same patient). Evaluate model answers under explicit instruction vs lowercase prompt. Compare changes in generated answers; compute patient-clustered 95% CIs. Labels derived from reports; code and exact prompts released.
AI.result: With explicit instruction, report availability reduces image-swap sensitivity: changes in 4.26% of trials when report present vs 20.94% without (paired increase of 16.7 points; 95% CI 15.6–17.7). Under lowercase-first-token readout, 4.70% vs 17.07%. Substitutions also alter continuous answer scores even if binary predictions unchanged. Direction replicates in two other model lineages.
AI.conclusion: Findings indicate that report content can drive perceived image-sensitivity in VLM evaluation; high sensitivity may reflect text cue reliance rather than true visual understanding. Labels based on reports limit conclusions about visual accuracy. Public code/prompts enable replication and further exploration across models.

title: Per-Matrix Optimality Is Not Enough: Three-Level Optimization for Low-Rank LLM Compression
comment: 16 pages, to appear at EMNLP 2026 Findings
summary: Per-matrix singular value decomposition (SVD) truncation is Eckart-Young optimal in the whitened Frobenius norm, but errors from independently compressed matrices compound through the block's nonlinear forward pass. Inspired in part by hierarchical variational optimization in quantum many-body methods, we introduce a three-level chain that widens optimization scope from individual matrices to Transformer blocks to the full model: whitened SVD~(L1), block-level joint optimization~(L2), and end-to-end language-modeling loss refinement~(L3), all from 256 calibration sequences, with no instruction or recovery data. On LLaMA-7B at 60% compression, the chain reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 42.1 to 19.1 to 11.4. The block-level stage acts as a regularizer: skipping it worsens Penn Treebank (PTB) perplexity by 24 points, a gap that additional end-to-end training did not close in our experiments. Perplexity gains hold across 20-80% compression, five architectures up to 13B parameters, and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, though the cross-architecture rows use architecture-specific configurations and the ratio sweep was not run under one common protocol. With more calibration data, skipping the block-level stage becomes competitive, revealing an offline compute--data trade-off. We therefore claim improvements only in perplexity and compression fidelity; downstream accuracy remains well below the dense model.

AI.tldr: Three-level hierarchical SVD-based compression for Transformer weights (L1 whitened SVD, L2 block-level joint optimization, L3 end-to-end refinement) yields large perplexity reductions under high compression; block-level optimization acts as a key regularizer; gains generalize across models and data, but downstream accuracy remains well below the dense model.
AI.motivation: Mitigate error compounding from independent matrix truncations in SVD and widen optimization scope from individual matrices to blocks to the full model, inspired by hierarchical variational optimization in quantum many-body methods.
AI.method: L1: whitened SVD truncation; L2: joint block-level optimization across Transformer blocks; L3: end-to-end language-modeling loss refinement using 256 calibration sequences with no instruction or recovery data; tested on LLaMA-7B at 60% compression; explored 20-80% compression, five architectures up to 13B; cross-architecture configs; ratio sweep not under single protocol.
AI.result: WikiText-2 perplexity improved from 42.1 to 19.1 to 11.4 under 60% compression; PTB perplexity worsened by 24 points if block-level stage skipped; gains persist across compression levels and architectures; out-of-distribution and in-distribution improvements observed; more calibration data could change the offline compute–data trade-off; downstream accuracy remains well below the dense model.
AI.conclusion: Three-level optimization yields perplexity and compression fidelity improvements under high compression; block-level stage provides regularization; results are promising but limited by downstream accuracy gap and protocol variability; more data could alter conclusions.

title: SAM3D-Part: Interactive Part Selection and Generation from 3D Objects
summary: Part-level control is essential for modern 3D asset creation, where objects are frequently edited, reused, animated, or fabricated through their individual components. In many such workflows, users need only several specific components rather than a complete object decomposition. However, existing 3D generation methods produce all parts regardless of user intent, while promptable 3D segmentation methods typically output partial surfaces instead of reusable complete meshes. In addition, image-conditioned part generators further struggle to preserve hidden geometry and accurate placement without directly conditioning on the source mesh. To address these problems, we present SAM3D-Part, a prompt-driven framework for selective part generation from input 3D object meshes. Given a source mesh and a part prompt, SAM3D-Part first encodes the source geometry into compact mesh features and aligns them with the rendered image, selective mask, and point-map observations via pixel-wise channel fusion. The fused representation conditions a feed-forward generative model to produce only the queried component as a completed mesh. To place the generated part back into the source coordinate frame, SAM3D-Part predicts dense per-voxel correspondences and estimates the part transformation from distributed spatial evidence rather than a single global pose code. For sequential multi-part queries, previously generated parts are stored in a part cache and reused as contextual constraints, reducing conflicts among independently requested components. Extensive experiments and ablations demonstrate that SAM3D-Part can significantly improve source alignment, reduce conditioning cost, and enable consistent selective part generation, achieving state-of-the-art. Code and weights will be available at https://github.com/Jiahao620/sam3d-part.

AI.tldr: Prompt-driven selective part generation from 3D meshes (SAM3D-Part) that yields complete, reusable parts by cross-modal fusion, per-voxel alignment, and a part cache, claiming state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Address the need for editing/reusing specific components of 3D objects without generating whole-object decompositions; current methods produce either full objects or partial surfaces, hindering reuse and placement accuracy.
AI.method: Encode source geometry into compact mesh features; align with rendered image, selective mask, and point-map via pixel-wise channel fusion; condition a feed-forward generative model to output the queried component as a complete mesh; estimate dense per-voxel correspondences and part transformations from distributed evidence; reuse previously generated parts via a part cache for sequential queries.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablations show improved source alignment, reduced conditioning cost, and consistent selective part generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: SAM3D-Part is a robust, prompt-driven framework enabling selective, reusable part generation from 3D meshes, with open-source code and weights forthcoming.

title: Task-Directed Residual AddUNet:Perfect-Reconstruction Routing for Full-Rate Representations
summary: This paper establishes a perfect-reconstruction (PR) interpretation of AddUNet and its full-rate realization, and introduces a Residual Full-Rate PR architecture for task-directed representation learning. The survivor--skip structure of a constrained additive U-Net is shown to be exactly equivalent to a critically sampled multirate PR filter bank. The full-rate formulation removes the complementary-subband restrictions of the critically sampled system while preserving PR. A Residual Full-Rate PR architecture is then proposed to progressively route task-irrelevant, nuisance, or redundant structure away from the task-facing survivor while retaining the routed information explicitly. Exact reconstruction is guaranteed for arbitrary shape-compatible linear or nonlinear routing operators, without requiring invertibility, a matched synthesis bank, reconstruction loss, or learned decoder. The resulting architecture decouples representation design from reconstruction design: conservation is structural, while learning is devoted to task-directed routing. The same formulation identifies an identity-shortcut ResNet with its residual output retained as a full-rate PR system. Experiments verify exact single-channel routing of linearly separable factors to machine precision. On TIMIT, the proposed front-end improves test PER from $28.60\pm2.09\%$ to $25.76\pm0.41\%$ with the recognizer and training protocol held fixed, while maintaining exact reconstruction. Speaker probing further shows that structural conservation does not itself imply task-specific invariance.

AI.tldr: Proposes a perfect-reconstruction (PR) view of AddUNet and a residual full-rate PR architecture for task-directed routing, rendering survivor-skip AddUNet equivalent to a multirate PR filter bank and enabling exact reconstruction with learnable, non-invertible routing.
AI.motivation: To decouple representation design from reconstruction design by enforcing exact reconstruction under arbitrary routing operators, enabling task-directed routing of nuisance components while preserving information.
AI.method: 1) Show survivor–skip constrained additive U-Net is exactly equivalent to a critically sampled multirate PR filter bank. 2) Extend to a full-rate formulation by removing subband restrictions yet preserving PR. 3) Introduce a Residual Full-Rate PR architecture that progressively routes task-irrelevant structure away from the task-facing survivor, without requiring invertibility or a matched synthesis bank. 4) Demonstrate that exact reconstruction holds for arbitrary linear/nonlinear routing operators and identify an identity-shortcut ResNet as a full-rate PR system.
AI.result: Exact reconstruction is guaranteed for the proposed architectures; experiments verify exact single-channel routing of linearly separable factors to machine precision. On TIMIT, the front-end improves test PER from 28.60±2.09% to 25.76±0.41% with fixed recognizer and training protocol, while maintaining exact reconstruction. Speaker probing indicates that structural conservation does not imply task-specific invariance.
AI.conclusion: The work decouples representation design from reconstruction design: conservation is structural, while learning handles task-directed routing. It also shows that identity shortcuts can be interpreted within a full-rate PR framework. The results suggest PR-based architectures can improve task performance (e.g., speech recognition) without sacrificing exact reconstruction, though invariance properties require separate investigation.

title: Human-Grounded Calibration for Long-Text Image-Text Congruence in Vision-Language Models
summary: Long-text image--text congruence scoring is increasingly important for vision-language systems that must evaluate whether detailed textual descriptions match visual content. However, raw similarity scores from dual-encoder models are difficult to interpret as calibrated congruence measures, especially under the modality gap between image and text embeddings. This paper proposes Congruency Score (CS), a lightweight calibration layer that maps image--text similarity evidence into a bounded score. Using DOCCI and Urban1k, we evaluate four frozen vision-language backbones and show that observed reductions in post-projection centroid distance do not uniformly improve image--text retrieval performance. Human-grounded evaluations on DOCCI further reveal a trade-off: direct post-hoc calibration preserves high association with human judgments, whereas selected projection-based configurations can reduce threshold-relevant slope and intercept distortions at the cost of retrieval performance and association strength. These results establish long-text image--text congruence scoring as a calibrated score-estimation problem, where retrieval performance, human association, and threshold calibration must be evaluated as distinct objectives. CS provides a lightweight way to expose and operationalize this separation.

AI.tldr: Calibrated Congruency Score (CS) maps image-text similarity to bounded scores for long-text congruence.
AI.motivation: Raw dual-encoder similarity lacks interpretability across modality gaps; there is a need for calibrated, threshold-friendly congruence measures aligned with human judgments.
AI.method: Introduce CS as a lightweight calibration layer; evaluate on DOCCI and Urban1k across four frozen vision-language backbones; compare post-projection centroid distance, retrieval performance, and human-grounded judgments; analyze trade-offs between direct calibration and projection-based configurations.
AI.result: CS yields bounded scores; reductions in centroid distance do not consistently improve retrieval; post-hoc calibration preserves human association; some projection-based settings reduce distortions but at the cost of retrieval performance and association strength; threshold calibration is a separate objective from retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Treat long-text image-text congruence scoring as a calibrated score-estimation problem; CS enables a minimal, separable calibration that clarifies thresholding while balancing retrieval and human-consistency.

title: LLM-Based Schema-Aware Split Learning for Privacy-Preserving Mental Distress Prediction Across Heterogeneous Surveys
summary: Rising societal and lifestyle complexity has been linked to a growing prevalence of mental distress worldwide. Educational institutions, workplaces, clinics, etc. collect large volumes of mental health survey data to understand and reduce this burden. Collaborative analysis of such data could yield effective generalizable predictive models. Privacy constraints and varied survey designs (i.e., different questions, scales, and formats) hinder direct integration. We propose a schema-aware split learning (SL) framework that preserves privacy, using a large language model (LLM) as a shared semantic encoder to harmonize heterogeneous survey schemas across institutions. We serialize each survey record into a natural-language description, unifying disparate survey schemas into a common format. The LLM is fine-tuned for mental distress assessment via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and partitioned across client and server. Clients retain the raw survey responses locally and run only a lightweight front-end, so original records never leave the institution that collected them. The resource-intensive backbone runs on the server, minimizing client-side computation. Using LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, the framework attains an average ANLS of 0.708 with only 2,000 training samples, surpasses federated learning (FL) in eight of nine settings, and cuts per-client computation by three orders of magnitude, while generalizing to unseen datasets. Overall, it enables accurate, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative learning from heterogeneous mental health survey data.

AI.tldr: Schema-aware split learning using an LLM as a semantic encoder to harmonize heterogeneous mental health surveys, enabling privacy-preserving, efficient cross-institution learning; achieves strong ANLS with small data and outperforms FL in most settings.
AI.motivation: Address privacy and heterogeneity obstacles in aggregating mental health survey data across institutions; goal is generalizable predictive models with minimal data leakage.
AI.method: Use LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct as a shared semantic encoder; serialize surveys into descriptive natural-language records to align schemas; fine-tune with LoRA; implement split learning with client/server; clients keep raw responses locally and run only a lightweight front-end; server handles the backbone.
AI.result: Average ANLS of 0.708 with 2,000 training samples; surpasses federated learning in 8 of 9 settings; reduces per-client computation by ~1000x; generalizes to unseen datasets.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables accurate, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient collaborative learning from heterogeneous mental health survey data and generalizes to new datasets.

title: MedDiME: Efficient Latent Diffusion with Adaptive Masking for Medical Counterfactual Generation
summary: Medical counterfactual generation modifies images to change model predictions for interpretability. However, existing diffusion-based approaches are often prohibitively slow and memory-intensive, making them difficult to apply in high-resolution settings. Moreover, existing masking strategies are tightly coupled with pixel-space representations, making them incompatible with latent-space diffusion editing. To address these challenges, we propose MedDiME, a latent-space classifier-guided diffusion framework that reduces computational and memory overhead while introducing a latent-compatible, gradient-driven adaptive masking mechanism for spatially precise medical counterfactual generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MedDiME achieves high-quality counterfactual generation with significant efficiency gains compared to prior classifier-guided diffusion baselines, achieving up to 40 times faster inference and 13 times lower peak GPU memory usage.

AI.tldr: MedDiME enables fast, memory-efficient medical counterfactuals by operating in latent space with classifier guidance and a gradient-driven, adaptive mask for precise localization, outperforming prior diffusion baselines in speed and memory use.
AI.motivation: Medical counterfactuals aid model interpretability but diffusion-based methods are too slow and memory-intensive for high-resolution medical images. Existing masking ties to pixel space and clashes with latent-space diffusion editing. A latent-space, gradient-guided approach can improve efficiency and precision.
AI.method: MedDiME leverages latent-space classifier-guided diffusion as the core framework, with a gradient-driven, adaptive masking mechanism that remains compatible with latent-space representations. This reduces computation/memory and enables spatially precise counterfactual edits without pixel-space constraints.
AI.result: Empirical results show substantial efficiency gains over prior baselines: up to 40× faster inference and 13× lower peak GPU memory usage, while delivering high-quality counterfactuals for medical images.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes classifier-guided diffusion practical for high-resolution medical counterfactuals by combining latent-space diffusion with gradient-driven adaptive masking, offering significant speed/memory advantages and enabling precise, interpretable counterfactual generation.

title: Learning Multimodal One-step Flow Policy via Value-weighted Optimal Transport
summary: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn a policy solely from fixed datasets, which often contain multimodal action distributions. Flow policies can naturally represent such multimodal behaviors, but learning an efficient one-step flow policy remains challenging: standard value guidance often leads to mode collapse or exploits overestimation bias in out-of-distribution regions. To address this, we introduce One-step Flow policy via Optimal Transport (OptiFlow), a framework for one-step flow policy learning as a structured sample-allocation problem. OptiFlow jointly trains a value-aware reference flow policy and an efficient one-step policy, coupling their action samples through state-wise entropic optimal transport. For each state, critic-estimated values define the priority of distillation target actions, while the action-distance cost ensures geometrically compatible pairings. By avoiding direct critic maximization, our transport-guided approach enables in-distribution exploitation by anchoring the one-step policy to high-value, dataset-supported modes without the risk of out-of-distribution divergence. Experimental results demonstrate that OptiFlow effectively captures optimal multimodal behaviors and achieves strong performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yonsei-DILLab/OptiFlow.

AI.tldr: OptiFlow learns a one-step, multimodal policy for offline RL by casting policy learning as a state-wise entropic optimal transport between a value-aware reference flow and a one-step policy, aligning high-value in-distribution modes while avoiding distributional collapse.
AI.motivation: Offline RL with multimodal action distributions often suffers from mode collapse and overestimation in OOD regions when learning a single-step flow policy. A principled mechanism is needed to exploit multiple high-value modes without diverging from the dataset.
AI.method: Propose OptiFlow: jointly train a value-aware reference flow policy and an efficient one-step policy. For each state, couple their action samples via state-wise entropic optimal transport. Use critic-estimated values to prioritize distillation targets and an action-distance cost to ensure geometric compatibility. This transport-guided approach anchors the one-step policy to high-value, dataset-supported modes without directly maximizing the critic.
AI.result: Empirically, OptiFlow captures optimal multimodal behaviors and achieves strong performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks. Code is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: A transport-guided, one-step flow policy effectively handles multimodal offline RL tasks by aligning sampled actions to high-value, in-distribution modes, mitigating mode collapse and OOD issues while preserving multimodality.

title: From Model Patterns to Abstract Semantics in Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
summary: Compositional Zero Shot Learning aims to recognize unseen compositions by recombining learned primitives. Recent methods rely on vision language models and attempt to explicitly model contextual variations of primitives through multiple representations. However, such approaches are limited by fixed variant capacity and competition between abstract and concrete semantics. In this work, we present a new perspective that views primitive variations as the context-driven activation of concrete visual cues rather than independent entities.
