Based on it, we propose CLEAR, a CLoze-style rEAsoning-based Re-ranking framework inspired by human perceptual processes. CLEAR extracts conditional variants from the primitive candidate set in a coarse-to-fine manner, performs cloze-style reasoning to infer high-level semantics, and re-ranks predictions to correct biases toward salient concrete primitives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLEAR consistently improves the Base Model and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the challenging C-GQA and MIT-States datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/buptLwz/CLEAR.

AI.tldr: CLEAR is a cloze-style re-ranking framework for compositional zero-shot learning that treats primitive variations as context-driven visual cues and re-ranks predictions to correct biases, achieving SOTA on C-GQA and MIT-States.
AI.motivation: Existing CZSL methods rely on multiple primitive representations and fixed variant capacity, leading to competition between abstract and concrete semantics and limited ability to capture context-driven variations.
AI.method: CLEAR uses coarse-to-fine extraction of conditional variants from primitive candidates, applies cloze-style reasoning to infer high-level semantics, and re-ranks predictions to align with context-driven cues.
AI.result: CLEAR consistently improves base models and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on C-GQA and MIT-States datasets; code is released.
AI.conclusion: A context-driven activation view of primitive variations paired with cloze-style reasoning improves CZSL performance and mitigates biases toward salient concrete primitives.

title: Privacy-enhanced federated learning via asynchronous aggregation and local differential perturbation
comment: Published in Proc. SPIE 14128, Third International Conference on Big Data, Computational Intelligence, and Applications (BDCIA 2025), 141283L. Event: BDCIA 2025, Huanggang, China. https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3106592
summary: This study proposes a privacy-enhanced federated learning framework to address secure collaborative training in distributed data environments. The framework integrates Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP), lightweight Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Local Differential Privacy (LDP) mechanisms to ensure data privacy protection during model training. Additionally, the framework employs an asynchronous aggregation strategy with version control to support distributed training in asynchronous environments. Experimental validation on the CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100 benchmark datasets demonstrates that the method maintains high classification accuracy (up to 82.6%) even under stringent privacy constraints (ε = 0.1), while reducing communication overhead by 21.3% compared to FedAvg. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework effectively balances privacy protection and model performance in distributed machine learning scenarios, providing a scalable technical foundation for large-scale distributed collaborative computing.

AI.tldr: A privacy-enhanced federated learning framework combining Dynamic Differential Privacy, lightweight Homomorphic Encryption, and Local Differential Privacy with asynchronous aggregation and version control; achieves strong privacy with competitive accuracy and reduced communication cost; validated on CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100.
AI.motivation: To enable secure, privacy-preserving collaborative training in distributed data environments while maintaining model performance and reducing communication overhead in asynchronous FL.
AI.method: Integrates Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP), lightweight Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Local Differential Privacy (LDP); employs asynchronous aggregation with version control; evaluates on CIFAR-10 and Purchase-100; compares against FedAvg.
AI.result: Maintains high classification accuracy up to 82.6% under a strict privacy budget (ε = 0.1) and reduces communication overhead by 21.3% compared to FedAvg.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable, privacy-aware framework for large-scale distributed learning that balances privacy protection and model performance while reducing communication requirements.

title: Circuit-MLLM: Topological Logic-Guided Latent-Space Visual Reasoning for Circuit Schematic Understanding
comment: Accepted at European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: Through pre-training on extensive text and image datasets, current multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on general tasks. However, circuit schematics present a unique challenge for MLLMs due to their dense component layouts and distinct topological logic, demanding fine-grained structural parsing to extract the electrical semantics. To address this, we propose Circuit-MLLM, a multimodal reasoning framework that reformulates circuit topology analysis as a process of device localization, path tracing, and sequential reasoning within the latent space. We introduce a circuit knowledge mining mechanism that deeply aligns the model's latent representations with structurally rich features derived from multi-granularity circuit vision experts, enabling the model to effectively internalize topological semantics. Building upon these internalized semantics, we devise a topology-guided sequencing strategy that decouples reasoning from the rigid raster-scan order, enforcing stepwise inference along the circuit's topological logic in latent space. Across diverse circuit analysis tasks, Circuit-MLLM consistently outperforms strong baselines, notably achieving a 25% higher average score than GPT-5.1, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our framework in circuit schematic topology analysis. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/IC-Yuan/Circuit-MLLM.

AI.tldr: Circuit-MLLM introduces a multimodal reasoning framework for circuit schematic topology analysis by device localization, path tracing, and sequential reasoning in latent space; uses circuit knowledge mining to align latent representations with circuit vision features; employs topology-guided sequencing; reports 25% higher average score than GPT-5.1; code released.
AI.motivation: Circuit schematics present dense component layouts and unique topologies that generic MLLMs struggle to parse; there is a need to internalize topological semantics and decouple reasoning from raster-scan order to improve circuit analysis tasks.
AI.method: Propose Circuit-MLLM that reformulates topology analysis as device localization, path tracing, and sequential reasoning in latent space. Introduce a circuit knowledge mining mechanism to align latent representations with features from multi-granularity circuit vision experts. Develop a topology-guided sequencing strategy that decouples reasoning from raster order and enforces stepwise inference along the circuit topology.
AI.result: Across diverse circuit analysis tasks, Circuit-MLLM outperforms baselines, notably achieving a 25% higher average score than GPT-5.1.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that aligning latent representations with structurally rich, domain-specific semantics enables effective circuit topology analysis, and provides a publicly available codebase for reproduction.

title: Discrete Beckmann Transport Models for One-Step Language Modeling and Reasoning
summary: Discrete diffusion and flow models are a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, but compressing many-step sampling into fewer steps typically requires distilling a pretrained teacher model. This caps the student at the teacher's quality and requires a costly two-stage training pipeline. We introduce Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM), built on a time-independent flow whose autonomous transport map provably carries any point in the ambient space to a fixed point on the vertices of the simplex in a single step. We show that this fixed-point property is characterized by a conservation equation whose residual can be minimized directly from data, removing the requirement for a teacher flow and time conditioning. Under this construction, a partially trained map corresponds to the flow truncated at finite time, so generation reduces to iterating one map until it reaches a fixed point. We further extend the map to a partial-context interpolant where additional function evaluations act as refinement steps rather than ODE integration steps. On language modeling and reasoning tasks, DBTM enables one- and few-step generation that improves quality and accuracy over discrete diffusion and continuous flow baselines.

AI.tldr: DBTM provides a single-map, time-independent transport model for discrete diffusion in language tasks, eliminating teacher-distillation and enabling one- to few-step generation with improved quality.
AI.motivation: Discreet diffusion/flow methods normally rely on distilling a pretrained teacher and time-conditioned steps, which limits quality and requires costly two-stage training.
AI.method: Introduce Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM) with a time-independent autonomous transport map that drives any point to a simplex vertex in one step. The fixed-point property is enforced via a conservation equation whose residual is minimized directly from data, removing the need for a teacher or time conditioning. A partially trained map corresponds to finite-time flow, so generation proceeds by iterating a single map to a fixed point. The map is extended to a partial-context interpolant where extra evaluations act as refinements rather than ODE steps.
AI.result: Empirically, DBTM achieves one- and few-step generation on language modeling and reasoning tasks, delivering higher quality/accuracy than both discrete diffusion and continuous flow baselines.
AI.conclusion: DBTM offers a teacher-free, efficient generation paradigm by leveraging a fixed-point transport map; it eliminates two-stage training, supports refinement via partial-context inputs, and improves performance in low-step generation scenarios.

title: Benchmarking Intra-Patient 3D Deformable Multimodal Image Registration
summary: Multimodal image registration is a key component of many clinical workflows, yet it remains challenging because corresponding anatomical structures often exhibit substantially different image intensities across modalities. In this work, we present a comprehensive benchmark of intra-patient 3D multimodal deformable registration methods across three datasets covering different anatomical regions and difficulty levels, including both synthetic deformation recovery and real clinical scenarios. We evaluate classical optimization-based approaches and modern learning-based methods, including recent deep learning and foundation models, using complementary metrics: Average Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), average 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and a modality-independent structural similarity measure based on the MIND self-similarity context (MIND-SSC). Results show high variability across datasets, with learning-based methods demonstrating superior performance on large synthetic benchmarks, while only limited improvements are observed in real pelvic registration. A key finding of this study is the consistent disagreement between geometric metrics (DSC, HD95) and image-based similarity metrics (MIND-SSC), highlighting that improved overlap does not necessarily imply better global multimodal correspondence. Furthermore, anatomy-guided approaches achieve the highest overlap scores but exhibit degraded performance outside of segmented regions, revealing a trade-off between label-driven alignment and global structural coherence. Overall, our results indicate that no current method achieves robust performance across anatomies and modalities. We demonstrate that intra-patient 3D multimodal registration requires multi-criteria evaluation, including deformation-based metrics, and remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive benchmark of intra-patient 3D multimodal deformable registration across three datasets, showing dataset-dependent performance; learning methods excel on synthetic data but not consistently on real data; metrics discordance between geometric (DSC/HD95) and image-based (MIND-SSC); anatomy-guided methods improve overlap but underperform globally; no method robust across anatomies/modalities; multi-criteria evaluation needed.
AI.motivation: Cross-modality image registration is difficult due to large inter-modal intensity differences; robust evaluation and benchmarking are needed to guide method development and clinical adoption.
AI.method: Evaluate classical optimization-based and learning-based registration methods, including deep learning and foundation models, on three intra-patient 3D multimodal datasets with both synthetic deformation recovery and real clinical scenarios; use DSC, HD95, and MIND-SSC as complementary metrics.
AI.result: Performance varies by dataset; learning methods beat traditional approaches on large synthetic benchmarks but offer limited gains in real pelvic registration; strong disagreement between DSC/HD95 and MIND-SSC; anatomy-guided methods yield high overlap but degrade outside segmented regions; no method achieves robust performance across anatomies/modality pairs.
AI.conclusion: Intra-patient 3D multimodal registration remains an open problem requiring multi-criteria evaluation; progress is dataset-dependent and generalizable methods are not yet established.

title: Safe Meta-Reinforcement Learning via Information Space Reachability
summary: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to adapt to unseen tasks with limited experience. Despite its promise, the application of meta-RL in real-world tasks is hindered by safety requirements, which have been underexplored in prior work. In this paper, we propose a safe meta-RL framework that explicitly accounts for safety during adaptation. Our key insight is to reason about safety in the information space, which captures both the physical state and the agent's belief over the underlying task. Within this space, we introduce a safety value function that measures the probability of the agent avoiding unsafe regions indefinitely. We show that this function satisfies a self-consistency condition and a Bellman equation, which make it learnable via meta-RL. Based on this formulation, we develop a safe meta-RL algorithm that learns the safety value function and leverages it for safety filtering and constrained policy optimization. Experiments on meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A safety-aware meta-RL framework that learns a safety value function in the information space to enable safety filtering and constrained policy optimization during adaptation.
AI.motivation: Meta-RL lacks safety considerations for real-world deployment; safety must be managed during adaptation as agents explore unseen tasks.
AI.method: Define a safety value function over the information space (state + belief over task) and show it satisfies a self-consistency condition and a Bellman equation; develop a safe meta-RL algorithm that learns this function and uses it for safety filtering and constrained policy optimization.
AI.result: Empirical results on meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method improves safety during adaptation while maintaining performance.
AI.conclusion: Safety-aware meta-RL is feasible by learning a safety value function in the information space, enabling filtering and constrained optimization during adaptation.

title: Don't Send What You Don't Need: Question-Guided Token Pruning as a Privacy Defense for Vision-Language Models
summary: Visual Question Answering (VQA) with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is increasingly used in privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained settings. Federated Learning (FL), Split Learning (SL), and U-Shaped Split Learning (USL) keep raw data local, but transmitting all visual tokens across a model partition remains costly and can expose private information. We propose QPriv-VL, a question-guided, privacy-aware token-pruning framework for FL, SL, and USL that prunes visual tokens before transmission based on task utility and privacy sensitivity. Its core component is a lightweight Dynamic Threshold Predictor (DTP) that jointly estimates a sample-specific pruning ratio and a token-level retention mask in one forward pass. DTP combines question relevance, computed from cross-modal similarity between visual patches and the pooled question embedding, with a sensitivity signal derived from frozen DINOv2 features. This allows the model to suppress potentially sensitive regions while preserving patches useful for answering the question, without requiring sensitivity labels. We evaluate QPriv-VL on GQA, OK-VQA, VQAv2, SLAKE, VQA-RAD, and PathVQA against four privacy attack families: FSHA, FORA, iDLG, and attribute-inference membership inference attacks. DTP matches or outperforms fixed-ratio pruning while using substantially fewer transmitted tokens. On VQA-RAD, it reduces membership-inference attack success from 0.99 to 0.76-0.79, lowers FSHA and FORA reconstruction PSNR relative to fixed-ratio pruning, and preserves competitive VQA accuracy using about 40% of the original visual-token budget. A sensitivity exclusion ratio of 1.20 +/- 0.18 indicates preferential removal of privacy-sensitive patches, while explainability analysis shows that retention adapts to question semantics rather than generic visual saliency.

AI.tldr: QPriv-VL introduces a dynamic, question-guided token-pruning framework for privacy-preserving VQA in FL/SL/USL. It uses a Dynamic Threshold Predictor (DTP) to jointly estimate pruning ratio and retention mask in one forward pass, leveraging question–patch relevance and a DINOv2-based sensitivity signal. It reduces privacy-attacker success and token transmission while preserving accuracy, without sensitivity labels.
AI.motivation: Reduce privacy leakage and bandwidth costs in privacy-sensitive, bandwidth-constrained VQA settings by pruning visual tokens before transmission, without requiring sensitive-label data.
AI.method: DTP combines cross-modal similarity between visual patches and pooled question embedding with a frozen DINOv2-derived sensitivity signal to predict a per-sample pruning ratio and a token-level retention mask in a single forward pass, enabling selective token pruning without sensitivity labels. Applied to FL, SL, and USL.
AI.result: DTP matches or exceeds fixed-ratio pruning while using far fewer transmitted tokens. On VQA-RAD, membership-inference attack success drops from 0.99 to 0.76–0.79; FSHA/FORA reconstructions improve (PSNR) relative to fixed pruning; preserves competitive VQA accuracy with ~40% of the original token budget. Sensitivity exclusion ratio = 1.20 ± 0.18, indicating preferential removal of privacy-sensitive patches. Explainability shows retention tracks question semantics rather than generic saliency.
AI.conclusion: DTP enables efficient privacy-aware token pruning for VQA across FL/SL/USL; improves privacy protection against multiple attack families while maintaining task performance, with low extra computation and without requiring sensitivity annotations.

title: Privacy-Aligned Personalized Federated Learning with Compact Adaptation and Variable-Length Gaussian Communication
summary: Record-level differential privacy exposes a structural misalignment in personalized federated learning when client-specific variation is low-dimensional while training repeatedly releases high-dimensional updates. In this paper, we address this misalignment by releasing a private client context once and confining repeated adaptation to a fixed coefficient space. Beyond dimensionality reduction, the factorized generator induces an adaptive optimization geometry that reshapes noisy updates, and controlled ablations show that most of its private-training gain is retained by radial evolution. To further reduce the communication cost, we realize the Gaussian mechanism for coefficient updates directly through variable-length quantization with finite expected code length, so that the quantization error itself serves as the required privacy perturbation rather than extra distortion. Across MNIST and CIFAR-10, our design matches or outperforms full-model private adaptation across privacy budgets and client heterogeneity, while reducing protected uplink by a factor of 2.67 at \(\varepsilon=16\) on CIFAR-10 with comparable future-client accuracy.

AI.tldr: A privacy-preserving personalized federated learning approach uses a private, fixed low-dimensional coefficient space and a factorized generator to adapt updates, achieving better communication efficiency and robustness to heterogeneity while preserving privacy through quantization-based Gaussian perturbations.
AI.motivation: To resolve a misalignment in record-level differential privacy: high-dimensional updates are released repeatedly while client-specific variation is low-dimensional, leading to inefficient privacy-utility trade-offs and high communication costs.
AI.method: Release a private client context once and constrain subsequent adaptation to a fixed coefficient space via a factorized generator. This generates updates with an adaptive optimization geometry (radial evolution). Employ variable-length quantization to implement Gaussian mechanism on coefficient updates, making quantization error the privacy perturbation. Evaluate on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with privacy budgets and heterogeneity settings.
AI.result: Matches or surpasses full-model private adaptation under similar privacy budgets and client heterogeneity. Achieves substantially lower uplink communication (2.67× reduction at ε=16 on CIFAR-10) while maintaining comparable future-client accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Dimensionality reduction coupled with a geometrically adaptive update mechanism and quantization-based privacy can effectively align privacy with learning dynamics in personalized FL, reducing communication and maintaining accuracy across standard benchmarks.

title: MambaMPD: A Mamba-Driven Segmentation Framework for Marine Pollution Detection from Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Accurate marine pollution detection (MPD) is essential for protecting coastal ecosystems and marine biodiversity. Vision Mamba models have shown promise in remote-sensing semantic segmentation by efficiently capturing long-range dependencies and global context, yet their potential for MPD remains underexplored. MPD is particularly challenging because of low signal-to-noise ratios, fragmented pollution patterns, and indistinct boundaries caused by the visual similarity between pollutants and the surrounding sea. To address these issues, we propose MambaMPD, an enhanced Mamba-based framework incorporating two complementary structural priors: Frequency-Aware Augmentation (FAA) and multi-scale Edge-Guided Attention (EGA). FAA integrates wavelet transforms into the encoder to decompose features into multi-scale frequency subbands, enabling the model to capture low-frequency contextual semantics and high-frequency structural details needed to identify small, low-contrast, and irregular pollution patterns. EGA adaptively fuses hierarchical, Laplacian-derived boundary cues with deep semantic representations, refining encoder features before decoding to sharpen boundaries and reduce ambiguity in visually confusing, spatially fragmented scenes. Together, these modules improve sensitivity to subtle pollution signals while preserving fine boundary structures. A U-Net-style decoder with squeeze-and-excitation attention and deep supervision progressively restores and refines semantic and spatial information across scales. Extensive experiments on two benchmark MPD datasets show that MambaMPD achieves higher mIoU than competing methods while requiring substantially less computation than foundation-model-based approaches. On MADOS, it improves F1 by 3.6% over OSDMamba; on M4D, it raises Oil Spill IoU by 6.82% over TransOilSeg.

AI.tldr: A Mamba-based marine-pollution detector (MambaMPD) with Frequency-Aware Augmentation and Edge-Guided Attention, achieving higher mIoU with lower compute than baselines.
AI.motivation: Marine Pollution Detection via remote sensing is hampered by low SNR, fragmented patterns, and boundary ambiguity; need efficient, accurate models that capture global context.
AI.method: FAA uses wavelet transforms in the encoder to decompose features into multi-scale frequency subbands; EGA fuses Laplacian-derived boundary cues with semantic features to sharpen boundaries; decoder is U-Net-style with squeeze-and-excitation and deep supervision.
AI.result: On MADOS: F1 +3.6% versus OSDMamba; On M4D: Oil Spill IoU +6.82% versus TransOilSeg; higher mIoU than competing methods; lower computation than foundation-model-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Combining frequency-aware and edge-guided priors yields improved MPD performance while preserving fine boundaries, and offers a resource-efficient alternative to large foundation models.

title: A Chosen Future Can Still Be Rewritten: Causal Writability in Video Models
summary: When a video model generates physically incorrect motion, did it fail to learn the correct motion, or did it learn it but fail to use it? We show the latter: the correct motion remains available inside the model and can still be made to control the generated video. We train on videos where red masses oscillate slowly and blue masses oscillate quickly, then test a red mass with fast observed motion. Even when the model generates slow motion in this conflicting case, a low-dimensional edit predicted from simple physical variables restores the correct fast motion. We call this ability causal writability. At fixed strength, we find a sharp depth boundary: the same edit changes the video before the boundary but not after it. This closure marks commitment for that write. The motion signal nevertheless remains, and a stronger downstream write can restore physical motion, while excessive gain overshoots. Early causal writability predicts which errors training later corrects: those errors are writable at more network depths than errors that persist. We reproduce both causal writability and its sharp closure in a pretrained 1.3B video model, supporting generality across model scale and training regime.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a latent physical representation in video models: even when outputs are physically wrong, the correct motion is still encoded and can be elicited via simple, low-dimensional edits—demonstrated as causal writability with a sharp depth boundary and generalization across scales.
AI.motivation: Understand whether motion errors come from failed learning or improper use of learned motion; investigate if physical dynamics are encoded internally and can be controlled post-training.
AI.method: Train on datasets where red masses oscillate slowly and blue masses oscillate quickly; test with a red mass exhibiting fast motion; apply low-dimensional edits derived from simple physical variables to steer generated videos; analyze the effect of edit strength across network depths to identify sharp commitment boundaries; test predictive power of early writability; reproduce findings on a large pretrained 1.3B video model.
AI.result: The model retains the correct motion inside its representations, and a simple physical-variable–based edit can restore the intended fast motion even when the output is slow; a fixed-strength edit shows a sharp depth boundary where it changes the output before the boundary but not after (commitment). The motion signal remains accessible, and stronger edits can fully restore motion; excessive gain can overshoot. Early causal writability predicts which errors future training can fix; results generalize to a larger pretrained model across scales and training regimes.
AI.conclusion: Motion errors do not erase internal physical representations; models exhibit causal writability, where small, physics-informed edits unlock correct dynamics. The sharp boundary indicates a commitment point for writes, and the phenomenon generalizes across models, offering avenues for interpretability and controllability of video generation.

title: V-ICAL Bench: Evaluating Video In-Context Learning for Multimodal Agents in Interactive Environments
summary: While In-Context Learning (ICL) enables models to adapt from exemplars without parameter updates, multimodal ICL remains largely underexplored, particularly regarding video demonstrations in interactive environments. For multimodal agents, learning from videos presents unique challenges: they must translate in-context demonstrations into executable policies, ground these policies in novel visual states, and iteratively refine actions based on environmental feedback. We introduce V-ICAL, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate video-based ICL for multimodal agents. Comprising 342 interactive tasks across 37 environments, V-ICAL utilizes human-curated demonstration videos as task-specific behavioral exemplars, evaluating agents through sustained interaction from a target initialization. The benchmark seamlessly connects in-context knowledge induction with core agentic capabilities, including state grounding, temporal memory, planning, and adaptation in dynamic environments. Extensive evaluations across 19 state-of-the-art multimodal agents reveal significant limitations: the best-performing model, Seed-2.1-Pro, achieves a score of only 54.4/100, while other leading models (e.g., Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.6) fail to surpass 50, far below the human baseline of 83.6. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that current agents struggle to reliably translate video exemplars into effective policies, failing to yield consistent performance gains. Ultimately, V-ICAL exposes a critical gap in the ICL capabilities of multimodal agents, underscoring an urgent need for future research.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark (V-ICAL) evaluates video-based in-context learning for multimodal agents in interactive environments; results show a large gap to human performance and limited benefit from video exemplars, underscoring the need for new methods.
AI.motivation: Addresses the underexplored area of multimodal ICL using video demonstrations in interactive settings. It aims to assess agents’ ability to translate video exemplars into executable policies, ground them to visual states, and adapt under feedback, thereby revealing gaps in state grounding, memory, planning, and adaptivity.
AI.method: V-ICAL comprises 342 interactive tasks across 37 environments. Demonstration videos curated by humans serve as task-specific exemplars. Agents are evaluated through sustained interaction from a target initialization, linking in-context knowledge induction with core agentic capabilities.
AI.result: Evaluations across 19 state-of-the-art multimodal agents show the best model (Seed-2.1-Pro) at 54.4/100; other top models (Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.6) fail to surpass 50. The human baseline is 83.6. Controlled comparisons indicate current agents struggle to translate video exemplars into effective policies and fail to gain consistent performance benefits.
AI.conclusion: V-ICAL reveals a critical gap in video-based ICL for multimodal agents and highlights an urgent need for methodological advances that enable reliable translation of video exemplars into dynamic policy execution in interactive environments.

title: The Router Within: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM
summary: Skills extend an LLM agent beyond its parametric knowledge, and the gain they promise rests on picking the right one. Deployed harnesses route by preloading every skill's metadata into the context, which disperses the agent's attention and caps the library size. Retrieval pipelines move the selection out of the context, but also out of the agent's capability. We show that the frozen agent LLM already carries the routing signal in its own forward passes, and that two linear maps suffice to read it out with no skill text in the context. Gavel (Glance And Verdict from a frozen LLM) reads it in two steps. A glance projects the task's and each skill's mid-layer states through the two maps, the only parameters trained, and scores the full library against compact per-skill banks that one forward pass builds at installation. A verdict then resumes the shortlisted skills' forward passes and reads the model's own likelihood and yes/no judgment, fused with the glance as a product of experts. Trained once, Gavel transfers zero-shot to three public benchmarks and SkillTraj, our new benchmark of 372 simulated agent trajectories. On Qwen3-32B it outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add 1.2B to 16B external parameters, by up to 13.4 points on written tasks and up to 21.9 when the need for a skill arises mid-rollout. Routing accuracy improves as the backbone does, and in a bash-agent harness the same 32B triggers the correct skill on Skill-Use more often than far larger frontier models running in Codex.

AI.tldr: Gavel shows that a frozen LLM already encodes routing signals for skills; using two lightweight linear mappings to read mid-layer state allows zero-shot skill routing without skill text in context, outperforming heavy retrieval and progressive-disclosure baselines with small parameters.
AI.motivation: Reduce context bloat and external parameter overhead in skill routing by leveraging intrinsic signals in the LLM's forward passes, enabling zero-shot generalization across tasks.
AI.method: Gavel trains two linear probes that project the task and skill mid-layer states through two maps to score a compact per-skill bank built at installation. A glance ranks candidates; a verdict resumes shortlisted skills and fuses likelihood-based judgments with the glance via a product of experts. All training is done once; no skill text is needed in the context.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B, Gavel outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rank pipelines that augment the model with 1.2B–16B external params, achieving up to 13.4-point gains on written tasks and up to 21.9-point gains when skill use is needed mid-rollout. Routing accuracy improves with stronger backbones; in a bash-agent setup, a 32B model triggers Skill-Use as reliably as much larger models in Codex.
AI.conclusion: Routing signals are embedded in LLM forward passes; two simple linear transforms suffice to read them, enabling effective zero-shot skill routing with minimal extra parameters and offering a competitive alternative to heavy retrieval/disclosure pipelines.

title: SURE-Map: Self-Correcting Streaming Geometric Foundation Model
summary: Streaming geometric foundation models are emerging as a compelling alternative to SLAM systems. Yet this streaming nature introduces a fundamental issue: each prediction is made from limited context, which is vulnerable to dynamic objects and weak textures. Small local errors accumulate into severe geometric distortion and long-horizon scale drift. We argue that reliable streaming reconstruction requires geometric foundation models to be not only predictive, but also self-correcting. We introduce SURE-Map, a self-correcting framework built upon two complementary principles. First, we explicitly model cross-view geometric uncertainty. Unlike conventional depth or point confidence, which primarily reflects the reliability of individual-view prediction, our uncertainty directly measures whether the jointly predicted pose and depth induce geometrically consistent cross-view pixel correspondences. Second, because local correction alone cannot eliminate slowly accumulating scale errors, we introduce multi-timescale self-correction: fast consecutive-frame inference preserves streaming efficiency, while sparse keyframe-window inference provides longer-range geometric evidence to periodically recalibrate the scale of recent trajectories. SURE-Map establishes new state-of-the-art performance for online feed-forward reconstruction across long-horizon benchmarks, reducing ATE-RMSE from 24.00 to 17.24 m on KITTI, 5.11 to 4.74 m on Oxford Spires, and 31.37 to 28.58 m on VBR, with further improvements to 15.17, 4.63, and 22.12 m when incorporating loop-closure refinement. Project page: https://mingkai-liu.github.io/projects/sure-map/.

AI.tldr: SURE-Map introduces a self-correcting streaming geometry framework that models cross-view uncertainty and uses multi-timescale correction to reduce long-horizon drift, achieving state-of-the-art online reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Streaming geometric foundation models operate with limited context, making them vulnerable to dynamic objects, weak textures, and cumulative drift. A self-correcting mechanism is needed to maintain long-horizon geometric consistency.
AI.method: Two principles: (1) explicit modeling of cross-view geometric uncertainty that assesses whether joint pose+depth predictions yield geometrically consistent cross-view correspondences; (2) multi-timescale self-correction combining fast per-frame inference with sparse keyframe-window recalibration to periodically recalibrate scale over longer horizons. Loop-closure refinement can further improve results.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art online feed-forward reconstruction on long-horizon benchmarks: ATE-RMSE reduced from 24.00 to 17.24 m on KITTI, 5.11 to 4.74 m on Oxford Spires, and 31.37 to 28.58 m on VBR; with loop-closure refinement further improving to 15.17, 4.63, and 22.12 m respectively.
AI.conclusion: SURE-Map demonstrates that coupling cross-view geometric uncertainty with multi-timescale self-correction yields substantial gains in streaming reconstruction accuracy, achieving new state-of-the-art results and highlighting the value of long-range geometric calibration in streaming settings.

title: Bellman Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). We introduce Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free method derived from Policy Mirror Descent (PMD). For autoregressive generation with terminal rewards, BPO uses the Bellman equations to reformulate PMD as a trajectory-level objective. The reformulation avoids estimating state values at intermediate states. We prove that it has the same unique optimal solution as the original PMD objective. We derive the practical BPO loss by approximating this objective. Its mismatch-correction weight is a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BPO.

AI.tldr: BPO is a critic-free reinforcement learning objective for autoregressive LLM generation with terminal rewards, equivalent in optimal solution to Policy Mirror Descent when using the Bellman reformulation, and demonstrated to enhance mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve LLM reasoning under verifiable rewards while avoiding the complexity of estimating intermediate state values, addressing limitations of traditional value-based RL in language generation.
AI.method: Derive Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO) from Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) for a trajectory-level objective in autoregressive generation with terminal rewards. Reformulate PMD using Bellman equations to avoid intermediate state value estimates; derive a practical, differentiable BPO loss with a mismatch-correction weight implemented as a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities.
AI.result: Theoretical equivalence: BPO shares the same unique optimal solution as the original PMD objective. Empirical validation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks shows improved performance, demonstrating effectiveness of the method.
AI.conclusion: BPO provides a practical, critic-free trajectory-level reinforcement learning objective that retains PMD’s optimal solution, enabling better reasoning in LLMs under verifiable rewards without intermediate-state value estimation.

title: VC-Attention: Value Smoothing and Softmax Casting for Low-bit Attention
summary: Diffusion Transformers deliver state-of-the-art video generation, but their long spatiotemporal sequences make attention the dominant deployment cost, and a deployable low-bit kernel must be accurate and fast. Accuracy is limited by outliers: a block's quantization scale is set by its largest entries, leaving typical entries confined to a narrow range of representable values. Prior work smooths queries and keys, but value outliers follow no fixed channel or spatiotemporal structure and remain the dominant source of output error. Speed is limited by softmax: low-bit Tensor Cores accelerate only the two matrix multiplications, so the high-precision exponential between them becomes the longest pipeline stage on datacenter GPUs. We propose VC-Attention, a training-free low-bit attention framework that addresses both by pairing Value smoothing with a fused probability Cast. V-Smooth reorders value tokens by lightweight online clustering, so the tokens in a hardware block quantize well together. It quantizes only the residual after subtracting the block mean, and restores that mean from the row sum the online softmax already maintains. ExpCast-FP8 maps log-domain scores directly to E4M3 probability codes with one fused multiply-add, eliminating the FP32 exponential and the format conversion. We implement VC-Attention for B200, B300, H200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090. Across Wan2.2, LongCat-Video, HunyuanVideo-1.5, and MiniMax-H3, VC-Attention improves fidelity over low-bit baselines, speeds up the attention kernel over BF16 FlashAttention-4 by 1.46-1.59x on datacenter Blackwell and Hopper and by 2.3-3.6x on workstation cards, and generates a clip 1.13-1.19x and 1.36-1.70x faster end to end.

AI.tldr: VC-Attention introduces training-free low-bit attention for diffusion transformers by combining value smoothing with a fused probability casting, yielding fidelity gains and substantial speedups over low-bit baselines.
AI.motivation: Reduce attention bottlenecks in long spatiotemporal diffusion models by addressing value outliers and softmax costs to enable deployable low-bit kernels without retraining.
AI.method: Two-part approach: (1) V-Smooth online clustering to reorder value tokens and quantize the residuals after removing the block mean; (2) ExpCast-FP8 maps log-domain scores to E4M3 probability codes via a fused multiply-add, avoiding FP32 exp and format conversions; training-free and hardware-aware implementation across multiple GPUs.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved fidelity over low-bit baselines; achieves 1.46–1.59× speedup of the attention kernel on datacenter Blackwell/Hopper and 2.3–3.6× on workstation cards versus BF16 FlashAttention-4; end-to-end clip speedups of 1.13–1.19× and 1.36–1.70×; validated across Wan2.2, LongCat-Video, HunyuanVideo-1.5, MiniMax-H3.
AI.conclusion: VC-Attention offers a practical training-free low-bit attention solution for diffusion transformers, balancing accuracy and throughput to enable efficient deployment of long-sequence video generation.

title: Portable Semantics, Private Dialects: Reuse and Negative Transfer in Latent Communication Between Language-Model Cells
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2608.20054. Code and evaluation records: https://github.com/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning ; checkpoints and fitted alignment maps: https://huggingface.co/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning-checkpoints
summary: In shared-genome language-model societies, restricted evidence visibility favors reusable, value-indexed latent packet interfaces, whereas the sole high-performing globally visible model in the parent study learned an episode-entangled code. This companion study asks whether independently trained societies share one packet language, where strict zero-shot transfer fails, and whether inherited interface state helps or harms later learning. First, a leakage-controlled causal interoperability audit over all 30 ordered pairs of six independently trained restricted societies -- under sealed held-out structure and a preregistered raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear alignment ladder -- shows the six semantically similar interfaces do not form one raw language: one same-initialization pair is exactly interoperable in both directions, a second shows asymmetric partial compatibility, and all 26 cross-initialization directions fail every frozen alignment rung. Second, within the tested decomposition and a single sealed source formulation, a source-span control localizes strict zero-shot failure to interpretation and execution of the new operator instructions. Third, in a matched adaptation factorial, the globally trained communication interface acts as a severe negative-transfer prior: reinitializing only the packet reader, writer, and mouth raises final depth-three accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857. Fourth, across two restricted checkpoints and two independently frozen target streams each, inherited interfaces never exceeded fresh-interface controls by the preregistered 0.10 margin. All primary conclusions are bounded to a near-transfer 17-state setting; the negative-transfer factorial concerns one globally visible parent-cohort checkpoint, while an appendix adds a post hoc tagged-global twin case study.

AI.tldr: A companion study tests whether six independently trained restricted-society packet-language interfaces share a single raw language; finds no universal interface, zero-shot transfer largely fails, and inherited/global interfaces can cause negative transfer; results are limited to a 17-state setting.
AI.motivation: Assess whether independently trained packet-language interfaces converge to a common, interoperable protocol, enabling zero-shot transfer, and to identify when inherited interfaces help or hinder later learning.
AI.method: Leakage-controlled causal interoperability audit across all 30 ordered pairs of six restricted societies, using sealed held-out structure and preregistered raw/orthogonal/linear/nonlinear alignment ladders. Includes a decomposition with a sealed source formulation, a matched adaptation factorial, and experiments reinitializing packet reader/writer/mouth. Two restricted checkpoints and two independently frozen target streams per condition; preregistered margins. An appendix adds a post hoc tagged-global twin case study.
AI.result: Six semantically similar interfaces do not compose a single raw language: exactly interoperable in one bidirectional pair; asymmetric partial compatibility in a second; 26 cross-initialization directions fail all frozen alignment rungs. Zero-shot failure localized to interpretation/execution of new operator instructions. Globally trained interface acts as a strong negative-transfer prior: reinitializing only reader/writer/mouth raises depth-3 accuracy from 0.169 to 0.857. Across two restricted checkpoints and two target streams, inherited interfaces do not exceed fresh-interface controls by the preregistered 0.10 margin. Findings bound to a near-transfer 17-state setting; negative-transfer factorial concerns one parent-cohort checkpoint; appendix includes a post hoc tagged-global twin case study.
AI.conclusion: Shared packet-language across independently trained societies is not achieved; zero-shot transfer is fragile; inherited interfaces offer no consistent advantage and can hurt learning. Results are domain-limited; broader generalization remains uncertain.

title: Integrating Multi-view Multi-light Surface Reconstruction into Cultural Heritage Workflows
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Accepted at VISART VIII, ECCV 2026 workshops
summary: Cultural heritage documentation increasingly relies on image-based 3D surface reconstruction, with photogrammetry software making such workflows accessible to archaeologists, conservators, and heritage technicians. These tools have been successful for conventional multi-view acquisition, but they do not routinely exploit richer multi-view, multi-light data, despite its potential for improving fine-scale surface reconstruction. This limitation is particularly relevant in heritage contexts, where controlled-light acquisition devices such as RTI domes are already used to capture illumination-varying image sets. The challenge is therefore to connect these existing acquisition practices with recent computer vision methods in a form that can be used within operational heritage workflows. In this work, we address this need by integrating state-of-the-art components from computer vision for multi-view, multi-light surface reconstruction into Meshroom, an open-source photogrammetry framework. Rather than proposing a new reconstruction algorithm, our contribution is to assemble and expose existing advanced methods, namely a complete photometric stereo ecosystem (calibrated, self-calibrated and universal), automatic object masking, and multi-view normal-and-reflectance integration, within a usable heritage-oriented workflow. The proposed system thus provides an intermediate software layer between computer vision research code and practical cultural heritage applications, making recent techniques easier to use and evaluate.

AI.tldr: Integrates photometric stereo and multi-view, multi-light reconstruction into Meshroom to bridge CV methods and heritage workflows, using established techniques (calibrated/self-calibrated/universal photometric stereo, masking, and multi-view normal/reflectance fusion) without new algorithms.
AI.motivation: Heritage imaging often uses illumination-varying datasets (RTI) but standard photogrammetry underutilizes them; need a practical, heritage-friendly pipeline that leverages recent CV advances.
AI.method: Assembles and exposes existing state-of-the-art components within Meshroom: complete photometric stereo ecosystems (calibrated, self-calibrated, universal), automatic masking, and multi-view normal-and-reflectance integration; acts as an intermediate layer between CV research code and heritage workflows.
AI.result: A functional, heritage-oriented workflow embedded in Meshroom enabling multi-view, multi-light surface reconstruction; easier to use and evaluate recent CV techniques in practice.
AI.conclusion: Provides a bridge between CV research and cultural heritage applications by re-packaging and integrating existing methods into an accessible workflow, rather than proposing new algorithms.

title: TRACE: Two-Stage Detector-Response Estimation With Angular Cosine Expansion for Ring Artifact Correction in Photon-Counting CT
summary: Detector response nonuniformity introduces systematic projection errors and ring artifacts in photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT). In measured PCD-CT data, residual stripe amplitudes vary slowly with projection angle, which fixed-bias models cannot adequately capture. We propose TRACE, a two-stage unsupervised sinogram decomposition method for estimating and correcting these response-related errors. TRACE represents stripes as a fixed bias plus low-order discrete cosine transform (DCT) components, using a small number of coefficients to describe angular variations at each detector element. A learnable analysis--synthesis architecture represents the ideal projections, while two-stage optimization separates them from fixed and then dynamic stripes. An angular-gradient soft orthogonality constraint suppresses correlated variations within the shared DCT gradient subspace, reducing the leakage of object structures into the artifact estimate. All parameters are optimized directly on the measured sinogram without paired training data. Experiments on measured QRM mouse phantom and porcine trotter data show that TRACE suppresses ring artifacts and improves image uniformity while preserving edge sharpness, soft-tissue texture, and trabecular detail.

AI.tldr: TRACE is an unsupervised two-stage sinogram-decomposition method to correct response nonuniformity in PCD-CT by modeling stripes as a fixed bias plus low-order DCT components, learned via a two-stage analysis–synthesis network without paired data, reducing rings while preserving detail.
AI.motivation: Residual stripe amplitudes in measured PCD-CT vary slowly with projection angle and fixed-bias models fail to capture them; there is a need for a data-driven, unsupervised correction that can separate fixed and dynamic stripe components without requiring training data.
AI.method: Model stripes with a fixed bias plus low-order DCT components per detector element. Use a learnable analysis–synthesis architecture to represent ideal projections. Apply two-stage optimization to separate fixed and dynamic stripes. Impose an angular-gradient soft orthogonality constraint to reduce leakage from object structures into the artifact estimate. Optimize directly on the measured sinogram without paired data.
AI.result: TRACE suppresses ring artifacts and improves image uniformity in measured PCD-CT data, while preserving edge sharpness, soft-tissue texture, and trabecular detail. Demonstrated on QRM mouse phantom and porcine trotter data.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides an effective unsupervised approach for correcting response-related artifacts in PCD-CT by decomposing projection data into fixed and angularly varying stripes using a compact DCT basis, with a learnable decomposition network and constraints to minimize leakage. It achieves artifact suppression without compromising structural detail and shows promise for broader applicability to PCD-CT systems.

title: LynnReal-Omni: Native multi-modal Video Generation for Agentic Visual Workflows
summary: Video diffusion models are stochastic and hard to control: precise content often requires repeated sampling without guaranteed success, and long-horizon scenes drift in appearance, interactions, and temporal coherence. Agentic visual creation provides explicit references, editable 3D scenes, or executable game states for stable control, but does not by itself guarantee high object or character fidelity. Combining the two can enable stable, high-quality generation. To realize this combination, we present LynnReal-Omni, a native multimodal video generation framework built on a 32B shared multimodal diffusion transformer that unifies text-to-video, image-conditioned generation, reference-guided generation, structural control, editing, degraded video restoration, and long-video generation. It accepts heterogeneous visual inputs, including appearance references, editable 3D renders, and game recordings, allowing agents to compose visual conditions within a unified model. We also train a dedicated 27B Flash shared multimodal diffusion transformer for real-time rendering. We build a systematic data pipeline for video cleaning, subject association, multimodal annotation, and aligned control construction, yielding a curated corpus of multi-shot audiovisual segments, and introduce MSAVP, a 100-prompt, 20-metric evaluation design that separates instruction following, generating plausibility, visual quality, temporal behavior, and audio coordination. LynnReal-Omni-Flash further reduces inference cost through model and decoding acceleration, including a lightweight VAE decoder; on one H100, warm generation and decoding of a 22-frame 540p video take 843 ms with LynnReal-Omni and 377 ms with Flash. These results provide a foundation for real-time streaming video generation, making LynnReal-Omni a unified, controllable, and efficient basis for agentic visual creation.

AI.tldr: Unified, controllable multimodal video generation via LynnReal-Omni; 32B shared transformer supporting text/video/image conditioning, references, and long-horizon coherence, with real-time 27B Flash model, data pipeline, and MSAVP evaluation.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion models are stochastic and hard to control; combining with agentic visual creation offers explicit references and structured control but fidelity is lacking; a unified framework can deliver stable, high-quality, real-time video generation.
AI.method: Build LynnReal-Omni (32B) and LynnReal-Omni-Flash (27B). Develop data pipeline for cleaning and annotation; support heterogeneous inputs (appearance refs, editable 3D renders, game recordings); introduce MSAVP evaluation; optimize for inference via VAE decoder and decoding acceleration; evaluate on 22-frame 540p video on H100.
AI.result: Demonstrates real-time streaming capability: 843 ms for LynnReal-Omni vs 377 ms for Flash on 22-frame 540p; supports real-time generation; MSAVP provides multi-dimensional evaluation; establishes a foundation for integrated, controllable video synthesis.
AI.conclusion: LynnReal-Omni-Flash offers a unified, efficient, controllable basis for agentic visual creation with real-time potential; enables stable content fidelity, temporal coherence, and user-guided control across modalities.

title: Anatomical Grounding and Leakage-Aware Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Alzheimer's Disease Classification from Structural MRI
summary: Deep networks trained on structural MRI for Alzheimer's disease (AD) staging often reach reasonable accuracy while attending to anatomically irrelevant regions, and multimodal models that add clinical tables frequently rely on variables that were used to assign the diagnostic label in the first place. We study both issues with a deliberately lightweight slice-based encoder (ResNet18 with a one-layer Transformer over slices) on 1,075 baseline T1-weighted scans from ADNI-1. First, we use FastSurfer segmentations as an anatomical reference: YOLOv8 models trained on segmentation-derived labels localize Alzheimer-relevant structures with mAP_50 above 0.96, and a Grad-CAM comparison shows that the image-only classifier frequently attends to the skull, orbits and background. Second, we adapt a CLIP-style image - tabular contrastive framework and organize ADNIMERGE variables along a label-leakage spectrum. Fusion with cognitive scores yields 87.3% three-way accuracy, which we treat as a leakage-driven upper bound rather than an imaging result; fusion with regional volumes yields 73.0%. We observe that the choice of contrastive target changes what the image encoder learns: on MCI vs. CN, the image-only head reaches 52.4% when the encoder is aligned to cognitive scores and 73.8\% when aligned to volumes, although no tabular input is used at inference. Third, restricting the input to a per-subject crop of the medial temporal lobe raises image-only three-way accuracy from 58.7% to 65.1%. All results come from single runs on a small balanced test set, and we report confidence intervals and the protocol differences that prevent direct comparison with published numbers.

AI.tldr: Aims to diagnose why MRI-based AD staging models rely on anatomically irrelevant regions and how tabular data can leak labels. Uses a lightweight slice-based encoder, segmentation-derived labels with YOLOv8 for localization, Grad-CAM interpretability, and a CLIP-style image–tabular contrastive framework across ADNIMERGE variables. Key findings show attention to non-brain regions (skull, background), leakage-driven upper bounds in fusion with cognitive scores, and that restricting input to medial temporal structures improves image-only accuracy. Conclusions stress leakage and label-target effects, but results come from single runs on a small test set, limiting generalizability and cross-study comparability.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the factors behind misleading high performance in imaging-based AD staging, specifically (i) reliance on non-neuroanatomical regions, and (ii) label leakage when combining images with tabular clinical data. The work also investigates how the choice of contrastive targets shapes the learned image representations.
AI.method: 1) Lightweight slice-based encoder (ResNet18 + one-layer Transformer) trained on 1075 baseline ADNI-1 T1 scans. 2) Segmentation-based localization: FastSurfer segmentations used as ground-truth-like labels to train YOLOv8; evaluate localization via mAP50; Grad-CAM used to compare attention between image-only models and anatomical references. 3) CLIP-style image–tabular contrastive framework: organize ADNIMERGE variables along a label-leakage spectrum; fuse image embeddings with tabular data (cognition vs regional volumes) and evaluate three-way accuracy on AD staging. 4) MCI vs CN analysis: assess how contrastive target alignment (to cognition vs to volumes) affects image-only head performance, without tabular input at inference. 5) Spatial cropping: restrict input to per-subject medial temporal lobe and measure impact on image-only accuracy. 6) Evaluation notes: single runs, small balanced test set; report confidence intervals and protocol differences that limit direct cross-study comparison.
AI.result: - YOLOv8 trained on segmentation-derived labels localizes Alzheimer-relevant structures with mAP50 > 0.96. Grad-CAM indicates the image-only model often attends to skull, orbits, and background rather than brain parenchyma. - Fusion with cognitive scores yields 87.3% three-way accuracy (treated as leakage-driven upper bound); fusion with regional volumes yields 73.0%. - For MCI vs CN, image-only head accuracy is 52.4% when the encoder is aligned to cognitive scores and 73.8% when aligned to volumes, despite no tabular input at inference. - Restricting input to a per-subject crop of the medial temporal lobe raises image-only three-way accuracy from 58.7% to 65.1%. - All results are from single runs on a small balanced test set; CI and protocol differences are reported, complicating direct comparison with published numbers.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that imaging models can leverage non-diagnostic regions, and that high performance with multimodal fusion may primarily reflect label leakage rather than imaging signal. The contrastive target materially shapes learned image representations. Spatial cropping to medial temporal regions improves image-only accuracy, but the study’s limited replication and small test set constrain generalizability. Future work should emphasize robust, replicated evaluations, explicit leakage controls, and standardized protocols to disentangle true imaging signal from leakage.
